El Salvador's president confirms and celebrates attack on home of key Haitian gang leader
El Salvador’s president says that his troops have demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, said Wednesday that his troops demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff. It wasn’t immediately clear if he was killed.
Bukele posted a video on X that depicts an old video of Jeff posing in front of his mansion in the Caribbean country and then cuts to Salvadoran helicopters flying toward it as they fire shot after shot, with big plumes of smoke rising from Jeff’s home.
“My gift to the Haitian people on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières,” Bukele wrote.
The 1803 battle was critical in helping secure Haiti's independence from France and transforming it into the world's first Black republic.
It wasn’t immediately known if Haiti’s police and army were involved. A U.N.-backed gang suppression force said that it wasn’t involved.
Jeff is considered one of Haiti's most powerful gang leaders. His real name is Jeff Larose, but he's known as Jeff Canaan, Jeff Gwo Lwa and Taliban. He has long controlled a community known as Canaan in northern Port-au-Prince, leading a gang of an estimated 200 members, according to the United Nations. His so-called Taliban gang based in Canaan is a very close ally of 5 Segond, which has provided it with reinforcements.
Diego Da Rin, a Haiti expert with International Crisis Group, said the attack on Jeff’s home was the obvious next step for Bukele’s operations.
Jeff built the home in mid-2024, complete with a pool emblazoned with his logo.
“It’s very easy to identify it by satellite,” Da Rin said. “It was a very defiant act by him.”
He noted that Jeff’s home is very vulnerable to an aerial attack, but it was built in a place where attacking it by land would have been very difficult.
Da Rin said Jeff was among a handful of gang leaders who have built mansions in recent years.
“In a way, they felt untouchable in their territory,” he said.
The use of explosive drones and helicopters, which Haitian police and military lack, has changed that.
Da Rin said he doubts Jeff was staying at the mansion when it was attacked early Wednesday given that on Nov. 8, Salvadoran troops attacked the home of Wilson Joseph, best known as Lanmò San Jou and leader of the 400 Mawozo gang. He wasn’t killed in the attack.
Da Rin said gang leaders have several residences and can always seek shelter in any home within the territory they control.
He noted that Jeff and Lanmò San Jou are allies and control the main roads north and east of Port-au-Prince that lead to other cities and towns, charging tolls that have become their main source of revenue.
Canaan was established as an informal community after a devastating earthquake hit Haiti in January 2010. Tens of thousands of people are estimated to now live there.
The attack comes a day after thousands of Haitians in Port-au-Prince and beyond marched in favor of Bukele, thanking him and his troops for fighting violent gangs.
On Wednesday, Haitians were again celebrating.
“Jeff is a criminal and I hope he died,” said Mario Jean-Pierre, a 45-year-old salesperson in Port-au-Prince. “We asked for help; Bukele answered us.”
Last month, Bukele deployed around 2,500 troops to Haiti after four of their own came under attack on Oct. 18 while deep in gang territory. They remain missing.
___
Associated Press reporter Evens Sanon in Port-au-Prince, Haiti contributed to this report.

The Delhi High Court has ruled that foreign nationals accused of overstaying their visas can’t be ordered to remain confined in detention centres as a condition for being released on bail.
Justices Navin Chawla and Arun Bhardwaj were hearing a reference sent by a magistrate from South Delhi District, who was clarifying whether foreign nationals accused of overstaying could be granted bail and what conditions could be imposed on them.
“Bail may be granted to a foreign national subject to reasonable conditions, including regarding the place of residence, restriction on movement, and periodic reporting, having regard to the gravity of the offence and the risk of the accused evading trial. However, a direction imposing a condition wherein the foreign national is restricted to a detention centre would frustrate the very order of bail and hence, cannot be imposed,” the November 18 order read.
According to the order, a Nigerian national was arrested for visa overstay as a result of an FIR filed at Police Station Tigri, New Delhi. It came on record that the foreign national had come to India in 2016 on a tourist visa for three months but continued living here even after the expiry of his visa.
When the man applied for bail, the magistrate hearing his case sent a reference to the Delhi High Court asking certain questions of law, like whether, if the foreign national was given unconditional bail, it would not result in legalizing his future stay in India without a valid visa.
The magistrate also asked whether, if bail was given to foreigners accused of overstaying their visas, certain conditions could be imposed on them, including keeping them in a detention centre till the trial was complete.
The advocate appearing for the foreign national argued that the man was entitled to bail and that he would apply for an extension of visa once he was granted bail. Advocate Aman Usman, appearing for the state, submitted that if bail was granted to a foreign national, he should be kept in a detention centre. Advocate Harish Prabhakar was appointed as the Amicus Curiae (‘friend of the court’) to assist the court.
After evaluating the relevant statutes and case laws, the high court noted that a foreign national who was charged for overstaying his visa would be tried for the offences committed before the trial began. Therefore, the court stated that while dealing with the bail application of such an accused, the trial court was considering offences committed in the past.
The high court held that granting bail to a foreign national accused of offences like overstaying his visa does not, by itself, mean legalising his continued stay in India or operate as a substitute for a valid visa and, as far as his continued stay in India in the future was concerned, that was for the Central Government to examine under the relevant laws.
The bench also stated that giving bail by itself would not mean that the foreign national got a right to remain in India without a valid visa and that the court was also empowered to impose conditions on bail.
According to the high court, in matters involving foreign nationals overstaying their visa, where the accused himself admits that his visa had expired before the date he expected it to expire on, such matters should not be treated differently than other criminal cases, and the accused could be released on bail, but “certainly not on the condition to detain him in a detention centre till the pendency of the trial.”

A thousand crores in annual revenue is a significant milestone for any Indian consumer internet company. And yet, crossing that mark has left ShareChat, Moj and QuickTV parent Mohalla Tech with a few more questions to deal with in the next year or two. In FY26, the company crossed ₹1,000 Cr in operating revenue for the first time, reporting ₹1,016.27 Cr, a 40.5% increase over the previous year. Yet its net loss widened to ₹1,978.40 Cr, raising an obvious question about the quality of that growth. Having said that, a large part of this loss came from share-based payments, which climbed 302% to ₹739 Cr in FY26 from ₹183.8 Cr in FY25, following an expansion of the company’s ESOP pool and additional grants to key employees. Whether the company crosses the profitability barrier in FY27 will be clear in about a year’s time, but what we know is that with ShareChat, Moj and QuickTV as its three products, ShareChat’s revenue story is changing. Mohalla Tech’s legacy chatroom business (ShareChat), built on in-app purchases and microtransactions continues to remain the biggest contributor, bringing in ₹471.76 Cr, but an acceleration was seen in subscription revenue for Moj and QuickTV, which resulted in a ₹292.72 Cr boost to the topline. Advertising revenue, once central to Mohalla Tech’s monetisation ambitions, took a backseat and declined to ₹251.79 Cr. In other words, the company behind ShareChat and Moj is no longer relying on external revenue levers such as brand partnerships and creators, but is looking to bring in more consistent revenue by selling short-form digital entertainment and microdramas. The diversification was not on the cards when it all began in 2015. Ankush Sachdeva, Bhanu Pratap Singh and Farid Ahsan founded ShareChat to tap into the regional language internet boom in India. When TikTok's ban in 2020 opened the door to short video, ShareChat launched Moj and then later acquired MX TakaTak. Today, it is riding the microdrama wave with QuickTV. It is monetising conversations, selling advertising against free content and charging consumers directly for microdramas. But there’s one crucial missing link and that’s to do with how the three main products acquire customers and therein lies a challenge for Mohalla Tech to fix in the long run. The company, once valued at around $5 Bn, is reportedly eyeing a $400 Mn IPO in late 2027, subject to achieving a full year of operating profitability in FY27. The company has seen all from layoffs, leadership exits and cost reductions, forcing the company to shift its focus from audience growth to monetisation and profitability. Now, the question is whether ShareChat's new revenue mix represents a clearing towards a path to profitability or is it a temporary shift before the next product comes along, as we have seen throughout the company’s lifetime. Subscriptions Turn Fruitful When QuickTV launched in February 2025, ShareChat was entering a new territory, chasing subscription revenue. Thus far in its lifetime, it relied on incidental revenue in its apps, whether it was in-app transactions by users or ad revenue from brands. QuickTV was the first push for direct revenue. And it seems to be working for Mohalla Tech. In FY26, subscriptions accounted for almost the entire increase in the company’s consolidated revenue from operations. Cofounder and CFO Manohar Charan revealed in a recent press and investor briefing that subscription had become the company’s clear third revenue stream after a great start. “And to be honest, that was the single largest force moving our revenue between last year and this year," Charan said after the FY26 results were announced in early November 2026. Besides QuickTV, the company also offers paid subscriptions through Moj Premium, but the latter is not yet a compelling revenue line. Microdrama seems to have hit the ground running. However, building a subscription business comes with a different set of challenges, particularly when it comes to acquiring paying customers. Charan claimed that while Moj spends around ₹14–15 to get a user to download the app, QuickTV subscription platforms can spend 6-7x higher to acquire a paying customer as the cost can be recouped through the subscription model. This makes it easier to acquire users profitably over the short term but more expensive over a long period. That long-term cost can take a toll on QuickTV and other microdrama platforms. Subscription-centric apps like microdrama platforms have to continuously invest in content to retain customers, and this can get especially expensive when there are multiple apps competing and offering similar microdramas and storylines. While AI is actively changing how microdramas are being made and therefore reducing costs, the economics are still not in the favour of the platform. It is estimated that producing a minute of microdrama using human actors costs ₹20,000–₹25,000, compared with ₹7,000–₹8,000 using AI tools and generative video models. While lower production costs could help platforms scale their content libraries and reduce long-term retention costs, they could also make it easier for competitors to produce similar shows, putting greater pressure on differentiation and even that initial customer acquisition. QuickTV operates on a commissioned-content model, with the company producing or commissioning around 30–40 shows every month. According to Charan, the QuickTV library has grown to roughly 1,000 shows. Moj, meanwhile, relies heavily on creator-generated content, receiving around 4,000 shows daily and offering a catalogue of approximately 5 Lakh shows across formats. The latter also gives Mohalla Tech an opportunity to identify popular themes and formats before committing larger production budgets. Charan said QuickTV has operated without burning cash since launch, though this remains to be verified since we were not given exact costs for QuickTV in terms of marketing and promotional spends. But Mohalla Tech is at a crossroads right now because of how QuickTV has performed. Subscriptions have revived its topline growth, but sustaining that momentum will require investing in retargeting, a clear content strategy and pipeline as well as other incremental spending to improve the subscriber experience, which will play a role in retention. If the past year has shown anything it is that users will pay for microdramas, but to keep them paying every month requires a lot more pieces moving in sync than just the right marketing pitch. Microdramas Fuel ShareChat's Advertising Recovery Advertising, ShareChat's other established revenue stream, faced a sharp slowdown in FY26. Revenue declined 13.1% to ₹251.79 Cr in FY26 from ₹289.83 Cr in FY25. The CFO attributed the advertising decline to the loss of real-money gaming advertisers following regulatory changes. Further, the company says advertising has begun recovering in FY27, supported by higher engagement and stronger monetisation. In Q2 FY27, advertising revenue is said to have grown by 40% YoY, while average ad revenue per user on Moj is claimed to have increased almost 2.5 times since May 2026. “We are seeing stronger monetisation from our existing user base, and will continue to prioritise investments that drive sustainable engagement and revenue without compromising profitability," Charan added. He expects full-year FY27 advertising revenue to exceed ₹350 Cr, but the run rate is not a full-year result and the outlook remains subject to seasonal demand. Free, ad-supported microdramas are central to boosting ad revenue. It is a clear strategy for Mohalla Tech if it gets its user acquisition right. This will allow the company to keep its ad inventory up-to-date and bring in more consistent revenue outside of the peak seasons. When it comes to QuickTV, AI is becoming central to monetisation and bringing in cost-efficiency on the production side. Not only is it playing a role in improving content discovery and therefore driving conversions to subscriptions, but it can help improve ad targeting. Charan said an ad-supported model could recover around 2.5 times user acquisition cost over 12 months, compared with roughly 1.6 times for a cautiously run subscription model. Moj was approaching ₹200 in annual advertising revenue per user, against the CFO’s estimate of ₹200–₹250 for YouTube in India. Though this number cannot be verified as YouTube’s average ad revenue per user is not disclosed. ShareChat is also experimenting with how brands advertise within microdramas using integrated storytelling or branded content. Other options include ads between episodes, programmatic inventory and interactive shopping formats backed by marketplaces. What Will Carry ShareChat Forward? Like we mentioned above, the caveat to ShareChat's return to growth is that it has yet to result in lower losses. Charan attributed the forex losses and roughly ₹548 Cr in interest provisions to dollar-denominated financing instruments, describing the latter as non-cash expenses. However, business development costs also surged to ₹334.80 Cr from ₹43.37 Cr, highlighting the spending pressures accompanying growth. Charan expects FY27 revenue to exceed ₹1,500 Cr, with approximately ₹25 Cr in full-year EBITDA profit. He also claimed the company used just ₹35 Cr of investor cash in FY26 and has been generating cash since September 2025. However, sustaining this momentum will become increasingly challenging as competition intensifies. Homegrown microdrama platforms such as EloElo, Kuku TV and Story TV are competing for paying subscribers, while global players including ReelShort and DramaBox are targeting the Indian market. Larger entertainment platforms, including JioHotstar, ZEE5 and Amazon MX Player, are also expanding into short-form storytelling. This could push up customer acquisition costs and content spending, particularly for QuickTV's subscription-led business. Consolidation can very well be on the cards as competition intensifies and investors increasingly scrutinise contribution margins. As we see with the OTT streaming industry, India is home to around 100 Mn - 150 Mn people who regularly pay for content online and even there a kind of subscription fatigue has set in, with users preferring to stick to one platform or only buying subscriptions through telecom bundles. It also adds more pressure on ShareChat, Moj and QuickTV to explore ways in which users can seamlessly switch between streaming, creator-generated content and chatrooms. Interestingly, the three Mohalla Tech platforms do not currently act as interconnected funnels. This will be a critical piece of operating leverage for the company in the long run. Charan explained that QuickTV primarily targets paying subscribers outside the company's existing ShareChat and Moj audience, acquiring them through platforms such as Instagram, Facebook and YouTube. Connecting this to the silos of ShareChat and Moj will give the company more bargaining power with advertisers as well as creators. This is why while ShareChat, Moj and QuickTV’s growth is undeniable, a stronger push by platforms such as YouTube or Meta could challenge that position because of their incumbency and the inherent moats that come with that position. But the milestones of FY26, the revenue trajectory and the fact that the company now reaches millions of social media users more frequently through three different apps offer plenty of reasons for optimism, even amid these questions.

The story so far: India continues to account for nearly a quarter of the world’s tuberculosis (TB) burden despite expanded diagnosis and treatment services, falling short of the national target of eliminating TB by 2025. According to the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Global Tuberculosis Report, released on November 12, 2026, an estimated 10.6 million people developed TB worldwide in 2025.
While India’s estimated TB mortality rate fell by 38%, from 28 deaths per lakh population in 2015 to 18 per lakh in 2025, the country diagnosed and notified 25.3 lakh cases during the year. However, the WHO has not published India’s estimated incidence for that year, as the figures are under review.

An analysis of more than 180 epidemiological studies examining the health impacts of air pollution across India has found that over 91% of them reported at least one adverse health association with air pollution exposure.
These studies, published between 1975 and 2025, also noted that health impacts extend beyond respiratory diseases to cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, pregnancy complications, impaired child growth, tumours, blood disorders, mental and neurocognitive disorders, among others.
The analysis, released on Friday, was done by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), an independent research organisation focused on revealing the trends, causes, and health impacts, as well as the solutions, to air pollution.
Notably, out of 180 studies, only 40 examined air pollution's impact on rural populations, of which 38 reported at least one adverse health association, indicating that air pollution's health impacts are not confined to urban areas.
Further, most studies were conducted on Delhi (26) to examine the link between health and air pollution. The national capital was followed by Punjab with 13 studies, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh with 11 each, West Bengal with 10, Tamil Nadu with nine, Karnataka with eight and Telangana with seven, the report said.
In a statement, CREA analyst Manoj Kumar said, "The findings highlight the need to move beyond a city-centric approach and explicitly include rural areas through a regional, airshed-based approach in the next phase of National Clean Air Programme (NCAP 2.0)."
Studies examined a range of air pollutants, with 45 investigating both particulate matter and gaseous pollutants. PM2.5 was examined in 32 studies, PM10 alone in four, and both PM10 and PM2.5 in 16.
Among studies examining gaseous pollutants, statistically significant adverse health associations were reported for increased mortality, acute respiratory hospital and emergency visits, asthma-related hospital admissions, and impaired lung function.
Beyond their direct health effects, gaseous pollutants such as SOx and NOx also contribute to secondary PM2.5 formation by undergoing atmospheric chemical reactions to form sulphate and nitrate particles, respectively.
Kumar said, "Air pollution mitigation must adopt a multipollutant approach, addressing gaseous precursors that contribute to secondary PM2.5 and ground-level ozone formation. This requires emission reductions at major sources, including industries, power plants, residential cooking, and other combustion activities."

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): Amidst the threat of E. coli contamination in Bhopal's drinking water, Bhopal Municipal Corporation (BMC) has shifted the most vulnerable over 22 km of water supply pipelines away from sewer lines.
The BMC had identified around 230 km of vulnerable water pipelines across the city, where drinking water lines run close to sewage networks, posing a risk of contamination in case of leakage.
Following the water contamination tragedy in Indore's Bhagirathpura, a statewide survey was conducted to identify locations where drinking water and sewer pipelines run close to each other. In Bhopal, the survey identified pipelines laid around 15 to 20 years ago.
As new colonies developed over the years, sewer networks were laid alongside existing water supply lines, increasing the possibility of sewage entering drinking water pipelines through leakages.
Taking lessons from the Indore incident, the BMC initiated a plan to relocate the vulnerable pipelines. The remaining work, covering approximately 200 km, is expected to be completed by next year.
Meanwhile, following the alleged detection of E. coli bacteria in drinking water in Vaishali Nagar, the BMC has now accelerated the replacement and relocation of ageing water supply pipelines running parallel to sewer lines.
Phase 1 completed, work on remaining network begins
According to the BMC water works department, the first phase of relocation has been completed, covering 22 km across different municipal zones.
The civic body has now started working on shifting additional pipelines located two to three metres away from sewer lines. The corporation is also replacing water supply pipelines that are more than 15 years old, depending on local requirements and the condition of the network.

A cancer medicine supplied to a retailer for ₹2,700 carries a maximum retail price (MRP) of ₹27,000. Who accounts for this tenfold difference? This was among the examples highlighted by the Supreme Court in September 2026, when it questioned the gap between the prices paid for medicines and what patients ultimately pay.
Subsequently, on October 17, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) announced a 30% cap on trade margins for 137 anti-cancer drugs, effective from November 9. This intervention could reduce prices substantially for some products. It also raises a broader question: how does India decide what medicines should cost?

Fintech major Razorpay is reportedly looking to file its updated DRHP as early as next week, following the SEBI clearance for its confidential filing. The Bengaluru-based startup is eyeing a potential market debut as early as February 2027, Bloomberg reported, adding that it is expected to begin investor roadshows immediately after the public filing. Inc42 has reached out to Razorpay for comment on the development. The story will be updated upon receiving a response. The report comes within days after the market regulator cleared the ₹6,000 Cr IPO that could potentially value Razorpay at around $5 Bn (₹47,000 Cr). Pertinent to note that IPO valuation is about 33% lower than the $7.5 Bn valuation it commanded in its last funding round in 2021. Razorpay had confidentially filed its draft IPO papers in June 2026. SEBI issued its observations on the company's filing on November 3, allowing it to proceed with the public issue. Founded in 2014 by Shashank Kumar and Harshil Mathur, Razorpay offers payment processing, business banking, payroll and lending solutions. It raised over $800 Mn from investors including Tiger Global Management, Y Combinator, Ribbit Capital and Lightspeed. The company reported a 65% YoY increase in operating revenue to ₹3,783 Cr in FY25 but slipped into the red, weighed down by ₹1,209 Cr in ESOP expenses and one-time costs linked to its domicile shift from the US to India. Financial numbers for the period since then would be more apparent when the company files its IPO papers. Razorpay is also exploring a 0.4% merchant discount rate (MDR) on eligible UPI transactions above ₹2,000 to boost monetisation. However, its rollout could be delayed until after the 2027 state elections amid concerns over merchant backlash. The central government, RBI and NPCI are yet to finalise an implementation date, despite much of the regulatory groundwork being complete. Beyond payments, Razorpay is expanding into AI-led products, including its Agent Studio platform for deploying task-specific AI agents. The company is looking to tap India's buoyant IPO market, where firms have raised around $18.6 Bn through initial share sales so far in 2026, nearing last year's record of $22.4 Bn.

When it comes to preventing malaria, researchers and public health officials have been hopeful about the potential of a monoclonal antibody, one injection of which could provide recipients with several months of protection against the parasite. Such a tool, experts have thought, could give babies a layer of defense even before they start receiving doses of the malaria vaccines that have rolled out in recent years.
New research detailed Thursday has cast doubt on that strategy.
Scientists tested the monoclonal, known as L9LS, in infants in Mali, finding that it was 78% effective versus a placebo in providing protection against the malaria parasite over the six-month transmission season, similar to what has been seen in studies of the antibody in older kids and adults.
However, they also reported that it interfered with the immune response the malaria vaccine R21 elicits, resulting in a 20% to 30% drop in antibody levels generated by the immunization, according to an abstract presented at the annual meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene.
While it’s not clear what the diminished immune responses seen in blood tests would mean for the real-world protection offered by the vaccine, researchers say they’re going to focus on groups other than babies as they plan the pivotal studies that could lead to L9LS being approved, which they hope to start in 2028.
“We have these other clear use cases, so let’s get those done and get it approved and we can come back and revisit this,” said Robert Seder of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, whose lab helped develop L9LS.
There is no panacea against malaria, and various strategies come with advantages and disadvantages that public health officials have to weigh as they think about which approach to prioritize and for whom, particularly given the limited funding for a disease that predominantly affects poor countries. The infection killed about 610,000 people in 2024, the majority of them children under 5 years old in sub-Saharan Africa.
R21 and RTS,S, the two malaria vaccines, are seen as major scientific breakthroughs — they are the first vaccines against any parasite — but they require multiple doses to be effective, the first of which comes at 5 months of age. They do, however, provide some level of protection for years.
A monoclonal, on the other hand, can provide several months of protection with just one dose, which could be enough to cover recipients for peak transmission periods. (In areas with year-round transmission, deploying antibodies might require two to three doses a year, experts say.) It could offer an alternative to the current strategy of giving children existing antimalarial treatments every month during high-transmission periods, which is a cheap and effective preventive strategy but that opens the door to adherence challenges.
“A monoclonal antibody, with only one shot, provides an efficacy over six months, and those six months correspond to the season of malaria in Sahelian regions,” said Kassoum Kayentao of Mali’s University of Sciences, Techniques, and Technologies of Bamako, one of the experts involved with the new research. “In terms of logistics, in terms of programmatical use, this could be a very good tool.”
The constraint with antibodies is that they are comparatively costly, though there are efforts underway to bring down the price of each dose as researchers head to pivotal trials.
The new study enrolled infants from 1 month to 12 months, gave them either a placebo or the L9LS monoclonal, and then doses of the R21 vaccine. That sequence was what created the issue, researchers said.
The malaria vaccines work by training the immune system to recognize a protein on the parasite known as the circumsporozoite protein, or CSP. The monoclonal L9LS also binds to the CSP. That meant that, when the infants who had been given L9LS later received R21, the antibody bound to the vaccine as well, essentially interfering with the full immune response it was meant to trigger, researchers believe.
Experts said there were still key groups of people who could benefit from a monoclonal and who could be the focus of future studies. Among them are pregnant people, as an infection during pregnancy can be dangerous for both parent and baby. Kids who are hospitalized with malaria are another target group. In the months after they’re released from hospital and as they recover from the infection-caused anemia, they are particularly vulnerable to severe outcomes from another malaria case. The current strategy of what’s called post-discharge malaria chemoprevention involves taking available preventive drugs every month, whereas one shot of a monoclonal as they leave the hospital could cover them for months.
André-Marie Tchouatieu of the Medicines for Malaria Venture, who was not involved in the study, said that, despite the issue seen with L9LS and the vaccine, it did not limit the potential impact the monoclonal and next-generation versions could have in reducing the burden of malaria broadly.
“Definitely there will be a use case,” said Tchouatieu, who this month co-authored a New England Journal of Medicine review outlining the advantages and challenges of different malaria strategies. “Every tool that can prove efficacy and safety will have a role to play in the whole strategy for malaria elimination.”

Millions in India celebrate Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights – in pictures
The spiritual triumph of ‘light over darkness’ is celebrated during Diwali, which people mark by lighting traditional lamps, decorating homes and gathering with family and friends
A child after lighting firecrackers in Hyderabad on Sunday as millions of people across India celebrate Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights. Photograph: Mahesh Kumar A/AP
People explode firecrackers on roadsides in New Delhi as air pollution remains high across India’s capital. Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
A student from a Hindu religious school lights earthen lamps in front of Mani Mandir – commemorating Lord Rama’s return to his kingdom, Ayodhya, after a 14-year exile – in Varanasi. Photograph: Niharika Kulkarni/AFP/Getty Images
Hindu devotees perform rituals, decorating floors with rangoli designs, in Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir.Photograph: Faisal Bashir/SOPA Images/Shutterstock
People burst firecrackers outside residential homes in New Delhi. India’s supreme court allowed the sale of certified green firecrackers, permitting their use only during certain hours throughout Diwali. Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
Devotees and families with sparklers and firecrackers during Kali Puja, which is observed in West Bengal on the night of Diwali, in Kolkata.Photograph: Sudipta Das/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
People celebrate Diwali in New Delhi. A complete ban on firecrackers is restored from 9 November as authorities seek to curb air pollution in India’s capital. Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

The Trump administration is pulling the nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the U.S. Food and Drug Administration over concerns that she lacked support to get confirmed by the Senate, STAT notes. The Senate’s health panel had been expected to vote on her nomination Wednesday, and the panel’s leader, Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), said on Tuesday that Overton had enough support to clear his committee and win confirmation. But some GOP lawmakers had reservations about Overton, a preventive care doctor who served in the Trump White House, due to her support for scaling back vaccine recommendations, her role in loosening restrictions on vapes, and her stance on abortion policy.
Merck plans to stop development of its experimental blood cancer drug, nemtabrutinib, after a review found the benefits may not outweigh the risks, Reuters says. An independent monitoring committee reached that conclusion after reviewing results from a late-stage study and Merck said its review of the full data confirmed the finding. The decision ends a broader development program for treating chronic lymphocytic leukemia and small lymphocytic lymphoma, including two other late-stage trials. Nemtabrutinib is an oral drug designed to block BTK, a protein that helps cancerous B cells grow.

(Bloomberg Law) -- New York City’s brand new law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, a union representing carriage operators and owners contend in a federal lawsuit filed Thursday seeking to block the measure.
The City Council-passed ban signed Thursday by Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) will phase out the 168-year-old industry before taking effect June 1, 2028 across all five boroughs. The law requires “humane disposition” of the horses, forbidding they be sold for slaughter or transferred to other carriage companies. Sixty-eight horse cabs currently operate in Central Park, employing roughly 200 drivers and up to 160 horses.
The statute will “immediately cripple” carriage owners and ignore property interests and contracts, industry union Transport Workers Union Local 100 said in its class action complaint filed in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York.
The union is seeking a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction blocking enforcement of the law until the court rules on the merits of the case. It’s also asking the court for expedited discovery.
The city’s law department said it’s reviewing the case.
The legislation, known as Romanch’s Law, passed following the death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who was killed over the summer after being thrown from a horse-drawn carriage in Central Park. The city has for decades tried to ban horse-drawn carriages — a Central Park tourist staple that’s been around since 1858.
Just Compensation
The new law doesn’t include compensation for the property — such as permits and licenses, stables, and horses — that’s now rendered “unusable,” the complaint said. It only talks about a potential compensation plan that could come later down the road. That’s a violation of the US Constitution, which bars a “taking” without just compensation, the union alleges.
It also “makes vague promises about a ‘transition plan’ that offers the carriage drivers affected only ‘help’ finding ‘employment opportunities,’” the complaint said.
Mamdani at Thursday’s public signing ceremony said the city plans to release a transition plan in April that will including a process for the city to buy back medallions — operating licenses and plates — from owners, a stipend for drivers and stable hands to attend workforce training and career development classes, and career counseling and entrepreneurship support.
The city will work directly with horse-carriage workers to receive and incorporate their feedback in the transition process, the mayor said. And the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene will oversee where each horse is sold or placed as they retire, he added.
“This is a new day for our city — one that will make the crown jewel of Manhattan’s parks safer while also recognizing the lasting legacy and contributions the horse-carriage industry has made in our city,” Mamdani said.
Advocates for Justice represents the Transport Workers Union.
The case is Chiarello v. City of New York, S.D.N.Y., 1:26-cv-10154, complaint 11/19/26.

Heavy fighting erupts in Haiti as armed forces fight gangs to regain control of key corridor
Armed forces in Haiti have launched an aggressive operation to remove powerful gangs long entrenched in a key corridor that connects the country’s capital to its western and southern regions
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Armed forces in Haiti launched an aggressive operation on Thursday to remove powerful gangs long entrenched in a key corridor that connects the country’s capital to its western and southern regions.
It is the first significant operation in the five years since violent gangs seized control of Martissant, located in the western tip of Port-au-Prince.
Haiti’s National Police posted a video on X stating that at least 34 suspected gang members were killed in Martissant during a fight with police officers working with a task force composed of members from Vectus Global, a private security firm founded by former U.S. Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince.
Local media reported heavy gunfire and explosive drones in the area as Haiti’s police posted a video of armored vehicles rumbling through the community.
Martissant is located along Route 2, the main road that leads out of Port-au-Prince to important western and southern cities. Thousands of people would travel through Martissant every day before gangs seized control of the area more than five years ago, disrupting the country’s economy as they prevented goods from entering or leaving the capital. Gangs have since charged tolls or randomly opened fire on cars or buses that dare cross through.
Ever since gangs seized absolute control of Martissant, aid workers and Haitian civilians have been forced to take alternative transportation or use rural back roads.
The fight to control Martissant began in June 2021, when gangs from Grand-Ravine and Village-de-Dieu attacked the Ti-Bois gang. Armed men set fire to homes, killed families, destroyed businesses and seized control of Martissant’s police station.
The clashes forced at least 19,000 people to flee their homes and affected some 800,000 people overall, according to a July 2022 United Nations report.
Several years ago, gangs operating between Tabarre and Carrefour would demand some $380 from those transiting through Martissant, according to a 2023 U.N. report.
Last year, Haiti’s Center for Analysis and Research in Human Rights noted that ever since Martissant fell, hundreds of public and private institutions were relocated and more than one million people were forced to flee their homes.
As the fight in Martissant continues, a U.N.-backed gang suppression force also has made recent inroads against gangs in a push to not only displace them but prevent their return.
“Operations are entering a new phase: increasing pressure on gang networks, dismantling more strongholds, and extending control over strategic areas,” the force wrote Thursday on X.
The gang suppression force said it’s working in places including Tabarre in Port-au-Prince and in Haiti’s central Artibonite region, which has come under repeated violent attacks by armed men.
The force said it has come under fire as it advances along Route 5, “removing obstacles established by gangs to isolate communities and control key routes.”
The force said it also cleared and secured a church and school that gangs had been controlling north of Gros-Morne.
“It is about restoring freedom of movement, reopening access to public institutions, and re-establishing State presence for communities that have endured years of gang control,” the force wrote Sunday on X.
Also fighting gangs are some 2,500 troops deployed by El Salvador last month when four of their own went missing after an Oct. 18 attack in Haiti’s capital.
Following orders by Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, the troops have attacked the main homes of two of Haiti’s most powerful gang leaders, Jeff and Lanmò San Jou, this month. Neither one was killed.
Thousands of Haitians poured into the streets of Port-au-Prince and beyond this week in support of Bukele, but experts have criticized the unilateral operations of Salvadoran troops and noted that the use of explosive drones has claimed a growing number of innocent victims.
A small group of Salvadorans are separately working with the gang suppression force.
In late September, El Salvador’s legislature passed a law authorizing the participation of that group in Haiti for another 12 months until October 2027. The law was championed by Bukele and overwhelmingly approved by the country’s congress, controlled by Bukele’s party.
The ongoing clashes with gangs continue as Haiti prepares for its first elections in more than a decade. The country hasn't had a president since Jovenel Moïse was killed in July 2021.

We weren't able to confirm, as of this writing, precisely how many barrels of lead azide would be exploded.
In mid-November, a rumor spread online that the U.S. Army had plans to set off two detonations to destroy an old cache of lead azide — a highly explosive compound — in Middletown, Iowa, on Nov. 20.
"The Army found 68 barrels of the explosive that had been stored at the plant for more than 20 years," one Facebook post read (archived). "Lead azide becomes more unstable as it ages and can detonate with slight movement or friction, making it unsafe to move off site."
The claim spread across other platforms, with several Snopes readers also contacting us for answers.
In short, the claim is true. Here's what we know:
Army confirms explosions will take place
The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant launched a campaign to inform the public about the upcoming explosions, including an open house on Oct. 15 and a notice (archived) on Nov. 15 warning people in the affected area to evacuate and inviting residents to shelter at the Armed Forces Reserve Center during the explosions if needed.
In a document titled "Keeping Our Community Safe," the Army described how plans to reduce harm from the explosion by using specialized water misters and cleaning and removing affected soil and debris once the operation ceases.
(U.S. Army)
The public warnings issued by the Army to residents in the area were as follows:
- Consider avoiding the affected area.
- If you are inside of the affected areas, avoid outdoor air by staying indoors.
- Keep windows and doors closed.
- If it is safe to do so, set heating and cooling systems to "recirculate" to minimize outdoor air exposure and maximize indoor air filtration until the plume passes by your community.
- Avoid unnecessary travel through impacted areas.
- After the US Army determines the air exposure period has ended, consider cleaning indoor and outdoor surfaces such as play surfaces for children and windowsills.
- If your car was parked outside, consider washing your car at a car wash to minimize your contact with potentially exposed surfaces.
Is the circulated 'blast zone' map accurate?
In the circulated map shown in the Facebook post above, the blast zone appears to stretch approximately 100 miles northeast from the blast site. We compared this map to maps the Army released ahead of the planned detonations and found they aligned.
(Facebook user Live Storm Chasers and U.S. Army)
As Nov. 20 draws closer, the Army's maps will be updated. Residents in the area were encouraged to regularly check for updates.
What is lead azide and how did it get there?
According to the Environmental Protection Agency, lead azide is a "hazardous waste that exhibits the characteristic of reactivity (energetic) and exhibits the characteristic of toxicity for lead." In a public notice (archived) Nov. 16, the EPA wrote:
The recrystallization of the stored lead azide has increased the material's sensitivity to friction and shock, and disturbing the containers of lead azide could create an unacceptable risk of unintentional detonation. The Army's evaluation of a range of potential alternatives for the treatment of lead azide culminated in the secretary of the Army selecting in-place, controlled, intentional detonation for the treatment of lead azide.
The material is used to initiate munitions, according to a Q&A document the Army published.
It's unclear precisely how the lead azide stores came to be stored at that underground location. While a number of media outlets reported that 68 barrels would be detonated, we were unable to confirm that amount. We contacted the Army seeking more context and information about the history of the lead azide stores and will update this story if we receive a response.
In March, the Army announced that experts were conducting a safety review for the "safe removal of a chemical compound currently at the plant."
On Nov. 17, local ABC affiliate KCRG reported that local activists were planning a "peaceful demonstration" against the planned detonations.
Group organizers were reportedly demanding:
- An immediate halt to the Nov. 20 lead azide detonation, at minimum until affected communities have had an adequate opportunity to review the risks and alternatives.
- Full transparency regarding the potential environmental and public health consequences.
- Independent environmental experts to review the proposed disposal method and evaluate safer alternatives.
- A comprehensive plan for independent air, soil, and surface testing in potentially affected communities.
- A commitment to clean up and remediate any lead contamination resulting from this operation, at no cost to affected residents and property owners.

IAF showcases air power, multi-agency coordination in major HADR exercise in Gujarat
Jamnagar, The Indian Air Force on Thursday showcased its growing air power and disaster-response capabilities through a large-scale exercise involving fighter jets, transport aircraft, helicopters and remotely piloted drones as part of a multinational humanitarian assistance and disaster relief drill in Gujarat.
The demonstration was part of 'Sahayata Setu 2026', the annual joint Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief exercise, being conducted at Air Force Station Jamnagar from November 17 to 19.
The multi-agency demonstration featured coordinated operations by the three armed services Army, Navy and Air Force the Indian Coast Guard, national disaster management agencies, civil administrations and representatives from friendly foreign countries.
Chief of Defence Staff General N S Raja Subramani said on Thursday that humanitarian assistance and disaster relief reflect India's commitment to human security and require coordinated efforts by multiple agencies.
"In today's disaster-prone world, effective response is not the ability of one agency alone. It requires a coordinated whole-of-nation approach," he said.
He said India's disaster-response efforts were guided by its Neighbourhood First policy and the vision of MAHASAGAR - an expanded global maritime vision, adding that the country had emerged as a dependable first responder in the Indian Ocean region and the Indo-Pacific.
He cited 'Operation Dost' in Turkiye and 'Operation Brahma' in Myanmar as examples of India's humanitarian assistance operations.
"Disasters do not recognise geographical boundaries. Our response hence needs to transcend them," he said, highlighting the importance of collective preparedness.
He said the exercise focused on joint preparedness, clearly defined responsibilities, interoperability and the effective use of technology.
"The real test of this exercise is whether we can translate coordination into timely action," he said.
Subramani expressed confidence that the lessons from the exercise would streamline preparedness and improve coordination among participating agencies.
The exercise simulated a disaster scenario, where participating agencies demonstrated different response stages, beginning with aerial reconnaissance and assessment of the affected area.
The Indian Air Force deployed Jaguar aircraft, C-130J Super Hercules transport aircraft, Mi-17 helicopters and remotely piloted quadcopters for the demonstration.
An Advanced Light Helicopter Mark IV, a platform operated by all three services, also took part, alongside the Indian Navy's Dornier aircraft and the Army's ALH and Cheetah helicopters.
The demonstrations included an Mi-17 V5 helicopter carrying a bucket to douse fires, supported by firefighting robots, while another Mi-17 1B helicopter airlifted an Army vehicle.
A Chinook heavy-lift helicopter demonstrated its ability to transport structures, including bridge components, to disaster-hit areas.
The IAF's Combat Free Fall Rapid Response Force personnel also conducted a jump from an AN-32 aircraft as part of the demonstration.
The multinational exercise, AJHE-26, is aimed at strengthening inter-agency synergy, operational interoperability and international coordination in responding to major disasters, including cyclones, earthquakes, floods and chemical emergencies.

Today was the day we’ve all been waiting for. Anthropic silenced the critics, at least for now. It's looking like one of the best venture outcomes ever, even though the biggest winners aren’t VCs.
How do you celebrate a multibillion-dollar return?
Hello. It’s Ben Bergman.
Bessemer’s Byron Deeter, Lightspeed’s Ravi Mhatre, and Menlo’s Matt Murphy were all at the Nasdaq today to ring in Anthropic’s wildly successful IPO. They each minted their firms billions of dollars on paper, some of the biggest VC gains in history. And what will they do to celebrate tonight? Wing it.
“Believe it or not, we’re in New York, and we don’t have a reservation yet,” Murphy told me when we caught up on a brief phone call between his TV appearances and meetings with limited partners. “It’s a little bit ad hoc.”
After today, they can certainly afford to slip the maître d some cash to score a table. Which one do you think will pick up the dinner tab?
Anthropic’s biggest winners are not VCs but Amazon, Google, and its seven cofounders. Anthropic’s Series B funding round was infamously led by FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried, who is now serving a 25-year prison sentence and would have been sitting on more than $40 billion.
Nonetheless, Anthropic’s valuation has soared to such heights that it still ranks among the best, if not the best, venture outcomes of all time. Aside from the aforementioned trio, Iconiq, GIC, Coatue, Sequoia, Spark, and Founders Fund are among the firms that made billions.
With such a long list of VCs who can brag about being early in Anthropic (even if they got in very late), it was a day of extreme FOMO for those who never invested or gave up the chance at a billion dollars because of their ex.
As for the VC trio, Murphy said they plan to eat some steak and enjoy a few glasses of wine before heading to the Morgan Stanley party, one of several banks that are celebrating tonight. He said Anthropic itself is not hosting a public celebration.
“A lot of the team is worn out from the IPO and headed back to their families and their jobs,” he said. “There's more recursive intelligence to be built, apparently.”
The buzz
Katie here. It’s hard to believe that the Anthropic IPO was almost overshadowed by another AI industry event, but the drama around Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia diverted a lot of industry attention. Most VCs I spoke to seem broadly in favor of Huang's return, given their general support for transformative founders. He also played a major role in the ecosystem by investing in and acquiring AI startups.
Yet Huang has an uphill battle, with ongoing investigations into his alleged misconduct with a possible spy. The board also maintains that Huang will not be offered his job back. However, there’s one caveat. Huang has the power to add two new board members. It remains to be seen whether he will proceed with that option and if that will be enough to tip the balance in his favor. This drama feels far from over.

The Pan American Health Organization has revoked the United States’ measles-elimination status after 26 years, because the country did not halt continuous transmission of the highly contagious virus for more than a year, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday (November 13, 2026).
The international health body did not immediately respond to a request from Reuters for comment on the report, which cited people familiar with the matter.
The reported decision by the Americas branch of the World Health Organization comes as the U.S. battles the highest number of measles cases it has seen in more than three decades.
Some 7,500 people in the U.S. have been infected with measles and 13 have died since 2025. That period coincides with falling immunization rates and rising vaccine hesitancy under U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has for years spread doubts, without scientific evidence, about the safety of measles vaccines.
As part of its evaluation, PAHO reviewed epidemiological and laboratory evidence to determine whether the same strain of measles had been circulating in the United States uninterrupted for 12 months or longer, a sign of local transmission rather than imported cases.
As of Thursday (November 12, 2026), 5,182 confirmed cases of measles had been reported in 2026 to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from 45 States, New York City and the District of Columbia, surpassing last year’s total of 2,289, making it one of the country’s worst measles resurgences in decades.
The U.S. achieved its measles-elimination status in 2000. A country can halt transmission when 95% of its population is vaccinated, creating so-called herd immunity that also protects those unable to receive the vaccine.
Two doses of the measles vaccine — by far the best way to prevent infection and transmission — provide 97% protection against the virus, which can cause blindness, deafness, brain damage or death.

When medical student Emmanuel Oyebadejo went to watch his friend's American football game, he had no idea he would end up being scouted himself for a sport he had never even played.
He wasn't even interested in it. In fact, while still at school in Manchester he'd delivered a speech titled 'I have a dream' in which he outlined plans to do "very well in basketball, return from the NBA and be the prime minister of the United Kingdom".
But now, four years later, he is being tipped to become the first Briton to be a first-round pick in the NFL Draft.
It is a rapid rise for the 22-year-old, who had to learn the game from scratch and win over his parents who "begged" him not to play and instead focus on his medical studies.
His biggest challenge at the start, though, was finding a pair of boots big enough for his size 16 feet.
It was 6ft 6in Oyebadejo's physique that had caught the eye of the coaching staff at Exeter Demons when he was a spectator for his friend's university game that was taking place at the club's home ground, The Crumb.
"I was talking to one of the other coaches, Jack Mullins, and we sort of turned around [and thought] 'that guy's freaking huge! We should go talk to him'," Lydon Ward-Best, one of the Demons' coaches, tells BBC Sport.
Oyebadejo had been a talented basketball player, playing for Manchester Magic - one of England's top junior clubs - from the age of 11 to 18. But by the time he was at the University of Exeter he was no longer playing competitively.
Lydon Ward-Best persuaded him to give a new sport a go.
"He started coming to training and just had the most ridiculous intro to American football I think I've ever seen," the coach adds.
A straight-A pupil, who had also learned the piano, guitar and drums while studying medicine, Oyebadejo had always been a quick learner.
"I always say that American football is kind of like violent chess," says Mullins, the Demons' current head coach.
"[Emmanuel] got the violent bit pretty quickly. He was fine at that - 'I am much bigger than you, watch me go'.
"The chess bit took a little longer because there's all these things that you have to think about."
But as Ward-Best puts it, "he's not just a big sort of jock athlete, he's a smart guy. He is so dedicated and disciplined with everything."
Oyebadejo played for the Demons at the end of the 2022-23 season, before the team went unbeaten in his first full season, 2023-24. When back home he also played for the Manchester Titans and helped them win the Britbowl in September 2023.
By December 2023, he decided he wanted to take things further. Could he make it in the United States? Would college teams be interested if he sent them videos of his highlights?
Coach Ward-Best told Oyebadejo it would be "tough", adding: "You know the percentages are not on your side here, but you are 6ft 6in and 280 pounds (20 stone), so you've got a better chance than most.
"I wanted to be realistic with him," he adds. "But I said I'd do whatever I could to help get him out there."
Emmanuel's father Oladini says he thought it was a "joke" and that he did not support him playing this "dangerous" game, explaining: "He had never played this game before. He'd only done it for a few months, so why would anybody from America want him?"
But they did.
There was interest from several colleges and Oyebadejo ended up at Jacksonville State, where he would study biology and play under legendary college coach Rich Rodriguez, having managed to win his parents round thanks to the influence of an uncle who lived in Dallas and understood the sport.
His first season was hit by injury but, despite coming up against players who have played American football since they were young children, his second was a big success.
As a defensive end, Oyebadejo's job is to get past the offensive linemen trying to block him and tackle the ball carrier or claim a sack - when a defensive player tackles the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage.
He recorded 4.5 sacks, forced two fumbles and had 41 total tackles during the 2025 season.
Now the big college teams were paying attention.
College football is America's most passionate sporting pastime. While the NFL plays on Sundays, the college game dominates Saturdays during the autumn months.
And Oyebadejo transferred to the University of Florida to play for one of college football's biggest teams in the most prestigious conference, the Southeastern (SEC).
The Florida Gators are three-time national champions, have about 50 former players currently in the NFL and get home crowds of 90,000 at 'The Swamp'.
Oyebadejo was undaunted as he burst on to the scene. He had 2.5 sacks in a win at rivals Auburn in September and followed that up by impressing in big wins over Mississippi and Texas, the latter in front of 103,989 people.
After barely being on the radar of NFL scouts at the start of the season, Oyebadejo's form has propelled him into contention to be an early-round draft pick in 2027.
NFL teams do not have youth systems or academies. Almost all players have come through the US college system and they are recruited via the NFL Draft when they graduate.
One of the biggest events in the American sporting calendar, the NFL Draft takes place over three days in April, with the 32 teams taking turns to select players across seven rounds.
First-round picks in April will be guaranteed a rookie contract of at least $19.1m (£14.4m) and they are often fast-tracked into starting roles. The contract values decrease in a sliding scale so, for example, a third-round pick (top 96) will be guaranteed $7.3m (£5.5m).
Among the latest prospects, ESPN's veteran draft analyst Mel Kiper has ranked Oyebadejo as the fifth-best edge rusher (defensive end). That is regarded as the sport's second-most important position behind quarterback - and therefore the second-best paid in the NFL.
The reason is that Oyebadejo has everything needed to be a starting defensive end in the NFL. Firstly, his height and weight are ideally suited for the grappling battle required in what is known as 'the trenches'.
He has very long arms (7ft wingspan), perfect for winning a wrestling match against the kind of enormous opponent he faces, and unusually for a man as big as him, he's extremely quick. That's the money-making trait.
Although he now weighs about 300lbs (more than 21 stone), it is believed he has a remarkable body-fat percentage of about 12%. All his measurables are seen as ideal for a defensive end, if not better.
There are simply very few people with Oyebadejo's physical talent, and given the fast-tracked nature of his rise in American football, he does not look as raw as you might expect.
"He's British and has only played the sport for three [full] seasons," says his mentor and former coach Ward-Best. "You'd therefore think he must be very green, but he doesn't look that way.
"The physical qualities are clearly there but he's worked a lot on mastering aspects of the position as well."
Menelik Watson, also from Manchester, holds the record for being the highest-drafted British player. He was the 42nd pick in 2013 and spent six years in the NFL, earning a total of $16.4m (£13.7m).
London-born Osi Umenyiora, the 56th pick in 2003, enjoyed an illustrious 12-year career - winning two Super Bowls with the New York Giants.
"I have spoken to Osi, he's a really cool guy," says Oyebadejo, who is also of Nigerian heritage.
"To be a first-round pick out of the UK, it would be amazing. It would do so much for the American football community back home."
Oyebadejo impressed again in an upset win at Kentucky on Saturday and has 4.5 sacks with two regular-season games left. Florida could then play in a 'bowl' game, an end-of-season exhibition.
After that, Oyebadejo is expected to participate in a physical-testing event called the 'scouting combine', where he will be assessed by representatives of all 32 teams in March.
The draft then begins in Washington DC on 27 April, and if Oyebadejo hears his name called, he will complete an unlikely journey and make his now fully supportive parents very proud.
"It's mad," says Ward-Best. "I've been doing this for 20 years and I've never seen anything like this. We almost have to pinch ourselves."
Oyebadejo has stayed in touch with his former coaches in Exeter. The Demons hold watch parties for Florida games and there is a real sense of pride over where his journey began.
"It was just complete chance that he wanted to wander up to The Crumb and watch a game, just being there for his mate," says coach Mullins.
"If those things didn't happen, we wouldn't be having this conversation. He would be four years into his medical degree."

Srinagar, Nov 19: Kashmiri singer-songwriter Faheem Abdullah has earned a place on the prestigious TIME100 Next India 2026 list, which recognises 100 emerging personalities making an impact across various fields.
The inaugural India-specific edition of the TIME list was unveiled on Thursday, bringing together emerging talents and influential voices from entertainment, business, science, sports, technology, advocacy and the arts.
Abdullah's inclusion marks a significant moment of recognition for Kashmir's contemporary music scene, highlighting his growing presence in the Indian music industry.
The TIME100 next India initiative recognizes a new generation of leaders and creative voices whose work is shaping their respective fields. According to the announcement, the selections were made by TIME journalists in India and internationally to highlight emerging Indian talent to a global audience.
The inaugural list also features several prominent personalities from the entertainment industry, including Alia Bhatt, Vicky Kaushal, Sai Pallavi, Nayanthara, Aryan Khan and filmmaker Payal Kapadia.

Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over?
- Published
Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment.
"People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC.
After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter.
"Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion.
Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next."
Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022.
But within less than two weeks, federal forces marched triumphantly into Mekelle. The TPLF made what it called a "strategic withdrawal" from the city and Tigray's other main towns so the army encountered little resistance. Hundreds of people are reported to have died in the conflict, including dozens killed by drone strikes and bombing raids by the air force.
Ethiopian government officials and supporters argue that the war is effectively over and that the only remaining task is to clear Tigray of TPLF elements.
Getachew Reda, a senior TPLF official who switched sides and is now an adviser to the prime minister, declared that the war in Tigray had ended and that stabilising the region should now be the immediate priority.
Cameroon Hudson, an analyst and consultant on African peace and security, says there are various reasons for the TPLF's rapid defeat.
"The TPLF has lost popular support at home. It is fragmented, it does not possess the advanced military technology necessary to match the ENDF [Ethiopian National Defence Forces]," he says. "It has lost many of its generals, strategic thinkers, finest diplomats and fighters, either through defections or arrests. The infighting within the TPLF leadership has caused significant damage."
Abraha Hailezgi, a scholar at Mekelle University, agrees. "The army lacks a clear political vision. In recent years, it has become associated with coercion, abuses, forced recruitment and arbitrary actions. As a result, many people have come to view the TPLF army as an adversary rather than a force acting on their behalf," he says.
Speaking by telephone from an undisclosed location, TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom denies that the group has lost.
Instead, he describes it as a deliberate tactical and strategic retreat. "This is not a defeat," he tells the BBC.
He says the TPLF "intentionally allowed the ENDF to advance deeper into the heartland of Tigray", where it can be isolated and confronted on favourable terrain. "We chose not to fight on terms favourable to the enemy."
The TPLF is preparing for a major counteroffensive, he says, adding that TPLF fighters have launched attacks against Ethiopian forces in several locations following their withdrawal from the region's towns, arguing that these operations demonstrated the group's continued military capability.
It is hard to get verified information from Tigray and the BBC is unable to report from there. But phone lines and the internet, which were cut when fighting broke out, have now been restored.
Residents in different parts of Tigray tell the BBC that fighting is continuing in central, northern and north-western parts of Tigray, with the use of heavy artillery and drone strikes.
Eyewitnesses around Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, report heavy fighting involving artillery and ground forces in recent days.
"We could hear heavy artillery fire from the Sheraro direction. People are concerned because there is no sense of security," a businessman tells the BBC on condition of anonymity. He adds that military convoys from both sides had moved towards Sheraro, while a motorcycle operator in the southern town of Yechila says military checkpoints are still active.
Memories of the devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war remain raw for many residents.
The conflict saw widespread human rights abuses and allegations of ethnic cleansing in Western Tigray, while estimates suggest the war claimed hundreds of thousands of lives.
As soldiers from Eritrea, accused of some of the worst atrocities in the previous conflict, and Ethiopia have reappeared in Tigray's towns, many residents describe a profound sense of fear and anxiety, saying the sight of the troops has reopened still-fresh wounds.
Military sources aligned with the federal army say operations against the TPLF are continuing, with recent fighting and troop movements reported in northern Tigray, near the Eritrean border, as well as across central Tigray's rugged highlands. They claim the TPLF's capabilities are being steadily degraded.
Security analysts and observers agree that unrest is likely to continue for some time. "I see a situation in which there could be a prolonged war in Tigray," Yared Tibebu, a well-known Ethiopian commentator based in the US, tells the BBC.
Yared argues that the TPLF has a long history of waging protracted armed struggles and believes the movement is once again preparing for a lengthy conflict. He believes that once the group has reorganised its military and political structures, it may attempt to resume offensive operations.
However he believes this will not happen for some time because of internal divisions - a suggestion dismissed by TPLF spokesperson Mikael.
Hudson rejects the idea that Tigray is heading towards a prolonged war but agrees that the region may not be truly peaceful for some time. "The TPLF may continue a low-level insurgency and guerrilla campaign, but that is not war. I do not think there will be a wider-scale conflict between the federal forces and the TPLF."
He says the TPLF no longer possesses the size, strength or military capability required to effectively confront federal forces, which he says have significantly expanded and modernised in recent years. "The TPLF has also lost much of its public support and cannot easily rebuild its ranks through recruitment," he says.
Yared, on the other hand, points to the TPLF's history of overcoming setbacks as evidence that the movement could recover to sustain a prolonged struggle. "The TPLF has overcome many major challenges in the past. It is wrong to conclude that it has no public support. It is a political movement with a history stretching back more than 50 years," he says.
What Yared sees as a strength, Hudson sees as a weakness, saying the TPLF is still "trapped in the past", and continues to behave as a dominant party within Tigray, even though the situation has changed. "It is a movement that has not evolved, modernised or expanded."
While Hudson argues that the TPLF is not equipped to sustain a major military campaign, the TPLF spokesman says the group obtains weapons and logistical supplies from the Ethiopian military. "We seize weapons from our enemy, and the weaponry that has entered Tigray will, sooner or later, become ours."
In early October, eyewitnesses told the BBC they had seen Eritrean troops in Tigray amid reports they were backing the TPLF. However, they appear to have returned home and Hudson thinks the country would be wary of becoming further embroiled in the conflict.
"First, Eritrea does not have unlimited resources. Second, the TPLF is no more an effective military force, and Eritrean leaders may have concluded that supporting it at this stage would not yield significant military gains," he says. "Third, Eritrea would have to consider the risk of provoking a confrontation with Ethiopia if it openly backs the TPLF."
Sources in the Ethiopia army tell the BBC that senior members of the TPLF's political leadership were briefly based in Eritrea, however, they say the authorities ordered them to leave in early November, shortly after President Isaias Afwerki returned from Russia. According to the sources, the move was driven by concerns that Ethiopia could use their presence as a reason to invade.
Hudson also argues that Eritrea's renewed diplomatic engagement with the US, whose relations with the TPLF have long been strained, could further discourage Asmara from providing meaningful support to the movement.
In September, seven Ethiopian rebel groups led by the TPLF announced the formation of a new coalition called the Alliance for Survival, aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.
Yared believes the alliance could give the TPLF the strength to keep on fighting. "Its members can combine their strengths. The TDF [the TPLF's military wing] has leadership experience and organisational capacity, while Fano [an ethnic Amhara militia] is believed to have between 70,000 and 80,000 fighters.
"If conditions emerge that allow the forces to co-ordinate effectively, the TPLF's current difficulties may not last long," he says.
Hudson, however, rejects that argument, insisting that the alliance is unlikely to alter the balance of power. "I don't think the TPLF can be saved by this alliance. The ethnic militias have not demonstrated the capacity, either individually or collectively, to pose a serious threat to federal forces. We should not underestimate the strength of the federal army," he says.
Abraha from Mekelle University argues that the conflict in Tigray will only truly be over if the federal government addresses the region's feeling that it has been marginalised, both economically and politically by the current government.
However, many Tigrayan elites and political observers remain wary of the federal government's intentions. They question whether the authorities in Addis Ababa are genuinely seeking to address Tigray's problems, or whether they are taking advantage of the region's weakness to boost their influence.
In the meantime, many ordinary people in Tigray say their priority is peace.
"Peace seems slow in coming. Most people are tired of politics. Whatever happens, we only want peace and a chance to rebuild our lives," says Firut from her beauty salon in Mekelle.
