A video purportedly showing Union Home Minister Amit Shah saying in the Lok Sabha that the government is more concerned about elections than the situation in Manipur is going viral on social media (here, here, and here). Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Union Home Minister Amit Shah saying in the Lok Sabha that the government is more concerned about elections than the situation in Manipur.
Fact: The video is from a Lok Sabha discussion on the Delhi Services Bill in August 2023. Amit Shah’s remarks about the government being more concerned about elections than Manipur were made sarcastically while criticising the opposition and accusing it of prioritising its political interests over democracy and the welfare of the nation. He was not expressing his own views or stating the BJP’s position. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to a video uploaded to Sansad TV’s YouTube channel on 03 August 2023. In this video, Amit Shah is seen wearing the same outfit and speaking against the same background as in the viral video. According to the description, Union Home Minister Amit Shah was responding to a discussion on the National Capital Territory of Delhi (Amendment) Bill, 2023, in the Lok Sabha. During the discussion, he also criticised the opposition.
At the 12:26-minute mark in the original video, Amit Shah can be heard making the same remarks as those in the viral clip. However, a careful viewing of the full video shows he wasn’t expressing his own views or explaining the BJP’s position. Instead, he was sarcastically quoting what he alleged to be the opposition’s priorities.
Amit Shah made these remarks to taunt the opposition. At the 12:28-minute mark, he says, “We’re not concerned about Manipur, we’re concerned about elections. We’re not concerned about democracy, we’re concerned about elections. Our party has no principles; we’re in politics solely to win elections.“
Before making these remarks, Shah was seen criticising the opposition over its response to the Manipur situation. In this context, he was accusing the opposition alliance of prioritising its political interests and the survival of its coalition over democracy and the welfare of the nation. Thus, the viral video omits the context in which he made these remarks, making it appear as though he was expressing his own views or stating the BJP’s position.
We also found multiple media reports (here, here) published in 2023, stating that the Delhi Services Bill was passed in the Lok Sabha on 03 August 2023. During the discussion, Home Minister Amit Shah launched a verbal attack on the opposition parties. The reports also stated that the bill was passed by a voice vote after opposition MPs staged a walkout.
To sum up, a video of Amit Shah criticising the opposition over Manipur is shared out of context as his own remarks on the BJP’s priorities.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday (November 19) urged Indian businesses to move beyond the domestic market, improve product quality, reduce import dependence and expand their global footprint, calling on industry leaders to make India First the foundation of their long-term investment decisions.
Addressing the 100th Annual General Meeting and Annual Convention of the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, PM Modi outlined opportunities across pharmaceuticals, agriculture, food processing, engineering, steel and aluminium.
He also challenged businesses to translate the benefits of tax reforms into higher salaries and more employment, while invoking Mahatma Gandhi's message of Swadeshi and self-reliance.
Here are the key takeaways from PM Modi's address:
PM Modi urged businesses to stop treating India's large domestic market as an assured destination for products, stressing that Indian consumers deserve the same quality of goods as overseas buyers.
He criticised the practice of selling products to Indian customers by describing them as "export quality".
"Do not take 140 crore Indians for granted as an assured market where anything will sell. Even today, sellers tell customers 'this is export quality' to convince them it is good. What do you take our countrymen for? Do they not deserve good quality? This mindset must change; my countrymen deserve top quality," he said.
He added that India's domestic market should serve as a launchpad for global competitiveness rather than become a comfort zone.
"Our domestic market must not become our comfort zone. It should give us the confidence to compete in global markets," PM Modi said.
The Prime Minister asked industry leaders to look beyond short-term business gains and prepare for emerging requirements in India and international markets.
He called on businesses to prioritise national interests while making long-term investment decisions over the next two decades.
"In every long-term investment decision of yours for the next 20 years, make India First your foundation," he said.
PM Modi said this approach would strengthen India's self-reliance while creating new opportunities for businesses.
He also warned that companies needed to prepare for a world where resources were increasingly being used as strategic instruments.
"In this era of the weaponisation of resources, securing the nation's future becomes the responsibility of all of us," he said.
PM Modi highlighted the government's tax reforms, including the reduction in the basic corporate tax rate and the income-tax exemption for earnings up to ₹12 lakh under the applicable provisions.
However, he questioned whether companies had passed on the benefits of these measures through higher employee salaries and additional hiring.
"We brought the basic corporate tax rate down from 30% in 2014 to 22%, and today there is no income tax on earnings up to ₹12 lakh. Did you increase your employees' salaries or hire more staff?" he asked.
He also highlighted improvements in tax administration, claiming that income-tax refunds that previously took several months were now generally processed within a week.
GST reforms had also reduced taxes on several products, supporting consumer demand and benefiting businesses, he said.
PM Modi urged India's pharmaceutical industry to reduce its dependence on imported active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), bulk drugs and drug intermediates.
Despite being known as the "pharmacy of the world", India continues to import billions of dollars' worth of pharmaceutical ingredients every year, he said.
"India is called the 'pharmacy of the world,' yet it imports billions of dollars' worth of APIs, bulk drugs, and drug intermediates every year," he said.
He asked pharmaceutical companies to identify ingredients that could be manufactured domestically and invest in new technologies and large-scale production facilities.
"In finished medicines, we have strength. Now we will have to build our capabilities in ingredients as well," Modi said.
The Prime Minister questioned why India continued to export raw materials while importing finished products, calling for greater domestic manufacturing and value addition.
"What kind of a country is this, and what kind of industrialists are we, if we export wheat and import bread?" he asked.
He cited opportunities in the steel and aluminium industries, noting that India exports iron ore but imports finished steel, while also importing specialised aluminium alloys despite having substantial bauxite reserves.
He urged companies to identify the grades of steel and aluminium products that India imports and develop the technology and manufacturing capabilities to produce them domestically.
PM Modi called on the corporate sector to increase investments in agriculture, food processing and procurement infrastructure to expand India's agricultural exports.
He said India's share of global agricultural exports remained at around 2-2.5%, highlighting the considerable room for growth.
"I would urge you to increase your industry's investment in India's agricultural sector. Set up reliable procurement systems with specific overseas markets in mind, and develop products for which there is demand there, so that Indian products can become our calling card around the world," he said.
He also highlighted the rise in processed food's share of India's agri-food exports from 13% to more than 20% over the past 12 years.
Businesses, he said, should focus on value addition and develop products according to the requirements of specific international markets.
The Prime Minister identified hand tools, power tools and machinery manufacturing as sectors where Indian companies could build a stronger global presence.
He encouraged large companies to help smaller enterprises develop manufacturing capabilities that meet international quality and scale requirements.
PM Modi also pointed to opportunities in manufacturing machinery for developing economies, particularly countries in the Global South.
Packaging equipment, irrigation systems and factory-related machinery were among the areas where Indian businesses could explore export opportunities, he said.
PM Modi asked Indian industry leaders to take advantage of the Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) signed with several major economies.
He said these agreements had opened new opportunities for Indian manufacturers and exporters, but questioned whether businesses had adequately prepared to exploit them.
"India has signed Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) with several major economies; doors have opened for you. Have you planned to seize this opportunity? If you do not take advantage of all my hard work, who will?" he said.
He urged companies to invest in overseas market research, understand consumer preferences and establish distribution networks to strengthen India's export presence.
Marking FICCI's 100th anniversary, PM Modi invoked Mahatma Gandhi's 1930 message of Swadeshi and self-reliance, saying Indian businesses needed to carry forward the same vision.
He questioned why the country still needed to emphasise indigenous manufacturing and self-reliance nearly a century after Gandhi advocated the use of domestic products.
"Imagine, 100 years have passed, but in 1930, Gandhi left us with this message, and today, so many years later, I too have to say the same thing. Is this your success or your failure? Don't listen to me; at least you could have listened to Gandhi!" he said.
He urged industry leaders to spread the message of Swadeshi and Atmanirbhar Bharat across the country.
Modi also urged businesses to move beyond any hesitation arising from their experiences with previous governments and openly communicate their concerns to the current administration.
"Your experience with previous governments has been so bitter that I am having to bear the consequences. This is not the old government; this is a government of friends. It knows how to honour friendship, and you are my true friends," he said.
He invited industry representatives to submit written suggestions on areas requiring further reforms, assuring them that the government was open to addressing their concerns.
Highlighting India's economic performance, PM Modi said the country had moved from being counted among the world's "Fragile Five" economies to becoming the fastest-growing major economy.
He cited a recent World Bank report, saying around 500 million Indians had moved out of poverty over the past 12-13 years.
He also highlighted merchandise exports of nearly $50 billion in October, describing it as the highest-ever monthly goods export figure.
"Today, India stands as the world's fastest-growing major economy, with projected growth of around 7%. In October, India's goods exports reached nearly $50 billion, our highest-ever monthly goods export," he said.
PM Modi added that international institutions, including Moody's Ratings, S&P Global Ratings, Fitch Ratings, the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank, had revised their growth projections for India upwards.
Concluding his message to industry leaders, Modi said FICCI's centenary was an opportunity to reflect on the contribution Indian businesses could make over the next two decades.
He urged companies to prepare for future domestic and global demand instead of concentrating only on sectors that already offered established business opportunities.
"Over its 100 years, FICCI has seen the country's industry achieve a great deal. Now is the time to decide what Indian industry can achieve in the next 20 years--how you can further increase your contribution to the journey of Viksit Bharat and Atmanirbhar Bharat," he said.
"Developed India is not a slogan; it is a commitment," PM Modi added.

New Delhi, Nov 19: Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi will inaugurate the First Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum on 20 November 2026 at around 5:30 PM at Purana Qila, New Delhi. He will also address the gathering on the occasion.
Being held from 20 to 22 November 2026, the Forum aims to celebrate the rich and interconnected civilisational heritage of the region, strengthen people-to-people ties and promote cross-cultural dialogue and cooperation.
The initiative builds upon the proposal made by the Prime Minister at the SCO Summit in Tianjin, China in 2025 to establish a dedicated platform for civilisational dialogue under the SCO framework. The proposal was subsequently welcomed in the Bishkek Declaration of SCO.
The inaugural ceremony will feature “Civilisations in Conversation - Cultural Show”, a presentation combining music, dance, visual storytelling and narration. Based on the theme “Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam - The World Is One Family”, it will highlight cultural connections across India and Eurasia.
The Forum will also feature exhibitions showcasing India's archaeological, artistic and literary heritage titled “ASTITVA – The Essence of Our Existence.” It will offer an immersive account of Delhi's history through archaeological evidence dating from 1200 BCE to 1200 CE, including excavated remains, artefacts, architectural fragments and other significant discoveries. The “Mahabharat Scroll Pavilion - Anant: A Rare 18th Century Mahabharata Scroll” will showcase an illustrated scroll reflecting India's rich epic and artistic traditions.
Four thematic sessions will be held on 21 and 22 November, bringing together scholars, academics, subject experts and cultural representatives. Discussions will cover cultural expressions such as music and performing arts, textiles, cuisine, traditional games; shared traditions in art and architecture; language and literary traditions, including scripts and manuscripts; and monastic trails and philosophical traditions

One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.
In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.
Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.
“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”
The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.
“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.
He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.
In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.
Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.
Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”
She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.
“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”

How much of India’s healthcare bill is being paid by the government, and how much still comes from households? Government health expenditure has more than tripled over a decade to ₹4.14 lakh crore, while the share of total health expenditure paid directly by households has fallen to 42.7%.

Advocates, traders and residents staged a protest near a bus terminus in Vaniyambadi town on Thursday, demanding an additional district court and a permanent building for the court complex.
The protest was held in the wake of the onset of the Northeast monsoon, when it could be risky to conduct court proceedings at the dilapidated Judicial Magistrate court. “Work to build a permanent court complex should be expedited. An additional district court should also be set up in the court complex”, said A.C. Devakumar, president, Bar Association (Vaniyambadi).
At present, Vaniyambadi has three lower courts that are located in different areas in the town. Each court, on an average, is located at least 1.5 km away from the other court. It has resulted in hardship for litigants, advocates, and court staff to commute from one court to another as some petitioners have cases in different courts that will be taken up on the same day.
The Judicial Magistrate Court, the oldest among three courts, was located in the Government Estate since the 1920s. The District Munsif court, formed in 1995, was functioning from a rented room in the Government Commercial Tax building. The subordinate court that was created in 2009 was also operating from a rented room in the town.
Every day, on an average, more than 150 litigants, mostly from Vaniyambadi taluk that comprises 45 villages, visit these courts. Around 75 advocates are working as regular practitioners. On an average, over 100 cases come up at each court every day. Currently, 1,500 - 2,000 cases are pending before each of these three courts.
Case bundles and court records get damaged during monsoon as the building is inundated. The court also does not have an audio system, to call for cases or parties. As a result, many litigants wait for long hours or leave as they are unsure about whether their case has been called.

JPMorgan Chase, Mastercard and Visa said Thursday that there were cyber incidents at the companies' third-party vendors. As a result, some customer data has been exposed.
Chase said in an X post that vendors who provide services to the banking giant "were the target of a cyber attack."
"Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," JPMorgan Chase wrote.
America's largest bank said there was no disruption to its services.
"Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring," it said.
A Mastercard spokesperson told Business Insider that the credit card firm was recently informed of an "incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses" from a "small subset" of cardholders enrolled in a certain benefit program.
"There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," the spokesperson said. The Mastercard spokesperson added that the exposure has been contained and that the company's teams were working with the provider to support the affected cardholders as needed.
A spokesperson for Visa told Business Insider that there was also an incident involving a third-party service provider in the Asia Pacific region.
"Visa's systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected," the spokesperson said. The spokesperson did not immediately respond to the question of whether other customer information was impacted.
It was not clear who the targeted vendors were, how many customers may have been affected, or whether the same hackers were behind the incidents.
Cybersecurity company SOCRadar told Business Insider that a ransomware group claimed responsibility for the incidents.
"SOCRadar's dark web monitoring identified posts on the leak site of a ransomware group calling itself n0n, claiming JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard as victims and posting sample data as proof," Ensar Seker, the firm's chief security information officer, said.
Seker said SOCRadar has not independently verified that n0n carried out the cyberattacks.
"The most immediate risk for consumers is targeted phishing that impersonates their bank or card provider," said Seker.
The cyberattacks follow a series of high-profile outages and a software bug at JPMorgan Chase that wreaked havoc on online banking services earlier this week.
"JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems — there is no evidence this is cyber-related," the bank previously said in a statement on Monday. "It is taking longer than usual to service some customers."
The bank said on Thursday that there is no connection between the cyberattack and the service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week.

In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.
Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.
“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”
Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role.
From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay.
Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.
Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa. In 2024, students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, made global headlines after they pulled off what was described as the world’s first successful gen Z-led revolution.
The protests began over a quota law but swiftly snowballed into a wider show of discontent against the increasingly autocratic rule of the prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. Two months later, Hasina resigned and fled the country by helicopter after being, as the Associated Press reported, “chased out by young protesters”.
Two years later and 4,000 miles away, students were at the helm of another revolution in Serbia, pushing back against a government that had steadily tightened its grip on the media and stuffed institutions with party loyalists.
Late last month, Serbia’s students’ movement was catapulted from the streets to the halls of power as they ousted Aleksandar Vučić in elections, bringing an end to his party’s 14 years in power.
Students and young people have long been at the forefront of the push for change, the analysts Cait Dallaire and Sebastian Dittgen wrote recently, citing the US civil rights movement and the 2011 Arab spring.
“What is unique about the current movement is the infrastructure of mobilisation: TikTok and X amplify and accelerate grievances; Discord servers and group chats enable decentralised planning; virtual private networks and mirrored content help organisers circumvent internet shutdowns,” they said.
It was this potent combination – young people in the streets and social media – that helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential election last month. After a bruising loss in the first round to the rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, there was dismay in the country’s political left.
That was until students from the Fluminense Federal University mobilised in a pro-Lula march, setting off a wave of similar actions across the country. Soon after, the congressman and Lula ally André Janones, 42, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” that attracted millions of people looking to help boost pro-Lula content on social media.
On the night of his victory, Lula recognised their power. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he said.
Some politicians have sought to engage gen Z from the start. In the US, Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for New York mayor combined a canny use of social media with a legion of about 50,000 volunteers that had young people at its heart. The New York Times wrote that “volunteering for Mr Mamdani’s campaign became a salve” for young New Yorkers as the campaign became not just about “mobilising, but socialising”.
It was a nod to the global context in which many gen Zers have come of age; one riven by conflicts such as the Israel-Gaza war, the escalating climate crisis and the rise of nationalism, while the rules that have shaped the international order since the second world war are fraying.
In recent weeks, youth-led protests have begun to sweep Europe, from school students in France demanding better conditions in which to work to those in Spain who pitched tents to rally for affordable housing. In Germany, thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the cost of living and call for more investment in education, health and climate action in a movement organised by a group calling itself Gen Z regelt!, or Gen Z will sort this.
Analysts have been swift to point to the link between the protests. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs, told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “In Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”
A similar note of disillusionment threads through India’s Cockroach movement, which began as an online satire and has since swelled into a show of force against the strongman government of Narendra Modi. Fuelled by social media and rooted in democratic ideals, the power of the movement was laid bare this summer after Cockroach-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.
Equally visible is the pushback by India’s security forces against the movement, detaining thousands, unleashing teargas and beating people with lathis, or wooden clubs. Authorities went to extreme lengths in October to keep them from gathering in central Delhi, barricading roads and shutting down the internet and public transport.
It was a window into another facet that has defined youth-led protests, as research suggests they tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others.
In France, lawyers and rights groups say several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons. After the 2024 protests in Bangladesh, UN human rights experts said as many as 1,400 people had been killed, mostly by security forces, while thousands more suffered severe, often life-altering injuries.
In a recent analysis, Civicus, a non-profit that monitors global civic freedoms, said: “Because they question the distribution of economic and political power, gen Z-led protests have invariably been met with state violence,” linking the violence meted out to young protesters with their focus on systems and institutions that have long been generally accepted.
In Morocco, more than 2,000 people were charged and many received harsh prison sentences after a 2025 movement known as Gen Z 212 targeted officials over corruption, neglected public services and the lack of opportunities. Weeks later, in Mexico, youth-led protests over corruption and crime led to clashes with police in which dozens of people were arrested.
The outcomes of both of these movements show the varying success of gen Z protests. But at times, the foundations laid in one protest have given rise to others. In the US, much of today’s youth organising was shaped by the pro-Palestine student movement, in which there were thousands of arrests, expulsions and suspensions. Many schools instated anti-protest policies amid a broader rollback of educational freedom on campus.
Students, however, have continued to push for change. Last month hundreds in North Carolina marched in the heat to the polls after their historically Black university was denied a polling site, while thousands across the country have responded to the Cornell 7 case by skipping class, protesting and launching occupations.
As Chenoweth of the Harvard Kennedy School noted, the wave of recent youth-led protests may mark the beginning of a “profound generational transformation in world affairs” – one that could be capable of countering the global trend of democratic backsliding.
Ultimately, however, as Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris recently told the Associated Press, the explosion of youth movements across Europe hints at a wider truth that has long been overlooked across the globe.
“We all agree on one point,” he said. “That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”

Senior IRS officer Prachi Saroop has sought voluntary retirement, drawing attention within the revenue department. She serves as Principal Chief Commissioner of the Mumbai CGST Zone. Saroop is among the senior-most officers of the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs. She was also seen as a contender for a seat on the board, according to The Secretariat. Saroop submitted a formal three-month notice to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman. She applied under Rule 43 of the CCS (Pension) Rules, 2012. Officials said she cited personal reasons and thanked the government for letting her serve India. She also acknowledged the support of her seniors and colleagues. According to The Secretariat, some staff believe repeated setbacks in board selection may have influenced her decision. Saroop was reportedly shortlisted and interviewed three times for a CBIC Member position. She did not secure a seat on the board. Her request comes ahead of another selection round for a CBIC Member, officials said. The process is expected in the coming weeks. Other officials pointed out that appointments follow a prescribed process. According to them, seniority alone does not determine who joins the board, the publication added. Prachi Saroop holds a Master of Science degree, according to her official service record. She entered Group A service on September 16, 1991. She started as an Assistant Commissioner in the Chennai Central Excise Zone in May 1993. She later handled Central Excise and Customs assignments in Delhi. Saroop became Deputy Commissioner in 2000 and Joint Commissioner in 2002. She served in the Directorate General of Audit in Delhi. She also worked as Deputy Secretary in the Department of Biotechnology on deputation. Her later assignments covered service tax, central excise, customs and vigilance in Mumbai. She served as Principal Commissioner in Mumbai Customs. She became Principal Additional Director General of Vigilance in Mumbai. She joined the Settlement Commission in Delhi in June 2023. In August, she became Chief Commissioner and was posted to Mumbai Customs Zone-III. She took charge as Principal Chief Commissioner of the Mumbai CGST Zone in April 2026. Social media users reacted to Prachi Saroop’s decision. Most reactions are more allegations than statements. “She has been superseded by her junior for the post of Member. Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.
Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.
The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.
Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.
The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”
Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.
The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”
Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.
“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.
Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.
Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
- Published
US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.
The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.
In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.
Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".
Trump praised the trilateral meeting calling it "a great and highly consequential trip", in a social media post while flying back to Washington on Air Force One.
In the same post, the president announced he would host a news conference to talk about the trip on Friday at the White House.
While in China, Trump met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend".
He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".
Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.

The opening remarks of the trilateral gave some indication about what was to be discussed during the closed-door meeting.
Before giving the floor to his fellow leaders, Xi said that "positive interaction among major powers is not a matter of choice, but a mandatory requirement".
Putin followed this by highlighting a shared interest in ending the Ukraine war and said the conversation would also touch on food and energy security.
China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.
Beijing has also repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's aggression.
Meanwhile, Trump closed by saying the presidents of three of the world's largest countries have a "special responsibility" to maintain productive dialogue.
"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said, adding: "We feel the opposite."
Trump referenced the three countries' nuclear capabilities and said they are "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth".
It is "vital" that they co-operate to "combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world", he said, adding: "That's what we're doing in Iran."
"We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon".
Trump then turned to Ukraine and said he and Putin have had a "long discussion" on the conflict there already.
He added that Putin "and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war".
Putin addressed the media following the trilateral meeting and described it as an "important chapter in the history of diplomacy".
He said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict in Ukraine - but he said Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to better understand Europe's position.
As the talks were under way in China, and even as Putin was holding his press conference claiming to be ready for peace, Ukraine's capital Kyiv was under attack from Russian drones.
Putin has repeatedly rejected all ceasefire offers from Ukraine, insisting on his maximalist demands which Kyiv and its European allies say are tantamount to de facto capitulation of Ukraine.
In Shenzhen, the Kremlin leader also vowed a "far more painful" retaliation in response to Ukrainian attacks on the bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea. A missile and drone attack on Tuesday destroyed its central road section.
There was no mention from Putin of almost five years of Russian attacks on power plants, bridges and residential buildings in Ukraine.
The Russian president also directly addressed comparisons between his meeting with Trump and Xi and the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the US met towards the end of World War Two.
"Nobody divided up the world at Yalta. It simply codified the realities that had emerged after WW2.
"And when it comes to today's conflicts, the realities on the ground will have to be accepted."
The Kremlin released a video showing Putin leaving the summit venue and saying goodbye to Xi.
"Thank you for organising this," Putin said. "I don't think anyone even expected everything to go so well."
Meanwhile, China's president described his meeting with Putin and Trump as "positive, constructive, and highly productive", according to the country's state broadcaster CCTV.
It added that Xi recalled "the history of fighting side-by-side during WW2", as the three leaders emphasised the importance of "cherishing the hard-won peace".
Thursday's trilateral meeting was reportedly the idea of Putin.
Some Russian newspapers called it a "diplomatic victory" as after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine many Western leaders were trying to isolate him.
The summit also marked the first time since Russia's war in Ukraine began that Putin took part in an international gathering attended by leaders from countries including Canada, Japan and Australia.
US lawmakers responded with frustration to Trump's warmth towards America's geopolitical adversaries.
"I was encouraged by some of the commitments that came out of the President's meetings in Asia, particularly the recognition that nuclear war must never be fought," Republican Senator John Curtis said in an emailed statement to the BBC.
But Curtis also said he was concerned about Trump's approach to the foreign leaders, adding that "Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends".
"We should not treat them as though they share our values or interests," Curtis, who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, added.
"Doing so risks undermining our national security, weakening trust with our allies, and sending the wrong message about where America stands."
Jeanne Shaheen, a ranking Democratic member on the same committee, chose harsher words in her comment.
"President Trump's 'friend' is a murderous war criminal," she wrote on X.

The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife
Ever argued with your spouse in the car? NPR's Nina Totenberg can relate.
She and her husband, David Reines, have been married for 26 years, and it's on the road where they're most likely to have a spat. "The car is awful," Totenberg told me, laughing. It comes down partly to the brakes. She taps them "way before" Reines does. And when another driver cuts him off, he sometimes wants to return the favor. Totenberg's advice from the passenger seat: "Don't take the bait."
It's so relatable. And as Reines put it, "You can't not have some conflict after 26 years. I think the secret is how you deal with it." (They began our interview for this episode of Your Turn by giving each other a kiss!)
As we ask "What comes next?" in midlife, who's standing beside us matters a lot. Kids leave home, careers shift, and relationships can change, too. So what does a good partnership look like at this stage?
David and Nina's Four L's
When people ask Reines why their marriage works, he points to four L's:
Love. "You gotta love each other."
Like. Do you actually like each other? For Reines, respect is part of this. He says he has total respect for her work, and she respects his career, too. He is a retired trauma surgeon and now keeps busy as a volunteer at the Library of Congress and serves on boards. Each of them also keeps a strong sense of self. "Although we meld," Reines says. "I still have me, and she still has her."
Lust. Physical intimacy matters. They kiss every day, hold hands, "all the time," and have held off on buying a king-size bed. In hotel beds, they joke, they can't find each other if the bed is too big.
Laugh. He says she has one of the best senses of humor he knows. They laugh together every day.
The Magic Six
I also talked with clinical psychologist Julie Schwartz Gottman who I interviewed for my book, Your Turn. She and her husband, John Gottman, co-founded the Gottman Institute and are two of the best-known names in relationship science, and co-authors of Fight Right: How Successful Couples Turn Conflict Into Connection, where they describe the "Four Horseman" which are four destructive communication patterns that can help predict the breakdown of a relationship.
Gottman points to research that shows many dual-career couples spend little time together and much of the communication can be transactional. Did you call the plumber? Did you walk the dog?
The Gottmans found that couples can improve their relationships by intentionally carving out about six hours a week together, and making changes to small, daily and weekly habits. They call it the Magic Six.
Some of these things may sound obvious, yet oftentimes these are the very things that can fall away when couples are too busy or distracted. And she says it's illuminating when couples actually track progress.
Partings (a few minutes each day). Before you leave in the morning, spend a few minutes communicating about what's happening in your partner's day.
Reunions (about 20 minutes a day). At the end of the workday, share a kiss or physical affection. Then have a 20-minute stress-reducing conversation about your day.
Admiration and appreciation (35 minutes a week). Spend about five minutes a day expressing genuine gratitude or naming a trait you admire in your partner. Or tell a story to remind each other.
Affection (35 minutes a week). That works out to about five minutes a day on physical touch, such as holding hands or cuddling before sleep.
Date night (2 hours a week). Have distraction-free time together to enjoy being together. It doesn't need to be dinner and a show. It can be a low-key hike, a museum visit or any activity you enjoy.
State of the union meeting (1 hour a week). Review what's going well as well as concerns or things that are not working, and then talk things out.
Listen. Don't Fix.
Many partners fall into the trap of trying to "fix" the other person's problems or tell them how to proceed. But the point of the daily conversation is to step away from this mentality.
"Most of us just wanna be seen," Gottman told me. "We wanna be witnessed." Jumping in with advice can cut off the conversation before your partner gets the chance to describe what's bothering them.
Instead, she suggests three simple words: "Tell me more."
It's an invitation, Gottman says. It tells your partner, "I really am interested in what you're saying." It shows them that you care.
Nina Totenberg and David Reines have their own version. Every night at dinner, they sit down and ask, "How'd your day go?" He calls Nina a good listener and she says she enjoys connecting this way and spending time together. They keep each other in check and serve as each other's confidant.
Find Your Rhythm
Gottman also had good news for couples who don't share every hobby. You can pursue different passions as long as you bring them back to the table and stay curious about each other. Some couples want lots of independence, and others want to do everything together. The key is to keep asking: Are you missing me? Do we need more time together, or less?
Totenberg and Reins have found their balance. They agree on watching British murder mysteries together. And when he wants a shoot-'em-up, she heads upstairs for Law & Order. Summer vacations on Cape Cod are friends-only, where they spend days doing what they each enjoy. Winter holidays are for her sisters and family.
As Totenberg put it: "If you find somebody that you really love who loves you back, you should grab that and run for all the world because it's ... an enormous gift."
So, if you'd like: give this a try: Ask your partner one open-ended question. Then say, "Tell me more."

TOI Correspondent From Washington: Elon Musk
 is seeking a divorce from MAGA, apparently on grounds of irreconcilable political differences. The man who once boldly declared himself “Dark MAGA,” bankrolled 
Donald Trump
, and wielded the chainsaw of DOGE, is now insisting he was never really one of them.
In what is the political equivalent of an uninstallation process, the multi-billionaire boss of SpaceX-Tesla has apparently concluded that being America's unofficial minister for disruption was not quite the career-enhancing investment he imagined. Speaking at The New York Times' DealBook Summit on Wednesday, he initiated a political course correction, describing himself as "quite moderate" and expressing regret at having spent an extraordinary amount of money backing Republican candidates in the midterm elections.
"Republicans were routed and the money I spent… I feel pretty foolish having spent so much money and not seeing much for it," he confessed. "If I could rewind the clock I would have spent less money."
Even for a multi-billionaire, the lolly he splurged was not exactly small beer. Musk reportedly spent approximately $446 million backing Republicans in the 2026 midterms, making him the biggest individual political donor in American electoral history. 
Much of that money went into trying to preserve GOP dominance in Texas -- where a lot of his tech assets are located -- and in Congress.
Voters had other ideas; only three of the nearly 50 candidates he backed won.
Pressed about his political identity at the summit, Musk did the tech version of a 404 error not found. "I'm not sure what MAGA means. But if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that," he said.
It did not appear so in October 2024, when Musk strode on stage at a Trump rally in Pennsylvania wearing a black MAGA cap and announced, with considerable theatrical passion: "I'm not just MAGA — I'm Dark MAGA." He subsequently became one of Trump's most enthusiastic financial backers, was rewarded with a prominent place in the president's inner circle and took charge of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), the administration's controversial cost-cutting operation. For months, he was a permanent fixture in the White House, turning up in the Oval Office, attending cabinet meetings and helping wield the administration's chainsaw against federal agencies and government employees.
It was an extraordinary political journey for a man who once cultivated the image of a freewheeling entrepreneur above party politics. But the romance eventually soured. Musk and Trump had a spectacular public falling-out in 2025, before patching things up. Now, following another electoral disaster, Musk appears to be rediscovering his independent streak.
There are several possible explanations for this sudden moderation. The most obvious is that losing elections is bad for business, particularly when one has invested nearly half a billion dollars in ensuring the other side loses. The Democrats' sweeping midterm victory has also changed the political geography of Musk's business empire. Texas, where Tesla and SpaceX have established major operations and where Musk has invested heavily, has elected Democrat Gina Hinojosa governor, ending decades of Republican control. Democrats also captured a Senate seat in Texas and made major gains nationally.
The new governor could bring greater scrutiny to Musk's sprawling Texas operations, including tax incentives, data-centre expansion and the controversial Starbase project. Musk, however, struck a conciliatory note, describing Hinojosa as a moderate and saying: "Things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor."
India is no stranger to Musk’s mercurial politics. He has repeatedly expressed admiration for PM Modi, spoken well of Indian professionals, and even backed the H1B visa program. But he has gradually soured on New Delhi, going so far as to suggest the government was favoring Indian business oligarchs in blocking his Starlink venture to protect their monopolies.
So while the Musk courtship may yet prove useful to New Delhi for the tech mojo and moolah he can bring, his latest flip is also a reminder that the world's richest man is nobody's ideological soulmate. His loyalties, like his business interests, are decidedly transactional.

Incoming House majority leader Katherine Clark stresses Democratic unity
Rep. Katherine Clark, D-Mass., on the Democratic Party's agenda for the new Congress
House Democrats needed a bigger room Wednesday to accommodate their newly expanded caucus, according to Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts.
Nominated to become the first woman to serve as House majority leader next year, Clark reflected on the moment in an interview with Morning Edition on Thursday.
"It was really looking at the diversity of that caucus, people who have been sent to Congress from all walks of life, that gives me the optimism and the energy that we can really deliver for the American people," she said.
Clark, who is currently the House minority whip, was nominated for House majority leader by a unanimous voice vote. Democrats also nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker and Pete Aguilar for majority whip.
The incoming leadership faces the challenge of lowering living costs while investigating alleged corruption in the Trump administration.
"Of course we can," she said when asked whether Democrats could accomplish both. "That's our responsibility."
She also called President Trump's description of himself as "Mr. Veto" a "stunning statement," expressing hope for bipartisan cooperation on healthcare.
But Democrats face divisions within their own ranks.
Jeffries won his nomination 251-11. Opposition came from incoming progressives including Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York and Adam Hamawy of New Jersey. They have pressed for Medicare for All, immigration enforcement reforms and an end to the war in Gaza.
The two leaders have differed over U.S. aid to Israel. In July, Clark voted for a Republican amendment that would have cut aid to Israel, while Jeffries opposed it.
Despite that disagreement and concerns among other Democrats about Jeffries' leadership, she emphasized party unity when asked whether the 11 votes against him could complicate Democrats' agenda.
"We are having conversations with every part of our new caucus, and they are united behind making life better for working people," she said.

Rosemary Nyirumbe became a nun when she was just in her mid-teens – and she felt her true vocation lay in rehabilitating children who had been through some of the worst trauma imaginable. So that’s what she did. In this episode Mike Wooldridge hears Sr Rosemary’s astonishing story. The feared rebel group, the Lord’s Resistance Army, started to terrorise the north of Uganda in the 1980s. Many children, girls as well as boys, were abducted and forced to become child soldiers. In many cases, the LRA forced them to commit atrocities, leaving them deeply traumatised. Many of the girls also bore the children of rebel leaders. As they started to return home, these children were often rejected by their families and communities, says Sr Rosemary. So she set about giving them a future and a hope: through enabling them to acquire skills like sewing, and by helping them see that God had not rejected them for the atrocities they had been forced to commit. More than once, Sr Rosemary put herself in enormous danger in order to fulfil her mission. But, she says, she also learnt that small acts of kindness can touch the hearts of even battle-hardened rebels.

Researchers have identified changes in the metabolic activity of the gut microbiome associated with exceptional longevity in humans, and found that amplifying the same activity in aged mice using engineered bacteria improved metabolic health.
Published in the journal Cell Metabolism, the team's study suggests that specific age-related changes in the gut microbiome may be protective adaptations rather than signs of decline, and could potentially be harnessed to support healthier aging.
Senior author Amir Zarrinpar, chair in circadian biology and medicine, and professor of medicine at the University of California San Diego, said while many studies on aging focus on what goes wrong as one grows old, the findings suggest "some changes in the gut microbiome may actually represent the body's attempt to preserve metabolic health".
"If we can identify those beneficial functions and safely strengthen them, we may eventually be able to develop new ways to promote healthier aging," Zarrinpar said.
The gut microbiome, the community of bacteria and other microbes living in the digestive tract, is known to change throughout life and plays an important role in metabolism and inflammation, among other aspects of health.
Studies have also found distinctive microbiome features among people who age exceptionally well.
The researchers focused on how gut microbes modify bile acids, substances produced by the liver that help digest fats but also act as signalling molecules in the body.
Studying young and aged mice, they found that aging was associated with an increased microbial activity linked to enzymes called bile salt hydrolases. These enzymes chemically modify bile acids, allowing them to influence pathways involved in metabolism, inflammation and the body's internal clock.
The team also found greater bile acid modification in the mice.
To determine patterns in humans, they reanalysed publicly available data from a human ageing cohort, analysing bile acid measurements from 48 young adults, 107 older adults and 125 centenarians.
The centenarian group showed higher ratios of modified bile acids than both younger groups. An analysis of microbiome data also revealed a greater abundance of a gene associated with bile salt hydrolase activity among centenarians compared with the older adult group.
Further, aged mice -- 82-week-old mice -- were introduced with a strain of bacteria native to the gut engineered to continuously produce bile salt hydrolases.
About 20 weeks after treatment, mice receiving the enzyme-producing bacteria had a significantly improved insulin sensitivity and modestly improved glucose tolerance, compared with mice receiving a non-enzyme-producing bacterium.
By 32 weeks, the treated mice also showed changes consistent with a lower body weight and fat mass and a greater lean mass. Other findings pointed to an increased use of fat for energy, improved mitochondrial function and changes in gene activity related to inflammation and the body's internal clock.

Russian arrested for spying on US defence company Palantir over Ukraine support
- Published
A Russian man has been arrested in California's Silicon Valley for allegedly attempting to spy on employees of a technology and defence firm that supports the Ukrainian military.
Igor D'iu is accused of acting as an agent of a foreign government to conduct a covert operation in Palo Alto, near San Francisco. The BBC understands that the company targeted was Palantir Technologies.
D'iu is also charged with stalking employees and possessing falsified identity documents.
The company is not named in charging documents, but is described as a publicly traded technology and defence company that produces software used by Ukraine in its war with Russia.
"The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian.
"We will not tolerate any efforts - by foreign governments or otherwise - to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations."
Prosecutors say that D'iu entered the US unlawfully via the Mexico border, after travelling there from Istanbul in June.
He was allegedly recruited through the Telegram encrypted messaging app. His handlers referred to Russia as "'the Motherland' and directed D'iu to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine".
On their instruction, he purchased computers, phones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software - tools he needed for his spy mission.
He then went to a coffee shop located near the company's offices in Palo Alto, where he photographed laptop screens of employees who were working there.
His handlers also allegedly "instructed him to position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity".
A source in the industry confirmed that Palantir was targeted, and added that the operation did not penetrate the company's private systems.
They added that the company has been "targeted extensively" by Russia over its involvement in Ukraine, and that the attacks are becoming "increasingly aggressive".
The source, who did not want to be named, said that this was the first time a Russian operative was found while on US soil attempting to spy on the company.
"I think the surprising thing is that they decided to take the risk of sending someone to the US," they said, in an attempt to get into the system "physically".
Palantir has not issued a statement in reaction to the charges.
D'iu also allegedly conducted surveillance of employees and their residences.
On 3 September, he followed a vehicle driven by one senior executive for nearly 30 miles. He fled after she drove to a police station. Police later obtained evidence that he had followed other employees' cars on previous days.
During the investigation, officials discovered identity cards that had been falsified - including a US passport, California ID card, and a Social Security card with the fake name "Hugo Landry Johns".
A raid on his home in October in East Palo Alto turned up two Russian passports, and a handwritten notebook that contained numerous home addresses of employees "family members' names, educational and employment histories, and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses", prosecutors say.
He faces two charges related his alleged work as a foreign agent, one charge of interstate stalking, and one count of fraud related to his identity documents. He faces over 15 years in prison if found guilty.

He has been held in jail since 2 November. It is unclear whether he has hired a lawyer who can speak on his behalf.
Palantir, which was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has interests in US defence and security, and has contracts with the Israeli military.
The arrest comes as espionage allegations roil the US tech industry, amid the news that Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic affair with a woman suspected of spying for China.
Last month, a former OpenAI employee was charged with planting a listening device in a company office. The man was later accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government.

Brussels- A cyberattack using software powered by artificial intelligence targeted the European Union in October, an official in Brussels said on Thursday, with some of the bloc’s digital tools still remaining offline.
The official did not elaborate on the cyberattack or say who could have been behind it. It was the first time the 27-member bloc reported a cyberattack using an AI tool.
“AI-assisted tools can be used and especially misused to detect vulnerabilities,” said Thomas Regnier, spokesperson for the European Commission, the executive body of the EU.
“Indeed, we can confirm that this was done with AI tools,” he added. “We have seen many global cyber attacks recently, and of course no one is immune to this.”
Regnier said the EU first detected the incident on Oct. 22 and that authorities launched an investigation while also imposing “preventative measures.”
“We temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored,” he said.
The investigation is ongoing and so far “we have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting commission staff as a whole,” he said. (AP)

A 10-year-old with a rare inflammatory blood vessel disease underwent surgery at SIMS Hospital, Chennai, to repair a large aneurysm of the aortic arch, the hospital said on Tuesday (November 17, 2026).
The patient was diagnosed with aortoarteritis, also known as Takayasu arteritis, a condition that causes inflammation and narrowing or enlargement of blood vessels. The aneurysm had enlarged significantly, causing breathing difficulty, palpitations, and difficulty lying down. The risk of rupture made urgent surgery necessary. The patient weighed about 18 kg, adding to the technical challenges of the operation. As the aneurysm was located close to the breastbone, opening the chest through the usual approach carried a risk of injuring the enlarged aorta. The surgical team first connected the patient to a heart-lung machine through blood vessels in the groin.
The patient’s body was cooled to 16°C using a technique known as deep hypothermic circulatory arrest. Blood circulation was then temporarily stopped for about 40 minutes, enabling surgeons to remove the affected section of the aorta and replace it with a Dacron graft. Lowering the body temperature reduces metabolic activity and the organs’ oxygen requirements, helping protect them during the period when blood flow is interrupted.
The patient was subsequently rewarmed, restoring his blood circulation. Post-operative assessments showed no damage to the brain, kidneys, intestines, or spinal cord, the hospital said. The patient has resumed normal activities without breathing difficulty but will require continued medication and monitoring to control the underlying inflammation and prevent further aneurysms.
The surgery was performed by a team led by Bashi V. Velayudhan, director and senior consultant, cardiothoracic surgery, along with Mohammed Idhrees, senior consultant, cardiothoracic surgery, and a team of anaesthesiologists and other specialists.

Amid a raging dispute over the India-UK trade pact, India is now imposing an effective duty of 162.5% on bulk Scotch whisky imports, Reuters reported. The development has left thousands of litres of whisky stuck at Indian ports and putting liquor companies in a difficult position despite a trade agreement that was expected to lower import costs.
The India-UK trade agreement, which came into effect in July, reduced tariffs on Scotch whisky from 150% to 75%. The move was expected to benefit companies such as Diageo and Pernod Ricard, which import Scotch in bulk and blend it with other spirits to manufacture popular whisky brands for India's $65 billion liquor market.
The disagreement centres on the customs classification of bulk Scotch whisky and whether it qualifies for the tariff concessions under the India-UK trade agreement.
Under the pact, tariffs on Scotch whisky imports were reduced from 150% to 75%. However, Indian investigators have argued that bulk Scotch concentrates should be classified differently from finished whisky.
According to Reuters, investigators contend that since May, these imports have come under a newly created customs category called "compound alcoholic preparations", which attracts a 150% tariff.
An additional consumption tax takes the effective duty to 162.5%.
Indian authorities have argued that bulk Scotch is merely a raw material used to manufacture blended whisky and other alcoholic beverages, and therefore does not qualify for the reduced tariff under the trade agreement.
Liquor companies, however, disagree with this interpretation. Pernod Ricard, Diageo and several Indian manufacturers believe all Scotch imports, whether bottled or brought in bulk, should attract the concessional 75% tariff under the pact.
The customs classification dispute has left thousands of litres of bulk Scotch in more than 80 shipping containers belonging to Pernod Ricard, Diageo and Bacardi stuck at Indian ports.
While investigations continue, companies can seek provisional release of their consignments by paying duty equivalent to 75% of the goods' value upfront and covering the remaining amount through bank guarantees, Reuters reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Pernod Ricard and Diageo have moved to arrange bank guarantees and other funding to secure the release of their blocked consignments and keep business operations running. Bacardi, meanwhile, was still considering its next steps.
The arrangement is creating additional pressure on companies' working capital. Smaller liquor manufacturers could face greater difficulties in arranging bank guarantees because they may need to provide collateral. These guarantees also have to be reported as contingent liabilities.
Bulk Scotch imports play an important role in India's whisky industry, as they are used by domestic manufacturers to produce Indian-Made Foreign Liquor (IMFL) whisky.
Around 80% of Scotch whisky imports from Britain by volume arrive in bulk, according to Reuters. Most of these imports are used to manufacture blended whisky by mixing Scotch with other spirits and ingredients.
These products are sold at considerably lower prices than fully imported Scotch brands such as Chivas Regal and Johnnie Walker.
This makes the tariff dispute significant for Indian liquor manufacturers as well as international whisky companies. A prolonged disruption in bulk Scotch supplies could affect production requirements and increase costs for manufacturers that depend on these imports.
The UK government has repeatedly said it is working with New Delhi to resolve the disagreement and ensure British businesses can export under the tariffs agreed in the trade deal.
A UK government spokesperson told Reuters that ministers were "urgently working with the government of India to resolve this issue to ensure UK businesses can export under the tariffs agreed in the trade deal".
The Scotch Whisky Association has estimated that Scotch exports to India stood at $335 million in 2024 and forecast that the trade agreement could increase exports by $1.34 billion over five years.

Parents jailed for torture and death of four-year-old girl in France in 1987
- Published
The mother of a four-year-old girl killed in central France and found along a motorway almost 40 years ago has been sentenced to 20 years in prison.
Halima El Bakhti, 72, was found guilty on Tuesday of "torture and acts of barbarity resulting in death without the intent to kill", French media reports.
The girl's father, 74-year-old Ahmed Touloub, was handed a 15-year sentence as an accomplice.
Four-year-old Inass Touloub was found along the A10 road in Suèvres in the Loir-et-Cher department on 11 August 1987. Her body bore multiple marks of abuse, including human bite marks, broken bones and burns with an iron.
She was buried in an unmarked grave near the location where her body was found. Unidentified for three decades, she was known only as the "Little Martyr of the A10".
Then, in 2018, she was identified after the DNA of her brother – tested in an unrelated case – matched with hers, leading to the arrest of their parents.
The trial took place in Loir-et-Cher Assize Court from 2 November, with the verdict delivered on Tuesday after several hours of deliberation.
During the trial, prosecutor Anaïs Allio emphasised that "not a single part of Inass's body was spared", and recalled the "sense of vertigo that overcame us all" upon viewing the "unbearable photographs" from the autopsy, France Info reports.
The jury concluded that the child's mother was suffering from impaired judgement at the time of the girl's death, which reduced the maximum potential sentence.
French media outlet France Info described the two defendants as sitting stoically in chairs before the court with their heads bowed as the reasoning behind the verdict was read out.
El Bakhti and Touloub have 10 days to appeal the verdict.
Inass's death sparked one of France's biggest ever investigations, with the girl's photograph posted in public places and an alert sent to more than 30 countries.

Many social science scholars have argued that nationalist and ethnic feelings would become weaker in the context of developed capitalism and modernity. However, we now know that nationalism continues to remain an implacable force. There is no dearth of literature about what nationalism means and how one makes sense of it. Here, we will look at two forms of nationalism and contextualise it by looking at the changing dynamic of nationalism in India.
Broadly speaking, one can refer to two kinds of nationalisms — civic and ethnic nationalism. The former is based on shared respect for values of liberty, equality, justice and fraternity and an unshakeable faith in the constitutional framework. It is inclusive, progressive, liberating and democratic. It seeks to bring together people who are otherwise extremely diverse in terms of their religions, social practices, languages, food habits, cultures etc. It takes special care to ensure that the marginalised and historically oppressed groups are accommodated within the nationalist framework. It also gives space to every identity to nurture itself unhindered.
On the contrary, ethnic nationalism focuses on essentialising and privileging a single identity via religion, language, or ethnicity and is therefore exclusionary, regressive, destructive and undemocratic. It poses physical and epistemic danger to those identities which do not fall within the dominant understanding of what nationalism is. Hitler clearly espoused ethnic nationalism (the superiority of Germanic Aryan race) which led to unspeakable atrocities being committed against Jews in Nazi-era Germany.
The nationalism that grew in India during the freedom struggle was largely civic in nature. It was an inclusive, liberating, and democratic project. There was a strong conviction that what was being sought was worth fighting for and morally and ethically justified. There was almost a touch of romance; one could not but fall in love with the ideals of justice, equality, freedom and secularism, which were the guiding principles of the nationalism that was experienced during the freedom struggle. It was an open invitation to explore. In this endeavour, science was to be a partner.
When the Constitution, which was a product of reasoned debates and contestations, came into existence, it unleashed enormous democratising possibilities. Its incorporation of fundamental rights and freedoms was a paradigmatic shift in a society which had and still has some of the most oppressive structures in the world such as the caste system. A democratic Constitution could have emerged only in the context of democratic nationalism.

In US, Pak national asks Rahul Gandhi if neighbours can move past ‘blame game’. His reply
Rahul Gandhi said said it was impossible for India to hold talks with Pakistan while innocent people continued to be killed.
India and Pakistan can work together but only if Islamabad stops supporting and encouraging terrorism in India, LoP in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi has said. Interacting with students at the University of Chicago on Wednesday, the Congress leader said it was impossible for India to hold talks with the neighbouring country while innocent people continued to be killed.
Gandhi was responding to a question from a participant who identified himself as a Pakistani national. He asked Gandhi whether the two neighbouring countries could “move beyond the blame game and work together for mutual benefit” without allowing external factors to exploit their differences.
“There is room, but there is a big problem, which is the support and encouragement of terrorism by Pakistan in our country,” Rahul Gandhi said. “And it is impossible for us to accept our innocent people being murdered and having a conversation with Pakistan. So the moment that stops, then a conversation can potentially begin.”
