Rahul Gandhi says India has become a ‘side player’ in global affairs
During the interaction, the Opposition leader also criticised the Narendra Modi government's foreign policy, saying India had become a "side player" in global affairs despite its size and international relationships.
Citing Pakistan's role in facilitating negotiations between the US and Iran, Gandhi said India should have been more actively involved in global discussions.
"India, by its size, naturally has a global voice and India should be actively involved in global conversations. But frankly, India has become a side player," he said. "I'm pretty shocked that Pakistan is busy negotiating with the Iranians and the Americans, and India's just looking," he added.
Pakistan played a key mediating role in the US-Israeli war on Iran that began in February. Islamabad hosted US-Iran talks in April and helped relay proposals between the two sides.
Rahul Gandhi said India should reclaim its historical role in global affairs, recalling its leadership of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM). Founded in 1961, the grouping brought together countries that sought to remain independent of the US- and Soviet-led blocs during the Cold War. India's first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, was among its founding leaders.

On X on Thursday, Gandhi said he was “pretty shocked” that Pakistan was negotiating with Iran and the US while India was “just looking”. He said India had a long history of independent foreign policy and should play an active role in global affairs.
“India has always had a sophisticated geopolitical understanding, right from independence. We had a mind of our own. Our foreign policy was guided by what benefits India,” he said. “By our size, our history and our relationships, we should be involved in these global conversations. But frankly, India has become a side player. We have stepped back from the stage. We have a voice and a view, but that view is missing.”
“There was already pain in India. The Iran war magnified it, pushing people over the edge. We cannot sit in India and remain unconcerned about what is happening in the rest of the world,” the Congress leader added.
Rahul Gandhi questions Modi's foreign policy
The Congress leader also questioned PM Modi's approach to foreign policy and said international relations should not depend on friendships between political leaders.
"Friendship is not the point. Who gives a damn about friendship? Do you really think that geopolitics is going to work because the guy is your friend? He's leading a structure. He's got a whole economic system under him. He's not going to make decisions based on whether he likes you or doesn't like you. So these are some of the things that disturb me," Gandhi said.
He clarified that he had no objection to leaders maintaining friendly relations but said understanding geopolitical realities and India's position in the world was more important.
"I don't have a problem with being friends with Mr Modi or being friends with leaders. Friendship is not that important. What's important is that you understand what's going on, who you are, and where you fit," he said.

Gandhi also spoke about the changing global security order, saying the next global architecture would involve several major powers and civilisations rather than being shaped by the West alone.
"The next global architecture will not be built by one civilisation alone. It will be shaped by multiple civilisations, with America, China, India, the Middle East and Russia all having a role to play," he said.

Staying fit and managing her health require constant attention to sleep, diet and exercise, she says. “It is tough to stay fit. Managing her condition requires constant vigilance.

ByShadab Khan
Srinagar- More than three decades after India amended its Constitution to strengthen village and municipal governments, a fundamental question remains: How much power do elected local representatives actually have?
Prof. M. Aslam, former vice-chancellor of Indira Gandhi National Open University, raised that question during a national seminar in Tirupati on Wednesday, pointing to the financial and administrative constraints that continue to limit grassroots democracy.
The seminar, organised by the Academy of Grassroots Studies and Research of India, examined the challenges facing local self-governance, with particular attention to the Devolution Index and finances. Prof. Aslam’s central argument was clear: India’s Panchayati Raj institutions need money, trained personnel and greater authority to fulfill the responsibilities voters expect them to perform.
The Ministry of Panchayati Raj’s Devolution Index, he said, provides an honest measure of how much power states have transferred to local governments. It examines six areas: institutional framework, functions, finances, functionaries, capacity building and accountability.
Finance, however, remains the weakest link in the decentralisation process.
Gram Panchayats have several potential sources of revenue, including property taxes, user charges, fees and income from common property resources. Many underuse these sources because elected representatives fear that collecting taxes could cost them votes.
That reluctance has consequences for accountability. Panchayats that depend heavily on government grants have limited financial freedom to decide their priorities, Aslam argued.
“A Panchayat that does not collect its own revenue will never be truly accountable to its own people,” he said, urging elected representatives to change their approach to taxation.
Government grants create another challenge. Finance Commission transfers remain essential to village development, but delays, restrictive conditions and utilisation certificate requirements make planning difficult.
A Sarpanch, the professor said, cannot plan a five-year term when funds arrive during the final three months of a financial year.
Even when money reaches Panchayats, shortages of trained accountants, engineers and technical staff often prevent them from spending it effectively. Inadequate digital infrastructure compounds the problem, leaving funds unused or causing them to lapse.
Prof. Aslam called for a dedicated cadre of Panchayat finance professionals, arguing that local governments need trained personnel rather than temporary administrative arrangements.
His proposed reforms extend to the structure of local governance itself. He urged governments to clearly map responsibilities, specifying who performs a function, who pays for it and who answers for its execution. He also called for trained secretaries, accountants and technical staff under the control of local bodies.
State Finance Commissions, he said, should be constituted on time, their reports tabled and their recommendations implemented. Digital Panchayats could improve budgeting, accounting, asset mapping and social audits, strengthening transparency in public spending.
He also called for stronger Gram Sabhas, describing them as the Parliament of the village. Participatory planning, social audits and citizen charters, he said, should give residents a greater role in decisions affecting their communities.
The seminar brought together former government officials, academics and public policy experts. S.M. Vijayanand, former chief secretary of Kerala and former Union secretary for Panchayati Raj and rural development, inaugurated the event. Former chief election commissioner T.S. Krishna Murthy and former Andhra Pradesh High Court judge G. Yethirajulu attended the inaugural session.
AGRASRI founder director D. Sundar Ram moderated the proceedings, highlighting the organisation’s 25 years of work in rural governance through research, training, education and advocacy.
Prof. Aslam framed local self-governance as a democratic commitment to giving people in India’s remotest villages the authority to decide their futures.
The challenge, he said, is to make Panchayats and municipalities genuine institutions of self-governance in the Gandhian sense.

Listed non-banking financial company (NBFC) Mufin Green Finance’s board has approved the acquisition of a 23% stake in insurtech startup BimaPay for a ₹65.8 Cr in an all-cash deal. Mufin Green Finance said that it expects to complete the transaction in the next three to four months, subject to the execution of definitive agreements and relevant regulatory approvals. It is pertinent to note that BimaPay operates under the umbrella of the broader Mufin Group. “.... With an RBI-registered NBFC as a shareholder, we can build products around how lending actually works rather than adapt them later,” said BimaPay cofounder and CEO Hanut Mehta. In a statement, Mufin said that he proposed investment will leverage synergies between the two entities and support the joint development and scaling of premium financing solutions. The transaction will look to combine the listed NBFC’s lending expertise with BimaPay’s tech solutions. “... An ownership stake lets us plan product, data and integration roadmaps over years instead of project cycles, which is what a lender growing at our pace needs,” added Mufin Green Finance managing director Kapil Garg said. The deal is a related-party transaction as Bimapay is a promoter-group subsidiary of Mufin, the listed NBFC said. Founded in 2022 by Mehta, Mohit Gupta and Kapil Garg, BimaPay facilitates financing solutions to enable individuals and businesses to pay insurance premiums in EMIs instead of upfront lump sums. It also works with lending partners and insurers to develop technology-enabled solutions. The startup last raised $2 Mn in an undisclosed funding round led by LC Nueva Investment Partners in 2024. On the financial front BimaPay reported revenue of ₹9.9 Cr in the fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26), up 203% from ₹3.2 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. According to Mufin Green Finance, the startup also reported a profit before tax (PBT) of ₹1.1 Cr in FY26. BimaPay operates at the intersection of lending tech and insurtech. The two segments are seeing healthy growth on the back of rising smartphone adoption, expanding credit and the rise of AI-driven distribution solutions. According to Inc42 data, the Indian insurtech market is projected to become a $307 Bn opportunity by 2030.

Listed insurtech giant PB Fintech’s cofounder Alok Bansal is stepping down as the executive vice-chairman and whole-time director of the company. In a statement, the company said that Bansal’s tenure will expire on March 31, 2027. PB Fintech also said that he will be appointed as a non-executive director on the company’s board starting April 1, 2027, subject to shareholder approval. In his resignation letter, Bansal cited his “personal desire” to step down from executive responsibilities as the reason for his departure. “PB Fintech and Policybazaar would not have been possible without Alok. He first shared his wish to step back five years ago, and I persuaded him to stay because I needed his support. I still do, and I am glad he will remain on our Board, while I understand his wish to step away from the day-to-day…,” said PB Fintech cofounder and CEO Yashish Dahiya. Reminiscing on his 18 year-long tenure at the company, Bansal said, “... Founders are lucky to get most of the credit and sometimes, a few brickbats as well, but the reality is that it takes the collective energies of the team to build something meaningful. PB Fintech has achieved far greater scale than I ever imagined, thanks entirely to the dedication of our team, the trust of our customers, and the support of our investors and partners”. An alumnus of IIM Calcutta, Bansal previously served at companies like Voltas, General Electric and Mahindra & Mahindra. He eventually cofounded Policybazaar (later PB Fintech) with Dahiya in 2008. Over his nearly two decades stint at the company, he oversaw the company’s rise into a multi-vertical insurtech company that closed Q2 FY27 with a net profit of ₹192.4 Cr and an operating revenue of ₹2,177.7 Cr. In a statement, the startup said that he was central to the company's strategy, fundraising and investor relations, especially during its public listing in 2021. The development comes amid a broader wave of cofounders quitting their startups and venture capital (VC) firms. Earlier this month, Unacademy Gaurav Munjal said that he was stepping down as the CEO of the edtech platform. Prior to this, Fireside Ventures’ cofounder and partner Vinay Singh also announced his departure from the investment firm after a nearly decade-long stint. In June this year, cofounders Hari Menon and Vipul Parekh stepped down from their executive roles at the Tata Digital-owned BigBasket. In the same month, fintech platform Setu’s cofounder Nikhil Kumar resigned from the day-to-day operations of the Pine Labs-owned platform. In April, used car marketplace Cars24’s cofounder and chief marketing officer (CMO) Gajendra Jangid also resigned from his executive role at the startup.

My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
- Published
When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.
They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.
"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.
But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.
This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.
Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.
Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.
After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.
"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.
The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.
The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.
After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.
Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.
This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.
After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.
This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre.
"She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.
Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.
He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.
"The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.
In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.
Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified.
"I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.
Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.
The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.
However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged.
"We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.
For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.
He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.
Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns.
"We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.
They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola.
Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.
After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust.
"I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact."
During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.
But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.
Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says.
"Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".
He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.
But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.
Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.
He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."
He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing.
"The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.
The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.
Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease.
"Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."

Survivors of Uganda's deadly landslide seek justice at the UN
- Published
Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.
The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides.
Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods.
The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.
The landslide struck Bududa in 2019, killing more than 53 people, including 33 children. Years later, survivors say every spell of heavy rain brings back fears of another tragedy.
William Tsama, one of the claimants, lost four members of his family members.
"My quest should be a lesson," he said.
"Victims in such situations, ignored by governments, can take them to court to compel them to help their citizens."
Uganda introduced a resettlement plan for landslide-prone areas in 2011, but progress has been limited, with relatively few people relocated.
Last month, it launched a new resettlement programme offering affected households 18 million Ugandan shillings ($4,300) to help them move to safer areas.
But some survivors have questioned whether the amount is enough to cover the cost of relocating and rebuilding their lives.
Under the programme, families can choose between receiving two acres of land, valued at 8 million shillings ($1,900), plus 10 million shillings (about $2,400) towards building a house, or taking the equivalent land allowance in cash, alongside the same housing grant.
The scheme is expected to benefit 1,410 households identified as living in high-risk areas.
The government has now given residents of designated high-risk areas two months, from November to December, to leave or face forced eviction.
The threat extends beyond landslides. The complainants say changing rainfall patterns and declining soil fertility have also affected farming, leaving many families struggling to secure their livelihoods.
"I want to get a new good place for my people, so even if I die, they will be okay. I am an old man, but I am doing it for my children," Tsama said.
The survivors first launched legal action in 2020 in Uganda, and received support from Ugandan environmental organisation Greenwatch three years later.
They are seeking compensation for lost family members and livelihoods, as well as emergency measures, including accessible early-warning systems in high-risk areas.
Greenwatch Executive Director Samantha Atukunda Kakuru Mwesigwa said the case is about changing how governments prepare and respond to climate-related disasters.
"Justice for claimants is not just about winning in court. It is about forcing government policy to keep pace with a changing climate, and ensuring loss and damage is no longer an afterthought in disaster management," she said.
The threat of climate-related disasters extends across East Africa.
In Kenya, floods and landslides killed at least 181 people between March and May 2024, according to the Kenya Red Cross. In Rwanda, floods and landslides killed 135 people in May 2023.
The dangers are also being felt further afield. In October 2026, a flash flood swept through Nepal's Gorkha district after a landslide blocked a river, washing away homes and infrastructure, and killing over 1,500 people.
"Disasters like the one in Bududa are only getting worse because of climate change – and they are happening all around the world, as we've seen recently and tragically in Nepal," ClientEarth lawyer Vesselina Newman said.
She said poorer countries, which have contributed relatively little to global emissions, are bearing some of the heaviest consequences of climate change and need greater financial support.
"High income countries must provide financial assistance and ensure that sufficient money goes directly to countries like Uganda, so they can roll out life-saving adaptation measures," she said.
The complainants say relocation must involve more than move people out of danger.
They want the government to protect their livelihoods, respect their land rights, and take account of individual needs.
The case is now before the United Nations Human Rights Committee, which will ask the Ugandan government to respond within six months.

In an intensive care unit, every second matters. A critically ill patient may be connected to several devices, including patient monitors, ventilators and infusion pumps, while laboratory systems and electronic health records continuously generate additional information. Together, these systems create a large and rapidly-changing picture of the patient’s condition. However, when the information remains fragmented across devices and platforms, clinicians may spend valuable time locating, verifying and reconciling data before they can act.
This makes interoperability a clinical priority in critical care, not simply an information technology requirement. Integration enables systems to exchange data, but true interoperability ensures that the information being exchanged is accurate, interpretable and clinically relevant. This can help care teams coordinate and prioritise interventions more effectively while reducing the need to move between multiple systems to assemble a clinical picture.

Premier League board members have reportedly been given additional legal protection amid the threat of action linked to Manchester City’s financial-rules case.
City is still waiting to discover its punishment after being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League regulations by an independent commission.
Eighteen of the 20 Premier League clubs are understood to have supported changes to the league’s articles at a meeting in London on Thursday, which extend protections provided to individual board members to enable them to freely carry out their duties.
The change comes after City sponsor Etihad said in September that it was considering legal action over the “damaging” implications of the commission’s guilty verdict against the club.
The airline was not named in the verdict, which found City had benefited from “sham” arrangements to inflate revenue and disguise costs to avoid breaching Premier League and UEFA rules.
City, England’s dominant club for more than a decade, has repeatedly denied wrongdoing and have appealed against the verdict.
Another City sponsor, Etisalat, was reported by the Times to be considering similar action earlier this week.

Ghana's new $60m presidential jet sparks public outrage
- Published
Ghana's government has defended its purchase of a new presidential jet amid criticism over its cost, as many citizens continue to struggle with the high cost of living.
The $60m (£46m) French-made Falcon 6X has sparked a political row, with opposition politicians accusing President John Mahama's administration of misplaced priorities.
But the government says the purchase is justified, arguing that Ghana's improving economy makes the aircraft affordable and is needed to replace an ageing presidential jet.
The controversy comes as Mahama's administration seeks to demonstrate an economic recovery after years of financial difficulties that forced Ghana to seek IMF assistance.
- Can Ghana's new president meet the voters' high expectations? 
  - Published7 January 2025
Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.
Parliament approved its purchase last December as part of a broader programme to modernise Ghana's military aviation fleet, which also includes four helicopters from Airbus.
The jet was welcomed with a water salute on Monday, but its arrival triggered criticism online and among opposition politicians over the cost and timing of the purchase.
While in the opposition, Mahama himself opposed buying a new presidential jet, prompting questions about why his administration has now gone head with the purchase.
Opposition MP Samuel Abu Jinapor questioned the government's priorities, saying the expenditure came at a time when many Ghanaians continue to struggle with the cost of living and youth unemployment remained alarmingly high.
"What was unacceptable in opposition cannot suddenly become acceptable in government merely because the occupants of power have changed," Jinapor added.
He accused the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) of hypocrisy, recalling how its senior figures had strongly opposed proposals for a new presidential aircraft when they were in opposition.
Jinapor also called for greater transparency over the procurement process, how the purchase was financed and the government's justification for the expenditure.
The purchase has also prompted sharp criticism on social media, with some users arguing the money could have been spent on more pressing public needs.
"This money can employ over 100,000 nurses and 200,000 teachers," an X user posted.
But the government has rejected the criticism, saying Ghana's economic circumstances have changed considerably since the NDC opposed a similar purchase.
Peter Lanchene Toobu, chairman of parliament's defence committee, said the party had never opposed acquiring a presidential jet in principle.
Its objection, he said, had been on the timing when Ghana was experiencing severe economic difficulties.
"We agreed in principle that we needed to purchase a new presidential jet," he said.
He argued, however, that Ghana could not justify the expenditure at a time when it was seeking a $3bn bailout from the IMF.
"The strength and macroeconomic stability of this country have enhanced our status in the sense that imports have become cheaper, and this is the right time," he added.
Toobu said the government had purchased the aircraft without borrowing, citing a stronger Ghanaian currency and improved economic conditions.
Government spokesperson Kwakye Ofosu also dismissed suggestions that the purchase was a misplaced priority.
He pointed to falling prices of construction materials and lower borrowing costs as evidence of the country's improved economic situation.
"When I was campaigning in 2024, and I was donating cement, it cost 115 cedis (£7.5) a bag. Today, for 80 cedis, you will get a bag of cement," he told JoyNews.
The controversy has also extended to the aircraft's interior, following claims that it has a dedicated bedroom and bathroom.
But Ofosu dismissed claims that the jet had such luxury facilities, saying the president has no intention of "bathing in the air".
"There certainly is no bathroom. President Mahama has no intention of bathing in the air," Ofosu said.
He explained that the jet has reclining seats that can be converted into sleeping arrangements but denied that it has a dedicated bedroom.
The government says the new jet will replace the 16-year-old Falcon 900EX, which has suffered recurring maintenance problems, including corrosion and leakages in its fuel tank.
The older jet was reportedly grounded in France for several months in 2025 while undergoing repairs.
Officials say the Falcon 6X has a longer flying range, reducing the need for refuelling stops on international trips and improving the reliability of presidential travel.
Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin, an economist at the University of Ghana said that while the president's safety was paramount, the timing of the purchase was difficult to justify amid severe austerity measures, high unemployment and widespread infrastructure challenges.
"The timing makes it a bit difficult to understand," he told the BBC, adding that the government should provide a cost-benefit analysis explaining why buying the jet was preferable to leasing one and how the decision serves Ghana's interests.

Footage shows derailed carriages after fatal train crash in Egypt
A train collision has killed at least seven people and injured dozens in northern Egypt.
Footage showed multiple overturned carriages and dozens of people surrounding them.
One train was travelling from Giza to the Fayoum oasis, south west of Cairo, while the other was heading from Cairo to Aswan in the south.
It is yet unclear what caused the accident but Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said an investigation was underway and would "hold accountable anyone who proves their negligence".

NEW DELHI: The Income Tax Department cannot tax a Mauritius-based investor's gains from selling equity mutual-fund units by treating them as gains from the sale of the underlying Indian shares, the Delhi High Court has ruled. The judgment, in favour of Emerging India Focus Funds, settles a ₹593.48 crore tax dispute over the treatment of such gains under the India-Mauritius tax treaty. A bench of Justices Subramonium Prasad and Renu Bhatnagar, in its 17 November judgment, rejected the department's argument that gains from mutual-fund units should be treated as gains from the sale of the Indian shares held by those funds. The court held that the fund owned mutual-fund units, not shares in the Indian companies held by the mutual funds. Gains from selling those units, therefore, could not be treated as gains from selling shares under the India-Mauritius tax treaty. “A unit holder of a mutual fund is, therefore, not a shareholder of the company. The unit holder only holds a unit in a fund which invests in shares or in any other securities,” the judgment notes. Emerging India Focus Funds is a Mauritius-based company registered as a foreign institutional investor with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi). It collects money from investors globally and invests it in Sebi-registered mutual funds. For assessment year 2022-23, Emerging India Focus Funds reported ₹593.48 crore in capital gains from selling units of equity-oriented mutual funds. It claimed the gains were not taxable in India under the India-Mauritius Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA). The Income Tax Department, however, argued that Emerging India Focus Funds had invested in mutual funds that put at least 65% of their money into Indian shares. When the fund sold its mutual-fund units at a profit, the department contended, the gains were linked to the Indian shares held by those funds. The tax officer consequently treated 65% of the ₹593.48 crore gain, or ₹385.76 crore, as taxable in India. The dispute then went to the Dispute Resolution Panel (DRP), which reviews taxpayers' objections to proposed tax assessments. The DRP agreed with the department that the mutual-fund units could be treated like shares for this purpose. It went a step further, however, holding that the entire ₹593.48 crore gain, rather than ₹385.76 crore, was taxable in India. Emerging India Focus Funds challenged the DRP's decision before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT). In June 2025, the ITAT ruled in favour of the fund, holding that mutual-fund units are distinct from shares. It said gains from selling those units could not be taxed under the treaty provision dealing with gains from the sale of shares. The Income Tax Department subsequently challenged the ITAT's decision before the Delhi High Court. The high court upheld the tribunal's view, holding that the treaty specifically covers gains from the sale of shares. It does not permit the department to look through mutual-fund units to the shares held by the fund and treat the sale of units as a sale of those shares. India and Mauritius signed the DTAA in 1982, and it came into force in 1983. The treaty determines which country has the right to tax income and capital gains arising from cross-border investments. Mauritius remains a major investment route into India. Between January 2000 and December 2025, it accounted for $185.21 billion, or 23.82% of India's cumulative foreign direct investment (FDI) equity inflows, making it the second-largest source after Singapore, according to government data. The sandpaper plot - who was there, who said what?
- Published
The sandpaper scandal, one of the biggest controversies in the history of Test cricket, continues to engulf Australian sport.
Fresh evidence from Cameron Bancroft - the culprit of the ball-tampering in South Africa in 2018 - has heaped pressure on Australia captain Pat Cummins, former coach Darren Lehmann and Cricket Australia.
In a detailed account of more than 4,000 words published in the West Australian newspaper, Bancroft alleges all the Australia players and coaches present in Cape Town eight years ago knew of the plot.
Bancroft's explosive testimony supports claims made by Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Chadd Sayers.
However, Cummins denied Khawaja's version of events in his own extraordinary news conference in Sydney last week. Cummins spoke to the media for 68 minutes in an address broadcast on live television.
Here, BBC Sport collects the most recent accounts of players and coaches involved in the saga that became widely known as sandpapergate.
Usman Khawaja
Batter Khawaja played all four Tests in South Africa and a total of 88 for Australia before retiring from international cricket earlier this year.
Revelations in his autobiography reignited debate around the sandpaper scandal and made headlines across the globe.
"It was all of us," Khawaja said. "Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.
"In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now.
"Even in the change rooms when I was talking to them after the game. I said, 'Take this as a team'.
"We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team, and so I was always of that stance."
- Whole Australia team knew of sandpaper use - Khawaja 
  - Published6 November
David Warner
Warner was Australia's opening batter and vice-captain during the 2018 series. He, along with captain Steve Smith and Bancroft, were the three players punished for the ball-tampering.
The Cricket Australia (CA) investigation in 2018 found Warner developed the plan and that he instructed Bancroft to carry out the cheating.
After serving his ban, Warner returned to play a further 133 times for Australia across formats, including three Ashes series and the 2023 World Cup win. He retired from international cricket in 2024.
In response to Khawaja's book, Warner said: "I thank you for what you've done. It's 100% accurate what you've said. Now everyone knows the truth."
He also accused Cricket Australia of a cover-up, describing the CA investigation as "rushed" and botched".
"As far as l am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," Warner said.
"If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?"
- Warner accuses Cricket Australia of 'cover-up' 
  - Published4 days ago
Pat Cummins
The Cape Town Test was the 13th of Cummins' Test career. A key bowler, he would go on to be named Australia's Test captain in 2021. It is a position he still holds.
Prior to Khawaja's book, Cummins and the other bowlers from Cape Town - Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon - had always denied knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper.
In an extraordinary news conference last week, Cummins called Khawaja's claims that the whole team knew about the plan "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense".
"I said that consistently for the last eight years," Cummins said. "I did not know that was happening.
"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."
Asked if he knew of any plans at any stage to tamper with the ball during the series against South Africa, Cummins said: "No."
Cummins also said he did not remember a meeting where Khawaja had called on the team to take collective responsibility - something his former team-mate claimed.
Cameron Bancroft
Opening batter Bancroft was playing his eighth Test in Cape Town, aged 25. He was the player caught using sandpaper on the field.
He played another two Tests after serving his ban and is still playing for Western Australia. He turns 34 this week.
In 2021, Bancroft said it was "self-explanatory" whether the bowlers knew of the plan, and on Wednesday he backed Khawaja's account, saying Cummins' news conference made him "feel angry, betrayed and alone".
Like Khawaja, Bancroft said sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa – the match before he was caught - and also said he had conversations with the Australia seamers about whether the ball was "swinging enough".
He said the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper. He also claimed that coach Lehmann and bowling coach David Saker were present in the initial discussions and that Bancroft's role was also discussed in a team meeting before day three.
In an account published by the West Australian on Wednesday, Bancroft wrote: "All the bowlers gave me feedback if my work on the ball was working. It was helpful.
"Is it going yet? It's not going yet, it needs more. So I would use the sandpaper more on the ball.
"There was even a time I was told to stop out of fear what I was doing was becoming too obvious."
- Bancroft sandpaper claims heap pressure on Cummins 
  - Published9 hours ago
Darren Lehmann
Lehmann was Australia coach at the time of the scandal. He was cleared by the CA investigation and said he had "no prior knowledge" of the plan to ball-tamper.
He resigned after the series and has been Northamptonshire coach since the start of the 2025 English season.
After Khawaja's revelations, Lehmann said: "I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball-tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years."
After Cricket Australia said it would hold an open forum, Lehmann said he has "nothing to hide".
Speaking on radio coverage of the third one-day international against England after Bancroft's account was published, Lehmann said: "I need to sit back, process it and work through each allegation.
"That's what I'll be doing over the next few days.
"I need to have a really good read of it. I need to make sure I'm saying what I want to say."
Steve Smith
Smith, one of the greatest batters of his generation, was Australia's captain at the time of the scandal.
After serving a 12-month ban, he returned for the World Cup and Ashes the following year and has stood in as captain at times since.
He was found to have been aware of the plan to cheat and to mislead the public and match officials.
Smith, who broke down in tears when apologising at a subsequent news conference, as cameras captured the emotional toll of the moment, has not spoken publicly since Khawaja's book was published.
Speaking about the episode in September this year, he said: "That was a traumatic experience in my life and when I hear the flash of a camera it makes me revisit that in a way.
"I've tried to kind of erase a lot of 2018 and what happened. I can't remember a lot about the series. I've tried to block most of it out of my memory bank."
Mitchell Marsh
Marsh was bowling when Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball in Cape Town. As an all-rounder, he was not part of the 2021 bowlers' statement.
Marsh was captain during Australia's recent ODI series against England and refused to answer questions on the topic before the series opener.
"I am not here to share mine [story] today," he said.
"I respect Uzzie [Khawaja] has told his story; my focus is on tomorrow. I am not here to go back on South Africa."
Following the conclusion of the series, Marsh did not take part in his post-match news conference, with 26-year-old bowler Jack Edwards taking his place.
Tim Paine
Paine was Australia's wicketkeeper during the South Africa series and was made captain when Smith was banned.
He served in the role until he stood down in 2021 over a historical investigation into sexually explicit text messages sent to a female colleague.
In his autobiography, Paine said the suggestion everyone in the Australia dressing room must have known about the sandpaper use is "rubbish" and claimed he first found out when images appeared on the big screen in Cape Town.
"Everyone out there was shocked when they looked up on the big screen and saw Cameron Bancroft with a piece of sandpaper in his hand," Paine wrote. "I was stunned. We all were.
"My heart sank, I was thinking, 'What the f***?' A sense of dread came over us all."
Bancroft said he discussed whether the ball was reversing with Paine during the second Test.
David Saker
Saker was Australia's bowling coach during the South Africa series.
Bancroft alleged Saker was present for discussions about the use of sandpaper and told the batter he needed to do more to the ball.
Saker was also England bowling coach as recently as last month's tri-series in Pakistan. He was an influential part of England's 2010-11 Ashes win.
In 2021, reflecting on the sandpaper saga, Saker said: "Obviously a lot of things went wrong at that time. There was a lot of people to blame. It could have been me to blame, it could have been someone else. It could have been stopped and it wasn't, which is unfortunate.
"Cameron's a very nice guy. He's just doing it to get something off his chest… He's not going to be the last. You could point your finger at me, you could point your finger at Boof [Lehmann]. Could you point it at other people? Of course you could.
"The disappointing thing is it's never going to go away. Regardless of what's said. We all know that we made a monumental mistake. The gravity wasn't as plain until it all came out."
Mitchell Starc
Starc was an integral part of the vaunted Australia attack in Cape Town and remains so in the present day. He is ranked as the number one bowler in Test cricket by the International Cricket Council.
Left-armer Starc repeatedly denied knowledge of the sandpaper plot, including in the statement released with Cummins, Hazlewood and Lyon in 2021, and in a news conference in the days after Khawaja's claims emerged.
Speaking on 10 November, Starc said: "Obviously, there's differing opinions of eight years ago. We were heavily grilled through the process at the time, and since, and I guess I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers, but where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed. My recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.
"I'll stick to what I said five years ago, what I said at the time, eight years ago. Clearly, there's different versions from different people, and I'll leave it where I left it back then."
Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon
Along with Cummins and Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon have remained part of Australia's first-choice bowling unit in the eight years since the sandpaper scandal, forming one of the greatest four-man attacks in Test history.
Seamer Hazlewood and off-spinner Lyon joined Cummins and Starc in releasing a statement in 2021, responding to an interview given by Bancroft to the Guardian newspaper when he said the bowlers' involvement in the sandpaper plot was "self-explanatory".
Neither Hazlewood nor Lyon has spoken publicly since the fresh claims from Khawaja, Warner and Bancroft emerged.
Their statement released with Cummins and Starc in 2021 said: "We pride ourselves on our honesty. So it's been disappointing to see that our integrity has been questioned by some journalists and past players in recent days in regard to the Cape Town Test of 2018.
"We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands.
"We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. It has gone on too long and it is time to move on."
Chadd Sayers and Jon Holland
A swing bowler, Sayers played his only Test for Australia after the sandpaper controversy erupted – the fourth and final match of the series against South Africa in Johannesburg.
Sayers, who retired from first-class cricket in 2021, spoke to Australian radio station SEN in the aftermath of Khawaja's claims, to corroborate the former batter's account.
Sayers claimed to have removed sandpaper from the field in the second Test against South Africa, the match before Bancroft was caught. He also backed up Khawaja's assertion that the entire Australia squad discussed the sandpaper issue after it was revealed in Cape Town.
Speaking on 15 November, Sayers said: "I am comfortable sitting here that I believe everyone in that side knew what was going on and what was being used.
"It was used in two Test matches and there were discussions in the changing rooms.
"After the occurrence in Cape Town, we all sat in the changing rooms after that day's play and, probably for 60 to 90 minutes, we talked about what had happened and I guess where to next."
Spinner Holland, who retired in 2021, was also a back-up bowler on the trip.
He also said there was a meeting held in the fallout from Cape Town about players taking responsibility.
"Once we got back to the hotel we did sit as a group [to discuss] what had happened and who was going to take the blame," Holland told newspaper The Australian.
"To Davey's [Warner's] credit, from what I remember, he did put his hand up and say he would take some of the responsibility, but not all of it.
"To be sitting there and seeing three blokes hung out to dry when you are supposed to be part of a team was a pretty hard watch."
- Australia's Sayers 'took sandpaper from field' 
  - Published3 days ago
Peter Handscomb
Batter Handscomb was Australia's 12th man on the day Bancroft was caught, making frequent trips between the field and the dressing room.
Bancroft's account alleges Handscomb was told by Lehmann, via walkie-talkie, to "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now".
Last week, following Khawaja's claims but before Bancroft spoke, Handscomb was asked for his recollections after making a century for Victoria in the Sheffield Shield against Western Australia.
On 11 November, Handscomb said: "I appreciate you have to ask these questions. I've had a nice day today, it's not really something that I want to comment on right now. I'll sort of just let the powers of be do their thing."
Graeme Hick
Former England batter Hick was part of the Australia backroom team on the South Africa tour of 2018.
Hick was made redundant by Cricket Australia as part of a series of cost-cutting measures in 2020.
Speaking to the Sydney Morning Herald last week, Hick said: "I have seen the various statements around the coaches, and I'm very disappointed with the broad nature of them.
"Khawaja puts it simply: 'It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us'. To me, what Khawaja is implying here is absolutely false.
"In regard to any discussions around the ball-tampering in Port Elizabeth or Cape Town, I will say in true honesty that I did not hear or know anything.
"My first knowledge of all this was, like many, when it appeared on the big screen in Cape Town as I was sat on the outside balcony at the time."

With the Air Quality Index (AQI) crossing 400 at some locations in Delhi, people whose work keeps them outdoors for long hours say they are experiencing breathing difficulties, persistent cough, headaches and burning eyes, often without adequate protection against pollution.
For traffic police personnel, domestic workers, roadside vendors, mechanics and gig workers, staying indoors is rarely an option.
Yogendra Kumar, a traffic inspector posted in outer north Delhi, said pollution-related health risks for traffic personnel persists throughout the year but increases significantly when air quality deteriorates.
“The impact on health is inevitable in the outskirts, as road dust also contributes to pollution alongside emissions. We have no safeguards apart from masks. Prolonged exposure causes breathing problems and a persistent cough,” he said.
Reena Chaudhary, a domestic worker in Palam Colony, said she began experiencing breathing difficulties on the night before Deepavali, with her symptoms worsening on the festival day.
“I leave home around 7 a.m. and return by 9 p.m. I began having headaches and burning eyes the day before Deepavali, particularly while passing through smoke-filled lanes between houses at night. On Deepavali, my condition worsened. I felt dizzy throughout the day, had a persistent cough and just wanted to lie down. But who would work if I did?” she said.
Ms. Chaudhary said she had to walk through smoke on Deepavali night with her dupatta wrapped around her face. Since then, she has been taking her daughter along in case she falls ill and is unable to work.
Ravi, a 21-year-old gig worker who attends college during the day, said he works through the night, picking up rides across the city to support his family.
“Even at night, I can see that the air is dense and heavy. At times, I have to stop near a green area, such as Vande Mataram Marg, just to be able to breathe,” he said.
Mukesh Yadav, an e-rickshaw driver in Palam, said road dust remains a problem throughout the year, apart from smoke from firecrackers and vehicular emissions.
“The area remains dusty even on normal days. Since Deepavali, I have been tying a towel around my face,” he said.
Mr. Yadav works eight to 10 hours a day, making several trips between Palam metro station and Kailashpuri, a one-kilometre stretch that witnesses heavy traffic.
“The only time I am not outdoors is when I am charging my e-rickshaw. I thought my cough was due to the cold, but everyone seems to be coughing, even the passengers. It could be due to pollution,” he said.
‘Pollution higher this year’
An analysis by the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) found that Delhi’s average PM2.5 concentration in the week preceding Deepavali reached 236 micrograms per cubic metre, the highest in three years. This was 97% higher than the 120 micrograms per cubic metre recorded in 2025 and 32% above the 179 micrograms per cubic metre recorded in 2024.
The study also found that time-bound restrictions on vehicles had failed to ease traffic congestion, with nitrogen dioxide, a marker of vehicular pollution, accumulating during the evening and remaining elevated until midnight, even after traffic had eased.
“Deepavali pollution is an annual tipping point, but elevated particulate levels before the festival this year show that baseline pollution is higher than in previous years,” said Anumita Roychowdhury, executive director (research and advocacy) at the CSE.
She said cleaner air ahead of winter and measures to contain episodic pollution spikes from farm fires and firecrackers could have prevented such severe pollution during seasonal weather changes.

AMRITSAR: As Sonia Gandhi’s memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, brings renewed attention to her personal journey and family history, a Sikh man has an unusual connection to her past.Sukhdev Singh Kang claims to have purchased the Maino family's ancestral home in Italy, which he says is Sonia Gandhi’s birthplace. Born on December 9, 1946, the former Congress president spent her early years in the Italian village, and Kang is now preparing to convert the six-room property into a museum dedicated to her family and early life.
Sonia Gandhi's birth home, a six-room building situated in Italy
Located in Lusiana, a village in Italy’s Vicenza province in the Veneto region, the house has gradually emerged as a point of interest for visitors, particularly from India. Kang has put up a board outside the property identifying it as the “Indian House, Place of Birth, 9 December 1946, Sonia Gandhi”.
Kang, who lives with his wife, son and daughter in Brescia, about an hour’s drive from Lusiana, said he purchased the property in 2020 but declined to disclose its price. He said the family had decided to convert it into a museum and had now obtained the necessary permissions to take the project forward. With Sonia Gandhi’s memoir drawing public attention to her personal journey, he feels this is the right time to develop the property as a museum.
Living room of Sonia Gandhi's ancestral home
“We want to meet Sonia Gandhi and her children, Rahul and Priyanka, to learn more about the family’s story and understand which personal belongings and other articles could be displayed in the museum. We want visitors to get a glimpse of her family background and early life,” Kang told TOI during his visit to Amritsar on Thursday.Born into an ordinary family in Lusiana, Sonia Gandhi’s journey has been extraordinary. Kang said her father, Stefano Maino, was a mason and building contractor, and there was little in her early life to suggest that she would one day emerge as one of the most influential women in Indian politics.From a modest Italian village, she went on to marry Rajiv Gandhi, become the wife of a Prime Minister, and eventually lead the Indian National Congress, one of the world's largest political parties. Her association with the Nehru-Gandhi family placed her at the centre of one of India's most influential political dynasties, marking a remarkable journey from a small-town upbringing to the corridors of power.
Sonia Gandhi's childhood home has been a point of conversation for the villagers and has also invited tourism interest
Kang said the family would be delighted if Sonia Gandhi and her children visited the property. “We are proud owners of Sonia Gandhi’s house. It is their family home, and we are ready to hand over the keys whenever they wish to come,” he said, adding that people known to the family in the village were also eager to meet her.Stating that over the years, the property has become a talking point among villagers, Kang said locals immediately identify it as “Sonia Gandhi’s house” whenever they see visitors from India, particularly Sikhs, understanding that they have come to see the former Congress president’s ancestral home.The growing tourist interest has also benefited the village economy, with visitors spending money at local eateries and accommodation facilities. Several prominent residents, including politicians, had attended the house’s inauguration, he said. The family also organises a function every year on Sonia Gandhi’s birthday, he added.
Kang said he spends 100 euros a month on a caretaker and pays around 1,000 euros annually in property taxes. Despite suggestions from some people to rent out the house for more than 800 euros a month or convert it into a gurdwara, the family has refused.
Current owner of Sonia Gandhi's ancestral home, Sukhdev Singh Kang
“We do not want to rent out our prized possession or change its character. We intend to preserve it as a place associated with Sonia Gandhi’s family,” he said.Asked about Sikh hardliners who hold the Gandhi family responsible for Operation Bluestar, Kang dismissed their criticism, saying only a handful of such elements were pursuing their own separatist agenda. He maintained that the operation was a decision of the government of the day and that blaming the Gandhi family personally for it was misplaced.For Kang, the property is not merely a real estate acquisition but an opportunity to preserve a small piece of the personal history of one of India's most prominent political figures.

Cowboy boots, cocktails and casinos - how do three US grands prix compare?
- Published
"The picnic blanket that you'd happily sit on in Austin will get confiscated by security at Miami and will end up wrapped around you in the chill of a Vegas night."
Cadence Kim from Dallas lives the reality of being an avid Formula 1 fan in the United States, in the three diverse locations the sport now frequents. She will be among the 300,000 spectators around the iconic Las Vegas Strip this weekend.
Las Vegas joined the F1 calendar in 2023, a year after Miami, while Austin has been home to the United States Grand Prix since 2012.
Kim has put in the hard yards travelling across the Atlantic to witness F1 in its European heartland. Now she is reaping the rewards of owners Liberty Media investing heavily in the three US races, which have all recently been awarded new long-term contracts.
"Following F1 from the US used to mean accepting a massive barrier to entry," Kim explains.
"It meant setting an early alarm and trying to explain to room mates why you were yelling at 20 rich men driving funny-looking cars very quickly. It was more of a niche sport with no natural gathering places for a community to watch. What bar is open at that time?
"Having three domestic races has changed everything. It has shifted F1 from a purely broadcast experience into something tangible. It becomes a week-long experience where a fan gets to engage with a like-minded community, attend parties in the evening, and do a meet-and-greet. You can walk a track, sit in a grandstand, purchase the overpriced merch, hear the engines and literally feel a part of something."
Watch parties and 30,000 steps a day
The community Kim is attached to is the ATX GP Club, formed in Austin by Maria Rodriguez and Julia Wezio, where watch parties help fans learn more about the sport and the drivers. With the longest running of the US races on their doorstep, at the Circuit of the Americas, she's ideally placed to compare all three venues for the fan experience.
"Vegas is a party," exclaims Kim. "The Nevada desert gets cold at night, so the cowboy hat doesn't make the trip, but socks, a hoodie and gloves do.
"Many of the teams have hotel partnerships so lobbies become team activation zones, and you might end up sharing an elevator with an engineer. The fan flow is well managed with everyone being funnelled through specific pedestrian walkways, but if you do have a ticket to watch the race at the track you are limited to staying only in that one specific zone.
"Vegas is known for its dining but that doesn't make it to the track. Ticketing forces you to consider some pretty rigid trade-offs. For example, sitting at Turn One means missing the musical artists and activations by the Sphere.
"As for Austin, you aren't restricted to a single assigned area but can walk almost the entire perimeter of the track. With each of the three races you get a local vibe integrated into the entertainment. It's not an artificially manufactured aesthetic in Austin, you're getting real Texas BBQ, smoked brisket and bedazzled cowboy hats.
"I've been once to Miami and would not consider going back unless it became a night race. The South Florida sun bakes both the track and the attendees during the daytime. Preparing for an outdoor trek is the best mindset. Treat it like a multi-day hike where you'll be logging 30,000 steps each day so comfortable shoes and water with electrolyte packets are a must."
'Vegas aligns so well with direction of F1'
The excitement level of racing at the Las Vegas Grand Prix in its opening three years has been as bright as the neon lights on the Strip. The debut race in 2023 was an instant classic, with the lead changing hands five times, and drama all the way to the line as Charles Leclerc overtook Sergio Perez for second place, behind winner Max Verstappen.
It was instant payback for F1, who had invested more than £500m in buying land and promoting the event. Despite complaints from some local residents and businesses over the disruption to the city streets, the gamble has paid dividends, according to Vegas-based podcast host and nine-time Le Mans 24 Hours driver Justin Bell.
"I was telling people, 'just wait'. It's like a big piece of Ikea furniture – once you do it once, it's so much quicker and more efficient the next time," Bell tells BBC Sport.
"The promoters did listen to the locals and worked out ways to get them involved, by offering discounted tickets and attempting to minimise the disruption. Let's face it, Las Vegas exists for one reason and that is to entertain visitors, and with the extraordinary economic impact it has I am sure the pros outweigh the cons for almost everyone involved."
That economic impact has been valued at $3.2bn for the Southern Nevada region over the three years, with each of the 175,000 visitors from outside Las Vegas spending an average of $2,400 on non-racing activities, according to figures from the 2024 race.
Bell, who presents the Drive to Wynn podcast from the luxury resort on the Strip, and used to guide celebrities like Drew Barrymore and Steve Carell in race cars on the Jay Leno Show, thinks Vegas has the perfect opportunity to position itself as the premier US race, despite it being the youngest.
"Vegas has such a leg up on the other two locations as a global entertainment hub, that aligns so well with the direction that F1 is heading as a brand," he says. "Miami is sexy and in theory has much going for it, but the track itself isn't in Miami so there are the usual inconveniences in terms of transportation.
"In contrast, I always recommended Austin to F1 newcomers as a track to visit first, because it is a purpose-built facility that is so easy to spectate at, with tons of room to walk around and watch cars from every angle all while eating a hotdog.
"From the first laps from 2023, it became evident that the Vegas track design was going to be great for F1. The mix of tight corners with that long straight down the iconic Strip invites breathtaking overtaking. Each successive year gets better."
Does US need an American F1 driver?
One of the burning questions, as to whether F1 can sustain its upward growth curve of popularity in the United States, is whether an American driver needs to be part of the elite 24 on the grid.
Logan Sargeant was the last American to drive in an F1 grand prix, in the Netherlands in August 2024. Contenders for future seats include Cadillac reserve driver Colton Herta, Jak Crawford and Ugo Ugochukwu, the 2026 Formula 3 champion.
"Thanks to Drive to Survive, this new breed of American F1 fan is attracted to the global superstar drivers," says Bell.
"They are exciting, handsome and wealthy. If the right American driver does make it to F1 he has to be a rock star both on and off the track. Colton might be fast enough but is he a media darling? I am not convinced that unless whomever he is ticks all those boxes, that it will really make a difference to the US fanbase. Americans like winners, not just participants."
Kim agrees that F1 is inherently global: "It doesn't bother me at all. I am a fan of an Australian and a Dutch driver while being an American with a Polish background. When I moved from Austin to Dallas this past summer, I wasn't handed a welcome kit by the Dallas Cowboys and told that now they expect my support.
"US representation already exists with Haas and Cadillac, but I don't think that we need an American driver on the grid for Americans to tune in and show up."
Crawford, Aston Martin's reserve driver, is one of those aiming to be that next American F1 star. Speaking to BBC Sport, he sees a growing percentage of younger drivers already leaning towards F1 ahead of the traditional Nascar and IndyCar series.
"I have a lot of kids and kart drivers coming up to me, and say that I inspire them, and I'm not on the grid full time. So I can't even imagine what that would be like if I was," Crawford says.
"I went to the first Austin race, in 2012, as a seven-year old. Back then it was hard to find how to watch F1 in the United States. Over time, as I raced in Europe, I became more passionate about it, and I grew up hand in hand with the popularity of F1 in the US.
"Austin is a phenomenal circuit. I'm biased as I'm from Texas. Las Vegas is cool, as a night race. I raced a lot there in karting, on a street circuit, and it's very cool driving past the big casinos at night."
'Miami wins, although Austin still feels like the soul of American Formula 1'
Analysis from BBC Radio 5 Live F1 commentator Harry Benjamin
Las Vegas is the Marmite of the three US races for me. You either love it or hate it, and somehow I manage to feel both ways about it over the course of the same weekend.
I've always struggled slightly with Vegas as a destination. Unless you're there for a very particular sort of weekend, I think the novelty can wear off surprisingly quickly. It's an extraordinary place to look at, but outside the circuit and paddock, the sensory overload can become exhausting. There are only so many flashing lights, casinos and enormous hotels you can take before you start craving somewhere a little more normal.
The timings don't help either. Everything happens so late, and the desert temperatures can be surprisingly cold once the sun goes down. Combined with the expense of the weekend, it isn't necessarily the easiest or most relaxing grand prix to attend.
However, one huge advantage of Vegas is that you barely need to get in a car once you've arrived. Apart from the journey between the airport and your hotel, so much of the grand prix experience is within walking distance. Compared with the traffic in Miami, that's a real luxury.
And of course, the moment you see Formula 1 cars racing down the Las Vegas Strip at night, an awful lot of those complaints disappear.
It is genuinely one of the most spectacular sights in motorsport. We've become so accustomed to seeing Formula 1 cars at purpose-built circuits or traditional street tracks, but watching them fly past some of the most recognisable landmarks in the world, illuminated by the lights of Vegas, is pretty extraordinary.
They really know how to put on a show, too. The entertainment doesn't simply stop when the chequered flag falls. The post-race spectacle is another part of the experience, and it's difficult to think of another grand prix that embraces that side of Formula 1 quite so enthusiastically.
For all my reservations about Vegas as a destination, I completely understand why someone would want to experience the race at least once. There really is nothing else like it.
Overall, Austin is where I'd send someone who loves the racing, Miami is where I'd send someone who wants the best all-round grand prix holiday and Las Vegas is where I'd send someone who wants to experience something they won't forget.
For me, Miami wins, although there's something about Austin that still feels like the soul of American Formula 1. And despite all my complaints about Vegas, there's absolutely no denying the spectacle of seeing those cars flying down the Strip at night.

The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.
On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.
Mark Brantley, the premier of Nevis, which has autonomous self-governance in some aspects, said he understood that the “country was given very little choice”, but did not “support the winding down of the program”.
The 42-year-old CBI programme, which St Kitts and Nevis pioneered, allows wealthy foreigners to obtain citizenship and ultimately a passport by investing in infrastructure and other development projects. It has brought billions of dollars into the country and in some years accounted for the largest share of government revenue.
In June, the European Commission wrote to the five Caribbean nations that currently operate CBI programmes: St Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and St Lucia. It warned that countries may lose visa-free access to its 29-country Schengen area if they did not phase out CBI.
In Friday’s statement, Drew blamed concerns over the programme on mismanagement by previous administrations, including years of underselling to undercut other countries, a controversial prison project, weak escrow protections and investment sums not being properly paid into the citizenship unit.
He said his government had led major reforms to the Caribbean’s programmes with international partners, including the US treasury, but argued that continuing the programme risked visa-free travel to parts of Europe and access to international banking. That could disrupt services allowing visitors to use overseas cards and families abroad to send money home.
Brantley, however, argued it was unfair for the EU to force St Kitts and Nevis to make a move without offering assistance to navigate the transition to other industries.
“I have not yet seen from the EU any corresponding suggestions of assistance. And we have to realise that these citizenship-by-investment programs, not only in St Kitts and Nevis, but … smaller countries of the Caribbean, have contributed significantly to our gross domestic product and also to ensuring that our people … can get adequate access to water and to education, to healthcare and the like,” he said.
Brantley described the 1 June 2028 deadline the EU gave the country to phase out the lucrative programme as “frankly ludicrous”.
In his statement, Drew said the CBI programme “did a lot of good, but it also created a danger”.
“When one source pays for half or more of everything, you are at its mercy. If it stops, everything stops. That is putting all of your eggs in one basket,” he added.
The prime minister said the government aimed to diversify its economy by strengthening tourism, yachting, and digital and creative industries, among others. He added that the sale of clean, geothermal energy is “at the heart of it” with drilling and exploration already planned.
“I will not pretend that the road is easy. Less CBI money means we must spend wisely and plan carefully. We will. Our plan is to make this change by growing our economy. Raising taxes is not part of that plan,” Drew said.
Antigua and Barbuda has also expressed willingness to end the programme, though it is trying to negotiate a longer transition period. The five Caribbean governments have taken differing positions on the EU demand. According to local media, Grenada has indicated it wants its programme to continue until 2032, while Dominica and St Lucia have responded to Brussels without publicly committing to ending their programmes.

Assam medical college dept withdraws order on marriage for PG trainees after backlash
The National Medical Commission's post-graduate medical education regulations of 2023 allows PG students maternity and paternity leave.
A department in the Assam Medical College and Hospital (AMCH) in Dibrugarh, the state’s oldest government medical college, on Wednesday night withdrew an order asking post-graduate trainees (PGTs) to postpone personal milestones like marriages till completion of their residency, hours after it was issued, sparking a controversy.
The order issued by Dr Prasanta Dihingia, professor and head of the department of medicine, said: "All PGTs are advised to defer personal milestones such as marriage until the successful completion of their residency tenure.” HT has seen a copy of the order.
It added: “Their primary focus during the tenure of their academic program should remain dedicated to clinical duties, patient care, academic pursuits and research requirements. All PGTs are expected to adhere to this advisory positively.”
Hours later, the department head issued a fresh order, saying the previous one was "withdrawn with immediate effect".
The development came amid criticisms from the students, with the United Doctors Front (UDF), an advocacy group of doctors, saying the order was not an advice to the students but meant to tell people to put their lives on hold.
The National Medical Commission's post-graduate medical education regulations of 2023 allows PG students maternity and paternity leave, casual leave, a weekly off, and reasonable working hours with adequate rest.
Dr Dihingia, however, said the order was “misinterpreted by some”. "The order was issued as advice from a senior member of the profession urging PGTs to focus on patient care and their academics. But it has been misinterpreted by some," he told HT.
"The PGTs have an annual quota of leaves as per rules and they will continue to get them. But some were found availing more leaves than sanctioned. There was no question of punishment," he said, adding that the principal of AMCH had sought an explanation from him in writing on the issue.
In a post on X, the UDF said: “It may be worded as advice. But it was issued on letterhead with a dispatch number by the office that also signs off on residents' leave, attendance and exam eligibility. No resident will read it as optional.”
It added: "The order also says something about the department that wrote it. If a resident getting married is seen as a threat to clinical duties and patient care, the problem is the workload and the staffing, not the wedding. PG residents are usually in their late 20s or early 30s. A three-year residency doesn't pause their lives, and women residents will feel this pressure most.”
The UDF also mentioned a Supreme Court ruling of 2018 in which it was stated that the right to marry a person of one's choice is integral to Article 21. It sought the NMC’s and Assam health minister Ashok Singhal intervention in the matter.
Set up in November 1947, AMCH is the oldest medical college in Assam and is considered among the best institutes for medical education in the northeastern region.
