The FAA fired several hundred employees in February 2025. However …
DOGE itself did not have the authority to make the firings. In all, 352 probationary employees — meaning those in their first year — were let go; 132 were reinstated the following month. According to the FAA, no airway transportation systems specialists, who maintain critical navigation systems, were among those dismissed.
In mid-November, following a nationwide ground stop ordered by the Federal Aviation Administration, social media users shared claims that the Department of Government Efficiency, a Trump administration initiative to cut government spending and jobs, laid off hundreds of technicians responsible for maintaining and upgrading critical air navigation systems.
"DOGE laid off 400 technicians in charge of maintaining and upgrading critical FAA navigational systems," one Facebook post (archived) read.
(Facebook user Tom Riley)
Versions of the rumor spread on multiple social media platforms, including X and Facebook. Some posts suggested the alleged layoffs contributed to the Nov. 13 ground stop. Snopes readers also asked about a possible connection between the layoffs and the disruption.
In short, the FAA fired 352 probationary employees in February 2025, but they were not 400 technicians maintaining critical navigation systems, as the posts claimed. According to the FAA, no airway transportation systems specialists, who maintain such equipment, were among those dismissed. The firings did affect employees in other aviation safety and support roles, and some were later reinstated. There was no evidence that the job cuts directly contributed to the Nov. 13 ground stop. As such, we have rated this claim as mostly false.
We have reached out to the FAA with questions about the firings and whether they affected FAA operations. We will update this article if we receive a response.
FAA fired fewer than 400 employees in February 2025
The job cuts mentioned in social media posts did happen, although the number of employees was slightly lower than social media users claimed. In February 2025, the Trump administration fired 352 probationary FAA employees, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. Of those, 132 were represented by the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union.
Although social media posts attributed the firings to DOGE, the initiative itself did not have authority to fire FAA employees. The FAA fired the employees as part of Trump administration's broader cuts to the federal workforce.
DOGE was, however, involved in discussions about the cuts. In a May 2025 interview with NBC's "Meet the Press," Duffy acknowledged discussing with Elon Musk — who led the DOGE initiative — which FAA positions should be protected from the cuts.
"We went back and forth, and Elon agreed, the president agreed," Duffy said. He also claimed the agency retained all positions considered critical to aviation safety, saying: "The FAA has 46,000 employees. And if you lost 350, is this affecting our safety mission? There's a lot of things the FAA does. But for us, safety is key. So, no, we've retained all those safety positions."
In response to our questions, the Transportation Department directed us to a Nov. 16 statement on X, which read:
MYTH: DOGE got rid of essential employees that made FAA less safe and effective.
TRUTH: The FAA has around 45,000 employees. Less than 400 were let go via DOGE, and they were all probationary, meaning they had been hired less than a year ago. Zero air traffic controllers or critical safety personnel were let go.
(X account @USDOTRapid)
The department also told us that the dismissals "did not negatively affect the Department in any way."
Who was affected by the FAA firings?
Contrary to social media posts, the dismissed employees were not 400 technicians responsible for maintaining and upgrading critical navigational systems.
According to the FAA's May 2026 workforce plan, no airway transportation systems specialists were terminated as probationary employees. Such employees are specialized technicians responsible for maintaining and repairing "radar, communications, navigational aids, airport lighting, backup power, heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) equipment."
The Transportation Department also confirmed this in an email to Snopes, stating, "No ATSS were terminated as probationary employees in February 2025 and the FAA has continued to hire and onboard ATSS since the start of this administration."
However, the firings did affect employees in other positions, including some supporting aviation safety and technical operations. According to the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists, 59 of the dismissed employees represented by the union worked in technical operations, 39 in flight standards, 19 in mission support services and 15 in air traffic services.
In an email to Snopes, the union provided the following breakdown of the affected positions and their responsibilities:
Aeronautical information specialists – evaluation, selection and preparation of navigation
maps, routes, chart, procedures and flight paths.
Maintenance mechanics maintain and repair the grounds and buildings where controllers and systems
specialists work. This requires detailed knowledge of specific trades such as carpentry, plumbing, and electrical.
Management & Program Assistants and Aviation Safety Assistants – maintain office records, office supplies, updates, logistics support and maintain data reports.
Environmental Protection Specialists – manage, supervise, or perform administrative or program work relating to environmental protection programs. They ensure compliance with environmental laws and regulations.
The union also clarified that the employees dismissed from the FAA's Technical Operations division worked as maintenance mechanics, environmental protection specialists and management and program assistants. "So no, none of them worked directly on navigation or communications equipment," the union told Snopes — referring to all 132 dismissed employees it represented.
Still, the fact that no airway transportation systems specialists were fired does not mean the other positions were completely unrelated to aviation safety. In March 2025 testimony to Congress, PASS President David Spero warned that the job cuts would increase workloads for employees already working in an understaffed agency, saying, "This action will increase the workload for frontline aviation safety workers and place new responsibilities on a workforce that is already stretched thin."
Another complication is the lack of a consistent definition of safety-critical positions. A September 2026 audit by the Transportation Department's Office of Inspector General found the criteria for classifying such positions varied across FAA offices.
Some employees were later reinstated
On March 17, 2025, the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists announced that the FAA was reinstating all 132 dismissed employees represented by the union, following a federal court ruling. According to the union, the employees were expected to return to work on March 20 and receive back pay.
In an email to Snopes in November, the union said that approximately 40 of those 132 employees were no longer represented by the union. "They could have found other employment before or after the court order, been reassigned to another FAA bargaining unit or taken a detail or promotion at the agency," spokesperson Liz Doherty told us.
Therefore, it remains unclear how many of the dismissed employees were still working for the FAA at the time of the Nov. 13 nationwide ground stop. We also asked the Transportation Department for updated figures on the reinstatements and the employees' current status. We will update this article if we receive a response.
No evidence firings caused the ground stop
As for the nationwide ground stop, there is no evidence that the February 2025 FAA firings contributed to the disruption. As we previously reported, the FAA said the problem involved its older communications network. In a Nov. 15 statement, the agency identified two possible locations connected to the disruption, including a site in Arkansas where contractor L3Harris was installing a new router. As of Nov. 19, the exact cause of the shutdown remained under investigation.
In a statement shared after the incident, the union said its represented technicians "were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop." The union also told us via email that it found no direct connection between the firings and the incident:
PASS sees no direct connection between the February 2025 terminations and Friday's ground stop. All the probationary employees are essential to the aviation ecosystem that keeps the National Airspace System functioning safely and efficiently. However, none would have been involved directly with the router upgrades that appear to have caused the ground stop.
Still, the FAA had broader staffing problems. In its May workforce plan (Page 8), the agency said it did not have enough employees to cover all shifts at 67 facilities. The report also found that airway transportation systems specialists worked an average of 115 hours of overtime in fiscal year 2025.
The union also stressed the need for more technicians, telling us:
PASS fully supports the modernization efforts undertaken by the DOT and FAA. However, the FAA agrees that the airway transportation systems specialist workforce is understaffed and earlier this year released that workforce plan calling for the hiring of 750 more technicians. The workforce needs to be fully staffed, funded and provided the resources need to continue performing their safety critical work.
However, there is no evidence that the February 2025 firings contributed to the November ground stop despite these broader staffing problems.

Divide and conquer - now maverick Erasmus plans online watchalong
- Published
Having been banned from the touchline for six matches, you will not find Rassie Erasmus at the Aviva Stadium when his South Africa side face Ireland.
Instead he will be hosting an online watchalong of Saturday's match, courtesy of a swiftly purchased domain name.
The South Africa head coach plans to stream his reactions live while watching on television from his team's Dublin hotel.
It is typical Erasmus. An unapologetic, unabashed show of defiance in the face of the authorities.
And he will not be short of virtual company.
Because, while Erasmus has run low of advocates elsewhere, his compatriots have rushed to his defence.
"Rassie was just asking questions," said former South Africa hooker Hanyani Shimange in the wake of Erasmus' ban for a scattergun series of complaints about the injustices suffered by his side.
"But you have to look at the facts. Where was the accountability for that refereeing performance [in the loss to France]?"
Naas Botha, legendary South Africa fly-half turned pundit, described Erasmus' punishment as a "debacle". "You can't tell me [officials] are untouchable," he said.
Supersport, which broadcasts South Africa's games domestically, published an article accusing Erasmus' critics of "pearl clutching", external and "shooting the messenger" with regards to the game's faults.
Despite slurring officials with a suggestion of match-fixing, Erasmus has the support of South Africa.
It is not surprising.
His feats with the team are astonishing.
South Africa were ranked sixth in the world when he took over in March 2018.
He arrived after a November tour in which they lost to Wales and were thrashed 38-3 by Ireland. New Zealand had racked up a record 57-0 win a few months earlier.
Erasmus turned the team around at speed, marrying their trademark up-front power with pace out wide.
They won the 2019 World Cup. The defended their title in 2023. They will go into the tournament in 2027 aiming for an unprecedented hat-trick. And few would bet against them achieving it.
Erasmus is relentlessly innovative.
Long before the sport's data revolution, he was coding game footage, picking up the technique from a friend who worked in the military. He has since developed Outfox, his own software which allows his teams to run through moves virtually on a screen away from the pitch.
Tactically, he has also been ahead of the curve. He pioneered the use of forward-heavy replacement benches, giving his team an edge in the final quarter of the match.
He saw the game-breaking potential of diminutive Sevens specialist Kurt-Lee Arendse and moulded Andre Esterhuizen into a genuine hybrid player, capable of playing in the back row and the backline.
Trick plays - forcing a scrum with a deliberate infringement off kick-off, or setting up a line-out in the middle of the pitch - have been part of Erasmus' arsenal.
Legally, he is across every possible loophole.
There was controversy before the match against France last weekend when he made use of the Nations Championships' looser regulations to swap his starting front row just over an hour before kick-off.
Previously, he demoted himself to water boy so he could run the touchline during the 2021 series win over the British and Irish Lions.
Former Springbok wing Bryan Habana worked under Erasmus at the Stormers in Cape Town.
"He is one of the master tacticians the game has ever seen," Habana told BBC Sport's Ireland Rugby Social.
"I don't always agree with how Rassie comes across, but I understand he wears his heart on his sleeve. He has got incredibly high standards.
"He's willing to be in the firing line to defend what he believes is right."
But there is no doubt, by the letter of the law, that Erasmus is wrong - certainly in terms of the platform and terms he chose for his complaints.
In July World Rugby introduced new rules around criticism of officials. It specifically targeted "comments which, viewed objectively, a reasonable person would conclude were an attack on the credibility or competence of the match officials".
Mentioning "match-fixing" undermines the officials in exactly that way.
Considering Erasmus' previous, including an hour-long monologue bemoaning officiating of a first-Test defeat by the Lions in 2021 and a series of tweets after a loss to France a year later, he may be fortunate to only be banned for six matches.
World Rugby, perhaps pre-empting the reaction in South Africa, was clear that it was not punishing Erasmus for asking questions.
"Robust, respectful debate is natural, but teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches," it said in its judgement.
"Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official's integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse."
For many South Africans, though, Erasmus is still an outlaw hero.
World Rugby, based in Dublin, is seen by them as tilted towards the north.
Australian Brett Robinson, the current chairman, is the first figure from outside the Six Nations countries to hold the organisation's top job since it became an elected position.
The World Cup has been lifted by South Africa on four occasions, but held there only once.
Japan coach Eddie Jones, Erasmus' fellow maverick, recently suggested Ireland's political clout, external was behind his team's home game being staged in Australia rather than Tokyo.
South Africa were a powerful voice against the possible moves to "depower" the scrum - a key part of the Springbok game - at a February conference to discuss future law tweaks.
Erasmus' public pronouncements have fuelled conspiracy theories weaved from those threads. They have also made an all-time great team harder for outsiders to love.
Whether it is a deliberate ploy is hard to tell.
Certainly Erasmus is a repeat offender, but his offences have also come in his second language. He is an Afrikaans speaker.
Some also see instinctive honesty rather than a premeditated ploy in his public speaking.
"He also has almost no filters, so he will speak his mind without fully appreciating the consequences of what he has done," his biographer David O'Sullivan told BBC Sport in 2023.
Whatever the motivation, the consequences keep coming - for Erasmus, but also the rest of world rugby.
Referees Nic Berry and Wayne Barnes, previous targets of Erasmus' criticism, have detailed the effects it had on them.
Berry described "a character assassination" that caused "immeasurable damage". He has not refereed a South Africa game in the five years since.
Barnes' wife and children were threatened over social media.
South Africa's latest appeal to their supporters not to abuse officials, external may be too late for referee Andrea Piardi and his television match official Matteo Liperini, who oversaw France's win on Friday.
There is a wider question too.
For a complex sport, the image of a world champion coach publicly criticising officials does not little to dispel a wavering viewer's assumption that it is too intricate and confusing to justify their attention.
South Africa will always line up alongside their rebel chief.
But the patience of the rest of the rugby world with Erasmus' antics is wearing ever thinner.

There is an uncanny similarity between Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), the virus responsible for the COVID-19 pandemic, and air pollution. During the pandemic, the virus entered our bodies through the air we breathed; harmful particulate matter and toxic gases enter through the same respiratory route. Additionally, both damage multiple organs, including the lungs, heart and brain. Yet, while COVID-19 prompted an unprecedented emergency national response, air pollution continues to be treated largely as a seasonal inconvenience.
The harmful effects of air pollution are well-established. An adult takes approximately 20,000–25,000 breaths daily, meaning that even a relatively miniscule worsening of air quality can have substantial health consequences over time. This alone should make improving the quality of air an urgent public health priority.

WASHINGTON — The White House pulled its nomination of Heidi Overton for commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration on Tuesday evening, startling senators on the health committee and introducing new questions about the future of the FDA.
The decision is a blow to an agency that thrives on stability and has been without a permanent head since May, though it was beginning to enjoy a period of relative normalcy under acting commissioner Kyle Diamantas. The FDA is on its third leader of this Trump administration, and whoever replaces Overton as nominee could be the fourth.
The FDA is facing a number of challenges. The user fees that fund the agency’s drug reviews need to be reauthorized, a process that may be complicated by Democrats’ sweeping midterm election wins. And leaders are confronting the rise of artificial intelligence in scientific research and push to compete with China’s biotech industry.

The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.
The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.
The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.
Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.
The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.
Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.
In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.
If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).
According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.
In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.
“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”
Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.
The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.
The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.
One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.
In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.
The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.
In order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.
On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.
The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.
During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.
Timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, said the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.
Sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, said the data presented by the Guardian raised important questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.
She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.
For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.
Strik said: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”
Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, said: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”
In a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission said the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.
Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.
It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.
Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.

Nvidia is going through it. The chipmaker’s iconic leader just resigned due to an international scandal, its stock has taken a hit, and it’s in a precarious position as it tries to maintain its dominance in the AI era.
Following Jensen Huang’s ouster, the company’s interim CEO and still-CFO Colette Kress has been tasked with stabilizing the deck. So far, Kress’s public-facing duties have included running the company’s third-quarter earnings call and hosting an all-hands meeting for Nvidia’s money-hungry workforce. And as part of her calming campaign, Kress has also been deploying a catchphrase that sounds like it was taken straight from the draft files of a summer of ‘24 Democratic campaign strategist: “We’ve got this.”
By WIRED’s count, Kress has publicly used the phrase three times in the past 24 hours, often putting emphasis or a little bit of zhuzh in it:
Tuesday’s earnings call:
“Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this.”
Wednesday’s all-hands meeting:
“Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. Our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change. We thank you all for the great quarter that we had. Just remember, we've got this.”
Wednesday’s all-hands meeting, again:
Kress ended Wednesday’s meeting by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game, all singing together.
“It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song… Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you that you will help sing it. But Nvidia, we’ve got this.”
Kress’s new catchphrase perhaps isn’t the most inspiring; companies that got this usually don’t have to remind people how much they got this twice in one meeting. It’s a collectivist’s version of “You got this,” a slightly less corny version of “Yes we can,” a saying that may well pose more questions than it answers. (We got…what?)
Nvidia investors, or any investor, might not have fist-pumped and said, “We’ve got this!” during a quick portfolio check these past 10 days. Anyone who has had the slightest hint of knowledge that Nvidia’s chips were finding their way into China is unlikely to be in a “We totally got this” mood at the moment.
Still, some Nvidia employees appear to be inspired by Kress’s mantra. “Damn right we got this,” Aaron Erickson, Nvidia’s head of NemoClaw engineering, posted on X on Wednesday. Vega Shah, who works in portfolio management for Nvidia’s venture capital arm, shared Erickson’s post and echoed the phrase, adding her own rocket ship emoji to the post.
And yesterday, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the board did not intend to reinstate Huang, despite some calls on social media and within the company to put Huang back in the top spot.
Which means that Kress, for the moment, has … got this.
Paresh Dave contributed to this article.

Ashton Kutcher's resumé is extensive — and he may soon be able to add one more title to that list: billionaire.
"Actor" is just one of the many bullets he'd list as part of a well-rounded career. Kutcher is also a producer, entrepreneur, and philanthropist, with various ventures in each of these fields. He also happens to be a very serious investor.
He's not the first celebrity to break into investing, but more than a decade in, Kutcher has made a name for himself in Silicon Valley. Business Insider's Bani Sapra previously called him the most active celebrity investor and, arguably, Hollywood's most experienced tech investor.
With the goal of helping connect the "little man" with new companies providing easy solutions to everyday problems, Kutcher began as an angel investor before co-founding two venture capital funds: A-Grade Investments and Sound Ventures.
Sound Ventures has invested $435 million into Anthropic, the tech giant behind Claude, since 2023. Before Anthropic's IPO on November 19, Bloomberg estimated that Sound's stake could be worth about $7 billion. While Kutcher exited Sound Ventures as a partner earlier this year, he remains in an advisory role, according to Inc., which means he could still stand to earn big in Anthropic's IPO.
Kutcher called the IPO "kind of cool" in a statement on X, adding that it was "years of work, micro victories and failures stacked on top of one another" and "the manifestation of trust."
"Thank you to those who didn't believe in us. You made us work harder," he said.
In June, he announced he was teaming up with Morgan Beller, a former partner at NFX, to start a new firm focused on AI, The Wall Street Journal reported.
From turning a $30 million fund into $250 million in six years to making early bets on Uber, Airbnb, and Anthropic, he's built a successful and lucrative investing career.
This is how he did it.
Kutcher's money prowess started young
Raised in Iowa, Kutcher comes from blue-collar roots. His dad worked at a meatpacking plant, and his mom was a schoolteacher.
As a kid, Kutcher juggled multiple jobs, including lawn mowing, janitorial work, and dishwashing.
Kutcher told Grow (the blog of micro-investing app Acorns) in 2018 that he saved $1,400 for a snowmobile at age 13. "I worked after school and on weekends for one and a half years, and put every cent into a savings account," he said.
Kutcher was studying biochemical engineering at the University of Iowa when he was scouted as a model, which ultimately led to his break in the acting world.
Today, at age 48, Kutcher has invested billions in startups, participating in dozens of funding rounds, leading Business Insider to previously call him the most active "Hollywood angel" in Silicon Valley.
"Focusing on this simple goal of identifying and enabling amazing entrepreneurs to create a better tomorrow is the crux of my investment strategy," Kutcher wrote in a 2018 blog post for Atrium, a legal and tech startup.
How and why he got started investing
Kutcher said he began investing because he wanted to connect new companies building solutions to everyday problems with the people who needed them.
"I spend a lot of time thinking about new and simpler ways to do things, but don't have enough time to execute on all those ideas," he told Grow. "So I found people who were executing on them and invested in their success."
Kutcher told The Telegraph in 2013 that he was particularly drawn to consumer technologies. "The companies that will ultimately do well are the companies that chase happiness," he said. "If you find a way to help people find love, or health, or friendship, the dollar will chase that."
That said, his foray into angel investing began when he founded the production company Katalyst in 2000, which led to Silicon Valley connections.
Kutcher poached Katalyst's digital chief from TechCrunch, who introduced him to the big names in Silicon Valley, Zack O'Malley Greenburg reported for Forbes. "I spent 90% of my time just listening," Kutcher told him.
Kutcher soon became familiar with the tech scene. In 2009, at the request of billionaire Marc Andreessen, he invested $1 million into Skype, 18 months before Microsoft bought the company and quadrupled the value, according to O'Malley Greenburg.
Mentorship changed his life and how he'd go on to invest
But Kutcher said his investing career hit a new level after reaching out to Silicon Valley angel investor Ron Conway for mentorship.
"He is one of the godfathers of angel investing," he told his website, A Plus, in a 2015 interview. "He completely opened up his investment portfolio to me and really started explaining to me how things worked and what his strategy was. He has probably been my biggest mentor."
From there, Kutcher went on to cofound venture capital firm A-Grade Investments with talent manager Guy Oseary and businessman Ron Burkle. Within six years, he turned a $30 million fund into $250 million, Forbes reported.
Kutcher and Oseary poured $1 million each of their own money into the fund, while Burkle contributed $8 million. A-Grade also received backing from experienced tech executives like Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt, as well as businessman Mark Cuban.
A-Grade focused on early-stage investments, according to TechCrunch. O'Malley Greenburg wrote that these start-ups had to have three defining characteristics: founders A-Grade wanted to work with; a problem-solving mission statement that would make the most of time; and a business model A-Grade could grow.
While there were a few failed investments along the way, such as BlackJet and Fab.com, A-Grade made many successful ones: $500,000 into Uber, $2.5 million into Airbnb, $3 million into Spotify, $300,000 into Warby Parker, and $1.5 million into Houzz, among many others. All five went on to become multibillion-dollar companies. (Uber, Airbnb, Spotify, and Warby Parker are publicly traded, while Houzz was last publicly valued at $4 billion in 2017.)
In 2015, Kutcher and Oseary took a more formal approach to venture investing, co-founding the venture fund Sound Ventures with $100 million from Liberty Media.
Investing other people's money instead of their own allowed "them to make bigger investments, invest in later-stage startups, and put more money into investments that raise follow-on rounds," according to TechCrunch.
By 2017, Sound Ventures was managing more than $100 million in investments, the Journal reported, and in 2026, it is reportedly managing around $2 billion. Sound Ventures' stake in Anthropic alone is worth $7 billion, and, per Yahoo Finance, an AI-focused fund the firm started in 2023 began with $240 million in capital.
Its portfolio has included Neighborly, a municipal bond crowdfunding startup, OpenGov, a financial tech company for local governments, and OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT.
Kutcher and Oseary told O'Malley Greenburg in 2016 they were taking a "typical carry" from Sound Ventures — likely 2% of cash invested and 20% of profits, plus performance bonuses.
The year prior, Kutcher had guest-judged on the investment show "Shark Tank" after Mark Cuban convinced him to audition.
Kutcher was originally hesitant about going on, but felt it "might deliver the opportunity to bring an audience to the show that might not normally watch it," he told A Plus. "It really is about entrepreneurship and, to me, the American Dream: that you can go off and start something with very little and build something great."
His episode aired in 2015. He ended up splitting a $200,000 investment with "Shark Tank" judge Lori Greiner for 15% each of Beebo, a shoulder strap that holds a baby bottle for optimal bottle-feeding.
Greiner used her expertise to improve packaging and presentation, while Kutcher used his name recognition, massive social-media outreach, and role as a new dad to get Beebo the customers it needed, Business Insider reported.
Kutcher has 3 rules when investing, all focused on what he sees in entrepreneurs
The first rule is that entrepreneurs must have an intimate understanding of both their product and their industry, he told A-Plus. They must also have a personality that will allow them to withstand failure and setbacks, he said.
Kutcher continued: "You can have the best idea in the world and absolute domain expertise and know how to do everything right, but if you want to do something great in the world, there are going to be obstacles; and you have to be a person who has ingenuity and sheer willpower to get through those times."
The third rule, he added, is that the entrepreneur must get along well with him.
But the real key to piquing his interest lies in how well an entrepreneur can spin a compelling narrative, he said at TechCrunch's Disrupt SF 2018.
"One of the critical tests that I try to run when I'm sitting across from a founder is: 'Can you sell me your idea?'" Kutcher said at the conference.
For Kutcher, the ability to convey a company's mission determines whether it can snag the best talent in a competitive job market. He sees telling the story of an early-stage company as integral to its future growth.
"If you can't sell me, how are you going to sell your first hire, your second hire, your third hire?" Kutcher asked. "How are you going to create the capacity for the rest of your team to sell those next hires?"
He's also doled out a lot of investing advice over the years, often recommending to invest in areas you have knowledge of.
On Chelsea Handler's Netflix talk show "Chelsea," Kutcher offered up his best investment advice: "Invest in the things that you know. If you drink beer all the time — if you go to microbreweries and you try all kinds of them — you probably know which ones are the best, and my advice is always to invest in what you know."
And for what you don't know, he advises finding out everything you can about it. That involves asking stupid questions. At a QuickBooks Connect conference, he said that when he was first introduced to key players in the tech world, he would ask every question he could think of.
Learning also requires paying attention. "If you're a stock boy in a grocery store and you see something flying off the shelf, find out who made it," he told Grow. "Find out why it's flying off the shelf. Do the investigation necessary to know whether or not it's something that is going to have ultimate value."
Kutcher told Grow you should invest in what you want to see become reality. "Worst-case scenario, you lose money — but at least you will get the life you want," he said.
When it comes to implementing that reality, Kutcher has said that while having a vision is important, making a plan is better. At the QuickBooks Connect conference, he advised starting with what you've done to work towards your vision or goal, then looking at what you can do next to finally achieve your vision. In other words, nail out the nitty-gritty details that get you from point A to B.
Of all his investments, Kutcher said he considers his relationships the best investment he's made
"Taking the time to get to know [people], what motivates them, what their challenges are," he told Grow. "These things are often overlooked. Investors get so wrapped up in returns and numbers that they forget that the true privilege of their position is to share a journey with exceptional people."
His philosophy on investing — and life in general — all goes back to his Midwestern roots. He said he wants to give back to those who need a helping hand.
"I'm very appreciative of the things I have," Kutcher said at QuickBooks. "I'm always fighting for the little guy, no matter what, because I always feel like I am the little guy. If you're lucky enough to be doing well, it's incumbent upon you to help folks who are struggling to grab that first rung on the ladder to start their climb."

Meta Quest adds 3D movie purchases and rentals to its TV app
The headlining film is a Billie Eilish 3D concert experience co-directed by James Cameron.
Meta has rolled out 3D movie rentals for its headsets. Users can now rent or buy films through the TV app on both the Meta Quest 3 and Meta Quest 3S.
The lineup of available titles is topped by HIT ME HARD AND SOFT: THE TOUR (LIVE IN 3D). Meta Quest will be the exclusive host for the 3D version of the Billie Eilish concert movie until December 31. The project is a big budget affair co-directed by the pop artist and James Cameron. It was shot with a custom system for 3D filming at range so that the show's live audience wouldn't be interrupted by cameras and the at-home viewers could still experience the sensation of being onstage along with Eilish.
Earlier this month, Disney began making its library of 3D films available on Meta Quest via the Disney+ app. Having more media embrace the tech is a welcome addition for fans of 3D (although it may have felt like an unnecessarily long wait). But today's announcement includes a note from Meta that the TV app will continue adding more content, including "thousands of titles and international availability coming with the launch of Meta VR Glasses in spring 2027."

PM Modi pays tribute to former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi on her birth anniversary
Indira Gandhi, India's first woman Prime Minister, was born on November 19, 1917, in Allahabad, now Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday paid tribute to the former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi on her birth anniversary.
In a post on X, PM Modi wrote, “Paying tribute to former Prime Minister Smt. Indira Gandhi Ji on her birth anniversary.”
Indira Gandhi, India's first woman Prime Minister, was born on November 19, 1917, in Allahabad, now Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh. She was the daughter of India's first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru.
A prominent figure in the country's political history, she served as Prime Minister from 1966 to 1977 and again from 1980 until 1984. She was succeeded as Prime Minister by her son, Rajiv Gandhi.
Karnataka CM pays his tributes
Karnataka Chief Minister D K Shivakumar also paid tribute to the former prime minister, recalling her contributions to India's political, economic and institutional development.
In a post on X, Shivakumar described Gandhi as the 'Iron Lady' and highlighted several milestones during her tenure, including strengthening agricultural production, expanding access to banking and supporting India's space and nuclear programmes.

"Paying my respects to the Iron Lady and former Prime Minister Smt. Indira Gandhi on her birth anniversary. As Kolkata choked on toxic air following Diwali and Kali Puja celebrations, West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari accused those raising concerns over firecracker pollution of being communists opposed to Hindu traditions. His remarks were consistent with the concerted push by a section of the Right wing to portray criticism of firecrackers as an attack on Hindu religious practices. However, among those complaining about noise levels and pollution in Kolkata were members of Adhikari’s own party and cabinet.
The Bengal CM made the remarks while addressing the media during a visit to the coastal town of Digha on Monday, where he had gone to attend an administrative meeting and visit the Kali Puja organised by the Shyama Prasad Mukherjee Traders Association.
Speaking to reporters, Adhikari said, “There has been an awakening of Sanatan in this state, and some people have a problem with that. The people making these allegations (about firecrackers) had turned Hindu religious festivals into cultural fests… These people do not apply ‘tika’ or religious markings on their foreheads, they do not wear ‘dors’ or religious threads on their wrists, nor do they wear tulsi beads around their necks.”
Adhikari further said, “The communists are raising this issue of firecrackers. We have controlled it in accordance with the Supreme Court’s directives. Firecrackers were burst in some places even after 10 pm, and the police took necessary action. We have stopped DJs, and we do not want environmental pollution. But people will have fun during Diwali. They will celebrate with lights and burst firecrackers. Where is the problem with that?”
While acknowledging that firecrackers had been burst beyond the time limit prescribed by the Supreme Court, Adhikari sought to deflect criticism by pointing to action taken by the administration.
“Those complaining that sound crackers were burst for a few hours longer than the time stipulated by the Supreme Court should know that the Pollution Control Board and the police are taking action against such violations. I would request those complaining about firecrackers to also congratulate the state government for stopping DJs. I will not say that DJ incidents did not happen in remote corners, but I did not hear them blaring, at least near the roads,” he said.
Firecrackers can Cure Diseases, Says Bengal Minister, then Apologises
According to the Supreme Court’s directives, only green firecrackers were allowed to be burst between 8 pm and 10 pm on Diwali. However, statements by ministers, the West Bengal Police’s deletion of a post urging responsible Diwali celebrations, and the general perception that a BJP government would not impose restrictions on Hindu festivals had collectively sent out a clear message: When it came to celebrating a majoritarian festival, the rules could be bent, if not ignored altogether.
BJP leader and Tollygunge MLA Papia Adhikary said on Monday, “Our honourable chief minister has said that people will definitely burst firecrackers. How can we celebrate Kali Puja without firecrackers? But we will burst them in accordance with the instructions of the local police station. Also, many diseases can be prevented simply by lighting firecrackers.”
Although Adhikary later apologised and backtracked on her statement, claiming that the media had misinterpreted her remarks, the message had already got across.
A section of social media users also began targeting dissenting voices who tried to reason with their fellow citizens. A user named Partha Pratim Kundu, who describes himself as a wildlife photographer, asked in a post how elderlies, children and birds and animals survived in earlier times when there was no curb on firecrackers.
Another Facebook user, Chayan Mukherjee, who hailed the chief minister’s indulgence on firecrackers, claimed in a post that “most of the Indian environmentalists and human rights activists, as well as professors at various institutions, receive funding from outside to oppose the country’s development.”
Domkal’s CPI(M) MLA Mostafijur Rahaman Rana had urged people to celebrate Diwali as a festival of lights, without noise and loud firecrackers. BJP MLA Tarunjyoti Tiwari gave the issue a communal twist by asking whether the legislator would also call for a ‘bloodless Eid’.
State BJP leader Keya Ghosh also criticised Mostafijur Rahaman for advocating a noise-free and smoke-free Diwali.
The lone CPIM MLA of West Bengal had wished smokeless, soundless Diwali.

The political messaging was accompanied by widespread violations on the ground. A large section of the public openly flouted firecracker regulations. Almost all media outlets reported that loud firecrackers were burst throughout the night severely inconveniencing elderlies, children and also pets, birds and stray animals.
Kolkata’s AQI reached 623 around 11 pm on Sunday night, reported The telegraph. At 12.51 am on Monday, IQAir classified the city’s air quality as hazardous, recording an AQI of 532, with PM2.5 at 342 and PM10 at 405. Both particulate matter concentrations were several times higher than the WHO’s recommended limits.
Left with no other option, residents in several localities took matters into their own hands, protesting against the rampant bursting of firecrackers and intervening to stop it. Facebook user Anitesh Chakraborty narrated his experience in a post.
Chakraborty went up to a neighbouring apartment’s rooftop around 1.45 am to ask people bursting firecrackers to stop. While some residents supported his objection, others on nearby rooftops mocked him with gestures and taunts. Nevertheless, the intervention succeeded in stopping the firecrackers. He observed that the rooftops of apartment buildings had become spaces where people felt free to flout restrictions, and argued people to raise their voices against such violations.
According to a report by the Times of India, by 1 am, the West Bengal Pollution Control Board had received 84 noise-related complaints, while Kolkata Police had recorded 434 complaints.
Police rounded up 371 people for bursting illegal firecrackers, arresting 205 of them. Another 387 people were arrested for disorderly conduct. Several commentators pointed out that the most effective way to curb the use of illegal firecrackers was to stop their manufacture and sale. This year, only 238.6 kg of such products were seized, compared to 853 kg last year.
Kolkata’s high-rise buildings were particular hotspots for violations of firecracker and noise restrictions. Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari himself acknowledged that the rules could not be enforced in every high-rise apartment building, as the state did not have enough police personnel.
Even hospitals located in silence zones were not spared. According to a report by The Telegraph, areas near hospitals such as B C Roy, R G Kar, M R Bangur and Sishumangal also faced onslaught of loud firecrackers.
To Celebrate Responsibly or Not? Bengal Police in a Fix
Signs of this situation had emerged earlier, when the West Bengal Police deleted a firecracker awareness post within hours of publishing it, as previously reported by Alt News.
Published on the morning of November 5 with the caption, “Please celebrate responsibly. It’s our Diwali too!”, the AI-generated poster featured two stray cats and a dog shivering due to the loud noise of firecrackers. However, it was deleted within three hours.
The post’s comment section was flooded with threatening messages directed at police and familiar Right-wing arguments, including questions about whether the police would also call for a ‘bloodless Eid’ and why the police and administration interfered only in Hindu festivals.
Similarly, Delhi Police, too, deleted a firecracker awareness post, while the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) removed a video featuring actor Dia Mirza advocating for a pollution-free Diwali from its social media accounts. Both decisions followed social media outrage from BJP-RSS supporters who claimed that the posts hurt Hindu religious sentiments.
A similar message by AISA leader Neha Bora also faced backlash from the far-right social media ecosystem.

BJP MLAs Complain about Noise Levels
Although a section of the Right wing encouraged unrestrained celebrations during Diwali and Kali Puja in the name of upholding Hindu traditions, some voices within the BJP struck a different note.
BJP leader and Sonarpur Dakshin MLA Roopa Ganguly tagged Kolkata Police in a post on Facebook stating she was unable to sleep because of the noise of firecrackers. However, the post is no longer available now.
State urban development minister Agnimitra Paul was seen roaming around the city in a police vehicle, attempting to curb the firecracker menace.
Paul said, “Please think about other people. Consider the condition of the elderly and the sick. The firecrackers are bursting so loudly that my heart is trembling.”
However, these interventions came too little, too late. The ruling dispensation had, through its rhetoric and its reluctance to enforce restrictions, effectively given people a free hand to flout the law, with the environment and public health bearing the consequences.

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.
Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.
But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.
He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.
The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.
"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

Srinagar, Nov 19: Three leopard cubs have been found dead in the Waripora area of Tangmarg in north Kashmir’s Baramulla district within two days, with preliminary post-mortem findings pointing towards suspected poisoning, Wildlife Department officials said on Thursday.
Range Officer Tangmarg, Shahid Sultan, said two female leopard cubs were recovered on November 17 after Police Station Kunzar informed the Wildlife Department about their deaths at around 4:30 pm.
“Immediately after receiving the information, I dispatched a team from our Tangmarg control room to recover the carcasses. Both cubs were brought to the control room and subsequently sent for post-mortem examination,” Sultan told KNS.
He said another call was received from Police Station Kunzar regarding a third leopard cub found dead in the same area.
“I personally visited the spot, recovered the carcass and brought it to our control room. The post-mortem examination was conducted the following morning,” he said.
According to Sultan, the three dead animals included two female cubs and one male cub, all recovered from the same locality.
He said preliminary examinations conducted by veterinary doctors had raised suspicion of poisoning, although the exact cause of death remained unconfirmed.
“The doctors have indicated suspected poisoning based on their initial examination. However, it would be premature to reach any conclusion until the final reports are received,” Sultan said.
He said the department had decided to conduct further forensic examinations to establish whether the deaths resulted from deliberate poisoning, consumption of contaminated prey or some other cause.
“Samples have been collected from all three carcasses and are being sent for forensic analysis. We want to establish the actual cause of death with certainty,” he said.
Sultan disclosed that preliminary examination of the stomach contents suggested the cubs might have consumed a dog before their deaths.
“The doctors indicated that the leopards may have consumed a dog. We have directed that the relevant samples also be examined to determine whether the animal carried any toxin or disease,” he said.
He said Wildlife Department teams had also inspected the surrounding area to look for possible poisoned bait or other evidence that could explain the deaths.
“We searched the entire area yesterday to ascertain whether any poisoned bait had been placed there and subsequently consumed by the leopards. So far, nothing of that nature has been recovered,” he said.
The Range Officer said veterinary examination had not revealed any visible injuries or external signs of assault on the carcasses.
He said the preliminary findings suggested possible toxic exposure, but laboratory confirmation was necessary before determining the circumstances surrounding the deaths.
“The matter is under investigation. Once the forensic and final post-mortem reports are available, we will share the findings,” Sultan said.
Meanwhile, responding to concerns over leopard movement in residential areas, Sultan said Wildlife Department teams were continuing night patrols in vulnerable locations and had installed cages following reports of sightings.
He said no fresh leopard movement had been confirmed in one of the areas where a recent attack had been reported, although field teams remained deployed.
Referring to the attack on a child, Sultan said the department had been patrolling the locality for several days and making efforts to locate and tranquilise the animal.
He said the incident occurred in an orchard away from the family's residential area while the child had accompanied his mother, who was collecting twigs.
Sultan urged residents, particularly those living near orchards and forest areas, to exercise caution during early morning and evening hours when leopards are generally more active.
He advised parents not to leave children unattended in vulnerable areas and asked residents to avoid unnecessary movement after dark.
He also urged people to clear bushes and accumulated waste near residential houses, which could provide shelter or attract animals.
“Our teams are monitoring the situation and conducting regular patrols. Any further development will be communicated,” he said.

The Mundka monitoring station of the Delhi Pollution Control Board recorded a PM2.5 concentration of 3,744 µg/m³ at 2 am on the Diwali night, which is 60 times the standard measure. Yes, you read it right. 60 times. Reports emerged the next day that 93 of the top 100 cities with worst AQI were from India following Diwali celebrations on November 8. AIIMS pulmonologist Vijay Hadda told ANI on November 9, “I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival.”
In any country with a functional government, this would warrant the environment minister to at least make a statement, even if not take direct accountability. Not in India.
Union minister of environment, forest and climate change, Bhupender Yadav, has remained conspicuously silent on the country’s deteriorating air quality before or after Diwali.
From the days preceding Diwali to four days after the festival when this article is being written, Yadav neither issued a single public appeal urging citizens to responsibly engage in celebrations, nor used his social media handles to spread awareness about the environmental consequences of bursting firecrackers or to address the mounting pollution crisis affecting major parts of the country.
Did Bhupender Yadav go Missing from Public Platforms?
Far from it. Yadav remained active on social media throughout this period. Between November 1 and November 12, he made 29 posts on his X account. Not one of them addressed the worsening air pollution, deteriorating air quality across Indian cities, or the need for public awareness and precautionary measures.
The days before Diwali are also crucial because pollution levels skyrocketing on the day of the festival and immediately after has become an annual phenomenon. It is reasonable to expect the minister holding the environment and climate change portfolio to make a public appeal ahead of Diwali, more so because firecracker pollution has been a matter of contention and has reached the Supreme Court in recent years.
Clearly, the Alwar MP thinks otherwise.
Modi Reigns Supreme on Yadav’s X Timeline
On November 7, observed as Chhoti Diwali, and November 8, the main day of Diwali, Yadav shared nine posts. These included amplification of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Diwali greetings to citizens, Modi’s Diwali celebrations and interactions with jawans at the CoBRA (Commando Battalion for Resolute Action) Operations Base in Karanpur, in Chhattisgarh’s Bastar district, as well as Yadav’s own festive greetings.
