I'm a human doctor with human intelligence. But I sure do like my AI notetaker
Dr. Mara Gordon, a family physician in Camden, N.J., answers reader health questions monthly. Send in your question to: thrive@npr.org.
Question: My doctor has started recording our office visits with an artificial intelligence scribe. She says it helps write notes in my medical record. I said yes when she asked if I was comfortable with it, but in hindsight I feel a little freaked out. Should I be worried about AI listening in on my private medical conversations?
Answer: AI scribes are all the rage in medicine right now. Doctors are using them to take notes everywhere from the gynecologist's office to the emergency room.
I admit I've been an eager adopter in my own primary care practice. I use an app on my phone that records my conversation with a patient and then uses AI to write a preliminary summary for the medical record.
It saves me time. But more importantly, I like using it because it helps me focus more fully on my patient. When I use the AI scribe, I don't have to talk and take notes at the same time – I can actually make eye contact with my patient rather than staring at the computer screen.
But I totally get why people feel uncomfortable with the technology. I share my patients' concerns about privacy and how AI scribes might impact the doctor-patient relationship.
I also worry that corporate health systems will put pressure on doctors to use any time we save with an AI scribe to squeeze in even more patients.
And like many people, I worry that artificial intelligence might one day put me out of a job!
Here's what you need to know.
How AI scribes work
When I use an AI scribe during a primary care visit, I first ask the patient if they're comfortable using the service. If the patient says yes, I start recording using an app on my smartphone. I usually set it down on the desk in the exam room.
The scribe uses a technology called "automatic speech recognition" which records our conversation and automatically distinguishes between the doctor's and patient's voices. (Sometimes, when the patient has a family member accompanying him, the app needs to distinguish between three – or more! – voices.)
When the visit ends, the recording is then transcribed. A large language model – the kind of AI technology that powers ChatGPT, but specifically geared toward medicine – converts the raw transcript into a medical note. These notes follow a standard format that is specific to the speciality and the type of visit. They reflect what the patient told the doctor, physical exam findings, and the doctor's medical decision-making.
What is the software like?
There are lots of AI scribes on the market, ranging from products embedded within the electronic medical record to free apps a doctor can download on her phone. Most scribes use a smartphone's recording capabilities to "listen in" on the conversation, although there are some that use a desktop computer or a separate recording device.
I use my personal smartphone for this purpose, as do many physicians I know. I downloaded the AI scribe software as an app on my phone. This causes occasional hiccups. For example, I've gotten notification pings from my book club's group chat while recording a patient visit – which made me make sure to put the phone in "do not disturb" mode whenever I'm using it for patient care.
What about privacy?
Even though I use my personal phone for scribing patient visits, our conversations aren't stored on my device. They're uploaded directly to a HIPAA-compliant cloud, where the data is then transcribed into the AI-generated clinical note. Most scribe systems then delete the recording and the note after a set period of time.
HIPAA-compliance is an important feature of all AI scribe services. It means that the computer program was designed in accordance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a federal law designed to protect patients' privacy.
The software company is responsible for safeguarding the data at every step of the process, from recording to generating notes. AI scribe companies encrypt the data, control who has access to it, and have systems to protect against "data breaches." It also means these companies are liable if the data is leaked.
AI scribes can make mistakes
Recently, I saw a patient who had metastatic cancer. Despite multiple conversations about his diagnosis with me, his oncologist, and his surgeon, he did not believe he had cancer. I had even – with his permission – called his spouse to tell her what was going on. He still did not accept it.
This kind of tricky clinical situation comes up on occasion, and the AI scribe did not get it right. Rather than reflecting the nuances of our conversation, the note that the scribe produced simply said that the patient had been misdiagnosed.
I often catch other errors that the software makes, like mistaking a patient's gender or age. Alarmingly, these scribes are also known for mistaking "I do" statements with "I do not." In medicine, this can be critical: The difference between "I do have chest pain" and "I do not have chest pain" can be a matter of life and death.
To better understand how AI scribes can contribute to errors in the medical record, I talked to Dr. Eileen Kim, an assistant professor of internal medicine at the University of California San Diego. Kim specializes in clinical informatics and thinks a lot about how AI might shape the future of medicine.
"You have a doctor who's overburdened, seeing way too many patients," she said. "They have this AI tool that's offered to them that seems like a great solution, but they don't have time to adequately review everything. It goes into the chart. Then you have another AI tool that's reading through all these notes. But they're wrong. And then it just propagates errors throughout the chart."
In my work caring for patients, I come across erroneous information in the electronic health record all the time. It's hard to know how much is related to AI and how much is caused by human error. But I think Dr. Kim is right to worry that AI scribes might make the problem worse.
Who is liable for errors?
As the doctor caring for my patient, I'm ultimately the one responsible for the content of the AI-generated note, so I always read them carefully before clicking "sign" and adding them to the medical record. Most AI scribe software makes doctors sign a user agreement stating doctors are liable for everything they write in the medical record, even if a scribe helps them with it.
When the AI-generated notes are factually accurate, I almost always end up editing them to make my clinical decision-making more clear. I'm happy to have robots help me with my administrative tasks, but I still take pride in being a human doctor with human intelligence!
Health equity concerns
Many AI scribes can only be used with English-speaking patients. Health equity advocates say they fear this means unequal access to the technology, which could further widen health disparities.
For example, the scribe allows me to look more at my patient and less at my computer, which might make a patient feel more comfortable disclosing a stigmatizing health concern. Or the opposite might be true, too: A patient fearful that an AI company is "listening in" to our conversation might be afraid to share sensitive information, which in turn could affect the quality of their medical care.
Are the recordings ever used for anything other than scribing?
As a security feature, most AI scribe companies delete the recorded conversations within a set period of time. This is to protect patient privacy and also protect doctors from lawsuits. There is widespread concern in health care that the transcriptions could be used in medical malpractice lawsuits.
But some researchers call the recordings "digital gold" that could be used to assess the quality of AI-generated medical notes or even to study broader questions about physician-patient communication.
For example, I'd love to know how other doctors handle tricky conversations with patients who are fearful of vaccines. There are theoretical best practices, but analyzing hundreds of thousands of office-visit transcripts could help doctors learn what actually works best in real life.
For now, recordings of regular doctors' appointments — unless you've been enrolled in a research study — are not used for research purposes.
Can I opt-out?
Most of my patients readily agree when I ask if it's OK to use the AI scribe software, but occasionally my patients have concerns. They worry that the data isn't really secure or that it could be used to identify them in the future.
If a patient doesn't want to use the AI scribe, it's no problem. I just take notes on the computer while they talk — it's what I've done for years before the AI scribes became available.
Opting out of AI in medicine more broadly may prove to be tricky.
"It's just everywhere," said Kim, the clinical information specialist. "It would be impossible to separate. We use it throughout the healthcare system."
Software that relies on machine learning is used for billing, for clinical decision-making, and for communication between the doctor's office and patients.
AI is often used in risk calculators, like clinical tools that estimate a patient's risk of, say, heart disease based on variables like cholesterol levels and blood pressure. AI is also common in "early warning" systems that notify clinicians their patients might be vulnerable to high-risk conditions like sepsis, based on vital signs and lab values.
Kim says it's basically impossible for patients to opt out entirely from having AI involved in their medical care, "unless you're so healthy that no risk calculators ever come near you," she said.
Will AI replace my doctor?
I asked Kim — a primary care doctor like me — if she thought AI would replace us in the coming years. If the AI scribe could learn to ask the same questions I do, could it generate a treatment plan as good — or better — as the one I recommend?
Kim thought AI might change how patients experience primary care. (Possibly for the better, she said, if AI scribes allow doctors to focus more on their patients and less on the computer!)
But ultimately, she thinks human intelligence is critical in medicine.
"It looks really good because it's really good at sounding like us, and it's really good at pretending to be us," she said. "But it's still just pretending in a way. There's no real brain."
I agree. I think the AI scribe technology has the potential to do both good and harm for health care. But the core of medicine is the relationship I have with my patients. No robot can replace that.
Dr. Mara Gordon is a family physician in Camden, NJ. Find her newsletter Your Doctor Friend on Substack.

The Prince of Wales’s Earthshot prize will host its forthcoming annual awards ceremony at a venue owned by the billionaire Ambani family conglomerate, drawing criticism from conservationists over their fossil fuel businesses and their foundation’s controversial mega-zoo.
A spokesperson for the Earthshot prize, which awards £1m to five winners every year to invest in conservation work, confirmed to the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay that this year’s ceremony will be held at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on 17 November.
The venue is part of Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, which also owns Jamnagar, the world’s biggest oil refinery in Gujarat on India’s western coast. The group’s philanthropic arm funds the 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo Vantara, which was founded by Mukesh’s son Anant Ambani and inaugurated by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, last year. The zoo is embroiled in a long-running controversy over its vast collection of more than 150,000 animals, which reportedly includes some of the world’s most endangered species – from the radiated tortoise, native to Madagascar, to the Spix’s macaw, endemic to north-eastern Brazil but now considered extinct in the wild.
Megan Carr, of the Wildlife Animal Protection Forum South Africa (WAPFSA), warned that using a venue owned by Reliance “could lend an unearned environmental prestige to a corporate group currently under question by the global conservation community”.
Conservation groups, including WAPFSA, have raised concerns about the speed with which Vantara has amassed so many animals, and about how they were sourced. The site, near the family’s oil refinery, houses more than 2,000 species of animals.
This week, the 32-member committee that governs Cites, the UN-administered body that regulates trade in endangered species, requested that India submit another report on the steps it is taking to address concerns relating to its imports of protected species.
The committee also requested the Cites secretariat review 11 cases where there are unresolved questions over how animals were sent to Vantara.
Joanna Swift, the executive director of communications at the Earthshot prize, said it had not sought a philanthropic partnership for its award ceremony venue and that it was paying the standard commercial rate to rent the space.
“The [Jio World Convention Centre] was selected because it allowed us to host the event in Mumbai while meeting the practical requirements of an event of this size. It offers world-class facilities, technical infrastructure and experience of hosting major international events, including environmental ones,” Swift said. “In February this year, JWCC hosted the first ever Mumbai climate week.”
Vantara, Kensington Palace and JWCC have been approached for comment.
Vantara has previously denied allegations of wildlife trafficking and says its purpose is “to rescue wild animals in distress, provide treatment along with lifelong care, and rehabilitate those fit for the wild”.
“With regulatory approval, we also breed select endangered or extinct-in-the-wild species, serving as a modern Noah’s Ark to ensure their survival under human care and restore wild populations through reintroduction,” Vantara says on its website.
Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo of allegations that animals had been acquired illegally or mistreated.
A later Cites fact-finding mission raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.
Susan Cheyne, the vice-chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s small apes section, said that Vantara’s model has not yet been shown to support conservation and “may be driving demand for wild animals in trade”.
“For gibbons and other primates, this matters a great deal. Moving animals out of their range countries into a private facility does nothing for wild populations unless there is a transparent, credible plan for those animals: for welfare, for any conservation breeding with clear goals, and for return to range states where that is possible. Real rescue and sanctuary work for primates is done by underfunded centres in range countries,” Cheyne said.
Daniela Freyer, co-founder of the German NGO Pro Wildlife, added: “Our planet is increasingly threatened by the overexploitation of wildlife and by climate change driven by fossil fuels. This week, the Cites Standing Committee, which oversees international wildlife trade, decided to keep India under its compliance procedure, as questions remain about the origin of some of the world’s rarest animals imported to Vantara. A prize whose goals include protecting nature and fixing our climate should be careful not to lend its reputation to these questions.”
Vantara had sought to lobby the UK, the chair of this week’s Cites meetings, attempting to persuade officials to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara, the Guardian and Mongabay reported earlier this month. Ministers were advised not to engage formally with Vantara, internal documents revealed.
The Earthshot prize, founded by Prince William in 2020, is billed as the most prestigious environmental award. William appeared on the BBC’s Graham Norton show last month to promote the prize, saying it was designed to “talk about urgency and optimism together”.
Swift said that it was vital to host an edition of the Earthshot prize in India.
“Mumbai is the sixth largest city on earth. It is home to exceptional environmental solutions and the people behind them, with an impact felt in India and around the world. Spotlighting progress like this, to the largest possible audience, is why the Earthshot prize exists,” Swift said.

Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex CEO
- Published
Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, backed the effort.
Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, adding to a list of supporters who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign.
Fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return.
But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in bringing him back after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs, including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy.
Meanwhile on Monday, the Trump administration said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from companies like Nvidia.
The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance. Since his departure, supporters have launched an online petition demanding his return.
Musk and Sweeny are among the more than 175,000 who have signed the open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.
The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by a make up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive.
They expressed concerns the ex-Nvidia boss "was removed without meaningful due process".
President Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.
"I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House.
The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips to train AI models.
The move came ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jingping this week.
The new rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted to China.
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy. However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.
The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times, external, though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.
The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.
President Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".
Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
'China plays games with us, so we play games with China'
On Monday, Trump said he did not know whether the women Huang had an affair with was a spy for China.
"They say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't, I don't know that," he said.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.
The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.
'A handshake with Jensen'
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.
"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X., external
"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."
But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".
Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.
Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.
In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".
Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.
For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

Recent news from Karnataka regarding the seizure of fake cancer drugs from a licensed distributor during a raid has understandably sparked concerns. Counterfeit drugs for serious conditions like cancer are a sensational and emotive issue, often provoking a demand for severe action, including death sentences for those involved in the distribution.
However, in this case, there is a serious reason to doubt the authenticity of the news reports about the recent seizure since the Government of Karnataka has not confirmed that indeed counterfeit cancer drugs were seized in the raid. While a purported list of the drugs seized was circulated on social media, it only contained antibiotics, not cancer drugs. The silence of the State Health Department on the news reports about the counterfeit drugs is insensitive to the dread and uncertainty being faced by patients receiving cancer treatment, not to mention the doubts of those wondering whether they lost their loved ones to cancer because of counterfeit drugs. The Department should clear the air on the matter by issuing a press release or holding a press conference. If counterfeit cancer drugs were indeed seized, the government should release the names of the drugs and the hospitals possibly affected. If not, it should at least communicate the same to the public. Letting the uncertainty hang without authoritative answers is not in public interest.

A Senate committee chaired by Ted Cruz (R-Texas) voted today to approve a Federal Communications Commission nominee, despite accusations that the nominee gave false testimony about her work as a legal advisor for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. Democrats attempted to prevent a quorum by not showing up, but Cruz proceeded with a Republican-only vote.
All 15 Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted to approve Trump nominee Danielle Thumann, while the committee’s 13 Democrats were absent. “We’re going to be doing our job today, even if the Democrats refuse to show up to do theirs,” Cruz said at today’s hearing.
Nominees are vetted in committees first, and then seek require majority approval from the Senate. Republicans are hoping to get Thumann confirmed before Democrats take Senate control in January.
Although the Senate Commerce Committee generally requires one minority member to be present for nomination votes, a spokesperson for Cruz said Senate rules allow the nomination to be advanced for a vote in the entire chamber. A spokesperson for Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), the top Democrat on the committee, said in response that “since 2005, Commerce Committee rules required that a quorum include one member of the minority for official action on bill, resolution, or nomination.”
Technically, the committee has operated with no rules during Cruz’s chairmanship because Cruz “failed to pass committee rules” for the current session of Congress, Cantwell’s spokesperson said. “Nevertheless, in practice it has operated in line with rules from the last Congress (and this provision, specifically, since 2005), including that a quorum with a member of the minority party must be present for official action on a nomination or legislation. False testimony allegation

Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump, California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway.
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.
Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep. Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News.
Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health, often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

The High Court of Karnataka has advised the security and police organisations to prioritise the mental health and well-being of personnel entrusted with firearms while asking the authorities to examine existing policies and take appropriate steps to strengthen the mental health and welfare measures for their personnel.
Justice Suraj Govindaraj passed the order while quashing the criminal proceedings against a 37-year-old CISF Sub-Inspector for attempting to kill herself in 2022 by using her service pistol while on duty in Mangaluru. She had attempted to end her life following years of severe mental distress over her inability to conceive a child due to a blocked fallopian tube.
Allowing her petition, the court set aside the lower court’s order and discharged her from the offence under Section 309 of the IPC (attempt to commit suicide). The court ruled that Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, creates a mandatory presumption of severe stress, placing the burden on the prosecution to prove otherwise. Since no such evidence was produced, the court held that continuing the trial would be an abuse of the judicial process.
‘Grief and anxiety’
“Personnel serving in these forces are also human beings. They have families, relationships, responsibilities and personal problems. They experience grief, anxiety, financial difficulties, marital discord, illness in the family and other difficulties common to human life. Wearing a uniform or undergoing rigorous training does not make them immune to such problems,” the court said.
Further, the court said that “the expectation that they must remain available for duty at all times and discharge their responsibilities, come rain or shine, irrespective of their personal circumstances or mental condition, requires a change in institutional thinking.”
The concerned organisations must ensure that accessible and confidential counselling, professional mental healthcare and timely treatment are available to personnel at all levels, including those posted in remote and difficult locations, the court said.
Signals of distress
Commanding and supervisory officers, the court emphasised, must be sensitised to recognise signs of distress and facilitate appropriate assistance, and personnel who undergo treatment or experience mental health difficulties must also receive suitable support for rehabilitation and return to duty, based on professional assessment.
“The welfare of personnel and the security of the public are not competing considerations. A force which looks after the mental and physical well-being of its personnel is better equipped to maintain discipline, operational readiness and public safety, the court said.

As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
- Published
Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.
For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.
Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.
The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.
For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.
Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.
Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.
Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.
Democrats, who will control Congress come January, have made their position clear. Last Wednesday top Democrat Ted Lieu told Politico the Trump administration had been "1,000%" too deferential to Nvidia, putting national security at risk, while fellow Democrat Zoe Lofgren suggested Congress would now be more likely to restrict sales of AI chips to China.
The BBC has approached the White House for comment.
Beijing's foreign ministry had described the spy claims as a "smear against China".
"The US should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades," spokesperson Mao Ning said last week.
The ministry also seemed keen to keep the meeting on track, saying the two countries had kept "close communication regarding interactions between the two heads of state".
Another 'spy balloon' incident?
For the last year, Trump and Xi have been seeking to stabilise relations after a damaging tariff war that almost brought trade between the two countries to a standstill.
The Trump administration's decision to permit sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China in late 2025 was seen as evidence that both sides were searching for areas of co-operation, even while competition intensified.
It was a rare move given Washington had spent years trying to limit China's access to the most advanced chips.
Many in the US have long viewed these chips as a national security issue, arguing they could strengthen China's military and surveillance capabilities. Jensen Huang, who rejects that claim, advocated lifting bans on the export of high-performing chips to China. Beijing argues the restrictions are an attempt to contain its rise.
Now that opening may be under threat.
History has taught Beijing and Washington that spy scandals rarely remain confined to the intelligence world.
Analysts in China already see echoes of an incident in 2023 when a suspected surveillance balloon drifted through the skies over the US before an American fighter jet shot it down. Beijing insisted it was a civilian meteorological airship that had strayed off course.
But a planned trip by then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken was cancelled and communication between the two governments deteriorated sharply.
The incident showed how quickly a security dispute could overwhelm diplomatic efforts and push relations into a deep freeze.
"The mere passage of a balloon sent American public opinion and politicians into a state of high alert, as if a "Chinese threat" were looming directly overhead," said the state media outlet, the Global Times this week as it made a direct comparison with the Nvidia scandal.
"No-one on the US side has ever apologised or taken responsibility for the genuine damage this caused to US-China relations," it added.
The state-run outlet also questioned why the Nvidia story had emerged so soon after "the hard-won detente" between Beijing and Washington, following a meeting between the two countries' leaders in September.
"Is someone behind the scenes pushing an agenda and stirring up confrontation?" it asked.
Trump-Xi summit unlikely to collapse
Both Trump and Xi have significant incentives to keep talking.
China's economy remains under pressure and is increasingly reliant on exports. Xi needs trade to keep flowing and this meeting is a key stepping stone to replacing the current trade truce that is due to expire in January.
Meanwhile Trump has repeatedly touted his close relationship with Xi and argued that maintaining dialogue is essential to managing competition between the two powers.
The US president is in his last two years and faces an uphill struggle to pass domestic legislation after the midterms. To counter this, he could be looking for some foreign policy wins.
He may also hope for Xi's help to end the war in the Middle East.
Neither side will want to be discussing intelligence concerns and technology controls instead of trade, investment and economic co-operation.
The summit is also being carefully choreographed by Beijing to show off its technological prowess in Shenzhen - a deeply symbolic choice of city.
It's home to some of the country's biggest tech companies and has become a showcase for Beijing's ambitions in AI and advanced manufacturing.
Also, given Washington's tighter restrictions on advanced chips, Beijing has options for retaliation.
One of its most powerful tools is its dominance of key rare earth minerals. China processes much of the world's supply for materials that are used in everything from electric vehicles and smartphones to military equipment.
Analysts have long warned that technological restrictions can trigger a cycle of retaliation in which each side reaches for its strongest economic leverage.
That would shift the current trend of US-China relations from engagement back towards mutual suspicion.

A video showing Akhilesh Yadav speaking to the media is being shared (here, here, here) with the claim that he was drunk while addressing reporters. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video shows Akhilesh Yadav in an intoxicated state while addressing the media.
Fact: The viral video is altered. The original video shows him speaking normally, and the audio has been altered to make his speech sound unclear. When the original video is heard at 0.75x speed, the audio matches the viral video. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to the same video, uploaded on 19 August 2026, on the official Facebook account of the Samajwadi Party. In this video, Akhilesh Yadav speaks in his normal tone. From the 50-second mark, he makes the same remarks heard in the viral video, but without the slurred tone.
Further, when we listened to the original video at 0.75x speed, we found that the audio matched the viral video. You can watch and listen to our edited video below.
We also found videos of the same interaction uploaded on 19 August 2026 by news agencies Bharat Samachar, IANS, and PTI. The microphones of these news agencies are also visible in the viral video. These videos show Akhilesh Yadav speaking to reporters after attending a Bhagwat Katha in Lucknow. He is seen speaking normally, without the slurred tone heard in the viral clip.
To sum up, this video claiming to show Akhilesh Yadav addressing the media in an intoxicated state is doctored.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows police officers beating two Muslim men, Junaid and Asif, with sticks, parading them on the road, and taking them away in Uttar Pradesh in connection with a harassment case. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Uttar Pradesh police beating two Muslim men with sticks and parading them on the road in connection with a harassment case.
Fact: The video shows police officers beating and parading Sahil Bhagoria and Sachin alias Ayush, who were arrested for opening fire outside the house of Sujal Khare in Valmiki Nagar, Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh, over an old dispute. Jitendra Solanki, sub-inspector at Madhav Nagar police station, confirmed to Factly that both accused are Hindus and that the incident has no communal angle and the video is unrelated to Uttar Pradesh. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple media reports (here, here, and here) featuring the same visuals. According to these reports, at around 3:30 am on 07 October 2026, Sahil Bhagoria and Sachin alias Ayush opened fire outside the house of Sujal Khare, a resident of Valmiki Nagar, Ujjain, over an old dispute. They were subsequently paraded from Valmiki Nagar to Desai Nagar, during which police officers beat them with sticks and pipes. A pistol was also seized from them. Jitendra Solanki, sub-inspector at Madhav Nagar police station, said police arrested both accused after CCTV footage of the incident surfaced. He further stated that the two men were criminals and had been arrested following a siege.
We then contacted Jitendra Solanki, sub-inspector at Madhav Nagar police station, who told Factly that both the accused are Hindus and that the incident has no communal angle. He dismissed the viral claim, clarifying that the video is from Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh, and not Uttar Pradesh.
To sum up, a video of police beating and parading two men in Madhya Pradesh is falsely shared as a Uttar Pradesh incident with a communal spin.

Veteran industry exec Tendo Nagenda is joining Proximity Media, as its new President. In this role, Nagenda will oversee all aspects of creative development and production across the company’s film, television and nonfiction divisions, reporting directly to the founders, to advance Proximity’s creative strategy and deliver their slate of projects. Nagenda will assume the role on November 30th.
“Tendo has spent his career working alongside talented filmmakers, championing original ideas and helping make projects that resonate with audiences around the world,” said Proximity co-founders Ryan Coogler, Zinzi Coogler and Sev Ohanian, Founders of Proximity Media, in a joint statement. “As Proximity continues to grow across film, television and nonfiction, we’re excited to have his creative instincts and experience helping guide this next chapter. He shares our belief in the power of storytelling to connect people, challenge perspectives and create meaningful impact, and we’re thrilled to welcome him to the team.”
As President, he will oversee Proximity’s creative divisions, guiding projects from ideation through production while helping shape the company’s broader creative and business strategy. The heads of Film, Television and Nonfiction will report directly to Nagenda, who will work alongside Terra Potts, who oversees Marketing, Operations and the In Proximity podcast, and Proximity Co-Founder Ludwig Göransson, who oversees Music.
Watch on Deadline
“I’m honored and excited to join Ryan, Zinzi, Sev and the entire Proximity team,” said Nagenda. “Their commitment to ambitious, meaningful storytelling reflects everything I’ve always believed in, and I look forward to building on what they’ve created, collaborating with extraordinary filmmakers and creators, and bringing compelling new stories to audiences around the world.”
Nagenda previously served as Vice President of Original Film at Netflix, where he helped build the streamer’s original film slate and oversaw a range of acclaimed projects, including Spike Lee’s Da 5 Bloods, The Old Guard, Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom, The Harder They Fall and Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery. Prior to Netflix, he served as Executive Vice President of Production at Walt Disney Studios, overseeing films across the studio’s live-action slate, including Beauty and the Beast, Cinderella, Saving Mr. Banks, Mulan, A Wrinkle in Time and Queen of Katwe.
In 2022, Nagenda founded 10 by Ten Entertainment, a production company focused on developing and producing original stories from distinctive and underrepresented perspectives. His first produced feature, The Book of Clarence, written and directed by Jeymes Samuel, was released theatrically by Sony Pictures in January 2024.
The appointment comes as Proximity Media continues to expand its slate across film, television and nonfiction. The company is behind the critically acclaimed blockbuster Sinners, which grossed more than $365 million worldwide, as well as Creed III and Academy Award-winning Judas and the Black Messiah. On the television side, Proximity recently secured a series greenlight for its highly anticipated reimagining of The X-Files for Hulu, Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel attached to star. The company also recently entered into a multiyear television deal with Netflix to develop an exclusive slate of scripted and unscripted projects. Its nonfiction projects include National Geographic’s Hurricane Katrina: Race Against Time, which became the network’s most-watched U.S. streaming title, along with Stephen Curry: Underrated, Homeroom and Anthem.

AI healthtech startup August AI has raised $12 Mn from Accel, Peak XV Partners, and Claypond Capital to expand its healthcare assistant’s ability to book appointments, find medicines, and follow up on insurance claims for users in the US. Founder and CEO Anuruddh Mishra announced the fundraise on social media alongside the rollout of the new capabilities. The startup claims to have helped 10 Mn people understand their health through its AI companion. The development comes after Inc42 exclusively reported in August that the startup was in talks to raise around $4 Mn from Peak XV Partners, with the terms still under discussion. August AI previously raised $3 Mn in seed funding from Accel and Claypond Capital, the family office of Manipal Group chairman Ranjan Pai, in October 2025. Founded in 2022 by IIT-BHU alumnus Mishra, August AI initially built an AI-powered health companion to help users understand symptoms, prescriptions, medications, and medical reports. The platform also offers personalised health insights, nutrition guidance, and medication reminders. It is now extending its offering to tasks patients must complete to access care, from finding a doctor covered by their insurance to locating prescribed medicines. According to Mishra, the AI agent calls doctors’ offices, checks availability, and books the earliest available appointment with the user’s approval. It can also call nearby pharmacies to compare medicine availability and prices, review medical bills for potential errors and savings, and follow up with insurers and hospitals on denied claims. The new capabilities are available in beta in the US, with users able to join a waitlist for access. Mishra said August AI spent 24,286 minutes on hold while finding in-network doctor appointments for early users over the past few weeks. This included 366 minutes for a single user. He also claimed the platform helped another user save $1,255 on an insurance claim. The administrative assistant builds on the startup’s existing US healthcare offering. In September, August AI launched August Care, a $39-a-month membership offering telehealth consultations, discounted laboratory tests, prescription services, and insurance guidance. The company says licensed physicians make clinical decisions within the service. August AI’s expansion comes amid increased investor interest in startups using AI to manage healthcare workflows, both for patients and providers. In September, Bengaluru-based Prodoc AI raised a seed round to develop agentic AI solutions for hospital workflows, including patient engagement, appointment conversion and care coordination. Meanwhile, US-based Confido Health raised $12.5 Mn in an extension round led by Z47 in October to expand its AI agents for appointment scheduling, insurance verification, prescription refills and other administrative tasks.

Shevchenko accuses Mudryk camp of 'baseless slander'
- Published
Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko has accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for an employee of the country's football federation to "falsely" take the blame for the winger's positive drugs test.
Tottenham winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.
The 25-year-old said he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.
In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk firmly placed the blame for his 20-month absence from the sport on his national association, which has led to Shevchenko's response.
In a statement, former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko, who is now president of the UAF, said Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally" and called on the player to retract his words.
He added: "His representatives repeatedly approached the UAF with a proposal to find an employee who would falsely take responsibility for the meldonium found in his doping sample.
"The UAF refused, as such a proposal contradicts the principles of our work."
He added that "numerous investigations and audits" undertaken as part of the case were unable to shed light on when or where the substance entered Mudryk's system.
In his interview Mudryk also claimed Shevchenko had offered him little support, blamed the association for leaks that emerged during the case and said its handling of the matter delayed his return to football.
However, Shevchenko went on to say that national team staff had complied with a request from Chelsea not to provide Mudryk with any medication while on international duty.
And he also challenged the former Shakhtar Donetsk forward to provide evidence "to back up his words".
"Head coach Serhiy Rebrov also approved for Mykhailo to have two of his personal specialists work with him at the training camps," Shevchenko added.
"These were the exact people who monitored his regimen and recovery, and helped him with his daily routine.
"The UAF completed all necessary checks in this case. We provided Mudryk's representatives with the information they requested and remained in contact with those working on the case.
"I know the people who have worked with the national team for many years. I trust them, because throughout all this time there have been no incidents in the team that could make anyone doubt their professionalism.
"If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it. If no such evidence exists, I expect him to publicly retract his accusations and apologise to the people whose honesty and professionalism he has called into question."
BBC Sport has contacted Mudryk's representatives for comment.

By Moke Corder & Molly Quell
The Hague – In a landmark judgement, the United Nations’ top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation and ordered the Southeast Asian nation to allow people who fled the violence to return home.
International Court of Justice President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention.”
The 15-judge panel of the World Court, which included Navi Pillay, the respected international jurist who won the Nobel Peace Prize last month, rejected Myanmar’s defence that the 2017 campaign was a legitimate operation against insurgents.
Iwasawa said that “the court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers.”
The decision marks the first time the court has ruled that a state committed genocide and comes as the World Court also is handling genocide allegations linked to the Gaza conflict and the war in Ukraine.
The atmosphere following the hearing was electric, with lawyers and members of the Rohingya, some of whom had travelled thousands of miles (kilometres) to attend the reading, hugging and crying.
“This is a great day for the Rohingya, and it is a great day for all oppressed people, everywhere, who have been told that their suffering does not count and that no one is listening,” said Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who sat in the court’s ornate, wood-paneled Great Hall of Justice for the nearly three-hour reading of the ruling.
The court also ordered Myanmar to commit to reparations including allowing Rohingya “safe, voluntary and dignified return to their place of residence.” It ordered Myanmar to investigate, prosecute and punish people found to have committed genocidal acts and to pay compensation to Rohingya. The amount will be decided in later court proceedings.
The court said that evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya.
The Muslim-majority African nation of Gambia launched the proceedings at the International Court of Justice in 2019, asking it to rule that Myanmar has breached the 1948 Genocide Convention, order the nation to end any illegal activities targeting the Rohingya and ensure those responsible for genocide are punished.
Brutal counterinsurgency campaign triggered the killings and expulsions
In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched what it called a clearance campaign in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The campaign led to accusations that security forces committed mass rapes and killings and burned thousands of homes.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred, the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part.”
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
The court’s rulings are final and legally binding, but it has no way to enforce them beyond reporting noncompliance to the UN Security Council.
The case could impact genocide allegations elsewhere
In a previous judgment in 2007, the court said that Serbia “violated the obligation to prevent genocide” in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when Bosnian Serb forces murdered some 8,000 mostly Muslim men and boys in the Bosnian town.
Judges at The Hague-based court have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.
“The International Court of Justice’s landmark ruling is long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military. The ruling also provides a significant precedent for victims of genocide, and other grave crimes, across the world in their own quest for justice,” said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch. ~AP

Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
- Published
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.
Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.
In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.
Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."
But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".
Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".
Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.
Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.
Zelensky and the three European leaders - Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron - were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."
The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".
"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.
He also said any attempts to divide Europe into sphere of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.

Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m after row over its Nazi history

Auction house Sotheby's has sold a painting by Vincent van Gogh for a record $190.4m (£144.8m).
The sale of Châtaigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom") shatters the renowned artist's previous auction record of $117.2 million set in 2022.
The historic sale in New York on Wednesday comes after an eleventh-hour agreement was reached to resolve a dispute regarding claims the art piece was previously sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.
Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Van Gogh's life. It is considered one of the most important works of art from that period to remain in private hands, according to Sotheby's.
It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.
The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.
Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.
Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.
A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.
"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.
Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.
It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.
The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.
Four other owners then had the painting.
The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.
The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.
“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”
So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.
1. Start with a presumption of innocence–or negligence
The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.
As the head of Internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One’s default position should be that it isn’t a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”
Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the Internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”
2. Look at status updates from organizations that might be involved
In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.
In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.
On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.
It can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech company may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.
Another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with issues. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products, Google Workspace, telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.
3. Check trusted sources of network data
When a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the Internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying issue. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon—but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net. Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his socialmediaaccounts.
When IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng says. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy update, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off Internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.
Even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what’s actually going on,” she says.
4. Look for claims of responsibility
Most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.
Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious Internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. In other cases, like the NotPetya or WannaCry worms—two of the worst cyberattacks in history—the hackers’ self-perpetuating code left behind ransom messages on machines that quickly spread on social media as the attacks unfolded. Ideological “hacktivist” groups—or state-sponsored hackers working for military or intelligence agencies but posing as hacktivists—also often take credit for their cyberattacks on platforms like X, Telegram, or their own websites. These messages then quickly spread to social media and through news reports.
Even these statements, however, should be taken as just another significant data point: Hacker groups exaggerate, misdirect, or lie when it serves their purposes. And some significant mass hacking incidents—such as the Mirai attack on the Internet infrastructure company Dyn in 2016 that took down thousands of websites—have been accompanied by no public message at all from the hackers responsible.
In cases where neither the perpetrator of a hacking incident nor its target has confirmed the attack, confirmation can sometimes come first from a government agency—such as the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency—or even from threat intelligence researchers at private cybersecurity firms. Government and industry investigators sometimes post their findings to their websites or share them with media, but it often takes days, weeks, or even months to come to confirmed conclusions. Hence, step five.
5. Sit tight and reserve judgment
If all these other measures of determining the cause of an outage don’t offer a clear understanding of the situation, the best approach may be patience. “It’s going to get a little conclusive at some point,” Madory says. “Sometimes you just have to just sit and wait.”
Aside from the time it takes for companies to admit to their screwups—or hackers to claim a win—the length of an outage can also sometimes offer a clue to its cause. A faulty update, power outage, or cascading bug can often be resolved quickly. Determined hackers who have maximized their damage, who shift tactics to outsmart defenders, or who may still be in a network they’ve breached can cause far longer and more severe outages. “A rollback takes minutes or hours,” Tomé says, referring to reverting to older code as a fix for a faulty update that introduces a bug. “Ransomware takes days or sometimes even weeks.”
In other words, as with all breaking news, when facts are in short supply, it’s better to maintain skepticism about early rumors or conspiracy theories and wait for more concrete evidence.
In the information vacuum that precedes that evidence, it can be easy to see connections between events that may just be coincidences. What are the odds, you may ask, that five major IT outages occurred on a sequential Thursday, Friday, Monday, and Tuesday?
For Doug Madory, who tracks those network outages every day of the week, that string of failures may just be a sign of the increasing complexity of technology—and how fundamentally our civilization has come to depend on it. “For better or worse, modern society is completely mediated through Internet-based services. They have outages from time to time. And that’s a reality I don’t think we’ll ever completely eliminate,” Madory says.
“If you’re immersed in that world of looking at outages for years on end, then they don’t really surprise you,” he adds. “You just try to understand what’s different about each one. And maybe what we can learn from it.”

Exposure to extreme heat during pregnancy can lead to severe outcomes, including preterm birth, stillbirth and congenital abnormalities in newborns, prompting experts at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) to highlight maternal health risks and call for targeted adaptation strategies.
The issue comes into focus as countries at COP31 prepare to discuss progress towards the Global Goal on Adaptation, a framework to help nations develop key adaptation measures, including those needed to address the health impacts of climate change.
However, translating growing recognition of climate-related health risks into action remains a challenge, particularly in the absence of adequate financial support.
According to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), only about one per cent of formal climate finance under its financial mechanism is currently directed towards health.
The broader issue of adaptation finance for developing nations is also expected to feature prominently in discussions in the coming days.
Speaking to PTI on the sidelines of COP31, Alan Dangour, Director of Climate and Health at the Wellcome Trust, said the foundation is seeking to highlight the evidence of heat-related impacts on pregnant women through three key areas -- elevating the issues as a risk for women, developing guidelines and preparing health systems.
“We have three key points: recognising that pregnant women are a particularly vulnerable group when it comes to climate-driven extreme heat, developing guidelines to help nurses, midwives and doctors respond to the challenges pregnant women face during heatwaves, and prepare health systems for a new world shaped by climate change, and identify the most vulnerable people so they are protected,” Dangour said.
He said pregnant women were not always recognised as a particularly vulnerable group and stressed that health systems must specifically account for their needs and risks during heatwaves.
“At the moment they are not recognised as such, and they need to be included in clinical guidelines. When it comes to data, we are keen that countries record the impacts of climate change on pregnant women and then work out how their guidelines and processes can protect them,” he said.
“That evidence is important because we can see what works and what doesn’t in different parts of the world, and share that knowledge,” he said.
Former World Health Organisation (WHO) chief scientist Soumya Swaminathan stressed the importance of highlighting the issue at COP31, saying the health impacts of climate change were already being felt and required immediate action.
“It is good that for the last three COPs or so we have had a day focused on health and climate, because everyone is increasingly recognising that the health impacts of climate change are already happening and need immediate action. They are also hitting certain vulnerable groups disproportionately, and pregnant women are one of them,” Swaminathan told PTI.
Citing studies showing that exposure to extreme heat can affect pregnant women's health, pregnancy outcomes and the health of newborns, she said the WHO had recently released a document identifying pregnant women as a high-risk group and recommending measures countries should take to protect them.
She also stressed the need to integrate climate and health data, saying policymakers must urgently begin linking exposure to extreme heat and air pollutants with their effects on human health.
“When heat and air pollution occur together in the same place, the impacts are three times as high as from either risk factor alone. India has many places with both heat and bad air pollution, so we must start looking at these data and correlating exposure to climatic and weather variables, such as heat and pollutants, with health outcomes,” the former WHO chief scientist told PTI.
Swaminathan said there was an urgent need for a research programme to address the issue, adding that sufficient evidence was already available to warrant action. She also called for the government's and states' Maternal and Child Health Programme to factor in heat exposure and take proactive and preventive measures to minimise its impact on pregnant women.
Youssef Nassef, Director of the Adaptation Programme at UN Climate Change, said the first 1,000 days, from conception until a child turns two, were considered the most critical period, as climate-related harm could begin even before birth.
“A lot of what we're talking about in terms of climate impacts generally, but heat in particular, has a severe impact on maternal health, on newborn babies. Unfortunately, in climate finance, about 1 per cent of formal climate finance under the financial mechanism goes to health. There is an incongruence between the needs, the demand and the supply,” he said.
Bhavreen Kandhari, an environmentalist and the co-founder of the ‘Warrior Moms’ movement, underscored that heatwaves have had a significant impact on pregnant women, particularly those living in more vulnerable areas or working in more vulnerable occupations, such as daily-wage workers, construction workers and farmers.
“Daily-wage workers, for instance, have to earn a living. They have to continue working because they simply cannot afford to stop. There is no looking back for them. Vulnerable mothers and other at-risk groups are not thinking about the future, but simply trying to survive this particular season, or, at most, looking ahead to the next one,” she said.
