A cyberattack using artificial intelligence targeted the EU in October, official says
An official in Brussels says a cyberattack using software powered by artificial intelligence targeted the European Union in October
BRUSSELS -- A cyberattack carried out with artificial intelligence targeted the European Union in October, an official in Brussels said on Thursday, and some of the bloc's digital tools remain offline.
The official did not elaborate on the cyberattack, or say who could have been behind it. It was the first time the 27-member bloc reported a cyberattack using an AI tool.
“AI-assisted tools can be used and especially misused to detect vulnerabilities," said Thomas Regnier, spokesperson for the European Commission, the executive body of the 27-nation EU.
"Indeed we can confirm that this was done with AI tools," he added. "We have seen many global cyberattacks recently, and of course no one is immune to this.”
Regnier said the EU first detected the incident on Oct. 22 and that authorities launched an investigation while also imposing “preventative measures."
Politico first reported the incidents. The news site said the attack lasted at least 10 days and affected translation and reimbursement tools as well as databases used for salaries and timesheets. Regnier declined to confirm that report.
“We temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored," Regnier said. So far, however, Regnier said that “we have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting commission staff as a whole.”
The EU agency CERT-EU oversees the digital security of the bloc’s various institutions, which all together employ about 40,000 people just in Brussels.

Gilead Sciences said on Monday it had signed royalty-free deals with three generic drugmakers to make its experimental Ebola prevention drug available in 127 mainly low- and lower-middle-income countries if it succeeds in trials and wins regulatory approvals.
The deals with Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, Eva Pharma and Ferozsons Laboratories cover obeldesivir, and include all African countries reporting cases in the current Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak. Obeldesivir has shown activity against several Ebola-related viruses in preclinical studies but is not approved for any use in any country.
A late-stage trial is testing the drug in people at high risk after exposure. The deals are intended to line up manufacturing and supply before trial results and regulatory filings.
Gilead is also expanding remdesivir licences to cover Ebola-related diseases if trial results are positive and regulators approve the drug. The company has donated more than 38,000 remdesivir vials to the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and Kenya, including more than 2,000 recently sent to Kenya for investigational treatment and post-exposure prevention.
Remdesivir is not approved to treat or prevent Ebola Bundibugyo disease, and its clinical effectiveness has not been established.

It has been a week of outages. From big tech giants like Microsoft and Apple to JPMorgan Chase and the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), high-profile disruptions at key digital installations exposed how fragile the global digital infrastructure could be. While these incidents have not yet been established as AI-assisted cyberattacks, Nikesh Arora, CEO of Palo Alto Networks, one of the world's largest cybersecurity companies, said that the events of week were far from a coincidence. “So what the (cybersecurity) industry tried to warn enterprises about six months ago is here. The events of this week so far are not a coincidence. AI is making it easy for hackers to attack multiple customers,” said Arora in post on X. Besides AI-assisted cyberattacks, he also blamed some of the outages on the a “deluge of patches” from vendors rushing to fix AI-discovered vulnerabilities. Noting that this “deluge” of patches was overwhelming IT teams, he urged the enterprises to test infrastructure across multiple AI models and revamp security operations centres. His comments brought the spotlight back on the growing threat of AI-led cyberattacks. By automating reconnaissance, writing exploit code on the fly and allowing threat actors to probe thousands of targets simultaneously, AI is drastically compressing the time between discovering a flaw and weaponising it – leaving human defenders struggling to keep pace. With new vulnerabilities surfacing every single day, how is AI making it harder for enterprises to keep pace with cyberattackers? Cyberattacks In The AI Era Cybersecurity expert Ritesh Bhatia, founder of cybersecurity platform V4WEB, believes that AI is not necessarily making cyberattacks more sophisticated. Instead, he says that the technology is accelerating techniques that attackers have been using for years. According to him, the change is primarily visible in three areas: speed, scale and realism. Tasks that earlier took days or months can now be completed in seconds, minutes or hours. Generative AI (GenAI) has also made phishing emails more convincing by eliminating grammatical errors that could previously alert recipients. Voice cloning and deepfakes further allow attackers to impersonate senior executives and issue fraudulent instructions. Bhatia also flagged the problem of what he described as “shadow infrastructure” or “shadow assets” at large enterprises – systems that remain untracked, forgotten or outside regular IT monitoring. AI-assisted scanning can help attackers identify vulnerabilities in these overlooked systems, he adds. Third-party vendors are another concern. Even large enterprises with strong cybersecurity teams often depend on smaller service providers that may not have comparable security capabilities. These vendors can become easier targets, particularly as AI lowers the barrier to learning hacking techniques. “What previously required multiple individuals with specialised skills can now increasingly be handled by a single attacker. The bigger concern is the scale at which these operations can be replicated across organisations,” said Manohar Reddy Pagilla, threat researcher at CloudSEK. He also added that the recent outages have highlighted the concentration risk across the global technology ecosystem. Pagilla further adds that from an attacker's perspective, compromising a technology provider serving hundreds of organisations can be more rewarding than targeting each business individually. Yet, the threat is no longer confined to external third-party vendors. As enterprises race to embed AI into their own workflows, they are inadvertently also expanding their exposure to cyberattacks from within. The Widening Enterprise Attack Surface Within enterprises, AI is opening up new fronts of vulnerability: accelerating how fast bug-laden software is shipped while simultaneously supercharging how quickly its code can be broken. Developers can now generate and deploy vast volumes of code with minimal human scrutiny. This has increased the odds of critical flaws (in authentication, payment logic, and API integrations) slipping into production before being adequately reviewed. Attackers, meanwhile, are using the same technology to probe multiple weaknesses at once, reverse-engineer applications, and map out attack paths in a fraction of the time it once took. "The same capabilities that make our security testing faster can also make attackers substantially more effective," said founder and CTO of Security Brigade Yash Kadakia. Compounding the issue of unvetted code is the rapid spread of AI across day-to-day business operations, a trend Akshit Kaushik, cofounder and CBO of Mitigata, flags as a major new blind spot. Enterprises are increasingly entrusting AI systems to handle customer queries, process refunds, generate code, and access internal databases. At the same time, employees are independently adopting unapproved “shadow AI” tools, often completely out of sight of security teams. Every new integration creates a fresh entry point. Kaushik warns that attackers can hide malicious instructions inside seemingly routine emails and documents, manipulating enterprise AI assistants into leaking sensitive data or executing unauthorised actions. To close these expanding gaps, he believes businesses must establish strict visibility and governance – tracking every AI tool deployed internally, auditing the data these systems can access, and ensuring their AI systems operate strictly within defined boundaries. What Should Indian Enterprises Do? For India, where banking, real-time payments, telecommunications, power, and public services are built on deeply interconnected digital infrastructure, the margin for error is shrinking fast. Security experts suggest that Indian enterprises must move beyond traditional perimeter defense and focus on three core pillars: Sovereign Resilience and System Modernisation: Kaushal Bheda, director at Pelorus Technologies, warns that India’s reliance on foreign software and cloud platforms for critical infrastructure introduces a distinct layer of geopolitical and supply-chain risk. To insulate sensitive infrastructure, he believes that Indian enterprises should aggressively upgrade legacy systems, continuously monitor networks, and invest in indigenous security products designed and controlled within the country. Proactive Cyber Hygiene and Threat Hunting: CloudSEK’s Pagilla advises organisations to immediately lock down their most common entry points: exposed credentials, unpatched internet-facing assets, excessive access permissions, and third-party vendor vulnerabilities. Rather than relying solely on internal alerts, he recommends augmenting existing security operations centres (SOCs) with external threat intelligence to detect and neutralise threats before they breach internal networks. Board-Level Incident Readiness: V4WEB’s Bhatia argues that Indian companies must shift their mindset from pure prevention to inevitable recovery. “Death, taxes and cyberhacks are bound to happen," he noted. According to Bhatia, Indian enterprises should regularly test data backups, rehearse restoration protocols and preparing clear crisis-communication playbooks for customers, partners, regulators and stock exchanges. "Today, the most important thing that companies should prioritise is incident response. When an incident happens, don't think that it won't happen. Are you ready to respond to it? Are you resilient enough? Have you tested your backups? Are you able to restore them?” added Bhatia. For Indian enterprises, therefore, the question is no longer simply whether AI can make cyberattacks more effective. It is whether their security teams, infrastructure, and leadership can respond at the exact same speed.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

The tightest survival scrap for years? Why it's not too early to worry
- Published
Despite being only 10 games into the season, sitting in the relegation zone even at this early stage is more worrying than you might think.
But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the fiercest relegation battles we have seen in a long time.
Two of the current bottom three, Crystal Palace and Manchester United, will resume their campaigns at the weekend with new managers after appointing Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino respectively.
Sunderland, wedged between the pair in 19th, have not pressed the panic button and have kept faith with Regis le Bris.
But is it too early to worry? We look at what the stats tell us about relegation battles in the past and what we can learn for the months ahead.
The bottom three may already be taking shape
Looking at every Premier League season since it changed to a 20-team league in 1995-96, the current bottom three have cause to be concerned.
In 19 of the previous 31 seasons (61%), only one of the bottom three sides after 10 games managed to avoid relegation.
For fairness and accuracy, the 'bottom three' are the three sides with the worst record after 10 games, not simply those in the relegation zone after matchweek 10, since in some seasons a team had played nine games by that point.
Only in 10 seasons (32%) have two or more of the bottom three stayed up - and that has not happened in any of the past eight campaigns. The last time more than one team avoided the drop was in 2017-18, when all three survived.
That has only happened twice, although only twice have all three sides been relegated.
Overall, of the 93 previous teams in the bottom three after 10 games, 41 survived and 52 were relegated - a survival rate of 44%.
It's not all bad news for the bottom three
This is the third time that Palace have been bottom after 10 games. On both previous occasions, they did not just survive but thrived, finishing 11th.
They did so under Tony Pulis in 2013-14 and under Roy Hodgson in 2017-18. Both managers, like Frank, were appointed early in the season following poor starts under Ian Holloway and Frank de Boer respectively.
The 2013-14 season is the only previous time that Sunderland and Palace were the bottom two at this stage. The Black Cats also survived thanks to a great, late escape under Gus Poyet.
This is the first time United have been in the bottom three after 10 games of a Premier League season.
Given the size and resources of the club, it is unlikely they will go down, although the team in 18th place at this stage have been relegated in each of the past six seasons.
Fans of all three clubs will hope for a repeat of 2017-18, when not only Palace but the bottom three improved significantly to finish comfortably mid-table.
Tight at the bottom - and in the middle
While history suggests only one of the bottom three will survive, there is also evidence to suggest that this might not be a standard Premier League season.
Palace have seven points, which is the most the bottom side after 10 games have had for 24 years. The bottom three all had eight points in 2002-03.
Sunderland's eight points is also the most that a side in 19th place have had for 16 years. Wolves had nine points in 2010-11 and survived in 17th.
In fact, only five points separate the bottom half of the Premier League, with Tottenham in 11th on 12 points and Palace bottom with seven – the smallest gap at this stage for 24 years.
The highest that a team in the bottom three after 10 games have finished the season is eighth - Bolton in 2003-04, Tottenham in 2008-09 and Everton in 2017-18 - which suggests it will be Conference League at best for Manchester United next season.
Then again, the table is so tight that only nine points separate Chelsea in fifth and Palace - the smallest gap at this stage for 16 years.
Given that fifth place has been enough to qualify for the Champions League in recent seasons, optimistic United fans may not be ruling it out just yet.
That means even sides who have started well could be involved in the relegation battle.
The most points a team have had after 10 games of a 38-game season and been relegated is 14 - Joe Royle's Manchester City in 2000-01.
The most recent team to start well but be relegated were Eddie Howe's Bournemouth in 2019-20, who were sitting pretty in ninth with 13 points at this stage but went down on the final day.
As mentioned, this season has both the 'best' bottom side in terms of points and the most compact bottom half of the table that we have seen at this stage since 2002-03.
In that season, West Ham were relegated on the final day with 42 points - the most a side have been relegated with in Premier League history.
Given the way this season is shaping up, 40 points might also not be enough to survive.

“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce.
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

New Delhi, Nov 19: India-US relations stand at a historic high point, with both governments working closely to build a fair, reciprocal and mutually beneficial trade relationship, a senior American diplomat said on Thursday.
Addressing the 23rd Indo-US Economic Summit here, US Deputy Chief of Mission Jason Meeks called for reducing trade barriers, ensuring fair market access and strengthening supply chain resilience.
“Our two governments are working very closely together to build a trade relationship that is fair, reciprocal and mutually beneficial,” Meeks said.
He said the two nations have made "real progress well beyond trading goods" and are partnering on energy, pharmaceuticals, critical minerals, advanced technology and manufacturing.
Meeks stressed the need to create an environment where American suppliers and technology can freely reach Indian manufacturers and consumers, while Indian firms can compete fairly in US markets.
“When trade is fair and reciprocal, workers and companies on both sides win,” he said.
Referring to the Pax Silica initiative, Meeks said the US, India and other countries recently signed the San Francisco Declaration to strengthen the partnership, underlining the importance of resilient supply chains.
Pax Silica is a US-led international coalition launched in December 2025 to build secure, resilient supply chains for artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductors, and critical minerals among trusted allies.
He said Indian manufacturers were emerging as reliable partners in global supply chains, particularly in automotive components, pharmaceuticals and electronics, while American companies were contributing technology, capital and expertise.
Inviting Indian companies to expand their operations in the US, Meeks said Washington was keen to attract investments in manufacturing, research and development and distribution networks.
“Whether you are looking at manufacturing, whether you're looking at research and development centres or distribution networks, the United States is open for business,” he said.
He also invited Indian businesses to participate in the SelectUSA Investment Summit, scheduled to be held from May 2-5, 2027, near Washington, DC.
Meeks said America's 250th anniversary and India's pursuit of Viksit Bharat presented an opportunity for both democracies to deepen economic cooperation and advance shared prosperity.

In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill.
When I log into Amazon today, I’m met with a vertical banner that reads: “ATTENTION NYC Council could add up to $5 per order” with a button that says “Act now.”
The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn’t specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I’m logged into Amazon.
Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses.
Clicking on “Act now” on Amazon’s homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states:
Right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.
It’s not unusual for Amazon to take a stance on political matters, and it has publicly opposed the Delivery Protection Act since April. What is new is Amazon using its online marketplace to push a political view. It’s uncommon to see a pop-up about legislation when visiting a shopping website.

AI startup Soket AI has raised $4 Mn (around ₹37 Cr) from Bajaj Finserv's applied research and innovation initiative Finserv Intelligence, and Pennant Technologies. The startup is working on building indigenous foundation models focused on mathematics, coding and reasoning. Bajaj Finance invested approximately $2 Mn in the startup, while Pennant Technologies, an investee company of Bajaj Finance, invested another $2 Mn in the round. Bajaj Finance Vice Chairman and MD Rajeev Jain said, “With Soket AI, we look forward to enabling India’s indigenous AI ecosystem, engaging with frontier research at an early stage, and bringing our scale and domain expertise to turn this research into practical solutions.” Backed by the government's IndiaAI Mission, Soket AI recently launched EKA-1, a 26-Bn-parameter foundation model under Project EKA, its flagship sovereign AI initiative. The funding comes as the startup looks to scale its foundation model research and develop AI systems for sectors such as financial services, cybersecurity, defence and enterprise technology. Besides, the $4 Mn investment will support applied AI research and enterprise deployments, particularly across financial services, cybersecurity, defence and enterprise technology. Besides financial backing, the strategic investment is expected to open opportunities for applied AI research enterprise applications and capability building by combining Bajaj Finance’s industry expertise with Soket AI’s foundational research capabilities. Founded in 2019 by Abhishek Upperwal, Soket AI is building a sovereign open-source AI stack that serves a gamut of Indian languages. Speaking to Inc42 earlier this year, the founder said that the idea is to crack the AI model for India first. Soket is among a limited set of Indian AI startups developing indigenous foundation models with support from the IndiaAI Mission. Earlier this month, ZenteiQ AiTech Innovations also launched Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B, two open-source multilingual models supporting English and 10 Indian languages. Unlike Soket's reasoning-focused EKA-1, ZenteiQ's models are designed as lightweight AI assistants that can run on-premises and on edge devices, including smartphones, without requiring continuous cloud connectivity. Meanwhile, AI unicorn Sarvam AI has also expanded its model portfolio with the launch of Prism, an open-weight decision model built on its Sarvam 105B model. The model is designed for enterprise workflows such as customer support routing, security checks and evaluating AI agent activity.

NEW DELHI: The BJP on Thursday launched a broadside against Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi over his remarks at an event in Chicago. BJP leaders claimed that Rahul Gandhi called Indian democracy "sick". The video put out by news agencies, however, showed that he had actually described the democracy as "sacred".In a social media post on X, BJP national spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari shared a clip of Rahul's address and termed him "leader of anti-India propaganda.""Rahul Gandhi called Indian Democracy 'sick' from foreign soil! Congress calls Indian democracy 'sick'. Rahul Gandhi has yet again proven he loves Parivar, & hates Democracy!" Bhandari said.
"Every time Rahul proves he is against Indian state, People of India & India's Democratic Fabric! Rahul Gandhi is Leader of Anti India Propaganda!" he added.Several BJP leaders also followed Bhandari in attacking Rahul, saying that the Congress leader was "moving towards senile mental dementia.""Rahul Gandhi himself is sick; he has been unwell for 10 years. He has developed an illness called obsessive-compulsive neurosis for the past 10 years, and now he is gradually moving towards senile mental dementia," BJP spokesperson Ajay Alok said.
"He has become incoherent. Look at him - he has no sense of place, time, or object. He thinks one thing in his mind, and something else comes out of his mouth. What was he even trying to say? Saying about his own mother that at every mile, Mummy used to sit in Papa's lap. Does Indian society speak like that or think like that? So, he is gradually losing his balance," he added.
What Rahul actually said
During an interaction with students at the University of Chicago in the US, Rahul Gandhi was asked why the opposition does not boycott elections if it believes they were being rigged.The Congress leader said Indian democracy was "sacred" to him and that he would need overwhelming evidence to even claim that it was under threat."Indian democracy is sacred. For me to even say that there is a problem in Indian democracy is difficult without 100, 200, 300 per cent proof," Rahul said."But what happens to all the opposition workers if we tell them, 'Okay, don't participate in the election?' If we say that we are not going to contest elections, we end Indian democracy that minute. And we don't want to end the structure of Indian democracy," he said.Rahul said the opposition's strategy was to highlight alleged electoral irregularities and continue contesting elections until people realise what he claimed was the dismantling of the system.
"So, our strategy is to expose what is going on and take the beating until the people of India realise that the system has been fully demolished," he added.BJP has repeatedly criticised Rahul Gandhi over his remarks during foreign visits, accusing him of maligning India and its democratic institutions.The latest controversy comes after Rahul raised allegations of "vote chori" during an earlier interaction at Columbia University, prompting BJP leaders to accuse him of insulting India and its democracy.Rahul was on a two-day visit to the US during which he interacted with students at Columbia University in New York on Tuesday and the University of Chicago on Wednesday.

Indian chess Grandmasters Nihal Sarin and Mitrabha Guha will retain their places at the inaugural Esports Nations Cup (ENC), after the Esports Foundation (EF) on Thursday said that every slot earned in the 2026 qualification season will be protected for the postponed event.
The ENC was originally scheduled to be held in Riyadh in November 2026 but was pushed back by a year in view of the security situation in West Asia. It will now be held in November 2027.
Nihal had secured a direct invitation through the ENC Rankings, while Guha came through a regional qualifier. Under the ‘Road to ENC 2027’ unveiled on Thursday, slots in solo titles such as chess stay with the player who earned them.
The two Grandmasters are part of an Indian contingent that has qualified in eight titles: Battlegrounds Mobile India (BGMI), Chess, EA SPORTS FC, Honor of Kings, MOBA Legends: 5v5!, Rocket League, Trackmania and VALORANT.
India received special invites in BGMI and Honor of Kings, while the MOBA Legends: 5v5! team and EA SPORTS FC player Charanjot Singh earned direct invitations through the rankings.
The Rocket League and VALORANT teams and Trackmania player Kunal Upreti (Spark) qualified through regional events.
Nations yet to qualify will get another route through regional online tournaments, which begin on February 26, 2027, and run for five weeks. Seven regional winners and one nation from the ENC Solidarity programme will advance to a final LAN qualifier.
In team titles, coaches can add eligible players to their squads. Updated rosters are due by January 15, and Finals line-ups by May 31, 2027. The ENC Ranking will award points for results in international club leagues, tournaments and national team competitions, and will decide group-stage seeding and future direct invitations.

About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest, several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory.
According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”.
The village they entered was within the Arariboia Indigenous territory in the north-eastern state of Maranhão, home to the Guajajara ethnic group.
Local community leaders said the villagers offered food to the group.
“They asked for yams and took them back into their forest,” said Survival International.
The NGO explained that the Awá typically subsist on hunting and gathering. However, they have faced increased incursions from illegal loggers, hunters and cattle ranchers.
A video of the encounter, filmed by Guajajara villagers and released by Survival International, shows a group of men, women and children at the edge of the forest.
Partially concealed by vegetation, they appear naked and are wearing necklaces. The men carry bows and long arrows.
“The physical condition of some members, particularly the children and the elderly, caused concern among the villagers, who noted clear signs of severe emaciation,” warned Coapima, an organization representing Indigenous groups in Maranhão.
Coapima highlighted the risks that unplanned contact poses to such groups, noting that they are particularly “exposed to diseases” against which they have little to no immunity.
Funai, the public agency responsible for Indigenous affairs, said in a statement sent to AFP that its technical teams were closely monitoring the situation and analyzing available information regarding the group’s health.
Survival International’s director, Caroline Pearce, said the group’s choice to emerge from isolation was a “troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger”.
She said the Awá were being driven into “an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction”.
According to the NGO, about 196 “uncontacted” peoples and groups, who choose to live in isolation, have been identified across 10 countries.
More than 90% of such groups live in the Amazon rainforest, primarily in Brazil, with others in Indonesia and India.
The Forest Guardians – a group of Guajajara people who have battled illegal invasions for years – warned in comments in the Survival International statement that “climate change, fires, deforestation and land encroachment” were affecting the Awá’s way of life.
According to Survival International, many of the guardians have lost their lives trying to protect the territory they share with the Awá.

Veteran executive and producer Tendo Nagenda will join Proximity Media as president, company founders Ryan Coogler, Zinzi Coogler and Sev Ohanian announced on Thursday.
“Tendo has spent his career working alongside talented filmmakers, championing original ideas and helping make projects that resonate with audiences around the world,” the Cooglers and Ohanian, who most recently produced the Oscar-winning film “Sinners,” said in a joint statement.
“As Proximity continues to grow across film, television and nonfiction, we’re excited to have his creative instincts and experience helping guide this next chapter,” the trio continued. “He shares our belief in the power of storytelling to connect people, challenge perspectives and create meaningful impact, and we’re thrilled to welcome him to the team.”
As president, Nagenda will oversee all aspects of creative development and production across Proximity’s film, television and nonfiction divisions, reporting directly to the founders. In addition to guiding the multimedia company’s slate of projects — including the highly anticipated “X-Files” series at Hulu, starring Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel, and Marvel’s “Black Panther 3” — Nagenda will also help shape the company’s broader business strategy.
Nagenda will work alongside Terra Potts, who oversees marketing, operations and the “In Proximity” podcast, and Proximity co-founder Ludwig Göransson, who oversees music. The heads of film, TV and nonfiction will report directly to Nagenda. He will assume the role on Nov. 30.
“I’m honored and excited to join Ryan, Zinzi, Sev and the entire Proximity team,” said Nagenda. “Their commitment to ambitious, meaningful storytelling reflects everything I’ve always believed in, and I look forward to building on what they’ve created, collaborating with extraordinary filmmakers and creators, and bringing compelling new stories to audiences around the world.”
Nagenda’s extensive entertainment resume includes key positions at Netflix and Walt Disney Studios. At Netflix, he served as VP of original film, where he helped build the streamer’s original film slate and oversaw a range of acclaimed projects, including Spike Lee’s “Da 5 Bloods,” “The Old Guard,” “Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom,” “The Harder They Fall” and “Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery.” Before Netflix, he served as executive VP of production at Walt Disney Studios, overseeing live-action films including “Beauty and the Beast,” “Cinderella,” “Saving Mr. Banks,” “Mulan,” “A Wrinkle in Time” and “Queen of Katwe.”
In 2022, Nagenda founded 10 by Ten Entertainment, a production company focused on developing and producing original stories from “distinctive and underrepresented perspectives.” His first produced feature was 2024’s “The Book of Clarence,” written and directed by Jeymes Samuel and released theatrically by Sony.
Nagenda’s appointment comes as Proximity Media continues to expand its slate across film, television and nonfiction. In June, the company entered into a multiyear television deal with Netflix to develop an exclusive slate of scripted and unscripted projects. Proximity Media’s television division is behind series including Marvel’s “Ironheart” and the animated “Black Panther” spinoff “Eyes of Wakanda”; the National Geographic docuseries “Hurricane Katrina: A Race Against Time”; “Stephen Curry: Underrated”; “Homeroom”; and “Anthem.”

A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its western neighbor.
Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”
Evasive and irregular turns
“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”
When police later questioned D’iu about the incident, the defendant allegedly said he saw a woman get into a car and thought she was “beautiful.” He then told the investigators that he followed her because he “wanted to ask her out on a date.”
Prosecutors didn’t name the company, but both Reuters and Bloomberg, citing unnamed people with knowledge of the case, identified it as Palantir. Ars is unable to confirm that reporting. Palantir representatives didn’t respond to an email seeking confirmation.

Democrats win Alaska Senate race two weeks after midterms counting began
- Published
Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's hard-fought Senate race, completing a sweeping victory for the party in the US upper house in the midterm elections.
The win gives the Democrats a 56th Senate seat following a tumultuous and controversial election in Alaska, which featured alleged spoiler recruitment efforts and unprecedented court battles.
It took two full weeks of counting to call a winner in the 3 November poll due to the logistical challenge of collecting ballots from across the state's remote expanse.
The Democratic win is the ninth Senate seat the party took from Republicans in this year's midterms, giving the party control of the US Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency.
A historic set of victories nationally also saw the party win back the House of Representatives.
In her victory statement, Peltola said the "status quo in DC is not working for Alaska".
She recalled speaking to "elders in tears about empty fish racks" and to parents in rural Alaska choosing between heating their homes and putting food on the table.
Peltola's campaign had come under fire after the New York Times reported Democrats attempted to recruit a candidate named Daniel J Sullivan, a complete political unknown residing in a small coastal town who shared a name with the state's current US Senator and incumbent, Dan S Sullivan, in an alleged attempt to confuse voters.

After legal challenges, state courts ruled the second Daniel J Sullivan could remain on the ballot, and election officials distinguished them on election materials.
Peltola denied having knowledge of the alleged plot but her campaign swiftly came under fire, and both the justice department and Alaska's Republican governor said they would launch investigations.
The Trump administration then filed a lawsuit attempting to stop the certification of the election results if the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan lost.
A federal judge, though, dismissed the case, following legal challenges from Alaska election officials as well as the Peltola campaign and voting groups.
Due to Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, voters confused about which Dan Sullivan was the incumbent could simply choose each man as their first and second choice.
If they did so, after the first round of voting was complete, tabulation would re-allocate any votes from the non-incumbent Dan Sullivan - who stood little to no chance of winning - to the US Senator.
Experts told the BBC that this process made it difficult for any potential spoiler candidate to have any impact on the results.
An analysis by BBC Verify found that even if every vote for the other Dan Sullivan had gone to the incumbent, Peltola would still have won.
The seat initially was one of several toss-up races that appeared as a must-win for Democrats if they wanted to gain control of the Senate - but by the time Peltola was called the winner, they had seats to spare.
With 99% of ballots counted, Peltola had slightly more than 50%, while Sullivan trailed on less than 46%.
Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney general and an ally of Trump, campaigned on his record of delivering energy and military investment for the state.
Peltola promised Alaskans a more independent voice in Washington.
"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," she said in her victory statement.
"I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families."

The claim spread after the Russian Embassy in the U.S. posted (archived) a photo of a U.S. flag hanging on the Millennium Gate Museum in Atlanta, Georgia. The embassy wrote:
🇷🇺 Russian flag has been put on the historical museum of Atlanta @MillenniumGate in memory of the Russian Ambassador to the U.S. Alexander #Darchiev at the initiative of President of the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts Rodney Mims Cook-Jr.
Alexander Darchiev was a Russian diplomat (archived) who served as ambassador to the U.S. since March 2025. CNN, citing the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, reported that Darchiev died "suddenly" on Nov. 11 after struggling with a chronic illness.
Following the Russiam Embassy's post, other social media users appeared to criticize the decision to fly the Russian flag in Atlanta. For example, the former Republican Representative for Illinois turned political commentator Adam Kinzinger wrote on Instagram, "Trump's pick to chair the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts" had hung a Russian flag "from an arch in Georgia while Russia is still waging war on Ukraine."
The claim also spread on Reddit and Facebook (archived, archived). Snopes readers searched our site about the claim.
Rodney Mims Cook Jr., who the Russian embassy said took the "initiative" to hang the flag and who other social media posts described as an "ally" of U.S. President Donald Trump, is the chairman of the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, which is a federal design review agency based in Washington, D.C. The CFA approved Trump's White House ballroom project in February and his proposal for a monumental arch in May.
However, Cook is also the founder and president of the Millennium Gate Museum, which hung the Russian flag. Therefore, it was unclear whether Cook took the initiative to fly the Russian flag in his capacity as chairman at the CFA or as founder and president at the Millennium Gate Museum.
CFA Secretary Thomas Luebke wrote via email to Snopes that the commission's jurisdiction was "almost entirely" in D.C. and that he did not know about "the activities of Mr. Cook at the Millennium Gate Museum in Atlanta, an institution for which he serves as President and CEO."
We contacted the Millennium Gate Museum to ask whether Cook made the decision to hang the Russian flag from the museum's arch in his capacity as the museum's founder and await a reply.
Because neither the CFA nor the Millennium Gate Museum had confirmed the Russian Embassy's claim that Cook personally decided to hang the Russian flag from the Millennium Gate in November directly to Snopes, we leave this claim unrated.
The New York Times reported on Nov. 18, citing an interview with Cook, that he arranged for the Russian flag to hang from the Millennium Gate Museum in memory of Darchiev. The flag reportedly came down on Nov. 18.
The Millennium Gate Museum said in a statement on its website that the Russian flag was part of its "long-standing diplomatic custom of marking the death of an accredited ambassador serving in the United States."
It was unclear whether the Millennium Gate Museum had flown a Congolese flag following the death of the serving Congolese Ambassador Serge Mombouli in September 2025, or when the museum had last honored that tradition.
Cook is a 2-time Trump appointee and 'Russophile'
Regardless of which authority Cook used to allegedly hang the Russian flag in Atlanta, it was fair to describe him as a Trump "ally." In an article in the New Yorker in July, Cook reportedly expressed confidence in Trump's design direction, saying that he would "leave us a legacy of such astonishing beauty."
Trump appointed Cook to the CFA in January 2026 after which the commission elected him as chairman. Cook had previously served on the CFA from 2021 to 2022 after being appointed by Trump during his first term.
The New Yorker article described Cook as a friend of Trump and an "unapologetic Russophile." Cook attended the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum, which the New Yorker described as "Putin's Davos," referencing the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum, in June.
It was unclear, owing to differing statements from Cook and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whether Cook attended SPIEF with the blessing of Trump or his administration.
Critique of public flying of Russian flag as US attempts to broker peace deal
According to the Russian Embassy, Darchiev and Cook "met numerous times" and bonded over shared culture and history between their countries.
Regardless of the reported bond between the two men, some social media users criticized the hanging of the Russian flag in Atlanta, which could be perceived as public support for Russia, at a time when the U.S. was once again trying to help broker a peace deal in the nearly five-year war between Russia and Ukraine.
Trump has publicly accused (archived) Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of dragging out the war because of "all of the money that Europe is famously giving him, and that Crooked Joe Biden gave him in the past."
Meanwhile, Trump publicly praised Russian President Vladimir Putin as a "friend" when the leaders met at the APEC Summit in China on Nov. 19.

Tessa Brown is visibly excited to talk to me about Germ DM, her secure messaging platform. It’s now available on Android, a major expansion for the small startup. Her eyes light up as she explains how her ambitious, three-person team—including an ex-Apple engineer who worked on iMessage—could pull off this platform expansion.
“It's essential to be able to talk to everybody, and that's really what this Android launch unlocks for us,” she says. Brown was previously a lecturer at Stanford University, and her cofounder, Mark Xue, worked on iMessage’s privacy provisions. The duo first launched the iOS app for Germ in 2023.
The platform expansion makes it easier to recommend Germ as an interesting alternative to Signal, especially for early adopters curious about trying new ways to message others and connect with the world.
My favorite aspect about Germ is that the platform doesn’t nudge you to attach a phone number. “Germ is a multi-identity messenger,” Brown says. “The way walled gardens are constructed means that every time you log into an app you get one identity that the app owns.” On Germ, it’s not about creating a permanent handle that you give to everyone; multiplicity is central to this messenger’s pitch.
The app revolves around “burner cards.” Each card works like a separate phone line built into the app. Instead of a dedicated number or a public handle, you can share these Germ cards in two ways: a QR code or a direct link. You can scan QR codes inside the app if meeting someone in person. For digital connections, you can generate a custom link tied to the card, from just one to 100.
After downloading the app, you create these cards by tapping on the green plus button under the Me tab. Choose the name, pronouns, and photo you want to use for that card. Cards associated with your Germ account are not mutually discoverable, and who you connect with on each card is private. As the name suggests, if you delete these “burners” at any time, the connections associated with that card will no longer be able to contact you, and those chats will be removed from your device.
The Germ network runs on Messaging Layer Security, built by the Internet Engineering Task Force as an end-to-end encryption standard. When you are exchanging those “burner cards,” you are actually exchanging cryptographic keys with your new contacts. However, Germ has not undergone a third-party audit, though Brown is open to doing so in the future.
“People want to share different parts of themselves with different people,” Brown says. “Queer folks get Germ immediately; it's not just queer people. It's also people who are gig workers and creatives that have multiple jobs.” Germ is built to share with people in different parts of your life and let them contact you in a central hub through distinct messaging channels.
Xue is serious about the work Germ put into building a secure platform, including addressing the looming issue of quantum computing. Essentially, security experts worry that super-powerful computers could break encryption protections and reveal previously private messages. Developers at large messaging platforms, like iMessage and Signal, have built protections against these quantum concerns. “What we've accomplished as a small team is we've reached the same level of security,” he says. Germ publicly laid out how the platform claims to be “quantum secure.”
Germ’s most recent success came from its integration with Bluesky. Since that social media platform is built on the Authenticated Transfer Protocol, Bluesky users can connect their existing handles to Germ and display it as a messaging button in their profile. This lets friends on the platform easily send you encrypted texts. While many users enjoy that platform-specific integration, Germ’s expansion to Android is a fresh opportunity to meet a new user base.
Brown already has her sights set on Germ’s next move: group chats.
“We’ve worked together this whole time over the belief that the future of communication is in private chats,” she says. For now, the platform supports one-on-one conversations, but the team is ready to build support for larger, group threads.
It might be hard to convince your group chat to switch to a new app, but flashing a QR code to a stranger you just met to continue a conversation could actually work.

China is hosting the world's leaders in its AI wonderland. Here's what they won't see
- Published
At 27, Huang Shihua is living the Chinese Dream.
He works as an engineer for a leading humanoid robot company in Shenzhen. The sprawling south-eastern metropolis is touted by China as the origin story for a high-tech future powered by artificial intelligence, robotics and home-grown innovation.
Drones soar across the sky to deliver your dinner, driverless taxis play relaxing music as you journey to your destination, and robots don't just hand you a cappuccino - they explain the origin of your coffee beans.
"We have created a miracle in Shenzhen," Huang says, surrounded by humanoid robots making coffee and playing chess. "Many young people from across China, full of passion and dreams, have flocked here."
Now they all spend their days figuring out ways to make robots smarter.
The Chinese call Shenzhen the "city of dreams". The moniker suits it: one of China's wealthiest, it is close to Hong Kong and the place where the country's explosive growth took off decades ago.
Its manufacturing inventory mirrors China's rise: cabbage patch dolls, then TVs, later iPhones, electric vehicles, drones and now the robots, which are drawing Huang and a new generation of Chinese ambition.
The "miracles" these young engineers are chasing are central to Xi Jinping's bold vision for China. So where better to show it off than Shenzhen, which will be centre-stage when US President Donald Trump, Russian leader Vladimir Putin and others arrive for a global economic summit this week.
And yet there is another side to this flashy, coastal city, a side that they will not get to see. Drive away from towering skyscrapers towards Shajing and Songgang, once the source of much of the world's electronics, and you will run into the challenges confronting Xi's China.
"Everyone feels life is hard," one construction worker tells us. "Lots of factories have relocated and workers lost their jobs."
China remains exceptionally good at making things - and Shenzhen is proof of that. But the city also holds the evidence for what ails the world's second-largest economy. The property crisis is not over, denting confidence in the future. This is one of China's most expensive cities but even here, our taxi driver tells us, his house is now only worth a third of its original price.
A weak property market and sluggish consumer spending mean many households are buying less. Factories are increasingly relying on exports while many manufacturers have cut production, downsized, automated or moved elsewhere in search of cheaper labour.
The result is a growing number of workers turning to temporary jobs in the gig economy, often with lower pay and fewer benefits.
"Shenzhen is not a magic place," says one delivery driver in his 40s, unwilling to give his name.
"Some say there is gold everywhere in Shenzhen, but it's not like that anymore. It's not a city where you can come and thrive. If you don't work hard, you won't have anything."
The BBC spent several days in Shenzhen exploring these two very different sides of China's progress: on the one hand is the dazzling promise of AI, and on the other are the anxieties of workers who worry if there will be room for them in the future it creates.
Wednesday is sandwich and bubble tea day in the offices of DexForce Technologies.
The elevator is packed with young engineers and developers headed to the right floor for the free carbs and sugar that will fuel their afternoon. They jostle past their creations en route: human-sized, yellow robots whose limbs fill every available corner.
"I believe that in a decade, robots will be able to better serve humanity by taking on highly repetitive or even dangerous tasks," Huang says. That could be anything from serving coffee to working in mines, and they are being trained for all of that in this laboratory for the future, where machines flail, jerk or lurch into motion as they learn to behave.
To him, "Shenzhen is another 'America'. Because, much like in the US, many young people have been able to realise their dreams and earn the wealth they desire."
This is what Xi wants to hear as he pushes China to lead the world in advanced tech. Shenzhen has indeed long been a place for seeking opportunity but Huang and his colleagues want to do much more. They don't simply want to continue China's manfuacturing supremacy. They want to transform it.
Beyond making "our lives more convenient and comfortable", Huang sees AI as helping "the entire world become one family - a global village. AI has the potential to foster equality and the prospect of AI-driven equality is, to me, the most exciting possibility of all."
Smiling enthusiastically, he explains how he hopes that robots can help emerging economies across Africa and South East Asia catch up by reshaping their production lines too.
This tech-charged optimism, which is everywhere in the building, jars with the uncertainty elsewhere in Shenzhen, where robots are nowhere to be found. Yet. But that's just the first of the differences.
In Huang's side of the city, tech and finance workers stroll to the office after a morning workout, sipping coffee that probably cost more than 30 yuan ($4.50; £3.40).
On the other side, scooters whizz through streets piled high with goods being shuttled between factories as vendors sell whole breakfast plates of spicy noodles for under 3 yuan.
Outside one of the city's tallest skyscrapers, 50-year-old Ms Lu has a phone to her ear and a pen in her right hand while grabbing a bag with her left from a delivery driver.
She shouts four key numbers at her co-worker: instructions for another Chinese woman who is waiting to take the delivery up the elevator to someone sitting at their desk.
This is the lunchtime rush outside SEG plaza, home to 70 storeys of thousands of tenants. Lu used to be one of them. "I ran a small business on the second floor. I sold circuit boards," she says. "But it's getting so hard to do business these days and the rental fees got higher."
Often likened to China's Silicon Valley, Shenzhen has seen rents soar with the influx of new capital, squeezing out smaller, more traditional businesses. At 50, Ms Lu couldn't find another job until the delivery drivers came to her with a plan.
The wait for the elevator can take half an hour – wasted money for a driver trying to fill as many orders as possible. So Ms Lu became a new layer in the ever-evolving gig economy.
"The delivery drivers bring food here to the building entrance. We pick it up and take it upstairs. The drivers pay us 2 yuan per order," she explains, always on the move. Delivery drivers earn between four to eight yuan per order, so Ms Lu gets a decent cut of their earnings.
"The lunch peak time only lasts two or three hours… if they use our service, they can get more orders done, and we can earn some money as well. But the market is bad. These days I only earn around 200 yuan per day."
An estimated 200 million Chinese workers, roughly 40% of the urban labour force, now depend on some form of gig work. Many delivery drivers in Shenzhen tell us they chose temporary work because there are fewer opportunities at factories than before.
"We need to adapt to the situation we find ourselves in," one driver told us, "rather than waiting for it to adapt to our needs." A group of them are waiting outside the gates of an e-cigarette factory to make industrial deliveries.
Others nod in agreement. Another driver says he has little choice: "I have two children to raise and I can't stop working. I don't have time to think about anything else."
Permanent jobs often require contributions to social security and pension, which reduces take-home pay. But gig work means more cash in hand and flexibile hours.
"Most workers prefer jobs with a fixed, shorter-term duration. It allows them the flexibility to resign and leave whenever they choose; they have no desire to become permanent employees," says job agent Li Xiaohe.
Increasingly, he puts up boards on pavements advertising temporary factory jobs that pay around 22 yuan an hour for assembling small electronics.
Although agents also appear to be in a shrinking pool, with several former shop fronts shuttered: yet another sign of the downturn in traditional manufacturing.
"Our business is perhaps not as optimistic as it once was," Li admits. "We can feel the effects of Shenzhen going through a transformation."
That transformation is hard to miss.
Drones buzz above the lush grounds of a purpose built "talent park" along the city's waterfront, dipping and darting as they deliver meals to a dedicated platform. Phones held high, tourists capture them landing with their lunch.
"This is amazing. The technology is just great. I wish we had this back at home," exclaims one Canadian tourist. Our coffee order - for a five-yuan delivery - arrives in just over 15 minutes, the drone landing seamlessly so I can pick up my order.
"I heard that many years ago, Shenzhen was a fishing village," says Anle, who is visiting from Vietnam. "Ha – no more fishing village," he laughs as he orders milk tea to be delivered by drone for him and his wife.
For all the ingenuity on display, it feels more like a demonstration of what is possible rather than a mundane reality. The deliveries, which are only possible in certain locations, stop at 20:00 local time. The driverless cars, which need a separate app to order, are also a novelty – they even offer you a massage when you are on your way.
At night, in the glow of a thousand dancing lights, the drones take on a different role. They fly above the park warning people to behave and not cause trouble.
Far from the glittering skyline, workers gather around plastic tables outside restaurants serving cheap hotpot and seafood skewers.
There are more expensive restaurants along the street, but they too have taken a hit. One owner told us business is down by more than 70% as workers are hesitant to splurge on dinner.
Many of them have spent decades here, including 58-year-old construction worker Mr Wu. He arrived in Shenzhen from Sichuan in the 1990s not long after China opened the city up to foreign businesses.
He was among millions of migrants from poorer provinces who came to work on production lines or build skyscrapers. They are still coming.
All the people we spoke to came from elsewhere. They often labour up to 14 hours a day and live in shared dormitories, sustained by the prospect of stable work and decent pay to send home to their families.
For these workers, the Covid pandemic, when Chinese manufacturing hit a record low, appears to have been the first turning point.
"After Covid, our salary dropped by at least a third," Mr Wu recalls, after which wages never fully recovered.
"I will continue to work," he adds. "As long as you keep working, you will have an income. More salary or not? It doesn't matter. As long as you keep working, you will have an income. If the economy slows down, we all slow down. If it grows, we all get better."
For all these decades, Shenzhen lived up to its bargain: work hard and your life would improve.
But now, in a city that is being redefined by automation and AI, that old promise feels less secure.

Actor Samantha Ruth Prabhu and filmmaker Raj Nidimoru have celebrated a traditional baby shower ceremony with their families as they prepare to welcome their first child. Samantha is currently in her third trimester.

Photographs and videos from the celebrations, shared by Raj’s sister Sheetal Nidimoru, show Samantha in a red outfit alongside Raj, his parents and extended family.
Sheetal, who posted a video compiling moments from the ceremony, wrote about how long she had been looking forward to the occasion. “When can we do this, Babu? I’d been asking my annayya for so long. And finally, it was time,” she said.

She revealed that family members who had been part of raising Raj and her travelled from different parts of the country to attend. “Our pinnammas and peddamma who helped raise us came from near and far for Matru Shishu Mangala Ashirvadam, to bless Sam and the precious little one already reigning over our hearts and soon, our Samrajyam,” Sheetal wrote.
The ceremony included traditional rituals rooted in the family’s spiritual practices. Sheetal described how gathering at the home altar to chant and sing was a part of the Nidimoru household’s daily life growing up, a tradition maintained by their grandparents, aunts and parents. “Whatever had happened that day, we sat together in prayer. It’s easy to run out of words to describe Rabindranath Tagore. The first non-European to win the Nobel prize in literature, Tagore was a Bengali poet, musician, novelist, philosopher, songwriter, painter, humanist and educator.
Born in 1861, Tagore left an indelible mark on the subcontinent’s literature, music, education and art. Among his enduring legacies are the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.
As Nobel laureate economist Amartya Sen once wrote, Tagore was “a towering figure in the millennium-old literature of Bengal”, whose songs resonate across eastern India and Bangladesh, while his ideas on education, nationalism and freedom of the mind remain relevant today.
Yet his work also made a deep impression on the literary world far beyond the shores of India. WB Yeats is said to have described Tagore as “greater than any of us”. Gitanjali, the collection of poems that won Tagore the Nobel prize that same year, was praised by the committee for its “profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse”. Tagore’s English translation was published in London that March and reprinted 10 times by the time the prize was announced in November.
Tagore’s life and works have, of course, been well documented, but a collection of material preserved in a private family archive is now being brought into public view for the first time at an exhibition by Christie’s, opening in Mumbai this month. The archive draws from Tagore’s visits to the family home of his protege, Maitreyi Devi, in the bucolic village of Mungpoo in Darjeeling between 1938 and 1940. He died in 1941.
The collection on display – artworks, manuscripts, letters, photographs and personal effects – offers an intimate glimpse into Tagore’s creative process and personal world in his final years.
I spoke to the exhibition curator, Nishad Avari, head of south Asian modern and contemporary art at Christie’s, about the stories behind the archive.
One instructive document Avari points to is a manuscript from 1940. It appears to be a draft of Tagore’s memoir Chelebela or My Boyhood Days, in which he reflects on his life – from growing up in a large family in Calcutta (modern-day Kolkata) to the rapidly changing world ushered in by electricity and the motorcar.
For Avari, what stood out was how the ideas in the document echoed the educational philosophy Tagore put into practice in Santiniketan (or Abode of Peace), the experimental school he set up about 100 miles from the state capital.
“He speaks about how education is like being in prison and that it should be open and free … about the idea of wonder and even fear as inspiring creativity,” Avari told me.
“That’s a direct relationship to Santiniketan and the open model of the school where people sat under trees with their gurus and learned in the open. Education didn’t feel like a restriction, prison or imposition,” he added.
Avari points to another detail that makes this particular document valuable. Of the 10 complete manuscripts in the exhibition, it is the only one dictated to Devi, whose father was a close friend of Tagore’s. For Avari, this speaks to their close relationship and the trust he placed in her.
“If you look at the collection as a whole, she has copies of almost every single one of his publications signed to her by him,” he says. The collection includes hundreds of letters, too: first between Tagore and her father, and later between Tagore and Devi herself.
There are doodles among corrections, Avari explains, which show how his literary practice fed into his artistic practice. Alongside the manuscripts and correspondence are vintage photographs and personal effects, including a kurta and a lungi that Tagore left behind at the family home.
Among the artworks in the collection is a portrait of Devi, particularly notable because Tagore’s figure studies were not generally attributed to specific individuals in the way that portraits by his nephews, Abanindranath and Gaganendranath, often were, Avari said. There is also a landscape depicting the forests of Mungpoo, which Tagore embraced as a retreat.
On the international art market, Tagore’s paintings command significant prices. This year, Sotheby’s sold one of his watercolours for £1.02m (Rs 12.97 crore), nearly four times its low estimate.
Institutions such as Visva-Bharati in Santiniketan and the National Gallery of Modern Art hold much of Tagore’s archival materials, making the discovery of a private archive particularly rare.
He hopes that making these materials public will offer historians, scholars and admirers alike additional perspectives on Tagore. “We hope to add to the understanding of the artist, their career, and in this case, of course, our understanding of the man beyond his art as well.”
Rabindranath Tagore and Mungpoo runs between 10 November and 18 December at Christie’s space in south Mumbai.

Freddy Birdy, a copywriter whose delightful words have earned him a devoted Instagram following, recommends writer and historian Malvika Singh’s cookbook, Cooking for My Firefly.
“This book isn’t about recipes, though it does include them. It is a voyage through another time and place, tracing the social fabric of India of the 60s, 70s and 80s, trickling down to today. Told in Malvika’s beautiful prose, it takes us to a time when people entertained in homes, not in restaurants; when dishes were cooked in-house and there were no caterers or party planners. An era long before Instagram posts, WhatsApp invitations, celebrity chefs and food delivery apps, when the point of having a party was simply to have fun. It is an archive of photographs, food, culture, gossip, movie stars, politicians, royalty, set against the spectacular backdrop of Malvika’s dining tables through the decades. I like to dip into it every now and then, much as one might do standing in a dark kitchen with the light of the refrigerator enticing you to midnight goodies.”

Tennis the saviour for player who tried to take own life before Wimbledon
