Warning: This article contains references to suicide
The clues were there. Leandro Riedi struggled to even force a smile after winning a match which moved him closer to the Wimbledon main draw.
These are the moments usually cherished and celebrated by a player ranked outside of the world's top 100.
The Swiss player's solemn reaction was jarring, but then nobody outside of his immediate circle knew what had happened a few days earlier.
Shortly before Wimbledon qualifying began in June 2024, Riedi had tried to take his own life.
Panic attacks had been plaguing the world number 137 for almost 18 months. Anxiety and self-doubt had been around for much longer.
The toll they were taking on his mental health meant he felt there was no other way out.
"I always had anxiety. I was always a shy person, especially when I was younger. I always had this mindset that I wasn't good enough," Riedi told BBC Sport.
"I always thought I needed to do something special. I have to be perfect. This was my mental battle all the time.
"February 2023 to November 2024 was a horrible period of time. I was always scared of having a panic attack. I had no control over it whatsoever."
Very few people knew the extent of Riedi's mental health issues until he revealed last week that he had attempted suicide.
The 24-year-old wants to make two things clear.
Firstly, he is not looking for sympathy. He has only decided to talk about his experience to "send a strong message" for others struggling with their mental health.
Secondly, he is now in a "very good" place, thanks to professional treatment he has received over the past two years.
"I hope nobody ever has to go through what I did - it's horrifying and scary," Riedi said.
"But I want to be an example it can turn out well."
The past - 'I don't know how I played at Wimbledon'
In his darkest moments Riedi found salvation in the sport which he started playing as a three-year-old growing up in Zurich.
"I felt really home at a tennis court - I was able to perform and I was able to play," he said.
"So tennis was my saviour in that time. It helped me to go out of my thoughts for one second and focus on doing what I love."
It goes some way to explaining why Riedi decided to still compete at Wimbledon so soon after attempting to end his life.
Looking back, he is unsure how he summoned the strength to play.
"My coach told me to go home. He was the only one who knew. But then what? Be sad at home?" Riedi said.
"I didn't want to go home. I wanted to stay and I wanted to play. It was a horrible, horrible week.
"After the first round I remember I just left and went to the hotel. Usually you're excited and happy about a win, but I couldn't speak."
In his hotel room Riedi continued to have troubled thoughts.
He credits his psychologist, who stayed awake with Riedi until 3am to make sure he was not alone, for saving his life.
Riedi went on to win his second qualifying match before losing in the third and final round. At first he felt the pressure was "lifted", but not competing created a void.
Riedi describes how he was "scared" to leave his hotel room for the next two weeks, only going out to collect food deliveries from the lobby.
Tennis continued to be the only force which Riedi thought provided purpose. He managed to leave London for a tournament in Sweden, banking on it "bringing happiness".
But, after winning a match in Gstaad, he started to realise that going on to court was merely a placebo effect.
The catalyst of change came a few weeks later when a knee injury - the first "big injury" of his career - required surgery following the US Open.
"It was devastating for me because I knew my one happiness - tennis - was gone," Riedi said.
"In tennis I always had to fight [my mental health] because I was still playing. I didn't want to show any weakness.
"Then I realised I didn't want to fight any more. I wanted to help it. I wanted to work with it."
The present - opening up to send 'strong message'
Focusing on tennis and receiving the support of his "closest people" helped Riedi through his most troubled times.
Reopening his psychological "wounds", and discussing his inner trauma with experts, has been the key to his recovery.
He no longer has suicidal thoughts. The panic attacks have stopped. He still has anxiety but possesses the coping mechanisms to prevent it being debilitating.
Riedi had been planning to open up publicly for several months. He still felt nervous when he hit publish on his social media post, but he has been heartened by an overwhelmingly warm response.
"I have got messages from all over the world. Someone texted me from India saying they saw the post and are going through something similar right now," Riedi said.
"They said 'Your message really helped me. It gave me some power to believe it's going to work.' That's exactly what I was aiming for.
"People think tennis pros have all they need. I wanted to showcase that it's OK not to be OK even though others think you have everything."
Riedi says his mental health struggles were caused by "private issues" in his life and were not a consequence of his career.
But, with players increasingly speaking out about mental burnout, he wants his words to drive further change.
The ATP already provides an in-house psychology and wellbeing service, which offers confidential support at tournaments and remotely.
If a mental health disorder prevents a player from competing for at least six months, they can apply for a protected ranking. It allows them to enter tournaments without penalty when they are ready to return.
Riedi says the governing bodies can "never do too much", but he thinks there is still an issue on the men's tour with reaching out for support.
"For me, mental health is like a muscle. If your knee is injured, you do surgery and take care of it," he said.
"If you're injured in your mind, it's like you can't speak about it. That's not good.
"I hope my message shows tennis players, or anyone, that speaking out isn't a weakness. It's actually the opposite. It's strong and brave."
The future - 'sky is the limit' after making peace
Since working on his mental health, Riedi has produced some of the best results of his career.
He came through qualifying to reach the last 16 of the 2025 US Open - his standout performance at a Grand Slam tournament - and climbed to a career-high world ranking of 116 this year.
The most poignant moment came in June 2025 when he returned to Wimbledon.
A year on from his suicide attempt, Riedi decided to stay at the same Chelsea hotel because he wanted "make peace" with what had happened.
"It was very emotional, but in a good way," he said.
"I was like, 'wow, when you really work on something, if you stay consistent about something, one year can do so much'."
This year Riedi's progress on the court has been hampered by a torn tendon in a wrist.
Being sidelined for six months led to some friends wondering why he does not stop playing professionally. He says his "love and passion" for tennis will not allow him.
Riedi says the "sky is still the limit" and plans to make his comeback at the start of 2027, using a protected injury ranking to enter Australian Open qualifying.
"I really had to go through big obstacles, but I'm very proud I did this at such a young age. I'm actually this guy who just likes life," he said.
"I love to do things. I want to be happy. I want to be excited for my future and not be scared."

Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (H5N1) has been confirmed in chicken samples collected from a poultry farm at Kattiyankuppam village in Kurinjipadi taluk of Cuddalore district.
“The National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD), Bhopal, had confirmed the H5N1 avian influenza virus in samples collected from a poultry carcass on November 5, 2026,” District Collector Sibi Adhithya Senthil Kumar told The Hindu.
The confirmation has triggered a full-scale containment operation, with the Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Services Department culling all birds in the affected farm and within a one-kilometre radius of the epicentre.
According to Mr. Senthil Kumar: “As many as 35,647 bird deaths were recorded in the affected belt till November 13, since the first case of sudden mortality was reported from a farm at Thamanampatti village in Thiyagavalli Panchayat on October 30.”
Samples sent to four laboratories
He added, “Veterinary teams that visited the farm on the day of the first report collected samples and sent them to the Poultry Disease Diagnostic Laboratory (PDDL) in Namakkal.”
As deaths mounted in neighbouring farms, further samples were routed to Poultry Disease Diagnosis and Surveillance Laboratory (PDDL) Erode and the Central University Laboratory (CUL) at Madhavaram in Chennai.
On November 5, a carcass sample was despatched to NIHSAD Bhopal, which confirmed H5N1 on November 13, he said.
Following the standard operating procedure under the National Action Plan, the district was divided into compartments to restrict the spread of the disease.
Culling and disposal
“Initially, we sent only one sample. But a total of 15 farms are affected, of which all the birds in 10 farms have already been wiped out. So only five farms remain, and we are going to cull all [the birds] anyway. As many as nine Rapid Response Teams have been deployed for this purpose,” the Collector said.
So far, 1,550 birds have been humanely culled, and the department is working to cull 100% of the birds in the epicentre farm and within the 1-km radius, in accordance with the Government of India guidelines, 2021.
The carcasses are being disposed of through deep burial in designated pits, with bleaching powder applied and biosecurity measures in place.
An official said that movement of birds to and from the affected farms has been strictly restricted.
All poultry farms in and around the affected area have been brought under intensive surveillance, and disinfection using VIRKON-S — administered orally to live birds and as a farm-level spray — has been carried out as a precautionary measure. Cleaning, disinfection, and fumigation of the affected premises are in progress.
The Cuddalore district administration has asked the public not to panic, stating that the outbreak has been confined to the Cuddalore compartment and that no confirmations have been reported from the other compartments so far.
Pamphlets have been circulated and residents have been advised to report any unusual bird mortality immediately to the nearest veterinary institution.
In the affected area, an advisory has been issued prohibiting restocking of poultry for three months. To monitor this, the Revenue Department and local bodies are involved at the village level, the official said.
Poultry farmers have been asked to strictly follow the prescribed protocols and cooperate with the containment efforts.
The situation is being continuously monitored by the Animal Husbandry Department under the supervision of the District Administration.

Few love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.
The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi, and you can read an excerpt from the book here.)
Belonging, published today, contains moving glimpses of Gandhi’s private grief. She writes about the loss of her first child, who died shortly after birth, and the chilling discovery of grenades in a room of their house after Operation Blue Star, the 1984 military operation against Sikh separatists at the Golden Temple in Amritsar. She also provides a ringside view of several turbulent chapters in Indian politics, not least the violent assassinations of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, in 1984 and her husband, Rajiv, in 1991.
Her book also revisits some of the darker episodes that have dogged the Gandhi family and the Congress party, including Indira’s imposition of the Emergency in June 1975, a 21-month period during which civil liberties were suspended, political opponents were jailed and the press was gagged, which caused fear and dismay across the country. In Gandhi’s account, it also caused a rift within the family.
Ultimately, Gandhi’s memoir is a vivid record of six decades of India’s political transformation from the Congress-dominated secular republic she moved to in 1968 until today, when Hindu nationalism has become the dominant political force under Narendra Modi.
Here are five key takeaways from her memoir and what they reveal about the state of Indian politics today.
Gandhi has had no real contact with Modi for the last 12 years
Gandhi’s account offers a glimpse of how deep the political polarisation runs in Indian politics today. In one revealing passage, Gandhi writes that she has had “practically no real contact” with Modi in the 12 years he has led the nation. In fact, at times when the two have been in the same rooms, such as the speaker’s small chamber, Modi “tends to look away, avoiding eye contact”, she says. On occasion, she adds, he has asked briefly about her health after a hospital stay.
For her, this breakdown is a departure from the past, when leaders on opposing sides of the aisle “would treat one another with cordiality”. After the 2001 terror attack on parliament, Gandhi immediately called then-BJP prime minister AB Vajpayee to enquire about his safety, a gesture he appreciated.
Gandhi sees an increasingly authoritarian style of politics, in which those in power seek to “belittle and torment” opponents. For years, Gandhi’s son, Rahul, has been the subject of BJP’s ridicule, which calls him Pappu, a derisive term intended to portray him as inexperienced and naive. She adds that similar things are happening elsewhere in the world, an observation that can be read in the context of US President Donald Trump’s use of personal insults and ridicule against opponents.
It’s lonely at the top for India’s female politicians
India has an illustrious history of women occupying top leadership positions, long before many other democracies. But their rise has often come at a cost – that of loneliness in navigating a male-dominated political world.
In the book, Gandhi describes a 2012 conversation with Hillary Clinton on the countrys’ female leaders and their backgrounds. In her recollections of Indira, she shares that, despite wielding authority, Indira could feel besieged and profoundly alone, and this was particularly acute, Gandhi writes, in the months leading up to the declaration of the Emergency by her mother-in-law.
Gandhi also writes of her own isolation, including when she decided to take on the leadership of the Congress out of a sense of duty to her family’s political legacy.
Those in power are increasingly stonewalling the press
Among the many ways in which Gandhi charts the erosion of India’s democratic conventions in Belonging, one particularly telling shift is the changed relationship between the media and those in power. She recalls a time when journalists had opportunities to question prime ministers directly.
In 12 years in power, Modi has not addressed a single press conference on his own. He has sat in on one press briefing at the conclusion of an election campaign, and appeared alongside US presidents at joint press encounters after bilateral meetings, where they took questions from the press. Modi has consistently avoided facing journalists in an open forum, and his media interactions have largely been one-on-one interviews with sympathetic, pro-government news anchors or in one much publicised exchange with a Bollywood actor who asked him how he liked to eat mangoes.
And it’s not just media …
The book’s publication has brought renewed attention to concerns about the space for free expression in contemporary India, and the extent to which apprehensions about repercussions may influence what can be said, written and published.
Penguin Random House India was to publish Gandhi’s memoir but withdrew from the project in August. Gandhi told the Guardian that it was “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and said it had dropped the book after she declined certain suggested edits. Penguin has disputed her account, saying that the suggestion it decided not to publish the book because of refused editorial changes “does not accurately reflect the circumstances”.
The book, released in the US by Alfred A Knopf, is being published in India by HarperCollins.
In June, Penguin had also pulled out of plans to distribute graphic journalist Joe Sacco’s The Once and Future Riot, about the 2013 Muzaffarnagar communal violence. The publisher cited an inaccurate map of India and unresolved citation issues. Sacco, however, blamed the decision on the “current political climate in India”.
She’s had quiet fallouts with the ‘thoroughly dishonest’
Western political memoirs, particularly by former heads of government or senior politicians, are often forthcoming in naming political adversaries, recounting private exchanges and offering candid assessments of colleagues. David Cameron’s 2019 memoir, For the Record, took aim at his former friend, Michael Gove, describing him as “mendacious” and a “foam-flecked Faragist”.
Gandhi, in contrast, is restrained. She writes warmly of the closeness between the Gandhi family and that of Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan, whose parents she lived with when she first moved to India, but she makes no mention of the subsequent estrangement between the two families. In another instance, she does not name the political leader she describes as “thoroughly dishonest” and who she says she trusted in 1999, when Congress unsuccessfully attempted to form a coalition government.
What else we’re reading about
Art | Art Mumbai runs from 12-15 November at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse. Among the highlights of this year’s edition is artist Baaraan Ijlal’s collaboration with the celebrated lyricist Javed Akhtar, turning his evocative Urdu couplets into paintings. The two will be in conversation with curator Ranjit Hoskote on Friday.
Government | The official bungalow of Andhra Pradesh’s chief minister, N Chandrababu Naidu, was renovated by a government-owned enterprise for Rs 6.5 crore (£518,000), according to the Indian Express (£). The renovation work on the Delhi property included was said to have had a major makeover.
Film | Bollywood’s ambitious rendering of Hindu epic Ramayana, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Sai Pallavi, was released on 5 November. Touted as the most expensive Indian film ever made, it earned praise from the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw, who described it as “thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular”.
Your Diwali celebrations
Readers from India and around the world on the festival of lights and tell us how they celebrated.
 In India, Diwali comes to you. You can see it in the streets, hear it in the neighbourhood and feel it in the atmosphere. In the UK, it is different. Life carries on around you. But traditions do not have to disappear when you move countries – they can change shape. A small light in a quiet room can carry the same meaning as an entire street illuminated for Diwali. Aman, Plymouth, UK
 My favorite part of Diwali back home was getting up before sunrise on Narak Chaturdashi and having a ceremonial bath, followed by a breakfast of traditional Marathi Diwali snacks. I have been living abroad for over 10 years now and it’s always a bittersweet time of the year where I miss my family and the general vibe of Diwali in India. But I am trying to build new traditions as one half of an Indian-Austrian couple, which includes trading the traditional boxes of mithai for Manner Schnitten and marzipan. Charu, Germany
 There used to be more of a community spirit to Diwali. As kids, we would be tasked with going door to door, exchanging sweets and snacks with neighbours (sometimes to our great displeasure, because it made for awkward conversation with those we had annoyed with our antics). Nowadays, the celebrations are mostly private. Group celebrations are walled off within exclusive clubs, families light their own fireworks almost competitively, and people send each other sweets through a delivery service. Samyuktha, Chennai

It’s hard to take one’s eyes off Muhammed Riswan when he’s at work. The 23-year-old football freestyler from Areekode in Kerala’s Malappuram district conjures tricks with the ball in a delicately choreographed dance. It glides between his feet, next it is rolling on to his back right before he leaps into the air to catch it with one hand.
Riswan, who’s been freestyling for eight years, is one of the two Indians to win Instagram Rings 2026 award recognising creators. The other is Chanel model Bhavitha Mandava.
Riswan’s big break came with a video filmed at Keralamkundu waterfall, where he pulled off a freestyle move before gracefully arching the ball into the water. The clip has since clocked more than 600m views. Last year, he was invited to watch his sporting idol, Lionel Messi, play in Argentina.

With several Veerashaiva-Lingayat community leaders up in arms against the book Basava Mantapa, alleging that it distorts the teachings and philosophy of Basavanna and insults him, the Karnataka Cabinet on Thursday decided to confiscate copies of the book by Ravi Hanj, which are in circulation. It has also cleared action against publisher-journalist Vishveshwar Bhat.
After a prolonged discussion in the Cabinet meeting, a decision to confiscate the book and take legal action against the author was arrived at, announced Deputy Chief Minister G. Parameshwara. “Normally, we do not take swift action based on petitions. But in this case a decision was taken since its impact is likely to be felt across the State,” he said.
Earlier in the day, the Basava Samiti not only demanded a ban of the book, but also filed a police complaint seeking action against the author and the publisher. In a social media post, BJP State president B.Y. Vijayendra had also sought action against the publisher and the author.
When asked why an expert committee was not set up and an immediate decision taken after the samiti petitioned Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar, the Deputy Chief Minister said that senior Ministers had discussed the issue in the Cabinet meeting. “This is only the inittial reaction and we will look into the legality later. Action has been taken as per the provisions of BNS. We could not be silent spectators,” he said.
Addressing a press conference in Bengaluru, Basava Samiti president Aravind Jatti said the book hurt the sentiments of the Lingayat community and Basavanna’s followers in the name of research. He also called for criminal cases to be registered against those responsible for disturbing peace in society.
“Mr. Hanj has attacked Basavanna, who propagated the ideals of equality, a casteless society, the dignity of labour and the concept of a parliament, by describing him in derogatory terms. However, following the backlash, he is now trying to apologise and promise corrections. We want neither. They have mistaken the peaceful nature of the Veerashaiva-Lingayat community for weakness. It is condemnable that the book has been presented as a work of research to disguise its objectionable content,” he said.
“What is happening now is an ideological conspiracy aimed at undermining the Sharana philosophy and Lingayat identity. We know who is behind it,” he said.
Mr. Jatti alleged that such objectionable developments had intensified since the government declared Basavanna the “cultural leader of Karnataka.”
Large and Medium Industries Minister M.B. Patil warned that attacks on Basavanna and the Lingayat community would no longer be tolerated. “We will take to the street and launch an intense agitation. Protests have already begun in several parts of Karnataka,” he said.
“It is condemnable that Veerashaiva Mahasabha president Shankar Bidari and former Kannada Sahitya Parishat president Manu Baligar attended the launch of such a book. It is up to the Veerashaiva Mahasabha to decide what action should be taken against Mr. Bidari,” he said.
MLA for Aland B.R. Patil said, “There have always been elements that cannot tolerate the ideals of Basavanna, Mahatma Gandhi and B.R. Ambedkar. Mr. Hanj has written the book with malicious intent and attempted to tarnish Basavanna’s reputation.”
Former Mayor of the London Borough of Lambeth, Neeraj Patil, and thinker J. S. Patil also called for stringent action against the author and the publisher.
Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Eshwar Khandre, who is also president of the All-India Veerashaiva Mahasabha, has welcomed the decision of the Cabinet. In a release, he said that a demand to remove Mr. Hanj’s videos on social media had been made in the Cabinet, and the Cabinet had agreed to write to the Centre to get it removed.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations' top court, on Thursday held Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya community in northern Rakhine State during the military's 2017 "clearance operations".
In its judgment on the merits in the case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar, with 11 states intervening, the court found that Myanmar had violated its obligations under the UN Genocide Convention.
The ICJ also ruled that Myanmar failed to meet its obligations to prevent genocide by individuals acting alongside its security forces, punish genocide and other acts prohibited under the Convention, and enact the necessary legislation to fulfil its obligations.
However, the court found that Myanmar had not directly and publicly incited private individuals to commit genocide against the Rohingya.
The judgment also held Myanmar responsible for violating the ICJ's January 23, 2020, order to prevent the destruction of and ensure the preservation of evidence related to allegations of genocide.
As part of its ruling, the ICJ ordered Myanmar to end any ongoing violations and take immediate and effective steps to investigate individuals reasonably suspected of committing acts prohibited under the Genocide Convention. It said those found responsible should be prosecuted and punished, if warranted.
The court also directed Myanmar to provide assurances and guarantees that such violations would not be repeated.
It ordered the country to adopt restitution measures for the Rohingya, including ensuring their safe, voluntary and dignified return to their places of residence and the reunification of families displaced within Myanmar or abroad.
Myanmar has also been ordered to compensate the Rohingya community and its members for the damage caused.
The court said the amount and modalities of compensation or other forms of reparation would be determined during a subsequent phase of the proceedings. Myanmar has been directed to submit a report to the ICJ within two years, detailing the restitution measures adopted and the amount and modalities of compensation.
Reacting to the judgment, Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard described it as a historic recognition of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya.
"Genocide. This is the unequivocal finding of the ICJ. After years of denial, impunity and suppression of truth, this ruling is a historic and authoritative recognition of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya and a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families," Callamard said.
She said the judgment should serve as a wake-up call for the international community and urged Myanmar to comply with the ruling.
"The Myanmar authorities must comply with the ICJ's ruling immediately. All other states, including ASEAN Member States, must also act to uphold it by meeting their own obligations under the Genocide Convention and general international law and doing everything within their power to prevent and punish genocide," she said.
Callamard also urged governments to halt transfers of weapons, security and surveillance equipment, as well as military and security assistance to Myanmar. She called on the UN Security Council to impose a global arms embargo and refer the situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The Gambia instituted proceedings against Myanmar in 2019, alleging violations of the 1948 Genocide Convention in connection with the military operations against the Rohingya in Rakhine State in 2017.
The ICJ ruled in July 2022 that it had jurisdiction to hear the case.
The military campaign in 2017 followed attacks by Rohingya militants on police stations in August that year. Myanmar's security forces subsequently launched operations during which thousands of Rohingya were unlawfully killed. Women and girls were subjected to rape and other sexual violence, men and boys were tortured in detention, and hundreds of villages were burnt down.
The violence forced more than 800,000 Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh. Amnesty International estimates that around 1.3 million Rohingya refugees now live in the country.
Amnesty International said the judgment was particularly significant because it marked the first time the ICJ had found a state responsible for committing genocide under the Genocide Convention.
The organisation also clarified that the ICJ proceedings concern Myanmar's international responsibility as a state and are separate from proceedings seeking to establish the criminal responsibility of individuals.
Callamard said the ruling should not bring efforts to secure justice for the Rohingya to an end. She stressed that survivors and victims were entitled to full and effective reparations, sustained international support and accountability for crimes under international law.

FIA announce introduction of full-time F1 stewards from 2027 ahead of Las Vegas Grand Prix
Formula 1's governing body, the FIA, has revealed full-time stewards will be used for the first time from next year; watch the Las Vegas GP weekend on Sky Sports F1, with Friday's practice sessions at 12.30am and 4pm

The FIA has announced it will introduce full-time Formula 1 stewards from 2027 with the aim of having "greater consistency in decision-making".
The use of full-time stewards has been a consistent talking point in F1 as different stewards, who adjudicate all racing and technical matters on a race weekend, are used at each event over the season.
There has been an argument that this can lead to inconsistencies in decision-making when it comes to imposing penalties, or the severity of a penalty.

But the FIA announced on Thursday, ahead of this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, they will begin to recruit full-time stewards with a phased introduction from next year with the aim of establishing 12-15 full-time stewards over the coming years.
Currently, there are four stewards drawn from a large FIA pool of officials and one of those is a former racing driver. The new structure will continue to use the knowledge of driver stewards at each event and the FIA say full-time stewards will "allow for deeper implementation of best practice and greater consistency in decision-making".
The news comes a month after the opening of the FIA Remote Operations Centre at Biggin Hill in the UK, following a reorganisation of Race Control in 2022 after the controversial 2021 season which saw Max Verstappen overtake Lewis Hamilton on the last lap of the season-ending Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.
"This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport," said FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.
"The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula One World Championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport.
"Following the milestone opening of the new FIA Remote Operations Centre and strengthening of officiating development through initiatives such as the FIA High Performance Programme, this development will help to build greater expertise and continuity within our stewarding structure, strengthening our ability to review and improve regulations, support the development of future officials and ensure the highest standards of consistent officiating across all our championships."

Whatever happened to the diamond that went missing in F1 crash?
- Published
Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?
If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula 1's biggest unsolved mystery.
A $300,000 diamond was last seen stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix and it still has not been found 22 years later.
Did someone pick it up? Was it swept up with all the debris? Did it slip down a drain? Was it even a real diamond?
Someone, somewhere, knows something.
The reason why a 1.4 carat diamond was attached to the most delicate part of a car that reaches 200mph in a race was straightforward: publicity.
Jaguar Racing's results on the track had been mediocre at best since becoming an F1 team in 2000 and by 2004 its parent company Ford had decided it would be pulling them out of the sport.
"My job flipped from primarily running the team to primarily selling the team and finding a new owner or they would shut it down," former team principal Tony Purnell tells BBC Sport.
"It was probably the worst year of my life. Particularly because for the first few months I was sworn to secrecy."
His team needed some good PR to divert attention away from performance and improve its appeal.
They had enjoyed a successful promotional weekend in Silverstone the previous season thanks to a tie-up with Terminator 3 and so director of communications Nav Sidhu was looking to recreate the magic with another bit of help from a movie.
"I'd heard on the grapevine, around about the winter of 2003, that they were making Ocean's Twelve and we discovered that they were shooting some of the scenes in Monte Carlo," Sidhu says.
"One thing led to another and before you knew it, we had agreed [a deal] with George Clooney, Brad Pitt and Matt Damon."
Sidhu had arranged with legendary Hollywood producer Jerry Weintraub to have the film's branding and stars take over the team for the Monaco weekend.
The film plot centred on an audacious theft of a diamond-encrusted Faberge egg. Sidhu decided he wanted some sparkle on his cars too at the most glamorous race in the F1 calendar.
Sidhu negotiated with diamond company Steinmetz that the two Jaguar cars would have gems - which would today be worth about $1m in total - attached to them.
What happened next, though, was not part of the script.
While the champagne corks were popping on nearby mega yachts in the principality, the diamonds were being hand-delivered into the garages. There were two that would be mounted on to the car and a larger gem just for the photos.
The diamonds for the cars were encased by steel and fixed to the nose cones. One on experienced driver Mark Webber's car and one on rookie Christian Klien's.
Webber was starting from 11th place in the grid and Klien - in only his sixth race - was starting from 14th. They weren't expected to challenge for the podium, but they were expected to bring the diamonds back.
Monaco's street circuit is demanding, with narrow roads, tight turns and a tunnel.
Overtaking is difficult and crashes are common - as Klien soon found out.
In a chaotic first lap, the Austrian made contact with one of the Jordan cars exiting the Mirabeau corner. This damaged the front of his car - where the diamond was - and led to a slow collision with the barriers at the famous Loews hairpin.
Klien climbed out unhurt but the front of the car was crumpled.
It was not long before Sidhu had the diamond company on the phone asking if they would get their diamond back.
"I can't remember what I answered, but it certainly wasn't 'yes'," he says.
He couldn't even get on to the track to have a look as the race had another 76 laps to go and only then would the car - which had been lifted off the track by a crane and left behind the barriers - return to the garage.
"I was consumed with getting to that spot as quickly as I possibly could," Sidhu says.
"That hour and a half waiting for the race to finish felt like a day and a half, every single lap was just like pulling teeth."
By the time he had the chance to have a look, there was no sign of the diamond.
But there were plenty of theories.
Theory: it was not a real diamond
Sidhu completely denies the rumours of a fake diamond.
"I've learned that any diamond company is not going to go out there, particularly in the public domain, and use fake diamonds because clearly there's a high risk of being caught," he says.
"Had we used a fake diamond in that car and what took place took place, then clearly the embarrassment and the disrepute it would bring Jaguar, and Formula 1 for that matter, was too high risk.
"There's been loads of conspiracy theories about was it a real diamond or was Christian told to crash his car and I think that's what's given the story its life - there's a mystery to this story and that mystery will always breed different theories."
Purnell backs up the legitimacy of the diamond, recalling a conversation he had with the managing director of the team, David Pitchforth.
"David said, 'Tony, it was definitely real because when they came to the office with it, I picked the diamond up, went to the window and scratched the window' because that's how to tell.
"Hearing that from Dave, I'm in no doubt it was the real thing that was put on the car.
"I don't know if one of our mechanics was switched on enough to make a fake, but I don't think so."
Theory: someone pocketed it
"I think somebody probably just picked it up, put it in their pocket and... they're probably smiling and thinking, 'it's in my drawer'," says Purnell.
"I do think also that a fairly large diamond zooming through at 100 miles an hour probably shattered. Somebody's got a little bit, somebody else has got another [little bit].
"Maybe, sadly, just some guy was sweeping up the road or one of those trucks with the brushes and it all went down the sewer.
"It did occur to me that the ultimate thing would be if Clooney, Pitt and Damon had contrived to steal it because it was so in line with Ocean's Eleven. But that was a fantasy too far."
There would have been hundreds, if not thousands, of people in the area because within an hour or so of the end of the race the circuit would have been returned to public roads.
Sidhu is pretty certain about what happened to the diamond: "Someone's picked it up.
"What people tend to do is, believe it or not, pick up bits of tyre rubber, you know, claim that as Michael Schumacher's front tyre rubber or whatever they can find.
"Somebody may have picked it up not having any idea it came off a car.
"There's a lot of diamonds in Monte Carlo. There's a lot of people walking around Monte Carlo with a lot of jewellery and a lot of stones.
"Somebody dropped a diamond in Monte Carlo. Well, they're not going to miss that, are they? Probably not."
Theory: Klien crashed on purpose
Sidhu says the cost of the damage to the car was more than the cost of the diamond, which reports at the time said was uninsured.
And points and a good result in the race were more valuable to the team and individuals than a diamond or the publicity a crash would bring. It was simply not worth crashing on purpose.
"For us, bringing two cars home, ideally in the points, had far bigger commercial benefits to us in terms of constructors' points, broadcast money, and more importantly, trying to retain our sponsors and trying to protect the integrity of the team," Sidhu explains.
Klien drove straight into the barriers right in front of the marshals so would not have had the chance to start looking for a diamond or picking it up even if he had wanted to.
"Christian didn't try and say all the brakes failed or anything like that, he's just said 'I made a rookie mistake'," says Purnell.
"He was a young guy, first time, made a mistake, it happens. Doesn't usually happen with a $300,000 diamond flying into the crowd or wherever it went, but I'm sure Christian wasn't really aware of the diamond.
"No amount of money would have got Christian to do that [crash on purpose]. He wanted to make a success of what he was doing."
While events were unfolding, Purnell had not really been thinking about the diamond.
His main concern that day was that one of his drivers had crashed and the other also did not finish, and that this was not a good look in terms of pleasing current backers or attracting potential buyers.
"When Christian went into the wall and then later Mark retired, my entire thinking was 'Oh God. What am I going to say?' The chairman of HSBC [Jaguar's then sponsors] was there, Sir John Bond. Jackie [Stewart] was there.
"It was all about 'how am I going to explain another bad performance? How am I going to say 'just stick with the plan? We know what we're doing, it will take time' because sponsors don't have time. They want success."
In the end, the missing diamond came to the rescue.
"No-one mentioned Jarno Trulli winning the Grand Prix, no-one asked how the Jaguars did. No-one was interested that Mark Webber's car broke as well. It was, 'where's the diamond?'" says Purnell.
"I remember talking to somebody in Detroit saying, 'fantastic publicity over here, you know we never hear anything about Formula 1 but it's on the newscasts, it's in the papers - fantastic'."
Asked if the diamond mystery had helped the eventual sale of the team to Red Bull six months later, he replies: "I think that helped quite a lot because it buzzed the Jaguar team and showed that huge publicity was possible even if you weren't doing so well."
Red Bull went on to become hugely successful, winning eight drivers' championships and six constructors' championships since joining F1.
"You couldn't design a better PR weekend," says Purnell.
Even if it was not quite how it was planned and there is still the small matter of a missing diamond.

This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
- Published
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.
For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.
Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.
And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.
Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.
His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.
But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.
Ukraine, the balancing act
First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year, to be on the agenda.
This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.
However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.
Beijing is still trying to maintain that it is neutral in this war and has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's full-scale invasion.
The US, especially under the previous Biden administration, and Europe have accused China of sending Russia components that it could use in its war in Ukraine, while also propping up the country's economy by buying oil and gas.
Xi wants to keep Putin close, but not too close because he also doesn't want Russia's problems to become China's problems.
China's growing nuclear arsenal
Donald Trump has already made it clear he wants the three leaders to discuss limiting the world's supply of nuclear weapons.
The US and Russia possess the world's largest stockpile of nuclear warheads. But China is rapidly expanding its own arsenal, which is raising alarm bells in Washington.
The last major US-Russian arms control treaty, known as New START, expired in February this year, triggering fears of an arms race. The agreement had set a cap to control the number of nuclear weapons in US and Russia's arsenal.
Trump would like China to be included in any new agreement, but Beijing has pushed back.
Xi's argument will be that his arsenal is considerably smaller than what Washington and Moscow own, and, therefore, it would be unfair for Beijing to be bound by their limits. China also believes it should have the freedom to develop its own nuclear capabilities.
This subject could complicate Xi's bid for China to be recognised as a leader on the world stage - because the US could argue that the status includes being a responsible nuclear power.
Will everyone stick to the script?
Xi will want to control the optics of this meeting, from start to finish.
Chinese officials like to nail down agendas with talking points and produce carefully choreographed speeches.
But in this unprecedented summit, Xi will have to live with two very unpredictable leaders.
Both Trump and Putin have their own agendas and the US President has already threatened to go off script.
There is a risk that they both dominate the meeting and Xi ends up looking like a host, rather than the architect of a major diplomatic moment.
Of course, Xi may be ready for this. It may even play into his hands.
The Chinese leader has been trying to portray himself as a stable global leader - at this summit he will be flanked by two men embroiled in wars they cannot seem to end.
So any unscripted moment could serve to highlight his preferred role as senior statesman.
Xi's problems at home
For all the attention, this meeting of three men with vastly different agendas is unlikely to yield any significant outcomes.
But the power it projects is important for Xi as he heads towards next year's Communist Party Congress, where he is expected to secure a historic fourth term as leader of the party and country.
He may hope to use this as propaganda at home, given the country is grappling with huge domestic challenges.
A country-wide property crisis has dented consumer confidence. Local governments are heavily in debt. Manufacturing has slowed and more of China's workforce has become dependent on flexible jobs with no pension or social security. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find work. Frustration and anxiety about the future bubble up routinely.
Xi does not have to deal with elections, and the country has not seen major protests in decades. But he will be concerned about his popularity within the party elite as these problems - and the palpable frustrations they produce - grow.
At a time like this, a photo-op with Putin and Trump may offer him proof that his country's "century of humiliation" is over. China is no longer a rising power, he can argue - rather, it is increasingly shaping the rules of a new era.

Somewhere out there, right at this moment, a couple is probably still negotiating the final terms of a contract that permits one partner to play Grand Theft Auto VI around the clock for an entire week following its Thursday release. Adults who grew up on the felony-based video game franchise are taking steps to secure sick days—and some, no doubt, are granting their own kids permission to stay home from school (despite warnings from their teachers). Streamers on Twitch and YouTube stand ready to conquer the enhanced and expanded virtual domain of Vice City, seeking out every last Easter egg.
So don’t be surprised if a console owner in your life is curiously unavailable between now and Thanksgiving. The 13-year-wait for this latest installment of the series has felt interminable enough to inspire a meme used in reaction to any surprising or unprecedented news: “We got [fill in the blank] before GTA VI.”
Especially within the tech and gaming industries, the expectation is that many developers won’t be clocking in on Thursday or Friday. (GTA VI officially launches for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S at midnight local time on Thursday, November 19, according to publisher Rockstar Games.)
“I’m not going to question whether folks are really sick on their sick days or how they spend a vacation day,” says Mike, an executive of a gaming studio with more than a thousand employees, who requested a pseudonym to avoid damaging professional relationships within the industry. “I want them to spend time engaging with the medium we love, and there’s no question that playing lots of video games helps you make video games.”
In October, the HR software company BambooHR concluded through data analysis and a survey of salaried workers that the PTO request rate for November 19 is nearly 13 percent higher than equivalent days in past years, while Xbox is running a promotional campaign in which gamers can generate notes from a Dr. Xbox (DJ Khaled in glasses and a lab coat) claiming that they have a “Vitamin G” deficiency and are unable to work.
A few companies are getting ahead of the productivity slump; the hardware and software manufacturer Logitech, for example, announced earlier this month that all 7,000 employees would be granted a paid day off for gaming, to be scheduled any time within a year or so. In announcing the policy, the company cited internal studies on the ways that gaming may potentially improve job performance and mental health.
Riot Games, the publisher behind League of Legends and Valorant, has likewise made arrangements for the blockbuster event. “We have an open PTO policy, and we’ve seen leaders encourage their teams to enjoy the first day of release,” Joe Hixson, Riot Games vice president of communications, tells WIRED. “On our main campus, we'll be celebrating with a special-themed lunch menu and snacks that pay homage to the game. We also expect to see people firing it up in our console rooms during breaks and after hours.”
Riot additionally offers the Play Fund, a stipend of $25 a month for employees to spend on gaming titles across platforms and genres. “It makes us better developers by deepening our understanding of what makes a great player experience,” Hixson says.
Mike tells WIRED that on in-office workdays, the company has a typical absentee rate of 5 to 7 percent due to vacations, illness, travel, and the like. He estimates that on Thursday, it will be more like 10 or 12 percent. “Now, on the Friday, will there be some number of employees who are ‘working’ when they’re at home but also suspiciously slow to answer messages while they have big chunks of their calendar blocked out for ‘deep individual work?’” says the studio leader. “Yeah, probably.”
But it’s hardly unusual in the business for people to select their days off to accommodate a major game release, Mike says. In 2023, he was out for three days to play The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, which he recalls as “paradise.”
That said, he notes that the next leap forward for GTA is no ordinary affair. The hype for this franchise, he explains, “breaks containment,” reaching people who have not bought a new title in years.
That’s why even companies without ties to gaming culture have been making allowances for so-called Grand Theft Auto Flu. On Monday, the social team for the luxury real estate firm Serhant posted a video of CEO Ryan Serhant (also the host of the Netflix reality show Owning Manhattan) agreeing with an employee that if the clip garnered 400,000 likes, the office would close for GTA day. “You’ll never get that,” Serhant predicted.
The post picked up 1.4 million likes within 24 hours, prompting an update on Tuesday: The firm would honor Serhant’s promise. “We are big supporters of our team, their passions both in and out of real estate, and all things culture and tech,” Serhant said in a statement to WIRED, noting that “13 years of anticipation deserves a day off.” The company announced a floating holiday to staff on Wednesday, to be used any time before the end of 2026.
Also on Wednesday, Arizona Beverages announced a sweepstakes for social media followers who may have felt they couldn’t afford to miss a work shift. Dropping a PTO request for GTA day in the comment section, the company said, would enter that person for a chance to win $500 to cover their lost hours.
With this level of fanfare, nearly 16 million preorders bringing in revenue of $1.5 billion, and expectations of 45 million sales in its launch quarter, GTA VI is poised to be the most significant entertainment event of the year and the biggest video game of all time. It’s little wonder, then, that some have warned about the global economy slowing down this week as fans ignore their email inboxes and Slack messages to indulge in some extended role-play as streetwise criminals. One economist has estimated that the GTA release could cost the US economy $1 billion in lost productivity.
Mike isn’t buying this, however, arguing that the hype about “how GTA will impact the GDP or cause a failure of the power grid or whatever are just silly.” He points out that “PC is the biggest individual platform, and the PC launch timing is still unclear.” Neither have Rockstar and Take-Two announced a launch date for the game’s online multiplayer mode; only the single-player experience will be available on Thursday.
Andy Garin, an associate professor of economics at Carnegie Mellon University, also finds the concerns about sluggish market activity to be overblown.
“Speculation about a hit to productivity around these kinds of events pops up a lot, particularly during the Olympics or World Cup, when time zone differences mean major events are during the workday,” Garin says. “I don't think the release date of GTA VI will be that different than these sort of events that happen all the time, particularly if workers are using their allotted PTO or scheduling flexibility baked into their jobs.”
Malcolm Robinson, who has a YouTube channel dedicated to gaming and works at a veterans hospital, tells WIRED that the GTA release just happens to fall on his day off. “I plan on playing it for about eight to 12 hours straight on the first night,” he says.
Others have had no difficulty setting that time aside. One redditor who works as the distribution coordinator for a chain of auto shops in Colorado and requested anonymity out of concern for professional consequences says that he would have called in sick on Thursday but had the option to use PTO. His supervisor asked if it was to play GTA, which he confirmed. “He was like, ‘I get it, enjoy,’” this gamer reports. He plans to play along with his girlfriend, who is also taking the day off, and is excited to “sink my teeth into it before the entire thing gets spoiled.”
James Lord, a data entry coordinator in Edmonton, Alberta, tells WIRED that he initially offered to let his team take Thursday off for GTA purposes. When none of them expressed interest in the game, he says, he “jumped at the opportunity” to claim the day for himself. He’s been playing Grand Theft Auto since the original top-down POV game for the PC came out in the late 1990s.
Lord, too, is wary of spoilers—he locked down his social media on Tuesday night to avoid any—but nostalgia and lifelong relationships are even better reasons to jump into GTA VI as soon as he can. He’s going to boot up the game while on a call with his brother, who lives across the country, and they’ll be joined by friends living in Pennsylvania and Texas. It’s a reunion experience that wouldn’t be possible without a break from the 9-to-5 job.
“We lead busy lives now,” Lord reflects, “so having to set time aside for the game of the decade is important to us.”
