Oakland, Nov 19: Anthropic priced its initial public offering at USD 83 per share Wednesday, valuing the artificial intelligence giant at USD 1.5 trillion in the biggest Wall Street debut of all time.
The pricing above the range initially projected by the company signals broad investor enthusiasm for AI stocks even amid some uncertainty in the market stemming from the ouster of Nvidia's CEO and worries about an AI bubble.
Anthropic said the offering consists of 980 million shares, roughly 956 million sold by the company and the rest by selling stockholders. Proceeds totalling USD 81 billion put Anthropic's IPO ahead of SpaceX, which raised about $75 billion in June.
The San Francisco-based maker of the Claude AI tool is set to make its debut Thursday on Wall Street. The company had set a price range of USD 70 to USD 78 per share, initially offering 825 million shares. The stock will begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT”.
Anthropic decided to barrel ahead with the IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public.
Then there's the spectacular downfall of one of the industry's biggest cheerleaders, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
“This is strong appetite for this major AI IPO in Anthropic, and it's a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia. The pricing shows strong demand among investors,” said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co.
The company's rival, OpenAI, is not planning to go public until next year.
Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial”.
Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited.
While the company has ample cash for now, it will likely run through it quickly if it cannot raise more soon, given its outsize spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend USD 900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including USD 70 billion in the next 12 months.
An IPO is essentially a way to raise money, instead of going into further debt. And borrowing has gotten more expensive. That's partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector's massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads.
Lenders fear that AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability.
Anthropic's IPO also means its employees can begin to sell their vested stock, a payout that will make many of them millionaires. The IPO could also give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion and potentially add billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela Amodei.
The offering consists of 980,000,000 shares of Class A common stock, 956,351,354 of which are being sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 of which are being sold by certain selling stockholders.
Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the US and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business.
Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI division have all lost more money than they've made because of the huge costs associated with building AI. That has fuelled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector.
Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up.
Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the internet within months.
Amid those fears, the regulatory environment could also change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session.
Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centres. And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors vowing to stop new construction.
Adding to the pressure is the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.
The goal of most companies, above all, is to do well for their owners. Usually that means making profits and growing the business. Anthropic says it too will consider its stockholders, but it will balance their interests against another fundamental goal: “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.”
Like its rival OpenAI, Anthropic is a public-benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good. How that will play out for companies worth potentially trillions of dollars is uncharted territory.
Anthropic has set up a long-term benefit trust that will have the ability to elect or remove a majority of the company's board of directors. The trust will not run the day-to-day operations of Anthropic. But its influence means the company could opt for strategies that may not make the most money for investors.
Market valuation for AI companies is going to be “up and down for many years to come, but more up than down,” said Rich Lesser, the global chair and former CEO of Boston Consulting Group.
“Exactly what the flow of that will be, it's very hard to predict,” Lesser said in an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday at the Semafor Silicon Valley & The World forum. “There's no question what Anthropic and OpenAI and Google and a number of the other players in this industry have done is pretty remarkable.”

Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
SHENZHEN, China and MOSCOW, Russia — President Trump joined Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China on Thursday – capping two days of talks characterized by high-minded tributes to the role of great powers in maintaining peace, even as the men who led them had a role in starting some of the most intractable conflicts around the globe.
"History tells us when great powers are at peace, the world is secure," said Xi in opening remarks before cameras. "When great powers clash, the world is in chaos."
Putin noted their nations could make a "significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world."
"In that sense and I think in lots of other ways, we are making history," said Trump, who called it a "special responsibility" for the three countries to work together.
Yet, they offered few solutions toward peace, with the leaders offering divergent agendas going in:
Trump wanted to talk about reducing nuclear weapons and his mission to keep Iran from obtaining them; Putin was looking to push for an end to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow; Xi was signaling he hoped to avoid wading too deep into either topic — preferring to showcase China's growing global clout with more general statements promoting peace and economic stability.
There were also topics to avoid: Trump refused to engage with journalists' questions over China's alleged role in an espionage plot to steal high end Nvidia chips.
In the end, the summit's key deliverable was arguably the image itself: the president of the United States gathering with authoritarian leaders from China and Russia for the first time in American history.
Summit speed dating
Despite being billed as a summit of "groundbreaking significance" by the Chinese hosts, sit-down talks between Trump, Xi, and Putin were relatively brief — with some of that time taken up by interpreters delivering simultaneous translation.
Trump's meeting with Putin lasted 42 minutes. His talks with Xi went about an hour. The trilateral group session went on for an hour and a half.
Still, it was enough time for familiar Trump bonhomie to emerge.
"Who's he? He's my friend," said a smiling Trump upon seeing Putin ahead of their bilateral meeting.
"We've known each other for a long time," added Trump after he and the Russian leader warmly shook hands. "And I think a lot of wonderful things can come of this. Or at least start."
Similarly, Trump told Xi "as long as you and I are in charge of things, we're never going to have a problem."
Both statements were tacit admissions the clock is ticking on Trump's remaining two years in office — with change coming even sooner to Washington when Democrats take control of Congress come January.
Getting there
The China gathering was first proposed by Putin during an October phone call with Trump — an offer to meet together with President Xi when China hosted the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in China that November.
For Putin in particular, the meeting was always going to be a coup: the latest sign that — with Trump and Xi's help — he has effectively chipped away at Western attempts to isolate him politically over his invasion of Ukraine.
Back in Moscow, state media showed footage of the three leaders huddled together seemingly on loop — proof that Russia had regained what the Kremlin sees as its rightful place among global superpowers.
Ignored by Kremlin-friendly media were hints at more subtle power dynamics at play.
Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac personally — returning a gesture Trump had given the Chinese leader during his recent visit in Washington — while Putin received a more scaled down delegation upon arrival to Shenzhen.
Similarly, Trump was offered the top spot next to Xi during the APEC group photo and sat next to Xi during the APEC dinner reception — with Putin positioned at a separate table.
Was it a slight to Putin? A calculated attempt to flatter Trump? A reflection of Russia's vastly weaker economy? Whatever the answer, Xi wasn't ignoring his Russian guest entirely.
The two gathered privately for two hours on Wednesday — a sit-down China-Russia watchers estimated to be their 50th meeting all told.
Xi and Putin also echoed each other in their public speeches— both touching on familiar themes of the dawn of a new "multipolar world" and criticizing the use of sanctions as a sign of Western influence on the wane.
A new Yalta?
From the outset, critics of the summit voiced concern that Trump, Xi, and Putin would seek to carve the world into each country's perceived sphere of influence.
In Russia, the event was billed as a potential "new Yalta" — a reference to a moment in 1945 when the leaders of the U.S., Soviet Union, and United Kingdom hastily agreed to a post-World War II order for Europe.
Instead, the Shenzhen summit reflected the far more fragmented priorities of its participants.
Trump made no secret he hoped to include China in arms control talks — what Trump calls "denuclearization" — at a moment when key landmark nuclear treaties between Russia and the U.S. have all expired.
The catch: his Chinese hosts had little interest in the issue.
Beijing has repeatedly rebuffed U.S. attempts to include it in negotiations with Russia — noting that its arsenal remains far below those of Cold War-era rivals Moscow and Washington.
Differences also extended to the war in Ukraine, where Putin had hoped to press for U.S. and Chinese support for a settlement tilted in Moscow's favor — including a redrawn security map for Europe that would amount to a rollback of NATO from Eastern Europe.
Xi has insisted Europe have a seat at the table in any negotiated settlement. Trump has largely relied on his trusted envoys — real estate developer Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner — to hash out the complexities of any peace deal.
Following Trump's meeting with Putin, a Kremlin aide would only say that Ukraine had been the focus of the discussions — adding the Kremlin leader had left "in an excellent mood."
It was hard to see why.
Just hours earlier, Ukraine carried out a missile strike on the lone bridge linking mainland Russia to the annexed Crimean peninsula for the third time this week — effectively disabling the structure for months to come.
The bridge is widely considered the Russian leader's pet project — a symbol of Russia's claim to territory illegally seized from Ukraine in 2014 rendered in steel.
Additional research by Jasmine Ling.

A Ukrainian barrage of missiles and drones collapsed a crucial segment of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s prized Kerch Strait Bridge—and Ukraine’s military pulled off the strike deep within Russian-occupied territory without relying on the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications to guide the missiles in.
On the nights of November 15 and November 16, coordinated waves of Ukrainian drones and missiles caused enough damage to collapse one of two steel arches supporting the Kerch bridge’s roadway for automobile traffic, according to an Institute for the Study of War update. Russian sources claimed several hundred Ukrainian drones first overwhelmed Russian air defenses to pave the way for remote-controlled missile strikes focused on the bridge, with the latter prominently including Ukraine’s homegrown Flamingo cruise missile.
The Ukrainian operation adapted a Russian battlefield innovation by using drones equipped with mesh radios to create an airborne communications network, according to the Financial Times. Each networked drone acts as a relay node to extend the communication link between human operators and remotely piloted missiles and strike drones. Russia began using the technique to support long-range drone and missile strikes on Ukrainian cities.
During the Ukrainian attacks on the Kerch Strait Bridge, the flying mesh network allowed operators located more than 250 kilometers away (155 miles) to remotely guide missiles and drones in evading Russian air defenses while also homing in on the bridge’s weakest structural points, according to the Financial Times.
Ukraine’s takedown of the bridge segment was preceded by weeks of preparatory strikes that systematically destroyed or degraded Russian air defense weapons, radars and electronic warfare equipment arrayed to protect the bridge. The November 15 night attack on the bridge also coincided with the largest Ukrainian overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of the full-scale war, Reuters reported.

The Best Theraguns and Therabody Devices for Rest and Relaxation
Featured in this article
Theraguns are the gold standard for massage guns, so much so that the name has become synonymous with the category. But Therabody, the innovative company behind Theragun, has expanded its repertoire to boost wellness for more than just sore muscles and pain relief. It now offers a suite of gadgets to alleviate eye strain, soothe menstrual cramps, and depuff your skin (to name a few). We haven't tried every product in their lineup—we're getting there—but we've put several to the test, and these are our favorites. Plus, most of these gadgets are FSA/HSA eligible and designed with USB-C charging.
While Theraguns are an excellent investment for active individuals, it's worth noting that percussive massage guns are available at lower price points. If you're not married to the Therabody brand, see our Best Massage Guns for alternative recommendations that won't break the bank.
Updated March 2026: I've added the Theragun Mini Plus, the JetBoots Pro Plus, the SleepMask, and the TheraFace Mask Glo as new favorites. I updated the Honorable Mentions section with more products. Prices and links were also updated.
Honorable Mentions
TheraFace Mask for $650: The TheraFace Mask is a cordless, hands-free light-therapy device that uses three wavelengths (red, infrared, and blue) to tackle different skin care needs. To distinguish itself from its competitors, the TheraFace Mask includes a built-in vibration therapy mode that massages pressure points around the eyes, brow line, and scalp for some added stress relief. It comes with removable eye shields and a sleek display stand, which makes it easy to store on your nightstand.
JetBoots Prime for $550: Compared to the JetBoots Pro Plus, the JetBoots Prime keeps it simple: You get four pressure levels (25, 50, 75, and 100 mmHg) and three durations (20, 40, or 60 minutes), all adjustable throughout your session through a built-in control panel. They’re wireless with a 180-minute battery life and can even be used while charging. Plus, they fold down into the included drawstring bag, making them portable and fuss-free to stow away.
WaveRoller for $180: Foam rollers are great for improving range of motion, increasing blood flow, and reducing muscle tension. You can buy a decent foam roller for significantly less, but the WaveRoller offers Therabody app integration for a personalized experience and five vibration frequencies. Designed for full-body use, it works best for warm-ups and post-workout recovery.
TheraFace Pro for $420: The TheraFace Pro includes six detachable magnetic heads for cleansing, microcurrent, percussive massage, and LED light therapy—blue light for acne, red light, and infrared for anti-aging. Former reviewer Haley Sprankle tested the facial device and said her skin was softer and brighter, but she also noted that no clinical studies prove that microcurrent is an effective facial treatment.
Theragun Mini (3rd Generation) for $220: I recommend the Mini if you’re new to percussive therapy or need something packable for travel. It's the smallest and lightest Theragun, with three attachments (standard ball, dampener, and thumb) and a soft-zip case that fits into a tote, gym bag, or carry-on.
Theragun Sense for $300: The Theragun Sense is slightly smaller (and lighter) than the Pro Plus, and it’s also impressively quiet. Some settings are almost silent, allowing for a discreet recovery session at whatever time of day without having to worry about bothering your housemates. It has the same LCD screen and breathwork features as the Pro Plus, too. The main difference here is that it's compatible with fewer attachments, but four heads are still more than enough for the active individual.
Theragun Pro (5th Generation) for $530: Therabody still sells a few older generations as well as refurbished models directly. You may find even older models for sale on Amazon. While we haven't tried them all, we think it comes down to price. Anything older than 2019 or 2020 releases might not be worth it unless the price is shockingly low. This Pro came out in 2022, so it's still a decent deep tissue massager. If you can find it on sale and don't need all the latest updates, you should be happy with this one over the Pro Plus.
What Am I Testing Next?
I'll be testing the Theragun Prime (6th Generation) for $330, the RecoveryTherm Cube for $160, and the RecoveryPulse Arm for $160.

Washington, Nov 19: Islam is projected to be the world's largest religion by 2035, surpassing Christianity, according to a new study released by the Pew Research Centre on Wednesday. Pew said if current trends continue, there will be more than 3.6 billion Muslims and just under three billion Christians worldwide by 2070.
The absolute number of Hindus in India and worldwide will rise from 1.2 billion in 2020 to 1.4 billion by 2070.
But the rest of the world's population -- i.e., all non-Hindus -- will grow at an even faster rate. As a result, Hindus will shrink slightly as a share of the global population, falling from 15 per cent in 2020 to 14 per cent in 2070.
The world's total population is projected to increase by 29 per cent between 2020 and 2070, with Christians growing by 30 per cent and Muslims by 80 per cent.
"The largest source of new members of major religions is not adults who convert to the faith, but babies who are born into the group," the Pew projections found.
During 2020-2025, the fertility rate for Muslims was 3.1 children per woman, followed by the rate for Christians at 2.5, Pew said. The average fertility rate for all other women was 1.6, below the 2.1 level considered necessary for each generation to replace itself.
If current demographic trends continue, the number of Hindus in India will increase by 176 million between 2020 and 2070.
While India's overall fertility rate has fallen rapidly in recent decades, Muslims in India still have more children per woman than Hindus do, the Pew research found. As per the Pew projections, Hindus comprise 79.4 per cent of India's religious composition in 2020 and the number is set to slide to 75.8 per cent by 2070.
Muslims comprise 15.2 per cent of India's religious composition in 2020, and that share is set to rise to 19.6 per cent by 2070. Outside India, much of the projected growth among Hindus will come from Pakistan (over five million) and the United States (over four million).
According to the Pew projections, the US will have the world's fifth-largest Hindu population. Nepal and India will remain the only two countries with a Hindu majority.
It forecasts that Buddhists will shrink both in number and as a share of the world's population, partly due to expected declines in the overall populations of China, South Korea, and Japan.
If recent trends continue, by 2070 more than half of the world's Christians will live in sub-Saharan Africa. The Democratic Republic of the Congo will surpass the United States as the country with the largest Christian population.
The United States will no longer have a Christian majority, though Christians will remain the biggest religious group in the country.
Pakistan will have the largest Muslim population, followed by India, Nigeria and Indonesia, which currently has the most adherents to Islam.
Many countries have seen a steady proliferation of the "nones" -- people who are atheist, agnostic or religiously unaffiliated.
Excluding China, which has a high proportion of "nones" but faces a sharp population decline, Pew said the ranks of "nones" elsewhere will grow by more than 180 million by 2070.
The "nones" already account for a majority of the population in 10 countries, including the Czech Republic, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Uruguay and Vietnam, according to Pew. South Korea, France and the United Kingdom are forecast to join this group by 2070.

You can edit Instagram Reels on Mac using Claude AI and the free Instagram Edits app. Install Claude Code, enable the app’s MCP automation server, and connect both. Then use simple text prompts to create projects, arrange clips, add transitions, titles, and effects, and export finished Reels in 4K.
The wait is over. The Instagram Edits app is finally available on desktop, but only on macOS, as of this guide. Instagram Edits is my go-to app not just for editing Instagram Reels, but also a reliable free video editor with all the features and a simple design.
Although the app is designed for creators and competes with CapCut, it has been limited to Android and iOS so far. The desktop interface is slightly different and can be complex for beginners. It took me a while to get used to it, but I have created a detailed guide to get started.
I also created a guide on how to connect your MCP, like Claude, to Instagram Edits to edit your videos, and it covers everything about this feature, including common setup errors. This guide is for beginners, so each step is comprehensive and detailed.

How to Connect Claude AI to Instagram Edits and Edit Reels on Mac
Before connecting your Instagram Edits app to the MCP server, ensure you have the following pre-requirements:
- A Mac with an Apple chip (M1 or newer) on macOS 15.1 or later. Currently, the Instagram Edits desktop app is only available for macOS, with Windows and Linux versions coming soon, but there is no expected release date yet.
- Download and install the Instagram Edits app from here

Part 1: Get Claude Code
Step 1: Open Terminal and type the command: claude –version, and press Return. If you see a version number, it means Claude Code is already installed on your device. You can skip to Part 2 to continue setup.
If you see something like zsh: command not found: claude, it means Claude Code is not installed on your device, or Terminal can not find it yet. Follow the next steps to install Claude Code on your Mac.
Install Claude Code: To install Claude Code, use the official Anthropic installer. To do that, open Terminal on your Mac and paste this command: curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Wait a few minutes, and then you will see a ” Claude Code successfully installed message in your terminal.
Check the setup notes below. If you see something like installation exists but ~/.local/bin is not in your PATH, it means the terminal still can’t find Claude Code yet.
Now follow the next two steps. If you don’t see such a note, you can quit the terminal, reopen it, and use this command to confirm that Claude Code has been successfully installed on your device: confirm claude –version. If you see a Claude version, it’s installed on your device. Then continue with part two.
Next, paste this command into the terminal and press Enter: echo ‘export PATH=”$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH”‘ >> ~/.zshrc

There is a six-year-old elephant seal in Tasmania named Neil who has a taste for light property damage during the winter months. Now, the state has a management plan.
Neil's annual “hauling out” and subsequent misadventures on the southeastern part of the island has delighted locals, making him a local mascot and a viral social media star.
But Neil’s on-land hijinks—as he experiences his yearly “catastrophic molt,” during which he, like all elephant seals, sheds and replaces his top level of fur and epidermis— has also created headaches for local officials. Neil, who weighs over 2,000 pounds, has destroyed walkways, flattened bollards, bowled through fences, and rammed vehicles. The enormous and growing public interest in Neil has also been a source of concern, as officials spend tens of thousands of Australian dollars to keep the public at a safe distance from him.
The Tasmanian government, finding itself in a precarious position, has finally decided to take action. The Department of Natural Resources and Environment published a 27-page dossier this week titled “Neil the Seal Management Plan.”
“The purpose of this Plan is to set out a framework for managing the resident elephant seal known as Neil in Tasmania, recognising the complex challenges associated with his recurring haul out period,” the dossier states.
Neil has a dedicated task force to monitor his whereabouts and according to the dossier, they would take a “non-intervention,” hands-off approach if he hauls out in a secluded location. They’d keep tabs on Neil from a distance, erecting signs around the area to alert the public of Neil’s presence while advising them to keep their distance. Should the public tempt fate and approach Neil, the task force can call in security personnel to keep people and the seal safe.
The second contingency plan is titled “on-site seal management,” which would be necessary if Neil comes ashore in a more public location, and has immediate access to roads and critical infrastructure that up the odds of molting-induced mayhem. One proposed management option involves “hazing,” which would essentially treat Neil like a frat pledge. The dossier doesn’t get into specifics—ostensibly there’s no paddling or eating a live goldfish involved—but highlights what it calls a “non-violent method of using deterrents and negative associations to disturb an animal, compelling them to move,” which can include “controlled visual, tactile and vocal stimuli where appropriate.”
The document also notes that Neil appears to be adapting to and thus eluding “standard management practices,” meaning that the task force needs to stay nimble in coming up with new methods to curb Neil’s taste for antics.
Tasmanian officials also propose “seal enrichment,” which they say would be used in tandem with other management options, to redirect “natural exploratory behaviors” (like engaging with infrastructure) towards decoy items “designed to withstand repeated interaction.”
Officials also say that despite their best efforts to avoid Neil-related interruptions to daily life, “significant events,” such as road closures, public safety incidents, relocation or translocation activities, or wildlife-born diseases, are still liable to happen. During such events, members of the public are advised to contact the Marine Mammal Hotline, also known as “0427 WHALES.”

Scientists use special tests to understand how autistic people see, hear, and process information. But many of these tests require participants to understand complex spoken rules, speak their answers out loud or fill out long written questionnaires. For instance, a standard perception study might ask a participant to watch a screen and say out loud which direction a cluster of dots is moving. A non-verbal autistic child cannot provide the required response, automatically excluding them from the research.
Now, Boston University researchers have tried to study perception without relying on language or conventional test-taking skills by turning a sensory test originally developed for rodents into a non-verbal online video game that adolescents across the autism spectrum can learn and play.
This holds special promise for India. A non-verbal, remote game bypasses the need to translate complex clinical instructions into dozens of regional languages, and allows researchers to reach autistic individuals far beyond the major metros where specialist centres are concentrated.

Tamil Nadu police file complaint against TVK cadres over Sothuparai dam videos
Police in Tamil Nadu’s Theni district have filed a complaint against TVK cadres over social media videos claiming water was released from the Sothuparai dam.
Police in Tamil Nadu’s Theni district have registered a complaint against cadres of the ruling Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) after videos claiming that water had been released from the Sothuparai dam for irrigation were widely circulated on social media, officers said on Thursday.
The complaint was lodged at the Thenkarai police station by public works department (PWD) officials, people aware of the development said.
According to investigating officers, the TVK cadres allegedly opened the sluice gates on Tuesday to release the water stored in the dam and were seen showering flowers as soon as the water was released. “A case has been booked over the release of the video and currently, investigations are on,” an officer told HT.
“The shutter is used to release surplus water after desilting the nearly 20-km-long canal, which is located nearly 1 km away from the dam. The canal is cleaned to ensure that the water directly reaches the irrigation tanks,” a PWD official said.
“However, the dam did not have surplus water and the water level was yet to reach a certain capacity for it to be released from the dam for irrigation purposes,” he added.
People aware of the matter in the ruling TVK said action against the cadres was taken based on the instructions of the party high command.
“Usually, members of the farming community clean the channel before opening the shutter in order to release the water. Some party cadres have also accompanied them and circulated the videos claiming that water was being released from the Sothuparai dam. What actually circulated on the social media is completely fake news,” a senior party leader told HT. He added that action was being taken against the party cadres who accompanied the villagers.
Sothuparai Dam is named after two words — food (Soru) and rock (paarai). It is located about 9 km from Periyakulam in Theni district, at the foothills of the Kodaikanal hills in the Western Ghats. It helps irrigate the entire area of Periyakulam. The water stored in the dam is a combination of rainwater, water from small streams flowing down the Kodaikanal hills and water released from Berijam Lake in Kodaikanal.
The dam has a small tunnel and irrigation canal, and the shutter is opened only during periods of heavy water inflow. The full storage capacity of the dam is 2.831 cubic metres.
The dam was originally conceptualised in 1920, and construction began in July 1982 but was halted midway in 1983. However, work resumed in 1997 and the dam was finally completed in 2001. On November 15, 2001, the reservoir reached full capacity, overflowing for the first time.
Meanwhile, the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) and Pattali Makkal Katchi (PMK) criticised the ruling TVK government.
AIADMK general secretary Edappadi K Palaniswami, in a statement, condemned the TVK government and the cadres for lacking the basic sense to understand that a massive surge of water from the dam would endanger the lives of people along the banks. He urged the TVK government to take strict action against all the cadres who were involved in the incident.
PMK president Anbumani Ramadoss, in a party statement, raised questions about how TVK members opened the dam without any concern or care about the consequences, and what the officials were doing before they opened it.
He said the TVK members who illegally entered the Sothuparai Dam and released water must be arrested. The Tamil Nadu government must prevent such incidents from happening in the future, his statement added.

Anthropic’s early birds are getting very rich
Anthropic’s expected $1 trillion debut would put it ahead of JPMorgan Chase and Walmart.
Americans have debated, derided, praised, and protested the frontier AI labs. But they’ve never been able to directly own a piece of one…until tomorrow at 9 am.
That’s when Anthropic, developer of the chatbot Claude, is expected to go public at a valuation of more than $1 trillion. That would immediately rank the almost-six-year-old lab among the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies — up there with the likes of Walmart and JPMorgan Chase.
It’s a major public test of what investors think Anthropic is worth, at a moment when a lot of people — policymakers, regulators, and technologists among them — are questioning the economic and social value of the AI industry. AI stocks have been shaky lately, and many of the new congressional Democrats have promised to take a tougher stance toward data centers and related technology.
But you wouldn’t know it from the hype around the IPO, which is on track to become one of the largest ever. Anthropic initially set a price range of $70 to $78 a share, then reportedly revised the offering at $83 per share as demand surged far beyond the number of shares available.
Investors are apparently betting that Anthropic has more growing to do. For ordinary buyers, that represents a chance to share in a company whose technology could cost us our jobs…if not our very existence on Earth. 💀
The biggest winners, however, will almost undoubtedly be the executives, employees, and early investors at Anthropic itself. The timing of the IPO helps with that.
Go a little deeper
Some of America’s most iconic companies went public very early in their lifecycles. (Think Apple, Amazon, and eBay, which all IPO-ed before they were five years old.)
But over the past two decades or so, many of America’s biggest businesses have instead grown in private. Between the early 2000s and 2025, the median age of a company at IPO doubled from six years in 2000 to 12 in 2025.
Analysts credit two main factors for these increasingly late-breaking IPOs. One is the fast-growing availability of private capital from venture funds, wealthy individuals, and other companies. Firms that once needed to go public to raise money to grow can now raise that money privately.
The other factor is the desire to maintain control over the company and its information: Private firms don’t have to file public financial reports or give public shareholders a vote on corporate matters.
But while that may be good for companies and their leaders, it’s not always or unambiguously great for the general public. Financial reports shed valuable light on how a business operates and where its risks lie, for instance.
There’s a financial downside for us normies, too. “The way I see it, the later a company goes public, the more of its growth gains accrue to private investors,” Brad Badertscher, a professor of accountancy at the University of Notre Dame who has studied IPO trends, said in an email to Vox.
Under this system, insiders like executives, employees, and early investors can nab shares at a low price while the company is still young and then benefit if its value goes up. Retail investors only join the party after much of that growth has already happened.
Of course, growth is never guaranteed. Early investors, private or public, also take on a lot of risk. And even now, several years in, new investors are still taking a substantial risk when they buy shares in Anthropic — a company that, in the grand scheme of recent IPOs, isn’t even that late to the process.
There’s the threat of greater regulation from a Democratic Congress. The fallout of the shake-up at Nvidia. The specter of a potential AI market crash (to say nothing about the aforementioned end of the world).
If would-be shareholders are bothered, however…you’d never know it! They’ve been waiting years to buy Anthropic stock, and they very much want in.

Environmental exposures during pregnancy and childhood, including tobacco smoke, indoor air pollution and dietary quality, may be associated with health outcomes such as BMI and behaviour, with many of these links persisting into adolescence, a new study has found.
Researchers, led by those at the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal), identified six prenatal and 42 childhood exposures associated with multiple outcomes and health families simultaneously.
The study, published in Science Advances, provides an atlas of associations between early-life environmental exposures and health, highlighting factors that may be relevant for prevention and policy action.
"Our approach allowed us to jointly analyse associations between the early-life exposome and multiple health outcomes instead of studying each one separately," first author Augusto Anguita-Ruiz, ISGlobal and University of Barcelona researcher, said.
The researchers used an outcome-wide exposome approach to study associations of exposures with health across four domains -- cardiometabolic, mental health, respiratory, and allergic problems.
The exposome refers to the totality of environmental exposures a person experiences throughout life, including factors such as diet, tobacco smoke and air pollution.
The exposures examined included diet, physical activity, sleep and other individual behaviours, as well as tobacco smoke, indoor and outdoor air pollution, chemical pollutants, metals and characteristics of the built environment.
The authors "identified a set of 'master regulator' exposures, such as maternal smoking, indoor air pollution, endocrine-disrupting chemicals, and dietary and urban factors, that influenced multiple health domains, with effects persisting into adolescence."
Senior co-author Valérie Siroux, researcher at the French National Institute for Health and Medical Research (Inserm), said: "Although no exposure was associated with all four domains, around one in three of the selected exposures was linked to more than one, suggesting that certain exposures can have broad and multisystemic effects on health."
Maternal smoking during pregnancy was associated with higher BMI and more externalising behaviours, such as aggression and impulsivity, in children during both early childhood and adolescence, as well as more ADHD symptoms during adolescence.
Higher maternal meat intake during pregnancy was also associated with several mental health outcomes and asthma in children, as well as wheezing and dermatitis during childhood.
Associations between environmental exposures and health parameters observed in early childhood were found to persist in adolescence.
The observation suggests that early environmental conditions may leave relatively durable health signatures, the researchers said.

Anthropic becomes most valuable AI firm as shares soar in stock market debut
- Published
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the public stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.
Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 per share, showing there is plenty of excitement around AI.
Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?
In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.5, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day, with shares hitting $97.
Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet (down 3%) and Amazon (down 3.9%).
The build-out happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.
The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.
"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."
While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.
The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate more quickly tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet.
It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.
As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.
The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.
That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.
Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.
With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.
"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.
So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth $1.5 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.
"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."
A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.
One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.
On Thursday, the same day Anthropic went public, a bipartisan group of lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.
A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.
Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.
Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".
"AI carries real risks," she added.
Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

In mid-November, a nationwide ground stop halted flights across the United States. In response, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called on Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for the Federal Aviation Authority. However, many blamed Duffy for allegedly opposing a bill that would give funding to the FAA in 2019, when he was a congressman.
A clip went viral in which CNBC asked Duffy about his purported voting record.
Duffy did vote against the 2019 bill that would have given the FAA more funding, and as a result we've rated the claim true. However, that is not the entire story. Duffy also voted in support of three previous bills that increased FAA funding.
Snopes reached out to the Department of Transportation. A spokesperson directed us to the 2025 PolitiFact story that highlighted three previous instances when Duffy supported funds for the FAA. A spokesperson for Duffy told PolitiFact that the 2019 bill only represented a small funding increase.
A CNBC anchor asked Duffy about his opposition to the 2019 funding, "When you were a congressman, in 2019 you actually voted against support for the Transportation, Housing, and Urban Development Agencies Appropriation Act, and that would've given more funding to the FAA. Do you regret that vote?"
In response, Duffy said:
I've seen those articles. All the FAA reauthorizations that funded the FAA, I voted for all of those. That vote was not a funding ― a proposal for the FAA. I was on the record voting for all the FAA funding. But the question is what is this Congress going to do?
Duffy referred to three previous instances in which he supported bills that gave additional funding to the FAA. In 2011, Duffy voted in support of the "FAA Modernization and Reform Act," which approved $63.4 billion to the FAA over the next four years.
In 2014, he voted in favor of the "Federal Aviation Administration Continuing Appropriations Resolution," which passed the House but not the Senate.
In 2018, he voted for the "FAA Reauthorization Act," which approved $96.7 billion in funding for federal aviation programs over five years.
In 2019, Duffy voted against the "Transportation, Housing and Urban Development, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act," which would have given $17.7 billion in total budgetary resources to the FAA. The House Appropriations Committee noted the funding amount was "$310 million below the fiscal year 2018 enacted level and $1.6 billion above the request."
At the time, Duffy did not give a reason for his "No" vote. When we asked the Department of Transportation to clarify over email, a spokesperson referenced his 2025 comments to PolitiFact, in which his office said the bill represented only a small funding increase.
Republicans opposed the 2019 bill for a range of reasons, including that U.S. President Donald Trump would have vetoed it. The bill—which bundled funding for various agencies and put up for a vote during a government shutdown—was passed by a Democratic-controlled House but stalled in the Senate.
On Nov. 14, Democrats questioned Duffy's call for additional funding for the FAA. Members of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure noted:
Congress approved $12.5 billion for the Department of Transportation to make necessary safety upgrades to our air traffic control system. Fifteen months later, the administration's obligated $4.3 billion but only spent $1 billion, leaving $8 billion unobligated and $11 billion unspent. Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?
Duffy said this was not true. In a CNN interview, he said:
I have no money in that $12.5 billion that I can use for a new architecture for telecom. I can't build new software to manage our airplanes in the airspace because it dates back to the 1990s, but there's no money for that. There's no money for towers. Our towers are old.
The spokesperson for the Department of Transportation emphasized to Snopes over email that in 2025, Democrats opposed the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, in which Republicans allocated $12.5 billion for air traffic control. The act passed with almost exclusively Republican votes. In September, Duffy had asked for $30 billion to upgrade the FAA systems. After the November ground stop, he upped the request to $50 billion.
In sum, Duffy has supported FAA funding in the past, but did vote against the 2019 bill.
For further reading, Snopes has reported on Duffy's other statements regarding the FAA as well as the unfounded claim that Duffy's son-in-law has ties to an artificial intelligence air traffic management tool.

Bulk Crap Uninstaller (BCU) lets you uninstall multiple Windows apps at once for free. Select unwanted apps, remove them in batches, and clean up leftover files to reclaim storage. It also supports quiet uninstallation, but review your selections carefully before deleting anything.
An easy way to free up storage on your Windows PC is to remove unnecessary apps — ones you no longer need. You identify the apps and delete them one by one. It’s pretty straightforward as long as you’re dealing with a couple of apps. If the number is higher, the method starts to feel tedious.
This is where a one-click uninstaller comes in handy, allowing you to delete multiple apps at once. Bulk Crap Uninstaller (BCU) is one such app. Here’s how it works and how to use it to bulk uninstall Windows apps on your PC.
What Is Bulk Crap Uninstaller, and What Makes It Better Than Other Tools?
Bulk Crap Uninstaller (also called BCUninstaller or BCU) is a bulk uninstaller that makes uninstalling multiple apps on your Windows PC at once incredibly easy. It can scan your computer comprehensively and find everything from Windows Store apps (pre-installed by Microsoft) and third-party apps to Steam games, portable apps, and Chocolatey packages. You can then select what you want to remove. This adds them to a queue, and the app handles uninstallation for you.
Bulk Crap Uninstaller stands out from other bulk uninstallers, including some paid alternatives, in a few ways. First, it can find broken or un-uninstallable programs and force uninstall them. Second, it can scan your file system and find leftover or orphaned items (files, folders, registry keys) left behind by apps you deleted manually. That way, you can safely and easily delete them and reclaim storage space. And third, it offers a “quiet uninstallation” mode that eliminates the need to click through dialog boxes and instead uninstalls the selected apps silently in the background.
How To Use Bulk Crap Uninstaller to Bulk Uninstall Windows Apps on Your PC
Bulk Crap Uninstaller is free to download and use. Go to the Bulk Crap Uninstaller website, and you’ll see multiple ways to download the app there. You can choose any method; the easiest is to download the installer from SourceForge. Next, run the installer and follow the on-screen instructions to complete it. Once installed, the app will require configuration. Configure it per your preference; you can change the settings later if you don’t like them. I recommend enabling the Select using checkboxes and Show items in groups options.
Once configured, Bulk Crap Uninstaller will scan your computer and populate a list of all installed programs, including hidden apps, Windows Store apps, Steam games, portable apps, orphaned shortcuts, and leftover registry keys. You’ll see additional details, such as size, version, publisher name, installation date, and certificate, next to each listing. You can use filters and sort options to filter out and sort items in a specific order.
Go through the list and tick the checkbox next to the apps you want to uninstall. The status bar at the bottom will show how many items you’ve selected and how much space deleting them will free up. Finally, click the Uninstall button at the top. The app will open a dialog box showing your selection. Hit Continue while checking (and changing, if required) the settings, and click Begin Uninstallation.
You’ll see a prompt asking if you’d like to create a Restore Point. Select accordingly, and the app will uninstall the selected apps. While it deletes apps, you’ll see the uninstallation status in a dialog box. At any point, if you want to cancel the uninstallation, click the Cancel button.
Once Bulk Crap Uninstaller finishes uninstalling the selected apps, it will ask if you want to delete the leftovers too. Review the listed files carefully, uncheck the ones you don’t want to delete, and click the Delete selected button to get rid of them. Be sure to back up your registry if you’ll be deleting leftover registry keys.
When you uninstall apps this way, you’ll need to click through multiple dialog box menus to complete the uninstallation. You can save yourself this hassle by clicking the Quiet Uninstall button instead of Uninstall after selecting apps for deletion. Bulk Crap Uninstaller will try — wherever possible — to uninstall apps silently. You won’t see visual confirmation in this mode.
Other Bulk Crap Uninstaller Features You Should Know About
For most people, the standard uninstallation process we checked out above is enough to get the job done. However, Bulk Crap Uninstaller has a few advanced features that can help you get the most out of the app.
For example, Bulk Crap Uninstaller offers a CLI version called BCU-console. It’s a great option for those who want to clean up their PC without dealing with multiple windows. Similarly, it lets you run an uninstallation script with your selected apps to automate deletion. This can be useful for cleaning up new PCs, too. Just feed the app a list of all the pre-installed apps from Windows, and it will remove them. You can go through Bulk Crap Uninstaller’s documentation to learn more about using scripts.
Bulk Crap Uninstaller can also run portably. So, you can put it on a USB flash drive and run it directly. This is handy when you want to uninstall apps on a PC running very low on storage space or one that isn’t connected to the internet and can’t download the Bulk Crap Uninstaller app.
Last but not least, Bulk Crap Uninstaller is highly configurable. As such, you can configure its behavior per your preference. Click the gear icon in the top toolbar to access the app’s settings. Here, you can change things like where to look for apps, which items to show/omit, and how the list appears. You can also configure the default behavior of quiet uninstallation and how many concurrent uninstalls the app can perform, among other things.
What I’m Not a Fan Of
I’ve used Bulk Crap Uninstaller on my PC for a while, and although it does its job well, there are a few aspects that I’m not a fan of and wish were better. The biggest one is that the app’s interface can seem intimidating, especially to first-time users. In other words, it looks more like a developer tool than a regular consumer app. It’s best to spend some time exploring different menus and options the app offers before jumping straight into uninstalling apps.
Then, there’s the risk of over-cleaning. Because Bulk Crap Uninstaller can scan deep system components, too, it’s important to double-check the selection — and not blindly trust the populated list — before uninstallation. You can configure the settings to minimize the risk. Another thing I’ve noticed is that the quiet uninstallation mode sometimes doesn’t work: some apps don’t obey it and keep popping up dialog boxes that require confirmation before uninstallation. Although rare, some users have complained about aggressive registry scanning, wherein Bulk Crap Uninstaller highlights shared keys (those used by other apps too) for removal. You can avoid this by reviewing the registry keys highlighted for deletion.
These aren’t drawbacks of Bulk Crap Uninstaller, though; they’re just a trade-off for its advanced capabilities. For this reason, it’s important to configure the app before you start using it and be completely sure about the actions you perform using it. You should also create a Restore Point when dealing with apps with broken uninstallers or stubborn leftovers. This way, if the cleanup goes wrong and renders your PC unusable, you can roll back to the last working state and undo the action.

Top House Democrat questions what Trump accomplished in Xi-Putin summit
Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., on Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping
Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, questioned Thursday what President Trump accomplished in his summit with the leaders of China and Russia, warning that the meeting could undermine U.S. alliances.
"I wish he had a plan and a strategy if he was going to meet with them and goals. Apparently, he does not," Meeks told Morning Edition.
His comments followed Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, which ended with few signs of progress on nuclear arms control or the war in Ukraine.
Meeks said he feared the leaders were discussing dividing the world into spheres of influence, potentially sidelining U.S. allies. He also questioned the lack of meaningful agreements on nuclear weapons and artificial intelligence safety.
Asked about the Nvidia scandal, Meeks said he would confront Xi over Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft and warn of possible retaliation.
"When it comes to our national security, that's where we draw a red line," he said.
Meeks argued that U.S. diplomats should have raised concerns about Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft before the summit to establish clear goals for the talks. In his conversation with NPR's A Martínez, Meeks also called for reducing tariffs on U.S. allies while pressing China to end its support for Russia's war in Ukraine.

A late-night fire at the ancestral home of a former Bangladesh interim leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate appeared to have been intentionally set, police said, as growing waves of violence and damage have followed a declaration by the ousted former prime minister that she plans to return. The fire occurred before midnight Wednesday at the home of Muhammad Yunus, who served as interim leader of the country for 18 months following a mass uprising that led to the resignation of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who was flown out of the country by the military on Aug. 5, 2024.
The fire in an abandoned, ground-floor room of Yunus’ house in Chattogram was spotted by a police patrol that immediately doused the flames, Police Inspector Mozammel Haque told local media Thursday. Police are investigating and additional details were not immediately available.The possible arson comes during ongoing political tensions following an announcement by Hasina that in December she will end her exile in India.
In an interview with The Associated Press earlier this month, Hasina said even death cannot prevent her from returning to Bangladesh.Hasina has requested a passport and national identity card to facilitate her return, but the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman insists she will not receive the documents and must be handed over by India under an extradition treaty. Police and BNP leaders blamed Hasina’s supporters for attempting to create anarchy ahead of her intended return.
Explosions of crude bombs, arson and roadblocks have taken place in the capital Dhaka and other locations throughout Bangladesh in recent weeks. Mass uprising led to Hasina’s exileYunus governed until February when his interim administration handed over power to an elected government under Rahman. He was given the temporary leadership role following a student-led mass uprising that ended Hasina’s 15-year rule.Hasina was sentenced to death on charges of crimes against humanity involving the deaths of hundreds of protesters in the uprising. Her political party, the Bangladesh Awami League, was banned by the Yunus administration.The Yunus administration and Rahman’s government requested her extradition from India, which did not respond to the requests.Rahman on Wednesday urged “democratic forces” to remain united to prevent Hasina’s party from returning to Bangladesh politics.
Renewed tensions are linked to Hasina’s intended returnProtests by Hasina’s supporters and violence were reported in at least 22 districts nationwide in recent weeks. On Wednesday, at least two BNP supporters died in a clash with Hasina supporters in the southwestern district of Narail, police and media reports said.Grameen Bank, a small-credit agency founded by Yunus that shared in the Nobel Prize award, also has come under attack.
The bank said in a statement Tuesday that at least 22 branches were targeted by arson attacks and vandalism between Nov. 10 and Nov. 17.At Hasina’s ancestral home in Gopalganj district, protesters have regularly blocked highways leading to the country’s longest bridge connecting Dhaka with southwestern and southern regions. Protesters recently torched a police station and repeatedly clashed with security officials. Hundreds of paramilitary border forces remained deployed in the district to maintain order.
Police in Dhaka on Tuesday arrested former Mayor Mohammad Sayeed Khokon, a Hasina supporter, and on Wednesday arrested former Hasina Cabinet minister and ally Nurul Islam Nahid.The country’s leading English-language newspaper, Daily Star, reported that the homes of former Hasina administration and party officials Dipu Moni and Sujit Roy Nandy were set on fire Wednesday.

Around one in five pregnant and lactating women in Assam’s Barak Valley and adjoining districts of Tripura suffer from suboptimal levels of ‘Thiamine’ (vitamin B1), according to a study by the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN), Hyderabad, highlighting a continuing public health concern in the region.
The study, ‘Re-Emergence of Thiamine Deficiency Among Pregnant and Lactating Women in Northeast India’, published in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, examined the prevalence of thiamine deficiency and its link to dietary practices in areas where beriberi cases have previously been reported, said a press release on Monday.
Researchers conducted the community-based study during 2023-24 among 1,083 women from 120 villages in Assam’s Barak Valley and neighbouring parts of Tripura. Thiamine status was assessed using biochemical and functional indicators to determine the extent of deficiency.
The findings showed that about 20% of participants had inadequate thiamine levels. Based on blood thiamine measurements, 4.9% were deficient, and 15.2% had marginal levels. A separate functional assessment produced similar results, with 8.5% showing severe deficiency and 12.1% marginal deficiency. Pregnant women were found to be more vulnerable than lactating mothers.
Thiamine is an essential micronutrient that supports energy metabolism and healthy nervous system function. Deficiency can lead to serious health complications, making adequate intake particularly important during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
According to Mahesh Kumar Mummadi, NIN scientist and lead author of the study, dietary assessments revealed that most women consumed rice-based diets with limited diversity. Practices such as consuming stored rice, repeatedly washing rice before cooking, chewing betel nut and drinking salted tea were associated with a higher risk of deficiency.
NIN director Bharati Kulkarni said the findings underscore the need to look beyond routinely monitored nutrients in maternal health programmes. She called for greater dietary diversity, regular nutritional surveillance and targeted supplementation in high-risk regions. Researchers also noted that since the study focused on areas with previously reported beriberi clusters, the findings may not be representative of all pregnant and lactating women across India.

Microsoft’s Ignite announcements this week went beyond the Office-in-Copilot overhaul with the reveal of the Windows Server 2028 Public Preview and its new security-by-default stance and what Microsoft calls Hardened Server Core. Windows Server 2028 will implement a default security framework that Microsoft says is aligned with hardened DoD benchmarks, such as the Defense Information Systems Agency’s (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG).
STIGs work by providing a standard security framework for system administrators to follow recommended guidance. In the past, Windows Server admins were left to start from a blank canvas and then implement hardening configurations for operations. Secure baselines were available but not the default. Microsoft says that concern is now managed: “The secure configuration is the starting state, not a project you run after setup. That closes the window where a newly deployed server sits exposed while it waits to be hardened.”
The new Windows Server 2028 hardened-by-default state will only be available for the Server Core installs. Windows Server Desktop Experience installs do not include the changed stance.
This isn’t to say that system administrators won’t still have the final say on which security protocols are activated, just that the default package now ships in a pre-hardened state. Kerberos is now the default over NTLM, with protections added to LSASS; TLS is automatically restricted to modern cipher suites; key exchange uses “hybrid post-quantum key exchange” based on the quantum-safe ML-KEM; and remote desktop authentication and PowerShell script block logging get stricter as well.

The introduction of a merchant discount rate (MDR) on select UPI transactions could be delayed until after the 2027 state elections, with the government concerned about a potential backlash from merchants and trade associations. Citing industry sources, Financial Express reported that the government, RBI, and National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) are yet to agree on an implementation date, despite much of the regulatory and operational groundwork being complete. Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Uttarakhand, Goa, and Manipur are due to go to polls in the first half of next year. A senior industry official cited by the publication described a deferment until after the Uttar Pradesh polls as a worst-case scenario. Discussions remain focused on finding a suitable rollout window. While minor modifications are possible after implementation, the official ruled out substantial changes to the framework. MDR is a fee charged to merchants for processing payments. Under the proposed framework, eligible person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above ₹2,000 would attract a 0.4% charge, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 and above. Transactions of up to ₹2,000, person-to-person transfers, and eligible small-merchant transactions would remain exempt. The rollout was initially scheduled for October 15 but was deferred until after Diwali, with NPCI citing the festive season. The payments body said it would notify a revised implementation date separately. Meanwhile, NPCI has notified the UPI Vyapaar Saksham scheme, which will use a portion of MDR collections to support QR code and soundbox deployment among small merchants. The scheme will run for three years from the implementation of UPI MDR. Shares of fintech companies Paytm, Pine Labs, and MobiKwik fell sharply in morning trade following the report of a possible further delay in MDR rollout. At 11:05 AM IST, the stocks were trading around 9%, 5%, and 7% lower, respectively. During the session, Paytm parent One 97 Communications fell as much as 9.1% to ₹1,715, while Pine Labs declined 5.5% to ₹159.90. MobiKwik parent One MobiKwik Systems dropped as much as 8.7% to ₹206.80.

The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) has warned of penal action against those failing to comply with the revised prices of 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs
The authority, which functions under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, has asked State drug controllers (SDCs) to strictly monitor the prices and submit their action taken reports by November 16, according to an official release on Friday (November 13, 2026).
The revised prices for the 137 anti-cancer drugs came into effect on November 9, 2026, following a gazette order issued on October 17, 2026. The order capped the trade margin on these medicines at 30%.

All manufacturers, stockists, dealers, retailers, hospitals, and medical institutions have been directed to comply with the revised prices and prominently display the updated price lists at their premises and on their websites.

Complaints regarding overcharging, shortage, or non-availability of medicines can be reported through the Pharma Sahi Daam app or portal, the NPPA helpline (1800-111-255), or via email at monitoring-nppa@gov.in, it added.

CBI brings back fugitive from UAE in 2008 Kerala murder case after Interpol alert
The CBI secured the return of Raghesh Unnikochan from the UAE after an Interpol Red Corner Notice was issued in connection with a 2008 Kerala murder case.
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has secured the return of a fugitive wanted in a 2008 murder case in Kerala after he was located and arrested in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), officers said on Thursday.
Raghesh Unnikochan was deported to India on Wednesday following an Interpol Red Corner Notice (RCN). At the request of Kerala Police, the CBI, which is Interpol’s nodal agency in India, had secured the publication of the RCN by Interpol.
“Unnikochan stayed absconding during the course of the murder investigation to evade legal proceedings,” CBI officers said on Thursday.
A chargesheet was filed against him before the competent court in the murder case, which had also issued an open-dated arrest warrant against him.
“The subject was being pursued for his involvement in the said case, and efforts were being made to ensure that he is brought to justice in accordance with the law,” a CBI officer said.
Kerala Police sent an escort team to the UAE to take over his custody and ensure his return to India. The escort team, along with Unnikochan, arrived at Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, on Wednesday.
Unnikochan and a few others were wanted in connection with a murder that took place on January 1, 2008, in Thirumangalam, Thrissur, Kerala. The accused, allegedly motivated by past enmity, attacked the victim with an axe, while the other co-accused assaulted him with deadly weapons, inflicting fatal injuries. The victim was taken to West Fort Hospital in Thrissur, where he succumbed to his injuries while undergoing treatment.
The CBI, as the National Central Bureau for Interpol in India, coordinates with law enforcement agencies across the country to facilitate international police cooperation. Since 2019, more than 281 wanted criminals, including 73 fugitives in 2026, have been brought back to India through Interpol channels.

Maintaining physical and mental capacities is key to ensuring that older persons remain functionally independent. With age-related conditions such as visual and hearing impairment, memory and mobility issues often remaining undetected or unaddressed in the elderly, the National Centre of Ageing (NCA), Guindy has started to focus on providing integrated care to help older persons maintain functional ability. This is in line with the World Health Organisation’s (WHO) integrated care for older people approach (ICOPE).
According to the WHO, numerous physiological changes occur, and the risks of experiencing a decline in physical and mental capacities (intrinsic capacity) and having more than one condition (disease) increase when people age. This could manifest as cognitive decline, limited mobility, hearing loss, malnutrition, vision impairment, depressive symptoms, urinary incontinence and falls. ICOPE is WHO’s approach to provide a continuum of integrated care that helps to reorient health and social services towards more person-centred and coordinated care. It supports optimising intrinsic capacity and functional ability in older age, it said.

The Karyavattom campus of Kerala University (KU) has emerged as a hotspot of dengue in the city, where over 50 cases have been reported since November 9. Health department suspects that this is a gross underestimation, as the transmission is likely to have begun weeks before
Intermittent spells of rain, followed by hot and humid weather, have led to the spike in dengue cases in Thiruvananthapuram, even when the general dengue case trend has been on a slow decline since July across the State.
In the last 10 days, Thiruvananthapuram district has reported 200 probable cases of dengue and 97 confirmed cases.
On Monday, following a meeting called by the Health department, which was joined by the Vice Chancellor, some KU syndicate members as well as public health experts of the School of Public Health under Kerala University of Health Sciences, it was decided to shut the Karyavattom campus and the hostel buildings for three days so that intense vector control measures can be taken up and a break in disease transmission can be achieved.
“District health officials and vector control teams had visited the campus and hostel and we found that solid waste management was a huge issue in the campus. Plastic disposable containers used for food delivery which are disposed of carelessly are emerging as a major contributor to vector breeding in urban areas.. Rain water stagnation in these containers which are strewn around is a major hazard. Indoor plants in hostel rooms, broken manholes and blocked drains leading to rainwater stagnation have all led to intense mosquito breeding inside the vast campus,” a senior Health official said.
The Health department has also decided to serve notice to the KU Registrar under the Kerala Public Health Act, for allowing the campus to be a breeding ground for mosquitoes and posing a public health issue
Teams from the Pangappara health centre have been at work on the campus since November 10 but the district vector control team and the Corporation health staff will be joining them now. Fogging will be done to kill adult mosquitoes and indoor space spraying inside the hostel room, which will be accompanied by a source reduction campaign, officials said.
The district health administration has identified several pockets of dengue within the city itself, where an abundance of breeding sources and intense vector breeding has been spotted
Health officials point out that several large government properties with vast, ill-maintained grounds are also turning out to be hotspots for dengue in the city.
“The Cliff House compound and the sprawling official bungalows around it are all major breeding grounds for mosquitoes. In the Cliff House, seven police personnel there on guard duty were down with dengue, following which a district health team had visited the location. In some of the bungalows where renovation works are going on, building materials and discarded parts of equipment are all thrown about carelessly, leading to rain water stagnation and mosquito breeding,” a health official said.
Health officials said that without public participation, source reduction and mosquito control cannot be taken up successfully.
Kollam district too has reported a significant number of dengue cases over the last 10 days.
In November so far, the State has recorded 739 confirmed cases and 2,056 probable cases of dengue and three probable dengue deaths.
