A Chinese executive is convicted in a case linked to a Bangkok building collapse
A Thai court has found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders guilty of illegally operating a business in Thailand
BANGKOK -- A court in Thailand on Wednesday found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders of a Thai subsidiary of a Chinese state-owned construction company guilty of illegally operating a business in Thailand in a case related to the collapse of a Bangkok office building last year.
At least 92 people died on March 28, 2025, when an earthquake struck the partially built high-rise, which was to house the State Audit Office. It was the only building in Thailand to collapse completely due to the 7.7-magnitude quake, which was centered in neighboring Myanmar.
The tower was being built by a joint venture between China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) and Italian-Thai Development. Executives from both companies are also facing separate proceedings over alleged wrongdoing related to the building’s collapse.
China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) and its director, Zhang Chuanling, were found guilty of violating Thailand’s Foreign Business Act by using Thai nominee shareholders to conceal the company’s foreign ownership and operating a construction business without the required permission. The Criminal Court in Bangkok fined the company and Zhang 1 million baht ($29,450) each and sentenced Zhang to three years in prison, while also ordering the company to cease operations.
The defendants had denied the charges and were granted bail.
China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) is a Thai-registered affiliate of China Railway No. 10 Engineering Group, part of the Chinese state-owned China Railway group, which operates internationally.
The court’s action comes after increasing public concern about Chinese influence over local business, especially through the use of Thai citizens as proxies to disguise their real ownership. In some cases, the concern extends to suspicion that such enterprises are fronts for illegal activities, including money laundering and online scams.
The involvement of Chinese companies in the building collapse and other construction-related accidents has drawn considerable attention. The most notable other accident took place in January this year on a line that is part of a Thai-Chinese high-speed railway project linking the capital to northeastern Thailand. At least 32 people were killed and dozens injured when a construction crane crashed onto a moving passenger train, derailing it.
Italian-Thai Development was also the construction contractor for the railway project, and a Chinese company handled design and construction supervision.
After the train accident, China’s ambassador to Thailand, Zhang Jianwei, said that China requires its companies to follow the rules when participating in overseas projects, and that Beijing is willing to “guide Chinese companies to actively cooperate with the Thai authorities’ investigation."
Wednesday’s court case also saw three Thai shareholders found guilty of acting as nominees for China Railway No. 10 (Thailand). Two were sentenced to six years in prison each and fined 2 million baht ($58,900), while the third received a three-year prison term and a 1-million-baht ($29,450) fine. However, the court reduced their sentences and their fines by one-fifth after they confessed to the offenses.

Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

People with diabetes could be at a 53% higher risk of Alzheimer's disease, compared to those living without the metabolic disorder, a review of studies has found.
Researchers, led by those from Australia's Curtin University, conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 studies. They found that if 1,000 people living with type 2 diabetes were followed for a year, an estimaated average of 4.7 would develop Alzheimer's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder in which memory and thought processes steadily decline with age.
Cognitive risk prevention should be integrated into diabetes care, they said.
"Individuals with T2D (type 2 diabetes) experienced approximately five AD (Alzheimer's disease) cases per 1,000 person-years and a 53 per cent higher risk of AD, supporting the rationale for integrating cognitive risk prevention into diabetes care," the authors wrote in the study published in the journal Alzheimer's Research and Therapy.
Study author Emmanuel Adewuyi, an investigator fellow at Curtin University's school of population health, said the review was important as it quantifies the relative risk and incidence of Alzheimer's in people living with type 2 diabetes.
"While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease and estimated how often new cases occurred," Adewuyi said.
"Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer's disease among people living with type 2 diabetes," the author said.
Databases including MEDLINE, CINAHL and Embase were searched from for publications since inception until April 2026. Forty studies, involving 27,102,559 data points, and looking at the incidence of Alzheimer's disease among people with diabetes or link between the two disorders were analysed.

Employees call out Google over AI Search in schools
The Alphabet Workers Union voiced concern over Google requiring its AI tools be bundled with Search.
Google continues to draw fire for its handling of AI features in its Classroom services for students. Earlier this month, Google set out a policy that would essentially require schools to have some AI features enabled in order for their students to use the company's Search tools. The argument from the business was that "Search and AI are deeply integrated" to the point that a blanket ban on AI at a school would make Search unavailable to its students. The claim seems to dismiss Google's decades of operation before it even launched Gemini and other public-facing AI tools. It's a controversial enough move that some of Google's own employees have spoken out opposing the decision.
Members of the Alphabet Workers Union, CWA Local 9009, released a statement today criticizing Google for its handling of the issue. "Any opportunity to drive positive change with AI in education will rely on educators having the freedom to choose how to implement it in their curriculum," the statement reads. "Cutting off access to Search for schools that don't wish to use AI will not help persuade our users, and will more likely result in them shutting out Google products altogether." More than 500 employees signed the petition, calling on Google leadership to "reconsider this decision, and allow schools to turn off AI features in Search without disrupting their ability to use search as a whole."
The concern about splitting from Google appears to be justified. According to The New York Times, school districts in New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago are all considering adopting an alternate search engine rather than cede control over how students use AI to Google.
It's also a reminder to that despite Google's attempts to make Gemini and its other AI products essential, they can in fact be turned off. It's just a matter of the company being unwilling to turn them off.

International health authorities formally announced on Tuesday that the US has lost its measles elimination status, a hard-fought public health triumph won in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. The loss had been widely expected by public health experts for months, and the decision was leaked by the press last week. Still, having the designation officially stripped stings.
After the announcement Tuesday, public health experts, doctors, and political leaders decried the dramatic backslide for the US, calling it “shameful” and a “national embarrassment.” News articles point to the staggering vertical rise of measles cases this year, currently over 5,400 cases, more than any other year since 1991. An explosive measles outbreak in Pennsylvania accounts for over 1,500 of those cases. There have been 10 confirmed deaths across three states, several deaths just in the last week.
But the measles data that caused the US to lose its status—the bits of it that are public at least—paint a darker picture of where the US is in its rematch with measles, the most contagious virus known on Earth. For one thing, almost none of the data from this year—the cases, the explosive Pennsylvania outbreak, the deaths—factored in to the loss. It was lost earlier. What’s happening now is a runaway epidemic.
Lost status
The US measles elimination status is a designation granted by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is a regional division of the World Health Organization. Last week a committee of experts assembled by the PAHO, called the RVC, met to review measles data for countries across the region, including the US. (RVC is short for the Measles, Rubella and Congenital Rubella Syndrome Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission.)
For their review of the US data, the RVC heard from an independent committee of experts from the US, called the NSC, which presented measles data collected from January 2025 onward. (The NSC is short for the US National Sustainability Committee for the Elimination of Measles, Rubella, and Congenital Rubella Syndrome.)
According to the PAHO, an elimination status is lost when epidemiological and laboratory data shows that a single viral lineage has spread continuously for at least 12 months within a country. At this point, the virus is considered to be reestablished or endemic. So, to withdraw the US elimination status, the RVC needed to see evidence that a single introduction of a measles virus led to a 12-month-long chain of cases, which requires a lot of data.
The full set of data the NSC presented to the RVC is private for now. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention needs to review and approve such data for public release, which can be a lengthy process that has not yet occurred.
The Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the CDC, did not respond to a question from Ars Technica regarding when the data may be released.
Private data
But Ars Technica spoke with the chair of the NSC, Noel Brewer, who tried to talk through the pieces of data in the NSC report to the PAHO that he could discuss—these are pieces that have already been made public at some point by others, such as by state health officials or researchers. Brewer said the NSC presented the PAHO with genetic data spanning January 2025 to January 2026, and also epidemiological data that extended to June 2026.
In a press briefing Tuesday, officials for the PAHO made clear that only some of the data presented by NSC factored into its assessment of the US elimination status. The RVC only looked at the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, which doesn’t include the massive outbreak ongoing in Pennsylvania, which began in April. “The number of cases in Pennsylvania did not actually contribute to the decision that was made by the Reverification Commission,” Rhonda Sealey-Thomas, PAHO’s assistant director, explicitly told reporters Tuesday. For 2025, the US reported 2,289 cases nationally.
Still, there was no ambiguity about the US losing its status; “multiple lines of data show clearly that the US has sustained transmission of measles,” Brewer told Ars.
Brewer, who is also the Gillings Distinguished Professor in Public Health at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, confirmed that the beginning of the end of US elimination was January 20, 2025, in Texas—that date was included in the letter PAHO sent to the US informing it of the loss of elimination status. That Texas outbreak was declared over on August 18, 2025, after 762 cases were confirmed in the state. But the virus carried on elsewhere and is still simmering.
“Since January 20, 2025, the US, Canada, and Mexico have been passing measles cases back and forth across borders,” Brewer said, and the national data shows multiple, “genetically distinct” measles introductions into the US. “However, there is one genomic lineage that predominates across the cases and ties many of them, the majority of them, together,” he said.
Key question
For people closely tracking the US measles status, a key question has been whether the big outbreaks that followed the initial one in Texas were clearly linked. If they were, it would be immediately obvious that the US had lost the elimination status; but if not, and the outbreaks were driven by different virus introductions, the US could have kept its measles-free status based on the technicality of how the status is defined.
Data that might hold the answer to this question has been elusive. The measles strain in Texas, D8-9171, appeared similar to the viruses seen subsequently in big outbreaks in Arizona and Utah. But the strain was also similar to those from Mexico and Canada. Generally, there can be relatively small genetic changes among measles viruses, and genetic data alone is not used by PAHO to evaluate elimination. In June, ProPublica tried to get at the answer itself, conducting its own genetic analysis of measles strains in the US. It concluded that “the measles virus still spreading in Utah as of this May is very closely related to the one that sickened Texans over a year ago.” But the outlet acknowledged this wasn’t a “smoking gun.”
To date, the question lingers. Brewer cannot yet explicitly disclose what the NSC reported to the PAHO about possible links between the Texas outbreak and any of the subsequent large outbreaks in 2025. That includes the one in nearby Utah or one in South Carolina, which began in October 2025 and ultimately tallied 997 cases by the time it was declared over in April 2026.
For its part, the PAHO did not respond to multiple requests for comment from Ars Technica on linkages between the outbreaks.
But in a twist, Brewer noted that the answer to the question might be moot; the lineage that started in Texas on January 20 might not be the only one that has been sustained and could have lost the country its status. There are “one or two that have gone on for more than 12 months,” he said.
Bleak outlook
With the designation now formally lost, health and medical experts are coming to grips with the reality that measles is once again endemic in the US. Details of how the US should move forward are up for debate; the US is now required to submit a “corrective action plan” to the PAHO, outlining how the country intends to regain its elimination status. But the fundamental solution is obvious and straightforward: The US needs to increase vaccination rates.
While the virus has been raging in religious communities with low vaccination rates, the entire US has seen slipping vaccination coverage. That makes it easier for the virus to gain a foothold virtually anywhere.
A protective vaccination rate is considered to be 95 percent; according to the latest data, only 92.4 percent of kindergartners were vaccinated with the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year. Only 10 states have MMR vaccination rates at or above the 95 percent threshold. Meanwhile, non-medical exemptions from school vaccination requirements have never been higher, at 4 percent. Currently, 24 states have exemption rates at or above 5 percent, meaning that even if they are able to vaccinate every single non-exempt child, they would still not meet the 95 percent target. And this is just the data for young children. The vaccination coverage for adults is another concern, and the data there is scarce. In Pennsylvania’s massive outbreak, 1,055 of the 1,561 cases this year have been in adults ages 18 and older (less than 1 percent of the cases were fully vaccinated).
While some health officials have noted optimistically that 92.4 percent in children is just a few percentage points from the target, the reality of bringing up vaccination rates is more onerous.
PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa stressed the point in the press briefing Tuesday: It’s “not the national average or the average in the state or even the average in a big city, you need to guarantee that in every community, village, you have this vaccination coverage up to 95 percent. This is very important,” Barbosa said.
The point has been demonstrated in the US. In 2019, the US came very close to losing its measles elimination status. Unlike now—when the virus is on a nationwide rampage, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases—in 2019, the US nearly lost its status from a single, large outbreak that spread in New York. Though it didn’t explode on a national level, it took 11 months to stamp out in those undervaccinated communities. In that year, the US reported 1,274 measles cases total.
The situation in the US has only gotten worse, and the outlook is bleak, Brewer warns. “The measles outbreaks in Canada and Mexico are winding down,” he noted. “However, in the US, our measles problem continues to accelerate. There is no end in sight.”
Beth is Ars Technica’s Senior Health Reporter. Beth has a Ph.D. in microbiology from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and attended the Science Communication program at the University of California, Santa Cruz. She specializes in covering infectious diseases, public health, and microbes.

Brazil's Senate approves Lula's $10 billion fiscal package after costly election spending
Brazil’s Senate approved on Wednesday a plan by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to control his government’s spending and increase revenues after his reelection late October
SAO PAULO -- SAO PAULO (AP) — Brazil 's Senate approved on Wednesday a plan by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to control his government’s spending and increase revenues after his reelection late October led market analysts to worry about Brazil’s economy. The 81-year-old leader came back with a series of incentives to voters after losing the first round of voting to Flávio Bolsonaro.
The Brazilian government’s fiscal package, which will also have to be approved by the lower house, introduces new rules to slow down the growth of spending, limits corporate tax breaks and closes loopholes. It seeks to improve the public finances by up to 60 billion reais (about $10 billion) next year.
Lula’s move is laying bare the challenges ahead of his fourth nonconsecutive administration, as it already has many critics left and right. Many of his supporters see the plan as a risk to welfare programs, while his critics among market agents deem it to be too shy.
Many analysts say Lula's fiscal package is too dependent on boosting revenues rather than cutting expenses. That perception has led to the depreciation of Brazilian assets in recent days, including the country's real currency. Lula is yet to announce who will be his finance minister for the new term.
Lula’s victories in 2002 and 2022 also sparked immediate depreciation of Brazilian assets, but stock markets eventually recovered from high losses.
Ahead of the runoff election, Lula rolled out costly initiatives, including a 15% increase in his flagship welfare program Bolsa Família, or Family Grant. That measure alone will cost 5.8 billion reais ($1 billion) this year and around 22 billion reais ($3.7 billion) next year, according to Brazilian government figures.
The minimum monthly benefit per family rose in October to 691 reais ($117) from 600 reais ($102). The average benefit will increase from 675 reais ($115) to 777 reais ($132).
Other major measures of the Lula administration included subsidized credit and debt-relief programs for small businesses and low-income earners, temporary federal fuel tax cuts, and proposed zero-fare weekend public transportation. Additionally, Congress passed legislation shortening the weekly workweek without cutting pay.
Low income voters were key for Lula’s victory. Students, who also led Lula’s charge to keep the presidency, took to Sao Paulo’s Brigadeiro Faria Lima avenue on Tuesday to protest against the government’s fiscal package. That artery of the metropolis hosts many of its banks and brokers.

Wales have made four changes to the side that made history against New Zealand for the Nations Championship fixture against Australia.
Head coach Steve Tandy has tinkered with the starting line-up that beat the All Blacks for the first time in 73 years at Principality Stadium.
Wales go with the same XV that opened the Nations Championship with a 28-21 victory against Japan.
Alex Mann comes in for James Botham at blind-side flanker, Aaron Wainwright is back from a leg injury at number eight, lock Ben Carter returns for the injured Adam Beard and Josh Adams gets the nod on the wing.
Botham was man of the match against New Zealand but his partner is expecting their first child this week.

Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese have heralded plans for new joint Quad military exercises designed to push back on China’s expansionist ambitions, with the US president promising the grouping with India and Japan will guarantee “peace through strength”.
Albanese met Trump, India’s Nahrendra Modi and Japan’s Sanae Takaichi in Manila late on Tuesday in talks about enhanced cooperation on AI, critical minerals, infrastructure and maritime security.
“These nations represent some of the most important partnerships in the entire world,” the US president said.
“They’re among the most successful nations in the world, and in certain ways among the most powerful nations of the world. Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific.”
Trump said: “As we continue to protect peace through strength, we are also working together to advance super intelligence, SI, the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the industrial revolution.”
The Australian prime minister praised Trump and said a new Quad business forum to be held in 2027 would build economic growth across the region.
Leaders in the group – established as China seeks to build its military might and exert influence across the region – say they will cooperate to maintain peace and stability with Beijing.
“When we work together for our common view in the Indo-Pacific of peace, security, stability, and prosperity, then the world will be a safer and more secure place, and the Quad has a critical role in achieving that,” Albanese told the summit.
The plan for new military exercises involving maritime patrol aircraft is likely to prompt strong criticism from China.
Albanese said Australia would deploy its P8-A Poseidon and P3-C Orion maritime patrol aircraft as part of the operation in early 2027.
Asked what he would tell Chinese leader Xi Jinping later this week about the plan, Albanese said military exercises were common.
“We want peace and security in the region. That’s the objective here. It’s not about any one country. It’s about our own sovereignty, but also about peace and security in the region,” he said
The Quad leaders want the group to present a multilateral coalition of resistance against Beijing, seeking to undermine its dominance, including in the South and East China seas.
Takaichi said the Quad would help shape the future of the region.
“We would like to realise a free and open Indo Pacific by strengthening resilience of countries in the region and promote their freedom to decide for themselves across a wide range of areas including maritime security, economic security, energy and critical and emerging technologies.”
Before the meeting, as the four leaders posed for a group photo, Trump praised Modi and Takaichi as “tough”, before gesturing to Albanese and saying: “We’re OK too.” Albanese laughed at the remark.
The first meeting of the Quad leaders since 2024 came as Albanese and Trump both prepare for setpiece engagement with China’s president later this week. Albanese will visit Xi in Shenzhen on Friday, a day after three-way talks between Trump, Xi and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Trump said he wanted talks with the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, but conceded he was not the host of the China summit and it was up to Xi to issue an invitation. The US president said he could have a one-on-one meeting with Putin “if it’s available”.
Quad military exercises would build on progress from the recently completed Malabar joint exercise near Japan, where sailors completed anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare drills.
Trump also talked up the Aukus nuclear deal with Australia. “We make the greatest submarines anywhere in the world, and we’re working with Australia and others on that,” he said.
Trump said the US was poised to catch up to China on rare earth production within 10 months, backed up by speedy progress from Australia, Japan and India.
He was accompanied by cabinet members Marco Rubio, Scott Bessent, Howard Lutnick and Jamieson Greer, as well as his new chief of staff, Stephen Miller.
Privately, officials believed the meeting alone showed the group was progressing. Australian officials welcomed the engagement of Trump in regional affairs as he enters the final two years of his presidency.
Trump took credit for reinvigorating the grouping, and said he placed a premium on relations with Albanese, Modi and Takaichi.
“When they have difficulty, when they want to tell me something, my phone is always open, and the Oval Office is always open to you, and you know that,” he said.
Albanese said before the meeting he would push Trump on ending the war in Iran, a conflict which has produced an unprecedented global energy shock and badly distorted conditions in the Australian economy.
It was Albanese’s first meeting with Takaichi since a weeks-long saga about comments he made on a podcast about her gift of melons presented to him during a visit to Australia in July.
Earlier, Albanese took part in the East Asia Summit where he called for regional partners to work together to boost AI protections. Trump, who calls the technology “superintelligence”, said it represented “the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution”.

Goa tourism minister seeks rethink on turtle nesting sites for 21 more beaches
Beaches identified as protected turtle nesting sites face several restrictions, including prohibition on setting up of beach beds in the intertidal zone.
Goa tourism minister Rohan Khaunte has called for a reconsideration of the state forest department’s proposal to notify an additional 21 beaches as protected sites for nesting of endangered Olive Ridley Turtles.
“Tourism and turtle nesting should co-exist. We love turtles, we love nature, we love the environment, but we have to have a balance. Certain things need to be relooked by the forest department. We have to ensure that the humans who rely on the tourism ecosystem for their bread and butter also survive – watersports, shack owners,” Khaunte said on Wednesday.
“Throughout the world when turtle nesting takes place, it is promoted very well as a tourism activity. We should use existing turtle nesting sites to boost tourism rather than establishing more at beaches where people already earn their livelihood,” he added.
There was no immediate comment from the forest department at the time of filing this report.
The proposal includes adding the beaches of Vagator, Calangute, Candolim, Keri, Miramar, Ashvem, Baga and Arambol in North Goa and Rajbag, Mobor, Cabo de Rama, Patnem, Baina, Palolem, Cola, Carmona, Cavelossim, Varca, Talpona, and in South Goa to its existing list of four beaches Morjim, Mandrem, Galgibaga and Agonda as designated turtle nesting sites.
Beaches identified as protected turtle nesting sites face several restrictions, including prohibition on setting up of beach beds in the intertidal zone, installation on any outdoor illumination, muted indoor lighting with opaque shields on the sea facing side and a prohibition on playing loud music and beach parties beyond 6pm.
Shacks are also directed to play a proactive role in ensuring conducive condition to the mare turtles besides information sharing with the forest department staff which monitors the entire coast.
The proposal has come under criticisms from tourism stakeholders, especially from those along the beach stretches of Canacona in the far south of Goa where all the beaches have been provisionally identified for turtle nesting. Canacona is home to the popular Palolem beach as well as that of Agonda, which has consistently been identified as among the best beaches by various travel aggregator sites.
Tourism stakeholders gathered at Palolem on Tuesday to denounce the forest department’s moves to expand the number of notified turtle nesting sites in Canacona.
“Fifty percent of Canacona’s economy runs on tourism since we have no other industrial activity here and nearly all of it is beach tourism. Notifying turtle nesting sites will severely restrict tourism. We demand that the Goa government withdraw this proposal within one month failing which tourism stakeholders will be forced to undertake a hunger strike and fast unto death,” Prashant Naik of the Goa Forward Party said.
“We have grown up on this beach. We don’t understand what could be behind the forest department’s latest move,” Simon Rebello, a tourism stakeholder and former chairperson of the Canacona Municipal Council, said.
“The hurdles that we face to obtain necessary permission will only be doubled and tripled. Tourism, which provides employment and business, will die a natural death, taking away the only source of livelihood for residents,” Ramakant Naik Gaunkar, a shackowner said.
The residents said they feared Canacona taluka’s economy would collapse if the proposal was implemented.
The state forest department has initiated and been holding sea turtle conservation programmes along the four beach stretches – Morjim and Ashvem in north Goa and Agonda and Galgibaga in south Goa since 1997.

UK firms owed thousands as Saudi-backed LIV paid golfers millions
- Published
LIV Golf - backed by more than $5bn (£3.8bn) from Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund - paid millions to players and executives in the weeks before filing for bankruptcy, while leaving a trail of unpaid bills from UK suppliers.
BBC Sport has seen invoices from five small businesses totalling hundreds of thousands of pounds, all of which were overdue before LIV made its final payments to players.
Global Infusion Group,, external a Buckinghamshire company that provided catering at July's LIV Golf UK event, is still owed £321,671, due on 7 August.
Suffolk-based BD365 Clean, external provided 108 cleaning staff and is owed £75,225, most of which was due on 20 July and 13 August.
"It just feels completely immoral," said Bonnie May, chief executive of Global Infusion Group.
"It really matters to a business of our scale. The impact has been huge, both personally and professionally."
Only $2m (£1.5m) has been earmarked so far by the Saudi owners to pay unsecured creditors, leaving many smaller companies unsure if they will receive anything at all.
Yet court filings reveal LIV made 59 payments to golfers on 31 July, amounting to $16.6m (£12.6m) and matching prize money for the same LIV Golf UK event.
A further $34.2m (£25.9m) went to players between 17 August and 3 September following tournaments in New York and Indianapolis, including $6.4m (£4.9m) to 2026 champion Jon Rahm just five days before the bankruptcy filing.
'How can they sleep at night?'
Four senior LIV executives also received retention bonuses totalling nearly $3m (£2.3m) in August.
"It's sickening," said Krissi Foskett, owner of BD365 Clean, who described the unpaid bills as "almost an extinction-level event" for her team.
"How can they sleep at night, knowing they are potentially putting companies out of business?"
Meanwhile, public records list more than £3,000 owed to Goodysphere,, external a family-run Yorkshire firm that provides a sensory bus designed to help autistic children who may find busy events overwhelming.
LIV Golf did not respond to our request for comment.
However, in August, LIV chief executive Scott O'Neil said he hoped they would be able to pay their suppliers.
"What I would say to them is we're doing everything we can to make sure we can do right by them and the work they committed."
'It's Saudi money, that’s safe as houses'
The controversial breakaway league had been owned and bankrolled by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) since its launch season in 2022.
But in April, the fund announced it would end its backing after the 2026 season, putting LIV's future in doubt.
"Our understanding was that the funding would take LIV through 2026," said Global Infusion Group's May, whose company had about 60 staff catering for players and broadcasters.
"We weren't aware the funding had already stopped and there wasn't enough to actually fulfil their obligations."
PIF's multi-billion-dollar investment helped it to lure some of golf's biggest names and disrupt the PGA Tour's dominance of the sport.
"It's Saudi money, that's safe as houses, we thought," said Foskett.
"Their head honchos came along and enjoyed hospitality. We were there cleaning up at one o'clock in the morning then back in at five in the morning, only to be treated like this."
PIF remains the majority owner of Newcastle United, while Saudi Arabia will host the 2034 Fifa World Cup.
"I'm sure the country won't want to be saddled with the characterisation that it doesn't pay its bills," said professor Simon Chadwick, who is an expert in the business and politics of sport across Africa, Europe and Asia.
"I do find it surprising that they would simply walk away. I think they would want to engage in some kind of remedial action, particularly in terms of managing their image and reputation."
Filmmaker Joe Bentley spent eight days from April working on a video for LIV's YouTube channel that is still online.
He is owed nearly £6,000, with £2,226 due on 31 July.
The video was part of the 'LIV Back' series, set up to "focus on the impact LIV players and teams are making off the course".
He filmed at two schools taking part in 'Little Sticks', a LIV outreach programme which aimed to provide golf equipment and training in areas of deprivation.
"You feel massively deflated, a bit cheated and undervalued," said Bentley.
"Everyone I dealt with at LIV was lovely. The first email I sent chasing was to a production coordinator or a manager and even she was appalled that we hadn't been paid."
Gateshead Council is also owed £1,912, due on 22 August, relating to 'Little Sticks'.
"Transformation is not a short-term process," said Professor Chadwick.
"If you're going to embark on investment programmes in community sport, grassroots sport, you've got to make a long-term commitment and those changes have got to take place."
What happens next?
LIV filed for bankruptcy protection in New Jersey on 8 September.
"The contacts we had sadly all lost their jobs," said Giles Mitchell, whose company, Office Pantry, supplied food to LIV's office on London's South Bank.
"We didn't hear anything from them and then their emails started bouncing back."
There was hope the competition could survive in some form with new investment, but in November LIV announced it was winding down operations.
In the bankruptcy filings, LIV estimated it had between $500m and $1bn (£380m-£760m) in liabilities and at least 1,000 creditors.
The largest 30 unsecured creditors alone were listed with claims of more than $64m (£49m).
"I think the message is loud and clear to somebody like me that, no, we're not going to get paid for any of this," said May.
"If anything did come our way, I'm thinking it's going to be pennies in the pound, nothing which will have any impact, or even cover our legal fees."
Who else is owed money?
Fourteen golfers were among the published creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims.
Rahm topped the list with a claim of $7.5m (£5.7m), which he agreed to give up as part of his deal to leave the league.
Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7m/£4.3m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m/£4.2m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m/£3.6m) and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m/£2.6m) also featured.
IMG Media, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, and British golf YouTuber Rick Shiels were each listed with claims of more than $1m (£760,000) too.
Meanwhile, BBC Sport understands the R&A is owed about £500,000 for advice on sustainable maintenance of courses used by LIV.
A hearing is scheduled for January to consider the wind-down plan, but creditors may have to wait longer to find out how much they will get back.
"I've had nights just sat there in tears, thinking, what is the point," said BD365 Clean's Foskett.
"How much comes in will honestly depend on whether or not the business will still be going at the end of January.
"I don't want to throw the towel in."

Putin vows 'far more painful' response to Ukraine's strikes on Crimean Bridge
- Published
Moscow's retaliation for attacks on the Crimean Bridge will be "far more painful" than Kyiv's strikes, Vladimir Putin has vowed.
In the early hours of Thursday, the double-arched, 12-mile bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea was hit for a third time this week.
A combined missile-and-drone strike on Tuesday destroyed the central road section of the bridge, collapsing part of it into the water and rendering it unusable for road traffic.
But at a press conference after historic talks with his Chinese and US counterparts in Shenzhen, Russian president Putin said Moscow's response would be even more significant.
Putin claimed the bridge was used exclusively for civilian purposes and not to transport military equipment, as Kyiv has alleged, or petroleum products.
Since illegally annexing the Crimean Peninsula in 2014, Moscow has used it as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles.
From there it has also carried out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplied its troops in southern Ukraine.
Commenting on the strikes on the bridge, Kyiv's defence ministry said that for Ukraine, they amounted to to "time gained and lives saved. The less that reaches the occupiers, the less hits our warriors."
The collapse of the Crimean Bridge's arch was the worst damage to be inflicted onto the structure in several years.
The bridge had long been in Ukraine's sights because it represents Moscow's pretensions over sovereign Ukrainian land, and because of its logistical importance in supplying Russian troops in the occupied Ukrainian southern regions.
It was built and unveiled to great fanfare in 2018, four years after Russia illegally annexed Ukraine's Crimea.
Thursday's strike was carried out with Neptune cruise missiles, Ukraine said. Russia's transport ministry said nobody had been hurt in the attack, and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge. Train services on the bridge were suspended but resumed in the afternoon.
Car traffic, however, will be prohibited for the foreseeable future as a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was dragged below into the sea when missiles hit the arch on Tuesday.
President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
The seven-stage operation first required the destruction of air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets which protected the bridge. Missiles and drones then dealt the structure the final blow.
In response to Tuesday's hit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
But the operation to repair it could take a long time, and it will likely have to be carried out under frequent Ukrainian fire.
Russia has regularly targeted Ukrainian civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022.
This week alone, as the Crimean Bridge was being hit, Moscow targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv.

Chemicals found almost everywhere in modern life pose a "global and growing threat" to human health and the environment, a landmark report based on over a decade of research has warned.
The report on "endocrine-disrupting chemicals" (EDCs) released by the United Nations Environment Programme and World Health Organization "conservatively" estimates the health and environmental costs of EDC exposure at over $1 trillion annually.
"The scientific evidence is clear: EDCs are a global and growing threat to human and environmental health," warns the report written by international scientists, calling current regulations "uneven and insufficient."
EDCs are chemicals that interfere with, mimic, or block the hormones that regulate the development and behaviour of our organs.
They are in everything from toys and makeup, to building materials and clothing.
The report released late Tuesday is the first such comprehensive look at EDC impacts in 14 years, and finds increasingly clear links between them and a range of diseases.
"The evidence is so strong that it's irrefutable at this point," said Laura Vandenberg, report co-author and professor of environmental health sciences at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.
The report examined thousands of studies on chemicals like bisphenols, phthalates and parabens.
Evidence of links between these chemicals and disease is strongest for certain neurological conditions and reproductive problems including sperm decline.
But there is also growing confidence that EDCs are linked to diseases like type 2 diabetes and asthma that have spiked globally.
"Because these changes are occurring rapidly, they are unlikely to be explained primarily by genetic change," the report says.
Sufficiently worrisome
Scientists looked at associations between EDC exposure and health conditions, as well as the mechanisms by which exposure could cause harm.
The findings vary, with "strong evidence" of developmental and neurobehavioral effects, but "emerging" links between EDCs and cardiovascular disease.
However, the overall risk is strong because EDCs are so ubiquitous and likely to impact health at tiny levels, Vandenberg said.
Among those most at risk are workers in the chemicals and recycling industries, particularly in countries with weak regulations.
A 2024 study by the International Pollutants Elimination Network NGO fitted participants with silicone wristbands that absorbed chemicals.
Lab tests of the wristbands found that plastic waste and recycling workers in Thailand and Kenya were exposed to over 20 hazardous chemicals, while even control subjects working in offices were exposed to at least 11.
There are around 1,000 identified EDCs, but experts say many chemicals have simply not been tested properly and their impacts remain unknown.
They are also concerned about "synergistic" impacts -- the way exposure to multiple chemicals may amplify health effects.
The "proverbial million-dollar question" is what level of EDC exposure triggers any given health impact, said Frederic Leusch, professor of environmental toxicology at Australia's Griffith University, who was not involved in the report.
But even absent an answer, Leusch believes "the hazard is sufficiently worrisome that we need to take action to reduce our, and our environment's, exposure."
It scares politicians
Many countries have regulated certain EDCs, often targeting bisphenol A, particularly in children's products.
But regulators have struggled to determine which chemicals should be regulated, and what an appropriate exposure level might be.
"It scares politicians, to some extent, because it's such a complicated area," said retired professor of environmental chemistry Ake Bergman, who worked on the previous editions of the EDC report in 2002 and 2012.
Like other experts, he warned there is no known safe exposure level for most EDCs.
"We have some that are really acting at extremely low concentrations."
In a statement, the International Council of Chemical Associations industry group called for "science-based" approaches to regulation that protect health and the environment "while enabling society to benefit from the products, technologies, and innovations that are essential to modern life and sustainable development."
Many EDCs are in plastics, and experts say oil firms are increasing plastic production as demand for fossil fuel energy falls.
"We need to stop the expansion of plastic production,... reduce exposures to EDCs, and ban the worst actors," said Tracey Woodruff, report co-author and professor at Stanford University.
"While more science is always needed, we don't need more science to act."

Indian students who have completed their medical education from recognised institutions in the Philippines can now appear for the country’s Physician Licensure Examination (PLE) and obtain a licence to practise medicine there.
The decision was confirmed by India’s Ambassador to the Philippines, Harsh Kumar Jain, who said the Philippine Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) shared the development last week. The move was described by Jain as an “important development in strengthening professional and people-to-people exchanges between the two countries.”
What does this step mean for Indian students?
This decision by Philippine authorities settles one of the conditions set by the National Medical Commission (NMC) for Indian students graduating from medical colleges in the Philippines to become eligible for the Foreign Medical Graduate Examination (FMGE) in India.
Kadwin Pillai, director of Pune-based overseas medical education consultant Transworld Educare, said that the step is significant for Indian students pursuing medical education in the Philippines, as it provides clarity on their eligibility to obtain medical registration in the country after completing their degrees.
Students and parents have wanted greater clarity on the professional options available after completing their medical education abroad and this progress will help them better understand the regulatory framework while planning their academic and professional journeys, he stated in a statement.
The development comes after a series of engagements between Indian and Philippine authorities concerning the recognition of medical qualifications and eligibility to practise medicine. It assumes significance as over 7,000 Indian students are pursuing higher education in the Philippines, with medical education being a major area of interest, said the statement.
Can Indian medical graduates practise in India after clearing PLE?
Indian graduates clearing the Philippines’ PLE will not automatically become eligible to practise in India. Students returning to India are required to meet the NMC’s eligibility requirements, including the prescribed examination, qualification and internship requirements.
Indian and Overseas Citizens of India (OCI) candidates who have obtained their primary medical qualification from an institution outside India will need to qualify the Foreign Medical Graduate Examination (FMGE), conducted by the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS).
Qualifying the FMGE is compulsory for obtaining provisional or permanent registration with the NMC or State Medical Councils and starting medical practice in India.

Fiona the hippo, one of America’s most famous zoo animals, has died after efforts to remove a knitted hat that she swallowed after it fell into her enclosure proved unsuccessful.
With surgery too risky for a full-grown hippos like Fiona, who weighed in the region of 2,500lb (1,113kg), veterinarians tried alternative method of getting the hat to pass through her system.
The hat fell near Fiona when a visitor to the Cincinnati zoo tossed it in the air, after which it bounced it off a ceiling fan and fell into the enclosure, according to the Associated Press. Fiona ate the hat and was initially asymptomatic.
Days later, however, she began to lose appetite and staff at the zoo were forced to feed Fiona more in the hope that she would eventually get the hat through her digestive system.
The zoo announced on Wednesday that the animal care team was using a vibration plate from a horse farm to help move things along, according to the Associated Press.
Fiona was sedated a second time on Tuesday for evaluation. After an ultrasound, veterinarians could see her intestines still trying push the hat through. They also used a 9ft scope colonoscopy to view her intestines as well.
“The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the zoo said on social media. Fiona remained out of her enclosure while she was receiving treatment.
Footage from the procedure released by the zoo on Wednesday shows her snorting and moving around her enclosure, which vets said was a sign of progress. Her hydration levels were being monitored.
“Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked, and they were happy to see her respond. Thank you for your continued love and concern for Fiona and her dedicated care team,” the zoo said.
This wasn’t not the first time Fiona’s health has been at risk. She became a global sensation after her premature birth in 2017, when she couldn’t stand on her own and weighed just 29lb at birth, 25lb less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
Fiona’s recovery had garnered support from across the country including, apparently, from Timothy, another hippo at the San Antonio zoo. Timothy sent well wishes via Instagram. “I know you’ve got some amazing people looking after you. We’re sending lots of love from Texas to the most beautiful hippo in the world. Hope you’re feeling more like yourself soon!”
Zoo staff had said updates on Fiona’s rally back to health would come as they received more information, reminding visitors to be careful when near habitats and to secure belongings.
In the meantime, the zoo asked visitors: “If something falls into a habitat, please notify a zoo staff member immediately.”

The Telangana State Women’s Commission (TGSCW) has initiated an inquiry into an alleged illegal oocyte donation racket in Hyderabad, issuing notices to eight Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) centres and egg banks over suspected irregularities in their donor records and procurement practices.
The Commission examined representatives of the eight institutions on Friday, November 13, after directing their managements to appear before it. However, TGSCW Chairperson Nerella Sharada expressed dissatisfaction after some centres sent staff members and other representatives instead of senior management, despite being specifically instructed to attend in person. The inquiry was subsequently adjourned after the institutions assured the Commission that their management would appear at the next hearing.
During Friday’s proceedings, the Commission scrutinised reports, records and details of egg donors submitted by the ART centres and egg banks. “Several irregularities and suspicious elements have emerged from the records examined so far,” said Ms. Sharada.
She also questioned claims made by the institutions that nearly 90% of their egg donors came from other States and donated their eggs voluntarily without receiving any remuneration or financial compensation. She said the claims raised several questions and warranted further investigation.
Health Department’s investigation
Commissioner of Health and Family Welfare, Sangeetha Satyanarayana, also attended the inquiry, during which Ms. Sharada sought details about the progress of the department’s investigation into the alleged illegal egg procurement practices. The discussions also covered shortcomings in the existing Assisted Reproductive Technology Act and its implementation, particularly the challenges in regulating and monitoring ART centres and egg banks.
Ms. Sharada said she would soon meet Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha and Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy to inform them of the findings and discuss corrective measures, including possible legislative amendments to strengthen regulation of the sector.
More ART centres likely to come under scanner
Ms. Sharada further said that the Commission has also received information indicating the possible involvement of several other ART centres and egg banks in the alleged racket. It plans to issue notices to their management and summon them for questioning as part of the ongoing inquiry.
“The Commission will not tolerate illegal practices that compromise women’s health, dignity and rights. We will continue the investigation in coordination with the concerned government departments to identify those responsible and ensure appropriate legal action,” she added.
