Here is a thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama from director Nitesh Tiwari, with music by Hans Zimmer and AR Rahman, based on the ancient classical poem about Rama, the avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu. It has often been adapted for live-action and animated movies in the past, though surely not on this scale, the current three-hour blockbuster being only the first half. (There are no musical numbers though.) The idea of aristocrats submitting stoically and yet playfully to exile in the forest has something Shakespearean about it, and if you are suffering from Homer-withdrawal after Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, a story about the noble Prince Rama finally vowing to wage war on a distant city where his wife has been abducted might just fit the bill.
Ranbir Kapoor plays the mythical Rama, a noble warrior and statesman who has been brought into being in the city state of Ayodhya as a bodily representative of Vishnu, and from the first his sense of destiny is overwhelming. But what exactly is that destiny? In broad terms, his fate is to face off with Ravana (Naveen “Yash” Kumar), king of far-off Lanka, a figure whose former slave status once triggered in him such a cosmically intense prayer for justice that Lord Brahma offered him the superpower of athletic strength and indifference to pain.
In Ayodhya, Rama marries the sweetly devoted Sita (Sai Pallavi), he enjoys an intense bond of comradeship with his brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey), and is the apple of his father’s eye; this is King Dasharatha (Arun Govil) who, careworn by affairs of state, is about cede the throne to Rama. But Rama’s stepmother Kaikeyi (Lara Dutta) furiously reminds Dasharatha that he promised the crown to Bharata (Adinath Kothare), the son they had together. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana are banished to the forest.
Over in Lanka, a toxic stew of plotting against Ravana is being stirred by his slippery, smirking brother-in-law Vidyutjihva (played by Bollywood veteran Vivek Oberoi), whom Ravana ruthlessly slays in single combat; this man’s widow Shurpanakha (Rakul Preet Singh), who is Ravana’s sister, is banished to the same forest where Rama is humbly eking out his civilian existence. She falls in love with Rama, using her witchy wiles to trick and bamboozle the happily married man, and this is to lead to a cataclysmic confrontation between Rama and Ravana.
With its giant canvas and some truly beautiful sunset skyscapes, this very enjoyable film has a little of Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings and even Disney’s The Lion King (the latter surely influenced the animal-kingdom tableaux). The bizarre flying machine piloted by Ravana (who does not have the ability to fly as such) has something engagingly Gilliamesque about it. As so often with Indian cinema, this movie reminds you of the forthright, unselfconscious storytelling energy that popular Hollywood films had in the 1950s and 60s, the era of sword-and-sandal. It’s a rather amazing adventure.

An advisory issued by the Department of General Medicine in Assam has asked postgraduate trainees (PGTs) to defer personal milestones such as marriage until the successful completion of their residency tenure, drawing criticism from the Federation of All India Medical Association (FAIMA).
The order, issued by the Office of the Department of Medicine, asks all postgraduate trainees to prioritise their clinical duties, patient care, academic pursuits and research requirements during their residency.
“This is for information to all Postgraduate Trainees (PGTs) of the Department of General Medicine that all PGTs are advised to defer personal milestones such as marriage until the successful completion of their residency tenure,” the advisory stated.
It further said that the primary focus of trainees during their academic programme should remain on clinical responsibilities, patient care, academics and research. All postgraduate trainees were expected to adhere to the advisory, it added.
Reacting to the order, FAIMA Doctors Association strongly criticised the recommendation and demanded its immediate withdrawal.
In a post on X, the doctors’ body said, “FAIMA strongly condemns this unreasonable advisory and demands its immediate withdrawal.”
Questioning the rationale behind the directive, FAIMA said resident doctors should be allowed to manage their personal lives alongside their professional responsibilities.
“Dear administrators, regulate duty hours, not the personal lives of resident doctors. Residency is a postgraduate course, not a vow of celibacy!” the association said.
Another student body, United Doctors Front (UDF), has criticised the order. In a post on X, they said if “a resident getting married is seen as a threat to clinical duties and patient care, the problem is the workload and the staffing, not the wedding.”
PG residents are usually in their late 20s or early 30s. A three-year residency doesn’t pause their lives, and women residents will feel this pressure most, UDF said.

Every year in Delhi, the arrival of the winter months also signals the beginning of what residents widely call “pollution season”. A thick toxic smog shrouds the city, home to 30 million people who have no choice but to breathe the poisonous air as they go about their daily lives, often while suffering from wheezy coughs, nausea and itchy eyes. While successive state governments have brought in measures intended to improve air quality, the situation has remained the same for more than a decade. Delhi is widely regarded as the world’s most polluted city. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Pollution season usually begins around the same time as Diwali, the Hindu festival of light. Amidst the plummeting air quality, people still gather in the markets for festival shopping and at festivities outside. Diwali is also known to cause a surge in the pollution levels, due to the tens of millions of cars that hit the roads and the use of firecrackers for the celebration. In previous years, firecrackers were banned, but this year the state government has allowed “green” firecrackers”. However environmentalists argue that these are still highly polluting.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The causes of Delhi’s apocalyptic pollution are multi-faceted. In recent years, one of the biggest causes has been vehicle emissions, from the almost 10m cars, rickshaws, motorcycles and trucks on the city’s roads. It is also the season where farmers in the neighbouring states of Haryana and Punjab often burn their fields to ready them for the next crop. These fires are illegal but still occur. Factory emissions, dust from construction and rubbish burning also contribute to the toxic air quality levels.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
So far, the air quality index (AQI) has already soared above 650, more than 30 times the limit the World Health Organization (WHO) deems to be safe. Air pollution is linked to numerous serious diseases, particularly respiratory, and hospitals have already reported a surge in patients suffering from breathing difficulties.The pollution season is expected to last until January, when the weather warms up.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
Millions of Delhi’s residents are poor families or migrant workers, who have no choice but to go out to work in the toxic air, often suffering long term impacts on their health. Doctors and campaigners have described the pollution as a “health emergency”. According to a study last year, at least 15% of deaths in the capital are linked to air pollution. Pollution now kills more people in Delhi than obesity of diabetes.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
As in previous years, the state government has introduced various restrictions to try and bring air quality levels under control. Coal and firewood have been banned as fuel. Construction has also been halted and so have older diesel and petrol cars. Offices have been instructed to get people to work from home to limit traffic on the roads. Trucks can often be seen spraying water on the roads. However, it is widely acknowledged that, so far, these restrictions have had little impact on the pollution levels. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
The pollution has been a problem for so long in Delhi that it has become normalised and people carry on with their daily lives in the toxic smog.Residents rarely wear masks outside and the parks will still be full of families and children and people exercising outside.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
While rich and middle class families will buy air purifiers for their homes, they are unaffordable for most poorer families who often live in makeshift tents or informal homes. As a result, breathing clean air during pollution season has become a luxury privilege in Delhi.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The pollution is not restricted to Delhi alone. All across north India, in states such as Punjab and Haryana, the air is also toxic due to coal-powered plants, vehicles and farm fires. Cities such as Amritsar in Punjab, on the border with Pakistan, also suffer from extremely dangerous air quality levels during the winter months. Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty Images
Campaigners say more money needs to be invested into proper public transport and better vehicle emission regulation in Delhi to tackle the root causes of pollution. Every year, the number of cars on Delhi’s roads keeps rising, releasing more harmful pollutants, and yet few the percentage of electric vehicles remains very low.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Delhi has an extensive bus and metro network, but it is not sufficient to cope with the huge daily demand and still has poor connectivity in many areas. Most people still rely on polluting rickshaws, cars and motorcycles to get them to the bus stops or metro stations. Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
Delhi’s topography – a city built in a bowl-like valley, which has little breeze or rain in the winter months – means most of the emissions get trapped over the city as the cold weather hits and cloak the city in brown smog. Some call it Delhi’s “death shroud”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
In past years, the state and national government has been accused of manipulating the data to disguise how bad pollution levels are in the capital. Last year, it was found that water was being sprayed around the air quality monitors, allegedly to bring down the readings. Campaigners and opposition politicians have alleged that a lot of data from the air quality measuring stations has gone “missing”.
Environmental campaigners have argued that much more extreme measures are needed to bring pollution under control, similar to how Beijing successfully cleaned up its air in recent years. However, others have argued this would have an economic cost that India, as a developing country, can not afford.Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
One of the plans being prepared by the government this year is to experiment with “cloud-seeding”, to create rain which would clear the skies. But many residents and campaigners say that until the root causes are tackled, these plans are nothing more than a “gimmick”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

Maharashtra puts non-essential construction on hold in 304 drought-hit talukas, prioritises relief
The Maharashtra government has directed district authorities to temporarily suspend non-essential new construction works in 304 drought-hit talukas and divert available funds for drinking water supply and other drought-mitigation measures.
A Government Resolution issued by the Planning Department on Wednesday said funds under the District Annual Plan (General) must be prioritised to finish incomplete water supply projects, strengthen existing water sources and ensure water and fodder availability for livestock.
Also Read | Maharashtra adds 2 more talukas to drought-hit list; count rises to 310
The state has identified 304 talukas as drought-affected, and the government said immediate measures were necessary to meet the drinking water requirements of citizens, livestock and other essential needs.
District collectors have been directed to review non-essential new projects, including parks, beautification works, new office and administrative buildings, cement roads, drains and other works involving substantial water consumption, and take steps to temporarily defer them in accordance with prescribed procedures.
Funds available for such deferred projects will be reviewed and reallocated to priority drought-relief works in the affected talukas, the GR said, adding that the exercise of reallocation must be completed by December 31.
The government has clarified that ongoing projects should not be stopped indiscriminately.
Authorities must take decisions on a case-by-case basis after considering contractual obligations, public safety, the stage of work, expenditure already incurred and possible compensation or financial liabilities, it said.
Essential works directly related to drinking water availability, strengthening existing water sources, creating necessary new sources, providing water and fodder for livestock, water conservation, irrigation, public health and emergency requirements have been exempted from the temporary suspension, subject to applicable rules and approvals.
The GR also gives priority to completing incomplete pipelines, pumps, electricity connections, storage tanks and distribution systems required to transport water from existing sources to scarcity-hit villages.
"Projects that can be completed during the current scarcity period and provide immediate access to water must receive priority. New projects that cannot normally be completed within the current financial year should not be sanctioned under the special priority framework," it said.
In exceptional cases, essential drinking water, livestock water or water-source creation projects may be considered even if they extend beyond the current financial year. However, the additional financial liability for 2027-28 must not exceed 10 per cent of the approved District Annual Plan outlay for 2026-27.
District collectors have been asked to convene meetings of district-level officials within seven days of the issuance of the GR and prepare an integrated taluka-wise and project-wise action plan within 15 days.
The government has also provided for expedited approval of urgent drought-relief measures. If convening a District Planning Committee meeting would delay an essential intervention, the collector can submit a proposal to the guardian minister, who heads the committee, for approval, subject to ratification at its subsequent meeting.
Collectors will have to review the progress of approved works and submit reports on fund allocation, expenditure and physical progress to the Planning and Finance departments by the 10th of every month.
The GR also mandates the publication of details of sanctioned works, funds, expenditure and progress on district collectorate websites or government portals.
The provisions will apply to the 304 drought-hit talukas and any additional talukas subsequently declared drought-affected or facing scarcity. The order will remain applicable for the 2026-27 financial year.

When 
Donald Trump
 picked 
JD Vance
 as his running mate in 2024, he chose a politician who had once described him as “America’s Hitler”. Two years later, Vance is not only the US vice-president but is also frequently discussed as a possible successor to Trump and the Republican Party’s “America First” movement.
The transformation has been striking. Vance has embraced much of Trump’s political agenda, from economic nationalism and restrictive immigration policies to scepticism towards America’s overseas commitments. Yet the war with Iran has demonstrated that the two men do not always share the same instincts on how that agenda should be pursued.
On the same page.
Vance has generally been more sceptical of prolonged military involvement. He has also sought to place greater emphasis on the domestic and economic consequences of foreign policy. These differences do not necessarily amount to a break with Trumpism. But they offer an indication of how Vance might seek to define the movement if he eventually has to lead it without Trump.
From critic to political heir
Vance’s transformation is central to understanding his relationship with Trump. In a report published in July 2024, Reuters recalled that Vance had publicly called Trump an “idiot” and described him as “reprehensible” during the 2016 presidential campaign. 
Reuters also reported that Vance had privately compared Trump to Adolf Hitler.
Timeline of Trump-Vance relations.
By the time Trump selected him as his running mate in 2024, however, Vance had become one of his most prominent defenders. Reuters described the choice as a signal that Trump wanted his Make America Great Again (Maga) movement to continue beyond his own presidency. Vance was increasingly being viewed within the Republican Party as a possible inheritor of that political project.
The ideological overlap is visible across several policy areas. Both men have challenged the traditional Republican preference for free trade, advocated tougher immigration enforcement and questioned the scale of America’s international commitments.
For Vance, economic nationalism is also about the position of American workers. His criticism of multinational corporations and the movement of manufacturing overseas fits into the broader argument that the US should prioritise domestic industry over the interests of global markets. This is a central theme of Trump’s political appeal as well.
Ukraine: a more pronounced scepticism
Foreign policy is where Vance’s views have, at times, been more clearly defined than Trump’s. Both have questioned the scale of American support for Ukraine and argued for an end to the war through negotiations. But Vance has been a more consistent and vocal opponent of continued US assistance.
In an interview in 2022, Vance said: “I don't really care what happens to Ukraine one way or the other.” Reuters quoted the remark in its July 2024 assessment of his foreign-policy positions. The agency also reported that Vance had argued Ukraine had little chance of regaining all the territory occupied by Russia and that American resources should instead be directed towards issues such as the US-Mexico border and competition with China.
Trump, too, has expressed scepticism about US aid to Kyiv and promised to end the conflict through negotiations. However, Reuters noted that, unlike Vance, Trump had not explicitly opposed the congressional aid package for Ukraine passed in April 2024.
Their preference for a negotiated settlement may overlap, but Vance’s opposition to American involvement has been more categorical. It is therefore important not to treat their positions as identical.
Vance’s wider scepticism towards overseas military commitments was also evident before he became vice-president. In a 2023 opinion article for The Wall Street Journal, he praised Trump for not starting wars during his first term. The Associated Press later cited Vance’s explanation for supporting Trump: “I know he won't recklessly send Americans to fight overseas.”
Iran: Where the differences became visible
The US-Israeli military campaign against Iran in February 2026 brought Vance’s foreign-policy instincts into sharper focus.
Trump argued that military action was necessary to prevent Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. Vance supported that stated objective, but the president himself acknowledged that the two had approached the decision differently.
Difference in outlook.
At a news conference on March 9, Trump said Vance was “philosophically a little bit different than me” and had been “maybe less enthusiastic about going” to war. Trump added: “I felt it was something we had to do. I didn't feel we had a choice.” The remarks were reported by the Associated Press.
Vance’s reservations had also been evident before the strikes. He had told The Washington Post that there was “no chance” the United States would become involved in a prolonged conflict similar to the Iraq war, Reuters and AP reported.
Once the operation began, however, Vance publicly backed the president. In an interview with Fox News, he defended the administration’s approach by arguing that Trump had clearly defined the military objectives.
“What's so different about this, Jesse, is that the president has clearly defined what he wants to accomplish,” Vance told Fox News, according to the Associated Press.
Vance’s role in the conflict later extended to diplomacy. He became a central figure in efforts to negotiate an end to the fighting and defended the preliminary agreement reached with Tehran. In June, he presented the agreement as a success, pointing to its potential economic benefits, including lower fuel prices and the resumption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump publicly joked about the political risks of giving his vice-president responsibility for the negotiations. “If it works out, I'm going to take the credit. If it doesn't work out, I'm blaming JD,” Trump said on June 17, according to the Associated Press.
The agreement did not bring a lasting end to the conflict. On November 2, Vance told reporters that he and Trump were optimistic about the prospects of a negotiated settlement. “We've certainly made some progress. We'll see if we can make some more,” he said, as reported by CBS News. Trump had also indicated on Truth Social that a deal with Iran “could happen”.
The position changed within days. On November 12, Trump said the United States did not need an agreement with Tehran and directed Vance to shift his attention from Iran to a domestic anti-fraud campaign.
“We don't need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that the United States had “got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!” Reuters reported that the directive came after Vance had been involved in efforts to resolve the conflict.
Beyond the immediate political fallout, the differences over Iran point to a broader debate within the Maga movement about the extent of America's military involvement overseas. Dr Ashok Sharma, a geopolitics expert and Visiting Fellow at the University of New South Wales Canberra at the Australian Defence Force Academy, said the disagreement reflected competing approaches to American foreign policy.
"The differences between Trump and JD Vance over the Iran war reflect a deeper ideological tension within the Maga movement. While Trump views military action against Iran as necessary to protect American strategic interests and prevent nuclear proliferation, Vance represents a more restrained, America First approach. He questions prolonged military engagements and their economic and political consequences", Sharma said.
Israel: Support, but not without limits
Vance’s position on Israel also requires a distinction between support for the country and agreement with every decision taken by its government.
In July 2024, Reuters described Vance as a consistent supporter of Israel, a position broadly in line with Trump’s. Vance had also supported sending aid to Israel while opposing a wider package that included assistance to Ukraine.
However, during the Iran conflict, Vance became more willing to question Israeli actions when he believed they could undermine American diplomatic objectives. In June 2026, he criticised Israeli strikes on civilian infrastructure in Beirut, suggesting that they risked damaging US-led peace efforts.
Vance made the broader argument more explicitly in September, when he addressed the All-In Summit. “We cannot let our Middle Eastern foreign policy be subservient to the State of Israel,” he said, according to The Times of Israel.
He also argued that Trump had shown a willingness to disagree with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu when he believed American interests required it. Vance’s comments were not a rejection of the US-Israel relationship. Rather, they reflected his argument that Washington should retain the freedom to pursue its own strategic priorities.
The midterm setback
The clearest public divergence between Trump and Vance emerged after the Republican Party’s losses in the November 2026 midterm elections. Democrats regained control of both chambers of Congress, and Vance identified the Iran war as one of the reasons for the defeat.
In a post on X on November 4, Vance wrote: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night.” He also challenged Republicans who believed the military operation had been worth the political cost.
“If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he wrote. CBS News reported that Vance identified four concerns among voters who had supported Trump in 2024 but switched to the Democrats: the Iran war, the cost of living and inflation, putting America first, and the US relationship with Israel.
Trump continued to defend the decision to launch the war, arguing that preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon justified the operation. In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, he acknowledged that Iran had been a factor in the election but said he had no regrets. “I don't think about it. I did the right thing. I would have done it again,” he said, according to The Guardian’s report of the interview.
Trump did not entirely dismiss Vance’s assessment. The Associated Press reported that he described the vice-president’s post as “good” and said: “I know how he feels about it.” However, Trump continued to defend the military campaign.
Vance's criticism of the Iran war has also raised questions about the political calculations behind his position. Prof Rajan Kumar, professor at the School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, told TOI that there could be multiple explanations, ranging from genuine disagreement over the war's consequences to an attempt by Vance to distinguish himself from a policy that may have hurt the Republican Party electorally.
"Vance may have raised the issue for two reasons. First, he genuinely believes that the Iran war was the principal reason behind the Republicans' defeat. Many within the party believe the conflict created a foreign-policy deadlock and contributed to domestic inflation through higher energy prices, hurting the Republicans in the midterm elections," Kumar said.
"The other explanation is political. If Vance is positioning himself as a potential Republican presidential candidate in 2028, he may feel the need to distance himself from a policy that contributed to the party's electoral setback and demonstrate that he does not agree with Trump on every issue," he added.
Kumar said Vance's position could also be interpreted differently by those who view his political trajectory as evidence of opportunism. Vance had criticised Trump before joining his administration, subsequently aligned himself with the president, and is now publicly highlighting differences over the Iran war.
"Many Republicans felt that traditional conservative values were not being adequately represented by Trump. However, they remained silent because of his strong electoral support and the fear that he could back challengers against them in primary elections. A few did speak out, but Trump has a habit of eliminating his own loyalists, including his former vice-president Mike Pence and former secretary of state Mike Pompeo".
The balancing act
Vance’s challenge is to distinguish himself from Trump without appearing to reject the movement that brought him to the vice-presidency. So far, his differences have largely been expressed through emphasis and approach rather than a wholesale break with the president.
On economic nationalism and immigration, he remains broadly aligned with Trump. On Ukraine, his opposition to continued US assistance has been more pronounced. On Iran, he supported the administration’s stated military objective but was more cautious about the prospect of a prolonged conflict and later became a leading advocate of negotiations.
The post-midterm disagreement, Sharma argued, raised a larger question about the direction of the Republican Party's foreign policy once Trump eventually leaves the political stage.
"The larger question is whether post-Trump Maga will continue Trump's assertive foreign policy or return to its original promise of avoiding costly overseas wars."
For now, Vance’s political position rests on two competing requirements: Maintaining the support of Trump’s voters and demonstrating that he can offer something beyond a continuation of the president’s own political approach. Whether that balance is enough to make him the movement’s next leader remains to be seen.

Extraordinary moment Trump greets Putin at Apec summit: ‘Who is he? He’s my friend’
Trump was all smiles when he met with the Russian leader ahead of an historic trilateral meeting with China’s Xi Jinping

Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin a warm reception when the leaders met for closed-door talks on the fate of war-torn Ukraine.
The U.S. president pointed, smiled and called out “Who is that? He’s my friend!” as he walked into a room with his Russian counterpart in Shenzhen, China, ahead of an unprecedented trilateral with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Trump said of Putin: “We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We know each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start. But I think they’ll come out of this.”
The Kremlin said after the meeting that the pair had discussed the ongoing war in Ukraine, and that Putin left in an “excellent” mood.
Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said the war was the main topic of conversation during their 35-40 minute tête-à-tête, and that they had also discussed the relationship between their two countries.
President Trump has sought to mediate an end to the nearly five-year conflict between Russian and Ukraine and this month restarted peace talks with diplomats from both sides.
But so far, talks have failed to produce a breakthrough, and allies fear Trump has been pressuring Kyiv to make concessions to its invader while lifting sanctions and cutting deals with Moscow.
Trump on Thursday also appealed to president Xi to help end the war and expressed hope that their three-way meeting with Putin would yield results.
“We're looking to both help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine,” the American president said. “I'd like to see it ended.”
Trump said both presidents felt strongly about oil having to flow through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been disrupted by the Iran war the US launched in February. Xi did not mention Ukraine or Iran in his remarks, and has long resisted directly weighing in on the European conflict.
The summit in Shenzhen has fuelled concerns in Europe that decisions affecting the war and the future of the continent could be taken without European input.
But Trump’s envoy Jared Kushner said on Thursday that he and Steve Witkoff would head to Berlin to meet with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders to discuss the conflict and talks.
Ukraine’s main allies in European are meeting for a ‘Coalition of the Willing’ summit to show support for Kyiv as Europe pushes for involvement in the US-brokered talks with Kyiv and Moscow.
German officials said the Berlin meeting would focus on reaffirming a commitment to robust and legally binding security guarantees, which would come into force following a ceasefire.
Its timing is intended to allow Ukraine's European allies to give a quick, joint response to any announcements from Shenzhen, they said.
The leaders of Germany, France, Britain, Poland and Italy and also NATO head Mark Rutte are expected to attend.
The United States and Europe, close allies for decades after the end of World War Two, have increasingly moved apart as Trump's administration has scaled back support for Ukraine and insisted its NATO partners pay more for their own defence.
On Tuesday, the differences were exposed when Germany and Britain rejected U.S. criticism of Ukraine's campaign of deep strikes on Russian oil infrastructure and commercial warehouses.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the Berlin meeting would signal that Ukraine's European allies maintain their firm support and that “we are united as ever in securing a just and lasting peace that sees an end to this senseless war”.
Britain will announce new details on a support package for Ukraine, including long-range drones capable of striking deep into Russia, as well as surveillance and logistical drones.

Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever
- Published
In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief.
Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks.
The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades.
Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party.
This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position.
The ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) has, however, rejected reports that its senior leadership had rejected a proposal to back Gen Kainerugaba as the next president, describing the claims as "completely false".
This has all fuelled speculation that the arrests are part of an effort to sideline military officers opposed to the general's presidential ambitions.
Others see the arrests as evidence of an anti-corruption drive in which senior commanders are held to account.
At the centre of the tension are two powerful powerful institutions: the military, where Gen Kainerugaba wields considerable influence, and the NRM, where questions about his political ambitions appear to be dividing senior figures.
A recent meeting of NRM's top leadership ended without agreement on a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Museveni's successor, according to the AFP news agency.
Five party sources who attended the closed-door meeting told AFP that a vote was abandoned after several members spoke against the proposal.
Uganda's news website ChimpReports, however, said that most members who spoke backed the general's potential presidency, although some questioned his readiness for civilian leadership.
In a statement on Thursday, NRM Secretary General Richard Todwong Awany confirmed that the party had met on 10 November to discuss "political, social and economic issues".
He dismissed reports that the meeting had rejected a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Uganda's next president, saying the party would communicate any decisions "through the right channel, at the right time".
Dr Gerald Bareebe, a Ugandan-born political scientist at Canada's York University, sees a connection between the arrests and political manoeuvring over Museveni's succession, often referred to as the "Muhoozi Project".
"Senior officers believed not to support the project have been arrested, detained or charged with corruption and treason," he tells the BBC.
He says the allegations against some officers were widely viewed as politically motivated, reflecting growing divisions within the military over the succession question.
Some of those detained have since been released, apparently after securing the general's forgiveness.
The detention of one of the country's most prominent former commanders, Lt Gen Peter Elwelu, has brought the crackdown into sharper focus.
The former deputy army chief was detained on 2 November over allegations that he had plotted to destabilise the eastern Teso region.
His fall from grace followed a series of social media posts by Kainerugaba, who accused him of treachery and announced that he had been stripped of his three-star rank and demoted.
"The traitor Peter Elwelu is hereby stripped of his ranks. He is demoted to Private," Kainerugaba wrote on X.
He also claimed that more than 20 soldiers linked to Elwelu had been arrested.
The announcement raised legal questions, with Ugandan media reporting that military regulations do not allow a senior officer to be stripped of his rank through a social media post.
The army later confirmed Elwelu's detention, saying they had recovered 15 guns, military uniforms and two pickup trucks linked to him. His family has rejected the allegations.
Elwelu is among at least a dozen generals and senior officers detained since April 2025, according to an investigation by Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper.
They include three former military intelligence chiefs who once oversaw some of Uganda's most sensitive security operations.

- The Ugandan general who lobs grenades on Twitter 
  - Published30 October 2022
Maj Gen James Birungi, a former head of defence intelligence and security, was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption.
He was charged before a military court but later released after Gen Kainerugaba announced that he had "forgiven" him.
Another former intelligence chief, Maj Gen Abel Kandiho, was detained in September this year over allegations of providing false intelligence and treachery. He remains in detention, according to the Daily Monitor.
His predecessor, Brig-Gen Charles Bakahumura, was also arrested in September over similar allegations, but was later released after the army chief announced that he had forgiven him.
Other officers have faced accusations ranging from stealing military fuel to taking money to spy on military communications.
The military has defended the arrests as part of efforts to tackle corruption and criminality within the armed forces.
Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa says the arrests reflect investigations involving different security agencies, rather than an army-led purge.
He argues that detaining senior officers helps protect witnesses and demonstrates the seriousness of the anti-corruption drive.
"Gen Muhoozi has the overall duty to permit the investigation team to arrest these high-profile people, in consultation with the commander-in-chief," Egesa says, adding: "The arrests are not summarily done."
But Bareebe sees a wider political motive, arguing that officers suspected of opposing to Gen Kainerugaba's presidential ambitions are being targeted.
"The result is a broad purge that has affected both serving and retired officers perceived to be anti-Muhoozi," he says.
He points to divisions between the elite Special Forces Command (SFC), which he says is largely loyal to the president's son, and army commanders who remain unconvinced about his succession.
The allegations against the officers are at different stages, with some facing charges, others in detention without publicly announced charges, and several having been released.
Bareebe also questions whether military trials can deliver independent proceedings.
"Many Ugandans regard the charges as politically motivated and therefore expect little justice," he adds.
He alleges that some officers have had charges dropped after closed-door negotiations with the president and his son, during which they were pressured to declare support for Gen Kainerugaba.
Government spokesperson Allan Kasujja dismissed the claims of a succession fallout as "hogwash".
Unlike his predecessors, who communicated through official military channels, Gen Kainerugaba frequently uses X to announce arrests, criticise public officials and comment on domestic and international affairs. Some have sparked diplomatic controversy.
On the night of 9 November, he turned his attention to Vice-President Jessica Alupo, demanding to take her job.
"Whoever is in that office should prepare to hand it over soon," he wrote, in posts that he later deleted.
He also questioned Alupo's loyalty and threatened her dismissal, adding that the government would operate "on military terms", if he became his father's deputy.
The following day, his X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, became inaccessible.
It was unclear whether he deactivated it himself, which he has done before, or the platform had suspended it.
Alupo remains in office and has yet to respond publicly.
Egesa says Gen Kainerugaba's controversial posts reflect his preferred style of communicating, but adds that security analysts are assessing their implications for Uganda's political and military stability.
Bareebe, however, sees them as part of a broader effort by the army chief to extend his influence into civilian politics.
He says the public confrontation with senior political figures illustrates how the succession debate was spilling beyond the army and into the ruling party.
Gen Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in March 2024, after previously commanding the SFC, which is responsible for protecting the president and strategic installations.
Under Uganda's military structure, he reports directly to Museveni, giving him considerable influence over the army.
Bareebe argues that the SFC's loyalty to the president and his son could prove crucial in any future transfer of power.
"The regular army remains important but has been sidelined by the SFC, which now functions as a personal army for Museveni and his son," he adds.
At the heart of the tension is the question of who will succeed Museveni, 82, who has ruled Uganda since 1986, when his rebel National Resistance Army seized power after a five-year guerrilla war.
He was sworn in for a seventh elected presidential term earlier this year, extending his rule into a fifth decade.
Gen Kainerugaba has been regarded as a possible successor and has indicated that he intends to seek the presidency in 2031, when his father's current term is due to end.
He also leads the Patriotic League of Uganda, a political movement that has mobilised support around his leadership.
But recent developments suggest that a transfer of power from father to son may be more complicated than his supporters anticipated.
At the recent meeting of the NRM leadership, one official reportedly urged Museveni to retire his son from the military and give him a civilian role to gain administrative experience, AFP reported.
Local media reported that some party officials consider Gen Salim Saleh, Museveni's younger brother, better suited for civilian leadership.
There is, however, no indication that he is interested in becoming president.
Others reportedly defended Gen Kainerugaba, pointing to his military leadership, anti-corruption campaign and grassroots political mobilisation.
Bareebe says opposition to the proposed succession has grown within the NRM, with both veteran figures and younger members concerned about what they see as an attempt to secure power through coercion.
He suggests Museveni's reluctance to move his son out of the military could reflect the importance of retaining control of the army during any transition.
"The underlying calculation appears to be that, so long as Muhoozi controls the SFC, he can use it to capture power even in an event of a contested transition," he says.
The military has been central to Museveni's hold on power, making the loyalties of senior commanders particularly important as succession questions intensify.
The family's military influence has also drawn attention to the possibility of a political dynasty spanning generations, with Gen Kainerugaba's son, Ruhamya, recently graduating from Britain's Sandhurst military academy.
The succession debate is unfolding against a backdrop of sustained pressure on the opposition.
Veteran opposition politician Kizza Besigye remains in detention on treason charges, which he denies.
Bobi Wine, who came second to Museveni in this year's presidential election, has gone into exile in the US, after being threatened by Gen Kainerugaba.
The government has consistently defended its security operations as lawful and necessary to maintain stability.
For now, Museveni remains in power.
But the arrests, his son's threats and competing accounts of divisions within the ruling party have intensified questions about how Uganda's next political transition might unfold, and what role his family may play.

A Delhi court has declared the election of AAP councillor Arun Nawariya from Pushp Vihar in the 2022 Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) polls void for not disclosing a criminal conviction in his nomination affidavit. The court also declared BJP candidate Naresh Sankla, who had finished second, elected from the ward, subject to verification of his eligibility by the State Election Commission.
“The voters have right to know that their candidate is convicted in such a serious offence,” Principal District and Sessions Judge Sanjeev Kumar Aggarwal of Saket court said in his November 18 order.
Nawariya had won from Ward 166 in Pushp Vihar, securing 13,721 votes against Sankla’s 10,114 in the December 2022 election.
Sankla had subsequently approached the court, alleging that Nawariya had concealed his conviction in a 2010 case registered at Ambedkar Nagar police station under Section 325 (voluntarily causing grievous hurt) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
Nawariya was convicted in February 2013. He was granted the benefit of probation and not sentenced to imprisonment. Three days later, he was released on probation for two years. However, in his nomination affidavit – Form 22 – he had written “Not Applicable” in the column seeking details of cases in which he had been convicted.
Nawariya’s counsel argued that Rule 18 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation (Election of Councillors) Rules, 2012, required a candidate to disclose only convictions carrying a jail term of one year or more.
The court, however, held that Form 22 required candidates to list all other convictions too. “If the respondent… was aggrieved with the requirement of said affidavit/Form 22 giving detail of criminal cases which was not covered in Rule 18, then he should have challenged the validity of said form 22 before appropriate authority or court of law,” the court said.
The judge said in the order that Navariya was “required to declare his conviction” in the affidavit and “has adopted corrupt practice by not disclosing” it.
Further, the court noted that Nawariya had failed to disclose a separate 2019 FIR registered against him by his wife under IPC sections relating to cruelty, criminal breach of trust and insulting the modesty of a woman. He had admitted to the case during cross-examination.
The Delhi BJP welcomed the verdict, saying the court had rightly declared Sankla the councillor from Pushp Vihar.
When contacted, Navariya said he would seek legal counsel before commenting on the verdict.

I return to my room as my mother-in-law leaves for her office in the building adjacent to our home. I am about to start my bath when I hear a series of explosions, as of firecrackers, but different. I freeze. Someone comes pounding frantically on my bathroom door. It is Ongmu, the children’s nanny, crying hysterically. I fling open the door, my heart thumping. She is gesticulating wildly, speechlessly, towards the garden.
I run along the path leading to Akbar Road. I see the white Ambassador car slowly moving towards the same path. I hesitate. I stop, heart in my mouth. Dread, panic, fear. I feel suffocated. I can’t breathe. I am about to collapse. No, no, I can’t. I have to walk to the car. I see her being carried into it. I understand; I scream.
I’m in the car now, crouching on the floor, facing her … Blood – blood on her sari, blood on her chest. Her large eyes are wide open; her face wears a surprised expression. She doesn’t move. I attempt to speak to her, to call out, “Mummy, Mummy”, but no word comes out. I try again; she doesn’t reply.
Her aides are in the front of the car, screaming. Heavy, slow traffic, the car barely moves, it has no siren. One red light, then another. Then the hospital. The gate isn’t opening. Chaos. We are stopped; someone looks through the window in a questioning attitude. They let us in.
We reach the emergency department, teeming with people. We are stopped again, not allowed in, we have to wait for our turn. Someone calls out to the driver, signals him to move forward. They identify us; she is placed on a trolley. We are led somewhere – an operation theatre? They ask me to follow. I’m taken to a room nearby. No, no, I want to stay by her, I insist. I want to know. I have to see. They don’t reply; they are immersed in their emergency procedures.
I feel confused, lost … I don’t recognise anyone there. I’m shivering under my dressing gown. I feel scared, my mind is racing. Where is Rajiv? I try to remember. I can’t, I can’t. The children, yes, they’re in school; they must be brought home. Oh God, no, no. Let them be safe, let Rajiv be safe … Whom do I tell, whom do I speak to? I sense someone in the room. I don’t know who it is. I try to speak, to put some words together; nothing comes out. “There’s blood all over her clothes,” someone says. Some clothes are brought in for me. I am helped into them in a nearby closet.
Hours go by, agonising hours. More people come in and crowd around. I signal a question to the doctor; he shakes his head. I understand, yes, I understand. I break into sobs, uncontrollably. Someone tries to calm me. I feel numb, cold.
At two in the afternoon of 31 October 1984, Indira Gandhi was declared dead. I was driven home to collect some clothes for her body to be changed into. On the way, a group of men tried to stop our car, banging on its windows. They were angry, shouting something I couldn’t understand.
At home, the children, Rahul and Priyanka, rushed to my arms in tears. When they had been abruptly picked up from school by black-uniformed commandos, they sensed a catastrophe. Once home, they saw some of the staff sobbing. They asked question after question. “Where’s Mama?” “Why have we been brought home?” “Where’s Papa?” “What’s happened?” “Where’s Dadi?” “You aren’t telling us the truth!” My friends Nina and Sterre had been with them, trying to calm them down, not knowing what to say to them. I wanted to sit with them and hug them, to break the news to them gently, but I was unable to – I had to go back; Rajiv was coming to the hospital.
Rajiv had been in West Bengal at a political rally when his cavalcade was stopped by a police patrol. He was told there was a message from Delhi to say he should rush back – a serious accident had taken place. He was driven to the helipad, from where he flew to Calcutta and then to Delhi. He’d heard on a BBC bulletin that Mrs Gandhi was wounded and in a grave condition. Nobody told him directly that his mother was no more, but he understood.
He landed at 3.30pm and was driven straight to the hospital. He walked in with other people, and I remember longing to be left alone with him for a moment at least. We held each other, and as he spoke to me, it sunk in that he was saying something I didn’t want to hear. “I have been asked … They want me to be sworn in as prime minister.”
I felt as if a knife had been plunged right into my heart. I felt a pounding in my chest, a rage welling up deep inside me. I was about to explode. I attempted to hold it in. “You have been asked to? How dare they ask? How dare they? Who are they? Why you, why does it have to be you? Why did you allow them to ask you? No, it cannot be; this time it’s not going to be!” Seized by utter pain and anguish, soaked in perspiration, I felt like throwing up. I wanted to scream, to ask for help. “Someone please help me put an end to this.”
I burst out crying, pleading, begging him with folded hands, “No, no, you can’t think of it. You have to stop them, you must refuse, you must say no – for the children’s sake, for yourself. You can’t do this to us. They will kill you; they will kill you, too!” I cried out. He replied, “They will kill me anyway.”
We brought my mother-in-law home. The dining room had been emptied out, and we laid her body down on the floor, her feet pointing south as Hindu custom decrees. The same evening at around 6.30pm, Rajiv was sworn in as prime minister of India. I was too broken to even register what was happening around me. His mother lay there, her body pierced with more than 30 bullet holes. I knew, I knew it then in my heart: Rajiv’s path would lead to the same end.

A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
He faces up to life in prison at sentencing.
Federal prosecutors said south Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The government said Sanon was the conspirators’ initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. Prosecutors also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.
Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but pointed out that the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.
Sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the US as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the midwest.
Haiti has not had a president since authorities said that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a night-time raid at their home on 7 July 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.
The election of a new president is scheduled for next year.
Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programs that were intended to help businesses during the Covid pandemic, according to court records. US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.
The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in south Florida with a former Haitian senator and several US businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies – Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU – for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.
CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.
By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian supreme court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.
Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.

On Nov. 10, the U.S. House of Representatives voted on articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has been the face of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran that began in February.
The impeachment effort failed in a 211-204 vote, which many Democrats blamed on 11 of their fellow party members who were absent from the voting chamber.
The 11 absent Democrats were Reps. Julia Brownley, Melanie Stansbury, Brittany Pettersen, Laura Gillen, Nancy Pelosi, Haley Stevens, Marilyn Strickland, Frederica Wilson, Jonathan Jackson, Steven Horsford and J. Luis Correa.
Social media users claimed some of those 11 missed the vote because they were attending an event related to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — a powerful pro-Israel lobbying group.
The event in question was reportedly hosted by Elect Democrat Women. According to the nonprofit OpenSecrets, the top donor to the Elect Democrat Women-affiliated super PAC, EDW Action Fund, was the United Democracy Project — a super PAC affiliate of AIPAC.
Drop Site News, a nonprofit investigative news outlet, reportedly obtained an RSVP list of the event showing that three of the 11 Democrats who missed the vote were present at the event: Brownley, of California, Stansbury, of New Mexico, and Pettersen, of Colorado. As of this writing, the reported RSVP list was not publicly available and Drop Site News did not reveal how it sourced the list.
Two of the representatives, Brownley and Pettersen, reportedly acknowledged attending the Elect Democratic Women event. However, none of them had responded to our requests for comment by the time of publication. Until we hear directly from the representatives' offices or primary evidence confirming their attendance emerges, we've left this claim unrated.
On Nov. 11, USA Today reporter Zach Schermele posted that Brownley told him she "left last night's Elect Democratic Women event for the Hegseth vote with plenty of time to spare" and that "when the traffic jam made it clear she might not make it in time, she and other lawmakers started texting each other." He reported that Brownley, 74, then got out of her car and started running, missing the vote by "seconds" (archived).
According to Denver NBC affiliate KUSA, Pettersen acknowledged she attended the event, saying in a statement, "Last night, I was late to the floor and there is no excuse for that. I was at an Electing Democratic Women event."
Stansbury posted a video on Nov. 11 apologizing for her absence, saying, "I know I should've been there at that moment." She blamed rush-hour traffic on Independence Avenue for her absence. She did not mention the EDW event, though her comments were flooded with users accusing her of attending it.
Because the reported RSVP list was not publicly available and Drop Site News did not reveal where it sourced the list, we are unable to rate this claim. We can, however, break down Drop Site News' findings and any other publicly available information.
The document Drop Site News reportedly obtained also included a "Run of Show" listing the event's schedule, which read:
Run of Show:
- 4:30 pm: Event begins.
  - Mix and mingle
- 5:00 pm: EDW Chairwoman Lois Frankel to give opening remarks.
  - Thank everyone for attending, supporting EDW, and our historic wins.
- 5:10 pm: Acknowledge all new members in attendance and have them answer questions.
- 5:30 pm: Guests resume mingling.
- 6:00 pm: Event ends.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., publicly posted the voting schedule on Nov. 10, which indicated the vote on the impeachment articles he introduced would take place at 5:30 p.m. (archived).
According to Drop Site's reporting, the event took place at Goldfinch Social, a venue in Washington, D.C., about 2 miles from the Capitol.

An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by immigration agents in San Diego on 4 November and transferred to a facility in Texas has been reunited with his family in California.
Representative Juan Vargas shared a photograph of the boy and his family in a social media post on Monda, writing: “11 days ago, an 8-year-old in San Diego was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in. He was separated from his loved ones and held in a facility in Texas. Today, he’s finally home.”
The Haitian Bridge Alliance, an immigration advocacy group, confirmed that the third-grader had been released from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody.
“An eight-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love – not in immigration detention. We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry,” Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said in a statement.
The third-grader at Fay elementary school was put in restraints and taken into custody by federal immigration officers at a check-in earlier in the month, according to video obtained by NBC News and an oversight letter Democratic lawmakers sent to the Departments of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services.
A spokesperson for the homeland security department said ICE took the child into custody “out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety”.
The uncle, the spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian, was unable to prove legal guardianship – and that officials were obliged by federal anti-trafficking laws to take the boy into care as an “unaccompanied alien child”.
The Haitian Bridge Alliance said the boy was in the care of his uncle and cousins after his father was deported last year.
“I’m so grateful that he’s home, but this should have never happened in the first place,” Vargas said in a second social media post, adding that he would be asking the Trump administration for answers. While he was detained, the child was “held in a facility in Texas, far away from his home in San Diego”, Vargas said.
Celebrating the boy’s return, Jozef of the Haitian Bridge Alliance told NBC News: “The aunt was literally crying, and she said: ‘I have not eaten since the Wednesday they took my baby.’ They haven’t been able to sleep because of that.” She added: “The cousins were there when they took him, and wondering: will they ever see him again? But today [Monday] they are able to see him again. They are able to hug him.”

Mountains of scientific evidence support both the negative and positive effects of our eating habits on our health. Research shows that a healthy diet can help those suffering from chronic health conditions like Type 2 diabetes, heart disease and high blood pressure.
This is where “food is medicine” comes in. Food is medicine, also known as “food as medicine” and “food prescriptions,” is a movement dedicated to providing healthy food – fruits, vegetables and sometimes healthy proteins – based on a clinician’s prescription in order to prevent, manage or treat specific clinical conditions.
Prescribing food to patients is intended to convey that food is just as important as medication for health and wellness.
As researchers whose work focuses on food access and health in rural communities, we have firsthand experience running food is medicine programs in our local area in northern Mississippi. This experience has shown us the benefits and limitations of these programs in our community.
Fighting food insecurity
Food is medicine programs can be delivered through curated food boxes, grocery vouchers and medically tailored meals. Most programs are collaborations between nonprofit organizations, health clinics and healthcare providers. The goal of food is medicine is to improve patient health, especially for those with chronic conditions, while reducing healthcare costs.
Increasingly, food is medicine programs have become lifelines for people with food insecurity. In 2024, more than 47 million Americans, including 7.3 million children, lived in food-insecure households – meaning they were at some point uncertain of having, or did not have, enough food for everyone in the household.
Internationally, the number of people experiencing hunger rises to roughly 673 million. Rural populations are more likely to be food insecure due to the loss of local grocery stores and distance from urban centers. Unlike a food bank, food is medicine programs provide only healthy foods, which are often curated by a dietitian, to optimize patient health.
Forward momentum
Though food is medicine isn’t formally connected to the Make American Healthy Again movement, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. has brought new energy and attention to the concept. In January 2026, the second Trump administration launched a campaign encouraging Americans to “Eat Real Food.”
But the food is medicine movement actually began more than 60 years ago. One of the early providers who prescribed food as medicine was civil rights activist and multiple Nobel Peace Prize winner Dr. Jack Geiger. In the 1960s, he co-founded community health centers in South Boston and the Mississippi Delta.
When government officials chastised him for prescribing food to patients in the Delta, Geiger responded, “The last time I looked at my textbooks, the most specific therapy for malnutrition was food.”
Since then, thousands of community organizations like Community Servings and Project Open Hand have provided healthy food to vulnerable community members.
In 2023, the president of the American Heart Association convened an advisory group of researchers and physicians to review current food is medicine research and suggest next steps for work in this area. This advisory has suggested that these programs could help prevent or manage chronic conditions, saving the U.S. healthcare system an estimated US$4.3 trillion annually.
Food is medicine has also started to gain international momentum. In 2025, the Rockefeller Foundation supported a meeting of international scholars, policy experts and practitioners that established the Food Is Medicine Global Alliance. This organization plans to help integrate, sustainably finance and routinely deliver food is medicine programs worldwide by 2030. So far, it has released several reports highlighting the current food is medicine environment and made resources available to providers looking to start their own programs.
Food is medicine in our local community
Food is medicine programs can use food from local farms or grocery stores, and the means of getting the food to patients varies. The four projects we have run to date have been relatively small and local.
One was a food box pickup program that supplemented fruits and vegetables for 55 households whose members demonstrated food insecurity. We followed the participants for two years and found statistically significant reductions in weight, waist circumference and triglyceride levels in the primary adult participants.
For two of our other programs, including one that is ongoing, we partnered with local farmers. One was a pilot test of a food box delivery program for housebound people. Both the recipients of the food and the farmers reported high satisfaction with the program’s delivery and felt the program strengthened community connections while also supporting local agricultural livelihoods.
What other researchers have found
One recent large-scale literature review identified 14 trials of food is medicine interventions and found that these approaches often positively influenced diet quality and food security.
Another review of food is medicine programs for people with diabetes found significant increases in fruit and vegetable intake and reductions in blood sugar levels. This data supports our own previous findings.
However, the effect of food is medicine programs on long-term health outcomes has been inconsistent, in part because many trials have been too small or not rigorous enough to determine causation. In some cases, the “dose” – that is, the amount of food provided – is limited by grant funding. Our food box pickup project supplemented only four to five meals each week, which may have been insufficient to significantly improve all health outcomes.
Moreover, it will be important for researchers to consider the logistics of making these programs work in various local food environments. Global factors like changing weather patterns and, more recently, delays in fuel and supplies from the Strait of Hormuz have increased prices of staple food products like cereals and vegetable oil and led to shortages of cooking oil in some countries.
Food is medicine can be appealing because it makes intuitive sense. But going forward, larger, high-quality studies are needed to adequately track clinical outcomes from the various types of food is medicine programming. If studies show food is medicine is beneficial, it could lead to a shift in how healthcare practitioners approach diet for patients with chronic illness. Access to healthy food would be considered as essential as medications for patients with chronic illness.
Meagen Rosenthal, University of Mississippi and Natalie Minton, University of Mississippi

- The claim that Elon Musk paid Democratic U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Michigan to endorse GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers is unfounded.
- Although Musk donated more than $445 million to Republicans during the 2026 midterm elections, data from the Federal Election Commission showed no evidence he had recently donated to Stevens.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Stevens and Musk and are waiting for responses.
Two days before the 2026 midterm elections, Democratic U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Michigan shocked her party by pulling support for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed — her opponent in the primary — and instead endorsing Republican candidate Mike Rogers.
As social media users tried to make sense of Stevens' reversal, a rumor (archived) spread that tech billionaire Elon Musk had paid Stevens $2 million to endorse Rogers instead of El-Sayed. Snopes readers also reached out to us to investigate the rumor's veracity.
Although Musk donated more than any other political donor in the 2026 midterms, with more than $445 million to Republican candidates, according to money-tracking nonprofit OpenSecrets — using data from the Federal Election Commission, we determined that there was no evidence Musk recently donated to Stevens. However, because we could not definitively prove he hadn't paid her in some manner, we leave this claim unrated.
We reached out to Stevens' team and to Musk's SpaceX company seeking comment and will update this story if we receive a response.
It's unclear precisely where the rumor originated, but it largely spread on social media. No reputable news outlet reported that Musk directed funds to Stevens. Some social media posts linked to in other posts had since been deleted, indicating the account that originated the rumor may have taken down the post.
Stevens has publicly criticized Musk in the past, introducing legislation in 2025 aimed at preventing him from "accessing the Department of the Treasury's payment system and Americans' most sensitive personal and business information." Despite her criticisms, she retained funds SpaceX donated to her House campaign and her leadership PAC between 2019 and 2024, according to the FEC. The company did not make any donations to her Senate campaign.
According to OpenSecrets, Musk has primarily given money to Republican groups and the super PAC he founded and funds, America PAC (archived). There is no public record indicating he directed money to Stevens ahead of the election.
Although the rumor that Musk paid Stevens to reverse her endorsement is unfounded, there is evidence that her decision to back Rogers stemmed from her and El-Sayed's split regarding U.S. support for Israel.
Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel, has received more than $36 million from the main super PAC of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, according to Track AIPAC, a grassroots campaign funding tracker. Opposing U.S. funding to Israel has been one of El-Sayed's strongest campaign points, while Rogers has maintained consistent support for Israel.
After Stevens released a statement (archived) demanding El-Sayed condemn a political advertisement criticizing Israel that El-Sayed maintained his team was unaffiliated with, El-Sayed said he no longer wanted Stevens to join him at a Detroit church appearance planned for Nov. 1.
Stevens endorsed Rogers that day.
"This is about Abdul getting angrier and angrier and saying, I don't want these people in my campaign," Stevens told CNN's Anderson Cooper after she endorsed Rogers.

The World Health Organisation warned on Friday (November 13, 2026) of surging respiratory illnesses in Gaza, with worse expected after heavy rains flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians.
“The numbers already show the pressure. Acute respiratory infections are 33,000 cases higher than at the same time last year,” Dr. Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told reporters in Geneva from Jerusalem.
Poor living conditions and severe overcrowding are driving up infections as Gaza’s population is squeezed into an ever-smaller area, WHO said. The crunch has worsened as the Israeli military expands its control by advancing the “Yellow Line” — a demarcation established under October’s U.S.-brokered ceasefire.
“That means people are living in more crowded conditions, where of course the spread between humans of a virus is much more prone to spread,” Ms. Van De Weerdt explained.
The Israeli military told Reuters the Yellow Line aims to protect Israeli civilians and army troops from threats and that adjustments to its location follow the ceasefire agreement and international law, and are not intended to harm the civilian population.
“The IDF categorically rejects the claim that it operates to deliberately reduce the area available to the civilian population in the Gaza Strip.”
COGAT, the Israeli military agency that coordinates aid, said that more than 93,000 tents and over 8,600 trucks carrying tarpaulin sheets, blankets and winter clothing have entered Gaza since the Board of Peace, UN agencies and NGOs launched the winterisation plan. Equipment intended for the reconstruction of Gaza will be permitted to enter only after Hamas has been fully disarmed, it added.
Last week COGAT said that it had stepped up efforts to improve sanitary conditions before the heavy rain, in coordination with international organisations.
Respiratory infections currently make up 11% of all consultations, with the WHO expecting cold weather, flooding, overcrowded shelters and poor ventilation to push these numbers higher.
“It is shocking that just a few days of rain really showed us what the coming months will bring. And winter has not even fully set in. The worst really is yet to come,” Ms. Van De Weerdt said.
Nearly a million displaced people in Gaza live in flood-exposed areas, and 400,000 of them are in locations that are considered at extremely high risk, according to the WHO.
The agency said flooding heightened the risk of contaminated water, while standing water gave mosquitoes and pests more places to breed. Dampness encouraged mould and bacteria that are major drivers of respiratory infections, especially in young children, it said.
While the majority of medicines are getting into Gaza, the WHO faces difficulty getting laboratory supplies, which it says are vital for diagnosing patients before they can be treated.
“To prevent outbreaks, we really call to let laboratory equipment enter Gaza today, so that we can avoid a public health disaster on top of a disaster.“
COGAT said Israel has facilitated the entry of all medicines requested by international aid organisations and has not rejected any requests received, adding that X-ray machines, oxygen generators, batteries, generators, and other equipment have entered Gaza.

Disseqt AI, which builds AI agents for AI governance and testing, has raised $8 Mn (about ₹75 Cr) in a funding round led by Gresham House Ventures. Sure Valley Ventures, Delta Partners, and Enterprise Ireland also participated in the round, along with angel investors like cricketer Rahul Dravid and senior executives from OpenAI, Palo Alto Networks, Salesforce, and Meta. The startup plans to use the fresh capital to expand its global enterprise customer base and scale operations across the UK and international markets. “Every enterprise is handing real work to AI agents, but very few can prove those agents are safe, fair and within policy. This gap often stops ambitious AI projects from going live, and it is what we built Disseqt to close … This funding lets us bring that standard to more enterprises around the world,” said CEO and cofounder Apoorva Kumar. Founded in late 2025 by Kumar, Manish Atri, and Cyril Treacy, Disseqt operates an independent governance and testing layer for enterprise AI agents. Essentially, it ensures that AI systems are behaving as intended and meet regulatory requirements. The platform enables compliance, security, and IT teams to test agentic workflows for vulnerabilities and data-leak risks prior to deployment. It can enforce real-time policy guardrails in production, block non-compliant outputs, and maintain audit trails independent of underlying model providers. While its commercial operations and headquarters are in Ireland, Disseqt’s engineering and AI teams are based in Bengaluru. It has customer-facing operations across the UK, Ireland and India, according to its website. Atri, its COO, is also India-based. Both Kumar and Atri are graduates of IIIT Allahabad. Besides, it has also partnered with major Indian IT companies like Infosys, Cognizant, HCLTech, Mphasis, and Tata Technologies as ‘Global System Integrators’ to deploy its platforms for their enterprise clients. This adds to the uptick in investor interest in AI startups. As per Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, AI startup funding more than tripled YoY to $438 Mn in the September quarter. The surging investor interest in AI comes even as the overall funding landscape remains relatively subdued, with the cumulative funding raised by Indian startups increasing by just 5% YoY.
