Taking Korea's toughest exam from behind bars
- Published
Students intently focus on maths formulas written on a board before lowering their heads and taking notes as the teacher works through a sum.
The teacher's voice and the scratch of pens fill the room.
At first glance, this could be any classroom in South Korea.
But thick metal bars cover the windows and the students are wearing blue prison uniforms and rubber shoes emblazoned with the words "Korea Correctional Service".
This is Mandela Boys' School, an education facility for young prisoners inside the Seoul Southern Correctional Institution in Guro, south-west Seoul. In South Korea, young people who are sentenced to imprisonment by a criminal court must serve their time in prison.
"The boys here have committed serious offences and received criminal sentences," Jeong Yeo-gyeong, a correctional officer in the Korea Correctional Service's social reintegration division, told the BBC.
"As well as theft, there is a high proportion of serious offences, including violence, bodily injury, sexual violence and robbery."
But by opening educational institutes like Mandela, authorities are hoping to give these young offenders a chance to better their lives after they serve out their sentences.
Opened by the justice ministry in March 2023, it allows boys who were aged 17 and under when their sentences became final to prepare for school equivalency exams as well as the Suneung - the country's notoriously difficult university entrance examination - while still serving their sentences.
Held every November, the Suneung is an infamous eight-hour marathon of back-to-back exams.
Students attempt about 200 questions across various subjects, which include Korean, maths, English, social and natural sciences, among others.
The country itself comes to a standstill - construction work halts, planes are grounded and military training gets suspended to facilitate an optimal testing environment.
A total of 551,864 people have applied to take this year's Suneung on 19 November.
Around 30 prisoners are enrolled in the Suneung preparation class at Mandela Boys' School, and 11 of them have applied to take this year's exam.
Park Soo-young (not his real name), a 17-year-old inmate, has been at the Mandela Boys' Suneung preparation class for two months and hopes to study social welfare.
He tells the BBC that he had dreams of becoming a police officer before committing the crime that landed him behind bars.
He says he could not bring himself to look properly at his mother during his trial. When he turned towards her after his sentence was announced, she was crying.
"Seeing her like that, I broke down too. I wondered how I was going to live from then on, and how I could look after my mother, who was on her own. I think I kept crying for about a week while I was in the detention centre."
Looking back on his offence, he says he feels "very ashamed that I couldn't control that impulse". If he could meet his younger self, he would tell him: "Control that impulse. If you do, everything will be different."
"I'd grab myself by the collar and shake myself as I said it."
He hopes the Suneung and university will offer him a chance to start again.
"Once I'm out, I need to cut ties with the friends and people I used to know and start a new life. I think university is the only way to do that. Going to university would let me leave the area where I used to live, move somewhere else and start something new. That's why I began studying again."
But he describes beginning Suneung preparation as "a struggle every day".
"But the teachers don't let anything slip past. They keep helping us until we understand. If I don't understand something, I put my hand up and they come over and explain it.
Sometimes, if I've missed something, I keep working at it on my own. If I still can't get it, I ask the students next to me to explain," he said.
Park's day begins at 06:30 with a morning check by prison officers. He starts memorising English vocabulary and working through Korean reading passages early in the morning.
"I learn English words whenever I can, even before breakfast. From 07:00, I work through a Korean passage, something like literature or speech. We have to come down to the classroom at 08:00, so we have another check and then come down for lessons."
During breaks, students make calls to their families or leave the classroom for scheduled visits. In the evening, they return for supervised study. Once the day's activities are over, they must go back to their cells together.
Park says he studies until 22:00 before finishing for the day. If he wants to study longer hours, he needs permission from a prison officer.
But even if gets a good result this year, Park will not be allowed to leave prison and attend university straight away. He is only due to be released in 2028, but plans to use this exam as experience and continue studying next year.
"This time, I want to experience how the Suneung works and how competitive it is. Then, next year, I'll work hard from the start so I can get in the year after that."
Some former students from Mandela Boys' School have managed to get into university, according to the justice ministry.
Others have continued their studies after leaving prison, including by enrolling in residential exam preparation academies.
The inmates are taught by a team of seven prison officers, all of whom hold teaching certificates. Each is responsible for a subject.
Visiting instructors provide classes in the humanities, arts and sport, while university student volunteers help with learning. Professional psychological counselling is also available.
Park Min-yong, who applied to work here in 2023, teaches science. And alongside Suneung lessons, he works with the students' to change their habits and behaviour.
One thing he often tells them is that they need to "learn how to become adults".
He believes that while studying in itself does not necessarily turn inmates away from a life of crime, the experience of having worked hard at something: staying with a concept that makes little sense, revisiting a wrong answer and continuing even when grades do not improve straight away, is valuable in itself.
"Studying properly means pushing yourself to your limits, and that takes considerable stamina and patience," he says.
"Whether they chose to do it or not, the experience of persevering, enduring and not giving up easily may help them to some extent when they face the difficulties of life after release."
He says the material they encounter while preparing for the Suneung also gives them new things to think about.
Korean reading passages cover literature, society, science and philosophy. Students have to consider a character's perspective, examine the evidence behind an argument and understand unfamiliar concepts. They also encounter explanations that differ from their own and have to reconsider what they think.
"They gradually learn that it's not just about their own personal view - that these concepts and relationships have been developed through a shared understanding among many people," Park said.
There are difficult moments too.
Park says students sometimes cheat in classroom tests even while he is watching.
"They cheat as if it's nothing. They give each other answers, even when I'm watching them. Some repeat it after being told off. There may be an element of doing it deliberately, but often they haven't thought it through. They don't think about the impact their actions or words could have on others."
The boys also have a strong desire for recognition, he says.
"It's all the time. 'Look how much I've done. Look how much my grades have improved. I've done this much - haven't I done well?' They're always like that. They're hungry for it."
Not everyone agrees with this initiative though.
One criticism is that young people who have not committed crimes also face fierce competition for university places: so there is some anger that the state provides offenders with separate education and opportunities to prepare for this exam.
Father Jeong Min-ha, of the Archdiocese of Seoul's correctional ministry committee, worked with Seoul Southern Correctional Institution from September 2023 until last year.
He acknowledges these criticisms.
"Studying gives them a sense of achievement and time to look seriously at their own lives. That's why I think it matters. I think that is the most important part of rehabilitation."
Of course, there is no guarantee.
Park recalls a student who had done well at the school but later returned to prison.
"He was doing well when he left, but in the end he came back. So something went wrong. I'd hoped he would carry on with what he'd been doing here, but he couldn't. That's disappointing."
According to the justice ministry's 2026 corrections statistical yearbook, 35.5% of prisoners aged under 20 who were released in 2021 were imprisoned again within three years. That was about 1.7 times the overall rate of 21.2%, and the highest of any age group.
But Park hopes the students will continue learning after they leave prison. "We don't know what the outcome will be," he says.
"They say the way to clear a glass of dirty water is to keep pouring clean water into it, rather than trying to remove each bit of dirt. I hope they fill their minds with good things, learn to use their energy and intellect in the right way, and put that learning into practice at the right time and place."
Additional reporting by Hosu Lee.

Srinagar, Nov 19: The Food and Drugs Administration (FDA), Jammu and Kashmir, has issued an advisory to railway authorities, directing that highly perishable food commodities be transported only through duly licensed Food Business Operators (FBOs) and under prescribed temperature-controlled conditions, with proper declarations and documentation.
The advisory follows the seizure and destruction of around 1,600 kg of frozen meat at Budgam Railway Station, where the consignment was allegedly transported through the railway parcel service by misrepresenting it as general goods.
In a press statement, the FDA said the action was taken after receiving specific information from Railway Police authorities. The frozen meat was found to have been transported without proper temperature-control arrangements to maintain the required frozen conditions.
A preliminary investigation revealed that the consignment originated from M/s Al Nida Foods, Ghazipur, Delhi, and was intended for Ayaan Manzoor, a resident of Bemina, Srinagar, through M/s Tultrav Courier Agency, Bemina.
The consignment had reportedly been booked under the general parcel category without disclosing the actual nature of the commodity, apparently to circumvent the prescribed requirements for transporting highly perishable food products under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
The FDA said inspection of the consignment and accompanying documents revealed discrepancies in the description of the commodity and violations of labelling norms, attracting provisions of Sections 53 and 61 of the Act.
It was also found that the transporter and intended recipient did not possess the mandatory FSSAI licences, attracting penal provisions under Section 63. Considering the potential threat to public health, the entire consignment was seized and destroyed through the Municipal Committee, Budgam, at a designated disposal site.
The department said notices had been issued to the concerned persons and entities, while further legal proceedings were being initiated under the relevant provisions of the Act.
The FDA also referred to similar enforcement actions undertaken during 2025, when frozen meat and meat products were seized from five establishments across Srinagar. These included 1,200 kg from M/s Sunshine Industries, Zakura; 500 kg from M/s Al-Taqwa, Lasjan; 1,400 kg from M/s M.M. Foods, Haji Bagh, HMT; 420 kg from M/s Niyaz Ahmad Kawa, Aali Kadal; and 520 kg from M/s Al-Azeem Enterprises, Manderbagh.
Following these seizures, legal proceedings were initiated against the respective Food Business Operators. The Court of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Srinagar, acting as the Adjudicating Officer, imposed penalties of Rs 4 lakh, Rs 5 lakh, Rs 4.40 lakh, Rs 1.25 lakh and Rs 17,500, respectively.
The department further stated that two samples collected from the establishments were examined by the ICAR-National Meat Research Institute, Hyderabad, and identified as buffalo meat.
To prevent such violations, the FDA had issued a prohibitory order on October 3, 2025, restricting the transportation, storage and sale of frozen food products without prescribed temperature-control arrangements and mandatory labelling under the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020.
Meanwhile, the department said it had conducted 12,778 inspections across Jammu and Kashmir during the financial year 2026-27, lifting 7,266 enforcement samples and 2,857 surveillance samples for analysis through NABL-accredited laboratories.
During the same period, 533 cases were instituted and 619 cases adjudicated, resulting in penalties amounting to Rs 1,00,42,231 under various provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act.
Following the Budgam incident, FDA field teams intensified enforcement activities, conducting 364 inspections, suspending nine FSSAI licences or registrations, issuing 21 improvement notices and recommending 31 cases for adjudication. More than 19 cases were also compounded under Section 69 of the Act.
The FDA also said that funding-related issues concerning manpower and laboratory requirements had been resolved after the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), Government of India, approved the action plan submitted by the department for the financial years 2026-27, 2027-28 and 2028-29.
The approval will facilitate the recruitment of laboratory analysts, microbiologists, drivers and other personnel, besides procurement of chemicals, consumables and glassware for the government food laboratories in Srinagar and Jammu.
The procurement process for laboratory manpower through the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) portal has reached its final stage, while the procurement of certified reference materials, chemicals and glassware is expected to be completed within two weeks, the department said.
Annual maintenance contracts for high-end laboratory equipment have also been executed with the respective original equipment manufacturers, while method validation is underway. Contracts for hiring drivers and laboratory analysts for Mobile Food Testing Vans have also been finalised, with personnel being deployed for operational activities.
The department said it was working to expand the NABL-accredited testing scope of the government food laboratories to 2,500 parameters by January 2027 and 3,500 parameters by March 2027. Additional NABL-accredited and FSSAI-recognised laboratories are also being empanelled to strengthen testing capacity and ensure timely analysis of enforcement and surveillance samples.
The FDA said it would continue intensified surveillance and enforcement to ensure compliance with food safety standards and appealed to consumers to share specific information about violations with the department for timely action.

The food which we choose to eat every day, the habits, how much we want to move… and staying consistent with that. I think even something like encouraging our children to be more mindful… giving them habits they can take with them as they grow. I think wellness is a byproduct of good habits for your body, and sustainability is for the Earth,” the entrepreneur said.

The Dreame X60 Ultra Complete offers powerful suction, heated-water mopping, a slimmer design, and smarter obstacle handling. At ₹1,34,999, it delivers an impressive cleaning experience with greater convenience, though the value of its premium features depends on your home’s needs.
When I reviewed the X40 Ultra, it was the first robot where I didn’t have to plan a backup round of cleaning. Months later, the L40 Ultra AE beat it on suction and mopping for Rs 20,000 less. The X60 Ultra Complete has to answer a question both reviews left open: what does a Dreame flagship do that the cheaper model does not?
On paper, quite a lot. It also costs more than twice what the L40 Ultra AE did, so the real question is whether the additions change daily cleaning in an Indian home or mostly change the spec sheet.
Table of Contents
Design and Build: Slimmer Robot, Smarter Moves
At first glance, the X60 Pro Complete looks like any other premium Dreame device. You get the familiar circular body, a large docking station, and a design that is more functional than flashy. But there’s one important difference. At just 7.95 cm tall, the X60 is noticeably slimmer than the X40 Ultra and L40 Ultra AE. And that’s thanks to the retractable navigation sensor that pops up when needed and slides back into the body when the robot needs to squeeze under low furniture.
This might sound gimmicky at first (remember OnePlus 7T Pro?), but it has a practical value. In 2026, most robot vacuums already do a decent job of cleaning open floors. The real challenge is getting under sofas, beds, and cabinets without getting stuck. The X60 needs just over 8 cm of clearance to enter these spaces with its sensor retracted.
The price of that slim body is a 235 ml onboard bin, which is significantly smaller than what we saw on the L40 Ultra (395 ml) and X40 Ultra (350 ml). That means the robot keeps returning to the dock to empty the bin more often than expected in heavy sessions, especially if you have a pet at home. Not a big deal, but the trips do add time.
The slimmer body isn’t the only trick up the X60’s sleeve. Dreame has also upgraded its obstacle-climbing system, allowing the robot to lift itself over raised thresholds and door tracks that might stop a regular robot vacuum. This is particularly useful in Indian homes, where bathrooms, balconies, and even some rooms have raised entrances.
Genuinely, this is a big step-up (pun intended) in the evolution of robot vacuums. But you should ask yourself this question: are the obstacles in your home tall enough to trouble a decent mid-range robot vacuum and require a top-of-the-line robot? So while the X60’s climbing ability is impressive on paper (single thresholds up to 4.5 cm and double-layer steps up to 8.8 cm), how much value it adds depends on the layout of your home. If your existing robot already moves between rooms without getting stuck, this upgrade alone won’t justify spending significantly more. In fact, your home’s layout, flooring, and the presence of pets matter far more than the specifications alone. We’ve covered these and other factors in our robot vacuum cleaner buying guide.
The dock is significantly shorter and wider than the L40 Ultra I tested last, and its gold-accented finish looks more at home in a living room than the matte black L40. The trade-off is the capacity: 4.2 liters of clean water and 3 liters of dirty water, down from 4.5 and 4 liters on the L40. The 3.2-liter dust bag is unchanged.
As I pointed out in my earlier Dreame reviews, the company continues to ship its robot vacuums with a bulky 16A plug, and the X60 Ultra Complete is no exception. Most Indian homes don’t have a 16A socket conveniently located where you’d want to place the docking station, making an adapter or a dedicated socket an unnecessary hassle for such an expensive product.
Cleaning Performance: Does the Extra Power Make a Difference?
Dreame has made a big deal of the X60 Ultra Complete’s suction power of 35,000 Pa, and understandably so. But having reviewed the X40 Ultra (12,000 Pa) and L40 Ultra AE (19,000 Pa), I’ve reached a point where raw suction figures don’t excite me as much as they once did. Both those robots were already capable of keeping my floors clean without much intervention. So with the X60, I was less interested in how much more powerful it was and more curious about whether that extra power translated into noticeably cleaner floors.
On tile and stone floors, the X60 Ultra Complete does an excellent job of picking up everyday dust, crumbs, and pet hair. The extending side brush also does a great job of cleaning along walls and around furniture legs, areas where robot vacuums often leave some dirt behind. Hair handling is noticeably better than on the X40 Ultra, which struggled with long human hair and clumps of dog fur.
Obstacle avoidance is something Dreame has mastered, and it’s no different on the X60. In my month-long testing, it easily avoided the usual suspects like cables, socks, and small toys. But that was the case with the cheaper L40 and X40 vacuums, too. While it handled thick carpets well, light fabric rugs were pulled towards its inlet a couple of times.
Two newer touches stand out on the X60 Ultra. The robot maps the house during its first clean, so there is no separate mapping run. Also, its proactive-light dirt detection spots hair and light liquids and adjusts cleaning. Image processing happens on the device, per Dreame, and the app shows when the camera is active.
Mopping Performance: Where the X60 Makes a Stronger Case
When I interviewed Manu Sharma, the head of Dreame India, he made an interesting observation: for Indians, a house isn’t truly clean until the mopping is done. And that’s where the X60 Ultra Complete brings some meaningful upgrades. Unlike the X40 Ultra and L40 Ultra AE, which used hot water only to wash the mop pads at the dock, the X60 actually mops the floor with water heated to 40°C. The pads spin at up to 230 RPM, apply 15 N of downward pressure, and extend towards walls and furniture legs to clean areas that regular circular mops often miss.
For everyday mopping, the results are quite impressive. Footprints, light spills, and the grime that builds up on floors throughout the day are handled well. Even some dried stains can be removed, although older, stubborn stains may need a second pass or a targeted zone clean. This is one area where the X60 makes a stronger case for its premium pricing, especially if you mop your floors daily rather than occasionally.
There is one catch, though. The X60 tends to leave floors noticeably damp after mopping. Not enough to make them dangerously slippery, but enough for water marks to show up on wooden-finish tiles. Thankfully, you can adjust the water level in the Dreame app, and I’d recommend starting with a lower setting before increasing it if needed. For homes with carpets, the mop pads can lift up to 21.5 mm to avoid wetting them. You can also have the robot leave the pads at the dock when vacuuming carpets, which is the safer option for thicker rugs.
Multifunction Dock: Almost Hands-Free, But Not Quite
A big part of what you’re paying for with the X60 Ultra Complete is its multifunction docking station. Once the robot finishes cleaning, the dock takes over. It empties the dustbin, refills the robot’s water tank, washes the mop pads, and dries them with hot air. This also makes the smaller onboard dustbin less of a concern, as the robot can return to the dock and empty itself whenever needed. It’s the sort of convenience that makes you forget how much work goes into keeping a robot vacuum clean.
But don’t mistake this for a completely hands-free system. During my testing, I had to refill the clean-water tank and empty the dirty-water tank roughly every other day. Your experience will vary depending on the size of your home, how often you mop, and the water settings you use. You’ll also need to replace the dust bag occasionally and clean the dock’s washboard and other parts. Then there are the recurring costs of dust bags, filters, brushes, and cleaning solution. Dreame includes a decent number of spare accessories in the Complete package, which is nice, but you’ll eventually need to buy replacements. For my usage of roughly 800 sqft home, that’s like replenishing every 6 months or so.
The dock itself is fairly large and needs a permanent spot in your home. Make sure there’s enough room to remove the water tanks comfortably, and preferably place it somewhere you won’t have to carry a tank full of dirty water across the house. These might sound like nitpicking, but when you’re spending this much on a robot vacuum, even small inconveniences are worth pointing out.
App and Battery Life: Plenty of Features, Room for Improvement
I’ve said this in my earlier Dreame reviews, and I’ll say it again. The Dreamehome app can do almost anything you want, but finding the right setting can sometimes be a task in itself. The X60 Ultra Complete is no different. You can clean individual rooms, set up no-mop zones, save up to four maps, and control the robot using Alexa, Siri, Google Home, or Dreame’s own “OK Dreame” voice commands. There’s plenty to play around with, but the app could really do with a simpler interface. Stain Recognition is still in beta, while Matter support is something Dreame has promised through a future software update.
There are some new pet-specific features, too. The X60 can recognize pet bowls, give extra attention to areas where pets spend time, and even locate your pet using its camera. You can also use the camera for live video and two-way communication. There’s an Apple Watch app for starting cleaning sessions and checking their status, along with phone widgets for quick access to cleaning routines.
As for battery life, the X60 packs a 6,400 mAh battery, the same capacity as the X40 Ultra and larger than the L40 Ultra AE’s 5,200 mAh unit. However, a bigger battery doesn’t necessarily translate into longer cleaning sessions, especially with all the extra features running. The good news is that charging is much faster than on the L40 Ultra AE. In my testing, charging times ranged from around 90 minutes to just over two hours, compared to roughly three and a half hours for the L40. Battery life itself isn’t particularly impressive for a flagship, especially in larger homes, but the robot can return to its dock, recharge, and resume cleaning from where it stopped. So, unless you’re in a hurry to get the entire house cleaned in one go, this shouldn’t be much of a concern.
Dreame X60 Ultra Complete Verdict: Worth the Price?
At Rs 1,34,999, the Dreame X60 Ultra Complete is not an easy robot vacuum to recommend, especially when the L40 Ultra AE costs less than half as much and already does an excellent job of keeping floors clean. But after spending time with the X60, I can see where the extra money goes. The slimmer design helps it reach places other robots struggle with, the improved obstacle-climbing system is useful for homes with raised thresholds, and the heated-water mopping is a meaningful upgrade over the X40 and L40. Add reliable vacuuming, better hair handling, excellent edge cleaning, and a multifunction dock that takes care of most of the dirty work, and you have a very capable cleaning system.
That doesn’t mean it’s without flaws. Despite the improvements, I still noticed some hair around the rollers. Mopping can leave floors wetter than I’d like, and stubborn stains may need another pass. The smaller 235 ml dustbin means more trips to the dock during heavy cleaning sessions, while battery life is good enough rather than exceptional. The Dreamehome app remains powerful but unnecessarily complicated, and the dock still needs regular attention. And yes, Dreame continues to ship a 16A plug, something I’ve complained about in my previous reviews. These aren’t deal-breakers individually, but they are harder to ignore at this price.
The X60 also faces some serious competition. In India, the Roborock Saros 20, Ecovacs DEEBOT X11 OmniCyclone, and Narwal Flow 2 offer their own take on premium robot cleaning. In the US, the Roborock Saros 20, Ecovacs DEEBOT X12S OmniCyclone, and eufy Omni S2 are worth considering against the X60 Max Ultra Complete. I haven’t personally tested these competing models, so I can’t tell you whether they clean better or worse than the Dreame. But based on their features, they’re certainly worth comparing before spending this kind of money.
And that brings me back to the question I raised at the beginning of this review. Does the X60 Ultra Complete do enough to justify its substantial premium over the L40 Ultra AE? For most homes, probably not. The L40 already handles everyday vacuuming and mopping well enough that the X60’s extra suction and smarter features won’t necessarily translate into noticeably cleaner floors. But if you have low furniture, tricky thresholds, pets that shed a lot, and want the most advanced cleaning system Dreame currently offers, the X60 makes a stronger case. You’re paying less for a dramatic improvement in cleaning and more for the ability to clean difficult areas with less intervention.
If you’re unsure which of these premium features you actually need, try our interactive robot vacuum buying checklist. It lets you choose features based on your home and cleaning needs, so you can decide where it’s worth spending more and where you can save.
The X60 Ultra Complete is an excellent robot vacuum, but it’s also a reminder that the best robot vacuum isn’t necessarily the most expensive one. It’s the one that cleans your home well enough that you stop thinking about cleaning. And Dreame had already come remarkably close to achieving that with its cheaper models.

- Slim design gets under low furniture
- Impressive obstacle climbing and avoidance
- Heated-water mopping with excellent edge coverage

In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down, and waiting for their rides home to arrive. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman.
Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and cancelled the alert, which notified not only other school officials on the chain, but also the Baltimore County Police Department, that no response was needed.
The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.
According to a lawsuit filed by the current and former students, Taki Allen, Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr., and Keith Winfield III, due to “both technological and human errors,” school officials called police to the scene anyway, and the cops responded with force.
At least six patrol cars arrived with lights flashing, and some cops emerged with guns drawn. The teens froze and cooperated, confused and scared for their lives, their lawsuit said.
“No one told the students what they were suspected of,” the lawsuit said. “Officers separated the students, ordered them to their knees on the concrete, handcuffed them, and searched their persons and property.”
Only after the cops failed to find a gun did students learn that it was the school’s AI gun detection system, Omnilert, that triggered the police response. Allegedly, one of the responding officers muttered, “stupid AI cameras” and “fucking Omnilerts,” while another told the students that “AI is not the best.” Finally releasing the students, one officer seemed to acknowledge that they had put the teens in danger.
“Hey, thanks for not running away, that would have been a real problem,” the officer allegedly said. Walking away, another joked that the boys should remember to “be careful with your chip bags.”
Teens traumatized
The cops did not just target the suspected gunman but apparently told the other teens that they were guilty “by association” when they asked why they were searched.
Suing to stop any other teens from facing allegedly life-or-death situations due to officials’ blind trust of AI, the teens have asked for an injunction barring BCPS from using Omnilert until they can effectively establish protocols to prevent police responses to false alerts.
The lawsuit alleged that students’ constitutional rights were violated, as students were unlawfully searched and detained.
Damon Hewitt, president and executive director of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law—a nonpartisan nonprofit that’s representing the teens in the suit—said that “overreliance on artificial intelligence technology mixed with inept communication and coordination among key officials is a toxic mix.”
The complaint noted that BCPS was among the earliest adopters of Omnilert, and officials have touted it as “the largest deployment of AI visual gun detection” as a means to supposedly protect students. Instead, they alleged that Omnilert is marketing a defective product as triggering “near-zero false positives” without effectively requiring the adequate human review that claim depends on.
“We need a reckoning on how AI is being used, especially concerning public safety and kids,” Hewitt said. “We are fighting to deliver justice in this case, but it also holds lessons for educators and police officials across the country who should think twice before putting our children’s fate in the hands of AI.”
All the teens feel less safe on campus and less trusting of police following the incident. They also suffered from physical pain—including ”deep red marks” on their wrists from handcuffs—as well as “acute and lasting emotional distress, fear, anxiety,” and “humiliation.” Further, the teens report that rumors follow them around, falsely claiming that there was a gun and damaging their reputations.
Car pick-up will never be the same. The student falsely flagged as the gunman, Taki Allen, “no longer feels safe waiting for rides or spending time outside the school after hours” and “frequently pays for rides home from private car services to avoid waiting for rides from friends or family.” Keith Winfield’s house was very close to the school, but his mother, Frieda Winfield, said his anxiety was so bad that he would call her “multiple times after football practice ended to confirm that she was on her way to pick him up.”
Frieda Winfield called for change following her son Keith’s chilling interaction.
“The police told my son this could have been a real problem,” Frieda Winfield said. “No child in Baltimore County should face this kind of danger while waiting outside his own school for a ride home from his mother.”
What went wrong?
The teens’ lawsuit targets Omnilert and responding Baltimore County Police Department officers. It also challenges Baltimore County Public Schools and individual school officials who allegedly failed to establish proper protocols to prevent a police response to a cancelled alert.
Later investigating, the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) for Education concluded that Omnilert’s system had no “bias.” But OIG acknowledged that the “delegation of authority” process that Kenwood High School set up didn’t stop its principal, Kate Smith, from noticing the alert, failing to see it was cancelled, and texting a school resource officer to deploy police 15 minutes later—all while acknowledging in that text that the object in the alert was “maybe not” a gun. Smith apparently was never trained on the Omnilert system, OIG’s report indicated.
The OIG agreed with teens that things should change. Immediately after the incident, an internal Omnilert training link was shared with BCPS staff, and OIG recommended that schools conduct bi-annual trainings moving forward.
They also recommended that the BCPS Department of School Safety “review its protocol” and reduce the number of individuals who receive campus gun alerts. That could help ensure “internal notification controls are followed” and police “are fully informed of a verified threat,” the OIG said.
Without changes, the OIG acknowledged that “the loss of alert notification controls could place not only BCPS staff and students at risk but could also place responding law enforcement in a potentially tragic situation.”
Another change offered a technical solution that may have prevented the tragic event. The OIG recommended that school officials switch to using the Omnilert app. Since Smith opened the alert in a text message window on her phone, they suggested that she could easily have overlooked the cancellation text message if her first instinct were to enlarge the image or review the camera footage.
These recommendations aren’t enough for current and former students suing, one of which remains an active student who claims the principal never apologized and instead made light of the incidents using cry-laughing emojis in texts with other school officials. Teens alleged that Smith should have known that more than “99 percent of OGD Alerts in Baltimore County Public Schools were false positives that required no police response,” as the OIG’s report said, and she should have prioritized students’ safety and verified the threat before calling in police.
“BCPS’s failures amounted to deliberate indifference to the constitutional rights of its students,” their lawsuit alleged.
The teens asked a court for an injunction barring the use of Omnilert until BCPS staff and police are adequately trained. In their complaint, they alleged that none of the officers on the scene had reviewed the camera footage before responding, and none of the officers informed of the alert cancellation intervened.
BCPS silent; Omnilert defends tech
BCPS declined to comment on the lawsuit, pointing Ars to a statement issued to parents following the incident. That statement did not directly apologize to students but did say the school would provide “ongoing counseling and emotional support” to them while promising to take steps to prevent future incidents.
Blake Mitchell, Omnilert’s vice president of marketing, told Ars that Omnilert is reviewing the complaint.
“What these four students went through on October 20, 2025 should not have happened, and we are truly sorry for the fear they and their families experienced,” Mitchell said. “We understand why they want answers.”
Mitchell said that Omnilert is “built to send anything that could be a firearm to trained people for review, because missing a real gun is the worst possible outcome.” He also reiterated that the OIG investigation found no bias in Omnilert’s system and seemed to agree that it was the school’s authority delegation that failed the students, not necessarily the technology.
“In this case, the school’s designated safety staff reviewed the alert and cancelled it within about two minutes, and everyone who received it was notified,” Mitchell said. “That is exactly why human review matters, and why a cancelled alert must stay cancelled.”
Len Kamdang of the Lawyers’ Committee representing the teens told The New York Times that teens want BCPS and Omnilert to acknowledge that “what happened to them was unacceptable.”
“This case is ultimately about how human beings allowed AI to substitute for their judgment,” Kamdang said.
As a mother, Frieda Winfield told a local news outlet that she was shocked by the incident, despite deliberately teaching her son to be cautious around police. The boys’ caution “saved their lives in my opinion,” she said.
“I was angry. I was fearful,” Frieda Winfield said. “The biggest part was fear, because they’re young men. Young Black men, and they were at school, and they didn’t understand why what was happening, happened to them.”
Kamdang told NYT that “for anyone with children, that is a scary, scary situation. For a Black student, especially a young Black man in America, that is a life-or-death situation.”
As AI tools are increasingly positioned as public safety solutions, the Lawyers Committee is pushing for police reform when cops or officials appear to be blindly trusting AI, their press release said. They noted that “this injustice also raises a broader concern regarding the use and reliability of AI-powered technology in public safety where accuracy is essential in life-and-death situations.”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

Salah scores twice as Egypt and Nigeria win Afcon 2027 qualifiers
- Published
Tolu Arokodare was the hero as Nigeria boosted their hopes of reaching the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) with a 3-1 home win over tournament co-hosts Tanzania.
With the East Africans already assured of a spot at the finals, the Super Eagles are battling for the one qualification spot available in Group L and have little margin for error after losing 3-0 in Guinea-Bissau in September.
Alhassan Yusuf kept his composure to slot Nigeria into a second-minute lead in Uyo from Ademola Lookman's pass, but the visitors equalised through Alphonce Msanga just after the half-hour mark.
Arokodare climbed off the bench at half-time and cleverly flicked home Wilfred Ndidi's low ball to restore the lead for the West Africans in the 52nd minute.
And the Ajax striker, who is on a season-long loan from Wolves, gave the Super Eagles breathing space eight minutes later when he controlled Moses Usor's cross from the left and smashed in from 12 yards out.
With three games played in the group, Eric Chelle's side are now one point behind leaders Guinea-Bissau, who drew 1-1 with Madagascar on Thursday.

Elsewhere, Mohamed Salah scored twice late on against Malawi as Egypt cruised to a 5-0 victory in Ali Maher's first match in charge.
Achraf Hakimi netted two stunning goals and Yassine Bounou saved a penalty to help Morocco continue their unbeaten start with a 5-1 win over Niger.
Meanwhile, Tunisia are in danger of missing out on the finals for the first time since 1992 after suffering a 2-0 defeat at home against Libya, and Kenya scored a last-minute equaliser to end South Africa's perfect start.
The third round of qualifying culminates with three games on Saturday, while the fourth round of fixtures are split across Monday and Tuesday.
Salah and Hakimi shine
Egypt reached the semi-finals of Afcon 2025 and the last 16 of this year's Fifa World Cup under Hossam Hassan but parted company with the 60-year-old earlier this month.
The Pharaohs had taken four points from their opening two games in Group B, with Salah substituted after an hour in their 0-0 draw with Angola before missing the win in South Sudan.
The former Liverpool forward returned as captain against Malawi, and Egypt cruised into a 3-0 lead at the break through goals from Nasser Maher, Omar Marmoush and Mohamed Hany.
Salah got on the scoresheet when he stooped to head in a cross from the left and rounded off proceedings by dinking in a penalty after Hamza Abdelkarim was tripped in the box.
Victory in Maher's first game at the helm puts Egypt three points clear of Angola, who take on South Sudan on Saturday.
In Group A, Morocco had also looked like they would ease to three points against Niger in Casablanca after Yassir Zabiri's early effort and a brilliant long-range strike from right-back Hakimi put them 2-0 up after 27 minutes.
But Mohamed Abdourahmane headed in to halve the deficit and Niger had a chance to level from the spot on the stroke of half-time after a handball by Noussair Mazraoui.
However, Atlas Lions goalkeeper Bounou moved to his left to keep out Youssouf Oumarou's penalty, and Hakimi made it 3-1 in first-half stoppage time with a dipping free-kick from distance.
Youssef En-Nesyri steered in the fourth in the 77th minute from a Hakimi pass and Ayoub Oufkir completed the scoring from close range in the final minute.
Earlier in Group A on Friday Gabon beat Lesotho to move on to six points thanks to two second-half goals from Denis Bouanga.
The LA FC forward smashed the right-hand upright with a penalty but broke the deadlock with a header a minute later and then scored from 12 yards when the Panthers were awarded a second spot kick.
Tunisia downed as McCarthy frustrates Bafana
Tunisia have appeared at a record 17 consecutive Afcons but are winless and bottom of Group H - another section with just one qualifying place on offer - after defeat by their North African neighbours Libya.
The Carthage Eagles could complain about refereeing decisions going against them in Sfax, with Ali Maaloul penalised for a shirt pull on Muad Eisay just before half-time and Ali Youssef converting the resulting spot-kick.
Tunisia had a goal ruled out following a marginal offside call in the second half and three minutes later a low shot from Hamdou El Houni made it 2-0 to the Mediterranean Knights.
Libya, who last played at an Afcon in 2012, climb to second in the table and go level on points with Uganda.
South Africa are a point clear of Guinea at the top of Group D after a 2-2 draw against Benni McCarthy's Kenya in Johannesburg.
Amos Wanjala's own goal gifted the hosts an early lead before Michael Olunga levelled from the penalty spot just before half-time.
Relebohile Mofokeng restored Bafana Bafana's advantage with 13 minutes remaining, but Kenya claimed a point when Ryan Ogam's low shot from 20 yards crept inside the left-hand upright in the 90th minute.
Elsewhere, Burkina Faso joined Benin on seven points at the top of Group F thanks to Elohim Kabore's 94th-minute winner against Mauritania in Ouagadougou.
Ethiopia upset Mozambique
Mali extended their winning start to go top of Group K after Mamadou Camara completed a 3-2 comeback win at home against Rwanda, who had led twice in Bamako.
Rwanda had won their first two fixtures and are three points ahead of Cape Verde, who registered their first points with a 4-2 victory over Liberia in Praia.
Ethiopia registered their first win to upset Mozambique in Maputo, with Kenean Markneh scoring the only goal in the 87th minute after Mambas keeper Ernan spilled a low shot from Carlos Damtew.
The East Africans move on to three points but remain bottom of Group J, behind Sudan on head-to-head record, while Mozambique are on four points and three behind leaders Senegal.
Zambia moved level on four points with Group I leaders Algeria after a 1-1 draw at home to Burundi. The North Africans have the chance to open up a three-point gap when they host Togo on Saturday.
In Group G, Comoros were held to a goalless draw by Congo-Brazzaville in Moroni. Cameroon lead the section on seven points, with Comoros on four, Namibia on three and the Congolese bottom on two points.

Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.
Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
Apple’s job listing describes an AI agent that can browse the web, work across apps, and call services.
An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhonemaker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks. Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same.
Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities, as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions.
“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing says. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.”
With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.

Ecuador’s football federation (FEF) has banned player Jhon Perlaza for eight years after he threw a stone that struck an assistant referee during a third-tier match last month.
The incident occurred during the 96th minute of the match between Perlaza’s side Club Ciudad de Yantzaza and Club Rio Aguarico FC on October 17. The match was abandoned after assistant referee Lenin Giovanni Ojeda Nunez was struck.
“The assistant referee suffered serious injuries that required surgery and a 60-day recovery period,” the FEF said in a statement on Wednesday.

The 3pm football blackout: outdated or still relevant in 2026?
- Published
After 60 years, is time finally running out on the 3pm blackout in football?
With pretty much every available television slot now exhausted, next year the Premier League and the EFL are set to hold serious discussions about its future.
There are concerns, especially within non-league football, that removing the blackout could have detrimental effects on attendances and finances.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham agrees, urging caution and suggesting the health of the football pyramid should come first.
But many Premier League fans feel they are short-changed, locked out of many of their team's fixtures just because they live in this country.
Go anywhere else in the world, and every single match is available live.
With streaming so prevalent, to some the blackout feels archaic.
Yet it is a complex situation, and many feel the depth of English football's pyramid is like nowhere else.
BBC Sport looks at the history of the blackout, why it is unique to British football and the arguments for and against keeping it.
How Match of the Day ushered in the blackout
It is the start of the 1964-65 season and the BBC launches a programme called Match of the Day.
Highlights of one match would be broadcast on BBC Two, a channel which at the time was only available in London.
Yet some clubs were concerned. Would fans still turn up to games?
Burnley chairman Bob Lord was the first owner to refuse to allow the cameras into Turf Moor. At the end of the season, several other clubs tried to block the renewal of the deal.
A compromise was reached and the BBC agreed not to reveal the televised Saturday match until all games had ended.
Shortly afterwards came the blackout for live matches.
Fast forward 20 years to 1987. With dwindling attendances across the European domestic leagues, partly influenced by crowd trouble, Uefa took up England's idea.
Article 48 was added to the Uefa Statutes.
Each country could designate a two-and-a-half-hour "transmission-free period", as long as at least 50% of matches in the top two leagues were taking place.
This was "designed to ensure that spectators are not deterred from attending local football matches of any kind and/or participating in matches at amateur and/or youth level".
Why does no other country have the blackout?
Today, the situation has gone full circle. The only leagues that apply Article 48 are England, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
The reason for this is simpler than you might imagine.
No other major country qualifies for the blackout - because no other major country has a kick-off time that runs from the top flight and through the divisions.
It is a tradition that is unique to football in the United Kingdom.
Let's take Germany, often held up as an example of a country with excellent attendances despite not having a blackout.
This misses a key point. The Bundesliga has its own kick-off slot, 3:30pm on a Saturday, and no other division plays at the same time. The 2. Bundesliga, for instance, has a standard Saturday kick-off time of 1:30pm.
Could you imagine English football replicating this?
The other top leagues are the same.
In Spain, it is rare for either of the top two divisions to have games that kick off simultaneously. Each match has its own slot, and is broadcast live.
In Italy, Serie A plays on a Sunday afternoon, and Serie B on a Saturday.
In France, Ligue 1 has Saturday night as its main time slot, Ligue 2 plays largely on a Friday night, and Ligue 3 on a Saturday lunchtime.
So there is no blackout, because the football calendar works in a completely different way.
Why the blackout is now under threat
The next television rights cycle presents a unique opportunity.
The deals for the Premier League, EFL and Scottish Premiership are all up for renewal in 2029-30.
There is the chance for all the top stakeholders to come together and agree to end the blackout.
Last year, Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said there were no plans to remove the blackout.
But this summer there was a clear shift in emphasis, with Masters admitting there would be talks with the EFL ahead of the renewal of TV rights.
Scottish football has gone first, with broadcasters invited to bid to show all matches live - and is open to those shown on a Saturday afternoon.
It will be another year before we discover what the Premier League and the EFL - which seriously considered ending the blackout three years ago - are prepared to offer to broadcasters.
So, why would the leagues need to offer up the Saturday 3pm slot to broadcasters? After all, the latest domestic Premier League deal was worth a record £6.7bn - an increase of 4%.
However, to achieve that figure, the Premier League had to make an additional 70 games available. In real terms, it means each live Premier League game is worth less than it was before.
Now every single game not shown at 3pm on a Saturday - and there are only 110 left - is on TV.
Could the Premier League need to offer more matches for the rights to keep their overall value?
If so there are two options: try to find more TV slots, or show games at 3pm on a Saturday.
Could the Women's Super League benefit too? It looked into playing a 3pm on a Saturday but could not find a way around the blackout.
Most of the competition's games are shown live already, with a greater concern being stadium availability and consistency of kick-off times.
'Football doesn't begin and end with the Premier League'
There is a danger that the issue of the 3pm blackout is viewed only through the lens of Premier League and EFL television rights.
But it goes much deeper than that.
Tom Greatrex, the chair of the Football Supporters' Association, says there are attendances in non-league football that some top flights in Europe "would look at jealously".
"We have one of the strongest football pyramids in the world, with excellent matchday attendances deep into the non-league game," Greatrex said.
"The prime minister is right to point out the value of the blackout to clubs further down the pyramid, and to urge caution over the impact rushed change could have on the overall health of the game."
BBC Sport understands that senior executives at the National League, which has a long-term global streaming deal with DAZN, are steadfastly against the blackout ending.
It has serious reservations, shared by the vast majority of its 72 clubs, that attendances would be impacted.
Included in this is transient attendance from season ticket holders of league clubs, who attend non-league football when their team is away from home, boosting receipts considerably.
The fear is this could be lost if all league games are streamed at 3pm.
Nicky Bloom, the chair of Northern Premier League side FC United of Manchester, worries that the issue is only viewed through the lens of top-flight football.
"Football doesn't begin and end with the Premier League," Bloom told BBC Sport.
"Every Saturday, thousands of people turn out to support their local clubs.
"For many of those clubs, the income from people coming through the turnstiles, buying a pint or something to eat is what keeps them alive.
"The 3pm blackout isn't about nostalgia. It's about protecting something that matters."
Bloom added that clubs in non-league football are huge community assets, and losing them would have an impact "well beyond 90 minutes on a Saturday".
Streaming could still be an opportunity for some clubs
Some clubs are more open-minded about what ending the blackout could mean for non-league football.
Others have changed the way they operate to get around it.
North West Counties League Premier Division side FC Isle of Man have stopped playing at 3:00pm on a Saturday so they can stream all their games live.
Brian Shotton, a director at eighth-tier Ashington FC, told BBC Sport that he would not be automatically against removing the blackout.
"I would still have concerns, because every person through the gate makes a difference," Shotton said.
"I don't think we should just assume it would damage non-league football, but equally you need to know what it could mean for clubs like ours."
Ashington, which have attendances of about 400, see gates rise by up to 25% when Newcastle are not at home - but they already see the impact of illegal streaming of the Magpies' games.
For the official broadcasters like Sky Sports, these supporters are seen as lost revenue.
There is an argument that the blackout drives piracy. Just how many of those particular fans would pay for a legal subscription is open to debate.
Added to that, there are now many weekends when when fewer than 50% of matches in the top two divisions are played at 3pm on a Saturday anyway.
For instance, on 28 November there are just two in the Premier League, and seven in the Championship.
Other non-league clubs, like Dorking Wanders and Hashtag United, have spoken of the opportunities ending the blackout could bring, such as more income streams and fewer inconvenient kick-off times.
But this, for now, seems to be a minority view. The concerns for the health of the entire pyramid, on attendances and finances, are real.
Once the blackout is gone, it is unlikely to come back.

Pochettino's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator
- Published
Manchester United fans have been given a unique and unexpected insight into Mauricio Pochettino's first training session after footage was captured by a drone flown next to the club's Carrington training ground.
Twelve minutes of the session was filmed by a drone operator and uploaded onto YouTube.
Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, are clearly visible, with the session filmed from a variety of angles and distances.
"For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it," said the drone operator.
"The drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn't fly over anyone or even near anyone so was a perfectly legal flight going by the CAA rules that regulates drone usage.
"The drone is correctly labelled, and I hold all the relevant licences, public liability and insurance required. As for leaking team news/tactics, it was half an hour into the managers first training session, there are many media there so certainly won't be the only footage of training released."
The session was also filmed by United's own media channel, who regularly film club training sessions.
Civil Aviation Authority guidelines include the following warning: "If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you're likely to be breaking data protection laws."
Manchester United have declined to comment.
Did we learn anything?
There were 10 outfield players working with Pochettino, although it seems unlikely it will be the starting line-up for Sunday's trip to Liverpool.
While Harry Maguire, Kobbie Mainoo, Amad Diallo, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo are regular starters, Ayden Heaven and Andrey Santos have had less involvement, and neither Joshua Zirkzee nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season. Jaume Camacho 17, who is yet to feature at senior level, was also with the group.
On an adjoining pitch, skipper Bruno Fernandes is shown in one group playing the 'rondos' game, where two players are in the middle trying to intercept the passes of the five players in a circle on the outside. Youngster Shea Lacey and last season's FA Youth Cup-winning skipper Dan Armer are also involved, along with England youth international Bendito Mantato.
Next to that is another group which includes more experienced players in Lisandro Martinez, Matthijs de Ligt, Youri Tielemans, Mason Mount, Leny Yoro, Noussair Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot.
The identical twins Jack and Tyler Fletcher are split between the two groups, with Pochettino's assistant Jesus Perez across both.
Not all the players were identifiable and United confirmed defender Patrick Dorgu was involved.

Rockstar Games has released Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6), a title expected to generate massive revenue. However, while the launch has sparked excitement among gamers, concerns about job security continue to trouble some of the developers behind the blockbuster game.
In an article for The Guardian, Nestor Uriarte, an animation programmer at Rockstar Games, highlighted the uncertainty surrounding employment in the gaming industry. He pointed out that contributing to one of the world's biggest video game releases does not necessarily protect developers from potential job cuts, particularly as studios continue to reduce their workforces.
"After the big day, we have had no indication that layoffs are coming, but It’s hard not to worry about what the future holds," Uriarte wrote.
Quick answers to key questions
Rockstar animation programmer Nestor Uriarte said that working on a major game does not guarantee job security. He pointed to widespread job cuts across the gaming industry in recent years.
Uriarte said employees had received no indication that layoffs were coming. He added that uncertainty across the gaming industry still made it hard not to worry about the future.
Rockstar North employees are voting on whether to secure union recognition. If approved, the union could represent more than 1,600 employees.
Uriarte said AI is changing how gaming studios work and raising questions about the future relevance of developers’ skills.
He noted that gaming companies worldwide have eliminated thousands of positions in recent years, with an estimated 24,000 jobs disappearing over the past two years. The scale of these cuts, he said, has left even employees working on highly successful projects concerned about their professional future.
"It says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off," he added.
The growing concerns over job security have also prompted employees at Rockstar North to consider collective action. Workers are voting on whether to secure union recognition, with the process expected to conclude on November 26.
If approved, the move could lead to the formation of one of the UK's largest recognised unions representing video game developers, with more than 1,600 employees.
Uriarte believes that organising collectively is crucial for workers to protect their rights and challenge decisions around redundancies. He argued that individual employees have limited influence when companies announce large-scale job cuts.
"The truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised," he wrote.
Rockstar has previously faced criticism over its workplace practices, particularly allegations of 'crunch culture'. The term refers to extended working hours and additional pressure on employees to complete games within strict deadlines.
Apart from mass redundancies and concerns about workplace conditions, the growing adoption of artificial intelligence is emerging as another challenge for video game developers.
Uriarte cautioned that the rapid development of AI is changing working practices at gaming studios and creating uncertainty about the long-term relevance of skills that developers have spent years developing.
"The rapid emergence of AI is transforming how studios work and raising fundamental questions about the future of our industry," he wrote.
Recent developments across the gaming sector have added to these concerns. Earlier this year, Electronic Arts (EA) reportedly cut several jobs following the release of Battlefield 6. Variety also reported last month that the company was planning to reduce around 3% of its global workforce as part of a wider business restructuring.
Data from Gaming Layoffs, a website that monitors job losses across the gaming industry, shows that 12,791 employees across 177 companies have lost their jobs this year. The website also reported that 40 gaming studios have shut down during the same period.
Fortis Games is among the latest companies to close its operations. According to GamesBeat, the shutdown this month resulted in around 440 employees losing their jobs.

Body of Melbourne Cup horse found dumped in Sydney skip
- Published
The body of a top Australian racehorse has been found dumped in a skip bin, hours after its trainer revealed the horse had died from colic.
In a video shared online, only two weeks after So You Are raced in the Melbourne Cup, the deceased racehorse appeared to be lying in a large metal bin surrounded by other household rubbish in Sydney.
Trainer Bjorn Baker - who shared news of the horse's death from colic on Monday - has said he was "deeply distressed" by the video, and called for a "full explanation".
Racing NSW, the state's industry regulator, said a preliminary investigation had found the horse was later properly buried, but called the way its body was handled "completely unacceptable".
"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said in an statement shared online.
"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."
So You Are had a successful run during spring, winning four times at respected races including the Rosehill, Randwick and the Bendigo Cup.
The five-year-old recently finished eight in the Melbourne Cup, which was won by Point of Law, a horse previously owned by King Charles III.
The racehorse had received urgent treatment after a severe bout of colic, but was "unfortunately unable to be saved" and was euthanised under anaesthesia, Racing NSW said.
"So You Are was then transported for burial, and was being held temporarily, awaiting burial, when these images were recorded," it said.
Burial at a licensed landfill is typically recommended for animals that die from euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process, according to the racing body.
"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner," it added.
In a statement, REC Equine Specialists - the hospital where the horse died - said a contractor had been hired to dispose of the So You Are's body.
"We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that."
"We have spoken with So You Are's owners and trainer to apologise personally."
The company added that it had stopped using the contractor, and was reviewing its processes to make sure they known exactly how horses are handled after leaving their hospital.
"No owner should have to go through what So You Are's connections have experienced this week. We will make sure it does not happen again."
Jowett's video appeared to be filmed at a public rubbish drop-off and land facility called Lucas Heights, in Sutherland Shire, south of Sydney.
The waste management company that runs the landfill site said So You Are's body had been moved to a skip bin in a permitted area, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported.
