Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.
The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.
It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.
The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.
The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.
The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecuties individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.
The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.
The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.
Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.
Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians”.
In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”
In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”
He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.
Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.
In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically.”
It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.
The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of the Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.
The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.
Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.
On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater US willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

How Premier League's big six keep getting richer
- Published
Ten games into the Premier League season, the top five places are dominated by big six clubs.
Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, have muscled their way in.
In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.
The six biggest clubs - Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal, Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.
And the gap is growing. Every season.
BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the big six have exploded, examines new trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.
Big six get richer and the gap grows
Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.
In England, Liverpool, Arsenal and United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.
Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham.
This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues.
Let's look at how the gap has grown.
We will use Everton, the only club not in the big six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.
This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.
In 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the big-six average and Everton was £120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to £442m.
So what has driven this huge escalation?
In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.
Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.
"The big football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said.
"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices."
Only 10% of Everton's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.
It means Everton, and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.
For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.
But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.
Champions League widens the gulf
It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.
This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.
But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.
When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.
This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or £713m, for the historically most successful clubs.
At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned £37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool £35.5m and Chelsea £33.3m. Newcastle received only £13.6m.
The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.
Their value pillar is projected to be worth £25m this season. But that will still be less than the big six clubs in the competition.
The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.
Stamford Bridge - Chelsea's big problem
Take a look at the financial trend of the big six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.
In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the big six.
Not just by a small amount. They were £74m behind Tottenham, and £200m below Liverpool and City.
Chelsea's problem is simple - seats.
Stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the big six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.
Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of £80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal.
Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their big six rivals, Chelsea's total matchday revenues are dwarfed.
"Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire said. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017.
"As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast."
Matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea, rising only £16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by £69m and Spurs, thanks to their new ground, by £85m.
"Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire said. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs.
"Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial."
Chelsea's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.
But there are signs that, financially at least, the big six could become the big five.
How new rules allow big six to spend even more
You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).
PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.
That has changed this season with squad-cost ratio (SCR).
There is a key difference with SCR, in that it allows a club to spend the money they generate on players. PSR limited losses so was more restrictive.
"This does make it a little easier for the likes of Villa and Newcastle to spend money," Maguire said. "But it is still heavily weighted in favour of the big six.
"SCR is different to PSR rather than better. For some people, change is advantageous. For others, it isn't."
So what does this mean?
The big six generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the other clubs. So they can spend hundreds of millions of pounds more on their squads.
This makes the big six even more powerful in the transfer market.
"Look at the clubs who voted against SCR - Brighton, Brentford, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Fulham and Leeds," Maguire said.
"It's very noticeable that those clubs have traditionally been very good at player sales, while they have tended to have lower matchday and commercial revenues."
Most of the big six - the outlier being Chelsea - are not remotely close to the Premier League's 85% SCR limit.
Surely this will inflate the transfer market?
If you give clubs more money to spend on transfers, the likelihood is they will do just that. And the numbers back that up.
Look at this summer.
Premier League clubs spent £3.5bn - not only a highest total for a summer window, but it almost smashed the record for a whole season, the £3.53bn set in 2025-26.
The annual accounting cost of previous transfers, or amortisation, has been rising year on year.
"Over the course of the last decade, transfer amortisation has more than doubled and close to tripled," Maguire said.
"Which means that on average, clubs in the Premier League are now spending, or now have a cost which goes into their SCR calculations of just under £100m."
Uefa fears that SCR will make matters worse, and have an inflationary impact across Europe.
And you can see why it is concerned.
In the summer 13 Premier League clubs broke their transfer record.
Brentford, Brighton, Palace, Leeds and Nottingham Forest all spent more than £40m on a player - unthinkable until recently.
Does this financial disparity really matter?
So we have learned that the big six have more money than ever, and the gap is so huge it is impossible for any other club to compete with them, financially at least.
And this is an important point: other than Villa and Newcastle, the other clubs are not trying to compete with the big six.
Clubs like Brentford and Brighton have shown that smart models are just as effective as fat wallets.
They sign the potential stars of the future, nurture them and then sell them to the big six.
Football's ecosystem recycles the big-six money through the transfer market.
But it is a precarious business for these other clubs.
"The smaller clubs have to get it right on a more regular basis than the bigger clubs," Maguire said.
"The big six can afford to make signings which are £60m and £70m, who turn out to be relative flops, and still have those players on high wages for several years."
And this is perhaps the key point about the vast finances of the big six.
The commercial power of the big six does not guarantee success. After all, United sit in the relegation zone.
Yet Mauricio Pochettino, their new manager, may well get the chance to revamp the squad despite the club spending £945m on players in the past five years.
The richest clubs can try to spend their way out of trouble. Again and again.
But the rest of the league are only a couple of bad transfer windows from catastrophe.
And that is the real gap between the big six and the rest.

The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.
The Paris-based agency found that the breakneck pace of the industry’s growth means that within four years AI datacentres will consume an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of electricity every year, or more than the annual electricity consumption of Great Britain.
Its influential annual report warned that the world’s energy future was less certain after the impact of the Middle East war, which it has described as the greatest energy market disruption in history.
“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said the IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol.
Instead, it will be reshaped by the policy decisions governments make after the crisis to meet the increasing demand for energy to power a growing global population, the rising need for air-conditioning and a booming AI economy, the IEA said.
Datacentre developers have emerged as the world’s biggest corporate buyers of renewable energy to help fuel their servers which have a connection to local power grids. Despite this, the report showed that the appetite for fossil fuels is expected to grow even faster, particularly in the US and China.
By the end of the decade, around half of the electricity needed to power China’s AI datacentres will come from coal power plants, according to the IEA. The rest will come from renewable energy, with smaller amounts from nuclear reactors and very little from gas plants.
In contrast, the US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. There were plans for about 180GW of new gas-fired power plants linked to US datacentres in August this year, the agency said. That is almost as much new gas capacity as the total now installed across the European Union.
As a result of the growth in fossil fuel generation for datacentres, emissions associated with this sector were on track to rise by 70% by 2030, the IEA said.
The appetite for gas power among US datacentre developers is more than 16 times higher than in Canada, where the IEA identified plans for 11GW of gas generation to power their servers. In the rest of the world, AI developers have put forward plans for new gas plants with a combined capacity of just 4GW, the agency said.
This is because renewable energy is expected to play a greater role in supplying datacentres outside the US and China. In the EU, the IEA expects datacentres to rely on renewables for about 70% of their electricity by 2030 – followed by nuclear power, gas generation, and a very small amount of coal power.
The agency based its forecasts for the notoriously opaque industry on data showing the annual global shipment of AI servers, which have climbed eighteen-fold since 2020. It also used space-based imagery to track the buildout of 93 large “AI factories” around the world.
Its analysis suggests that the world’s datacentre capacity has climbed tenfold in the last 24 months to 17GW. By the time the AI factories were completed, their combined capacity was likely to be about 50GW, the IEA said.
The world’s existing stock of datacentres, including those with AI-optimised servers, now stands at 120GW, with 80% of this capacity in China, the US and the EU. A further 120GW will be built by the end of the decade under the IEA scenario often considered its central base case, of which three-quarters will be AI datacentres.

After Nepal's epic flood, they're restoring their community ... and their lives
"I thought I wouldn't survive," says Januka Dhital.
Just minutes before that terrible thought, Dhital was busy preparing snacks. She ran a catering service out of her house in Uttargaya, Nepal, and was getting ready for an event later that day. Her work was interrupted by a man on a scooter, warning of a flood. She stepped outside to look.
"When I turned around, I saw darkness, dust and what looked like the entire hillside coming down," she says.
She grabbed her young son and hopped onto the back of the man's scooter. They raced to higher ground, eventually reaching safety. But she didn't know if her husband and daughter were safe, since they were at work and school when the waters came.
"It felt unbelievable"
After hours of waiting and searching, they were all reunited. Her husband was naked, covered in blood and badly injured, she says, but alive.
"It felt unbelievable that our family had survived," says Dhital. But the wall of water and mud that descended from the mountains had obliterated their home, along with thousands of others. "We have lost everything. We have nothing now."
Dhital and her family are among the 100,000-some people whose lives have been upended by the devastating floods sparked by glacial melt, a phenomenon made worse by climate change. At least 1,500 have died, and more than 5,000 are still missing. Thousands are still living in temporary shelters or tents.
The flood damaged or destroyed seven health facilities, 23 schools, 10,000 toilets and 64 water systems, according to the United Nations. And there are early signs that malnutrition is spiking as winter approaches.
"The magnitude of devastation is unimaginable," says Shyam Pathak, a chief of health at UNICEF. The din of helicopters circling the wreckage looking for survivors has faded, he says. International attention and aid has fallen too, sources on the ground say, as the response turns to the arduous, but intimate work of helping these communities stitch their lives back together.
This disaster is somewhat unique, Pathak says, in that many of those doing the work are trying to rebuild their own lives at the same time. Dhital is one of them.
"I felt like I was losing my mind"
In the immediate aftermath of the flood, Dhital and her family moved into a holding center, one of a couple dozen that housed the displaced. They stayed there for about a month before moving into a relative's house. Those days were not easy.
"For almost a month, I felt like I was losing my mind," she says. "More than money, I am in great need of work."
She found that work through Helen Keller Intl, a nonprofit that's helping the response. After a short training program that included mental health support, she began helping her community rebuild. There's a lot to do.
"I go out into the community, we work with postpartum mothers, pregnant women and children under five," says Dhital. "This is the only thing keeping me going right now."
One of her jobs is screening for malnutrition among survivors.
Preliminary data suggest a notable increase. In Naukunda Gaunpalika, for instance, moderate acute malnutrition — a condition that can slow growth, weaken the immune system and become life threatening without treatment — appears to have gone up from 0.8% in June of this year to 8.7% in October, says Pooja Pandey Rana, who directs Hellen Keller's work in Nepal. These are likely conservative estimates too, she says.
"It's a big jump," says Pandey Rana, and likely driven by fallout from the flood.
In addition to losing homes, many families lost the gardens or local farms they relied on for nutritious food. "As a result, they have to depend on dried and packaged foods, such as instant noodles and biscuits," says Dhital. Poor sanitation and lack of clean drinking water is an issue too, she says. And many have lost their livelihoods, so they don't have money to pay for food.
Workers like Dhital are handing out supplies and cash to families in need. In some regions, that's a challenge.
Many of the communities along the flood's path were connected by bridges. More than 100 of them are now destroyed, according to the U.N. And for many living higher up the slopes, mountain roads were a lifeline that have now been severed.
"There still are places, especially in the upper north part of the impacted areas, which have been cut off by the flood," says Ayush Joshi, who works for the non-profit Save the Children in Nepal. "There is still a challenge to deliver food and life saving support to these areas."
"Our hearts cannot bear to see the destruction"
Pushmaya Tamang is a community aid worker trying to reach those areas. Often, she must cross the makeshift bridges hastily constructed to make up for the damage.
"The bridge shakes, making it difficult for elderly people to cross," she says. "It becomes dangerous when people try to cross the bridge from both directions at the same time. It almost overturns, making it extremely frightening."
Such damaged infrastructure is a start reminder of what's been lost, she says. Tamang is from a village in Nuwakot that's essentially gone after the floods.
"Our hearts cannot bear to see the destruction," she says. "The village that was once full of colorful lights and life has now become gloomy and dark."
Tamang's heart is heavy with grief over the loss of her younger sister, too. Many of the families she helps in her work with Helen Keller are also grieving unimaginable loss, she says.
"When we visit other affected families, we do not even know what to say or how to talk to them," she says. "We do not have the words to comfort or console them."
Many survivors need significant mental health support, says Pathak of UNICEF, which is teaming up with other aid organizations to mobilize health workers who can provide counseling. Like Dhital and Tamang, many of them are trying to help rebuild their communities while dealing with their own trauma.
"A hallmark of this response is that the health workers, despite being the victim themselves, are back to the work," says Pathak. "This has helped a lot."
"Everything has been wiped out"
Winter poses distinct challenges for survivors.
Colder temperatures are threatening those who still live in temporary shelters or flimsy tents. "Winter in these areas is very harsh," says Joshi. "Exposure to cold, overcrowded living, poor ventilation in the tent, damp bedding and inadequate clothing can also increase health risk."
Responders are winterizing tents and getting families into safer shelters, says Joshi, in addition to providing food and medical care.
In the longer term, there's the question of rebuilding what was leveled.
"We still haven't really seen [plans] on where to rebuild, how many homes are needed, how do we fix the water systems, how do you rebuild the schools?" says Pandey Rana of Helen Keller. "Like everything has been wiped out."
Preliminary estimates put the cost of rebuilding at roughly $5 billion, a steep figure for the small nation. The U.N. Climate Fund, aimed at helping countries harmed by climate change, approved $20 million for recovery. Domestic and international donors have contributed over $100 million in additional funds, but it's still far short of what's needed.
For now, aid organizations are focused on the immediate needs of survivors. Tamang says the daily work helps keep her going amid so much loss.
"What else can I do," she says. "Life goes on, and we have to accept what nature has brought upon us."

A Chinese scientist who concealed the death of a six-year-old girl in a gene-editing trial has been sacked following a government probe, according to state media.
The girl died last year after receiving experimental gene therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition -- which was not disclosed in published research, an investigation found in July.
Neuroscientist Zilong Qiu, the trial's lead researcher, had made no mention of the girl in a paper published in the prestigious journal Nature, according to the joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch.
Qiu was dismissed as deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institute affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, state broadcaster CCTV said Friday, citing a statement from Shanghai authorities.
The reported statement included only Qiu's surname, but referenced the Nature study published on February 18.
Qiu was given a five-year suspension from participating in scientific projects and recorded in a database for "serious breaches of research integrity", the report said.
Another researcher on Qiu's team was sacked and handed a five-year suspension, while several others with ties to the hospital where the trial took place were also punished.
The child who died had a rare neurodevelopmental condition called Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, according to the report.
The hospital's ethics committee had approved a gene-editing trial to treat the disorder in January 2025, the report said.
The committee terminated the study after the girl died in March due to complications from gene therapy.
Shanghai authorities found that Qiu's team failed to properly inform the hospital of possible safety issues from earlier tests on primates, according to the report.
AFP has reached out to Qiu for comment.
The July investigation by Science and Retraction Watch found that the girl's parents, who paid more than $800,000 to fund the experiment, were not adequately informed about the risks.
The scandal is a blow to China's ambitions to rival the United States as a biotech power following the 2018 scandal around He Jiankui, a biophysicist who secretly produced gene-edited babies.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday used the launch of popular video game Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) to highlight India's development journey, comparing economic, infrastructure and technology indicators from around 2013-14 with the latest figures. From India's inclusion among the "Fragile Five" economies to its current position as the world's fastest-growing major economy, from 2.82 GW of solar capacity to 175 GW, and from 20% railway electrification to 99.6%, Modi used the gap between the releases of GTA 5 and GTA 6 to present what he described as India's progress over the past 12 years. In an apparent attempt to connect with younger audiences, the prime minister drew parallels between GTA 5, released in 2013, and GTA 6, launched on Thursday. The comparison was shared through a social media post featuring illustrations of an aeroplane, train, rocket, solar station, mobile phone, road network and ship, among other things. "Between GTA 5 and 6, here is how India upgraded," he said. The prime minister said India, which was earlier described as part of the "Fragile Five", is now the world's fastest-growing major economy. He also highlighted a decline in poverty, saying it stood at 27% earlier, while extreme poverty has now fallen to 2.6%. On sanitation, Modi referred to the Swachh Bharat campaign and the construction of toilets, particularly for women. He said sanitation coverage had increased from 39% to 100%. Renewable energy and infrastructure were among the other areas highlighted in the comparison. Modi said India's solar power capacity had increased from 2.82 GW to 175 GW over the period. He also pointed to the growth of the country's space sector, saying India now has 440 space startups. The earlier-period graphic displayed the words "Sorry! no result found" in the corresponding section. Railway electrification, according to the prime minister, has increased from 20% to 99.6%. The prime minister also highlighted the reduction in mobile internet costs. He said the price of 1 GB of data had fallen from ₹308 during the 3G era to ₹7.51. On defence, Modi said India had moved from being a major importer of defence equipment to exporting arms and defence equipment to more than 80 countries. On internal security, the prime minister said the number of districts affected by Naxalism had also declined. "Then, 182 districts (were) Naxal affected, now zero district," he said. At the American Heart Association’s recent annual meeting, the overarching theme coming from the center stage, bathed in Pantone red, was one of high-profile neutral findings.
As I listened to the results of the STREAM trial — which found that older adults without a history of heart attacks or strokes who stopped taking statins didn’t have significantly different outcomes from those who continued taking them — I jotted down that the study continued the theme.
But as the Kaplan-Meier curves were cast onto the screen, something felt off: The curves diverged, rather than stayed together. Theoretically, this scenario can happen in noninferiority studies, where researchers are testing whether an intervention offers similar outcomes compared with a standard. De-prescribing statins in this group, by the expectations set by researchers at the beginning of STREAM, was technically noninferior, but nevertheless, still inferior. The patients randomized to stop taking their statin did worse compared with those who continued. Even the trial’s data safety monitoring board suggested that patients who have stopped their statins should talk to their doctors about resuming their medications.

The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989.
Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones.
India’s meteorological department has released an alert for a depression located in the Bay of Bengal with the potential to develop into a cyclone. We know each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start. But I think they'll come out of this," Trump told Putin, according to Reuters. "He's my friend," he added. The meeting comes ahead of Trump's talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and a proposed trilateral meeting involving the three leaders. Quick answers to key questions It is a proposed meeting between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. It is scheduled to take place in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Possible topics include nuclear arms control, the Iran war, global trade and the Russia-Ukraine war. Supply-chain security, economic cooperation, artificial intelligence and technology governance could also be discussed; no official agenda has been announced. The meeting brings together the leaders of three major powers and could open discussion on issues affecting global security and stability. It is also described as a historic first trilateral meeting between the leaders of the US, China and Russia. The US does not expect the meeting to produce an agreement, though Trump is expected to raise nuclear weapons reduction and proliferation. China has been reluctant to join formal arms-control negotiations. It is uncertain. White House officials said Trump was not expected to raise the war, but Trump suggested he might bring it up; no official agenda has been announced. Earlier, Trump had described the proposed trilateral meeting as an opportunity to explore areas of cooperation among the three major powers. "And here in China, I look forward to a historic trilateral meeting with President Xi and President Putin later today to discuss more opportunities for all three. So, we look forward to that, very much forward to that," he had said earlier. While no official announcement has been made on the agenda of the proposed trilateral meeting, discussions are expected to cover several issues, including nuclear disarmament, the Iran war, global trade and the Russia-Ukraine war. The leaders could also discuss supply chain security, economic cooperation, artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure and technology governance. "He [Trump] will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, told reporters during a briefing call, according to CNBC. White House officials have also said that Trump is not expected to raise the Russia-Ukraine war during the meeting. However, Trump has suggested that he could bring up the issue, Reuters reported. Speaking to Fox News, Trump said he would not seek help from Russia and China to bring the Iran conflict to an end. Earlier on Wednesday, Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomed Trump at Shenzhen airport, the first time he has personally received a visiting leader at the airport since becoming president. The two leaders also shared a brief hug. The meeting in China also comes days after a major controversy erupted in US after an alleged Chinese spy "honey trapped" former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The fall out of the affair resulted in Huang's exit from the company and tighter US control over the export of advance American-made semiconductors. The last chimpanzees owned by the U.S. government and still living in a laboratory will be moved to a sanctuary next year, a move that comes more than a decade after the National Institutes of Health agreed to end its funding for biomedical research on chimpanzees.
Beginning early next year, nearly three dozen chimpanzees housed at the Keeling Center for Comparative Medicine and Research in Bastrop, Texas, will be transferred a 200-acre federal sanctuary operated by Chimp Haven, in Keithville, La., which is the only such sanctuary in the U.S.
“Completing their transfers will fulfill NIH’s commitment, announced in November 2015, to retire all NIH-owned chimpanzees to sanctuary,” said NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya in a statement.

A federal judge said that he will issue a ruling “as soon as I can” as to whether the Kennedy Center can proceed with its plan to close the arts complex for two years for renovations, amid fears that President Donald Trump ultimately will move to demolish the 55-year-old arts complex.
U.S. District Court Judge Christopher Cooper issued an injunction earlier this year that barred the center from closing unless its board conducted a more thorough analysis of its impacts on programming and other operations. The judge also ordered that Trump’s name be removed from the complex, with a tarp now covering the front facade after crews removed the lettering to comply with the order.
The Justice Department, representing the center, is seeking to lift the injunction, arguing that the board vote in August and September to close the center sufficiently examined all of the options, citing a report from Delta Consulting Group. The report concluded that a two-year closure would be much less expensive than keeping the center open during construction, a process that would take four years.
Watch on Deadline
“The court contemplated the exact course of action the center took here,” William Jankowski, attorney for the DOJ, told the judge.
An attorney for Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-OH), an ex officio board member of the center who is challenging the board’s actions, argued that, despite the third-party Delta analysis, the board still has not considered the impact of a closure on such things as fundraising and programming.
Nathaniel Zelinsky, Beatty’s attorney, said that the board “keeps rubber stamping the same decision.” Trump, who is the board chairman, announced the closure plan in February, but Beatty’s legal team has claimed that the decision was not motivated by the renovation, but to mask the embarrassment of a drop in revenue after Trump’s name was added to the center’s official moniker.
Zelinsky also pointed to another analysis conducted by real estate firm, which showed that a four-year renovation plan that kept the center open would be far less costly than the Delta analysis. He said that the board never were given the JLL report before their August vote, but Jankowski told the judge that it still led to the some conclusion in recommending a two-year closure.
The center itself has had scant major programming since July, and the sprawling main building has been off limits to the public since September. The center says that the closure is temporary due to safety concerns, after a portion of the indoor ceiling plaster collapsed following rainstorms, as well as concerns of deterioration of supports for exterior soffit panels.
Meanwhile, the center is going ahead with its annual Kennedy Center Honors, but in an alternate venue: The Capitol One Arena. The event is scheduled to take place on Dec. 7 and air on CBS on Dec. 27. The center also plans to proceed with the Mark Twain Prize, an annual ceremony honoring comedians and humorists, next year, Jankowski told the judge.
Trump has stirred concerns over demolition of the center after he raised the prospect in social media posts. He also was photographed on Air Force One in September reviewing a poster board that featured the lettering, “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED.”
While the DOJ attorney argued that Trump’s remarks are not relevant to whether to lift the injunction, the judge still expressed concerns. In September, he ordered that he be given at least a 30-day notice before any such drastic changes be made to the center.
Norm Eisen, who also is representing Beatty, told reporters that they were trying to prevent a scenario like what happened to the White House East Wing, which Trump ordered demolished last year to make room for a new ballroom, and the East Potomac Golf Course, where the National Park Service abruptly cut down hundreds of trees on a site that the president wants to remake into championship links.
“The most important takeaway: There is no question in my mind that this judge, under any cirumstances, is going to allow the demolition of the Kennedy Center, just that East Wing or East Potomac Golf Course wrecking ball scenario,” Eisen said.

With Putin in the room, Carney condemns Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine
Speaking at APEC summit, Carney tells Putin what he thinks of Ukraine war
Prime Minister Mark Carney condemned Russia's war with Ukraine while Russian President Vladimir Putin, the man prosecuting that war, was in the room for leaders' speeches at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China.
Carney's speech principally focused on the government's efforts to boost the economy and make the country a more favourable place to invest for Asian partners.
However, toward the end of those remarks to the plenary session on Thursday, he veered into the yearslong conflict that has threatened Ukraine's territorial integrity, killed tens of thousands of soldiers and civilians and shaken the global economy.
"Sustained prosperity also depends on a stable international environment. Geopolitical crises, including Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine, continue to have material economic consequences across the Asia-Pacific and beyond," Carney said, according to a copy of his prepared remarks shared by the Prime Minister's Office.
Wars like Putin's "underscore the importance of reliable partners who respect international law and territorial integrity while building resilience among like-minded countries," he said.
This is believed to be the first time these two leaders have ever been together in the same space since Carney became prime minister.
Before making those comments, Carney was more pointed in a news conference when asked about Putin's claim that sanctions on his country are ineffective and "a thing of the past."
"Mr. Putin can ask his financial institutions, he can ask his oligarch friends, he can ask his hockey players whether or not sanctions are a thing of the past. I think he'll find out that they're very real, they're biting and they're absolutely necessary because of his illegal and unjustified war. Canada is speaking with action," Carney said.
Carney and United States President Donald Trump leave the family photo at the summit, which also included Russian President Vladimir Putin. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
When asked if he was willing to be blunt with Putin face-to-face, Carney praised former prime minister Stephen Harper's 2014 decision to personally chastise Putin for invading Crimea.
At the time, Harper said to Putin: "I guess I'll shake your hand, but I only have one thing to say to you: you need to get out of Ukraine."
According to an account of that moment in Harper's recently published memoir, Putin told him in response, "I'm not in Ukraine."
"Well, that's why it's a waste of my time to talk to you," Harper said he told the Russian leader.
Carney said he was willing to say something similar.
"If I have the occasion to be next to him, I will make that clear. But it is already clear, and not for the first time, Vladimir Putin is lying about the situation on the ground. Sanctions are very real and they're going to continue to increase as long as this war goes on," he said.
After his speech taking issue with Putin's war, Carney did pose for the usual leaders' family photo as the summit wrapped.
Putin was one row down and two leaders over from Carney, but it wasn't apparent if the two ever spoke.
The Russian Embassy in Ottawa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
World leaders including Carney, Putin, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are seen posing for the family photo on Thursday. (Greg Baker/Getty Images)
Since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin has largely avoided international summits where Kyiv's Western allies are present. He hasn't been to APEC, for example, in years.
But he was in Shenzhen, China, this year for a rare trilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping where the war with Ukraine was a major focus.
Putin also had a one-on-one meeting with Trump, who greeted the Russian leader at the start of their bilateral discussion by saying: "He's my friend," a comment that has been roundly condemned as inappropriate given Putin's alleged war crimes.
Trump shakes hands with Putin as Xi looks on before the APEC summit welcome banquet. (Iori Sagisawa/AFP/Getty Images)
Trump hailed the visit as "Highly Consequential" on social media as he returned to Washington. But it wasn't clear what, if anything, had been accomplished beyond a vague commitment to avoid nuclear war.
Xi said the meeting focused on "promoting world peace."
Putin, for his part, said the countries "hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace."
Leaders from the Coalition of the Willing, comprising some 34 Western nations supporting Ukraine in this war, met later Thursday to discuss the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting.
Carney was in the air on his way back to Canada but his defence minister, David McGuinty, attended in his place.
According to a readout from McGuinty's office, the minister "reaffirmed Canada's unwavering support for international efforts and emphasized that any peace agreement must preserve Ukraine's sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity, while strengthening rather than weakening Euro-Atlantic security."
Canada's position is that Ukraine "must be fully involved in decisions regarding its own future," the readout said.

- The claim that the guards at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier follow strict rules, such as taking exactly 21 steps in their march, never swearing and never drinking alcohol on or off duty, is a mixture of truth and falsehoods.
- The rumor stems from a post previously fact-checked by Snopes that has made the rounds on social media since at least 2004. It gained steam in November after a group of visitors led by U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was chastised by one of the tomb guards for not maintaining "an atmosphere of silence and respect."
- Snopes found that while the guards at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier do follow a strict regimen in the course of their duties, the rules aren't quite as stringent as the claim suggests.
On Nov. 11, footage captured a U.S. Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Virginia reprimanding Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and his entourage after one of them talked and laughed on the steps of the monument. Soon after the video spread, Snopes readers searched our site for information about the rules that govern the tomb guards.
First, some background on the monument. The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is located in Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia. In 1921, the military first laid to rest a soldier of unknown identity there with an inscription reading "Here rests in honored glory an American soldier known but to God." The tomb is intended to honor unidentified war dead and includes the remains of three soldiers of unknown identities who died in World War I, World War II and the Korean War.
Beginning in 1984, the tomb also held the remains of a soldier killed in the Vietnam War. In 1998, after DNA testing confirmed his identity, his remains were disinterred and returned to his family.
A variation of an old Facebook post spread online in 2026, claiming to detail a set of complex rules governing the tomb's guards. Snopes readers also sent us a list of rumors about them. The post stated:
(Facebook user "Whispers of Life/Incredible Stuff")
Snopes covered variations of these questions back in 2004 and concluded the post contained a mixture of true and false information. Below, we look closely at each question and break down the rules for being a guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier:
How many steps does the guard take during his walk across the Tomb and why?  
He takes 21 steps — symbolizing the 21-gun salute, the highest military and foreign tribute.
- True. The guard takes 21-step walks past the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier because 21 is a number of special significance. Snopes previously discussed the origins of the 21-gun salute, which dates back to cannon weaponry salutes in the 14th century.
How long does he pause before turning to walk back and why?  
He waits 21 seconds, again in honor of the same tradition.
- Mixture. The guard doesn't do an about-face, and the wait is actually 42 seconds. Instead, the guard marches 21 steps across the black mat, past the unknown soldiers of World War I, World War II and Korea and the crypt of the unknown soldier of the Vietnam War. The guard turns 90 degrees (not about-face) to face east for 21 seconds. The guard then turns 90 degrees again and faces north for 21 seconds. After a moment, the guard paces 21 steps north, turns and repeats the process. At each turn, the guard places the rifle on the shoulder nearest to visitors to signify that he or she stands between the tomb and any threat.
Why are his gloves damp?  
They are lightly moistened to ensure he never loses his grip on his rifle.
- True. The Society of the Honor Guard (a nonprofit organization focused on preserving the tomb's history) FAQ confirms this is correct.
Does he keep his rifle on the same shoulder, and if not, why?  
He always carries it on the shoulder farthest from the Tomb. After each crossing, he performs an about-face and moves it to the outside shoulder.
- True. The guard shifts the rifle before each 21-step walk to ensure that it is always carried on the outside shoulder, the one away from the tomb, to signify that the guard stands between the tomb and any threat.
How often are the guards changed?  
Every 30 minutes, 24/7, 365 days a year.
- Mixture. As Snopes previously reported, from 1926 through 1937, the tomb was guarded only during the day. Since 1937, it has been guarded 24 hours a day, every day of the year. According to the Arlington National Cemetery, the guard is changed every hour on the hour from Oct. 1 through March 31, and every half-hour from April 1 through Sept. 30. When the cemetery is closed at nighttime, the guard is changed every two hours.
What are the physical requirements for a Tomb Guard?  
Applicants must be between 5'10" and 6'2" and have a waist no larger than 30".
- Mixture. The Arlington National Cemetery website states: "Each soldier must be in superb physical condition, possess an unblemished military record and be between 5 feet, 10 inches and 6 feet, 4 inches tall for men or 5 feet, 8 inches and 6 feet, 2 inches tall for women, with a proportionate weight and build." The rules do not specify waist size.
They devote two years to the Tomb, live in the barracks beneath it, and must refrain from drinking alcohol on or off duty for the rest of their lives.
- Mixture. As we reported previously, the average tour of duty for a guard is shorter than the two-year period claimed here. The Society of the Honor Guard states: "The average tour at the Tomb is about 18 months. However, there is NO set time for service there. Sentinels live either in a barracks on Ft. Myer (the Army post located adjacent to the cemetery) or off base if they like. They do have a living quarters under the steps of the amphitheater where they stay during their 24 hour shifts. If they are of legal age, they may drink except while on duty."
They can never swear in public or dishonor the uniform or the Tomb. After two years, they earn a wreath pin signifying their service — fewer than 400 are currently worn. If they violate the code, they must relinquish the pin.
- Mixture. The "wreath pin" is the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier Identification Badge or "Tomb Badge" and it is rarely awarded to guards. According to the Arlington National Cemetery website: "Tomb Guards, members of the 3d U.S. Infantry Regiment (The Old Guard), earn the Tomb Badge for passing five testing phases and demonstrating high proficiency in Army and Tomb Guard knowledge. Tomb Guards who earn the badge are called Sentinels." There is no rule against swearing, but the identification badge can be taken away, even after the recipient has left the service. The Society of the Honor Guard says the badge is permanently awarded after a sentinel has served nine months as a sentinel at the tomb. Around 600 have been awarded since the late 1950s, about 10 badges per year. The Society notes that "while the TGIB can be revoked, the offense must be such that it discredits the Tomb of the Unknowns. Revocation is at the 3rd Infantry Regimental Commander's discretion and can occur while active duty or even when the Sentinel is a civilian."
Their shoes have thick soles to protect against extreme temperatures and metal heel plates that create the crisp click when they halt.
- Mixture. According to the Society of the Honor Guard: "The shoes are standard issue military dress shoes" and "have a steel tip on the toe and a 'horseshoe' steel plate on the heel."
Uniforms must have zero wrinkles or lint and are inspected in a full-length mirror. For the first six months, guards do not speak to anyone and do not watch television. Their off-duty time is spent studying the 175 notable individuals buried at Arlington National Cemetery, memorizing who they are and where they rest.
- Mixture. Tomb guards are allowed to talk to people and watch television. There are no rules prohibiting this on their off-duty hours. Any soldier wishing to become a sentinel undergoes rigorous training, including several hours a day of marching, rifle drill and uniform preparation, and every tomb sentinel is expected to be completely versed in the history of the tomb and of Arlington National Cemetery. According to the Arlington National Cemetery website, while still on-duty but not guarding the tomb, "the Tomb Guards spend their duty time in quarters below the Memorial Display Room of the Memorial Amphitheater, where they study cemetery history, clean their weapons and help the rest of their relief prepare for the changing of the guard." The Society of the Honor Guard also notes, "It takes the average Sentinel 8 hours to prep their uniform for the next work day." Tomb guards have even remained on duty in extreme weather situations. In 2003 during Hurricane Isabel, soldiers guarding the Tomb refused to go off-duty and seek shelter.
In sum, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier has a long and storied history and the soldiers tasked with guarding it follow a strict regimen. However, the rules in their daily lives are not as stringent as claimed in some social media posts.
Snopes archives contributed to this report.

Following a terrorist attack on November 11 at a Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) checkpoint in Jammu and Kashmir’s Kulgam district, a video went viral on social media with the claim that retired Indian Army officer and journalist Pravin Sawhney described Indian military and counter-terrorism drives in the valley as “false flag operations”.
Social media users claimed that Sawhney said that operations against the Kulgam attack, the Balakot airstrikes, and Operation Sindoor were orchestrated for political gains.
X user @RedDeFactoIND (Red Vanguard) shared the viral clip, which shows an interview conducted by The Wire. (Archive)
𝗘𝘅-𝗔𝗿𝗺𝘆 𝗢𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗲𝗿 𝗗𝗿𝗼𝗽𝘀 𝗕𝗼𝗺𝗯𝘀𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗹🚨: Pravin Sawhney in Recent Interview for Wire said, “Another false flag, just like Pulwama and Pahalgam,This is a pattern”
Indian journalists and influencers are now openly questioning the government’s narrative.
The voices from within are getting louder.
#CRPFSoldiers #CRPFCampAttack #kulgamattack #Kulgam #KulgamTerrorAttack
— Red Vanguard (@RedDeFactoIND) November 12, 2026
In the viral clip, the interviewer can first be heard saying (translated from Hindi): “Sushant, I want to know from you…the theme of your latest essay is the politicisation of army…During the false flag operations like Balakot and Pahalgam, the way the Bharatiya Janata Party used the military for political gains. My second question is that today while there is a war-like situation in the world…is testing the Pralay missile is an indication of a new false flag operation?”
“On one side China is occupying [Indian land], on the other there are CJP protests…Rahul Gandhi…,” the interviewer goes on to say before his voice is abruptly cut off.
The interviewee then seems to respond with, “Two things are very clear. One, for false flag operations like Balakot and Pahalgam, Operation Sindoor was launched but the Indian army failed. Second, my answers are within your questions.”
Several other users on X and Facebook also circulated the same video with identical claims. Among them were X handles @KaurUdhoke3 and @HinduReformer, along with multiple public Facebook pages focusing on South Asian geopolitics. [Archives: 1, 2]
Fact Check
A closer look at the viral video reveals noticeable lip-sync discrepancies and an unnatural, monotonous cadence in the voices of both men in the interview, which are salient features of AI-generated audio manipulation.
Further, columnist and strategic affairs expert Sushant Singh has been misidentified in the viral video as Pravin Sawhney. In the viral video itself, the interviewer refers to the interviewee as Sushant, and not Pravin. Below is an image of Sawhney, who does not appear in the viral clip.
On November 13, Singh himself took to X to debunk the clip, clarifying that the video was AI-generated, and highlighting that users had also misidentified him.
This is AI generated video of an old interview, which completely fabricates my conversation with @ashubh. This Pakistan-made AI video clip not only gets my identity wrong but creates what was never said.
The original full interview of March 2025 is here: https://t.co/Y6teNLJDfg
— Sushant Singh (@SushantSin) November 13, 2026
In his post, Singh also attached a link to the original YouTube interview from which the visuals were taken. Alt News examined the original video uploaded on The Wire’s official YouTube channel in March 2025.
Comparing the viral clip with the March 2025 interview confirms that the visual frames, including Singh’s attire, the background setting, and lighting, are identical. However, the audio track in the viral clip has been changed using AI.
In the original interview, Singh makes no mention of Kulgam, Pulwama, Balakot, or any ‘false flag operations’. Instead, he is heard discussing civil-military relations and institutional oversight.
To sum up, a manipulated video of journalist and strategic affairs analyst Sushant Singh is circulating on social media with users misidentifying him as journalist and FORCE editor Pravin Sawhney. The claim that the speaker in the video termed India’s counter-terrorism measures in Kulgam and Pulwama ‘false flag operations’ is false as well.

Apple TV expands its racing coverage with the all-female F1 Academy
The platform will air “every qualifying session and race throughout the season.”
Apple TV will stream the 2027 F1 Academy season, which is an all-female racing championship. The platform will air "every qualifying session and race throughout the season." F1 Academy began in 2022 and has since blossomed in popularity. Apple says it's now the second-most-followed series after Formula 1.
The season begins on March 19 with the Jeddah Corniche Circuit race in Saudi Arabia. It ends on November 20 with the Las Vegas Strip Circuit race. All told, the platform will stream seven full races and accompanying qualifying sessions.
"To have a global brand like Apple recognize the potential of our sport and commit its platform and resources to helping us reach new audiences is a powerful statement of how far we have come and where we are heading," said F1 Academy's managing director Susie Wolff. "Visibility remains fundamental to our mission. When young girls can switch on their screens and see women racing, competing, and succeeding, it changes what they believe is possible."
Apple has not, however, announced a companion docuseries just yet. Both Netflix and Disney+ have aired shows about F1 Academy in the past. This has certainly helped boost the championship's popularity and raise the profile of racers like Alisha Palmowski and Emma Felbermayr.
This is just the latest move to strengthen the partnership between Apple and Formula 1. The streamer is the exclusive US home for F1 races and related content. It offers both live and on-demand coverage, including practice rounds, sprint sessions and the actual races.

An iOS update did include a "Remote Control" feature that appeared to be enabled automatically.
The feature was introduced as part of the iOS 26 update, not iOS 27, and it does not allow users to remotely access a phone's "activity." Rather, it expands the functionality of the previously existing "Live Listen" accessibility feature. It is only available on devices signed into the same Apple account.
A rumor has circulated online since October that Apple released an update automatically enabling an option for outsiders to remotely access a phone's activity.
The claim spread on social media platforms such as Facebook (archived) and Instagram (archived). Many of the posts offered warnings about the feature and instructions on how to turn it off, like this one (archived) from a Facebook user:
If you have an iPhone and installed the iOS 27 update, you might not know that Apple turned ON the option for someone to remotely access your activity on your phone.
In short, Apple did put out a "Remote Control" feature in an update, but not iOS 27, as posts claimed. According to their Settings app, the feature released in iOS 26, and the assertion that the feature allowed "someone to remotely access" activity on users' phones was overstated. As such, we have rated this claim as mostly false.
(Screenshot from iPhone/Snopes illustration)
We reached out to Apple for more information about the "Remote Control" feature and to ask whether the iOS 26 update automatically enabled it across all devices. We will update the story if we receive a response.
According to the Apple Support website, Live Listen allows an iPhone to "act like a microphone," allowing users to "hear a conversation in a noisy area or even hear someone speaking across the room." It was originally intended to work with hearing aids, but was expanded in iOS 12 to include AirPods or Beats earphones.
The iOS 26 "Remote Control" setting added new functionality to the feature, allowing Apple devices like iPads and Apple Watches to view and control Live Listen sessions, as long as they are nearby and signed into the same Apple Account.
For example, a student in the back of a noisy lecture hall could put their phone next to their professor at the start of class and remotely control a Live Listen session from their iPad signed into the same Apple account, allowing them to pause, resume and view a transcript of the picked-up audio without getting up from their seat.
Live Listen is situated within the "Accessibility" menu, indicating that Apple intended the feature especially for those with hearing-related difficulties.
(Screenshot from iPhone)
Remote control of a user's Live Listen session can only take place if that user's device is currently connected to AirPods or Beats, and it only provides access to a transcript of audio near the user's iPhone. A bad actor who gained access to a device signed into a user's Apple account could start a Live Listen session on that user's device using "Remote Control," but based on our testing using devices with iOS 26, a pop-up announcing the session appears on that user's device. Clicking on that pop-up brings the user to Settings, where the user can turn the feature off. The range of the "Remote Control" feature also seemed to be limited, meaning the bad actor would also need to be close to the user — in our test, within earshot. Because of this, there is little risk of someone using the feature nefariously.
Based on user testimony and our own testing, the feature did appear to be automatically enabled as of the iOS 26 update. However, official Apple developer notes (archived) for the update made no mention of the terms "Remote Control" or "Live Listen."
For further reading, Snopes investigated the extent to which incognito mode protects users' data, and found it might be less than most users expected.
