Aakasamlo Oka Tara movie review: There is no Telugu word for what Krishna, played by Dulquer Salmaan, does in Aakasamlo Oka Tara. There is no English word either. It is not a sacrifice because sacrifice implies loss, and Krishna does not see his actions as a loss. It is not support, because support sounds structural and cold, like a pillar holding up a building. What Krishna does is closer to gardening. He tends, he waters, and he waits. He does not decide what grows. He just makes sure the soil is right, and light gets in. And then, one day, something extraordinary rises from the ordinary ground he has been tending for years, and he does not stand in front of it. He stands beside it. That is the whole of Aakasamlo Oka Tara. That is also, if you are lucky, the whole of love.
Kalpana, played by debutant Satvika Veeravalli, is a girl from a small Telugu village with a dream that the people around her find easier to dismiss than to understand. She wants to become an astronaut. However, her father believes that educating his daughter is a waste of money, and decides to get her married at the age of 16
Krishna, played by Dulquer Salmaan, enters her life through marriage. Somewhere in the early days of their marriage, he recognises something in Kalpana that the rest of the world has not bothered to look at: she is serious. Her dream is not a childhood fantasy she forgot to outgrow. And Krishna, without fanfare or a background score to underline the moment, makes a decision. Her dream becomes his project.
Dulquer Salmaan delivers one of his most selfless performances. Krishna is not a character designed to generate applause. What he has is a presence, steady, warm, unshowy, that makes you believe in the relationship and therefore in the film. It is the kind of performance that works precisely because it does not call attention to itself. Dulquer understood that this film does not belong to him, and he played accordingly.
Satvika Veeravalli, in her debut, shoulders a great responsibility. The film rises or falls on whether the audience believes Kalpana’s dream, and that belief has to come entirely from Satvika, and she delivers. She plays Kalpana not as a symbol of empowerment but as a person: stubborn, vulnerable, frightened and brave, often all within the same scene. It is a debut performance that announces a talent worth following.
Shruti Haasan brings a quiet gravity to Rohini. It is a role with less screen time than the billing suggests, but Shruti makes every scene count. She plays the character as someone who recognises in Kalpana the same fire she once had in herself, and her interactions with Satvika carry an unspoken mentorship that the film wisely chooses to show rather than explain.
The emotional core of this film is genuine. When Aakasamlo Oka Tara asks you to feel something, the feeling has been earned. Scene by scene. Moment by moment. The film does not manipulate you into tears with swelling music and slow-motion flashbacks. It builds its emotional case the way Krishna builds his support for Kalpana: quietly, consistently, with the confidence that if the foundation is solid, the structure will hold.
The relationship between Krishna and Kalpana is the film’s greatest achievement. It avoids every trap. It is not a romance where the man saves the woman. It is not a social drama where the woman’s success exists to make a point about gender. It is a marriage, real, imperfect and lived every day, where two people figure out what they owe each other and what they are willing to give. That balance is extraordinarily difficult to write and even harder to perform, and both Pavan Sadineni and his actors get it right.
However, the supporting world around Krishna and Kalpana could have been richer. Beyond Shruti Haasan’s Rohini, the characters who populate their lives feel functional rather than fully dimensional. A more textured supporting cast would have given the film additional depth and made the small-town world feel more complete.
GV Prakash Kumar’s music is a significant asset. The songs fit the emotional texture of the film without interrupting its narrative flow. The background score is particularly effective in the more intimate moments, lifting the scenes without overpowering them. There is a restraint in the score that mirrors the restraint in Dulquer’s performance, and the two work in concert.
Sujith Sarang’s cinematography gives the small-town setting a warmth and lived-in quality that serves the story well. The visual language is understated, never reaching for a beautiful shot at the expense of emotional truth.
Also Read – ENE Repeat review: Vishwak Sen’s gang can’t recreate the magic of the original
Gunnam Gangaraju’s dialogues deserve specific mention. The conversations between Krishna and Kalpana feel natural. They sound like things real people would say to each other in real kitchens, and that naturalism is one of the film’s quiet but crucial strengths.
Aakasamlo Oka Tara is as close to a perfect Telugu film as 2026 has produced. Aakasamlo Oka Tara’s central relationship is one of the most beautifully realised in recent Telugu cinema. Take your family. Take someone you love. Take someone who once held the ladder steady for you. This is a film for them.

Special Police Officers (SPOs) Rashpal Kumar (45) and Babi Chand (57), posted with the Special Operations Group in Kishtwar, Jammu and Kashmir, went missing on 10 November while heading to an Army operational base. Their bullet-riddled bodies were recovered near a nullah on 12 November, with their service weapons missing. On 14 November, their bodies were brought to their native village, Kiyar, in a dumper without coffins, reportedly without any senior police officer accompanying them. Locals alleged that no stretcher was provided and that they had to arrange one from the Army. The manner in which the bodies were transported triggered outrage and grief among residents, with BJP MLA Shagun Parihar reportedly confronting police officials over the treatment of the slain personnel. Their last rites were subsequently performed with full honours (here, here, here, and here).
Amid this outrage, a video purportedly showing CRPF SDG Sandeep Khirwar is being shared on social media with the claim that he said the bodies of the SPOs martyred in Kishtwar were transported in a dumper because there was no other option, as all vehicles in the area were occupied, and that the families should be grateful for receiving the bodies of the slain personnel. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows CRPF SDG Sandeep Khirwar saying the bodies of the martyred SPOs were transported in a dumper due to a lack of vehicles and that their families should be grateful for receiving them.
Fact: The video is digitally manipulated. The original video shows CRPF SDG Sandeep Khirwar expressing grief over the death of the two SPOs, paying tribute to them, assuring support to their families, and promising efforts to ensure justice. He does not make any remarks about the bodies being transported in a dumper due to a lack of vehicles or the families being grateful for receiving them. Analysis using AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya, indicated that the viral audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated, confirming that fabricated audio was added to the original footage to falsely attribute these remarks to him. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify whether CRPF SDG Sandeep Khirwar made any such statement, we searched Google using relevant keywords. However, we found no credible news reports or official statements corroborating the viral claim.
We noticed the viral video carries an ANI watermark. A keyword search led us to an ANI post on X (archived), dated 16 November 2026, featuring the same footage of CRPF SDG Sandeep Khirwar, wearing the same attire and speaking against an identical background.
In the original video, Khirwar speaks about the recovery of the mortal remains of the two missing SPOs in Kishtwar. He expresses grief over the loss of personnel, pays respect to the fallen, assures support to their families, and states that efforts will be made to ensure justice for them. The original footage contains no remarks about transporting the bodies in a dumper or about the families being grateful to receive them.
We analysed the viral video using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya. The analysis indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated, suggesting that fabricated audio was added to the original footage to make it appear as though CRPF SDG Sandeep Khirwar was making the remarks about the transportation of the bodies of the SPOs martyred in Kishtwar in a dumper due to the lack of available vehicles, and that their families should be grateful for receiving the bodies.
To sum up, this viral video of CRPF SDG Sandeep Khirwar making remarks about the SPOs’ bodies being transported in a dumper is digitally manipulated.

Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days
A federal judge has extended her block on construction of President Trump's D.C. arch for two weeks, another short-term victory for those who don't want to see the 250-foot structure break ground.
D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended her temporary restraining order on Wednesday, the day before it was set to expire. She originally stepped in to block construction on the night of Nov. 5, after the National Capital Planning Commission and National Park Service gave the arch final approval and the Trump administration said construction could begin imminently.
Chutkan's new five-page order prevents the administration from "initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility-installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity" at Memorial Circle through Dec. 3.
"The judge's order recognizes that the conditions that called for emergency relief two weeks ago remain unchanged," Nick Sansone, the Public Citizen attorney representing the original plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said in a statement.
The extension gives Chutkan more time to consider plaintiffs' request for a longer-term preliminary injunction, which would prohibit construction as the lawsuit against the arch plays out.
That lawsuit started earlier this year with a challenge from a group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian, but has expanded in recent weeks.
In late October, the governments of D.C. and Virginia filed another lawsuit, which was combined with the original. And nine members of the Kennedy family joined the fight last week, saying the arch will block historic sightlines and cast shadows over the graves of John F. Kennedy and others at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.
"This is one man who wants to build this arch. He's violated every rule. If this is a great idea, then bring it before Congress, follow the rules and get it approved," Max Kennedy, a son of Robert F. Kennedy, told NPR's All Things Considered.
Opposition to the arch — from area residents, veterans, local officials, Democratic lawmakers and more — has grown in recent months as the structure hurtled through the federal approval process.
Critics take issue with the arch's scale and location, saying it would interrupt the solemn and historic vista between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. Plaintiffs argue the structure violates several laws — including the Commemorative Works Act and D.C.'s Height of Buildings Act — and is fundamentally illegal without approval from Congress.
The Trump administration has not sought that approval, arguing the arch is covered by Congress' authorization in 1925 of a pair of 166-foot columns at the same location, which were never built.
In court filings and a recently unveiled website, the administration characterizes building the arch as a matter of urgency — both to complete that century-old vision and to facilitate national security. Trump said in September that the arch would double as a military complex, but the plans that got final approval this month don't include any details to that effect.
In a declaration this week, Ricky Buria, chief of staff to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, told the court that the agency is "currently in the planning process to determine how to integrate national defense uses … into the Arch without changing the existing plans for the Arch."
White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR on Thursday that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."
The arch is one of several construction projects that Trump has pursued with vigor in his second term. Some of them, like the White House ballroom and Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, are well underway. Others, like the Kennedy Center closure and East Potomac golf course redevelopment, are held up by various legal challenges.
Democrats have said they will use their forthcoming majority in Congress to push back on Trump's construction agenda, including by blocking federal funding. But experts say the fate of many of these projects will ultimately be up to the court.
'Time is of the essence' at East Potomac
Trump's dream of redeveloping a municipal D.C. golf course into a championship-level venue is also temporarily on hold, despite his repeated social media pronouncements that the park would close and work would begin on Nov. 15.
Another D.C. district judge, Ana Reyes, intervened Saturday to order the administration to keep East Potomac Park open for two weeks, on the eve of its indefinite closure.
But the golf course itself is currently unstaffed, since its operator lease expired on Sunday. That hasn't stopped locals from showing up and teeing off, finding creative ways to mark the holes after the flagsticks were removed from the course.
Reyes has ordered both parties to weigh in on whether she has the authority to order the government to keep the golf course open.
On Wednesday, the Trump administration officially appealed Reyes' restraining order as it had promised. That order is currently set to expire on Nov. 28, the Saturday after Thanksgiving.
Noting that timing, the plaintiffs in the case — local golfers and historic preservationists — have asked Reyes to extend her order by another two weeks, until Dec. 12, while she considers the underlying legal issues and decides whether to issue a longer preliminary injunction.
The government, on the other hand, said "the court already has everything it needs to promptly consider a motion for preliminary injunction" and has proposed a schedule that would enable her to issue a final ruling by Nov. 28.
In the meantime, the administration took another step forward in the federal review process on Thursday. The Interior Department presented its plan for the golf course to the Commission of Fine Arts, one of two federal agencies which would need to approve the project.
Commission Secretary Thomas Luebke said some 700 members of the public submitted comments ahead of the meeting, all but three in opposition to the golf course proposal.
The biggest concerns had to do with making the park less accessible to golfers of all levels, as well as cyclists, runners and picnickers who use the park's perimeter loop, which would be eliminated. There were other concerns about the impact of major road races — like the Marine Corps Marathon — that use that road, the loss of historic cherry trees and the cost of the project (the Interior Department said deferred maintenance alone would cost $43 million but did not specify how much the renovations would cost).
Over a dozen other people spoke out in the room, sharing their personal experiences with the park, raising questions about gaps in the presentation and urging the commission to defer or outright reject any plan that does not leave the perimeter loop intact.
Commissioners — all of whom were appointed by Trump — did not have the quorum needed to vote on preliminary approval. Several offered praise for the idea of beautifying the space and overhauling the golf course, but questioned whether this plan is the best way to do it.
Vice Chair Rodney Mims Cook, Jr., a Trump ally, said there seems to be enough space in the park to accommodate the aspects that people care about, like preserving the historic mini-golf course. His comments prompted applause from many of the people who had crowded into the meeting room.
Cook asked the Interior Department to bring alternative designs to its next meeting, in late January. The administration has said it plans to present the same proposal to the National Capital Planning Commission at its meeting in early December.
Administration officials said in Thursday's meeting, as they have in previous court hearings, that their plan is not yet finalized. Judge Reyes, however, is not convinced and accused the administration of already taking steps to carry it out, like cutting down hundreds of trees.
Plaintiffs in the case argue the administration has violated federal environmental law by splitting the project into smaller parts, like the tree removal, to bypass necessary reviews. And they say the administration skipped required legal steps in its rush to close off most of the park, which Reyes seemed to agree with in her order.
"In its haste to meet an arbitrary deadline, the Government has likely violated at least the National Environmental Policy Act and the Administrative Procedure Act," she wrote.
Trump has repeatedly described the East Potomac golf course as decrepit and dangerous, and challenged Reyes' authority over the project. Over the weekend, he reiterated that Reyes was appointed by President Biden and slammed her decision as "highly destructive and political."
"Why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course, one that is mocked all over D.C.(and far beyond!), instead of quickly turning it into a great and admired one?" Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Time is of the essence, or golf seasons, jobs, prestige, and much money, will be lost!"
Government lawyers asked Reyes to recuse herself from the case in mid-October, accusing her of bias and hostility. She denied that request on legal grounds. Tensions between Reyes and the administration have dominated this case so far, with the judge ordering a misconduct inquiry into whether government officials and lawyers misled the court about its plans for the park.
Government lawyers have pushed back, telling the court Thursday that such an inquiry is "not necessary."

Can Nigeria's president regain voters' trust after painful first term?
- Published
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched his re-election manifesto, promising to grow the economy, tackle insecurity and address housing shortages.
The plan targets 6% annual economic growth by 2031, 78,000 additional security personnel and 200,000 affordable homes.
Titled From Reform to Prosperity, the manifesto builds on Tinubu's first-term economic reforms, including the removal of the fuel subsidy, which has pushed up living costs.
Nigeria is due to hold a general election in January 2027, with Peter Obi and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar among Tinubu's main challengers.
The manifesto, launched on 10 November by his party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), reflects the government's bid to win back the trust of Nigerians.
Elected in 2023, Tinubu undertook a series of economic reforms, including the removal of fuel subsidies, the harmonisation of official and parallel foreign exchange rates, and tax reforms.
"That manifesto was trying to get Nigeria back on its feet, given the condition of the country at that time, slipping into austerity," Joshua Osiyemi, who heads Tracka, a platform launched by the BudgIT Foundation, which is a non-profit organisation that aims to make government financial data easier to understand.
The reforms, although considered necessary by some economists, have been painful for many Nigerians.
"Fuel prices went up, and everything that Nigerians consume skyrocketed," Osiyemi told the BBC.
"Most Nigerian families are saying they cannot survive on 10,000 naira [$7.40; £5.50] a day," he said, referring to a survey conducted by his organisation.
Analysis by Nigeria's International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) found that the price of imported rice rose by 184% between May 2023, when Tinubu took office, and October 2025. Other staples, including beans, garri (cassava flour) and bread, also recorded substantial increases.
In a sign that the reforms might be starting to pay off, SBM Intelligence, a security risk consulting firm, found that the cost of preparing a pot of jollof rice fell by 11.5% between June and September 2026, the sharpest decline it had recorded in the 10 years it has been running its Jollof Index.
However, this has not translated into significant relief for most households.
"Nigerians spend more and more of their income on basics," said Ikenna Okonkwo, head of research at SBM Intelligence.
The reforms were praised by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for their effectiveness.
Nigeria's headline inflation stood at 14% in September 2026, according to the National Bureau of Statistics, down from a high of 34% in 2024. The gap between the official and parallel exchange rates has also narrowed.
Tinubu has said the removal of fuel subsidies freed up more than one trillion ($740m; £550m) naira in government resources in just the first two months.
Following widespread complaints about the rising cost of living, he recently said he would work to reduce the cost of fuel but denied that this was a return to the subsidy. For decades, many Nigerians have seen cheap fuel as one of the few perks of living in Africa's largest oil producer.
His administration subsequently announced a 125bn naira intervention package for small businesses, including grants for smaller enterprises and loans for manufacturers.
Atiku has criticised Tinubu's decision to remove the fuel subsidy.
"My position stands! I will restore subsidy to make life easier and affordable for Nigerians," Atiku wrote on X.
However, restoring the fuel subsidy could prove challenging given Nigeria's economic realities.
"The current budget for Nigeria in 2026 is about 68.32tn naira, with 15.8tn going towards debt servicing. So, we are not fiscally strong enough to say that we want to return to the subsidy," Osiyemi said.
While Tinubu's reforms are lauded for restoring some stability at the macroeconomic level, they have also created instability in households.
Two months away from elections, the cost of living and economic hardship are the major issues for many voters.
"These kinds of things can get punished in polls," said Okonkwo of SBM Intelligence.
To address this, Tinubu promised to lower the cost of living, grow the economy by 6% and halve youth unemployment if he wins re-election. Achieving these targets will require increased oil and agricultural production.
But much of Nigeria's agricultural production is concentrated in the north, where insecurity has made farming increasingly difficult.
Osiyemi says many farmers are reluctant to return to their fields.
"They're not sure whether when they go to their farms, they have the chances of also coming back home, to meet with their family."
To address insecurity, Tinubu proposes recruiting an additional 28,000 military personnel and 50,000 police officers.
"The security situation, especially in the north, is more complex than a matter of just recruiting more soldiers," Okonkwo said.

The threats include jihadists, kidnap gangs and conflict between herders and farmers in central Nigeria.
Insecurity is also a major priority for Obi, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, who came third in the 2023 presidential election and attracted significant support from young Nigerians.
He unveiled his 2027 Governance Agenda on 10 November, under the campaign slogan "A New Nigeria is Possible", placing national unity at the top of his priorities, followed by security.
"Nobody will kidnap school children and disappear into the bush. If you kidnap children and go into the bush, you will not be alone there. We will come after you," he said.
Further, delivering on those ambitions will also depend on improving electricity supply, particularly for businesses and industries. Tinubu promises to increase available electricity generation towards 10,000MW.
"There is nothing in the manifesto about where that investment is going to come from because it will cost a lot of money," said Okonkwo.
Another huge challenge facing Nigeria is the power sector, which has suffered from years of underinvestment.
The Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission says the country had installed generation capacity of 13,625MW at the end of 2024, but generated an average of just 4,223MW during the year.
Nigeria's power sector has failed to produce at capacity due to ageing infrastructure, inadequate maintenance, gas supply constraints and funding challenges.
The government has also privatised electricity distribution, but distribution companies have struggled to invest in infrastructure, including local transformers and metering systems, partly because of low profit margins.
"The government cannot increase tariffs to an extent where people will revolt, and that also keeps investors away because they don't look at the Nigerian power sector as somewhere that they can make money," said Okonkwo.
Unreliable electricity supplies force many households and businesses to rely on generators, pushing up the cost of living and doing business.
The manifesto also promises to build 200,000 affordable homes. This is a fraction of Nigeria's estimated housing deficit, which a technical committee set up by the housing ministry put at 14.9 million units in 2025.
For Nigerians to feel a meaningful improvement in their lives, the reforms will need to go beyond the promises outlined in the manifesto, analysts say.
"Some of the items in the manifesto seem bloated, but if they can be committed to it, I want to believe that quite a number of these items that they have here are very much achievable," Osiyemi said.
"The big thing, if the APC wins, which they have to do and is a tall order, is to regain the trust of Nigerians," Okonkwo said.
Nigeria's 2023 presidential election saw Tinubu declared winner with 8.79 million votes, ahead of Atiku and Obi. Tinubu's victory came amid growing economic hardship after eight years of Muhammadu Buhari's APC government.
"APC were able to win because opposition was divided between two very strong candidates with two regional bases. In the end, we still go down to basic questions like the region you are from and tribal sentiments," Okonkwo said.
As Nigeria heads towards the 2027 elections, Tinubu, Atiku and Obi are once again central to the contest, but the opposition faces a familiar challenge - building a united front and support beyond regional strongholds.
"It will play out like it did in 2023," Okonkwo said.
"The APC are in a stronger position being the incumbent party and the momentum that some of the opposition candidates had in 2023 has faded."

The reproductive-autonomy jurisprudence as evolved by the Supreme Court under Article 21 of the Constitution is rich yet narrow, focusing primarily on one side of the problem. In Suchita Srivastava v. Chandigarh Administration (2009), the Court held that reproductive choices may be exercised to procreate as well as to abstain from procreating. In X v. Principal Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Department (2022), the Supreme Court extended the right to abortion to unmarried women as an exercise of ‘decisional autonomy’.
These, and nearly all other landmark cases are concerned only with an existing pregnancy. The freedom to pursue parenthood through medical treatment, however, has surfaced only at the margins. The Delhi High Court, in 2023, allowed parole of a life convict to attempt IVF, by recognising a “right to parenthood,” but only as a claim against a barrier the State itself had erected. No court has yet asked whether the State may leave a citizen’s access to infertility care entirely to their own purse. Can a right available to the fertile but structurally withheld from the infertile be called a universal right?

Leicester, which now plays in the third tier of English football, issued a statement on Wednesday saying the club and BC Game had “reached a mutual agreement to conclude our commercial partnership with immediate effect”.
“The decision follows constructive discussions between both parties in recent days, during which we recognised our differing commercial priorities moving forward,” it said.
The club thanked BC Game for the “constructive approach taken in reaching this agreement”.
The statement did not refer to the supporters’ stated objections.
Leicester shocked the sporting world when it won the Premier League in 2016, following up with an FA Cup triumph five years later.
But the club has fallen on hard times in recent years and is currently 11th in League One.

The Bombay high court on Thursday directed Bank of Baroda to maintain status quo on documents sought by Bavaguthu Raghuram Shetty in his $15 billion lawsuit against the lender. The direction came after Shetty alleged that bank officials were involved in the fraud at his company, NMC Healthcare, and sought access to those records. Counsel for Shetty sought immediate inspection of records in Bank of Baroda’s possession, including loan guarantees, arguing that they could help establish the lender’s role in the alleged transactions. The bank, meanwhile, assured the court that the records would be preserved without alteration until the next hearing on 17 December. Senior counsel Birendra Saraf, appearing for the bank, said there was no reason to believe that records would be destroyed, pointing out that proceedings relating to NMC were also taking place in Abu Dhabi. Shetty's counsel argued that the “massive” amount of funds being transferred from NMC Healthcare was impossible without the involvement of officials of Bank of Baroda’s Abu Dhabi branch. He also said that the bank’s system raised around 150 alerts over suspicious transactions, but all of them were closed without investigations. “There were 150 alerts that their computer generated, depending on the nature of the transaction with regard to the syphoning of money laundering transactions. Each of them was closed without investigation,” he informed the court. A single-judge bench of Justice Arif S. Doctor, after hearing both sides, declined immediate disclosure of the documents and ordered that status quo be maintained over the documents listed in Shetty’s application. On 29 October, Shetty also filed two interim applications in the Bombay high court, requesting a court-monitored forensic preservation of electronic records, and disclosure of relevant bank records, including electronic communications, transaction data, emails and records from banking and payment systems. He has also asked the court to appoint a commissioner to inspect and preserve these records. In his second application, Shetty has sought an order directing the bank to furnish the security amount he has claimed, or any such amount as fixed by the court. He stated that he wanted the bank to set aside the claimed amount in a reserve that would not be available for distribution. He argued that the bank could later rely on the absence of a provision to resist payment of any amount awarded by the court. Shetty, the founder of NMC Healthcare and UAE Exchange, has accused Bank of Baroda and its officials of helping former NMC executives move money out of the healthcare group. His suit also names former NMC executives, including Prasanth Manghat and Promoth Manghat, among 26 defendants. Shetty has sought $15 billion in damages, including compensation for financial losses and reputational damage, along with 18% annual interest. NMC Healthcare, once one of the largest private healthcare providers in the UAE, was listed on the London Stock Exchange before entering insolvency proceedings in 2020. After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.
When testing the agent, staff warned that Muse appeared to be accessing encrypted private messages that users did not expect the bot to review, could be mixing up conversations between users, and even potentially sharing sensitive information users would never expect to be exposed.
Some unexpected Muse outputs responded to questions that staffers never asked.
“Hmmm,” one Meta staffer wrote in an instance where Muse sent the definition of “money laundering” unbidden. “Got a random ping from Muse about something I definitely did not ask for… .”
In at least one case, Muse told a staffer surprised by a similarly out-of-context offer to message a seller about a coffee table that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.”
According to Reuters, that employee flagged the troubling output, writing, “this was ‘not my conversation’” and “expressing concern about a ‘possible cross-account context leak.’”
Raising the most concern were random outputs that appeared to share private user data. For example, a perplexed Meta staffer chatting with Muse about fishing got a random extra response, seemingly sharing balances from two unknown bank accounts. That output said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
At least one staffer said they lost money testing Muse, Reuters reported. That staffer reported that Muse “accidentally rolled me into a premium insurance plan” for their dog that charged them $888 per month instead of their prior rate of $200. “Couldn’t recover,” the staffer said.
Meta’s spokesperson, Daniel Roberts, told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents,” and internally employees were told that “the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with users in between sessions.” In those cases, an AI team member said the hallucinations were “unfortunately” biased “towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks.” In some cases, instead of bank details, Muse hallucinated bitcoin balances, the team member said.
A Meta spokesperson told Ars that “employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products. Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Speaking to Reuters, Roberts reiterated that “many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations” that Meta had already addressed.
But Roberts declined to respond to Reuters’ questions on the prevalence or persistence of the issues the AI team member discussed. And Reuters’ report emphasized that the outlet independently was “unable to establish whether Muse was giving users other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.”
Muse issues arose soon after September launch
Meta started receiving privacy-related complaints from Muse users in September. An Inc. Magazine reporter, Jason Aten, was shocked when it became clear that Muse was digging through private messages on his Mac without permission, reporting that he instead “explicitly” chose to deny Muse that access. As Meta delayed responding, the agent claimed it was simply parsing text in push notifications, but Aten found that “wasn’t true.” Rather, the agent was syncing messages from a local database, which Aten said was activated without his knowledge.
Eventually, a Meta spokesperson, David Singleton, responded to Aten on social media. Singleton insisted that Aten must have opted into granting “macOS system-level Full Disk Access” with the “Messages connector” enabled, if Muse was reading his private messages.
But Aten said the response wasn’t good enough.
“Email me, David,” Aten responded. “Full Disk Access off. Muse synced 187k lines from my messages chat [database]. Something’s not great. Also, that Full Disk Access doesn’t say anything about your message database, and I specifically gave Muse a goal that had nothing to do with messages, so it had no business doing that even if I had given it permission.”
Around the same time, Singleton responded to another user warning that his Muse appeared to be hacked. In that case, the user said that Muse tried to access an email service after claiming the user asked it to.
“I didn’t even open the app today at all,” the user wrote, vowing to delete the app and report it to Apple. “This is crazy.”
In a lengthy response providing more technical details, Singleton confirmed that Meta had received “a few reports” of such cases “where people thought their Muse was hallucinating or leaking other people’s data.” As he explained, the issues arose after Meta deployed an update giving Muse instructions on “how to engage with the user and ask them for confirmation before taking specific actions.”
It seems those instructions “landed on every message, not just messages pertaining to those specific actions, so its impact was wider than intended,” Singleton said. Also: “the way this instruction was provided to the model was done in a way that the model was not expecting (i.e. was not trained to expect).”
“We investigated with urgency and determined that this was caused by a bug introduced in the product that caused the model to hallucinate and was NOT a security or privacy issue,” Singleton wrote. “The bug has now been fixed.”
Aten warned that even though you can’t rely on Muse to explain its own behavior, the agent’s response coupled with Meta’s did little to rebuild trust after the shocking intrusion into his private messages.
“If we grant Singleton’s premise that I managed to unknowingly click something that enabled this capability, I still think that’s really bad,” Aten wrote. “You should not design your system in a way that people end up surprised by this kind of thing.” And if you do, you should not make “user control the central pitch” for marketing Muse, Aten suggested.
“If an AI agent is going to read my private messages, there should be a moment when it clearly asks me whether that’s okay,” Aten wrote.
Reuters warned Signal intrusions are ongoing
Since Muse launched in September, it has been downloaded more than 10 million times, tapping Meta’s vast user network to quickly become one of the most-used AI agent tools.
But staffers warned Meta that users may be blindsided by some actions the agents take, depending on the operating system the app is connected to. For example, one staffer was surprised to find that “Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system.” That, too, gave access to private message preview text the staffer had not intended for the agent’s review.
Meta says that Muse users can trust the company to keep their data private. It also warns users that Muse can make mistakes, while building into its terms that users are responsible for actions taken by Muse (like maybe buying things you don’t want or making doctor’s appointments you don’t need). The tech giant said it’s continuously updating user protections, conducting internal testing, and prioritizing user safety.
However, Reuters worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute to test if they could replicate that Meta staffer’s and others’ Muse experiences. On Android devices, they found that Muse could read Signal messages by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead relying on permissions granted during initial setup.
On iPhone, requests were blocked, Reuters reported. But on Apple’s macOS, Muse repurposed “settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers” to retrieve messages, including screenshot tools.
That testing “indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others,” Reuters reported. Overall, Meta seemed to be interpreting permissions from Muse users “broadly,” Reuters concluded, in ways that privacy advocates and regulators may disagree with.
Signal President Meredith Whittaker told Reuters that Meta launched Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity.” She demanded that Meta make changes to give app developers like Signal “consistent technical ways” to “mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents,” Reuters reported.
Part of that change would require operating systems to enforce rules that app developers set to rope off AI agents from sensitive data, Whittaker suggested. And following Reuters’ reporting, both Apple and Google are already weighing potential changes to “give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents.”
Apple, in particular, seemed disturbed by how Muse may be manipulating accessibility tools for people with disabilities. In October, Apple had already announced changes coming in response to users complaining about Muse accessing private messages without their knowledge or explicit consent. At that time, Apple concluded that “some developers were using the Full Disk Access feature in ways that could put users at risk.” And they promised to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
“We are committed to ensuring users understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple said.

‘The Jhulan effect’ — that’s what a near-obsessive search for the next Jhulan Goswami in the Indian women’s cricket ecosystem is called in jest. Who wouldn’t want another speedy maverick cut from the same cloth as the Bengal superstar? Tall, quick, incredibly disciplined, handy with the bat and, perhaps most importantly, commendably fit until the very end.
Jhulan, who walked into the sunset as the leading wicket-taker in ODIs with 255 scalps, belongs to a bridging era in Indian women’s cricket when pace bowling wasn’t the trendy option. Spinners headlined proceedings, while pacers were the fillers.
“In the beginning of my career, Amita Sharma [the incumbent selection committee chair] and Rumeli Dhar were there alongside me. Then came Snehal Pradhan and Shikha Pandey, followed by Mansi Joshi, Meghna Singh and Pooja Vastrakar, who made space in the team. India was always considered a spin-bowling side. That myth changed when our generation — Ami, Rumi and me — came in. Our pace attack started being talked about,” Jhulan tells Sportstar.
Cut to 2026, and India is a flourishing cradle for seamers.
While raw, explosive pace is not yet as abundant as India would like, bowlers with control, variations and gusto have emerged from various parts of the country. The existence of the Women’s Premier League (WPL) has only fanned the flames of a desperate need that was identified close to a decade ago: developing a pace pool that can pose problems for opponents, especially on international wickets.
However, India seems stuck in an unimaginative loop of emerging talent getting caught in the quicksands of injury and losing valuable time at the topmost tier of the game.
Pooja, Amanjot Kaur and Kashvee Gautam have missed World Cups due to persistent niggles and lengthy recoveries, while others, like Renuka Singh Thakur, have had patchy game time due to workload issues and stress fractures. A depleted pace attack, among other factors, left India red-faced after another group-stage exit at the T20 World Cup.
When Jhulan was settling into the sport, players had no access to speed-gun metrics. Indians are masters of jugaad (hacks), and this issue had one too.“We often procured them when we toured abroad. Before that was possible, I used to tell our coach, Sudha (Shah) ma’am, to note our speeds and keep from broadcasting them. I also spoke a lot to the opponent batter and would ask how the ball felt. The ball needed to hit the sticker of the bat. I wanted to beat the batter, come what may. In the nets, I also always asked the keeper, and tried to train with one facing me. Today, things are much different,” she notes.
Now, empirical tools are widely used. CricViz consistently places Jhulan in the 125-128 kmph range, despite competing in an age where modern-day staples such as nutrition monitoring, biomechanical experts and strength-and-conditioning staff were hard to come by. One outlier reading even puts her at 132.1 kmph during the 2016 Women’s T20 World Cup.
Among Indian pacers since the 2000s, Amita Sharma has a recorded fastest speed of 128.90 kmph, while Shikha Pandey’s top speed is 124.35 kmph. Kranti Gaud and Arundhati Reddy, with 119.62 and 118.51 kmph respectively, are the closest to the 120 kmph mark. But the former — young and still developing her game — has struggled with consistency in control. Arundhati, meanwhile, relies more on disciplined rhythm and variations to stay economical, take wickets, or both.
But is the search for a speedster who can match or, better still, surpass this benchmark possible in a system that forces its talents to bowl slower?
Winning or developing?
Some of India’s best spinners today — from Deepti Sharma and N. Sree Charani to even Poonam Yadav — started out as medium-pacers. However, factors such as a relatively small build or the tendency to concede runs because of their pace steered these players towards spin.
“After close to 10 years of senior cricket, I found a coach who told me to become a leg-spinner,” Ananya Upendran, former cricketer and lead scout for Delhi Capitals, says.
“I had a teammate, Sravanthi Naidu, who started off as a medium-pacer but switched to left-arm spin and got picked for India. She then came back to the domestic system and bowled two full seasons of pace. She switched to left-arm spin again and got picked for India once more. It’s so annoying, but hopefully that trend is changing,” she shrugs.
“We don’t use pacers enough in domestic cricket,” declares Neetu David, former chief selector of the women’s national team (2020-2025). Incidentally, 12 seam-bowling options were handed debuts across both white-ball formats during her committee’s tenure.
“Even today, we tell State associations to give pacers at least 10 overs, even if they bowl in spells of two, three or four overs. If they don’t play in the States, it gets tough to bring them up to the national level. But States want to win championships, and that’s understandable too. Coaches worry about results ruining their record. They find their spinners are more proficient wicket-takers and turn to them. Rajeshwari Gayakwad used to open the bowling for Team India,” Neetu recalls.
Pace brings an unpredictability that both Ananya and Neetu feels domestic decision-makers largely wish to avoid. The ball could beat not just the batter but the fielders too, running away to the boundary.
“I can tell you from my own state, Uttar Pradesh, where we had very good pacers, but the earlier coaches used to say, ‘You are too erratic and bowling too fast. Please slow down and just swing it.’ So the kid would start thinking: If my catches get dropped, there’s no point; the coach will drop me from the team,” Neetu explains.
Shikha corroborates this experience.
“We play in smaller grounds, with 55-yard boundaries and fast outfields. There were so many instances when I would bowl, just miss the stumps or get an inside edge. I might have a slip and a third in place, but the edge would hit a hand and run away for four. That four would be remembered. I had mentors like Purnima Rau who encouraged me to bowl fast, but that was in a domestic system where only one medium-pacer would be fielded.”
“I just hope our girls get really strong and start hitting spinners too,” she quips.
Neetu’s tenure also saw the BCCI organise several pace-bowling camps, which brought age-group talent under the Board’s ambit for monitoring and high-performance training. But a foundational change in the selection process itself was also needed.
“When V.V.S. Laxman took charge at the National Cricket Academy, which later became the BCCI’s Centre of Excellence, we discussed clear criteria for every player. For spinners, that was 12-15 wickets, and a similar bar was set for pacers too. But we had to tell him that pacers don’t get enough match time or overs. So the criterion was relaxed to a lower wicket bracket. We brought in specialist coaches to work with these girls. We even had Australian bowling consultant Troy Cooley at the NCA and later with the women’s team too,” she says.
Doubling up as all-rounders
“The runs bowlers get for you are the ones that give you games,” Shikha Pandey recalls former head coach W.V. Raman telling the team. She remembers a tense international match in which she and spinner Radha Yadav stitched together a crucial 17-ball, 22-run stand to snatch a three-run victory.
For years, India’s inability to make its tail wag has been a bête noire. As a result, domestic coaches no longer view batting as a luxury for fast bowlers; it is an absolute prerequisite for survival.
Sukhwinder Singh Bawa, coach to medium-pacer Nandni Sharma, explicitly trained her to finish tight games under pressure. In the nets, he created situational simulations — 15 runs needed off 10 balls — forcing Nandni, who bowls a clever 110 kmph seam-up delivery and a dipping slower ball in the low 80s, to master lower-order hitting.
“My trademark has always been developing all-rounders, from Yuvraj Singh to Reema Malhotra,” Bawa explains. “The idea was to ensure selectors saw that she could bat, maybe even promote her higher up the order.”
Nagesh Gupta, coach to international seamers Amanjot Kaur and Kashvee Gautam, is equally blunt about the national setup’s demands. “The team suffers because the batting thins out after number six. Just bowling is a tough pathway now. Everyone is bowling — so who in the pool can bat well? Producing all-round performances in pressure games is a necessity.”
This push reflects a global game increasingly dominated by pace-bowling all-rounders — from South Africa’s Marizanne Kapp and Annerie Dercksen and England’s Nat Sciver-Brunt and Issy Wong to Australia’s formidable assembly line featuring Ellyse Perry, Annabel Sutherland and Nicola Carey, among a host of others.
It’s a tough balance. Nagesh’s academy trains 55 girls in the 8-10 age bracket, of whom 25 are pure batters and 16 are pace bowlers.
But in India, this dual requirement has not settled in seamlessly and has come at a steep physical price. Nagesh notes that as young seamers rise through the ranks, the demands of bowling express overs and contributing with the bat can trigger severe workload issues.
Gaps at the grassroots
“The spike in injury rates is natural and will continue for a few years. The women’s game has exploded, and bowlers are now expected to do something different from what they trained for,” Welsh high-performance fast-bowling coach Steffan Jones says.
“There are biological differences, and so pace programmes for men and women, or boys and girls, need to accommodate them. India largely has a one-size-fits-all approach,” he explains.
“Early specialisation is a problem in India. A youngster who likes cricket takes it up, and that’s it. The robustness and athleticism needed for it are never developed. On the other hand, in England, for instance, a young bowler would probably do a lot of gym work and training, but not enough bowling. No country has really nailed the balance,” says the newly announced Mumbai Indians bowling consultant.
After the 2017 ODI World Cup, Shikha Pandey approached Jones hoping to unlock higher speeds. His recent work with Indian men’s team all-rounder Nitish Kumar Reddy, whose marked improvement in pace was there for all to see, underlines that this can be done. But the parallels end there.
“Nearly 20 per cent of ball speed comes from your run-up. Too many female bowlers have short run-ups. So if you’re removing the momentum you get from a proper run-up, the force goes somewhere else. That’s potentially the crease, with angular momentum and rotation, which takes a lot out of the body because this depends on strength and muscle.
“Women can run as well as men, just a bit slower. If we’re discouraging them from running and attacking the crease, we’re making the game harder for female fast bowlers,” he says, citing run-up tweaks as one of the elements he worked on with Shikha.
An Australian study on non-elite female pacers shows that, unlike men — who generate velocity by bending forward at the waist — female seamers show no statistical relationship between forward trunk flexion and release speed. Instead, 89 per cent of speed variation in female pacers is driven by delayed arm circumduction and torso rotation.
“Female bowlers should be encouraged to have a more midway or front-on bowling action. We can’t teach them to be side-on, with the back foot parallel to the crease. I call them hip-and-knee-dominant bowlers. Men run with their pelvis open. But the female body can’t get its foot around because it needs a lot of internal hip rotation and strength, which the female body often can’t do. I encourage my trainees to be more like jumpers and sprinters, not side-on bowlers.”
But the route to that is not about overdoing any one element. “Practice doesn’t make perfect; practice makes permanent,” he underlines, advising against overbowling young cricketers and emphasising the need to “bulletproof the body” instead.
Matt Mason, former England women’s pace-bowling coach, found the lack of foundational bowling work a challenge. “The first difference between men and women is how they’re brought into the game. They haven’t bowled as many overs as young men. Usually, the age-group programmes available to boys aren’t available to girls. Males bowl more and so have built a little more resilience. Add the biomarkers that are different for both genders to this. What we’ve found is that when we put our athletes in safe positions, we put them in better positions to perform well,” says Mason, who is now with London Spirit in The Hundred.
He cites Freya Kemp as an example of a pacer who took up 50-over cricket and made her international 50-over debut in the span of a few months. That would never happen in the men’s game.
“Women and girls recruit a lot of their physical strength to bowl fast, whereas men don’t. Men use the technical model far more efficiently. The girls rely on strength and rotation. So that means they have to be very strong because they’re going to use those muscle groups. But then, obviously, we know there’s a gap in that area as well. The frustration for me is that, at the very beginning of their cricketing journey, potentially in the 12-14 age group, some of these habits have already formed. That’s where our coaches need to be,” he adds.
Repeatable actions also do not guarantee adaptability in high-pressure situations. This is Jones’ biggest gripe with how training systems work.
“A net session or an intensive training block is still not up to match-day intensity. It isn’t preparing bowlers. The stress of competition, crowds and the context of a match cannot be replicated in the nets. But the game still runs on this notion that we need to bowl more and train more. If you get a bowler to go at the stumps for an hour, I promise you the deliveries they bowl in the second 30 minutes will not be hard enough. Fast bowling is a mental activity too. It’s about going flat out for a few seconds and then having full recovery,” Jones argues.
Jhulan’s own experiences corroborate this.
“As a new-ball opener, we barely got new balls to train with in the open nets. So, learning to control was done on the go in matches and was quite challenging. I’d have people casually tell me, ‘You’re going too fast and erratic. Bring down the pace, swing the ball more.’ With all due respect, I quite happily ignored them,” she gushes.
The many deaths of pace
In a batter’s universe, a bowler’s currency is the dot ball. Accuracy over speed, then, becomes the formula to dry up runs.
“You’re given these cones and asked to bowl 30 balls in that box. When you’re young and quick, you’re not accurate. And if you want to finish that session, you have to do as told. Pace dies in that compromise,” Ananya adds.
Visakhapatnam-based pacer Shabnam Shakil, who emerged as a credible raw-pace option at the U-19 level, is a case in point.
“We just bowl young quicks into the dust. Look at Shabnam. She’s been playing cricket non-stop since 2022. She was clocking 113 kmph at one stage. Her body is developing. She was invariably in every state and NCA-level camp. It’s good to see faith in them this way and a desire to keep them in the system. But we need to remember these are developing women and we shouldn’t push them ahead until they are ready. The 5 kmph drop in pace she had at one point, with a heavily strained action, was inevitable,” Ananya explains.
Shikha believes age tiers exist for a reason. Promoting youngsters should also come with pragmatism.
“Shabnam was playing U-16, U-19, U-23 and senior cricket at the domestic level. She wasn’t getting any wickets, but was directly fast-tracked into the senior team. I keep harping on this. You have an U-23 side because you don’t want players dropping off after U-19, but you don’t want U-19s playing seniors all the time either. Their development needs to follow that physical gradation too, sometimes,” she points out.
It doesn’t help that fast bowling has been quantitatively identified as the single most injury-prone role in women’s cricket, according to an Australian review of shoulder injuries from 2015 to 2023.
Furthermore, a study conducted at the University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg, found injury prevalence reaching up to 53.8 per cent among pacers. Among the potential problem areas, lower-back pain affects up to 53.9 per cent of elite female pacers, while shoulder pain impacts up to 46.5 per cent.
Take Pooja’s case. Long viewed as India’s premier pace-bowling all-rounder, she has spent years navigating a relentless cycle of injury and return — most recently enduring an 18-month layoff following surgery to repair a torn supraspinatus tendon in her bowling shoulder, a textbook casualty in a sport where rotator cuff-related pain accounts for 59 per cent of all time-loss shoulder injuries among seamers. She’s also had previous surgeries on both knees.
During her recovery, Royal Challengers Bengaluru signed her for the WPL strictly as a batter. Working under England seam legend Anya Shrubsole, she gained a vital psychological lifeline.
“My pace was all over the place, but RCB told me my batting was enough,” she recalls. “That confidence came at a time when I felt inadequate for this game.”
“Injuries toh hoga (injuries are inevitable). Look at the spurt in matches and series now. We played two or three series tops, and then there was the odd year with ICC events or tournaments like the Asia Cup. Now that number has tripled, and so has the intensity,” Jhulan argues.
There’s an incongruence in the way injuries are handled in this environment, according to the veteran pacer.
“The issue is that players get injured, work on recovery and slot right back into the national side. Game time there becomes wonky, and you give it your all in the odd chance you’re given. That actually isn’t good for your recovery. This is where the domestic system should be used. Go back, play games and work your way out of the injury. We have the infrastructure to monitor and tweak things there, in synergy with the national side.”
Learning from the best
India has plenty to learn from its two main international adversaries.
Australia, easily the mecca of pace in women’s cricket purely because of the quantity of credible pacers it regularly produces, has more granular initiatives such as Project130. A partnership between Cricket New South Wales and the University of Technology Sydney (UTS), its stated objective is to plug the research gap that pushes cricket to condition female bowlers according to frameworks designed for men. The venture aims to help female fast bowlers reach the 130 kmph-and-above spectrum and stay there, while keeping injuries to a minimum.
England’s Women’s Pace Bowling Programme, launched in 2024, has also been working closely with tier-one counties to groom and induct pace-bowling talent into the mainstream. An important additional focus of the initiative is identifying taller athletes transitioning from sports such as netball and basketball, and tapping into their natural potential for bounce and, maybe even, raw pace.
It helps that their domestic teams are closely intertwined with franchise systems and, by extension, the national side’s interests. The Women’s Big Bash has State-based teams, making the pathways uncomplicated, as does England with its county setup.
India’s WPL, in this regard, stands out. With just five teams carrying the ambitions of a nation of 1.4 billion, calls to add another team (or two) got a renewed push after the recently concluded auction for the 2027 edition.
Ananya is still undecided about whether the WPL is purely a boon for Indian pace bowling.
“In the initial stages, not many franchises looked at grooming as a priority or at building players over four to five seasons within the setup. It’s a new tournament, and teams are still finding their feet. We’ve started seeing that change slowly now. The next couple of years, and perhaps the addition of teams, will make a difference to how much ownership teams take of their players’ growth arcs.”
The road ahead
Mason hopes the system will eventually render someone like him redundant, where bowlers won’t need him anymore — something a coaching-intensive setup like India’s can adopt. He cites Lauren Bell’s example while illustrating how a bowler who never really set her own fields is now a free-thinking phenom. Likewise, he cautions against changing bowling techniques for the sake of it, suggesting intervention only when necessary. Both are areas where Indian systems still have considerable catching up to do at the domestic level.
Neetu and Jhulan, apart from sharing an almost military-level precision in their bowling, also believe players should learn to deploy their skills on flatter tracks without the usual creases on the forehead.
“The modern game values runs, which is why these wickets are a lot more popular now. I’m not praising myself, but back in my time, people used to say that David could turn the ball even on a cement wicket. I feel even today, despite it being a batting wicket, as a bowler, you can still do well there,” Neetu says.
“International cricket is played on flat tracks, right? The younger kids coming through need to hone their skills on flat tracks, so let that be an added challenge. Spinners can maximise turners, and seamers can make use of moisture early in the morning to effect some damage. We see bowlers often clueless on flat strips. We want to avoid that,” Jhulan adds.
She also vehemently denies that height is a prerequisite for a pacer, despite an Australian study titled ‘In-match analysis of elite female cricket pace bowlers’ identifying height as the single best physical predictor of release speed. It explains that 53 per cent of speed variation in female fast bowlers is due to longer lever arms. Taller bowlers also have higher run-up velocities.
“Look at Shabnim Ismail [the South African pacer who bowled the fastest recorded delivery in women’s cricket, at 132.1 kmph during WPL 2024, according to official broadcaster JioHotstar]. She’s not tall, but she bowls so fast. She is a genuine seam bowler. She runs so smoothly. I often feel there are springs under her feet,” she adds.
A new appreciation for speed also brings with it a rush of people claiming they can help players go up a few gears.
“First, assess whether the action is injury-inducing. Once the action becomes safely repeatable, drills for fast bowling, such as brace-leg or arm-delay routines, can be done. Posture can be fixed as well, and we can safely see a 4-5 kmph increase. That’s the maximum you should aim for. Many academies claim to make a 15 kmph increase possible. Do not fall for that. Fast bowling is a natural thing, and you must listen to your body,” Nagesh warns.
Most importantly, Jhulan believes, it is perhaps high time India separated its pace pool by format to ensure smoother team outcomes and, more importantly, player welfare.
“We need 10-15 players in a seam-bowling pool whom India can use rotationally. Place players in ODI, T20I and Test duties, respecting their strengths and limitations. Batting roles are so well-defined. Do that with bowlers too. And the push India had a few years ago to make the top and middle order bowl as well was novel. It gives the captain options and contingency plans,” she explains.
Pace bowling in the women’s game has long needed greater intent. The next step may not be finding another Jhulan, but building a pool deep enough that India never again depends on one. Only then will the chase for 130 kmph become realistic.

Best Buy is selling Blu-rays directly through its website and in physical stores again after exiting Blu-ray and DVD sales in 2023.
The Best Buy website’s movie section currently lists 15 Blu-rays (including one two-pack) that are “sold & shipped by Best Buy.” New titles available include The Odyssey (2026), Project Hail Mary (2026), Supergirl (2026), Super Mario Galaxy (2026), and Obsession (2025). Best Buy is also selling some older titles on Blu-ray, including It’s a Wonderful Life (1943), Saving Private Ryan (1998), and The Godfather (1972).
Most of the Blu-rays are available for purchase online and can be delivered to an address or picked up at a Best Buy store within a few days. As of this writing, The Odyssey appears to be in stock at Best Buy stores, as it’s currently listed as available for pickup within as little as an hour.
Ars Technica reached out to Best Buy to ask whether customers can expect the store to continue selling Blu-rays moving forward.
In October 2023, Best Buy announced that it would stop selling Blu-rays and DVDs online and in stores starting in 2024.
“To state the obvious, the way we watch movies and TV shows is much different today than it was decades ago. Making this change gives us more space and opportunity to bring customers new and innovative tech for them to explore, discover and enjoy,” a Best Buy spokesperson said in a statement issued at the time.
Last year, the Best Buy website started selling Blu-rays and DVDs from third parties via its online marketplace.
Numerous other companies have reduced or ended their Blu-ray and/or DVD businesses in recent years. Target, for instance, only sells the discs in stores during special occasions (like holidays or for big releases) now. Disney outsourced its DVD and Blu-ray business to Sony, which subsequently stopped selling recordable Blu-rays to people, and DVD rental company Redbox went out of business.

Despite being entirely preventable through vaccination, tetanus continues to claim tens of thousands of lives globally each year, introduction of the domestically manufactured Td vaccine is expected to strengthen adult immunisation and sustain protection under the National Immunisation Programme. | Image used for representational purpose only
| Photo Credit: REUTERS
Tetanus and diphtheria are two preventable diseases. And still, they surface years after childhood vaccinations. As antibody levels decline over time, especially against diphtheria, could the introduction of the Td vaccine signal a crucial point in closing this long-overlooked gap in adult vaccination and protection?
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), maternal and neonatal tetanus has declined significantly over the past two decades. But thousands of people still die from the disease each year, with newborns being especially at risk, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Diphtheria also continues to cause outbreaks in areas where immunity wanes or vaccine coverage is insufficient.

Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo?
- Published
As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments.
She is thinking about getting around more easily.
The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast.
For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient.
"Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.
But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport.
It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo.
Under agreements brokered by US President Donald Trump, DR Congo and neighbouring Rwanda have committed to greater economic cooperation, including more transparent mineral supply chains and regional infrastructure development.
The wider plan envisages linking these initiatives to the railway, which transports minerals from Central Africa to Western markets via Angola, rather than east to China as most do currently.
The hope is that formalising the mineral trade and encouraging investment could help curb illicit markets that have helped finance armed groups and fuel instability.
But can a railway built to move minerals to global markets also deliver peace and prosperity?
The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito.
Its importance has grown as demand for copper and cobalt rises, driven partly by the global transition to cleaner energy, as both are critical ingredients for all kinds of electrical components.
"The timing matters," says Johannesburg-based political risk analyst Wellington Muzengeza
"Electrification and the energy transition have increased the strategic importance of copper, cobalt and reliable mineral supply chains."
DR Congo is the world's largest producer of cobalt and one of its biggest copper producers, along with neighbouring Zambia. The US sees the corridor as a means to diversify mineral supplies and reduce reliance on China, which dominates much of the world's processing capacity.
A US-DR Congo strategic partnership identifies the route from the Congolese town of Sakania to Lobito as a priority for mineral exports, while the economic framework agreed by DR Congo and Rwanda envisages connecting regional infrastructure and trade initiatives to the corridor.
The project has attracted over $750m (£570m), including funding backed by the US International Development Finance Corporation and the Development Bank of Southern Africa to upgrade railway tracks, signalling systems and trains.
The railway, built in 1902 under Portuguese colonial rule, was originally designed to transport goods and minerals from Central Africa to the Atlantic coast. After years of disruption during Angola's civil war, it was rebuilt and fully reopened in 2015.
The US first got involved in the project under former President Joe Biden but backing has continued under Trump.
At Lobito's mineral terminal, the renewed ambitions are already visible.
When the BBC visited, a train carrying about 12,000 tonnes of copper cathodes from DR Congo had arrived. Workers moved the refined copper sheets into a warehouse before they were loaded on to ships bound for international markets, mostly the US.
The cargo is handled by Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), which has a 30-year concession to operate freight services along the corridor and manage the mineral terminal.
Chief operating officer Nicholas Gregoir says freight volumes have more than doubled since the company took over in January 2024.
LAR expects to transport about 200,000 tonnes of copper through the corridor in 2026.
For mining companies, the railway offers a shorter route to international markets.
"The Lobito Corridor is the shortest route for both Zambia and the DRC," to the Atlantic, says Kátila Vanessa Monteiro da Silva Neto, executive director of the Lobito Port Authority.
Zambia, Africa's second-largest copper producer, also plans to connect its Copperbelt to Lobito through a proposed 830km (515 mile)-railway.
But a more efficient route to market does not automatically translate into economic transformation.
"Joining a corridor is not the same as industrialising," Muzengeza says. "The test is not simply whether Zambia gains another route to the sea. It is whether that route helps build a stronger economy."
Some Angolans believe the railway's greatest value could lie in what it offers businesses and communities beyond mining.
"I call it a corridor of development," says businessman Adérito Areias.
The railway passes through some of Angola's most productive agricultural regions.
Better transport links could help farmers reach larger markets and reduce losses.
"If there isn't an artery carrying products from the interior to where there is demand, those products simply rot where they are produced," Areias says.
But the challenge is turning that ambition into reality.
The Port of Lobito handled about 1.8 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, of which around 158,000 tonnes was minerals. Its mineral terminal can handle up to 3.6 million tonnes annually.
"The port already has the capacity," says Neto. "What we need now is sufficient railway capacity and rolling stock."
For residents along the route, the benefits have been immediate.
State-owned railway operator Caminho de Ferro de Benguela (CFB), which runs passenger services, carried a record 1.6 million passengers in 2025.
LAR says it directly employs nearly 1,000 people, 98% of them Angolan.
"This job allows me to support my family," says Domingos Canhama, a father of four and a forklift operator at CFB.
"I can put food on the table, maintain a home and help support my father," he says.
Muzengeza argues that the bigger opportunity is developing local businesses in engineering, maintenance, warehousing and agricultural processing.
"Businesses in Angola need access to the railway, not just proximity to it. That means feeder roads, electricity, storage and predictable services," he says.
But can minerals and their movement along the railways line help deliver peace to eastern DR Congo, where the battle for control of mineral resources has fuelled decades of conflict?
Most recently, this has seen the M23 rebel group seize control of many mineral-rich areas.
The Congolese government says neighbouring Rwanda is backing the M23 in order to gain access to DR Congo's mineral wealth. Despite overwhelming evidence, Rwanda denies backing the M23.
The Trump-backed agreements between DR Congo and Rwanda seek to promote transparent mineral supply chains, cross-border investment and regional infrastructure, with the aim of ensuring mineral wealth does not finance armed groups.
"The US wants reliable access to minerals essential to defence, advanced technology and energy systems, while reducing dependence on supply chains in which China has substantial influence," says Muzengeza, the political risk analyst
"Lobito is therefore more than a railway but an infrastructure that can reshape trade routes and commercial power."
At a meeting in Paris in November, DR Congo urged the US to turn its strategic partnership into tangible investments, arguing that success should be measured by completed projects rather than signed agreements.
"We want the partnership to support local mineral processing, electricity access for households and businesses and peace in the east," said DR Congo's Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba.
Even if more minerals move through formal channels, better infrastructure alone would not resolve the political and security tensions driving the conflict.
There is also the question of who captures the wealth. Much of the copper and cobalt transported from DR Congo through Lobito is destined for processing and manufacturing outside Africa.
While Angola can earn transit fees and create logistics jobs, much of the higher-value activity takes place elsewhere.
"When you export raw materials, you are also exporting jobs and knowledge," Angola's Foreign Affairs Minister Téte António tells the BBC.
Areias shares that concern.
"We should not export lithium but export batteries," he says, arguing that the corridor should help develop local processing and manufacturing rather than simply accelerate raw material exports.
Back in Catumbela, such debates can feel distant from everyday life.
For Julia, the railway already means cheaper journeys and easier movement.
But its ultimate success will depend on whether it can deliver more than faster mineral exports.
Whether it can also help secure lasting peace in eastern DR Congo, where the minerals are mined, remains the bigger test.
