- The criminal profile in GTA 6 tracks how professionally or recklessly Jason and Lucia behave as criminals.
- The four different states of the GTA 6 criminal profile are Professional, Aggressive, Violent, and Psycho.
- Jason and Lucia have separate criminal profiles, and their individual behavior can affect parts of the story.
In most GTA games, from GTA San Andreas to GTA 5, you might steal a car, rob a store, and accidentally flatten out half a sidewalk full of pedestrians. GTA 6, however, lets you put a little more thought behind the kind of criminal you want to become. So, here is a detailed explanation of the GTA 6 Criminal Profile mechanic, including all five ratings, focus bonuses, and consequences.
What is the GTA 6 Criminal Profile?
The criminal profile in GTA 6 is a new system that tracks how Jason and Lucia conduct themselves as criminals.
There is a neat distinction between the criminal profile in GTA 6 and the honor system in Red Dead Redemption 2. While the latter is based on Arthur Morgan’s morality, Rockstar has taken a different approach this time around. The Criminal Profile in GTA 6 is based on how professional you are as a criminal.
The criminal profile system in GTA 6 considers several factors, including how often you kill civilians, attack police officers, use lethal force against enemies, harm animals, and cause unnecessary destruction.
Moreover, this system is a metric that measures how clean your crime was. There is no good or evil here. In simple terms, if you leave the crime scene without a trace, you’re an expert; but if you leave after a bloodbath, you’re an irredeemable psychopath.
The criminal profile mechanic in GTA 6 also appears to be separate from Jason and Lucia’s relationship system.
GTA 6 Criminal Profile States and Ratings
There are five different states or ratings for the criminal profile in GTA 6. While the first four of these stages can be reversed, the final one is permanent. The five states in the criminal profile are as follows, and they are represented by different devil GTA 6 icons.
| Criminal Profile Icon | Name | Description | 
|---|---|---|
|  | Professional | Avoiding unnecessary violence and completing crimes with minimal casualties | 
|  | Hardened | Using force when necessary without deliberately creating chaos | 
|  | Violent | Frequently resorting to lethal force against enemies, civilians, and defenseless animals | 
|  | Psycho | Causing widespread destruction and killing innocent people and defenseless animals | 
|  | Irredeemable | The final criminal rating for characters who continue the Psycho behavior | 
Here’s a detailed description of what all the criminal ratings mean in GTA 6.
Professional
Professional is the most disciplined criminal profile in GTA 6. It rewards players who prefer stealth, non-lethal takedowns, and controlled approaches. Here, you don’t shoot everybody in the room; rather, you intimidate or restrain them using a weapon in GTA 6 and complete the job.
To maintain this rank, avoid killing enemies unnecessarily, use dialogue to defuse confrontations, and stay undetected whenever possible. However, if combat becomes unavoidable, you can use Jason’s ability in GTA 6 to focus on arms or legs to incapacitate the enemies with non-lethal moves.
The biggest advantage of this profile is that you can still surrender to the police when an encounter goes wrong. So, you have more room to make mistakes and work your way back up.
Hardened
Hardened is the middle ground between a professional criminal and someone who continuously resorts to violence. If you repeatedly choose physical force when a calmer approach was available, you push Jason or Lucia to this state.
For instance, killing an armed opponent during a confrontation won’t necessarily make you a Violent criminal but will push you up to the Hardened state. Similar to Professional, this state rewards you with more Focus for non-lethal incapacitations and stealth encounters.
The difference between a Professional and an Aggressive state is knowing the difference between violence being an option and treating it as the first thing on the menu.
Violent
Violent is where your criminal behavior starts becoming considerably more destructive, and you’re no longer concerned about avoiding casualties. You reach this state when you start resorting to lethal force frequently against enemies, police officers, and civilians.
Rockstar has already shown how GTA 6’s gore and dismemberment are significantly more brutal, so turning every robbery into a massacre can create harsh consequences. However, there’s still a distinction between Violent and Psycho, as the latter is reached when you harm defenseless individuals without any reason.
During this state, you earn bonus Focus for aggressive combat, like performing more headshots, instead of moving covertly.
Psycho
Psycho is one of the most dangerous criminal profile ratings in GTA 6. You might reach this stage when you’re consistently causing excessive violence and chaotic behavior.
If your everyday heists and other missions include going far beyond what is necessary, you’re probably heading toward this stage. Repeatedly killing people without a reason, attacking those who pose no threat, or turning minor encounters into shootouts could push your character toward this end.
In this state, you earn a focus bonus for every headshot you make during your missions. You can still return to more professional stages, even after reaching Psycho, simply by conducting crimes in the most efficient manner without raising alarms or killing the innocent.
Irredeemable
Irredeemable is the final and most consequential criminal profile rank in GTA 6 that you can reach if you like to play the classic old-school way. This is the point of no return for both Jason and Lucia that permanently breaks the criminal profile as you know it.
You can reach this stage by continuing to commit excessive violence after becoming a Psycho. Repeatedly killing civilians, destroying vehicles with groups of people nearby, and causing widespread destruction can push your character here.
So, unlike Red Dead Redemption 2, you can’t just finish half of the GTA 6 map and then repair your reputation by greeting strangers for five minutes. There are no focus bonuses at this point.
Moreover, before reaching Irredeemable, time slows down, and the Psycho icon begins to crack. You’ll then receive three warning stages as the icon deteriorates before it finally changes into the dark gray Irredeemable stage. Now, the only way to return to normal gameplay is to load a saved file from before the transformation.
What Raises the Criminal Profile in GTA 6
One of the most important things is to understand that committing crimes won’t automatically make your criminal profile worse.
For example, you carry out a restrained approach that includes completing a robbery without killing people, avoiding collateral damage, and leaving once you’ve completed the objective. The money is secured, the escape route is clear, and there is minimal evidence of Jason and Lucia being at the crime scene. This is a completely Professional approach, and it won’t raise the criminal profile stage.
Whereas, if you see a GTA 6 NPC with a weapon and violently confront them, decide to knock out the cashier who gave you a funny look, and begin a war in the neighborhood, it will drag your profile to the Violent or even Psycho stages.
Does Criminal Profile Affect Jason and Lucia Differently?
Yes, another interesting detail about the GTA 6 criminal profile is that Jason and Lucia do not share a single criminal profile. Each character can develop their own state.
This means you might make Jason a highly disciplined professional while developing Lucia with a more violent reputation, or vice versa. This can be interesting, because Rockstar has already given the two separate identities. The approach might suit them more, with Jason being a trained army veteran and Lucia being a fighter.
This makes the GTA 6 criminal profile more interesting than simply slapping an honor meter. That concludes our guide on GTA 6’s criminal profile. If you want to learn more about other major mechanics, the GTA 6 wanted system guide is there to help you out.
Is GTA 6’s criminal profile the same as Red Dead Redemption 2’s honor system?
No, the criminal profile in GTA 6 is inspired by some of the ideas behind the RDR 2 honor system, but it is not a morality meter. It focuses on the type of criminal you are and how efficiently you carry out the missions.
What are the GTA 6 criminal profile states?
The four standard states in the GTA 6 criminal profile are Professional, Aggressive, Violent, and Psycho, all of which are reversible. However, beyond this, there’s a fifth Irredeemable state that can permanently lock the profile for the whole game, meaning you cannot reverse it for either Jason or Lucia.
Do Jason and Lucia have different criminal profiles in GTA 6?
Yes, Jason and Lucia have separate criminal profiles. That means if you consider developing a character solely on an aggressive side, it can later affect how the main story unfolds.

By any measure, it is one of the most extraordinary political stories of our age: a shy Italian girl locks eyes with the scion of an Indian political family, falls instantly and steadfastly in love, “transplanting herself” as a result, suffers soul-shattering tragedies, then takes the reins of power in the world’s largest democracy. It is a life that spans the extremes of privilege and distress, and half a century of seismic national history.
No wonder publishers have been keen to secure the memoirs of the famously guarded Sonia Gandhi, soon to turn 80. Yet when the chance came, the deal with the country’s biggest publisher, Penguin Random House India, fell through at the last minute over what it termed “an impasse over a particular issue” in the text, with HarperCollins stepping into the breach. For those unfamiliar with the sensitive political context, the Nehru-Gandhi family has been in charge of India for about half the eight decades since independence – and the principal opposition to Narendra Modi’s prickly BJP regime for the past 12 years.
As it turns out, Belonging does not read as incendiary. It errs, rather, towards discretion and legacy-building. It is also, at its best, a heartbreaking story of love and loss.
Gandhi’s voice is measured and generally frill-free. Flourishes do accompany the meet-cute at a Greek restaurant in Cambridge in the mid-1960s that sets off the story. “That January Sunday, which was to change my life,” she writes, “the sky [was] a beautiful azure dotted with puffy white clouds as in a Tiepolo fresco.” The introduction to fellow student Rajiv Gandhi was “a bolt of lightning”.
And, as in a film, there is parental resistance. Sonia’s father, a businessman who worked in construction in a small Italian town, is a second world war veteran, nicknamed Maino the Lion. A 1998 New Yorker profile by Patrick French, briefly a collaborator on Belonging, had him down as “an unrepentant fascist” until his death. Well, was he? We don’t get to find out. Wherever expedient, Gandhi maintains her strategic silence.
Stefano Maino, at any rate, is “padre padrone” – literally, “father master”. When he hears about his middle daughter’s love interest, he brings “his fist down on his writing table” with a shout of “Basta!” And yet, he buys her a ticket to India the moment she turns 21.
On the boy’s side is the person who would come to be described as the world’s most powerful woman, Indira Gandhi, the daughter of India’s first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru. Barely has Sonia landed in Delhi than Indira decides the pair must wed (the news reaches the Mainos via radio; Signor Maino stays away). Indira then manages Sonia’s first pregnancy, directs the name-giving ceremony – you get the picture. Gandhi refers to her, factually, as “my mother-in-law”, but, subverting the stereotype, she becomes a devoted daughter. Walking us through her induction into elite Indian family life, she draws an affectionate portrait of this formidable 20th-century figure.
But family and party allegiance are a distorting lens through which to view history. Charged events, such as Indira’s crushing of a huge railway strike, acquire a benign gloss. The 21 tumultuous months of the 1975 Emergency – which saw members of the opposition arrested, civil liberties curtailed, the press censored, while a despotic nepo-baby (Sanjay, Indira’s younger son) ran amok – are rendered with a brisk calm. Tenderness is reserved for the repercussions on the family in its subsequent period out of power.
Sanjay’s death at 33, just after Indira’s return to power in 1980, leaves the matriarch broken. “In her eyes [Rajiv] was the only one who could come to her rescue.” Gandhi does not interrogate the hereditary approach to democratic politics, but she does recount, affectingly, the fight to protect herself and Rajiv – a commercial pilot with no greater ambitions – and their two children from the inferno.
In the book’s strongest scene, she waits disoriented in a crowded hospital in 1984, “shivering under my dressing gown”, having ferried her mother-in-law’s bullet-ridden body there. Indira was slain by her Sikh bodyguards in revenge for ordering the army into the Golden Temple, Sikhism’s holiest site. As Rajiv embraces her with the words “they want me to be sworn in as prime minister”, Gandhi feels “a rage welling up deep inside me”. “They will kill you too!” she says. “They will kill me anyway,” he replies. The “they” is unspecified, and gives these pages an air of foretold tragedy.
Rajiv’s eventful term plays out under this death cloud. It starts with a pogrom against Sikhs, spearheaded by Congress leaders. Gandhi goes some length to eulogise her husband’s tenure: in reality, it was a troubled and contradictory record. Rajiv was 40, severely underqualified, and grieving. Miscalculations abounded, among them clumsy religious manoeuvring that played into the Hindu-nationalist BJP’s hands, and a military entanglement in Sri Lanka designed to end the civil war with Tamil separatists.
And that death cloud never blows way. The children are withdrawn from school; Gandhi, perpetually anxious, finds her hands trembling in public; Rajiv is once shot at. When he loses the election his successor vindictively withdraws his special security cover. Their son Rahul (the current leader of the opposition) predicts the worst. At a rally in Tamil Nadu in 1991, a Tamil Tiger operative makes to place a garland around Rajiv, then 46, with explosives strapped around her body.
The graphic photograph of the aftermath of that scene is seared into Indian memory. Thanks to the vigilance of her children, Gandhi has never seen it. “I had become the child to be protected, they the parents,” she writes, in a wrenching section. Years later, when she collapses in Japan, a nurse is startled to find her grown children lying on either side of her on the small hospital bed.
Gandhi’s first reaction on hearing the news about Rajiv? “I wanted to die.” Gradually though, she picks up the smithereens of her life. As the remaining Gandhi elder, she picks up the pieces of the splintering Congress party, too.There are few parallels to a life as singular as this. A century ago, Congress had its first foreign-born female president, the British theosophist Annie Besant; farther afield, Janet Jagan, the American-born Jewish wife of Cheddi Jagan herself became president of Guyana – but both women were political activists to begin with. Gandhi, in her words, “had no right – except for the fact that I carried the family name”.
The exhortations to Gandhi to take over the party reveal plenty about Congress culture, and they are eventually successful: the spectator becomes the player. We watch her bone up on her Hindi, lead campaigns, stitch up alliances (including with a party sympathetic to the Tamil Tigers), and combat the BJP, which brands her, among other things, a “Monica Lewinsky” who would establish a “Rome Raj”. In 2004, she leads an alliance of parties to victory.
To her children’s horror, Gandhi is badgered into nearly accepting the post of prime minister. Instead she handpicks a candidate, Manmohan Singh, while keeping charge of the party (eventually leading it for a staggering 22 years) and chairing the ruling coalition as well as an advisory council that keeps a hand on policy levers.
“It had been my choice to become Indian,” she reflects after the long night of the soul that leads her to decline the premiership – a source of fascinated speculation over the years. “I made it out of love for a man, but that love came to encompass his family and his country. And it was this love for India that had demanded the most from me.”
Belonging comes into its own when unpacking those demands, and showing the transition from grief to its successor emotion, resilience.

Omnichannel fast fashion brand Style Union’s parent Nexon Omniverse Ltd has raised ₹485 Cr (nearly $51.8 Mn) in its Series E funding round co-led by Venturi Partners and Elev8 Venture Partners. In a statement, the platform said that the round comprised both primary and secondary components. Style Union plans to utilise the fresh capital to expand its offline store network across key metros in West and North India. "This is a defining moment for Nexon Omniverse and for Style Union… With their backing, we will take Style Union beyond its southern base into West and North India and into millions of new households across the country." said Nexon Omniverse whole-time director Rajesh Seth. Founded in 2022 by former operations head of Future Retail Rakesh Biyani and his wife Ekta Biyani, Style Union sells apparels for men, women and kids through its own website as well as offline stores. With its core footprint in South India, the brand operates 200 physical stores across Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, among other cities. The platform claims to have closed FY26 with over ₹1,150 Cr in revenue. It competes with the likes of Tata-owned Zudio, V-Mart and Vishal Mega Mart. The funding comes as a growing number of Indian D2C fashion and lifestyle brands are expanding beyond online channels and building omnichannel businesses. Startups are increasingly using physical stores to improve brand discovery and customer experience while continuing to leverage ecommerce for scale. On the back of this, the space continues to attract healthy investor interest. Israeli military launches rare ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
- Published
Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents.
Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.
Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety.
It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.
Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".
"IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added.
Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement.
In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says.
Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.
A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.
- Israel moves Yellow Line deeper into Gaza, satellite images show 
  - Published16 January
Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second to the north in Gaza City, and the third in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.
The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".
At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.
Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.
The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.
The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

After reports that the 2027 summit of NATO heads of state in Albania was canceled, a rumor spread that the organization had canceled all upcoming summits to prevent U.S. President Donald Trump from sharing intelligence with Russia President Vladimir Putin.
Putin opposes NATO, which he sees as a direct threat to Russia's security and influence. In a 2022 speech, he said the expansion of NATO was the reason for his invasion of Ukraine.
Several social media posts claimed the reason for the summits' alleged cancelation was Trump's lack of integrity. One X post said "NATO has canceled all upcoming summits until Trump leaves office, amid concerns that sensitive information shared during these meetings could be passed along to Vladimir Putin" (archived):
Meanwhile, Snopes readers searched the website and emailed, seeking clarity on the rumor.
It is true that NATO reportedly said it would skip its 2027 leadership summit, which was initially scheduled to take place in Albania, according to a Nov. 15 article by The Associated Press.
The article cited tensions among NATO member nations regarding the U.S.-Israel war on Iran, Russia's ongoing war on Ukraine and disagreements about defense spending. NATO members agreed to spend at least 3.5% of their gross domestic product on defense by 2035; as of 2025, only seven of the 32 countries reached or surpassed that level, a NATO report showed.
It is also true that an Oct. 21 report by The Atlantic said tensions at the North American Aerospace Defense Command — NORAD, a U.S.-Canadian military organization designed to cooperate on air and maritime defense — were boiling over. The story said Canada was having difficulty staffing its NORAD posts due to its personnel's distrust of the U.S. NORAD's headquarters are located in Colorado Springs, Colorado.
However, it appeared people spreading the rumor had conflated parts of these two different stories, though it's worth noting that neither report cited leaks to Putin.
Snopes found no evidence that concerns Trump would share NATO intelligence with Putin were the reason for canceling the 2027 summit. In addition, it was unclear whether a NATO leadership summit in 2028 — the last year of Trump's second term — would also be canceled.
For these reasons, we've left the claim unrated.
In response to our inquiry about the rumor, a White House spokesperson told Snopes via email that it was "obviously fake."
We also reached out to NATO, NORAD and the office of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama seeking more details and await responses.
NATO summits do not happen every year
It is worth noting that NATO leadership summits have not taken place every year since the organization's foundation in 1949. The organization has skipped several years. Meanwhile, some years saw more than one summit, for example in February 2022, in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine, followed by another in Brussels a month later and a third in Madrid in June 2022.
Meanwhile, ministerial meetings happen more frequently. In December 2026, foreign affairs ministers of the member countries (including the U.S. secretary of state) are scheduled to gather in Brussels, Belgium, where NATO is headquartered. Defense ministers also met in June 2026.
Further, such summits can be elaborate and expensive affairs due to security concerns, the AP cited NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte as saying.
Meanwhile the article in The Atlantic suggested the distrust among Canadian military staff regarding NORAD was the symptom of a larger breakdown in military cooperation between Canada and the U.S. Among several affronts to the U.S.' northern neighbor, the story cited Trump's threats to annex Canada and the tariffs he imposed on Canadian products.
For further reading, Snopes has covered several rumors about NATO, including the claim that one of its officials said Europe would take every U.S. base if Trump annexed Greenland.

As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit
When the White House announced big improvements in the number of people dying from fatal drug overdoses earlier this week, officials pointed to hopeful new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showing U.S. drug deaths have plunged to their lowest level in roughly a decade, saving nearly 50,000 lives each year.
But leading drug policy researchers say the White House statement also made misleading claims about the timing and cause of the remarkable public health success when it said that gains occurred primarily over the last 18 months due to policies enacted under President Trump's leadership.
"The historic decline in drug overdose deaths demonstrates that America is unequivocally winning the fight against illicit drugs," White House Office of National Drug Control Policy director Sara Carter said in a statement.
Carter credited heightened border security under Trump and claims of success dismantling "narco-terrorist" organizations for the recovery. "Critically, this represents a an approximately 41.5% decrease in total drug overdose deaths compared to the peak under the previous administration," the statement said.
What the White House failed to disclose is that declines in overdose fatalities began much earlier, under the Biden administration, with most of the gains occurring before Trump returned to office.
"Since the spring of 2023, we have seen a steady decline in overdose deaths," said Vanda Felbab-Brown, a drug policy expert at the Brookings Institution. "The fact that it has been sustained is very important."
Fentanyl crisis on Biden's watch, then a pivot toward fewer deaths
According to CDC data, reductions in drug deaths began in 2023 and have continued steadily for at least 39 consecutive months — not 18 months as the ONDCP statement said. By the time Biden left office, fatal overdoses had already dropped by roughly one-third, an improvement described by addiction experts at the time as unprecedented.
Nabarun Dasgupta, a street drug researcher at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, was one of the first scientists to detect the stunning drop in overdose deaths. He said the trend toward fewer deaths began in some regions and among some demographic groups as early as 2021 and rapidly gained momentum nationwide.
"It was really the period early 2024 through spring 2025 where we were seeing the greatest rate of decline that we've ever seen," Dasgupta said.
Deaths from fentanyl smuggled into the U.S. from Mexico first began to rise in 2013 during President Obama's time in office and accelerated during Trump's first term. Fentanyl overdoses spiked sharply the first two years of Biden's presidency, during the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite progress, fentanyl remains the leading cause of drug deaths nationwide.
Dasgupta, Felbab-Brown and other and addiction experts credit the Biden administration for rolling out policy responses that included wider access to healthcare, making the opioid overdose medication naloxone more readily available, and negotiating a deal with China that disrupted the flow of industrial chemicals used to make fentanyl.
The Biden team also scored significant drug interdiction wins against the Mexican cartels that smuggle fentanyl. "We have certainly been seeing over many years, going back to the Biden administration, important efforts to crack down against them," said Felbab-Brown.
Dasgupta and Felbab-Brown both said improvements in reducing drug mortality have continued under Trump. They said it's important to have an accurate timeline of the overdose crisis because researchers are still trying to understand why deaths involving fentanyl surged and why so many fewer people are now dying.
White House on Biden role in declines
NPR asked the White House about progress in the fentanyl fight under Biden. In an emailed statement, ONDCP director Carter, a former podcaster, journalist and Fox News contributor, blamed Biden for failing to secure the U.S.-Mexico border and for allowing drug deaths to surge in the first place.
"While drug overdose deaths eventually began to decline following the peak, the Biden Administration doesn't get to take credit for overseeing the highest drug overdose numbers in history, then bringing them down from their own failure," Carter said.
Responding to CDC data showing drug deaths began to plummet much earlier than stated the White House announcement, Carter said "this could be misinterpreted as progress on a graph, but it was not progress."
According to Carter, the Trump administration is now well-positioned to build on overdose death reductions made over the last three years, in part by maintaining border security and by continuing to "relentlessly attack" drug gangs.
"We are dismantling and eliminating the violent cartels and drug trafficking organizations through coordinated operations," she said.
But Felbab-Brown at Brookings said she doesn't share the Trump administration's confidence that there has been significant progress "dismantling and eliminating" narco-terrorist organizations.
"I cannot think of one narco-terrorist organization that has been dismantled," she said. "They all continue operating and they are all very strong. They all continue smuggling drugs."
Military experts have also questioned the effectiveness, and legality, of Trump's ongoing strikes against civilian boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, described as smuggling vessels by the Pentagon.
Dasgupta, the addiction researcher at UNC, said he's also concerned about whether progress reducing drug deaths can be sustained next year as the Trump administration implements deep cuts to Medicaid passed by the Republican Congress.
The Congressional Budget Office has estimated the cuts could mean as many as 10 million Americans losing access to health insurance coverage.
"Medicaid is the largest funder of addiction services in the United States," Dasgupta said. "Cutting Medicaid eligibility or making it harder to access forms of effective addiction treatment is guaranteed to leave people out in the cold."

A 29-year-old woman from Manuguru, who was rushed to hospital after suddenly losing movement in her right arm and leg, regained significant mobility within hours after doctors at two government hospitals coordinated to administer emergency stroke treatment within the critical window.
Rajani’s ordeal began on an ordinary morning when she suddenly developed slurred speech and complete weakness on her right side. Recognising the signs of an acute stroke, doctors acted swiftly to prevent permanent brain damage.
She was first taken to Area Hospital, Manuguru, where Sai Kumar, a General Medicine specialist, identified the symptoms and arranged an urgent referral to Area Hospital, Bhadrachalam, nearly 60 km away, for emergency treatment.
Recognising the narrow window for intervention, M. Ramakrishna, medical superintendent of Area Hospital, Manuguru, coordinated directly with Tejaswi Gadde, physician at Area Hospital, Bhadrachalam, to facilitate her transfer.
At Bhadrachalam, doctors immediately conducted a CT scan to rule out bleeding in the brain before administering clot-dissolving medication. With Rajani still within the recommended 4.5-hour treatment window, doctors administered intravenous Tenecteplase at 2 p.m., around 3.5 hours after the symptoms began, said G. Ravi Babu, District Coordinator of Hospital Services (DCHS), Bhadradri Kothagudem.
The response to treatment was encouraging. Before the intervention, Rajani had no detectable movement in her right arm or leg, with her muscle power recorded at 0/5. Following thrombolysis, her muscle strength improved, and she regained the ability to move the affected limbs against resistance, though full strength is yet to return.
She remains under close neurological observation. The case also highlights the availability of advanced emergency treatment in government hospitals serving remote and tribal areas. The thrombolytic medication, which costs around ₹45,000 in the market, was administered to Rajani free of cost.
Dr. Ravi Babu appreciated the doctors, nurses and supporting staff at both hospitals for their prompt decisions and coordination. “Such interventions demonstrate how teamwork between government healthcare institutions can help deliver advanced, life-saving treatment even in geographically remote areas,” he said.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”
The PSA is voiced by Academy Award® and Emmy Award® nominee Steve Carrell, who voices the character Gru in the Despicable Me franchise. The PSA will be localized into multiple languages including Spanish, French, Portuguese and Arabic, among others.
“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. It is an honor to partner with the WHO and UN Foundation to remind people around the globe to protect themselves, each other and our communities during this pandemic. I am also appreciative to Participant for helping to organize the collaboration and to my partners at Comcast/NBCU for helping to amplify this important message,” said Illumination Founder and CEO Chris Meledandri.
Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.
"As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of COVID-19, one of our most powerful weapons is kindness," said Elizabeth Cousens, President & CEO of the United Nations Foundation. "We are delighted that the Despicable Me characters are letting their love show and showing ways to keep themselves and their communities safe during this unprecedented time."

Indore (Madhya Pradesh): In a major community-led initiative to strengthen security and curb theft, anti-social activities and drug abuse, 100 CCTV cameras have been installed in Goma Ki Phel, located in Ward 47 of the city. Of these, 50 cameras were installed through public participation, while residents contributed another 50 by installing cameras at their homes.
The CCTV surveillance network was inaugurated by MLA Mahendra Hardia and police commissioner Santosh Kumar Singh. “With this initiative, the entire locality will now come under an extensive camera surveillance network, helping the police keep track of suspicious activities and investigate criminal incidents,” said mayor-in-council member and Ward 47 corporator Nandkishore Pahadia.
The initiative aims to address growing concerns over drug abuse among youngsters in working-class settlements, besides preventing theft and other criminal activities. Drug addiction has reportedly pushed some young people into selling valuables from their own homes, causing financial and emotional distress to their families.
The CCTV network is expected to help the police monitor suspicious movements and deter anti-social elements. It is also expected to strengthen the sense of security among women, girls and other residents.
Police commissioner calls for public participation
After the inauguration, Hardia and the police commissioner interacted with residents at Kabir Chowk in Goma Ki Phel. They discussed public safety and the importance of community awareness. Appreciating Pahadia's initiative, Singh said the police were always with the public and that effective crime control was possible only through mutual trust and cooperation between citizens and the police.
He said the CCTV network would connect Goma Ki Phel with the surveillance system of Tukoganj police station, helping personnel monitor incidents and assist in investigations.
Similar drives planned in other wards
Hardia praised the residents for contributing 50 cameras from their own resources and said that coordination between citizens, elected representatives and the police could transform Goma Ki Phel into a safer and model locality. He also urged youngsters to stay away from drugs and anti-social activities and focus on education and constructive pursuits. He added that similar joint initiatives would be undertaken in other wards with police support to strengthen security and curb crime.

Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the Kharkiv region.
The BBC is the first international broadcaster to enter the pipeline where this subterranean battle is taking place.
With a diameter of just over a metre there's enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line – and which are making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.
The BBC's defence correspondent Jonathan Beale reports from near Kupyansk, where he went underground with the 13th Khartiia Operational Brigade.

World Toilet Day is a funny idea with a serious goal: A world awash in toilets
Twenty-five years ago, Jack Sim was flush with excitement. (Please pardon the pun.)
The Singapore entrepreneur was looking for a meaningful project and came upon this thought from the prime minister: "He said we should measure our graciousness according to the cleanliness of our public toilets," Sim recalls.
Thus was born World Toilet Day. The goal was more than cleanliness. It was access, too — billions of people do not have a safe and sanitary toilet to use.
Enshrined as an official U.N. day in 2013, World Toilet Day aims to get people talking and thinking about a topic that maybe is a taboo in polite conversation.
Let's eschew the euphemisms
World Toilet Day is all about peeing, pooping and addressing menstrual hygiene in a clean and safe manner — followed by the "conveyance" of excreta to a sanitary disposal system, notes Kate Olive Medlicott, the sanitation and waste team leader within the WASH team at the World Health Organization. Human diseases are shed in sewage, so a top-notch sanitation system is critical, says Medlicott. Cholera is linked to sewage. Polio is, too.
This year's World Toilet Day theme is "Sanitation and Gender Equality: Safe Toilets, Equal Futures." Even though everyone suffers when they can't find a toilet, the menstrual cycle creates additional complications. If schools or offices lack a safe and sanitary place to attend to period needs and to dispose of period products, girls and women may opt to stay home.
There is another gender issue. Sofia Calltorp, the U.N. Women global head of humanitarian action, says: "When women and girls do not have access to safe toilets," they leave their home and look for a public toilet or a secluded space to do their business, often venturing into unsafe areas. "There is a huge impact in terms of being exposed to harassment or violence," Calltorp says. She points to refugee camps as a place where this issue often arises, with unlit toilets that aren't differentiated by gender.
Now you might well ask: Has World Toilet Day made a difference?
The toilet titans we interviewed say yes, it has, just by talking about toilets in the public arena. The U.N. has stated that access to safe sanitation is a human right. And in just about every country, progress has been made in improving access to sanitary facilities. Since 2015, 1.2 billion people have become part of the world of safely managed sanitation systems.
What are the next steps? Kellogg Schwab, who specializes in water and wastewater contaminants of public health concern at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, stresses that governments should be a force for change but that it shouldn't be top down. It should also be … oh, forgive me again … bottom up. Schwab suggests giving money to communities to figure out what solutions they can come up with to improve the toilet and sanitation situation. There will be flops. But there will be successes that can be scaled up.
So maybe one day — Medlicott of WHO thinks in 50 years or so —- Earthlings will look back and say, How curious that in a world of wealth there were not enough safe and secure toilets.
A toast to toilets
Let's end by reflecting on the present day.
"World Toilet Day is my favorite day of the year," says Medlicott. "People find it fun and funny but it's really important to celebrate and act on something we take for granted."
If you're among the population where toilets are plentiful, she suggests pausing to think of a moment — it's happened to all of us — when you needed a bathroom and couldn't find one. Maybe that incident has turned into a funny story you share with friends. Now imagine if it were to happen every day.
I am deeply thankful that all I need to do is walk down the office hallway to find a clean and private loo.

For three months, Suraj Kumar’s job was to feed discarded clothes into shredding machines in Panipat, an industrial city in the north Indian state of Haryana. Clothes discarded in the US, Canada and Europe arrive in the city to be torn back into fibres and spun into yarn, feeding a textile recycling industry that supplies markets across the world.
Suraj, 19, had travelled from West Bengal state to work in Panipat’s factories, following his cousins and friends who had already found jobs there. He hoped to earn enough to send money home to his parents. But in late August, an electrical short circuit in the machine propelled him into the shredding mechanism. The accident crushed both arms.
“I wish I had died rather than lost both my arms,” Suraj says. An only child, he had hoped his job in Panipat would support his parents. Instead, he fears he has become a financial burden on them. The work he had taken up to help his family has left him dependent on others, with no certainty about what his future will look like.
By some estimates, Panipat processes more than 1m tons of used clothing from across the world every year, making it one of the world’s largest textile recycling hubs. In the city’s 20,000 factories, employing about 300,000 people, discarded clothes are shredded into yarn and made into finished products, including home furnishings for brands such as H&M Home, Ikea, Primark, Tesco and Walmart.
But the fast-fashion industry, built on buying more and more clothes and wearing them less, carries a devastating cost for workers tackling its waste. Ramesh Chaudhary, an environmental activist who has worked in Panipat’s labour department, has been tracking reports of injuries and amputations across the city for the past five years. He estimates that at least one worker a day loses a limb, rising to as many as five on some days.
“Every day, we come across cases of workers injured inside factories, sometimes losing a hand or a leg, and sometimes even dying,” Chaudhary says. He gathers his information through a network of labour contractors who supply workers to factories across Panipat. But not all news of injuries reaches him, he says, suggesting the scale of the problem could be greater.
Between 17 and 24 August this year, the Guardian monitored reports from 11 private hospitals and two government hospitals in Panipat. In that period, six cases of textile workers with severe limb injuries were reported: two had lost an arm, another man lost both, one lost a hand, one lost a leg and the sixth their fingers.
Such injuries are common in Panipat’s factories, says Chaudhary, because machinery often lacks the necessary safety mechanisms. If a worker gets caught in a spinning machine, he says, cutting the power may not stop it immediately. By the time the machine comes to a halt, a worker may already have catastrophic injuries.
During numerous visits to spinning units and factories, the Guardian did not see anyone wearing any kind of safety gear. None of the workers interviewed reported having safety training.
India’s 1948 Factories Act places a duty on factory owners to protect workers’ health and safety. It requires serious workplace accidents to be reported to the authorities. But the effectiveness of safety oversight remains a concern, says Sandeep Sachdeva, co-founder of the Safe in India Foundation, which works to reduce industrial injuries.
“Factories are often audited by buyers, especially where quality and critical components are involved, and inspected by government industrial safety and health departments. Buyer audits tend to focus more on commercial requirements and product quality than on workplace safety or working conditions,” he says.
“Government inspections are selected through a central software system, but inspectors are now required to inform factories before visiting. Their role is now that of a facilitator-cum-inspector – a shift that undermines the effectiveness of inspections, particularly in factories with unsafe working conditions.”
For workers, losing a limb means losing their livelihood. Ramashankar Singh, who is in his fifties, from Chapra in Bihar, spent 18 years in Panipat’s factories before an accident last year led to him having a leg amputated.
It happened when a hot ball bearing fell on his foot. Ramashankar’s injury was first just wrapped in discarded cloth, before the factory owner sent him to a pharmacy.
The wound worsened as the infection spread. When Ramashankar approached his employer again, the owner agreed to arrange treatment and admitted him to a private hospital. By then, the infection had progressed so far that doctors had to amputate his leg above the knee.
“The factory owner said he would give me another job, possibly as a cook or a security guard at the factory,” Ramashankar says. “But that never happened.” The owner also said he would help him secure a government disability pension, but he has received no pension since the accident and relies on a prosthetic leg provided by a charitable organisation.
After so much of his life spent in a factory, Ramashankar says: “I have almost forgotten how to live without work. Much of my day now passes lying on my bed, staring at the ceiling fan.”
He also struggles with guilt that he has become a burden on his family.
India’s textile industry is the country’s second-largest source of employment after agriculture, directly employing more than 45 million people. An estimated 92% of its workforce is informally employed. In Panipat, more than 90% of workers are employed informally, says Ina Bahuguna, programme manager at the Estonia-based Reverse Resources, which monitors the city’s textile waste.
“Formal employment contracts and the social security benefits that accompany them, including pensions, are largely limited to workers in management, clerical roles and some specialised jobs, such as tailoring,” says Bahuguna.
Most workers on the factory floor lack these protections, leaving those who suffer serious injuries particularly vulnerable. Without formal employment or adequate social security coverage, they are left without employer-backed compensation, rehabilitation support or a source of income.
The Guardian asked several factory owners why they hired workers on a contractual or piece-rate basis rather than in permanent positions, and most cited the workers’ seasonal migration, saying some did not return to Panipat after travelling home.
For workers who sustain life-changing injuries, getting employers to pay for medical treatment can be a struggle. Indrapal Singh, who lost his arm in 2017, had worked in Panipat for 15 years, two and a half of those at the factory where he was injured. His hand was caught in a Chinese-made carding machine, which tore away the skin. He was given a painkilling injection but, as the infection worsened, his arm had to be amputated. The factory owner refused to pay his hospital bills.
Indrapal spent six years fighting his case through the courts, but says he received no compensation. The police told him that he had signed documents withdrawing his complaint, something Indrapal, who says he cannot read or write, disputes.
“I lost my arm, fought for six years, and in the end, all I got was a government pension of 5,700 rupees [£45]. The factory owner has faced no consequences, and the factory continues to operate as before,” he says.
Chaudhary says: “Workers have very little bargaining power when they are up against factory owners who are not only financially powerful but sometimes politically influential too. For many workers, taking them on in a legal fight is simply not an option.”
Arvind Kumar, the officer in charge at one of Panipat’s 12 police stations, says three workplace injury cases have been registered at his station so far this year. One involved the death of a worker. “Fewer than 1% of workplace injury cases reach the police and are formally registered,” he says.
Most cases, the officer says, are settled outside the formal legal system. Workers may receive a one-time payment towards medical bills, but then are generally left to manage the long-term consequences of their injuries on their own. The police rarely get involved.
For now, Suraj Kumar’’s family are grateful that the factory owner covered his hospital bills. They are not sure whether to register a police complaint.
“He [the owner] is like God to us. He is paying for our boy’s treatment,” says his mother, Sita.
Suraj struggles to imagine what comes next. “I thought that if I worked hard for two years, I could buy myself a motorcycle. I had so many things I wanted to do with my life. I never thought I would have to start by figuring out how to live without my arms.”

Imagine having a medicine that could help manage your child’s rare genetic condition, but being unable to afford it because a year’s treatment costs as much as ₹9 crore. For seven families in India, that situation could soon change.
Seven children diagnosed with Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome (AHDS), a rare genetic disorder, are set to receive a year’s supply of the medicine tiratricol free of cost on November 30, following an initiative led by Hyderabad-based paediatrician Dr. Sivaranjani Santosh and Access to Medicines India.
The development is significant not just because the families will receive the medicine without paying for it, but also because its cost has been brought down through pharmaceutical compounding in the Netherlands. While the commercial version of the drug costs approximately ₹4.68 crore to ₹9 crore per child annually, the compounded formulation is estimated to cost just ₹2.5 lakh per child for a year.
The medicine has been prepared by Transvaal Pharmacy in The Hague, Netherlands, with support from the Netherlands-based Pharmaceutical Accountability Foundation (PAF). The first batch will be handed over to the parents of the seven children along with the necessary documentation and individual import permissions. The families have secured approvals for one year of treatment. As the compounded medicine has a shelf life of six months, it will be imported in two batches.
How did a ₹9-crore treatment become available for ₹2.5 lakh?
The initiative began after Arav, a child under the care of Dr. Sivaranjani, was diagnosed with AHDS, also known as MCT8 deficiency. The condition is caused by mutations affecting the MCT8 gene, which plays an important role in transporting thyroid hormones into brain cells. Tiratricol, also known as TRIAC, acts on thyroid hormone receptors and may help overcome some effects of the deficiency. It also helps minimise complications associated with peripheral thyrotoxicosis.
Although the medicine was available in Europe, its commercial price put it beyond the reach of most Indian families. Arav’s mother, Pavitra Sirolkar, had to arrange approximately ₹12 lakh to ₹13 lakh for just one month’s supply of the medicine from Germany. Dr. Sivaranjani initially approached paediatricians, endocrinologists and paediatric neurologists to explore ways of procuring the drug. Doctors at Christian Medical College (CMC), Vellore, where five other children with the same condition had been identified, were also approached.
Attempts to obtain the medicine through pharmaceutical company Egetis Therapeutics and its compassionate-use programme did not succeed. The situation eventually prompted Dr. Sivaranjani to take the issue to social media. On September 7, she posted an appeal seeking help for the family and urged people to tag the Prime Minister, Union Health Minister and other government representatives. The appeal gained attention, bringing it to the notice of PAF.
The foundation subsequently explored the possibility of preparing the medicine through pharmaceutical compounding using the active pharmaceutical ingredient. Transvaal Pharmacy conducted test batches and developed a formulation for the seven children. The initial group included Arav and five children receiving treatment at CMC Vellore. A seventh child, aged one year, was identified after his father contacted Dr Sivaranjani following her social media appeal.
Who is funding the treatment?
According to PAF, the total cost of providing one year’s treatment to all seven children is €14,200, approximately ₹15.08 lakh. Of this, Dr Sivaranjani raised approximately ₹6.09 lakh in India, while PAF undertook to raise the remaining €8,600, approximately ₹9.13 lakh, in the Netherlands. The medicine will be provided to all seven families free of cost.
Will the medicine become available in India?
While the November 30 handover addresses the immediate treatment requirements of the seven children, Dr. Sivaranjani believes that importing the medicine cannot be a permanent solution. She plans to approach the Union government and work with Access to Medicines India and other organisations to explore the possibility of getting the medicine compounded in India and making it accessible to more children.
“How can a medicine be available in the world but not be available for our children? We should get the medicine compounded in India and make it available for all the children with this condition,” she said.

The computer gaming world hasn’t heard much from Will Wright (SimCity, The Sims) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright’s subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA. Now, well over 15 years later, Wright is starting to promote his next digital simulation, which will use generative AI technology to craft a game-like experience from players’ memories.
MyMems, which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright’s previous projects by “turn[ing] the simulation inward,” as Wright’s Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning. The game will mine memories provided by the player to create digital people that can then form teams to solve puzzles in the game world.
“If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?” Wright says by way of example in the release. “If I had to build a bridge across a short chasm, which three people from my life would I choose to help me?”
In an accompanying announcement video, Wright talks about how the “plausible behavior” in a game like The Sims still didn’t effectively capture the nuances of people he encounters in real life. “It was nowhere near them understanding my claustrophobia or why my sister and I fought so much… We’re actually taking parts of your life, your memories, your experiences, people you know, and turning that into a game that’s very personal.”
Wright said MyMems will be able to extract generalized themes from your memories into self-contained areas that Wright compared to the various parts in a theme park: Sports, vacations, injuries, memories, and deaths could all be the basis for their own zones to play in. Players will also have the option to create worlds based on shared memories with family, friends, and co-workers, for example.

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

The Union government’s health expenditure more than tripled to ₹4.14 lakh crore in 2023-24, from ₹1.30 lakh crore in 2013-14, according to the latest National Health Accounts (NHA) estimates released by the Health Ministry.
The estimates also showed the share of out-of-pocket spending by households dropped by 21.5 percentage points over the same period, highlighting a significant transformation in the country’s healthcare financing.
As a share of total health expenditure, out-of-pocket spending fell from 64.2% in 2013-14 to 42.7% in 2023-24.
“The simultaneous increase in public healthcare financing and decline in the proportion of spending borne directly by households reflect India’s progress towards a more accessible, affordable, and financially protective healthcare system,” the Ministry said in a statement. It said out-of-pocket expenditure declined from 43.4% in 2022-23 to 42.7% in 2023-24.
“The sustained downward trend reflects the expanding role of government-supported healthcare services and financial protection mechanisms. Initiatives aimed at improving access to free and affordable treatment, medicines, diagnostics and hospital services are supporting efforts to reduce dependence on direct household spending,” it said.
Private insurance growth
The government’s share in total health expenditure increased by 14.9 percentage points over the decade, the estimates showed, while per capita government health expenditure rose from ₹1,042 in 2013-14 to ₹2,959 in 2023-24, an increase of nearly three times. Social security expenditure on health rose from 6% of total health expenditure in 2013-14 to 11% in 2023-24.
This includes government-financed health insurance schemes such as Ayushman Bharat-Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana, State insurance schemes, social health insurance, and medical expenditure for government employees. Private health insurance expenditure grew even faster, with its share rising from 3.4% to 10.2% over the decade.
Focus on primary healthcare
The government’s expenditure on primary healthcare stood at about ₹1.53 lakh crore in 2023-24, underscoring the increased focus on primary and community-level healthcare, the Ministry said.
Initiatives such as Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, free drugs and diagnostics, the Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme, the Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana and AMRIT pharmacies had contributed to efforts to improve access to affordable healthcare, it said.
The Ayushman Bharat-PMJAY had also strengthened financial protection by providing cashless hospitalisation benefits to eligible beneficiaries, it added.
The NHA Estimates for India 2023-24 are the 11th round of estimates prepared by the NHA3 Technical Secretariat, which operates within the National Health Systems Resource Centre of the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. They are prepared using the internationally recognised System of Health Accounts 2011 framework.

A video has gone viral across social media platforms with the claim that a group of Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangha (RSS) activists vandalised a restaurant in West Bengal.
The clip was shared by X handle @Deshmukh_0 on November 13 at around 6:07 pm, with the claim that the members of the RSS raided and vandalised the restaurant following an altercation with the owner over non-payment of dues. The RSS men had eaten there but refused to pay, the post claimed. (Archive)

The post garnered 106,700 views and over 2,000 reshares.
The 25-second-long clip shows a mob breaking glass panes and ransacking the space. The caption, written in Hindi, says when the owner asked for payment, the RSS members accused the restaurant of wrongly serving them chicken.
The same clip was shared by X user @yadavanoop08, with the claim that certain “RSS goons caused a ruckus” at a restaurant in West Bengal after they were asked to pay their bill. (Archive)
पश्चिम बंगाल के ड्यूर्विंग होटल में RSS के कुछ गुंडों का हंगामा,
होटल द्वारा बिल मांगने पर RSS के गुंडों ने ये आरोप लगाकर दुकान में तोड़फोड़ करने लगे कि खाने में चिकन दिया गया है।
सालो की औकात अगर बिल देने की न हो तो खाना ही क्यों खाते है। https://t.co/o3KquCIEn7
— PDA परिवार (@yadavanoop08) November 13, 2026
Several other users also shared the video with identical claims on X.
Fact Check
In order to determine the veracity of these claims, first, we ran a reverse image search on some of the keyframes of the viral clip. This led us to images of a restaurant called Durbin Bangla located in Dhaka, Bangladesh.
Below is a comparison of a frame from the viral video and an image of the restaurant we found online.
The viral video also contains footage of the incident shot from outside the restaurant. We examined keyframes from this clip and compared them with photographs of the outside facade of the restaurant available online. See below:
These comparisons prove conclusively that the restaurant shown in the viral clip is not in West Bengal, but in Dhaka, Bangladesh.
Further, the viral clip shows a police officer in a green uniform in the midst of the chaos. This matches the uniform worn by Bangladesh police.
A keyword search then led us to several news reports (The Daily Star, The Financial Express and Dhaka Tribune) on a mob attack and vandalism at Durbin Bangla restaurant in Dhaka’s Mohakhali on November 13, 2026.
The Daily Star reported that a disagreement over a vacant seat at the restaurant eventually escalated into a heated conflict, followed by a clash with the restaurant employees and vandalism at the restaurant.
To sum up, the viral video is from Bangladesh. It shows an incident at Durbin Bangla restaurant in Dhaka. The claim that a group of RSS members is seen vandalising a restaurant in Bengal over non-payment of bill and being served chicken is false.

Greetings from a Berlin square, where an artist's statue watches over children at play
If you were listening to this, you'd hear what isn't pictured: the whoops and wails of children playing on the swings and slides behind me, all under the watchful eye of Käthe Kollwitz cast in bronze. The German expressionist lived just off this square in Berlin — named after her, Kollwitzplatz — and, at the turn of the 20th century, her children probably played here, too.
In the wake of World War I, Kollwitz's lithographs, woodcuts and sculptures fixated on the suffering and futility of war. They depict undernourished, wide-eyed children in the protective arms of mothers whose anguish is etched into their faces. Her statue, The Grieving Parents, stands in Belgium where her son Peter died at the front, aged 18.
As I turn my back briefly on the playground and aim my camera at Kollwitz, a boy jumps into the shot, up onto the statue's plinth. Playing hide and seek, he conceals himself behind Kollwitz. His friend finds him quickly and the two boys chase each other around the statue, inadvertently embracing Kollwitz like she does her own boys in her lithograph renderings.
The Kollwitz statue's presence is calm. She sits, charcoal in hand, poised to draw the happy hubbub of children growing up in a city that is safe. But with wars not so far away and Germany bringing back military service for a new generation, I feel a sudden urge to wrap my arms around my own child, just as Kollwitz did.

Myanmar faces historic genocide verdict at UN court over Rohingya massacres
- Published
When the judges of the International Court of Justice read out their verdict in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar on Thursday, they could make history.
In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.
But no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.
"It would be a judgment of landmark importance if The Gambia were to win this case," says Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court. "It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state."
The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality.
I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.
Their accounts of killing, torture and mass rape by Burmese soldiers have been thoroughly documented by human rights groups and a United Nations fact-finding mission, external.
I have on many occasions interviewed ethnic Rakhine people about their animosity towards the Muslim population, and I have documented the systematic obliteration of what remained of Rohingya villages by the Myanmar state.
But the question posed at the UN's top court, the ICJ, is whether all of this amounted to genocide.
The ICJ was established in 1945 to help settle disputes between states, not to try international crimes. However, it was chosen to address the attacks on Rohingyas in Myanmar because there were few other avenues of redress for the victims.
Myanmar authorities have denied accusations of ethnic cleansing or genocide, saying they were only responding to terrorist actions by Rohingya militants with so-called military "clearance operations".
A UN report in 2018, based on hundreds of interviews, said the army's tactics were "grossly disproportionate to actual security threats". It said top military figures in Myanmar must be investigated for genocide in Rakhine State and crimes against humanity in other areas. Myanmar rejected the report.
As Myanmar was not a signatory to the International Criminal Court, it was not possible to file a case there against the officials accused of atrocities in Rakhine State.
Instead in November 2019 The Gambia, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Co-operation, filed a case at the ICJ, arguing that all states are bound by the Genocide Convention, so all have an interest in upholding it.
It accused the state in Myanmar, not just the military, of genocide.
This was a novelty in international law; a state not directly affected by an act, arguing that it had legal standing to make a complaint because it was indirectly affected by any violations of such an important convention.
Myanmar objected to this argument, but the ICJ judges ruled that The Gambia was eligible to file the case.
The case drew even more attention when the Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, who at the time headed the elected government in Myanmar, chose to lead the initial legal defence of her country at The Hague in person, for which she was widely criticised.
She had very limited influence over the actions of the Myanmar military in Rakhine State, but her refusal to condemn them dismayed many of those who until then had admired her courage and adherence to democratic principles.
Since she was deposed by a coup in 2021 and placed under arrest the defence has been led by a new team appointed by the military.
Historically, proving that genocide has been committed has been very difficult. Judges apply a high bar to this.
Typically, where there is no explicitly genocidal programme, like that of the Nazis, the judges require that the evidence presented at court must be such that the only reasonable inference from the actions of the defendants is that they had genocidal intent.
When Bosnia-Herzegovina filed a genocide case against Serbia at the ICJ in 1993, it took the court 14 years to conclude that while incidents like the 1995 massacre at Srebrenica did amount to genocide, there was not sufficient proof that the state of Serbia had genocidal intent, though it was found to have failed to prevent genocide.
Myanmar's lawyers and Aung San Suu Kyi have argued something similar.
Suu Kyi said that The Gambia's team mischaracterised a complex conflict and military operation, and that while she accepted that war crimes may have been committed against the Rohingyas, that is not proof of genocidal intent.
But Arsalan Suleman believes the weight of evidence his team gathered is enough to meet that high bar.
"What we presented to the court was the long history of discrimination targeting the Rohingya, and how that history, and the policies connected with it, provide a background to understand the government's language, rhetoric, propaganda, and policies that were part of the 2017 'clearance operations'," Suleman said.
"We discussed the 1982 citizenship law, and the tightening noose of discriminatory laws that restricted access to education, healthcare, livelihoods, and travel - all of which made life really impossible for the Rohingya and, we argued, was one of several indicators of genocidal intent."
What happens if the court does find in favour of The Gambia?
Myanmar would then find itself tarnished by having committed "the crime of crimes", as sitting on the same bench as Nazi Germany, the Rwandan Hutu militants and the Bosnian Serbs at Srebrenica.
That might seem a setback for Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, who above all was responsible for the military's operations in 2017, and who has been trying to improve his dismal international image in recent months.
There is no right of appeal against an ICJ verdict. However, there is also no penalty that follows an ICJ verdict.
The Burmese coup leader is focused mostly on rebuilding relations with neighbouring Asian countries, who are unlikely to pay too much attention to such a verdict, and much less on rebuilding relations with Western countries who do care.
But for the huge Rohingya diaspora this verdict matters a great deal.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of the Rakhine town of Buthidaung in 2017 and now lives in Canada.
"For the Rohingya, this trial is a moment of acknowledgement of our suffering after years of denial. The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades, not just this year."
He and other Rohingya activists hope that a ruling in favour of The Gambia will prompt more co-ordinated action by other countries to find a resolution which allows them to go home to Rakhine State, in safety.
More than a million are stuck in wretched camps in Bangladesh, barred from employment as international funding dries up.
But the obstacles to realising this hope are formidable.
Rakhine State has been ravaged by a conflict between the military and the insurgent Arakan Army, which now controls most of the territory. It is supported by the indigenous Rakhine population who are very hostile to the idea of the Rohingyas coming back.
Many Rohingya villages have been completely destroyed. And international support for them has faded over the years. Even an unprecedented genocide verdict at the world's highest court cannot change that reality.
