The Kashmiri wazwan, an array of dishes adding up to 4,500-5,500 calories partaken during festivals and weddings, is one of the key cultural factors contributing to a spike in cases of diabetes in Kashmir, experts said.
Kashmir’s social life is organised around large, meat-centred feasts, most visibly the wazwan served at weddings or on Eid. Diabetes Simplified for Kashmir, a book released on World Diabetes Day (November 14), said the multi-course meal can run to over 30 mutton and chicken preparations, with the calorie intake “several times the average daily requirement”.
“Such exposure accumulates rather than occurs in isolation, and repeated post-prandial glucose and lipid excursions of this magnitude plausibly contribute to the region’s rising dysglycaemia burden,” the book, co-authored by endocrinologists Mohammad Hayat Bhat and Shahnawaz Mir, and cardiologist Nasir Shams, stated.
J&K has witnessed a spike in the incidence of diabetes in the past three years. The Union Territory screened more than 2.15 million people for diabetes; 48,623 individuals have been diagnosed to have diabetes, according to data from the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. In 2025-2026, 2.84 million people were screened and 85,948 were found to have diabetes. “In the past three years, J&K added 2.18 lakh new patients to its diabetes burden,” the Ministry’s data suggested.
Apart from more universally seen factors, including poor physical activity and consumption of tobacco, the book identifies Kashmir’s unique lifestyle among the contributing factors.
“Kashmir’s daily plate remains rice-centric with rice typically supplying the bulk of meal volume and carbohydrate load. Large portions of rice translate directly into high postprandial glycaemic load,” it said.
“Type 2 diabetes prevalence in Kashmir has risen sharply within a single generation. A survey in 1999 found known diabetes in just 1.89% of adults, with 4.25% undiagnosed. Recent Indian Council of Medical Research-INDIA data show 7.8% prevalence,” the authors said, attributing the rising incidence of Type 2 diabetes to lifestyle in Kashmir.
The book noted that such a rapid shift cannot reflect genetic change. “It points instead to a compressed nutrition and lifestyle transition, as subsistence agriculture and labour-intensive living have been replaced by urbanisation and declining physical activity, while traditional dietary patterns — rice-centric meals, salt tea, preserved winter foods, and elaborate festive feasting — persist largely unchanged,” the experts said.
They also attributed the rise in cases of diabetes to Kashmir’s winters. “The glycaemic and fat load of the traditional meat and generous portion sizes do not act in isolation. Their convergence with a pronounced winter sedentary period appears to produce a compounding rather than merely additive metabolic burden across the Kashmiri annual cycle, in which periods of highest intake coincide with the lowest levels of expenditure,” they added.
Seasonal confinement and winter lifestyle patterns in the Kashmir Valley’s prolonged winter, which are marked by heavy snowfall and sub-zero temperatures for several months, compress daily life to indoor spaces, warmed by the hammam, a built-in masonry hearth, and the kangri, a portable wicker-encased firepot carried beneath the pheran, a long woollen robe.
“Large meals could be risky or other sudden triggers for heart attacks. Overeating should be considered as a heart attack trigger, much in the same way that extreme physical activities and severe anger episodes can provoke an attack,” the doctors warned.

Japan sends up jets after alleged Russian incursion of its airspace
- Published
Japan says it launched fighter jets and "strongly" protested after two suspected Russian aircraft violated its airspace early on Tuesday.
South Korea also says it deployed fighter jets, while Taiwan says it "responded" to Russian military aircraft detected in their respective air defence identification zones.
These are unofficial buffer areas beyond territorial airspace where governments identify approaching aircraft for security purposes. Moscow has yet to comment.
The alleged incursions are a reminder of Russia's military power ahead of the Apec economic summit in China this week, which Vladimir Putin will attend alongside US President Donald Trump.
Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft, off the south-western Okinoshima island, were a "serious infringement of Japan's sovereignty" and "completely unacceptable".
The last such incursion was in 2024, when a Russian military patrol plane entered Japanese airspace off Rebun island, Hokkaido.
Taiwan says its military "responded accordingly" after two Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone, also on Tuesday.
South Korea says it sent up jets after an unspecified number of Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan. The aircraft departed without violating South Korean airspace, authorities said.
It is unclear if the three neighbours were responding to the same or different aircraft.
The East China Sea contains self-declared, overlapping air defence identification zones between China, Taiwan, Japan and South Korea.
Foreign military aircraft are expected, but not legally required, to notify governments before entering such air defence identification zones.
Tensions are flaring between Japan and Russia, which are locked in a decades-old territorial dispute over a cluster of islands in the Pacific Ocean.
For months, Moscow has been ratcheting up the pressure on Tokyo.
In August, Putin paid his first visit to one of these islands, prompting sharp rebuke from Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. In October, Russia detained a Japanese journalist on spying allegations.

Waymo pauses service in San Francisco after robotaxis get stuck on flooded streets
This isn’t the first time the company’s robotaxis have caused chaos in the city.
Waymo has temporarily paused its robotaxi service in San Francisco due to issues dealing with flooding on some streets, according to an X post from District 5 Supervisor Bilal Mahmood and a message in the Waymo app. The interruption in service follows several incidents of Waymos blocking intersections because they're seemingly unable (or unwilling) to drive through water.
Riders who want to get picked up are now greeted with a message in the app that says "we're paused for now due to weather" and that service will resume "when road conditions improve and the forecast looks clear." San Francisco is currently dealing with heavy rain and flooding as the region heads into what forecasters expect could be a record El Niño winter.
Ahead of the pause, videos posted on X showed a Waymo stopped in the middle of a flooded crosswalk, forcing cars to drive around it. Another Waymo idled in the middle of a road and instructed its rider to stay inside.

Engadget has asked Waymo to comment on the stalled robotaxis and the issues it's facing with San Francisco's current weather. We'll update this article if we hear back.
Waymo previously paused service in San Francisco in December 2025, when a power outage led to similar instances of robotaxis blocking city streets. The company has also dealt with flooding in the past. In May, Waymo recalled nearly 4,000 vehicles and paused its service after a robotaxi drove into a flooded road in San Antonio. The company issued a software update to address the issue, but later had to pause service in Atlanta when a Waymo drove into a flooded street again.

The pause only affects the city, but it comes just a day after the California DMV restricted Waymo from the state's freeways, prompting the company to pull its robotaxis off freeways in all of its markets.

This week, the Trump administration made it significantly harder for Chinese companies to access some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. For years, tech firms like Alibaba and ByteDance could rent computing power from data centers overseas, allowing them to use powerful Nvidia chips they were generally prohibited from physically importing into China. This is known as remote access.
But under new plans announced on Monday, overseas data centers that want to provide large amounts of computing power to China will have to get special licenses and deal with other annoying new kinds of red tape. The White House also imposed stricter rules on shipments of advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore and Malaysia, where US officials suspect significant levels of smuggling may have taken place.
These are not new policy ideas, and similar proposals have been kicking around in Washington for a while. But the timing of Monday’s announcement is impossible to ignore. Yes, this is about Jensen Huang’s sex life.
As you’ve probably heard by now, the Nvidia cofounder resigned as CEO last week after admitting he had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. Alice previously worked at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which offered remote access services and is suspected of engaging in chip smuggling.
The scandal may have been so embarrassing for the White House that officials felt compelled to demonstrate they had the situation under control. Apparently, the cheating scandal of the century was the motivation they were missing. (A White House spokesperson previously told WIRED that the new rule would “crack down on the smuggling of advanced US SI chips” and “help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.”)
It started in the fall of 2022, when the Biden administration unveiled a set of rules that would radically alter the future of AI and who was allowed to build it. The goal was to choke off China's access to the advanced chips needed to train the world's most powerful AI models, as well as the equipment required to manufacture those chips.
It's worth remembering just how radical this approach was at the time. For decades, the US had used export controls to keep sensitive American technology away from specific military programs, governments, and blacklisted companies accused of carrying out human rights abuses. But the Biden administration was attempting something far more ambitious: using Washington's influence over the global semiconductor industry to hold back the world's second-largest economy from competing at the cutting edge of one of the most important new technologies in generations.
The strategy rested on a relatively simple idea. Training the most advanced AI models requires enormous amounts of computing power, and American companies like Nvidia dominate the market for the chips that provide it. By restricting China's access to those chips, Washington hoped to preserve America's technological lead.
Four years later, the US certainly cannot claim total victory. But boy, have things gotten messy. Part of the problem is that Washington tasked the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), a relatively small, underfunded agency within the Commerce Department, with leading enforcement of the controls. The bureau had a budget of just $235 million in 2026—a paltry sum compared to what Nvidia rakes in in a single week.
The bureau's job only got harder as the Biden administration introduced successive rounds of increasingly complex restrictions, scrambling to tighten the rules as chipmakers found increasingly elaborate ways to get around them. But one of the bureau's biggest challenges was fighting what became a booming industry for smuggling AI chips into China.
At BIS, Megaspeed has become a poster child for the problem, although it's far from the only company suspected of involvement, or even the largest, according to a person familiar with the matter.
According to Bloomberg, roughly 50,000 of the estimated 136,000 AI chips Megaspeed imported into Malaysia and Indonesia in 2024 and 2025 weren't accounted for in Nvidia's initial inventory checks. It's not clear where they may have ended up. (Nvidia later said it had found at least some of them.)
Even if all of the unaccounted-for chips ended up in China, they would represent only a fraction of the advanced semiconductors believed to have been smuggled into the country over the past few years. Researchers at the Institute for Progress estimate that, by the end of 2026, China could have accumulated smuggled computing power equivalent to roughly 1 million of Nvidia's high-end H100 chips.
But all along, Chinese companies didn't necessarily need to smuggle chips into the country to use them. They could just rent computing power from data centers in other countries, and best of all, the practice didn’t violate US export controls. This wasn’t some hidden loophole—every policymaker and researcher who worked on the chip restrictions was deeply aware of it. So why let the practice continue?
For one, renting computing power can be more expensive and cumbersome than owning the chips outright, especially for companies that need to train large AI models over long periods. Some analysts argued that allowing Chinese firms to use American technology overseas could help keep them dependent on it instead of pushing them to develop domestic alternatives. Restricting access would also be difficult to enforce and could hurt US technology companies.
Now, Washington is moving into this territory anyway. Monday's announcement represents another significant expansion of US efforts to control China's technological development. In 2022, Washington set out to prevent Chinese companies from acquiring certain American chips. Four years later, it’s trying to regulate how Chinese companies use those same chips, even when the hardware never enters China.
Whether that's a good idea depends partly on how much the original restrictions have actually accomplished.
There is evidence that export controls have made it considerably harder for Chinese AI companies to acquire the kind of computing power of their American competitors. But assessing the precise impact of the policies has proven to be extremely difficult.
This strategy comes with a lot of risks, and like with everything else in life, there are real winners and losers. For example, forcing US chip companies to cut off Chinese customers has come at a cost to American companies. In a study of earlier US export restrictions, researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that affected American suppliers struggled to replace lost business in China with new customers elsewhere. They estimate that the restrictions wiped $130 billion from the companies’ combined market value, while also hurting their profitability and employment.
The restrictions have also given China a very powerful incentive to find ways to compete in AI without relying on American technology. Huawei, for example, developed a way to link powerful chips together to create larger, more powerful megachip systems. The Chinese AI lab DeepSeek proved to the world that finding ways to make training more efficient could help developers build competitive models with fewer resources.
I worry that the Trump administration will soon find that it has gotten out over its own skis. It’s now trying to control not only which chips Chinese companies can buy from American companies, but also how they can use American technology anywhere it may be in the world. I’m not sure that is the kind of responsibility I want to bestow on anyone in response to what happened in one person’s sex life.

The days of carrying an entire military arsenal in your pocket are finally over. Rockstar Games is taking a more grounded approach to weapon management in GTA 6. This adds realism to how you plan your robberies and heists. While infinite inventory is gone, the GTA 6 weapon wheel is sticking around with some visual tweaks. So, learn everything about the GTA 6 weapon wheel and inventory system.
How Does the GTA 6 Weapon Wheel Work?
The GTA 6 weapon wheel keeps the familiar radial format, but with a more minimalist and colorful design instead of its predecessor’s circular wheel.
Instead of offering access to all GTA 6 weapons you own, this wheel helps you manage the ones you can carry at a time.
Here’s a quick overview of how the GTA 6 weapon wheel and inventory system works:
- You can carry up to two handguns or pistols at a time.
- You have two long-gun slots for rifles and other larger firearms.
- Only one weapon in GTA 6 can be slung back, while the second can be held in your hands.
- Alongside firearms, you can carry a single melee weapon, explosives, and throwables.
- For items, you can carry masks, headgear, outfits, bags, eyewear, and even smokes.
- The GTA 6 item wheel also allows you to keep a few health and energy-related consumables.
- Later in the story, you can purchase larger backpacks and duffel bags to store additional stash and valuables.
When you press and hold the L1 button on PS5 or the LB button on Xbox to open the weapon wheel, you’ll notice two separate weapons and items tabs. So, you can choose between available guns, explosives, and supplies without navigating a layer of menus.
The interface also displays other information like your health bar, stamina, and the focus ability in GTA 6 in the top-left. Whereas on the top right, you can view your bank account balance and cash wallet money you’re currently carrying in the form of small GTA 6 HUD icons.
Switching between the Weapon Wheel and the Items Wheel is easy and can be done by pressing the RB or R1 button on your Xbox or PlayStation controller. Once the interface is open, you can simply navigate between the weapons to equip and use them during your run.
What Items Can You Access Through GTA 6’s Weapon Wheel
The GTA 6 weapon wheel isn’t just about firearms. There’s an Item tab alongside that brings useful equipment into the same interface. The official footage shows how Lucia and Jason put on a disguise every time they’re attempting to commit a crime. This brings up another aspect in the game where the cops remember your face and other attributes.
So, the Items tab keeps a bunch of wearables such as a bandana face wrap, a pair of sunglasses, a cap, or anything else that you can wear to efficiently and easily lose a cop in GTA 6. It may also keep body armor and throwables, but that’s not confirmed yet.
Apart from the objects present in the Items tab, you can find a bunch of consumables in the bottom left corner of the same weapon wheel interface in GTA 6. On PlayStation, you can use the Square and Triangle buttons, and on Xbox, you can use the X and Y buttons to access these consumables.
How Does the GTA 6 Inventory System Work?
The biggest difference between GTA 6 and GTA 5 is how many weapons you own and how many you can carry physically.
Both GTA 6 protagonists, Jason and Lucia, have a limited personal loadout. Both main characters can carry 2 handguns and up to 2 long guns each.
Since your inventory is a lot more realistic than before, one of the two long guns will always be slung across the back while the other requires holding it visibly.
Needless to say, NPCs will surely react to visible guns on your character and may affect your GTA 6 criminal profile if they call the cops on you.
Here, your vehicle or car in GTA 6 also plays an important part in inventory management. While you can’t pull out additional weapons from your pocket, you can use your car’s trunk in GTA 6 to store items in your vehicle and retrieve them when needed. This is one of the ways to increase the inventory space in GTA 6.
So, you need to make efficient strategies before starting a mission. Carry shotguns for close-quarters robberies, while a rifle could be more useful for a longer firefight. You also need to consider adding some healing supplies in GTA 6 as emergency options.
So, what are your thoughts on the weapon wheel in GTA 6? Tell us in the comments below.

Even as Christian communities continue to face attacks allegedly from Hindutva groups across various parts of West Bengal, Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) state president Samik Bhattacharya on November 15 issued a warning to Christian missionary school, saying it they were found promoting “anti-India activities”, they would not be allowed to function.
“If any Christian missionary school, due to religious reasons, promotes anti-India activities, we will not let that school run,” he said while addressing a gathering at Birsa Munda’s birth anniversary celebrations in New Alipore, Kolkata.
“Guardians should become alert that an official at a school placed a Pakistani flag on the table of his chamber… in a school here in Kolkata. Please correct yourselves… We will let this happen in West Bengal no matter how powerful they are. All Christian missionaries can take to the streets; we are not opposed to any religion, but sitting in our state, in our country, we will not let you insult saffron [colour]… We will not allow it.”
Prior to issuing the warning, Bhattacharya claimed that a woman BJP worker was prevented from entering a “prestigious school in Kolkata” for wearing a saffron saree. “A prestigious school in Kolkata…I am not naming the school right now because a few days later I will sit outside its gates. One of our sisters, our BJP worker who was seen wearing saffron attire…was told [by the school] that ‘wearing these saris, you cannot come to school, you cannot pronounce the name of lotus flower while teaching the students.’ This is happening in the land of Kolkata where several eminent personalities have walked,” he said.
He further went on to insinuate that Christians were continuing to uphold British mentality in India. “It’s been 75 years since the British left the country, but the mentality has not left. You have come here; you are holding your establishments; you are Catholics, you are Protestants; you can propagate your religion. But remember, this government is not Babur’s government. This government is not trying to uphold British legacies. West Bengal has an independent government,” he said.
A report published by The Telegraph stated that the BJP president alleged that a reputed college in Kolkata was carrying out religious conversions in Asansol forcibly through “allurements”. “There is an obhijato (elite) college in Kolkata whose principal is carrying out religious conversion in Asansol. This cannot be allowed to continue. This is not the government of the Trinamool Congress, this is not the Left Front government…We are against political intervention in any educational institution. We want schools to create their own curriculum,” the report quoted him.
Bhattacharya, however, did not name any Christian missionary schools or colleges or provide any evidence behind the severe allegations he levelled against the community.
Upon being asked about Bhattacharya’s allegations against Christian missionaries, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on November 17, Tuesday, told the media, “…I get information on this and verify the facts. If the information is true and a written complaint is filed, if an individual did it, action will be taken against the individual; and if it was done institutionally, we will withdraw the NOC given to the institute.”

Christian Bodies Condemn Remarks, Issue Statements
The Bangiya Christiya Pariseba (BCP) in a statement on November 18 reacted to Bhattacharya’s statement saying “sweeping accusations without evidence” maligned a peace-loving community and endangered social harmony, and demanded “specific facts, accountability, and immediate legal action”.
BCP posed eight questions to Bhattacharya and the state administration, questioning the lack of legal action against alleged perpetrators of illegal conversion, if any, and the silence over recurring vigilante attacks on Christians. It asked why attacks and vandalism of prayer meetings by ‘militant groups’ had not been condemned, whether such groups were allegedly being used to intimidate Christians, and sought the status of FIRs filed in connection with alleged threats and attacks against the community in the state.

Concerns Ahead of Christmas
Following Bhattacharya’s remarks, Paritosh Canning, moderator of the Church of North India and bishop of the Calcutta diocese, on Sunday sought chief minister Suvendu Adhikari’s intervention against the rising number of attacks against the Christian community in West Bengal. “A viral video has recently come to our attention. While we cannot verify its authenticity at this moment, the remarks recorded in it feature four grave allegations: claims of widespread religious conversions, an accusation that a…principal is involved in conversion activities; an allegation regarding a person wearing a saffron sari coming to a school; and a sweeping insinuation that even though the British have left, Christian missionary school administrators continue to carry a ‘British mentality,” read a statement by the representatives.
“At a time when vigilantes and hooligans are taking the law into their own hands across various districts — vandalising and launching brutal attacks on peaceful prayer meetings under the false pretext of forced conversions and desperately trying to build a fabricated narrative — the Christian community is both shocked and deeply angered to hear such an incredible, hate-mongering and aggressive speech from a usually balanced and sagacious leader like Samik Babu,” it added.
Speaking to Alt News, Moloy D’Costa, secretary of the West Bengal Association of Christian Schools and vicar-general of the Roman Catholic archdiocese of Calcutta, said, “The comments made by Mr Bhattacharya are vague. Every school has its own dress code, and there is no universal colour code. The authorities should either provide evidence or identify specific institutions and take appropriate action against them, rather than making general statements that vilify an entire community and a network of institutions.”
D’Costa also pointed out, “Several leaders in the party attended Christian missionary institutions; have they converted to Christianity? Converting to Christianity is a lengthy process. Simply visiting a church or sprinkling water is not part of that process. Accusations of forced conversion are being made from all sides, yet not a single case has been reported where anyone has been proven guilty of such actions.”
National Christian Council (NCC) state general secretary Arpan Rana strongly condemned Bhattacharya’s remarks on Christian missionary institutions, stating that “sweeping allegations without evidence” risk fostering suspicion and hostility towards the Christian community.
Rana told Alt News that Christian institutions were primarily invested in “education, humanitarian service, moral development and nation-building, not forced religious conversion,” adding that students from diverse religious backgrounds have studied in these institutions without abandoning their faiths. “Thousands of students from Hindu, Muslim, Christian and other communities have received education from these institutions while preserving their respective religious identities,” he said.
He also termed the portrayal of Indian Christianity as a legacy of British colonialism ‘historically misleading’, noting that Christianity existed in India long before colonial rule. “We expect scholarly arguments backed by evidence, not broad political claims. If any institution is found to engage in unlawful conversion, we support impartial investigations, but the entire Christian community should not be collectively accused,” he added.
Akin to other Christian associations in the state, Rana, on behalf of the NCC, urged the state government to protect Christian institutions, churches and communities, and ensure they can celebrate Christmas peacefully.
As precautionary measures, the BCP also advised churches to inform local authorities about upcoming programmes, establish a community alert system, ring church bells thrice if suspicious groups enter church premises, immediately notify police, and install CCTV cameras at vulnerable points. It also urged members to seek legal aid from BCP, maintain discipline and peaceful conduct, refrain from retaliation, and involve neighbours of all faiths and civil society members in Christmas celebrations to foster communal harmony.
Alt News has been documenting instances of hate crimes against the Christian community in West Bengal since early this year. Instances of violence, attacks, vandalism, and intimidation have often been carried out by Right-wing groups including Bajrang Dal, Vishva Hindu Parishad, and others, against individuals practising Christianity, house churches, and small Christian communities. However, in most of the cases we have reported, police action has been sparse, with fresh instances of harassment emerging regularly.

DOJ accuses Russian national of spying on and harassing Palantir employees
He allegedly took photos of their work laptops and even once followed a female employee for 30 miles.
A Russian national has been indicted for spying on and harassing the employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company, according to the Department of Justice. While the agency's announcement didn't name the specific company, Bloomberg reports that it was Palantir, and that the Russian national was told to do so over Ukraine's use of the company's software for wartime purposes.
Igor D'iu was reportedly recruited by the Russian government through Telegram, where he also received orders on what to do, the DOJ says. He traveled from Istanbul, Turkey to Mexico City, from where he illegally crossed the border to the US in June 2026. On US soil, he was made to purchase laptops, phones, remote access software and wireless networking equipment. He was told that that the company he was monitoring "was providing weapons to fight against Russia in Ukraine."
The Russian officials he was in contact with told him to visit a coffee shop near Palantir's Palo Alto office and take photos of its employees' laptop screens. They also made him switch on his laptop at designated areas near the company's offices, so they could remotely access and collect information from the devices of employees in the vicinity.
His assignment included the surveillance of Palantir employees and their homes, as well. In September, he allegedly followed a female employee in a car for more than 30 miles. D'iu's home was searched on October 8, where authorities found two Russian passports and $18,035 in cash. Authorities had also intercepted packages for him shipped from overseas, containing a fake California ID card and an authentic US passport altered with his photograph.
Palantir, a tech company, is controversial for providing governments, law enforcement and the military products they can then use for mass surveillance. Wired previously reported that ICE used a database built by the company to compile dossiers on people accused of observing and protesting its activities. According to Bloomberg, the US uses Palantir's technology to offer targeting support to Ukraine. In addition, Ukrainian forces in Kyiv use its products for various purposes, including the removal of unexploded Russian mines in the country.
D'iu has been charged with "one count of conspiracy to act as an agent of a foreign government, one count of acting as an agent of a foreign government without notice to the Attorney General, one count of interstate stalking and one count of fraud in connection with identification documents." He is scheduled to appear in federal court on November 24.

Tehran- Iran has called on regional countries to prevent the United States from using their soil to launch aggression against Iran rather than criticise the Islamic Republic for exercising its inherent right to self-defense.
The Iranian Foreign Ministry released a statement early on Thursday amid the recent exchanges of fire between Iran and the US, as well as deadlock in negotiations aimed at ending the nine-month-old war.
The ministry said it “condemns the irresponsible approach of certain regional parties, which criticize Iran’s legitimate defensive operations while disregarding the existing realities and overlooking the United States’ acts of aggression against Iran.”
It also called on the regional states to “prevent the United States from using their territories and military bases to prepare for and carry out acts of aggression against Iran instead of complaining about Iran for exercising its legitimate right to self-defense.”
Meanwhile, the Foreign Ministry reaffirmed Tehran’s respect for the national sovereignty and territorial integrity of the countries in the region.
The failure of regional countries to prevent the United States from using their territories and facilities to conduct acts of aggression against Iran is not only contrary to the principle of good-neighborliness but also constitutes an “act of aggression” under Article 3(f) of the Annex to United Nations General Assembly Resolution 3314 (XXIX) (1974), it added.
The ministry further emphasized that so far, “the Islamic Republic of Iran, out of due consideration for the principles of good-neighborliness and the interests of the Islamic Ummah, has exercised utmost restraint and confined its defensive strikes exclusively to American military bases and assets located in these countries.”
Additionally, it strongly condemned the acts of aggression carried out by the US military against locations along Iran’s southern coast over the past few days.
In order to safeguard the country’s national sovereignty and territorial integrity, the Iranian Armed Forces launched crushing reprisal strikes against US Patriot systems, along with drone and missile launch platforms at two American military bases in the region, which served as launching points and logistical support facilities for acts of aggression against the Islamic Republic, it continued.

Elon Musk says record $446m spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'
- Published
Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.
The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive was the election's top individual donor, giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.
Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of the both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.
The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.
Musk was speaking virtually, external at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.
"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."
This marks a major shift in tone by Musk, who has previously been seen wearing a Maga hat.
"I'm not just Maga, I'm dark, gothic Maga," he joked at a Trump rally in 2024.
For several months at the start of Trump's second term in the White House, Musk served as an unpaid "special government employee" and Senior Advisor to the President, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to cut government spending.
In October 2026, the Pentagon named Musk as a co-lead of a future of warfare study called Project Meridian, while he continued to travel with and advise Trump.
Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.
The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.
Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.
In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governor promised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings, as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.
Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.
One of the most striking midterms wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas.
According to BBC analysis, Musk had spent at least $45m in support of Paxton.
Texas is where key operations for Musk's car company Tesla and rocket and technology firm SpaceX are based.
Musk said on Wednesday that he believes Texas' new governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, is "going to be quite moderate".
Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, ending more than three decades of the party's control of the state.
The Tesla boss added : "I don't think she's a far-left governor. And based on everything I've heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor."

Elon Musk accuses Ukraine of being 'untruthful' about Starshield disruptions
He said that Ukraine is trying to use SpaceX’s consumer Starlink service for military purposes.
Elon Musk has accused Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelenskyy of being "untruthful" about Starshield disruptions hampering the nation's ability to defend and fight back against Russia. The SpaceX CEO told The New York Times' DealBook Summit that Ukraine is actually trying to use the company's consumer Starlink service, not Starshield, for military purposes.
"From the beginning, I've said that Starlink is a civilian system," Musk told interviewer Andrew Ross Sorkin. "It is not meant to be used for offensive drone strikes that kill people. If you want to do that, you need to use Starshield, which is a separate system that is controlled by the US government. But do not ask me as a private individual to make kill decisions."
Musk's comments come amid a lengthy disruption to Starshield in Ukraine. Last month, Zelenskyy posted on X that speed limits on Starshield were imposed along the war's entire front line and in Russian territory, saying any terminal moving faster than 161 km/h (100 mph) would lose its connection to the satellite network. "Unfortunately, this is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine," Zelenskyy said at the time. "We are trying to establish all the circumstances with the American side."
Sorkin reminded Musk that Zelenskyy referred to the system being slowed down as Starshield and not Starlink. "That's false... [Zelenskyy is] not always truthful," Musk replied. "What he is actually saying is he wants to use Starlink for offensive military operations."
The last time Starshield was slowed on October 14, SpaceX and The White House blamed each other for throttling speeds, but nothing was ever confirmed. Citing US officials, Reuters had reported that the order came from inside the White House. Later on, though, The Wall Street Journal's sources said that Musk himself ordered the slowdown.
Later in October, Ukraine pushed back against allegations that it had misused Starlink for offensive attacks. An official said that pre-existing restrictions on the systems would have made it "physically impossible" for Ukraine to use Starlink to strike in Russian territory as Musk described.

Morphine and codeine are opium compounds naturally found in poppy plants. In other words, South Korea pulled Trader Joe's popular seasoning because it contains poppy seeds. It is also worth noting that the ban reportedly happened in 2022, not 2026.
In November, a claim spread online that South Korea had banned the popular Trader Joe's "Everything but the Bagel" sesame seasoning blend after the country determined the product had morphine and codeine in it.
As social media users on Facebook shared rumors that South Korea's customs officials were "actively confiscating" the product, Snopes readers wrote in and searched the website to verify the alleged ban.
According to South Korea's official food safety website (archived), Trader Joe's everything seasoning is, in fact, banned from the country due to "detected components" of morphine, thebaine and codeine within the product.
Thus, we have rated this claim as true, with the caveat that morphine, thebaine and codeine are opium compounds that are naturally present in the poppy plant. In other words, South Korea has banned the seasoning because it contains poppy seeds. (According to credible reports, so has Singapore.)
Both The New York Times and The Washington Post reported that South Korea officially listed the seasoning blend on its banned foods list in 2022, not in 2026, and that Korea's customs officials have previously confiscated the product.
However, this claim may have started spreading online again due to the Korea Herald's August report that police in Seoul had blocked the sale of the Trader Joe's seasoning on secondhand e-commerce platforms. The BBC and other international news outlets also picked up the Herald's story.
We reached out to South Korea's primary airport — Incheon International Airport in Seoul — for more information about its confiscation policy for products with poppy seeds and await a response.
How to find information on banned products
The South Korean government has an online searchable database of food products blocked from entering the country because they are deemed "hazardous."
A search using the keywords "everything but the bagel" returned three results, all of which were Trader Joe's products: Everything but the Bagel Sesame Seasoning Blend, Everything but the Bagel Nut Duo and Everything but the Bagel Seasoned Kettle-Cooked Potato Chips.
Translating the webpage using Google Translate revealed that the "detected components" listed in Everything but the Bagel Sesame Seasoning Blend were morphine, thebaine and codeine.
Here's the specific page (archived in Korean) for the seasoning in question within the database:
(South Korea Ministry of Food and Drug Safety)
It's unclear why the "Registration Date" is listed for 2025, rather than 2022. South Korea's Ministry of Food and Drug Safety was not reachable. 
South Korea's poppy seed ban vs. U.S. rules
South Korea's Narcotics Control Act defines poppy and all alkaloids, or organic compounds, "extracted from poppy and its processed substance" as narcotic drugs. The U.S. embassy in Korea warns travelers that "food products containing poppy seeds, including popular bagel seasoning blends, are considered illegal in Korea."
"Attempting to travel into Korea with these products could result in a criminal investigation resulting in fines, entry and exit bans, or even imprisonment," the embassy says on its website.
Parts of the poppy plant, including a milky white fluid, contain opiate alkaloids like morphine, codeine and thebaine. According to the Drug Enforcement Administration, unwashed poppy seeds can "contain dangerous amounts of opium alkaloids."
However, the FDA states that the actual poppy seeds "contain little or no opiate alkaloids inside." The agency also does not advise consumers to avoid poppy seeds, although it cautions against misuse:
Although FDA is aware of some reports of consumption of poppy seed-containing foods being associated with negative health effects, FDA is particularly concerned about the misuse of poppy seeds. Specifically, opiate alkaloids on poppy seeds may pose particular risks when misused. Consumers should not make poppy seed "tea," as this practice has been linked to serious adverse events, including death.
While poppy seeds won't get you high, according to experts, drug tests are far more sensitive and may pick up on trace amounts of opiate compounds.
We asked Trader Joe's about how it determines that its bagel seasoning does not have unsafe levels of opium alkaloids and await a response.
According to the American Spice Trade Association, poppy seed processing in the United States usually involves mechanical cleaning to remove opioid alkaloid residue, periodic testing for opiate compounds and "microbial reduction treatments to comply with food safety requirements" (see pages 5 to 8 of a 2025 report the association sent to the FDA).

The Karnataka government has recently issued a joint circular, with multiple concerned departments on board, on measures to ensure the well-being of students across all schools, colleges, hostels, residential schools, and training institutions in the State.
These measures include conducting mandatory check-ups for all girls in schools by a gynaecologist, the provision of sex education, and the creation of awareness among children regarding child rights, issues concerning teenage pregnancies, the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, child marriage, and the Child Helpline (1098). Furthermore, the installation of CCTV cameras has been made mandatory in all schools and colleges.
A warning has also been issued stating that failure to prevent — or negligence in addressing — cases of child marriage, teenage pregnancy, and incidents falling under the POCSO Act, 2012, will result in both legal action and disciplinary proceedings against the officials concerned.
The circular is a culmination of a series of measures initiated in June 2025 over concerns about rising cases of child marriage and teenage pregnancy in the State.
Child Protection Committee
Among the measures prescribed is the formation of Child Protection Committees in educational institutions across the State. The committee, comprising parents, children, and teachers, must meet once every three months, and the proceedings of these meetings should be duly recorded, the circular noted.
Schools and residential schools must install complaint boxes and take measures to address the grievances of girl students. It has been mandated that experienced and qualified counsellors be appointed in schools and Pre-University (PU) colleges to address the mental health and other challenges faced by adolescent students. Teachers must persuade parents to re-enrol girls who have dropped out of school and ensure that they continue their education until the age of 18. They must also take measures to prevent school-going children from being subjected to child labour.
Children should be provided with appropriate education to help them understand and identify issues such as crimes against children, child labour, child trafficking, sexual abuse, and child marriage through both formal and informal educational curricula. They should also be taught to recognise any form of abuse, violence, discrimination, or exploitation directed against them, whether within educational institutions or elsewhere, the circular said.
“If a girl student in a school or residential school remains absent for more than three days without providing any notification, the principal must inform the gram panchayat and the child helpline (1098) in writing. The Health Department has stated that appropriate legal action must be taken against shops selling abortion pills without a doctor’s prescription, as well as against doctors and members of the public involved in unauthorised abortion activities,” the circular said.
Substance abuse
Additionally, the guidelines emphasise the need to raise awareness among children about the dangers of substance abuse and drug addiction, alongside conducting regular screenings for such issues. They stipulate that such awareness should also be integrated into the school curriculum.

Duffy said during a nationwide ground stop in January 2023 that the FAA needed competent people, not more funding. He was not transportation secretary at the time. More than three years later, in November 2026, he said his department needed more money during a nationwide ground stop that occurred on his watch.
In mid-November, a video montage spread purportedly showing U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy making contrasting statements about funding for the Federal Aviation Administration.
Some of the compilation's clips, said to be from 2023, supposedly show him saying the FAA needed more competent people, not more money, amid a nationwide ground stop that lasted less than two hours on Jan. 11 of that year. Duffy was not transportation secretary at that point. He appeared to be criticizing former President Joe Biden's administration.
Other parts of the video montage show Duffy nearly four years later, speaking as transportation secretary, requesting $50 billion in funding following the Nov. 13, 2026, outage that led to a nationwide grounding of flights lasting roughly five hours — the longest such stoppage since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.
People shared versions of the compilation video on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Reddit (archived) and TikTok. One Snopes reader asked, "Was Sean Duffy on Fox News Jan. 11, 2023, saying the FAA doesn't need more money but more competent people?"
To answer that reader's question, yes, the story is true. The clips in the video montage are real, meaning they were not created or manipulated with artificial intelligence tools.
Comedy Central's "The Daily Show" first posted the edited compilation video on Nov. 16 (archived).
A partial statement from the Transportation Department appears later in this article.
Duffy's 2023 remarks
A search of the Internet Archive's TV News Archive website, which hosts historic footage of news programs, confirms that Duffy did say the remarks in the video montage that were said to be from 2023. On Jan. 11 of that year, he told Sandra Smith, the host of the Fox News show, "America Reports" (from the 2:36 mark onward):
They got billions of dollars, the FAA did, over COVID. And now they're going to come back and say, "We want even more money to fix this crisis that we weren't able to handle when, you know, for what, three hours in the morning, aircraft couldn't fly." I don't know that it's more money, Sandra. I think it's just having competent people in leadership and throughout the building that can make the organization function, and you don't have that right now.
Origin of November 2026 clips
The additional clips in "The Daily Show" video montage truly originate from recent broadcasts, as well. They show Duffy speaking about the grounding of flights in 2026.
During a Nov. 13 White House news conference regarding the ground stop, Duffy said, "I want $50 billion" (7:11), "Let's get the money" (7:51), and "I want $50 billion" (9:35). These clips appear between 0:13 and 0:16 in "The Daily Show" compilation video.
Other clips show Duffy saying, "I need additional money" (6:53) on "Fox News Sunday," "Congress can find a way to find the money" (5:27) and "All we need is the money" (7:57) on ABC News' "This Week With George Stephanopoulos," and "I need more money" (2:19) and "All I need is the money" (4:08) on NBC News' "Meet the Press." These clips appear between 0:20 and 0:26 in "The Daily Show" compilation video.
The final clip of Duffy confirming his $50 billion ask (from 0:26 onward in the video montage) aired on CBS News' "Face the Nation" (9:25) on Nov. 15.
Snopes contacted the Transportation Department to ask if the comparison people were sharing is fair. A spokesperson responded by comparing Duffy's record to that of former Transportation Department Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who served under Biden during the January 2023 ground stop. That statement, criticizing Buttigieg, ended with, "Secretary Duffy pointed out the obvious: Buttigieg had no plan to fix the FAA. The Trump administration does."
For further reading, we previously examined whether Buttigieg's transportation department spent $80 billion on diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives while delaying air traffic control upgrades.

Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic and unprecedented decision.
The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.
The ICJ president, Yuji Iwasawa, said a majority of nine judges on the 15-seat court found that “the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya”.
The 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, arriving with reports of mass killings of adults and children, gang-rapes and burned-down villages.
Nearly a decade later, in a refugee camp in Bangladesh, crowds of Rohingya people watching on outdoor TV screens leaped up in celebration and applause as the final verdict was read out.
One Rohingya survivor, Yousuf Ali, had travelled to the court to hear the verdict. “Today, we have finally been heard, and it is a profound relief,” he said. “This judgment gives hope to our children and the next generation of Rohingya. But our fight is not over.”
Governments had been anxiously awaiting the decision handed down in the Netherlands, where the UN-run court is based, in part because the ruling will set a precedent for genocide claims, notably a high-profile case against Israel.
In what could become a crucial factor for the Gaza case, where Israel claims its mass killings are part of a counter-terrorism operation, judges dismissed Myanmar’s claims of carrying out legitimate military operations against insurgents.
Genocide, defined after the Nazi Holocaust by a 1948 UN convention, is harder to prove than war crimes because it requires evidence of specific “intent” to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. Iwasawa said during the reading of the decision that the court was “fully convinced that Myanmar committed acts falling under … the genocide convention with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar”.
After the ruling, Britain’s foreign minister, Ed Miliband, said the government was expelling Myanmar’s defence attaché and called “urgently” for a session at the UN security council, the body that has the power to enforce ICJ rulings.
The case was raised by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, on behalf of Myanmar survivors. It rested on claims of genocidal statements and “patterns of conduct” that showed attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state, including gunning down people as they fled and blocking their return.
In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear from survivors who had travelled from camps in Bangladesh. More than a million Rohingya still live there, in the world’s largest refugee settlement, and fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Buddhist-majority Myanmar.
Refugees who had fled to Bangladesh told the Guardian in 2017 of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, mass graves and the drowning of children in a river. That village, which satellite footage later showed had been burned down, was one of several analysed by rights investigators and built a case for genocide.
During hearings, the Gambian justice minister, Dawda Jallow, told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”. “It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”
Legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to “prevent births”. Investigators have said gang-rapes and soldiers’ mutilation of women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.
The court appeared to back that assessment, accusing the military of using sexual violence to “physically and mentally impair the willingness and ability of the [Rohingya] population to procreate”, referring to cultural stigma for rape survivors. Myanmar had also imposed other measures to restrict births, the court ruled, such as limits of two children per Rohingya family.
Myanmar has denied carrying out a genocide, claiming its actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted guerrilla-style attacks. Its military responded with massive “clearance operations”.
However, judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the international criminal court (ICC), which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states, on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
During a reading of the decision that lasted more than two hours in a packed Great Hall of Justice in The Hague, Iwasawa called for Myanmar to provide reparations and restitution. This included allowing the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, returning or replacing their property, and providing physical and mental rehabilitation.
The ruling was also significant as it formally classified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group under international law, something they have been denied by Myanmar, which refers to them as Bengalis or foreign migrants.
Reached by phone shortly after he left the courtroom, the lead counsel for the case against Myanmar told the Guardian the mood had been emotional in the room as the judgment was read out in front of his legal team, which included Rohingya.
“This is the ICJ recognising their history of discrimination, recognising them as a group, recognising the horrific violence they endured and suffered,” said Arsalan Suleman. “It was a really emotional moment for them and the whole team. We felt the weight of the court’s judgment.”
Israel and its chief ally, the US, have been closely following the Myanmar case, as the decision provides the strongest hint of how judges could assess the Gaza case, brought by South Africa. UN independent investigations, as well as genocide scholars, have already said Israel has committed acts of genocide in Gaza.
A judgment finding Myanmar had breached the convention has been predicted to lead to the US imposing sanctions on ICJ judges, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay.
Washington had considered the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration. However, the Trump administration has been on the offensive against international rights bodies, including imposing sanctions on the ICC.
Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the 1990s Balkan wars fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops at the Srebrenica massacre.
Other UN tribunals have established genocide in only a handful of cases since the Holocaust, including Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge rule in the 1970s and the 1994 mass killings in Rwanda.

More people are getting the flu. Should you get a flu shot before you travel?
Heading out of town for the holidays? There's still time to get your flu shot
More people are getting the flu than usual this fall, according to the latest influenza tracking numbers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
"Flu started a bit early this year, so it's out there and spreading," Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of infectious diseases at the Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville. "So people who are thinking of Thanksgiving travel need to get their protection as quickly as possible."
The flu shot takes about ten days to reach its full efficacy, so there's still time to get one before Thanksgiving, Schaffner says. And the sooner someone gets it, the better – especially because people will be gathering in enclosed spaces for the holidays.
AAA predicts that this year, around 82 million people will travel more than 50 miles over Thanksgiving break, including 73 million by car.
Getting the vaccine doesn't mean someone won't get the flu – but it does mean they'll be less likely to wind up in the hospital from influenza-related complications. Those include pneumonia and secondary bacterial infections.
"It can strike a healthy person at any age and put them in the emergency room. Flu is like that," Schaffner says.
People at the highest risk are seniors, young children and people with underlying health conditions.
Schaffner also says not enough people are getting their COVID boosters.
"Somehow they think that COVID has disappeared," he says. "But the people who are admitted to my hospital with COVID are invariably people who are not up to date with their vaccinations, as with flu. That COVID vaccine helps keep you out of the hospital. It is still a threat. It hasn't gone away."
People should have no trouble finding available vaccines for the flu, COVID and the highly contagious respiratory syncytial virus, RSV, at their local pharmacies and health care providers' offices, says Claire Hannan, the executive director of the Association of Immunization Managers, adding that vaccination season is in "full swing."
"Now is definitely the time to get vaccinated," says Hannan. "Influenza is circulating, people are traveling, people are getting ready for Thanksgiving, the holidays. And the best protection you can get is from the vaccine."

Merck and Isomorphic Labs, the artificial intelligence drug designer built on a Nobel winning technology that can model how molecules will bind to proteins, said Thursday that they are entering into a research collaboration to discover small molecule candidates for an undisclosed oncology target of “strategic importance.”
The partnership — only the latest such deal between a pharma giant and Isomorphic — will bring together the latter’s proprietary drug design engine and existing wet lab data from Merck, officials from both companies said. Merck will handle the preclinical and clinical development, manufacturing, and commercializing of any products.
“It is a target of high interest to us, a target where we have deployed internal efforts, and we think the pairing of those datasets with the Isomorphic drug discovery engine technology could be a very powerful pairing,” said George Addona, global head of discovery, preclinical development, and translational medicine at Merck.
The aim is to use Isomorphic’s modeling and compute capabilities to expedite the discovery process. “At the end of the day, the ability for us to identify new ways to discover better molecules faster is truly, truly exciting,” Addona said.
Under the agreement, Isomorphic will receive an undisclosed upfront payment and is eligible for later payments tied to research, development, regulatory, and commercial milestones, as well as tiered royalties on net sales. Isomorphic also has the option to co-fund development activities for higher royalties.
The announcement comes days after Isomorphic announced it had raised $5 billion in additional private funding, and six months after having raised $2.1 billion. Its other pharma industry research partners include Novartis, Eli Lilly, and Johnson & Johnson.
While Isomorphic has its own internal drug development program, broadening its reach through external partnerships is a critical part of its strategy, according to the company’s chief research officer, Sarah Skerratt.
“We always say that we’re here to ‘solve all disease,’ but we’re not going to do that in isolation. … The only way we’re going to solve our mission is to have partners that can enable that journey with us,” Skerratt said.
For Adonna, the partnership reflects how quickly AI is maturing — a sign that the technology is being used “in ways that we could only have dreamed of a few years ago,” he said.
Isomorphic, which spun out from Google’s DeepMind in 2021 and is now based in London, is best known for the development of AlphaFold, an open-access AI program that predicts the 3D structures of proteins from their amino acid sequences. This year, Isomorphic released its proprietary commercial platform for drug developers, called Isomorphic Labs Drug Design Engine. The IsoDDE system is intended to tackle some of drug design’s toughest challenges, like discovering hidden pockets on proteins and estimating how strongly a molecule can bind to its target.
Isomorphic’s founder and CEO, Demis Hassabis, was awarded the 2024 Nobel Prize in chemistry for developing the AlphaFold model.
