In the span of less than 24 hours, two Trump administration nominees have suffered sudden blows—Trump’s pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration and his pick to lead the National Science Foundation.
Late Tuesday evening, Axios reported that the White House had abruptly withdrawn its controversial nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the FDA. Overton, a top conservative domestic policy aide in the White House, has drawn criticism and skepticism from Republicans and Democrats alike over her stances on vaccines, abortion, vapes, and birth control. Overton opposes abortion—though perhaps not strongly enough for some Republicans—and supported Trump and Kennedy’s decried anti-vaccine policies and statements, vexing Democrats.
In her confirmation hearing in September, Overton consistently stonewalled senators on every topic, refusing to directly answer even softball questions from friendly Republicans, leaving lawmakers on both sides of the aisle openly frustrated. The questions she dodged included those on how she would handle the FDA’s current safety review of the abortion pill, mifepristone, which extensive data has established is extremely safe. She also wouldn’t say whether she agreed with Trump when he falsely claimed the measles vaccine is “quite lethal” or that children are given vaccine doses the “size of a soda bottle.” Overton repeatedly refused to answer whether Trump could ever be wrong.
Axios quoted a senior Trump administration official as saying that Overton’s nomination was dropped because she “lacks the support on the Hill to move forward with her confirmation.”
The Senate’s Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee, chaired by Bill Cassidy (R-La.), was scheduled to vote on Overton’s nomination Wednesday. In a social media post Tuesday night, after her nomination was withdrawn, Cassidy said he believed she had a “viable confirmation path.” But he said the nomination was “abandoned” after some anti-abortion senators sought commitments from her that they couldn’t get. “The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments,” Cassidy said.

- The claim that Sean Duffy's son-in-law, U.S. Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso, owns or has a stake in Air Space Intelligence, the company behind a new artificial intelligence-powered air traffic management tool for the FAA, is unfounded.
- The claims spread after the Nov. 13 nationwide ground stop, with some social media posts linking the outage to the company's campaign donation and FAA contract. The FAA denied that ASI's software caused the shutdown.
- ASI's PAC did give Alfonso's campaign $2,500 — not $12,500, as some posts claimed — before the firm won an FAA contract worth up to $875.95 million. But neither Alfonso nor Duffy has reported a stake in the company.
- Federal records show that the FAA received 12 offers for the contract. We found no evidence that Alfonso received the contract or that the campaign donation influenced the decision. Alfonso's team told us via email he had no part in awarding the contract and said no laws or House ethics rules were violated. The FAA said in a statement that its contracts go through "a rigorous, competitive process guided by nonpartisan career experts and personnel" and that ASI received this contract following an "innovative challenge with three vendors."
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces.
In mid-November, following a nationwide halt to U.S. flight departures, social media users shared claims about connections between Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy; his son-in-law, U.S. Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso, a Wisconsin Republican; and Air Space Intelligence — the company behind a new artificial intelligence-powered system used by the Federal Aviation Administration.
On Nov. 13, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop after communications problems affected air traffic control facilities. The incident happened three days after the agency announced the nationwide expansion of an AI-supported traffic management system called SMART, developed by ASI.
Some posts claimed Alfonso had financial ties to ASI or received the FAA contract through Duffy, while others linked the company to the shutdown. For instance, one Facebook post (archived) read:
On Friday, the FAA grounded every plane in America.
The AI air traffic system at the center of it belongs to Air Space Intelligence. In June, Sean Duffy's department gave them an $875 million contract.
Before that, the company's PAC donated to Duffy's son-in-law, 26-year-old Michael Alfonso. He just won Duffy's old seat in Congress.
Americans deserve answers.
Another post (archived) on X stated, "Sean Duffy's son in law owns the AI company responsible for this FAA disaster yall."
Versions of the claim circulated on multiple social media platforms, including Reddit, X, Instagram and Facebook. Snopes readers also asked whether Alfonso or Duffy owned ASI, whether Alfonso received a multimillion-dollar FAA contract and whether campaign donations influenced the deal.
In short, Air Space Intelligence's PAC did contribute to Alfonso's campaign in March, and the company later received an FAA contract worth up to $875.95 million. However, we found no evidence that Alfonso owned ASI or that the donation influenced the contract award. The FAA also denied that the company's SMART system caused the Nov. 13 shutdown, and rather pointed to problems with its older communications network.
Alfonso's team said he had no part in awarding the FAA contract and that the campaign donation broke no laws or ethics rules, adding, "Nobody trades an $875 million federal contract for a $2,500 check." The FAA said in a statement that "each FAA contract goes through a rigorous, competitive process guided by nonpartisan career experts and personnel." We have also reached out to Air Space Intelligence and will update this report if we receive a response.
Here's what we know about the rumor:
ASI's PAC donated to Alfonso's campaign
According to a filing with the Federal Election Commission, Air Space Intelligence's political action committee donated $2,500 to Alfonso's congressional campaign on March 31:
(Federal Election Commission)
Alfonso's campaign also reported the same contribution:
(Federal Election Commission)
Some social media posts and articles, however, mentioned a larger sum of $12,500. That likely stemmed from a Raw Story article, which cited that amount, but later issued a correction.
News outlets reported on Alfonso's campaign donations even before the FAA shutdown. For instance, in March, ProPublica reported that his campaign received money from lobbyists and companies with interests before the Department of Transportation.
Did Alfonso or Duffy have financial ties to ASI?
Some social media posts claimed Alfonso owned Air Space Intelligence. Snopes readers also asked whether he invested in the company or benefited financially from its FAA contract.
However, we found no evidence supporting these claims. Neither Alfonso nor Duffy was listed among ASI's founders or executives. Alfonso's financial disclosure from April also didn't list any investment in ASI, although it only covered the period until October 2025. Similarly, Duffy's 2026 financial disclosure didn't list ASI among his investments.
In a statement to Snopes, Alfonso said, "Family ties don't earn anyone special treatment, and my father-in-law knows better than anyone that I think for myself." His team did not directly answer whether he ever owned shares or had any other financial interest in ASI.
Who received the $875M FAA contract?
Some social media posts claimed that Duffy awarded a multimillion-dollar FAA contract directly to his son-in-law, sometimes describing it as a no-bid contract. For example, one Bluesky user wrote, "In a surprise to no one, Sean Duffy gave a No Bid contract to his son-in-law to install the AI program into the FAA's system."
However, the USAspending.gov database showed the contract was awarded to Air Space Intelligence, not Alfonso:
(www.usaspending.gov)
The contract began on June 23 and could run for 12 years. Its maximum potential value is $875.95 million, but this does not mean ASI has already received all of that amount.
"No laws or House Ethics rules were violated," Alfonso's team told us via email, adding that "By law, PACs can give up to $5,000 per election. Nobody trades an $875 million federal contract for a $2,500 check."
According to federal records, the FAA received 12 offers before awarding the contract to ASI. The records classified the award as competitive, although they did not identify the other bidders or explain how ASI was selected. Bloomberg reported "the startup beat out larger competitors Palantir Technologies Inc. and Thales SA."
The FAA said in a statement that: "each FAA contract goes through a rigorous, competitive process guided by nonpartisan career experts and personnel. The FAA awarded the contract to Air Space Intelligence (ASI) following an innovative challenge with three vendors who demonstrated the highest levels of reliability, operational performance, and efficiency." The agency did not say whether Duffy was personally involved in the decision, or whether there was any potential conflict of interest involving him or Alfonso.
The FAA announced its search for a company to develop the system in September 2025, months before ASI's PAC donated to Alfonso's campaign, and announced ASI as the winner in June. We found no public evidence that the donation influenced the contract award.
Alfonso's team said he had no part in awarding the FAA contract, pointing out that he was a congressional candidate at the time, and not a government official. In a statement to Snopes, Alfonso also said, "I can't be bought," adding that he would consider each bill separately, including any future FAA funding requests, and "vote based on what's best for Wisconsin."
What caused the Nov. 13 FAA shutdown?
The FAA said its new AI system, SMART, did not cause the nationwide flight shutdown on Nov. 13. During a news briefing the next day, Duffy explained it "is a system that's not tied into or connected to the systems that went down yesterday. It's a tool that gives a prompt to one of our flight managers that they can accept or deny, but it's just better information flowing to them," summarizing that "SMART had zero impact on the occurrences yesterday."
Similarly, ASI wrote on X on Nov. 13 that the "current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC."
According to a Nov. 15 statement, the issue involved the FAA's older communications network. The agency identified two possible locations connected to the problem: a site in Arkansas, where contractor L3Harris was installing a new router, and another in Texas. L3Harris confirmed in a news release it was cooperating with the FAA's investigation. As of this writing, the exact cause of the shutdown was still under investigation.

Moving beyond test preparation, listed edtech major PhysicsWallah (PW) has now said that it is establishing a “greenfield digital” university. In an investor presentation, the edtech platform said that the digital university has already been notified by the Punjab government. The digital university plans to offer 16 undergraduate, postgraduate, diploma and certificate courses including BCA, BBA, B.Com, BA, M.Com, MCA, MBA, among others. The edtech major also claimed that the nearly 15,000 sq ft campus will be self-financed and will operate on an asset-light model. Admissions are slated to begin in July 2027. The listed company has opted for a digital delivery model that pairs online degrees with competitive exam preparation (such as B.Com-CA and BA-UPSC combinations). “After Class 12, many learners take a degree elsewhere. PWDU (PW digital university) keeps them with PW, from exam prep to a degree to a career,” read the presentation. PW has received authorisation from the state government under the “Punjab Private Digital Open Universities Policy”. The digital university will have a 3 acre physical campus, but it will serve only as the headquarters for administrative purposes. No regular classes will be held on campus. The announcement came on the same day as the company’s maiden Investor Day in Mumbai. At the event, the company outlined an ambitious target of ₹9,000 Cr to ₹10,000 Cr in revenue by fiscal year 2029-30 (FY30). This implies a 2.5X jump from the ₹3,900 Cr top line that the company reported in FY26 The company expects this growth surge to come on the back of its online business, which it projects will contribute around “two-thirds” of its total revenue by FY30. At its maiden Investor Day in Mumbai, the edtech giant said that it expects its revenue to rise at an compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) of more than 25% between FY27 and FY30. It is also targeting an EBITDA margin of over 20% by FY30. “Our FY30 ambition is about profit growing faster than revenue. We will stay disciplined with capital and report our progress every year,” said PhysicsWallah chief financial officer (CFO) Amit Sachdeva. Over the next three to five years, PW plans to focus on premiumisation to drive higher average revenue per user (ARPU), leverage AI to drive efficiencies, scale vernacular courses and tap into the pre-foundation (Class 6 to Class 8) and upskilling markets. The bullish outlook comes as PW reported a consolidated net profit of ₹143.6 Cr in the second quarter (Q2) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27), up 106% from ₹69.7 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Meanwhile, revenue from operations also rose 18.2% to ₹1,242.3 Cr in the quarter under review from ₹1,051.3 Cr in Q2 FY26.

The story so far: After 26 years of holding on to its measles elimination status, the United States lost this distinction. On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organisation (PAHO) revoked the United States’ measles elimination status. This was after over 5400 cases of measles were reported in the U.S. in 2026.
This is the highest annual total since 1989-91, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention(CDC). As per data put out by the Unicef, 96% of cases are in unvaccinated people or those with unknown vaccination status. Children under five account for 18% of cases and those aged 5-19 for 40%.

Microplastics in the Yamuna in Delhi are accompanied by a complex mixture of organic chemicals, including pharmaceutical residues, pesticides and industrial effluents, with many of these substances classified as human-health and environmental hazards, according to a new study by University of Delhi researchers.
The study, published in the 'Journal of Hazardous Materials Advances' in September 2026, examines microplastic pollution and associated chemical profiles at eight locations along a 48.8-km stretch of the river in Delhi -- from its entry at Palla to its exit at Asgarpur Jagir -- highlighting how pollution patterns vary across agricultural, residential, industrial, recreational and forested areas.
Researchers recovered 2,289 microplastic particles from the samples, with an average abundance of 3.18 particles per litre. The analysis identified 321 distinct chemical compounds across the samples, of which 50 were detected in extracts of recovered microplastic fractions at four or more locations.
Of these 50 compounds, 36 corresponded to structures with Global Harmonized System (GHS) hazard classifications, covering categories such as carcinogenicity, reproductive toxicity, acute toxicity and aquatic hazards.
Seven compounds were detected across all eight sampling locations, including 2-naphthylamine, lidocaine and monobutyl phthalate, the study found.
The researchers also identified pharmaceutical compounds such as atomoxetine, domperidone and telmisartan, along with agrochemical-related substances, including diuron and thiamethoxam.
Radhey Shyam Sharma, head of the Department of Environmental Studies at University of Delhi and one of the co-authors of the study, said the findings highlight the need to look beyond microplastic particles and examine the complex chemical mixtures present in river ecosystems.
"The microplastics problem, along with this cocktail of organic and inorganic substances, needs to be looked at through the lens of mixture toxicity. The land-use pattern has also been explored in the study," Sharma said.
He stressed the importance of nature-based solutions, including strengthening vegetation along riverbanks and protecting natural river ecosystems, to minimise pollution-related risks.
"Vegetation ecosystems can help prevent pollution from entering the river. Natural ecosystems and riverbanks need to be strengthened to minimise these risks. The focus should be on nature-based solutions," he said.
The study found significant variations in microplastic abundance across the eight locations. The highest concentration was recorded at the recreational-hydraulic site near the barrage, followed by a floodplain area where multiple drains converge.
The lowest abundance was recorded at the agricultural entry point at Palla and a forested stretch of the river.
The researchers noted that the Delhi stretch of the Yamuna receives inputs from 22 tributary drains carrying partially treated or untreated sewage, agricultural runoff and industrial effluents, contributing to the diverse pollution profile.
Polyethylene and polypropylene were the predominant polymers identified, accounting for 44.1 per cent and 27.3 per cent, respectively, of the spectrally identified particles.
The researchers cautioned that the detection of hazardous compounds does not, by itself, establish actual exposure or ecological risk. The chemical findings were based on screening-level identification and require further confirmation through quantitative analysis.
They also pointed out that microplastic abundance alone cannot capture the chemical complexity of river pollution, underlining the need for spatially detailed monitoring of both particles and associated chemical substances.

As U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., announced his bid to serve as the next speaker of the House following Democrats' sweeping congressional victories in the 2026 midterm elections, social media users were quick to claim he received money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — a pro-Israel lobbying group.
Posts on X, Instagram and Facebook accused Jeffries of working for Israel's interests as a major recipient of AIPAC funding. Snopes readers also searched the site and emailed us seeking the truth about the matter.
A petition circulated online, garnering more than 930,000 signatures as of this writing, asking Democrats to select someone else as speaker. "Picking our own speaker who does not represent Israel first, is where we start," one of the top comments on the petition read.
The claim was true — Jeffries has received money from AIPAC. He has an extensive history with the lobbying group, and they have publicly expressed mutual support.
We looked at the official Federal Election Commission record (archived) of Jeffries' campaign funding, and found AIPAC had given many thousands of dollars to Jeffries over the years.
OpenSecrets, a nonprofit aimed at tracking money in U.S. politics, estimated Jeffries had received approximately $1.74 million through 2024 from pro-Israel donors generally, putting him slightly ahead of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. TrackAIPAC, an organization focused specifically on AIPAC and other pro-Israel lobbyists, connected $1.5 million in such donations to Jeffries.
AIPAC identified Jeffries by name in a congratulatory post on Nov. 4, writing on X (archived) that "AIPAC members are determined to expand their political activism in the cycles ahead."
Jeffries has a long history of support for Israel, telling a crowd in 2014: "Israel today, Israel tomorrow, Israel forever." He told the American Jewish Committee in June 2023 that he'd been to Israel six times, more than any other country he'd visited. "I'm from New York City, where we consider Jerusalem to be the sixth borough," he reportedly said.
The Times of Israel reported on Nov. 6: "While some in that younger generation have pushed for a tougher US stance on Israel, Jeffries does not belong to that camp and is likely to toe the line set by his predecessor Pelosi, Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and US President Joe Biden, who have long made a point of boasting their pro-Israel bona fides."
As U.S. voters, particularly younger constituents, signal increasing opposition to U.S. support for Israel amid its war in Gaza — which the U.N. declared a genocide — it remains unclear how this will shape Jeffries' stance on Israel.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) on Thursday sought an additional 60 days to continue its investigation into Twisha Sharma's death. However, the district and sessions court in Bhopal asked the agency to first furnish details of the investigation conducted over the past 90 days. The application was submitted before additional district judge (ADJ) Pallavi Dwivedi.
Advocate Ankur Pandey, representing Twisha Sharma's parents, said, "CBI had demanded an extension of 60 days for further investigation. But the court has asked CBI for details of investigation of 90 days."
Pandey further said that counsel for Giribala Singh and Samarth Singh had filed an application seeking separate cells in Bhopal Jail, citing safety concerns.
The application was submitted before the Bhopal court on Nov 14. The jailer has since submitted a report to the court. According to Pandey, arrangements have been made for them in accordance with the jail manual.
The CBI, in its application, stated that it had filed a chargesheet on Aug 18, 2026, along with a request for additional time to conduct further investigation. The court had taken cognisance and allowed the request.
According to the CBI application, forensic examination of the digital video recorder (DVR) and closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage from the residence is still required to verify continuity and investigate alleged tampering.
The agency is also awaiting forensic data extraction from Twisha Sharma's iPhone at the Central Forensic Science Laboratory (CFSL) in Delhi.
Twisha died at her husband's residence in Bhopal's Katara Hills on May 12.

The two rival factions of the Trinamool Congress have become embroiled in a war of words over the party’s twin-flower symbol that has been frozen by the Election Commission of India (ECI). Diamond Harbour MP Abhishek Banerjee and Mamata All India Trinamool Congress on November 18 said that the original electoral symbol of the party will ultimately remain with Mamata Banerjee.
“The original name and electoral symbol had always been with Mamata Banerjee and will continue to remain so in the future. Just wait for seven days. We will prove how manipulations were made in filing affidavits to establish the right over the original party name and original electoral symbol. We will display that on the big screen,” Mr. Banerjee told media persons.
Mr. Banerjee has claimed that the faction of the party led by Ritabrata Banerjee filed affidavits with the help of the West Bengal Police. The Diamond Harbour MP had claimed that the alleged attack on his residence on November 7 was intended to interfere with the filing of affidavits, staking a claim over the affidavits.
Leader of the Opposition in the West Bengal Assembly Ritabrata Banerjee said that the symbol does not belong to either faction and Mr. Banerjee will not be able to stake claim over the symbol in seven births.
“He has said that they will get the symbol in seven days, they will not get the symbol in seven births,” the LOP, which represents the Democratic Trinamool Congress, said.
The ECI on September 17, 2026, had barred both factions, the Mamata Banerjee-led faction and the Ritabrata Banerjee-led faction of the party, from using the party symbol and name in the bypolls in Nandigram and Rejinagar in West Bengal which were scheduled on October 6. The very next day, on September 18, the Mamata faction got the name ‘Mamata All India Trinamool Congress’ with ‘football player’ as its symbol, while the Ritabrata grouping was allotted the name ‘Democratic Trinamool Congress’ with the symbol ‘envelope’.
Both the factions of the Trinamool Congress have submitted truckloads of affidavits to the ECI, which includes support by party members, MPs and MLAs. Ritabrata Banerjee claims support of 65 of the 80 MLAs of the party. The faction of Mamata Banerjee has the support of a handful of MLAs and MPs who have not defected to NCPI or joined the BJP after the West Bengal Assembly polls of 2026.

Union minister for road transport and highways Nitin Gadkari has urged states to adopt the Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines, 2025, citing their potential to expand livelihood opportunities amid crackdowns on bike taxi operations across several states. The remarks came during the 'RIDE – Moving India Forward' event in New Delhi, organised in collaboration with Uber, Ola, Rapido, Bharat Taxi, Zomato, Swiggy and Porter. Gadkari said aggregator platforms have already generated 4 Cr jobs following the introduction of the government's policy framework, despite its adoption by only two states. "If the whole country accepts this, then 10 Cr jobs will be created. And the food and other delivery apps working in this are different. So, if 10 Cr and 8-10 Cr are there, then 18 Cr jobs will be created here," the minister said. He added that these platforms could generate employment without requiring government capital expenditure. “Not everyone can get a government job. Not even so many governments have jobs," Gadkari said. The minister said he has written to state governments, urging them to adopt the framework and enable app-based mobility services to create livelihoods, particularly for people from socially, economically and educationally disadvantaged backgrounds. He also highlighted the expansion of app-based services beyond passenger transport into food and goods delivery, creating opportunities for employment and entrepreneurship. He cited e-rickshaws and e-carts as examples of technology transforming traditional occupations and reducing physical hardship. Gadkari further emphasised the need to strengthen last-mile connectivity in rural areas, arguing that better access to transport services could help people travel to schools and cities, while enabling farmers to take their produce to urban markets. "Children will be able to go to school. They will start coming to the city. If they can bring their milk, fruits, flowers, vegetables to the city, then the economy can change," he said. On regulation, he said the ministry’s objective is to support the sector’s growth while protecting drivers and passengers, and called on companies to share suggestions to improve the framework. “The aim of the ministry is not to control anyone. All of us should come together, think together and work together,” he said. State-Level Bike Taxi Crackdowns Gadkari's push for wider adoption of the aggregator framework comes amid regulatory uncertainty and enforcement action against bike taxi operators across several states. In Kolhapur, the RTO seized 10 two-wheelers allegedly operating as Rapido bike taxis and said no bike-taxi app had been granted permission to operate in the district. In Odisha, the Crime Branch directed Uber and Rapido to discontinue their bike taxi services, terming them unauthorised over the alleged commercial use of private, non-transport two-wheelers. Meanwhile, Karnataka's bike taxi dispute remains before the Supreme Court, with the state challenging a January 2026 High Court ruling that allowed operations to resume. In August, the state’s transport department inspected 220 two-wheelers in Bengaluru, booked 71 and seized 70. In May, Maharashtra’s transport minister Pratap Sarnaik urged the state's cybercrime department to shut down bike taxi services operated by Ola, Uber and Rapido and file FIRs against their management. What The Guidelines Cover Issued on July 1, 2025, under Section 93 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the guidelines provide a framework for states to license and regulate aggregators. They prescribe five-year licences, a ₹5 Lakh grant fee and security deposits of ₹10-50 Lakh, depending on fleet size. Surge pricing is capped at twice the base fare, while drivers using their own vehicles must receive at least 80% of the applicable fare. Aggregators must provide ₹5 Lakh health insurance and at least ₹10 Lakh term insurance for drivers. Requirements also cover training, tracking, panic buttons, round-the-clock support and grievance redressal. Drivers can work across platforms. Clause 23 lets states permit private motorcycles to carry passengers through aggregators under Section 67(3), subject to driver checks, licensing, insurance and training. States may levy daily, weekly or fortnightly fees. This is optional, rather than nationwide permission for private bike taxis. Other aggregator vehicles require applicable permits, including contract carriage permits for cars carrying paying passengers. Subsequent amendments allow apps to offer voluntary tipping only after a trip, with the entire amount credited to the driver. They also require an option to choose a driver of the same gender, wherever available, including female drivers for women passengers.

Bengaluru-based deeptech startup Enerzolve Smart Technologies is in talks to raise around $16- 20 Mn (₹150-186 Cr) in a fresh funding round led by existing investor Jungle Ventures, sources familiar with the development told Inc42. The round is also expected to see participation from other existing investors, while there is a possibility of a new investor joining the startup’s cap table, the sources said. The name of the new investor is yet to be determined. Inc42 reached out to Enerzolve and Jungle Ventures for comments on the deal. The story will be updated based on their response. The proposed round comes less than a year after Enerzolve raised $5.1 Mn in a seed funding round co-led by Jungle Ventures and Kae Capital in January 2026. The latest fundraise, if completed, would mark a significant jump in the capital raised by the startup as it looks to scale its energy infrastructure business. The startup had earmarked its erstwhile raised seed capital to scale manufacturing, securing certifications for its smart grid and energy storage product lines, and strengthening its engineering and product development capabilities. It also planned to deepen its business development efforts and build relationships with utilities, EPC companies, private DISCOMs and storage developers. Founded in 2024 by Abhay Adya and Anupam Kumar Bhatt, Enerzolve builds semiconductor-powered hardware and embedded systems for smart grids, renewable energy infrastructure and battery storage. Its product portfolio spans three segments — instrumentation, power electronics and energy storage. These include smart meters, protection relays, grid analysers, battery management systems, power conversion systems and inverters. The startup also offers original design manufacturing (ODM), system integration and customised engineering solutions for utilities, industrial players and infrastructure companies. The B2B firm targets clients in segments like DISCOM, EPC and battery storage developers. It is also working on developing its core intellectual property across silicon, firmware and power electronics. The proposed fundraise comes amid growing investor interest in India's energy infrastructure and hardware ecosystem. The expansion of renewable energy capacity, smart meter deployments and battery energy storage projects is creating demand for indigenous power electronics and grid management solutions. For Enerzolve, the fresh capital could help accelerate product development, manufacturing capabilities and commercial deployments as it looks to establish itself in India's evolving energy infrastructure market.

On the intervening night of November 8 and 9, over 250 PM2.5 data points from Delhi were missing on the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) website, according to an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
Scientist and air quality analyst Manoj Kumar tweeted the statistics in the early hours of November 9. According to him, out of the 59 monitoring stations, as seen on the official website of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), only 14 stations reported complete data, while the remaining 45 had at least one missing hourly observation.
Missing hourly PM2.5 data raises concerns over Delhi’s air quality assessment.
Since midnight on 8 November until 5 am on 9 November, 227 hourly PM2.5 observations were missing across 59 CPCB monitoring stations in Delhi. Only 14 stations reported complete data, while the remaining 45 had at least one missing hourly observation.
A key concern is that many missing readings occurred when concentrations approached the monitoring instruments’ upper measurement limit of 1,000 µg/m³. These observations should not simply be treated as missing when calculating hourly or daily averages or deriving AQI. Doing so could underestimate pollution levels. For a conservative assessment, such readings should be flagged as potentially exceeding the measurement range, with 1,000 µg/m³ considered as a lower-bound value rather than treating them as zero or excluding them without qualification.
Mundka recorded the highest number of missing hourly observations (10), followed by Dwarka Sector 8, IIT Delhi, Nehru Nagar, Pusa IITM and Uttam Nagar, with eight missing hours each.
There is also an unusual pattern at some stations. IGNOU Maidan Garhi, Cantonment Area, Siri Fort and Tikri Kalan recorded PM2.5 concentrations below 30 µg/m³ (Cleanest) during parts of this episode. Given the pollution levels elsewhere, these readings warrant verification for possible instrument or data-quality issues before being used in final averages or AQI calculations.
Reliable air-quality assessment during pollution episodes requires both complete data and transparent treatment of readings that exceed instrument measurement limits.
— Dr. Manoj Kumar (@manoj_kumar_nr) November 9, 2026
Air Quality Index, or AQI, turns air quality data for eight pollutants into one number and one name, providing an easy-to-understand picture of air quality. According to the All India AQI Dashboard, the pollutants are PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, Pb, and NH3. (Lead is not monitored at every station.)
Delhi’s average AQI on the night of Diwali was as follows, according to the CPCB.
However, between 1 am and 3 am on the Diwali night, over 30 monitoring stations were not showing any PM2.5 data. Over the course of the night, more stations failed.
A day after, as the mystery of missing data caused an outrage, the hourly air quality readings missing from the CPCB website became available on the Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) website, which showed that the PM2.5 concentration went up to a staggering 3500 micrograms per cubic metre and beyond, which is around 60 times its standard value.
Below is the reading from Mundka station:
Below is the reading from JNU station:
Why does the Missing Data Matter?
India’s air quality figures come from monitoring stations run by state pollution control boards and committees, such as DPCC in Delhi. Stations send their readings to CPCB every 15 minutes. CPCB calculates each station’s AQI by finding a sub-index for every pollutant and taking the highest one. It then publishes the results on its portal, the SAMEER app and its daily bulletin.
A sub-index is the AQI score for a single pollutant on its own. Each pollutant is measured in different units and has a different “safe” range. For example, PM2.5 is in micrograms per cubic metre, and CO is in milligrams per cubic metre. So CPCB converts each pollutant’s reading to the same 0-500 scale, and that converted number is its sub-index.
If the PM2.5 has a sub-index of 75, SO2 has 63, and NO2 has 38, the station’s overall AQI is the highest of these, so here it is 75, driven by PM2.5. One bad pollutant is enough to push the AQI into a worse category, even if the others are fine.
If one looks carefully at the above screenshot from 12 midnight on November 9 from the Anand Vihar monitoring station, one would see that the 24-hour average of the PM2.5 pollutant is the 24-hour average AQI for that particular monitoring station. One would also note that the highest average sub-index determines the AQI.
Now, if PM2.5, which gives a measure of fine particulate matter in the air and is also highest during Diwali due to the bursting of firecrackers, goes missing, the average AQI reading underestimates the pollution in the air to a great extent. According to a Hindustan Times report, if one considers the released readings, Delhi’s AQI for 24 hours until 9 am on November 9 was 384 on a 500 scale against the 370 figure published by CPCB.
Why did the Data Go Missing?
According to Kumar’s post on X (shared when the missing data had not been released), Mundka recorded the highest number of missing hourly observations (10), followed by Dwarka Sector 8, IIT Delhi, Nehru Nagar, Pusa IITM and Uttam Nagar, with eight missing hours each.
Interestingly, the highest reading also came from Mundka at 3,744 µg/m³ at 2 am on November 9. JNU was at 3,023 at 4 am the same night and NSUT’s West Campus at 3,008 at 5 am. Eleven of DPCC’s stations went past 2,000 micrograms per cubic metre.
The CPCB released an official statement on November 10 addressing the data gaps, saying that particulate analysers like PM2.5 were calibrated for 0-1,000 µg/m³. Under the automated validation, hourly readings beyond that range are treated as “outside range” and left out of the computation. CPCB conceded this “may appear as a data gap” during extreme episodes like Diwali firecracker bursting. Those hours don’t count towards the 24-hour average for that station. It also stated that the methodology for processing data beyond the system’s design range is “under review”, with internal deliberations underway.
On November 11, Kumar posted on X, if the 255 missing PM2.5 data points were replaced with 1,000 µg/m³, the upper measurement limit cited by CPCB, the average showed a 49% increase, from 269 to 400 µg/m³.
Alt News spoke to Kumar, who also told us that while the DPCC continued to record data above 1000 micrograms per cubic metre, it was the CPCB, the body ultimately entrusted with calculating and releasing AQI findings, that did not register it. “DPCC had measured and displayed PM 2.5 concentration above 1000 on that day. But it was not reflected on the CPCB website.”
Explaining the process and the gaps, Kumar said, “Let’s say that the instrument’s operating range is between 0 and 1000. But if it is going above 1000, there will be some uncertainty, but uncertainty can be estimated.”
Even in his November 9 post, Kumar made the point that the readings had gone missing as the concentration readings approached 1000. “These observations should not simply be treated as missing when calculating hourly or daily averages or deriving AQI. Doing so could underestimate pollution levels. For a conservative assessment, such readings should be flagged as potentially exceeding the measurement range, with 1,000 µg/m³ considered as a lower-bound value rather than treating them as zero or excluding them without qualification,” he wrote.
Furthermore, to calculate AQI, one would need to have at least 16 hours in a day, if not all 24 hours of data. So missing out on important data points during peak pollution periods underrepresents the AQI value.
It’s also worth noting that aur quality monitoring is not cheap: A 2018 Hindustan Times report put the cost of a conventional station at up to Rs 5 crore.

Muslims will outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, report says
Muslims will soon become the largest religious group on the planet, according to a new report by the Pew Research Center released today.
Christians will be the second-largest cohort by 2035. The Muslim and Christian populations are both expected to grow, but researchers anticipate Muslims will grow faster.
If recent demographic trends continue, Pew expects the world's Muslim population will reach 3.6 billion by 2070 while the Christian population will be just under 3 billion.
The Pew Research Center arrived at its projections using data from national censuses worldwide, combined with data on fertility rates and religious switching patterns. The projections also use findings from United Nations reports and global migration estimates, along with Pew Research Center's earlier studies on religious migration.
Hindus and Jews are projected to grow in absolute numbers but decline as an overall percentage of the world population. Buddhists, meanwhile, are expected to shrink in both number and portion of the global population in the coming decades.
Some of these trends, according to Pew, can be explained by population growth trends. For instance, most of the population growth in the 21st century is expected to occur in Africa.
By 2070, more than a quarter of the global population will live in sub-Saharan Africa. The vast majority of those who live there are either Christian or Muslim. The region's high fertility rate and lengthening lifespans mean the numbers of both faiths there are expected to grow, with the Muslim population growing faster than the Christian one.
In fact, Pew projects that by 2070, the Democratic Republic of the Congo in sub-Saharan Africa will surpass the United States as the country with the largest total number of Christians. The Pew Center's religion research director Alan Cooperman calls this a "global change in what one might think of as the center of gravity of Christianity."
Birth rates drive religious shifts
Pew points out that differences in fertility rates have major effects on religious populations. Around the world, Muslims tend to have more children than people of other faiths. In recent years, the fertility rate for Muslims has been 3.1 children per woman. The average rate for non-Muslim women has been about 2 per woman.
Among the other religious trends anticipated by 2070 in the Pew Research Center's report: The overall populations of China, Japan, and South Korea will shrink, and their Buddhist populations will shrink by half. And, an increasing portion of the world's Jews will live in Israel. In 2020, 46% of global Jewry lived there, but Pew projects that by 2070, 62% of Jews will live in Israel.
One of the more surprising projections is that while the percentage of people who identify as having no religious affiliation will increase in many countries, the global population of "nones" is expected to drop. The reason for this is that a very large portion of the religiously unaffiliated live in China, and that country is expected to have dramatic population losses in the coming decades due to dropping birth rates there.
U.S. religious trends reflect overall global patterns
The report also details how religious change will affect the United States. Pew says the U.S. will no longer have a Christian majority by 2070, yet Christians will remain the largest single religious group in the country. Christians are expected to decline to just under 48% of the population. (They currently make up 62% of the U.S.) During this same period, the percentage of the population of those who are religiously unaffiliated is expected to rise to 41%.
The anticipated population change in the U.S. among Christians and the religiously unaffiliated will be driven mostly by people changing their religion rather than by birth rates, according to the report. Christians tend to shed more adherents than they gain through what demographers call "religious switching," most of whom switch to being religious "nones" rather than taking on another tradition.
The U.S. is expected to become increasingly religiously diverse, with Pew projecting that both Muslims and Hindus in the country will outnumber Jews by 2070 if current demographic trends continue. 
Correction Nov. 18, 2026
A previous version of this headline incorrectly said Muslims would outnumber Christians by 2070. They will outnumber Christians by 2035.

Thanks for tuning into our live blog of Apec summit currently under way in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.
There is plenty more to come, so don’t go away, but here is a quick summary of what we know so far.
Chinese president Xi Jinping opened the Apec CEO summit on Wednesday with a speech calling for freer trade and greater cooperation around AI. “We should not only eliminate trade and investment barriers... but also promote inclusive and balanced development,” he said. “We should actively build partnerships for scientific and technological innovation, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence and promote a green and low-carbon transition.”
Russian president Vladimir Putin also addressed the summit, speaking after Ukraine destroyed the vital Kerch road bridge linking occupied Crimea to Russia in a major blow to his four-year-old war. Putin followed Xi on stage with a speech that described Western powers as “former hegemons”. He said Europe was in a “humiliating decline” and that anti-Russian sanctions imposed after his invasion of Ukraine had backfired, instead making his country stronger.
Xi and Putin headed into a meeting after their opening addresses, according to Chinese and Russian state media.
The much-anticipated trilateral meeting between US president Donald Trump, Xi and Putin will take place on Thursday. The three men are due to meet on the sidelines and potentially discuss Russia’s war with Ukraine and the US war in Iran, as well as other flashpoints such as trade, AI and nuclear weapons.
The meeting has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the US, Britain and the Soviet Union that formalised spheres of influence, set the stage for world order after the second world war and became shorthand for great power deals imposed on smaller countries.
It is unclear whether North Korean leader Kim Jong-un will attend the talks, but Trump has floated the possibility. On Wednesday US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the US president was willing to engage, but he did not confirm whether a meeting had been set in Shenzhen.
Trump said on Wednesday that the US has just concluded a “very big trade deal” with the Philippines, but he did not provide any details, and Manila did not announce any agreement. “We’ve just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made so far, and it is a fair deal for both countries,” Trump said during a state luncheon at the Philippine presidential palace. Trump is set to arrive in Shenzhen on Wednesday evening.
Trump announces new trade deal with Philippines as he heads to China
As Trump makes his way to China, he has posted a message on his Truth Social platform reflecting on his visit to the Philippines and his meeting with president Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
The US president wrote:
I am now heading to China, from the Philippines, where we had a wonderful meeting on Trade, National Security, and other subjects. I am pleased to announce that we made a new and completely different Trade Deal with the Philippines, one that will be a true landmark and, in particular, a Deal that will be great for our Farmers and those in the business of “Energy.” President Marcos is a powerful leader, and a man of high integrity and substance. It was an Honor to be with him, and his beautiful wife and son.”
Trump has suggested this week that he could meet North Korean leader Kim Jong-un in China, but there has been no official confirmation from Beijing and Pyongyang has only published photos of its leader visiting a ski resort.

Donald Trump has said he doesn’t want to talk about Nvidia, the AI giant at the centre of a global espionage scandal, but AI will surely be on the agenda.
Countries have called for stronger governance and regulation of AI, as worries grow about its potential for military use and the risks posed by rogue autonomous-agent tools.
The China-US talks could build on the AI “communication channel” agreed when Trump and Xi met in Washington in September, Reuters reports.
The next step should be to agree on what constitutes a reportable incident, who has authority to communicate, how quickly notifications must occur and how information can be verified without disclosing sensitive capabilities,” said Marina Zhang from the University of Technology Sydney.
Media reports have also suggested Xi, Putin and Trump may discuss the use of AI in nuclear weapons command systems.
Trump’s predecessor Joe Biden and Xi had agreed in 2024 that any decision to use nuclear weapons should be controlled by humans, not by AI, the White House said.
Taiwan’s representative Stan Shih, founder of computer manufacturer Acer, is expected to arrive in Shenzhen with a delegation this morning.
Among the 21 Apec member economies, Taiwan’s participation is particularly sensitive, given that host country China claims the self-governing democracy as its territory.
Taiwan joined Apec in 1991 under the name “Chinese Taipei” and remains a full member despite its limited diplomatic recognition. Home to TSMC, the world’s leading contract chipmaker, the island plays a crucial role in the global supply of advanced semiconductors essential to AI, a key focus of discussions at the summit.
Ahead of the summit, China reiterated that Taiwan’s participation in Apec must adhere to its “one-China principle”, a position rejected by Taipei, which insists that its participation as a forum member is not subject to Beijing’s policy.
A Tuesday poll shows that 71.8% of respondents in Taiwan supported the government’s participation in the Shenzhen summit on “equal and dignified terms.”
Taiwan could also come up in talks between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the summit on Thursday.
Asked on Tuesday whether Taiwan had communicated with Washington ahead of Trump’s talks with Chinese and Russian leaders, Taiwan’s foreign ministry spokesperson said communication channels with the US are “running smoothly” and the ministry is closely monitoring Trump’s meetings at the summit.
Trade tensions are likely to loom over the Apec summit this year, just a year after Trump and Xi Jinping reached a tenuous truce in their trade war on the sidelines of the last Apec summit in South Korea.
But that deal expires in January.
The leaders’ “priority” would be “keeping the truce alive”, especially with another Trump-Xi meeting expected at the G20 summit in Miami in December, said Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), as reported by Reuters.
Countries like Canada are also expected to be looking to broaden their trade partnerships – including with China – to reduce dependence on the United States.
Trump has of course upended global trade order by imposing wide-ranging tariffs on many countries.
Kim Jong-un had plenty to gain from his three meetings with Donald Trump during the US president’s first term in office.
Seven years on from their last meeting, along the heavily armed border dividing the Korean peninsula, speculation is mounting that the North Korean leader will end their estrangement at this week’s Apec summit in Shenzhen.
But some analysts are casting doubt on the likelihood of a fourth Trump-Kim meeting in the Chinese city.
After making rapid progress with his country’s nuclear and missile programmes and forming a loose “axis of upheaval” with Beijing and Moscow, what, they ask, would Kim have to gain from another encounter with his American counterpart?
Apec’s Chinese hosts say they have no information on a possible bilateral, while the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to play down the prospect, saying preparations for a dialogue between Kim and Trump did not mean it would happen.
Trump, who floated the idea just before leaving Washington on Monday, has raised the prospect of a resumption of nuclear diplomacy before, yet the men have not met since their brief meeting along the DMZ in June 2019, months after they failed to agree on how US would compensate Pyongyang for dismantling its nuclear arsenal.
Speculation that Kim would make an appearance alongside other world leaders increased, however, after a report by Russia’s Interfax news agency quoted the Kremlin as saying Vladimir Putin could meet Kim if he attended the Apec summit.
The Kremlin “wouldn’t do that unless they were certain he was going to meet”, Sydney Seiler, a former US national intelligence officer for North Korea, now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Reuters. “I’m pretty confident something’s underway.”
Others North Korea experts were more skeptical. Kim would have nothing to gain from a trip to Shenzhen except photo opportunities, said Kim Dong-yup, a professor at Kyungnam University’s Far East Institute. “Let’s say they offer to remove sanctions. But sanctions are already not working. There’s nothing to gain for Kim. Why would he go and open himself up to potential uncertainty?”
North Korean state media have been silent on the speculation. Official photos released this week showed a smiling Kim, accompanied by his wife and daughter, perched on an armchair in the snow at a ski resort near the North Korea-China border.
Wearing aviator shades, a cigarette dangling from his fingers, Kim did not give the impression he was ready to resurrect his “friendship” with a weakened US president.
As mentioned earlier, Zelenskyy is undeniably concerned about the Apec trilateral meeting between the Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Ukraine’s foreign minister Andriy Sybiga said earlier this week that a meeting between US, Chinese and Russian leaders would “only encourage Putin to continue this war”.
Beijing has said the three leaders will discuss “safeguarding world peace”, but US officials say Trump is not expected to bring up Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Beijing, insisting it is a neutral party, has never denounced the Russian invasion, and has instead called for peace talks.
“Beijing will remain respectful of Russia’s own aims in the war and balance that with growing calls from Europe to exert a little more influence in that regard,” NTU’s Loh said, as reported by Reuters news agency.
Putin would probably have the most to gain from the trilateral meeting, ASPI’s Lee added.
Just being at the table with Trump and Xi would elevate Russia’s standing and potentially shift the conversation toward a broader great-power bargain over European security.
Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?
That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday.
Some have likened the impending trilateral (pictured below) to the 1945 meeting between Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt that that in effect carved up postwar Europe, between a communist-ruled east and a democratic, capitalist west.
Among those concerned about the meeting, he writes, is Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse.
The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has arrived in Shenzhen for the Apec summit, and confirmed he will join a leaders’ “family photo” despite the presence of Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Albanese said he would respect the wishes of host country China and take part, echoing the explanation of the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney. But, Albanese said would make clear Australia’s view on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
This is a big power intervening in an illegal way to try to assert its will and underestimating the will and courage and conviction of the Ukrainian people to fight for their national sovereignty.
After Tuesday’s Quad summit in Manila, Albanese talked up the cooperation of middle powers in this week’s roster of international summits.
Absolutely there is a role for middle power diplomacy, and we’ll see at Apec, the engagement that we’ll have with countries such as Canada and Mexico, Korea, Japan.
They are important partners for Australia.
Albanese is due to meet China’s president Xi Jinping on Friday.
Donald Trump, meanwhile, has not arrived in Shenzhen yet, writes our correspondent Rebecca Bailey, reporting from the Chinese tech hub.
He was last seen at the start of talks with Philippine president Ferdinand Marcos Jr in Manila, where Reuters reported he said he was not concerned about the situation in the hotly contested South China Sea.
The US alliance with the Philippines has never been better, Trump added.
The US leader also touted an expansion of defence cooperation with Manila and suggested US nuclear technology could help ease the country’s energy woes.
Speaking to the press in Manila, US secretary of state Marco Rubio has addressed speculation that North Korean leader Kim Jong-un will attend the Apec summit.
Asked how serious the idea was, Rubio said:
It’s serious in the sense that I think the president has never viewed meeting and talking to someone as a concession. He has often made the case – and I think rightfully so – that, how are you going to solve problems with people you have disagreements with if you don’t speak to them, if you’re not willing to engage with them?
I think there’s been this conventional thought in American foreign policy that if you meet with someone, you give them credibility; if you meet with someone, you somehow are saying that everything they’re doing is good or right. And that’s not the way the president views it, and I’m glad he doesn’t view it that way.
The president views it this way – if we have a problem with North Korea, the only way we’re ever going to solve it is if we engage with them. Now, that may not be possible, and I’m not telling you that there will be a meeting tomorrow. I’m just saying that that’s – the president is willing to meet and discuss, as he did during his first term. Whether that will lead to a positive outcome, we’ll never find out if we don’t try. And it may not happen, but he’s prepared to do it. He has made that clear in the past.
Presidents Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin have just begun talks, according to state media from both countries, reports our correspondent, Rebecca Bailey, from Shenzhen.
Earlier Putin told the Apec summit he expected tomorrow’s much anticipated trilateral meeting with Trump and Xi to be “highly useful”.
The Russian president took to the stage after Malaysia’s prime minister Anwar Ibrahim for a punchy speech that took aim at Russia’s detractors and pitched expanded economic cooperation with Apec.
Western sanctions imposed on Moscow since his 2022 invasion of Ukraine have “failed” and Russia has come through “with dignity”, he said.
He added:
In a contemporary world full of turbulence, amidst the fragmentation of the global economy, and at a time when military-political risks are on the rise, what is desperately needed is unity rather than division, equality rather than hegemony, partnership rather than isolation, and dialogue rather than ultimatums.
Well, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) club has 21 members that represent more than 50% of global GDP and are home to about 2.7 billion people.
China, Russia and the US are three of the largest members. Others include Australia, Canada, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Singapore, and Vietnam.
Read below our handy short explainer on how it all started.
The Asia Group’s George Chen is at the CEO summit and sent the Guardian some thoughts on Xi’s speech, which he said was “largely expected”, featuring technology and innovation prominently.
Xi positioned China as “a force for stability and predictability in an increasingly uncertain world”, he said.
He added:
While Xi never mentioned export controls, Nvidia or the United States directly in his speech, the underlying message was unmistakable: China intends to pursue a more open and cooperative approach to technology development. That message is likely to resonate with many countries in the Global South and reinforces Beijing’s effort to contrast its technology strategy with that of Washington.”
Xi Jinping calls for freer trade, greater cooperation on AI
Rebecca Bailey
President Xi Jinping addressed the Apec CEO summit this morning. His speech called for the elimination of trade and investment barriers, as well as greater cooperation around artificial intelligence.
He also emphasised the importance of the World Trade Organization, and said China was expanding its imports of quality goods and services.
We should not only eliminate trade and investment barriers... but also promote inclusive and balanced development.
We should actively build partnerships for scientific and technological innovation, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence and promote a green and low-carbon transition.”
We’re back for day two of the Apec CEO Summit in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen. Today the summit will be addressed by APEC leaders, with President Xi Jinping set to give a keynote speech.
Bilateral meetings will continue on the sidelines, although the most eye-catching – Xi and Donald Trump, and the US-China-Russia trilateral – won’t be until Thursday. Vladimir Putin arrived in Shenzhen this morning, greeted by a red carpet, soldiers and pom pom-waving dancers dressed in fuchsia and blue. Communist party politburo member Cai Qi, often described as Xi’s right-hand man, was there to meet him.
Trump will leave Manila, where he has been attending the Asean forum, later on Wednesday. The Associated Press reports that he has expressed excitement about his own welcome ceremony: “I hear we’re going to have quite a landing,” he told reporters. “It’s going to be a beautiful thing.”
Aside from the high-level hobnobbing, delegates are “working around the clock” to agree on a joint statement for Thursday, a senior Apec official told Reuters on Tuesday.
Carlos Kuriyama, director of the Apec policy support unit, said all 21 Apec members agreed on the need to ensure trade is “not only open, but also fair”.
He said they were also discussing the safe and responsible use of artificial intelligence.
They are working very hard to make sure that we can have a common language.”
It’s been a big week already for diplomatic summits, with the most anticipated among them, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leader’s meeting, starting today in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.
Some observers have noted that we could be about to witness a Yalta 2.0, a reference to a major 1945 wartime conference attended by Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin.
That’s because the leaders of the US, China and Russia – namely Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin – will meet for trilateral talks at the summit to discuss the wars in Iran and Ukraine, denuclearisation, economics, tech and trade.
Trump has also floated the possibility of meeting North Korea’s Kim Jong-un in what would be their first meeting of his second term.
Here is a quick recap of the latest before the event kicks off:
China’s foreign ministry said the leaders “will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance”. The ministry added that: “Stronger communication among China, Russia and the United States, along with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.”
The Kremlin said: “The significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate.” But it has dismissed comparisons with the 1945 Yalta meeting saying they were just “games of political scientists”.
In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said.

The monthly medicines bill for the mother of one of us comes to approximately ₹2,900. This month, a chance visit to the Jan Aushadhi outlet near home came as a pleasant surprise. The bill for the same monthly list of medicines was ₹663, a near 23 per cent of the usual spend. It provokes a question: how does a bill fall by more than three-fourths?
The bill is not a fluke. It is the visible end of a long chain of efforts by the Government of India to make medicines affordable for the common people. The Jan Aushadhi scheme, launched in 2008 and revamped in 2015, has put low-cost medicines within the reach of people across the country. It banks on a manufacturing base that has made India the largest supplier of generic medicines in the world. What remains to be done is increasing health expenditure as a percentage of the GDP to ensure meaningful outreach.

Eternal-owned quick commerce platform Blinkit has started delivering download codes for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), the latest instalment in Rockstar Games’ open-world action-adventure series, in select areas across 11 Indian cities, a day ahead of the game’s global release tomorrow. The development was announced by CEO Albinder Dhindsa today, as the Eternal-owned platform looks to tap into demand around the launch. “It took 13 years for GTA 6 to be released. In the meantime, we built Blinkit so that you can get the game delivered in minutes,” he said. GTA 6 is currently available on Blinkit in select areas of Delhi, Gurugram, Faridabad, Ghaziabad, Noida, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Mumbai, Pune, Kolkata, and Ahmedabad. The company plans to expand availability to more cities between November 18 and 19, Dhindsa added. The deliveries will see customers receive a physical box containing a digital download code for the game, rather than a traditional game disc. Buyers can redeem the code through the PlayStation Store and download the game before it unlocks in India at midnight tonight. Rockstar Games is releasing GTA 6 on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, while Blinkit’s listing is for PS5. The quick commerce platform is offering the PS5 Standard Edition of GTA 6 for ₹5,999. From Ambulances To GTA 6: Blinkit Looks Beyond Groceries Blinkit has increasingly used unconventional launches and quirky campaigns to stretch the idea of what a quick commerce platform can deliver. In January 2025, the company launched a 10-minute ambulance service in parts of Gurugram, initially deploying five ambulances equipped with oxygen cylinders, defibrillators, emergency medicines and paramedics. It also ventured into document services, allowing users to order printouts and passport-size photographs through the app. Blinkit also launched a ‘Scream for Ice Cream’ challenge, allowing users to scream into their phones to unlock discounts on ice cream brands. The campaign turned a routine purchase into a social media-driven activity. These launches help Blinkit stand out in the increasingly crowded quick commerce market, where it competes with Zepto, Swiggy Instamart, Flipkart Minutes, Amazon Now and BigBasket. India's quick commerce market is projected to reach $40 Bn by 2030, driven by hyperlocal fulfillment (typically under 10-30 minutes) through dark stores and rapid expansion beyond groceries into higher-margin categories, as per Swiggy CEO Sriharsha Majety. In Q2 FY27, Blinkit’s net order value rose 79.3% YoY to ₹20,940 Cr, while revenue grew 93.6% YoY to ₹19,152 Cr. The business posted an adjusted EBITDA profit of ₹184 Cr against a loss of ₹156 Cr a year earlier. Blinkit added 308 dark stores on a net basis during the quarter, taking its network to 2,751. Eternal expects the count to cross 3,500 by March 2027 and reach about 5,000 by March 2028.

Christian Bale says portraying Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis in “Madden” is one of his favorite roles from his four-decade career. That’s extremely high praise considering Bale’s resume is longer than a CVS receipt, and includes winning an Oscar (for “The Fighter”) and playing Batman three times.
So why did Bale enjoy playing the eccentric football team owner so much?
“He had so many just wonderful contradictions,” Bale told Variety at the Amazon MGM Studios film’s world premiere earlier this month. “He was such a strong character. He liked to intimidate people, you know; he said all this ‘Just win, baby’ and ‘Dominate.’ It’s a game of psychological intimidation and fear.”
On the flip side, Davis had “one of the biggest hearts of anybody,” Bale said. “He took care of people. He kept this very quiet. He didn’t really like people knowing about how much he cared for others.”
In truth, Davis, who owned the NFL team for 39 years, from 1972 until his death in 2011, lived the mantra of “Once a Raider, Always a Raider.” Bale explained: “He kept caring for [players] after they were long gone from the roster. But he was just an icon. He was a trailblazer, and he seemed to know what he wanted to do in life from a very, very early age and did it. It’s quite incredible and very, very unique.”
In “Madden,” now playing in theaters and streaming on Prime Video, director David O. Russell explores the special bond between Davis and the Raiders’ Super Bowl-winning coach John Madden (Nicolas Cage). The film follows their relationship as it evolves from owner and coach to a deeper, though sometimes complicated, friendship when Madden retires from coaching and starts a career in the broadcast booth.
Since Bale and Cage are both famous for diving deep into their characters, O. Russell encouraged them to riff on set. One of their ad-libs made the trailer, with Bale’s Davis introducing Cage’s Madden to a hot new rap group — N.W.A. Another, riffing on the fact that Madden’s tour bus was loaned from Dolly Parton and the pair sing “9 to 5,” was left on the cutting room floor — though O. Russell wants to release it if the studio can clear the rights.
“I’m used to working with David, and I love it,” Bale said. (“Madden” marks the actor and director’s fourth collaboration, following 2010’s “The Fighter,” 2013’s “American Hustle” and 2022’s “Amsterdam.”) “David writes beautiful scripts, so we obviously do that. But then he’s often shouting new lines out at us. He loves it when we start going off script as well, and so it creates a real atmosphere of fun and creativity, and it ends up looking incredible, having been imbued with life.”
Aside from the focus on football, “Madden” also spotlights Al Davis’ love story with his wife Carol Davis, portrayed in the film by Sienna Miller.
“What was so moving was their absolute devotion to each other,” said Miller. “Al lived and breathed football. That was No. 1. The only thing that would keep him away from a game was his love for his wife.”
That devotion was epitomized when Carol suffered a stroke in 1979. “[Al] stayed by her bed. He slept in the hospital. He did not leave her side. I guess you’d hope that was the case, but the world stopped for him,” Miller said. “It was that love that I wanted to bring into the film.” [Carol Davis recovered and, after inheriting ownership of the team from Al, led the Raiders until her death in 2025.]
As much passion as the Davises had for each other, they also had a passion for fashion. “Madden” includes a goofy montage where Al and Carol try on a myriad of snazzy ’80s getups, but the sequence doubles as a genuinely sweet tribute to their love. Did Bale take any of Davis’ jackets or his signature pinky ring home from set?
“I didn’t take any of the jackets, but I did take Super Bowl ring,” Bale admitted. “That’s in a very nice little box on a shelf.”
After Davis, Bale is soon set to take on another legend — playing Lt. Vincent Hanna in Michael Mann’s long-awaited “Heat 2.”
“I was very reticent because I thought, ‘Oh, these are legends. These are icons. Like, how can you compete with that?’” Bale said about taking on a role originated by Al Pacino. “Talking with Michael, well, he’s written an absolutely brilliant script. He’s a phenomenal director, and I thought, ‘All right, I’m a coward if I don’t try doing this.’ So, I’m enjoying figuring out how to play that one.”

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

Bhanushali Studios Limited, founded by producer Vinod Bhanushali, is entering the international production space with CAPTIVATED, a true-crime drama featuring Hollywood actors Al Pacino, Isla Fisher and Blake Ritson. The film marks the company's international production debut and is being made in association with Los Angeles-based 32Red Entertainment.
Bhanushali Studios makes international production debut with Al Pacino and Isla Fisher starrer CAPTIVATED
Directed by Dito Montiel, known for A Guide to Recognizing Your Saints and Fighting, the film also brings together cinematographer Stefan Ciupek, whose credits include Slumdog Millionaire and Rumours. Inspired by the 1973 kidnapping of John Paul Getty III, CAPTIVATED revisits one of the most notorious abduction cases of the twentieth century. Michael Mammoliti, Producer and Co-Writer of CAPTIVATED and Co-Founder of 32Red Entertainment, highlighted his personal connection to the story. He said, “For me, this project is deeply personal. Manasvi Mamgai, Co-Founder and President of 32Red Entertainment, also spoke about the collaboration between the two industries. She said, “Having worked across Indian cinema and Hollywood, it's especially meaningful to bring these two industries together on a project like CAPTIVATED. Our partnership with Vinod Bhanushali is an exciting step toward more collaborations between India and Hollywood.”
The film is produced by Michael Mammoliti and Manasvi Mamgai of 32Red Entertainment, alongside Andrea Bucko and Nicky Weinstock of Sweetheart Entertainment, and Cassian Elwes, known for producing Dallas Buyers Club.
