Top UN court set to rule in a case alleging Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
The United Nations court is delivering its judgment on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya nearly a decade ago
THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- The top United Nations court opened a hearing Thursday to deliver its judgment on whether Myanmar committed genocide in a brutal offensive against the Rohingya Muslim minority.
The president of the International Court of Justice, Japan’s Yuji Iwasawa, formally declared the hearing open in a packed Great Hall of Justice. The reading of the 15-judge court’s decision is expected to take three hours.
The Muslim-majority African nation of Gambia launched the proceedings at the International Court of Justice in 2019, asking it to rule that Myanmar has breached the 1948 Genocide Convention, order the nation to put an end to any illegal activities targeting the Rohingya and ensure those responsible for genocide are punished.
Myanmar has defended its military campaign, calling it a legitimate counterterrorism operation that did not amount to genocide.
The judgment comes while the World Court also is handling genocide allegations linked to the Gaza conflict and the war in Ukraine.
“Genocides have similarities in how they are committed so this decision will have an impact on other cases,” said Melanie O’Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia.
In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched what it called a clearance campaign in northern Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The campaign led to accusations that security forces committed mass rapes and killings and burned thousands of homes.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred, the court will have to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part.”
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Gambia has asked for reparations for the Rohingya, including ordering Myanmar to grant them full citizenship and the right to return home.
The court’s rulings are final and legally binding, but even if it grants Gambia's request in full, it has no way to enforce it beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council.
A finding of genocide would be the first time the International Court of Justice has passed such a judgment. In 2007, the court said that Serbia “violated the obligation to prevent genocide” in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when Bosnian Serb forces murdered some 8,000 mostly Muslim men and boys in the Bosnian town.
Judges at The Hague-based court have also been asked to weigh in on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.
Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya human rights activist who fled Myanmar as a young child with her mother in the 1990s, said the demands in the Myanmar case are rooted in her community’s desire for recognition and dignity.
“Because so far, we’ve just been pushed around into this limbo state,” she said. “It’s been almost 10 years now that Rohingya have been living in very, very precarious conditions across the Asia-Pacific.”

NCLT or NCLAT cannot ask flat buyers to repay the financier without first examining the “unholy” bank-builder nexus, said SC
NEW DELHI: In a big relief to lakhs of homebuyers, SC has ruled that in housing projects that remained incomplete despite banks releasing major portion of loan instalments to rogue or insolvent builders, the commercial courts, NCLT or NCLAT cannot ask flat buyers to repay the financier without first examining the "unholy" bank-builder nexus.The order came from a bench of CJI Surya Kant, and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana on a petition by homebuyers in Krishna housing project, Gurgaon, by Raheja Developers, which has gone into insolvency proceedings.The petitioners said the bank had started recovery proceedings against them in a commercial court in Saket, New Delhi, even though they had not yet got their flats.The CJI-led bench said, "It is the bounden duty of the commercial court to determine the nexus between the builder and bank officials and to see whether the bank disbursed the loan amount to the builder strictly in terms of the tripartite agreement."It said unless a categorical finding is returned that the homebuyers are in default, no interim direction regarding payment of instalments can be issued. "We direct the civil court not to take any coercive action against the petitioners or similarly placed homebuyers without first determining the above-mentioned issue," it said.As per the tripartite agreement between buyers-builder-banks, the financier was to disburse the loan amount directly to the builder in proportion to the progress in construction on ground.
However, in many cases, because of builder-bank officials nexus, the financial institutions released loan amounts against each flat buyer much more than the money that should have been disbursed to the builder given the stage of construction of the housing project.When the project remained incomplete for decades, the bank filed recovery suits against homebuyers who, without getting the flats, kept paying EMIs and house rent. A decree in the suit would mean fastening crippling financial liability on the homebuyers.In Sept last year, a Justice Kant-led bench ordered a CBI inquiry against a large number of builders and banks across India for colluding to misuse the tripartite subvention scheme and fleece the homebuyers even when the projects remained incomplete for decades.
On Thursday, the bench found its sympathy for the homebuyers has virtually opened the floodgates of litigation and thousands of them suffering under the tyranny of builders and banks have rushed directly to SC. It said, "Our hands are full and we may not be able to handle fresh litigation."In a similar case from Bengaluru involving over 4,000 homebuyers, it protected homebuyers against possible recovery proceedings from banks as the housing project remained incomplete for nearly a decade despite the petitioners paying 95% of the cost of the flat. After granting protection, the bench asked the petitioner's counsel to move Karnataka HC for appropriate relief.

New Delhi, Nov 19: Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Thursday inaugurated a two-day key anti-terror conference, which will deliberate on "cross-border terrorism" besides the development of future-ready counter-terrorism strategies and the strengthening of institutional capacities to meet emerging national security challenges, among others.
Held annually, the conference has steadily grown into a significant gathering of operational forces, agencies working in the field of counter-terrorism, and experts from the technical, legal and forensic domains.
It offers the agencies/forces an opportunity to collectively examine matters that have bearing on national security and the threats arising from terrorism.
In keeping with the 'whole of government approach', the conference places particular emphasis on fostering synergy among all stakeholders. It seeks to establish formal as well as informal channels that enable coordinated and concerted action against terrorism.
The conference also aims at contributing substantive inputs towards the formulation of future policy, a statement issued by the Home Ministry has said.
The conference sessions will address a range of subjects, including obtaining evidence from foreign jurisdictions, the application of digital forensics and data analysis in counter-terrorism investigations, and the effective management of trials, it said.
Sessions will also cover countering radicalisation and emerging hybrid threats to national security.
"Further sessions will examine the tools, techniques and case experiences involved in disrupting terror financing networks, as well as the development of future-ready counter-terrorism strategies and the strengthening of institutional capacities to meet emerging national security challenges," said the statement issued on Wednesday.
The conference is being organised by the National Investigation Agency (NIA) as a part of a continued effort to bolster the nation's collective response to terrorism.
This year's conference deliberates on the theme "cross-border terrorism", it said.
The conference will also host a capacity-building training programme for state police personnel and practising professionals. The programme has been designed to equip participants in several areas. These include applying the new criminal laws in terror investigations, using digital evidence in prosecution, and trial strategy and management.
"The programme will also cover special provisions relating to the investigation of terror cases, common challenges posed by the defence, the protection of witnesses, and the initiatives taken by the government to improve prosecution," the statement said.
Over the two days, the deliberations will enable law enforcement agencies to share their experiences, highlight good practices in handling counter-terrorism matters, and draw upon lessons learnt from terror investigations.
The conference is being attended by senior police officers of states and Union Territories, officers of central agencies and departments dealing with counter-terrorism, and experts from allied fields including law, forensics and technology.

A crude bomb was allegedly hurled by ABVP activists at a bookstall set up by the Students’ Federation of India (SFI) in College Street, Kolkata’s principal hub of bookshops and publishing houses, late on November 18.
Titled Sangrami Boipotro (Literature of Struggle), the stall was set up by the Calcutta University unit of the SFI to commemorate the November Revolution. ABVP activists allegedly attempted to vandalise the stall, accusing the Left student outfit of selling ‘anti-national’ books, resulting in day-long tension in the ‘boi para’.
The confrontation began around 11 am on Wednesday and continued late into the evening. Tensions escalated when ABVP activists allegedly hurled a firecracker, locally known as a ‘chocolate bomb’, into the SFI stall as activists, including women, were packing up the books before closing for the day. Video footage shows the firecracker exploding in a small burst of flames and smoke filling up the area.
The incident took place in the presence of a large contingent of Kolkata Police personnel. SFI activists alleged that the police attempted to shield the ABVP activists. The Right-wing student organisation, on the other hand, claimed SFI activists had assaulted its members and vandalised its bookstall.
Reacting to the allegations and counter allegations of violence, BJP state president Samik Bhattacharya said, “These are matters related to student politics. They are young. Political movements were never entirely peaceful here. These things happen.” He also said ABVP was not related to the BJP.
The SFI’s Version of Events
According to SFI activists and videos circulated on social media, the confrontation began around 11 am. The bookstall was scheduled to open at that time, with senior Left leader Biman Bose slated to inaugurate it.
However, as SFI activists were setting up the stall, a group of ABVP activists gathered outside the main gate of Calcutta University, which opens onto College Street, and attempted to prevent them.
To contain the situation, a contingent of Kolkata Police personnel formed a human barricade between the two groups. Videos show ABVP activists repeatedly raising slogans and displaying aggression. However, the police did not remove them from the spot.
Around 1 pm, tensions appeared to ease somewhat, with ABVP workers setting up a makeshift bookstall a few metres away from the SFI stall. The two stalls were positioned on either side of the university’s main gate, with the ABVP stall to its left and the SFI stall to its right. Police personnel placed metal barricades in front of the SFI stall to prevent a direct confrontation between the groups.
Around 2 pm, Left leaders Biman Bose and Sujan Chakraborty visited the stall.
However, as Bose was leaving, ABVP workers were heard raising slogans such as “Biman Bose Go Back” and “Slap Biman Bose across the face with shoes”.
The ABVP protest blocked a section of College Street. Its activists allegedly charged towards the SFI stall several times in the presence of police personnel. They also threw water and eggs at the stall, staining a National Flag at the venue and several books, the Left outfit alleged.
Around 7 pm, the situation escalated with the ABVP gathering allegedly hurling bricks, wooden sticks and water bottles towards the SFI enclosure, while police personnel continued to maintain a barricade between the two groups.
Videos also show plastic chairs being hurled form either side.
Around this time, SFI activists were packing up the stall for the day when a ‘chocolate bomb’ was seen flying towards it from the direction of the ABVP gathering.
The firecracker exploded inside the SFI enclosure, producing a flash and filling the area with smoke. The explosion further escalated tensions, with SFI activists seen rushing towards the ABVP gathering. Police personnel struggled to pull them back and prevent a direct confrontation.
Following the incident, the SFI decided to lodge an FIR at the nearby Jorasanko police station. Activists also organised a protest march from College Street to the police station.
According to SFI activists, police initially resisted registering a written complaint but eventually agreed following their sustained pressure.
SFI activists further alleged that after they had left for the police station, ABVP workers vandalised the stall site, damaging tables, benches and chairs.
The SFI is scheduled to reopen the bookstall at the same location on Thursday. It will remain open until November 20.
Trouble Erupted on November 17 as well
According to SFI sources, the organisation has been setting up the bookstall at the same location for the past four years. This year, too, its members informed the Joint Commissioner of Kolkata Police about the stall and its schedule through an email. They also paid the requisite fee to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) for setting up the stall. However, on Monday, the police informed them that they would not be allowed to erect any permanent structure at the site.
On Tuesday morning, a contingent of Kolkata Police personnel arrived in front of Calcutta University and attempted to prevent SFI activists from setting up the bookstall.
Around 12:30 pm, SFI activists blockaded College Street and began selling books while sitting on the road.
This led to a scuffle with the police, following which 41 SFI activists, including the organisation’s West Bengal state secretary, Debanjan Dey, were detained and taken to Lalbazar, the headquarters of Kolkata Police.
In response, the SFI organised a mobilisation outside Lalbazar, demanding the release of those detained. Around 6 pm, all 41 activists were released.
According to SFI activists, the joint commissioner of police held lengthy discussions with them, following which it was agreed that they could set up the stall without erecting any permanent structure. They were also asked to ensure that the stall did not obstruct traffic on College Street.
The SFI activists attempted to set up the stall on Wednesday in accordance with these conditions. However, their efforts were disrupted by ABVP activists, who objected to the organisation’s programme.
The ABVP’s Response
ABVP further alleged that SFI activists had destroyed books on Swami Vivekananda, claiming that its own bookstall had been set up to encourage reading among students. It accused the SFI of sabotaging an initiative intended to promote education.
The Facebook page of ABVP Paschimbanga also shared a clipping from Bengali news channel TV9 Bangla, which purportedly showed Arunava Dutta, an ABVP national executive council member, being assaulted by SFI activists.
In a separate post, ABVP shared a video showing a stone being hurled from near the Left book stall.
In a separate Facebook post, ABVP Paschimbanga condemned what it described as attacks on its activists at Calcutta University, Calcutta Medical College and Presidency University. “The throwing of bombs inside university campuses and the targeted attacks on ABVP activists by SFI and Left organisations are deeply alarming and condemnable,” the organisation said.
In the video, ABVP national secretary Shravan B Raj said, “The SFI and Left extremist groups are unleashing violence on ABVP karyakartas.”
Vandalism at Calcutta Medical College
In another incident on the same day, intern doctors at Calcutta Medical College, located adjacent to Calcutta University and barely a 100-metre from the site of the book-stall clash, alleged that ABVP-backed miscreants entered the college campus and assaulted them.
The incident came amid a protest by students and junior doctors against show-cause notices issued to eight interns who had spoken out against alleged mismanagement at government hospitals following the stampede at a Durga Puja pandal which claimed 19 lives.
According to a Facebook post by the West Bengal Junior Doctors’ Front, the college principal and other senior officials had initially agreed to withdraw the notices after acknowledging a shortage of medicines. However, following a phone call from a “higher authority”, the principal reportedly refused to issue a written order confirming their withdrawal. This prompted students to stage a sit-in protest.
The post alleged that around 70–80 outsiders subsequently entered the campus, vandalised property and assaulted interns and medical students, leaving several injured. It further alleged that the principal left the campus under heavy police protection while the attackers continued their rampage in the presence of police personnel.

A day after the Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena protested against Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi’s memoir over references to Hindutva ideologue V D Savarkar, the Congress on Thursday hit back by citing excerpts from Bunch of Thoughts, written by former Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief M S Golwalkar.
Congress national secretary and Telangana co-in-charge Sachin Sawant questioned why the Shinde Sena had not objected to Golwalkar’s book, claiming it described Savarkar’s Hindutva as negative and referred to him as a “traitor”.
“If Shinde Sena feels Savarkar has been insulted, then in his book Bunch of Thoughts, the second Sarsanghchalak of the RSS, Golwalkar, stated Savarkar’s Hindutva was negative and referred to him as a ‘traitor’ . Will the Shinde Sena tear the book , which calls Savarkar a ‘traitor’? And will it walk out of the government aligned with Sangh ideology?” he asked.

కాంగ్రెస్ నాయకురాలు సోనియా గాంధీ రాసిన ఆత్మకథ ‘బిలాంగింగ్: ఎ జర్నీ ఆఫ్ లవ్’ 10 నవంబర్ 2026న విడుదలైంది. ఇటలీలో ఆమె బాల్యం నుండి 1965లో కేంబ్రిడ్జ్లో రాజీవ్ గాంధీని కలవడం, ఆ తర్వాత భారతదేశానికి వచ్చి ఇక్కడి సంస్కృతికి అలవాటు పడటం వంటి అనేక విషయాలను ఈ పుస్తకం వివరిస్తుంది. మొదటి వారంలోనే ఈ పుస్తకం 2 లక్షల కాపీలకు పైగా అమ్ముడయ్యాయని పబ్లిషర్ హార్పర్ కాలిన్స్ సంస్థ పేర్కొంది.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, ఈ పుస్తకాలను కాంగ్రెస్ కార్యకర్తలు కిలోల చొప్పున ముంబైలోని ఫోర్ట్ మార్కెట్లో దుకాణదారులకు అమ్మారని, అయితే వీటిని కొనడానికి ఎవరూ ముందుకు రావడం లేదని, అందువలన వీటిని స్క్రా ప్లో(తుక్కు) అమ్ముతున్నట్లు ఒక దుకాణదారుడు చెప్తున్నట్లుగా ఉన్న వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ఒకటి సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: సోనియా గాంధీ ఆత్మకథను ఎవరూ కొనని కారణంగా ఈ పుస్తకాలను ముంబైలో తుక్కాగా అమ్ముతున్నామంటూ దుకాణదారుడు చెప్తున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ ప్రచారంలో ఎలాంటి నిజం లేదు. ఇది ఆర్టిఫిషియల్ ఇంటెలిజెన్స్(AI) టెక్నాలజీతో సృష్టించిన ఫేక్ వీడియో. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా ఇందులో పుస్తకం పైన ఉన్న అక్షరాలు అసహజంగా ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. అలాగే, దుకాణదారుడి చేతి వేళ్లు కూడా ఒకదానితో ఒకటి కలిసిపోయినట్లుగా ఉన్నాయి. ఇంకా పాదచారుల కదలికలు కూడా అస్పష్టంగా ఉన్నట్లు చూడవచ్చు. సాధారణంగా AI తో రూపొందించిన వీడియోలలో ఇటువంటి పొరపాట్లు కనిపిస్తాయి.
దీని ఆధారంగా, ఈ వీడియోను AI డిటెక్షన్ టూల్స్తో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) పరీక్షించగా, ఇది AI తో రూపొందించిన వీడియో అని నిర్ధారించబడింది.
అలాగే, ఈ వీడియోను ఫేస్బుక్లో అప్లోడ్ చేసిన పోస్ట్ (ఆర్కైవ్) కింద “AI Content” అనే లేబుల్ ఉండటాన్ని చూడవచ్చు. దీన్ని బట్టి, వైరల్ వీడియో నిజమైన ఘటన కాదని, ఇది AI ద్వారా రూపొందించిన వీడియో అని నిర్ధారించవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, సోనియా గాంధీ పుస్తకాలను తుక్కుగా అమ్ముతున్నారంటూ షేర్ అవుతున్న ఈ వీడియో AIతో సృష్టించబడింది.

Sustained top-tier performance. Huge screen. Keeps cool. Dedicated gaming features and controls. Plenty of stamina.
TIRED
Boxy and slippery design. Bloatware. Only two platform updates.
Mobile gamers don’t have many dedicated gaming smartphones to choose from, so Nubia’s Redmagic series stands out. This big, boxy phone offers cutting-edge performance, long battery life, and a large display. You also get touch-sensitive shoulder buttons, RGB lighting, and gaming-focused software features.
Sadly, Nubia has followed every other phone manufacturer this year, offering minimal iterative improvements while jacking up the price significantly. While this series has always been a clear bargain for gamers seeking the best chipset, it’s harder to swallow the compromises lurking here (camera, software, update commitment) when the price starts at $949.
Groundhog Day
Photograph: Simon Hill
The Nubia Redmagic 12 Pro sports the same boxy design as its predecessors, just a teeny bit slimmer and lighter. I’m a fan of the translucent industrial aesthetic and RGB lighting, but it’s not something I really want in my everyday phone. I had exactly the same issues with the 12 Pro as I had with the 10 Pro I reviewed two years ago. It’s very big, so you really feel it in your pocket, and it can be awkward to handle, especially when you’re trying to scroll one-handed. It’s also the most slippery phone ever. Every time I put it down, the 12 Pro slowly starts to slide away.
The big positive of this design is that it feels great in landscape orientation for gaming. The thick frame is easy to hold. There are touch-sensitive shoulder buttons on the top edge, and Nubia has a dedicated Magic Key for gaming mode, though you can customize it to launch the camera. This used to be a switch, but is now a red button. It’s still flanked by the round power button. Sadly, there’s no headphone port.
Photograph: Simon Hill
It’s refreshing not to have a camera bump on the back, though this inevitably adds to the slipperiness, and this glass sandwich quickly gets covered in finger smudges. Nubia has toned down the lighting a little, but you can still customize it for all sorts of activities. There’s a powerful cooling fan inside, with two vents to expel hot air, but the 12 Pro still somehow scores an IP68/69 rating for dust and water resistance.
The 6.85-inch OLED display is completely uninterrupted, with no notch or cutout camera to break it up. There’s an effective fingerprint sensor at the bottom and a less effective selfie camera under the top of the screen. The screen can hit a 185-Hz refresh rate, but only a handful of games actually support it. Most of the time you’ll be capped at 120 Hz. It supports HDR with 5,000-nit local peak brightness for highlights, but overall brightness is capped at 1,900 nits. Overall, it’s a lovely display, and a pleasure to play games or watch movies on. The Dolby Atmos–certified stereo speakers are decent for a phone.
Pro Performance
Perhaps the biggest enticement is Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset, paired with Redmagic’s RedCore R5 chipset and 12 or 16 GB of RAM. You won’t find a faster Android phone right now, and the Redmagic 12 Pro can even give the iPhone 18 Pro a run for its money. Benchmark scores topped the Android charts, above phones like Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra.
I had no issues playing Asphalt Legends and Wuthering Waves with settings cranked to the max. I also tried PUBG Mobile, one of the titles that can support that 185-Hz refresh rate, and it was smooth sailing. The 12 Pro keeps its cool, even after an hour or so of challenging gaming. Aside from the fan and vapor chamber for cooling, Nubia added dual-loop liquid cooling. You do get some fan noise and thermal throttling, but the 12 Pro has enough grunt to satisfy even the most hardcore of gamers.
Nubia includes a dedicated game space called Gravity X, triggered by that red button, where you can map those pressure-sensitive shoulder buttons and optimize the settings for your favorite games. It’s packed with options and even includes an anime companion and AI assistant called Mora. Even more exciting, it has an embedded Steam emulator, so you can log into your account and potentially play Steam games on the 12 Pro, though not everything works. It’s also easy to connect a gamepad, mouse, and keyboard, or a second screen.
To keep you gaming for longer, the 12 Pro boasts an enormous 8,400-mAh battery. Even with hours of gaming, I made it to the end of every day with something left in the tank. With careful use, you could easily push this phone to two days. There’s no charger in the box, but it supports up to 80-watt wired or wireless charging if you spring for a Redmagic charger. It took me an hour and 17 minutes to charge it from dead, but you can hit around 50 percent in half an hour. Sadly, it doesn’t support Qi2 magnets, so you’ll need a flat wireless charging pad.
The Caveats
To get top-notch performance at this price, you’ll have to accept several compromises. Let’s start with the camera. While the main 50-megapixel camera is quite good, and there’s a 50-megapixel ultrawide, the flat design doesn’t leave room for a telephoto lens, so you can only get 2X zoom by cropping. The main camera will satisfy folks who only snap the odd photo, and it does well in most conditions. The ultrawide is fine for group shots, but its smaller sensor means performance suffers in low light. The 16-megapixel front-facing camera is hidden under the screen, and it’s fine for video calls or well-lit selfies, though shots often look a bit muddy.
Photograph: Simon Hill
Nubia Redmagic 12 Pro, main camera.
The real problem with the 12 Pro’s camera is the processing. Use the terrible portrait mode or zoom in too far and you’ll see how badly it handles image processing. Nubia lacks Google’s expertise in this space, so a camera system that sounds similar on paper produces far worse photos in reality. Nubia’s colors often look a bit off, it really struggles with mixed lighting, and shots tend to be noisy or oversharpened. Video recording is quite good with the main camera, but stabilization was a little poor in some of the videos I shot.
Another big turnoff with the 12 Pro is the software. Redmagic OS 12 sits atop Android 17, and it’s mostly OK, though I wish Chinese manufacturers didn’t feel the need to imitate things like Apple’s Liquid Glass. The interface also has some bad translations. What’s worse is the prevalence of absolute junk bloatware and the subpar update commitment. Nubia is only promising two years of platform updates and three years of security software updates in the US (five years in the UK).
Our best Android phones guide includes many more well-rounded options than the 12 Pro. You can even buy a Pixel 11 Pro XL on sale for the same price right now. But the 12 Pro is all about gaming, and to that end, it offers the best performance-and-screen combo you can get today. Whether the gaming features, cooling tech, and overall style add enough value depends on you. That same chipset will roll into more phones soon, and most of them will have a better camera and longer software support, but they’re likely to be more expensive, like the forthcoming Motorola Signature 27 at $1,600.
For buyers in the US, check your carrier bands. The 12 Pro should be fine with T-Mobile and its associated MVNOs, but it may not work well, or at all, with some other carriers. It also doesn’t support eSIM, so you need a physical SIM card. The 12-GB RAM and 256-GB storage model is $949; upgrading to 16 GB and 512 GB costs $1,049, and the 1-TB model is $1,199.

Six months after an Ebola outbreak was declared in Congo, the disease remains out of control and efforts to contain it are faltering.
More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to Government data. It is the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.
Basic containment measures, including contact tracing and isolation, remain inadequate, raising doubts about authorities' ability to halt the outbreak. Experts say there is little chance of bringing it under control within the next year.
By the time the outbreak was announced in mid-May, 43 deaths had already been recorded, suggesting the virus had circulated undetected for an extended period. It has since spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces, moving at a pace aid groups have likened to wildfire.
New hotspots continue to emerge, stretching an already strained health care system.
Questions over funding and management
Community transmission remains high. According to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, 80% of new cases are being detected outside health surveillance, meaning most infections have not been tracked by authorities.
One-third of deaths occur at home or elsewhere in the community, where burials and other procedures are often conducted without specialist supervision, increasing the risk of transmission.
Health workers have repeatedly gone on strike over pay that is months overdue, sometimes leaving patients with confirmed infections without treatment.
Aid groups have also questioned how the response is being managed. Last month, the Africa CDC raised concerns about more than $700 million in Ebola aid that remains unaccounted for.
“A troubling disconnect between the considerable resources mobilised for the response and what is actually reaching patients, frontline workers, and communities continues,” said the humanitarian organisation Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF.
Children face high death rates
Children are particularly vulnerable to Ebola, especially those with preexisting conditions such as malnutrition, experts say.
Most children affected by the disease have not received specialised care, contributing to high death rates.
According to UNICEF, children accounted for 35% of deaths recorded through November 4. Children under 5 accounted for 21% of all deaths, and nearly 72% of infected children in that age group have died.
Conflict and attacks hamper response
Health workers face difficult conditions as Ebola prevention and containment measures clash with social and cultural practices.
Since the outbreak began, health workers have been attacked, some fatally, adding to the dangers of working in an already volatile region. Health facilities have also come under attack.
The outbreak has been concentrated in eastern Congo, particularly Ituri and North Kivu, where communities face both the epidemic and armed conflict.
Fighting between Government forces and hundreds of rebel groups, including the Rwanda-backed M23, had already helped create one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises. The Allied Democratic Forces, an Islamic State-affiliated rebel group, also attacks civilians.
The virus's rapid spread has raised fears of wider transmission across Africa. Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda have confirmed cases, making this the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak on record.

Monica was not prepared for a caesarean section. She had done everything right and had been assured of a vaginal delivery. Then two weeks before the expected date of delivery, she had to be rushed to the emergency for a caesarean. Monica felt that she had completely lost control of the situation. She found herself alone in an intensive care ward away from her baby, who was in the neonatal ICU and described her birth experience as being extremely traumatic. She is now unable to bond with her baby and keeps questioning herself. Am I such a terrible mother? Will I be like this lifelong?
Priya became pregnant after multiple IVF procedures but did not disclose the pregnancy to anyone till the third trimester, as she didn’t want to jinx it. After a healthy baby girl was born, Priya continued to be anxious and could not trust anyone else to take care of the baby. She would be hypervigilant, and even the smallest change in the infant’s spit-up or breathing would make her panic.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Bollywood superstar Aamir Khan has entered into a high-value residential rental agreement in Mumbai, leasing three luxury apartments in Santacruz (West) for a combined monthly rent of Rs. 38 lakhs. Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.
Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.
Speaking outside the recently reopened US embassy in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Wednesday, Hegseth said: “It’s a great honor to be here as the first United States secretary of war this century to set foot in Venezuela. Just one year ago my presence here … would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable.
“In fact, exactly one year ago today … [Maduro] stood on a stage not too far from here and yelled mockingly, ‘Come and get me!’” Hegseth recalled, before adding sarcastically: “Well, we answered that call.
“The reality is that … January 3 is the day that will go down in history as a day of liberation for Venezuela,” Hegseth claimed, although Maduro’s allies continue to hold power with US support.
Earlier in the day, Hegseth was welcomed to the Miraflores Palace by Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who became acting president with Donald Trump’s blessing after his abduction.
In the aftermath of the deadly US attack, Hegseth was one of the bluntest Trump administration voices when it came to celebrating the invasion. “Maduro had his chance … he effed around and he found out,” the defense secretary bragged.
Speaking at the palace, Hegseth struck a more conciliatory tone as he vowed to deepen cooperation with Venezuela’s new leaders in brief comments that were broadcast by the state broadcaster VTV.
“I stand here on behalf of President Trump, who sends his greeting and looks forward to the opportunities, not just militarily … but also economically: the incredible resource capabilities that your country has, that we look forward to unlocking together with you,” Hegseth told Rodríguez and senior cabinet members, including the defense and foreign ministers, Gustavo González López and Oliver Blanco.
Hegseth said his visit to Rodríguez’s “beautiful country” was designed to re-establish and increase “defense cooperation” between “two great militaries” that less than a year ago were briefly at war. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that Trump officials were trying to negotiate a long-term US troop presence in Venezuela as part of their push for regional hegemony.
“I appreciate your leadership and commitment to your country,” Hegseth told Maduro’s successor, a once outspoken anti-imperialist leftist who has overseen an unlikely realignment with Washington since her ally was grabbed.
During her five-minute address, Rodríguez, whose oil-rich country is widely seen to have become a US protectorate after January’s invasion, made no mention of Maduro, who is behind bars in New York City.
But referring indirectly to his capture and the subsequent reconciliation with Washington, she told Hegseth: “Thanks to the political and geopolitical maturity of our governments, we have – in a very short period of time, just a few months – turned what were very difficult and very tough times for our people, into an extraordinary space for cooperation and mutual benefit.”
Rodríguez hailed the “historic” energy deal her government recently struck with Trump, who has called it “the biggest oil deal in world history” as well as “the spoils” of his “conquest” of Venezuela.
Hegseth claimed the agreement, which reportedly involves 65bn barrels of reserves, “makes the strait of Hormuz a non-factor for the western hemisphere”.
Critics of Rodríguez’s political movement painted Hegseth’s visit as a humiliating act of genuflection for a president with no choice but to roll out the red carpet for the man whose troops captured her boss.
Writing on X, Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent Venezuelan journalist, said Hegseth’s visit was designed to underscore Washington’s “direct administration” of her country.
“Ten months after Nicolás Maduro’s capture, Washington no longer needs to fire shots to remind everyone who is in charge: the mere presence on Venezuelan soil of the architect of the January incursion reaffirms that the country’s operational sovereignty is subject to the White House’s directives,” Reyes said.
Reyes suspected the visit also carried a message for members of Venezuela’s armed forces. “Domestically, the trip forces the military high command to legitimize the man who directed the extraction of their former commander in chief,” she said. “In this regard, I wonder whether it might be a message of discipline intended to prevent any pockets of resistance in the barracks.”
Trump’s attempts to expand his Shield of the Americas anti-cartel coalition of Latin American governments suffered a major blow last month with the defeat of his far-right ally, Flávio Bolsonaro, in Brazil’s presidential election. The leftwing winner, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has indicated his country will not join the initiative.
But Venezuela’s interim government is in little position to resist. During his surprise visit to Venezuela, Hegseth said Venezuela had gone from being “our most aggressive regional threat to [being] a compliant security partner”. He praised Rodríguez for working “closely, pragmatically, and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela”. Hegseth claimed US and Venezuelan armed forces would work together to attack “narco-terrorists” operating on Venezuelan soil, vowing: “We will hunt you down. We will find you. And we will kill you.”
Concluding her speech at the palace, Rodríguez told her foe-turned-friend: “Thank you, secretary, and I wish you a lifetime of happiness.”

Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.
The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.
The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.
The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.
The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.
Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”
Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.
“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.
The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.
Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.
“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”
Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.
The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”
Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.
The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.
A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.

Owono did not deserve 12-match ban - Pique
- Published
FC Andorra owner Gerard Pique says goalkeeper Jesus Owono did not deserve the 12-match suspension he received following his challenge which resulted in the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
Owono, 25, was sent off after colliding with De Miguel late on in the second-tier match between Andorra and Tenerife on 2 November.
De Miguel died the following day, aged 30, and a disciplinary committee from the Spanish football federation confirmed Owono's ban last week.
In a video posted on social media, Pique said players past and present, plus coaches and other goalkeepers, felt the incident was "an accident".
The former Spain and Barcelona defender added: "I truly believe that imposing the maximum sanction on Jesus for this action puts him in a situation he does not deserve, because he is not to blame for all of this having happened."
- Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision 
  - Published3 November
- Goalkeeper involved in fatal collision gets 12-game ban 
  - Published3 days ago
The 12-match suspension was the maximum punishment Owono, 25, could have received, as the disciplinary committee could only consider the offence on the pitch and not "the tragic outcome of the incident".
Following the decision, Tenerife manager Alvaro Cervera said he accepted the regulations do not specifically account for what happened, but acknowledged the ban "might feel light".
Pique also highlighted a recent on-field incident in Spain, when Albacete winger Jose Corpas accidentally kicked Sabadell midfielder Quadri Liameed in the head during a Spanish second division match.
Nigerian Liameed was knocked unconscious but was later discharged from hospital following medical checks, while Spaniard Corpas was shown a straight red card and handed a three-match ban.
"Fortunately Quadri is fine, the consequences in this case were not fatal, and the committee decided to sanction Corpas with three matches," Pique said.
"With all this, my reflection is: what is being sanctioned, the action or the consequences?"
Owono has withdrawn from Equatorial Guinea's squad for Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Zimbabwe this month, and Pique said it was unlikely he would return to action as soon as his suspension is served.
He added: "Jesus is going to need far more than 12 matches before he is available and able to compete.
"No sanction is going to bring [De Miguel] back to us."

Datacentres around the world will be responsible for generating 70% more carbon emissions over the next four years, reported The Guardian, citing the International Energy Agency (IEA). This comes as the US and China increasingly turn to fossil fuels to meet the growing energy demands of their AI ambitions. Reportedly, the agency warned against datacentres, which are expected to consume twice as much electricity by 2030. It added that these datacentres would end up taking an additional 350 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity every year by the next four years, which is reported to be more than Great Britain's annual electricity consumption. IEA, in its annual report, mentioned that the global energy landscape would depend on government decisions following the disruption caused by the Middle East conflict, which it described as the biggest energy market disruption in history. Rising energy demand, increased use of air-conditioning and the expanding AI industry are said to influence decisions, the report added. On the other hand, the demand for fossil fuels is expected to grow faster, especially in the US and China, as per the publication. By 2030, coal is expected to supply around half of the electricity required by China's AI datacentres. The remaining power is said to come from renewable sources alongside small contributions from nuclear energy and gas. The US is expected to depend on natural gas for about 60% of the electricity needed by AI datacentres by the end of this decade. The usage of fossil fuels to run datacentres is expected to push emissions by 70% by 2030, the IEA concluded. In the European Union, renewables are said to account for nearly 70% of the electricity consumed by datacentres by 2030. Nuclear power and gas will provide the remaining supply and coal will contribute only a small share. The IEA analysis also pointed out that global datacentre capacity has increased tenfold over the past two years to 17GW. These identified AI facilities, when completed, could have a combined capacity of around 50GW. The world's existing datacentre capacity, including facilities with AI-optimised servers, stands at 120GW, reported The Guardian. Out of this, 80% of this capacity is concentrated in China, the US and the EU. Another 120GW of capacity is reported to be added by 2030, with AI datacentres accounting for three-quarters of the expansion. U.S. stocks slumped on Thursday (November 19, 2026) after Anthropic’s super-sized IPO failed to revitalise faded enthusiasm over artificial intelligence, as an early spike in its share price ebbed.
All three major U.S. stock indexes ended the session sharply lower, with the benchmark S&P 500 logging its fifth straight session of losses.
The S&P 500 was on course to post its steepest weekly loss since April 2025.
Anthropic’s debut, the largest IPO on record, was priced on late Wednesday (November 18, 2026) at $83 per share and was widely viewed as the next high bar to clear for the AI trade. The stock opened at $111.50 shortly before noon. After the company’s market valuation briefly surpassed $2 trillion, its momentum began to lose steam.
“The Anthropic IPO is attracting gobs of attention,” said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital in St. Louis, Missouri.
Even so, Ellerbroek’s enthusiasm for the AI trade has waned.
“My beliefs about the growth in data centre capex spending have come down a little bit over the last month or two,” he added. “Nvidia’s crisis situation is a big deal. The midterm elections have had an impact. Data centres are going to be more expensive to build and they’re going to be built more slowly.”
Advanced Micro Devices shares tumbled after investigative outlet Hunterbrook said its affiliated fund, Hunterbrook Capital, had taken a short position in the company.
Most chipmakers were lower, including Micron and Broadcom, among others.
Nvidia marked its sixth straight session of losses after the chipmaker’s upbeat revenue forecast did little to lift sentiment.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index closed lower. Neocloud firms CoreWeave and Nebius sustained steep losses.
In other stocks, Palo Alto Networks shares jumped after the cybersecurity firm raised its 2027 revenue guidance. Walmart dipped after the retail giant’s annual sales forecast disappointed investors.

Next week, the Commerce Department is expected to release its personal consumption expenditures (PCE) report, which includes the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the PCE price index. Analysts expect the report to show year-on-year core inflation of 3.2%, well above the central bank’s 2% annual target.

Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026 earlier this year. The new Act represents a significant shift from the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019. The 2026 amendment removes the principle of self-identification and demands a medical board’s recommendation; a selection from prescribed categories; and certification by a District Magistrate. It fundamentally changes legal recognition for transgender persons from self-identification to medical assessment. While the 2026 Act does increase protection, it changes the philosophical foundation of transgender rights — from recognition based substantially on autonomy and self-identification towards recognition mediated by medical and administrative authorities.
The definition of “transgender” as introduced in the Amendment Act is in contradiction to established international evidence and guidelines laid down in the World Health Organization ICD-11 and the World Professional Association for Transgender Health Standards of Care Version 8.

Social media posts about this announcement failed to make a distinction between calendar year 2026 and fiscal year 2026. The Department of Veterans Affairs announced in November that nearly 49,000 homeless veterans have been permanently housed in fiscal year 2026, which runs from Oct. 1, 2025, to Sept. 30, 2026.
Social media users are spreading a rumor that under U.S. President Donald Trump, the Department of Veterans Affairs has provided permanent housing to nearly 49,000 veterans experiencing homelessness "in 2026 so far."
Posts on Facebook and Instagram claimed the data came "directly from the Department of Veterans Affairs."
"These are not temporary shelters or short-term beds. They are permanent housing placements for veterans who were living on the streets," said one popular post.
(Facebook page David J Harris Jr.)
This claim is mostly true, although it gets the timeline slightly wrong. The Department of Veterans Affairs announced in a Nov. 12 news release (archived) that the agency "permanently housed 48,968 homeless Veterans across the country in fiscal year 2026 – an average of more than 4,000 Veterans housed per month."
The federal government's fiscal year 2026 ran from Oct. 1, 2025, to Sept. 30, 2026. Since posts claimed the VA provided housing to nearly 49,000 veterans in 2026 "so far," it appears the claims misunderstood the VA's announcement to mean the calendar year of 2026, not the fiscal year.
Posts online also implied that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration's efforts represented an outpouring of support for housing veterans. One post even claimed that Trump "took money meant to house illegal aliens and used it for our veterans."
It is true that the VA's data indicates that the second Trump administration has housed a few thousand more veterans per fiscal year than former President Joe Biden. However, the Trump administration has a mixed record of following through with its promises to support the VA's decades-long efforts to end homelessness. It is also worth noting that housing veterans experiencing homelessness is a bipartisan policy issue.
Since fiscal year 2019, the VA has housed at least 38,000 veterans a year. The Trump administration's high rates of housing veterans followed a year-over-year increase under Biden, per the VA's own data from its November news release, which Snopes visualized in the line graph below:
Contextualizing the numbers
Veteran homelessness has steadily dropped for decades — and Congress has steadily increased spending in support of the VA's goals to end veteran homelessness, appropriating approximately $3.2 billion in fiscal year 2025. In fact, both Biden and Trump's first administration put out news releases touting record lows in veteran homelessness under their respective presidencies.
The Department of Housing and Urban Development uses a "Point-in-Time" count — a count of the number of people without a home on a single night — to estimate the number of veterans without stable housing. According to the most recent HUD data available, 32,495 veterans experienced homelessness on a single night in January 2025. That's the lowest number of veterans counted since HUD first began recording Point-in-Time data for homeless veterans in 2009, per the VA, and a 56.1% decline since 2010.
According to the VA, the Point-in-Time data compared to the VA's housing data from 2024 and 2025 indicates "a significant increase in the number of Veterans needing homelessness assistance that VA and its partners were able to just keep ahead of."
Federal officials have consistently stated that a primary reason for the VA's success in housing veterans is a voucher program between the VA and HUD known as HUD-VASH, or the HUD–Veterans Affairs Supportive Housing program, which combines housing vouchers with VA case management and support services. HUD-VASH began as a collaboration between the two departments in the 1990s; Congress has appropriated funds for the program since fiscal year 2008.
In fact, as of 2026, Congress has funded 20,900 more HUD-VASH vouchers than are being used, according to three Democratic senators who want to loosen eligibility requirements.
The VA also attributes its success to community grants for programs that support housing. The second Trump administration awarded more than $2 billion in grants to organizations dedicated to reducing veteran homelessness.
"Under President Trump, VA is working harder than ever to get homeless veterans off the streets and back on the path to self-sufficiency," VA Secretary Doug Collins said in the VA's November news release.
That news release notes that Trump's VA established a $29 million fund to provide assistance to homeless veterans in the HUD-VASH program. It also touts supposed efforts to create a center for homeless veterans on the West Los Angeles VA Medical Center campus, although NPR reported in May that Trump's budget gave no money toward the center. The LA Times reported in September that the project, financed through VA funds and California state tax credits, would create only 24 units of housing for $1.25 million per apartment.
Furthermore, Trump has come under fire among veterans and their advocates for institutionalizing homeless veterans, making various budget cuts impacting VA programs and ending a home loan program (that was eventually replaced by a new program to help veterans avoid foreclosure).

The AI start-ups fixing India's broken roads and messy land records
- Published
In 2020, Sanjay Mandava flew down from Chicago to Chennai in southern India to resolve a personal land dispute.
Over the next few months, he was running around between government offices to access a dozen records that would conclusively prove that the property belonged to his family.
Just a sale deed dating back to when his parents bought the land was not enough. Authorities asked him to produce a string of other documents.
Frustrated by the experience, he built Landeed - an AI-led digital platform that enables users to aggregate fragmented, multi-source land-records, verify titles and conduct legal checks at the click of a few buttons, across 24 states in India.
He's solving a problem that is uniquely Indian.
"In the US or UK, when you purchase a property, the government verifies ownership. In India by contrast, we follow presumptive titling - the buyer is responsible for establishing ownership. A sale deed merely records the transaction - multiple other documents may be needed to prove title," Mandava told the BBC.
These include building certificates, property tax receipts and land survey maps among others.
The system is rife for misuse - property disputes account for a bulk of civil litigation cases in the country where some 80% of household wealth is held in real estate.
Landeed has mapped large swathes of India using geo-spatial technology and data from state land revenue departments, registration offices, survey records and municipal databases.
Using this, it has linked registered properties to their official land identification and survey numbers and ownership records.
An additional AI-layer can read these titles, extract information and spot inconsistencies within minutes - a process that takes lawyers and brokers several days.
With the largest repository of title data in the country, consisting of 1.8 billion documents, the app is now used by millions of individual and enterprise customers while doing real estate transactions.
The app is among a burgeoning list of Indian start-ups trying to address some of India's most complex challenges in sectors ranging from legal-tech to healthcare, infrastructure, education and agriculture using AI.
Unlike the US and China which have a global dominance in building frontier language models like ChatGPT, India's AI revolution is happening downstream in data centre infrastructure and consumer applications rather than in research.
Start-ups are solving issues for everything from pothole detection to tribal language translation to assisting overworked public-health professionals with medical tasks - often working with highly fragmented, multilingual datasets in extremely cost sensitive industries.
Bengaluru-based YouTube teacher Gaurav Sen's AI app detects potholes using a dash-cam, satellite-based navigation and an AI vision model to analyse images.
It then identifies civic officials responsible for fixing them and sends them this data. He got viral attention recently given how widespread the menace of potholes is across India's urban sprawls.
On last count, there are at least half a dozen other similar offerings that map and report road damage to authorities across the country.
"A municipal corporation can take the app and use it on public buses and taxis, to access real-time, updated data on road conditions," Sen told the BBC.
In Mumbai on India's western coast, Fractal Analytics - among the few Indian listed AI companies - has deployed its AI tool "Vaidya" in hospitals run by the local civic authority.
The app allows citizens to receive AI-generated, simplified summaries of their lab reports in multiple languages, identify nearby healthcare facilities based on their needs and gives doctors AI-guided pre-consultation support such as medical history and medication details of patients.
It also provides hospital administrators with a public health dashboard based on aggregated, anonymous insights from lab reports accessed through its tie-up with municipal hospitals, giving them crucial visibility into emerging infections or other disease trends.
This boom has led to a surge in funding for AI start-ups - up 265% year-on-year according to Inc42, external, a start-up information platform. They raised over $1bn in the first nine months of this year amid a relatively muted fundraising environment for the broader ecosystem.
Yet, these companies face an uphill task in commercialising their ideas and taking them beyond pilot.
"The cost of building in India is sometimes much higher than what Indian customers are willing to pay," Fractal's co-founder Srikanth Velamakanni told the BBC at his sprawling office overlooking Mumbai's film city.
"The computing power needed to run an AI model is the same whether it is built in India or the US - but American customers have a far bigger paying capacity than those here."
Indian AI founders are also being forced to build around scarcity, with availability of high quality chips at the right scale and price, a major impediment for many.
"I believe I am building one of the most impactful things for this country," says Mandava.
"But I am starved for GPUs [chips that perform millions of calculations and help train AI models]. I have a hellish time trying to acquire them," he says.
The country has promised its start-ups 38,000 GPUs through its government-led AI mission, external, but demand for this compute power is far greater than supply.
Cumbersome regulation and bureaucracy are other major challenges.
Without these fundamental issues being addressed, there's a risk that Indian AI companies will build shallow solutions that a next generation of founders will immediately make redundant, say experts.
"Someone like a Google will probably laugh if I tell them of my pilot. To make it sustainable and hard to replicate, it will have to be much more sophisticated," says Sen, displaying a self-awareness of where his product currently stands.
From a lack of experienced talent to the struggle to turn successful pilots into recurring government contracts to heavy dependence on expensive foreign technology, Indian founders are powering through many odds.
"We can still do it. We don't want protection, but propel us, give us the weapons to compete against the best," Mandava says, when asked what he wants from policymakers.
"To quote Jay-Z - I can't help the poor if I'm one of them," he adds.
