In the wake of the Make America Healthy Again movement’s midterm wipeout, a top leader suggested the heavy losses came down to being outspent by wealthier, more powerful rivals. But a Stat report on MAHA’s own spending in the run-up to the election raises questions about whether the group’s priority was ever winning elections in the first place.
The dive into the financial documents reveals that the MAHA PAC, led by Tony Lyons, spent more on allies, boosters, meals, luxuries, and its affiliated nonprofit than it did on political candidates.
The findings are in stark contrast to an announcement from Lyons in the spring that he was heading a $100 million fundraiser to boost MAHA’s clout in the midterms. In reality, MAHA PAC took in $3.2 million. During the election cycle, the PAC spent more than $10.5 million, with over $7 million coming from money it had collected previously.
According to Stat’s findings, of the $10.5 million the MAHA PAC spent on the midterms, less than a tenth—roughly $1 million—went to messaging on political candidates, which are expenses called “independent expenditures.”
Andrew Mayersohn, a committees researcher at OpenSecrets, called the spending “pretty unusual,” explaining that “Major super PACs spend most of their money on independent expenditures.”
MAHA perks
In some cases, the scant political spending was dwarfed by spending on luxuries. For instance, in a key House race in Northern California, MAHA supported Kevin Kiley over his political rival, pediatrician Richard Pan. Despite calling the race “the most direct ideological confrontation” between MAHA and its opposition “anywhere on the 2026 ballot,” the PAC only spent $49,900 to back Kiley. That’s a little less than the $50,100 it spent at Mastro’s Steakhouse, an upscale restaurant that offers $110 porterhouse steaks in Washington, DC. Further, it’s less than a third of the $155,900 the PAC spent at Ned’s Club, a luxury club near the White House that has become a popular gathering spot among Trump officials.

Pakistan's solar revolution seems unstoppable - but there's a problem
- Published
Jewellery, glimmering silverware, sofas and an air-conditioning unit. Three months after his wedding, Faisal Shahzad's home in rural Punjab is bursting with gifts from his bride's family, as part of the dowry.
But the most prized possession is tucked under the bed: a 340W solar panel.
"In the summer we ran it from 08:00 in the morning until the evening," he says, adding they didn't need to use grid power at all during the day. "We ran our air cooler on it all day."
Pakistan has seen a boom in imported solar panels, which glisten from the rooftops of homes and hospitals; from farmers' fields to industrial complexes.
From 2018 to 2025, the share of electricity generated from solar energy in the country rose from 1% to 28%, according to Pakistan-based think tank Renewables First, with some seven million households now owning panels.
People used to gift motorbikes or other household items at weddings, Shahzad says. "Now they give a solar panel and an air cooler. It has almost become a must."
Alongside the solar panel he still uses the national grid to meet his energy needs, particularly as he lives in a house with his family and brothers' families, who often use multiple appliances simultaneously. But in a country where the average wage is just under 40,000 Pakistani rupees (£110; $145) per month, bills are becoming unaffordable, rising to 15,000-18,000 rupees.
This year, COP31 is pushing the world to move away from fossil-powered vehicles, boilers and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment. And while Pakistan has become a poster child for solarisation, the national grid system is experiencing knock-on eﬀects.
The power grid death spiral
The big pivot to solar wasn't driven by government policy but by individual Pakistani households. Most people we spoke to said they installed panels to escape soaring electricity prices from an often unreliable national grid.
Electricity tariffs have more than doubled in a few years, says Muhammad Hassan Dajana, industry liaison at Renewables First, while the cost of Chinese solar panels has "decreased by 93%".
"People have just found another way to be able to survive," says Energy Minister Awais Ahmad Leghari. "It's a very healthy thing. We have adapted to the situation. The people have reacted and responded in a very economically viable and efficient manner."
While the solar boom brings clear benefits, particularly for a country that imports huge amounts of fuel, there are worries too.
Pakistan needs to avoid the so-called utility death spiral.
When people buy less energy from the national grid, fewer customers are left to cover the fixed costs of maintaining it. That can force prices up - which in turn encourages even more people to switch to solar.
Over time, this can lead to a two-tier system in which those who can't afford to buy panels face ever-rising bills, while the national grid becomes an increasing burden on the state.
"You'll have a white elephant in the form of a state-owned enterprise that requires a lot of public funding to just stay afloat," says Dajana.
Pakistan's government says the costs are already being felt.
"In just the past two years, the exodus from the grid has cost the rest of the consumers more than $500 million [£378m] a year," says Leghari. "That's a very big burden."
The government doesn't want to pull people away from solar, he explains, but wants the grid to be more competitive to be able to offer better energy prices.
Private power producers, which feed into the grid, have been heavily criticised inside Pakistan for locking the country into costly, inflexible contracts. Producers themselves point to broader structural problems like poor grid maintenance as contributing to higher bills. Leghari says the government has renegotiated most of the contracts and is now focused on making the grid more efficient with better storage, less waste and more innovation.
Leghari wants the country to run on "up to 90% clean power" by the end of 2036 - including renewables and nuclear - with dependence on imported energy reducing from 26% to 4%.
The solar power boom in Pakistan and the Philippines
Cheap solar panels, mainly imported from China, are transforming lives and slashing electricity bills across Asia.
Solar-powered business
But as the government tries to improve the grid, solar is still expanding with widespread adoption in industry.
Kohinoor Textiles Mills in Islamabad, which is powered by a sea of huge blue solar panels, is one example. Utilities manager Sabawoon Khan describes them as his "baby", pointing at construction work levelling the ground for more panels.
When the sun shines, the mills' hundreds of machines are powered entirely by solar energy, Khan says. The heavy-furnace-oil engines they once relied on sit mothballed in a warehouse.
But there are limits. When it's too cloudy or polluted, and during the night, the company takes more energy from the national grid. In the coming weeks, like other firms, it will start using industrial batteries which can store excess solar energy.
"We needed to reduce our energy costs and this was one way to do it," says Taufique Sayeed Saigol, the mills' CEO, who adds the plan is not to disconnect from the grid altogether.
"The state unfortunately doesn't have the resources so we can't really say that we blame everything on the state. We do some of the things ourselves."
Critics accuse the government of moving the goalposts on solar power. Previously, households could feed excess electricity into the grid and earn credits, which were then used to offset the cost of grid power when the sun wasn't shining. That policy changed earlier this year.
"Initially their policy was very helpful," says Arif Ehsan Malik, president of Faisalabad's chamber of commerce. "But then the policy changed. Now they have started purchasing at a lower rate and selling back at a higher rate."
Malik says that makes a big difference for small and medium businesses. Leghari counters that the costs of the initial model didn't add up; the electricity the solar producers put into the system was much cheaper than the electricity they ended up taking out of it.
"Those profits were coming at the cost of the rest of the consumers of the grid. Had we not changed those regulations, the rest of the consumers would have been burdened by at least 150 to 200 billion rupees a year, say, two years from now."
Despite admitting that the first wave of solar adoption was a "surprise" to the government, Leghari says he has no fear that solar could outrun their plans, saying it has been incorporated into their 10-year forecasts and the numbers leaving the grid have slowed.
Pakistan has big ambitions for solar; there are plans to open solar battery factories around the country and encourage more electric vehicles.
But it's also at a crossroads.
"There are two paths ahead," Dajana says. One is a future where solar and the grid work in parallel, demonstrating how a gradual energy transition can succeed. The other is where Pakistan becomes a cautionary tale, burdened with a costly, declining grid.
Shahzad's solar ambitions for his home in rural Punjab certainly have not slowed.
"We plan to get another 10-15 panels and install them on the roof, then connect a full system with batteries and back up.
"The plan is to be fully self-sufficient."

The spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is threatening modern medicine despite progress in combating drug-resistant bacteria, senior World Health Organization officials said Monday, November 16, 2026.
WHO officials said countries had expanded efforts to tackle AMR, but warned that progress in prevention, diagnosis and the appropriate use of antibiotics remained too slow to meet global targets.
Bacteria have long evolved resistance to medicines designed to kill them.
The widespread use of antibiotics in human health, animal husbandry and food production has accelerated the problem, making AMR one of the leading causes of infectious-disease deaths worldwide.
"Antimicrobial resistance is widespread and threatening the future of modern medicine," said Jean-Pierre Nyemazi, interim head of antimicrobial resistance at the WHO. "Unlike COVID-19, which was very visible, drug-resistant infections have been taking people's lives for years without us noticing it and raising the alarm as we should," said Nyemazi.
In 2021 alone, AMR was directly responsible for more than one million deaths and linked to some 4.7 million others, said the agency.
A WHO investigation in 183 countries into the progress of the fight against antimicrobial resistance this year revealed that nearly nine countries in 10 had a national action plan against the phenomenon. In 2017, the figure was only around four in 10.
But only 42 countries -- less than one in five -- said they had a plan that was financed, implemented and monitored, said Pravasha Prakash, an AMR technical officer with the global health agency.
"Countries are moving forward in every step but progress still needs to be speeded up to reach the 2030 targets," she added.
Poor access to diagnostics
One of the main weaknesses remains access to diagnostics. Only 36% of countries had a national reference laboratory capable of testing for resistance in all bacteria and fungi monitored by the WHO -- well short of the 80% target set for 2030.
"Without testing, clinicians must treat without knowing the cause of infection or which antibiotic will work," said Sylvia Bertagnolo, head of surveillance for AMR at the WHO.
The latest global surveillance data show that in 2023, one in every six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections flagged to the WHO was resistant to antibiotics used to treat it.
As a result, the WHO has announced the release of two new tools designed to help countries strengthen their diagnostic capacities.
The first defines the tests that should be available at every level of the healthcare system, from primary care centres to referral hospitals. The second compiles 73 laboratory procedures, from sample collection to the identification of pathogens and antibiotic susceptibility testing.
The WHO has estimated that AMR could cause some 39 million deaths between now and 2050.
There needed to be improved use of existing antibiotics, at a time when the development of new treatments is failing to keep pace with the rise of resistance, it said.
Infection prevention, vaccination, improved access to water and sanitation, and the appropriate use of antimicrobials are the main levers to combat the issue, it added.

Two days after Diwali was celebrated across India, on November 10, Tuesday, the nation woke up to grim newspaper headlines and reports highlighting the sharp deterioration of air quality across major cities. According to reports, 93 Indian cities appeared among the world’s 100 most polluted locations, several parts of Delhi reportedly witnessed a staggering Air Quality Index (AQI) of 3,000+, and six cities recorded an AQI above 1,000 at 9 pm on Diwali night.
Newspaper reports suggested that despite bans and restrictions, the bursting of firecrackers remained untethered across states, resulting in not only a severe surge in air pollution, but major fire accidents, noise pollution, and several people, stray animals and birds suffering burn injuries.
The front page of the Delhi edition of The Times of India on Tuesday led with a report headlined ‘Delhi pollution on Diwali rockets to worst in 5 yrs’.
“Delhi saw its most polluted Diwali day in five years, with AQI touching 376 at 4pm Nov 8, the worst since 2021. The city, however, narrowly escaped its worst post-Diwali pollution day in five years, with Monday’s AQI touching 370 at 11am before improving to 344 by 4pm, better than 2025’s post-Diwali air quality,” the report read, while highlighting that “several monitoring stations failed to report crucial AQI data”.
The front page also carried reports on the death of 10-year-old Rishi Garg in Delhi’s Narela after suffering a deep injury on his chest while bursting a firecracker; the hourly PM2.5 concentration at Jahangirpuri surging to 4,985 µg/m³ on Diwali night, which is 83 times the daily national ambient air quality standard; and X “locking” the account of TOI photojournalist Anindya Chattopadhyay after he posted visuals of smog in Delhi, citing violation of its rules.
The Mumbai edition of the paper on Tuesday reported “a record number of firecracker accidents” across the city on Diwali, with the headline ‘390 fires caused by crackers across Mum region on Diwali’. The report highlighted that the local train services on the Western line were disrupted due to a fire damaging signalling cables between Virar and Nalasopara. It noted that over 60 people suffered burns across Mumbai Metropolitan Region and over 30 stray animals and birds sustained burn injuries due to crackers, among various other major accidents and mishaps across MMR.
Similarly, the Kolkata edition led with a story on firecracker-related noise complaints. With the headline, ‘This Diwali, city seeks max number of noise complaints’, the report highlighted the widespread bursting of banned high-decibel firecrackers across the city, well beyond the permissible hours, making Sunday night one of the noisiest in recent years. Kolkata’s air quality deteriorated sharply over the same period, with readings lying between the “very poor” and “severe” categories from Sunday night to the intervening morning, and PM2.5 rising from 74 to 409 in Ballygunge and 115 to 444 in Salt Lake within a span of 2 hours, the report highlighted.
The front page Delhi edition of The Indian Express on Tuesday carried the lead story on pollution with the headline ‘Delhi wakes up to toxic post-Diwali air, 8 stations in ‘severe’ zone’. It reported that the capital had recorded its “worst” Diwali-day air quality in the last five years. Pollution levels rose sharply after sunset and remained elevated into the following morning, with PM2.5 concentrations touching nearly 5,000 µg/m³ at some monitoring stations. India’s 24-hour national ambient air quality standards prescribe a safe limit of 60 µg/m³ for PM2.5 and 100 µg/m³ for PM10.
The lead story of the Hindustan Times carried the headline, ‘Delhi pollution monitors went dark as AQI surged on Diwali’. According to the report, 43 of Delhi’s 59 air quality monitoring stations went “blank” on Diwali night just as PM2.5 readings surged towards 1,000 µg/m³. The data gaps reportedly affected the calculation of the capital’s daily AQI, raising questions about the reliability of pollution monitoring during peak pollution hours.
The front page also featured reports on Punjab recording nearly 200 stubble burning incidents on November 9, Monday; the sale of firecrackers continuing in Delhi despite a Supreme Court ban; and the rampant bursting of firecrackers leading to an increase in ambient noise levels across most monitoring stations in Delhi.
The Telegraph featured a collage showing the contrast of visibility of Delhi’s India Gate before and after Diwali, with photographs taken on October 30 and November 9 respectively. With the lead headline reading ‘Diwali cocktail of cacophony’, the front page reports covered the aftermath in both Delhi and Kolkata, highlighting data gaps in Delhi’s pollution monitoring during peak pollution hours and administrative inaction in Kolkata.
“Slackness in the seizure of banned fireworks. Stalls selling crackers at almost every neighbourhood. Lackadaisical police response to noise complaints. Political endorsement at the highest level in the name of religion. Several factors made this Diwali the most deafening in years, according to environmentalists, former pollution control board members, Opposition politicians and ordinary Calcuttans,” the report read.
The Telegraph reported that this Diwali celebration was Delhi’s most polluted Diwali in five years. It noted that, over 18 hours, from 10 pm on Sunday to 4 am on Monday, 59 air quality stations in the national capital should have recorded 1062 hourly readings; however, around 24% are missing from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data.
On Kolkata’s exceeding noise pollution levels, the report stated that “even a minister and an MLA from the BJP complained of the “unbearable” noise…However, asked about the rampant violation of noise pollution norms, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari politicised the issue, saying it was the “communists” and those unnerved by the “stupendous rise of Sanatan” that were complaining.”

The Hindu on Tuesday carried a standalone image of thick smog enveloping Rashtrapati Bhavan on Monday morning with the caption ‘Pollution unlimited’. On Page 6, it further reported that air pollution levels in Delhi had spiked to 200 times the World Health Organization’s recommended limits during Diwali.
Hospitals Report Burn Patients; Doctors Raise Concerns
“I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival,” Dr Vijay Hadda, professor, department of pulmonary medicine and sleep disorders at AIIMS, told ANI on Monday.
He said that the green crackers reduced emissions by only 30 per cent, but as far as the particulate matter was concerned, 70 per cent of the emissions remained the same as conventional firecrackers. He raised concerns over people breathing this ‘poisonous’ smoke and said, “You should understand that you are simply inhaling poison and exhaling it.”

The general public forgets, and even policies remain somewhat in a grey area, making it difficult to understand how they should be interpreted. Overall, the situation is not good at all. In the aftermath of Diwali, doctors in Delhi began reporting an alarming number of juvenile patients, including newborns, arriving with breathing difficulties, even as hospitals are witnessing a significant rise in respiratory illnesses. According to reports, 397 patients with Diwali-related injuries were treated at four major hospitals in Delhi. The cases included burns, firecracker injuries and eye trauma.
AIIMS reported 42 burn injury cases by 11 am on November 9. Of these, 37 were caused by firecrackers. Eleven patients sustained major injuries, while 31 had minor injuries. Eight were admitted, including one in critical condition. Moreover, 18 of the 42 patients were under 18, including six below the age of 10. An eight-year-old child at AIIMS was in critical condition after sustaining burns over 45 per cent of their body surface area. Safdarjung Hospital recorded 135 burn injury cases. Of these, 129 were attributed to firecrackers and six to traditional diyas. Seven patients sustained major burns requiring hospital admission. The hospital also treated 35 children with firecracker-related injuries in its outpatient department.
Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital treated 41 patients with burn injuries from 9 am on Saturday. 18 of these injuries were reportedly caused by firecrackers, with two patients requiring admission. Eight patients were hospitalised overall, while approximately 10–12 of those treated were children. Guru Tegh Bahadur Hospital reported 172 patients with firecracker burns and other Diwali-related injuries within 24 hours. Among them were 25 children and 56 women. Thirty-four patients also suffered eye injuries.
The toll was not limited to burn injuries. The Dr Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences at AIIMS received nearly 110 patients with eye injuries on Sunday and during the early hours of Monday, most of them with firecracker-related ocular injuries. 18 patients suffered corneal perforations or lacerations and underwent surgical intervention.
In Pali, Rajasthan, sparks from firecrackers being burst on a road reportedly reached a firecracker shop near Swarn Mandir in Falna town, gutting three shops and killing two people. One person sustained burn injuries and three others were initially reported missing.

Cummins' Australia captaincy at a crossroads - Agnew
- Published
Australia captain Pat Cummins, much like his fellow bowlers, is in the eye of the sandpapergate storm at the moment.
The reason is simple to me. The very notion that Cameron Bancroft - the most inexperienced batsman in the Australia team at the time – would use sandpaper on the ball against South Africa without the bowlers knowing has never made sense.
It has never seemed remotely plausible to me, as a former bowler, that the bowlers didn't know what was happening in Cape Town in 2018. It just doesn't seem possible.
Therefore, this day of reckoning was always going to come.
Let's be clear - as long as there has been cricket, there has been ball-tampering. There is no point hiding from the fact.
Back in the day it was about shining the ball, maybe using something like a sweet to get a sheen on one side.
Reverse swing was a ball-tampering game-changer. There was a requirement for a wearing process, roughing up and drying the ball.
But, to get one thing straight, whether a ball is being tampered with or not, it belongs to the bowlers. It is the bowling attack's weapon. As much as a bowler would not fiddle with a batsman's bat – sanding an edge or changing the grip - a batsman would not work on the ball without the knowledge of a bowler.
Some might wonder why revelations relating to the sandpaper controversy have not come to light before.
In response to that, I would say it would have been very difficult for a player in the Australia team to go public at the time. They would have been worried about their own futures, their careers.
Only when a player has retired, or believe their time as an international cricketer has come to an end, do they feel more comfortable to speak up.
I have also seen suggestions that Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner have had their guilt diminished by what has emerged in recent days, that they took bullets for their team-mates.
Smith was captain and should have been in control of his team. Warner cooked up the sandpaper idea. Bancroft executed it. If they did take bullets, they were bullets they deserved.
Now, the spotlight has fallen on Pat Cummins, whose agent has repeated his client's version of events in the last 24 hours.
The junior bowler at the time, Cummins has ascended to the captaincy, often joked to be the second-most important job in Australia, behind only the prime minister.
Cummins is not a typical Australian captain. He is not abrasive, or in your face. When he says he has worked hard to correct the image of his team, he is credible. Then again, he missed a trick to really prove Australia are no longer a win-at-all-costs outfit with the Jonny Bairstow stumping in the 2023 Ashes Test at Lord's.
After everything he said in public, and the way he has been backed by Cricket Australia (CA), there seems to be no obvious suggestion Cummins has considered resigning, or that he will be sacked.
He is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on 9 December.
Looking ahead to that match, it is difficult to see how the build-up will be anything other than a circus, dominated by questions about sandpaper, who knew what and who said what to whom.
The litmus test for Cummins will be the public reaction. Remember, that Test is being played in Bancroft's home city, in the state of the newspaper where his 4,000-word testimony was first published.
If Cummins is still in his position by then, the response of the Perth crowd to the captain will be very interesting.
Even if Cummins does get through that, the Australian media will not let up. This is a huge story, one of the biggest in the history of Australia sport. The press will bang away until they feel they have got the truth.
And what about next summer's Ashes? If Cummins is tossing the coin at Trent Bridge on 18 June, then he is extraordinarily resilient.
Right now, I can't imagine that happening. He has said he never wants to talk about sandpaper again, which is ludicrous when you think what he will face on that tour: scrutiny from the media, constant baiting from the crowds.
Cummins will have to decide if he has the stomach for all of that, and whether he can see it through.
His way out could be to resign, without admitting guilt. To say the speculation has become a distraction for the team and the pressure is taking a toll on his family life – we have seen more pictures from Australia overnight of Cummins being confronted outside his home.
Cummins could perhaps continue in the ranks, just as Warner and Smith did. A resignation without an admission of guilt may also take the heat off the other bowlers – Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon.
Whether Cummins continues or not, questions will remain for others who were in Cape Town, Cricket Australia and the whole culture of the sport in that country.
Looking now at what happened in 2018, it appears there was an attitude in the Australia camp that they were fireproof, that they could get away with anything.
Credit goes to their media manager Kate Hutchison, who, according to Bancroft, made a stand about what was going on and knew what would happen if and when the Aussies got caught.
What about the others involved, coaches who were supposed to guide and protect young men? Darren Lehmann and his position at Northamptonshire, or David Saker, who has recently been working with England.
Cricket Australia has seemed so reluctant to get involved. If the big idea was to give individuals the opportunity to "tell their truth" behind closed doors, it is surely dead in the water.
What about telling THE truth? Nothing else is good enough.

Wider access to diabetes technology needs policy support, experts say
Continuous glucose monitors and automated insulin delivery systems drastically improve glycaemic control and cut hospitalisations, yet steep out-of-pocket costs and socioeconomic disparities leave a massive adoption gap
Technology can improve monitoring and support treatment decisions |Image used for representational purpose only
| Photo Credit: Wikimedia commons
Diabetes management is moving beyond periodic finger-prick tests and clinic visits, with technologies such as continuous glucose monitors (CGMs), insulin pumps and mobile applications providing more detailed information on glucose levels and helping patients make day-to-day decisions about their care.
CGMs use a sensor placed on the arm or abdomen to measure glucose levels at regular intervals, offering a picture of fluctuations through the day and night. Insulin pumps deliver insulin continuously, while automated insulin delivery systems combine CGM readings with algorithms to adjust insulin delivery. Mobile applications can bring together information on glucose levels, food intake, physical activity and medication.

The Best Smart Bed Doesn’t Sleep on the Job
While they may not be able to levitate or act like a Jetsons-style robot personal assistant (yet), smart beds these days come pretty close to accomplishing both. Like adjustable mattresses, smart beds offer modifiable firmness and the ability to raise and lower the head and foot. These days, though, smart beds offer so much more, integrating features like dual-climate control, sleep tracking, and massage therapies.
The best smart bed is, by far, the Bryte Balance Pro Smart Mattress, and if you’re looking for the most luxurious, it’s the Tempur-Pedic Tempur-ActiveBreeze. Let me break it down for you below.
For more old-school mattresses, check out our guides to the Best Mattresses, the Best Organic Mattresses, and the Best Mattresses for Back Pain.
Updated November 2026: I’ve updated product information and the FAQ section. Discontinued products were removed, and I updated specs, prices, and links.
What Am I Testing Next?
I’m currently testing the Eight Sleep Pod 6.
Honorable Mention
Personal Comfort’s Rejuvenate is a solid adjustable mattress for side sleepers. It doesn’t offer any additional features or sleep-tracking capabilities, so it doesn’t truly qualify as a smart bed in my book.
Nevertheless, the Rejuvenate is a side-sleeper-friendly option because of its deep memory foam layers that contour to the body. If you want to sink in while still relying on the 45 firmness levels to ensure you're getting the support you need, this is it. Former WIRED reviewer Julia Forbes found a medium-firm 30 to be ideal for a healthy spine alignment when side sleeping.
What About Personal Comfort’s Adjustable Base?
An adjustable base is available as an add-on and helpful if you opt for one of Personal Comfort’s specialty bed sizes, such as the Queen Flex-Head or King Flex-Head. It’s the only way to move the head and foot of the Rejuvenate, as well as implement adjustable lumbar support, pillow tilt, and massage features.
Julia tested the Power Flex 4. It provides a firmer feel right around the midsection, and its lumbar adjustment setting really amps up back support. She did find the massage features to be uncomfortable, though, describing them as “increasingly aggressive vibrations, akin to tectonic plates.”
FYI, Personal Comfort often runs a bundle promotion.
FAQs
Should I Use a Sleep Tracker With a Smart Bed?
Some smart beds offer contactless sleep tracking, which eliminates the need for an additional wearable. That said, they do carry some limitations. They’re generally not as accurate as contact-based trackers and can overestimate sleep stages and miscalculate duration. They often can’t track the same breadth of physiological measurements as smartwatches and smart rings do. And they can misattribute data from a partner or pet sharing the bed. But they’re convenient, especially if you dislike wearing trackers to bed.
Personally, I still sleep with my Apple Watch Series 12 and/or Oura Ring 5 to bed to compare. But, if I forget to wear either, my smart bed is auto-tracking my slumber in the background.
Do I Need an Adjustable Base to Go With My Smart Bed?
You are very likely going to want an adjustable base to go with your smart bed in order to enjoy everything your smart bed has to offer. This is especially true if you are purchasing one with the expectation of being able to move the top and bottom of the bed into different angles, like “TV watching” and “zero gravity” settings.
What’s the Difference Between an Adjustable Bed and a Smart Bed?
Generally speaking, adjustable beds and smart beds are similar in that they both can raise or lower different sections of your mattress, with a remote control or companion app. Smart beds take it up a notch by incorporating additional features, such as sleep tracking, temperature control, and automated adjustments.
Can a Smart Bed Work for All Sleeping Positions?
Smart beds often come in adjustable firmness levels, and therefore can work for all sleeping positions. However, just like with any other mattress, the fabric technology is a huge deciding factor when it comes to comfort.
For example, the Bryte Balance Pro is a much better choice for stomach sleepers or if you have a heavier body type. Coil support simply does not compare to even the firmest of inflated air chambers, which are usually what make smart beds' firmness levels “adjustable.” On the other hand, the Rejuvenate has a softer feel right off the bat because of its memory foam layers, making it ideal for side sleepers who need pressure relief.
Do I Need Wi-Fi Connectivity for My Smart Bed to Work?
Yes—if the power goes out, your smart bed will likely go offline. Smart beds are factored into smart home technology, meaning they rely on Wi-Fi for full functionality, especially to track sleep data and maintain the firmness level you've chosen.
What Does WIRED Do With the Mattresses After Testing Them?
These smart beds were provided for free as media samples, and we either return them to the company or donate without personal benefit when testing is done. Most of these beds went to nurses, students, families in need, or those with medical conditions that were affecting their sleep.

GTA 6 feels vastly different from past entries, and even seasoned veterans may be overwhelmed by its settings. Rockstar has introduced the deepest controller customization options in the series yet, so tweaking them can make a big difference. Here’s our guide to the best controller settings for GTA 6 on PS5 and Xbox.
Early GTA 6 Controller Settings to Change First
If you want to get into the action of GTA 6 right away with the initial default settings, we’ve got a list of these seven early settings that you can tinker with in under a minute. Of course, these are part and parcel of the best beginner tips to play GTA 6, but we offer you an in-depth look at all of them.
Changing these controller and gameplay settings in GTA 6 can make your movement, driving, and gunplay feel sharper and smoother.
| Setting | Menu Path | Recommended Setting | Why Change Right Away | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Control Scheme | Settings → Control Scheme | Classic (or keep Default) | Moves Run/Sprint back to X/A if clicking L3 feels awkward after years of GTA 5 | 
| Movement Speed | Settings → Gameplay → Movement | Jog (or Run) | Stops Jason and Lucia from defaulting to a slow walk every time you push the stick | 
| Stand & Sprint | Settings → Gameplay → Movement | Off | Prevents accidental sprint presses from popping you out of stealth crouch | 
| Look & Aim Sensitivity | Settings → Controller | 8 to 9 Look / 7 to 8 Aim | Speeds up sluggish 180-degree turns while keeping your reticle steady during ADS | 
| Stick Deadzones | Settings → Controller (DualSense) | 2 to 3 (check for drift) | Eliminates sluggish center-stick lag without causing camera creep | 
| Fishing & Nitrous | Settings → Gameplay → Accessibility | Hold (Fishing) / Press (Nitrous) | Saves your analog sticks from wear during fishing and makes vehicle boosts instant | 
| Motion Blur & Camera Shake | Settings → Camera / Display | 0 or 1 Blur / Shake Off | Keeps fast camera turns crisp and readable on 30 FPS console builds | 
While these settings are recommended to begin GTA 6 with if you’re on a time crunch, you don’t need to overhaul every single slider in the controller menu at once. Start with the above-recommended settings first, play for 15 minutes, and then dial up your sensitivity, input curve, and DualSense settings we have listed for you below to play GTA 6.
Recommended GTA 6 Controller Settings to Use
To access controller settings in GTA 6, head to the Pause Menu → Settings → Controller, and you’ll open the most expansive controller customization you’ve ever seen in a Rockstar title. However, if you mess up any setting, fret not; you can always set every setting back to default with a button press, since it’s easier than using a GTA 6 cheat code.
Look, Aim Sensitivity, Acceleration, and Response Curve
GTA 6 provides players with acceleration sliders for its separate camera movement and ADS cam. Several players like these parked at their default 7 value, but I like to go a bit experimental with them; that is far more balanced than the sluggish default approach.
| Setting | Default Value | Recommended Value | Advantage | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Horizontal Look Sensitivity | 7 | 8 to 9 | Lets you check alleys and spin around quickly in firefights | 
| Vertical Look Sensitivity | 7 | 7 to 8 | Keeps vertical movement controlled without flinging the camera at the sky | 
| Horizontal Aim Sensitivity | 7 | 7 to 8 (1 step below Look) | Stops your crosshair from overshooting moving targets | 
| Vertical Aim Sensitivity | 7 | 6 to 7 | Makes micro-adjustments for headshots much easier to land | 
| Look Acceleration | 7 | 6 to 7 | Keeps full-tilt camera turns smooth and predictable | 
| Aim Acceleration | 7 | 5 to 6 | Lowering this prevents sudden speed spikes when tracking strafing enemies | 
| Aim Response Curve | Standard | Linear (or Precision) | Gives finer control near the center of the stick with fast turns at the edges | 
Choosing the right Aim Response Curve makes a bigger difference in GTA 6 than cranking up raw sensitivity. Standard baseline gives your stick movement a gradual ramp-up from the center to the edge. If you only want a slow and light speed boost, then stick with this.
However, if you want more fast-paced action and want raw 1-to-1 muscle memory like when you play competitive shooters, go for Linear, as it maps stick tilt directly to camera speed with zero artificial smoothing.
But since GTA 6’s gunfights are more precision-based, choose Precision as it slows down small inputs near the center of the analog stick, while ramping up fast at the outer edges.
Important Tip:
Change your sensitivity first, get comfortable with it, and only then swap your response curve. Changing every setting at the same time may make it tough to understand which one helped you.
Vibration, Haptics, Deadzone, and Adaptive Triggers
When you scroll to the bottom of the controller tab in GTA 6 on your PS5, you’ll find a dedicated DualSense Wireless Controller Features section. Rockstar has packed GTA 6 with a surprising amount of detail here, including stick dead zones and a brand-new driving trigger option.
| Setting | Default Value | Recommended Value | Advantage | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Vibration & Haptics Strength | 10 | 7 to 8 (or 10 for immersion) | Preserves road texture and weapon recoil without fatiguing your hands over multi-hour sessions | 
| Deadzone (Left Stick) | 4 | 2 to 3 | Makes character movement kick in faster on light stick pushes | 
| Deadzone (Right Stick) | 4 | 2 to 3 | Removes dead center play so small aim corrections register right away |

Do not blindly go with a zero deadzone setting. If you’ve just bought a DualSense, your old one still may have a significant amount of stick drift. Drop both deadzones down to 2, take your thumbs off the sticks, and watch the screen for a few seconds and notice if the camera moves. If it does, keep bumping up the deadzone setting by 1 until it stops.
You can also check out our guide on how to fix stick drift on your controller if you’re plagued by it while playing as Jason or Lucia in GTA 6.
Inverted Controls (Look, Movement, 3D Map Rotation and Aircraft)
Right above the DualSense section, GTA 6 splits inversion into four separate toggles: Look, Movement, 3D Map Rotation, and Aircraft Movement. Leave the first three on Default unless you always play inverted.
Pay special attention to Aircraft Movement, which defaults to On independently of your normal camera settings. If you hop into a helicopter or plane for the first time and immediately nose-dive into Leonida Keys, open this menu and flip Aircraft Movement to Off.
Best GTA 6 Combat and Targeting Settings on Controller
Now that you’re done with the controller settings, it’s time to head to the Gameplay tab to set some must-have settings to play GTA 6. Head to Pause Menu → Settings → Gameplay to access these settings.
Since Rockstar gives you full control over how aggressively the game helps your aim, leaving everything on full Lock-On may feel heavily assisted even on casual runs. So you need to switch to these recommended GTA 6 controller combat and targeting settings:
| Setting | Default Value | Recommended Value | Advantage | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Targeting | Partial | Partial (or Lock-On for casual play) | Nudges your crosshair onto nearby enemies without taking over your camera completely | 
| Aim Assist Strength | 4 | 4 (scale of 0 to 5) | Keeps mid-range and long-range firefights smooth at 30 FPS | 
| Lock-On Time | 4 | 4 | Gives you enough time to snap and follow through before assistance fades | 
| Lock-On Target Switch | Off | On (for Lock-On) / Off (for Partial) | Lets you flick the right stick to cycle targets during chaotic shootouts | 
| Shooting Assist | On | On (turn Off for pure Free Aim) | Smooths out bullet magnetism and tracking during sustained fire | 
| Drive-By Assist | On | On (turn Off for pure Free Aim) | Makes shooting from moving cars and bikes far more manageable on thumbsticks | 
| Quick Draw | On | On | Lets you fire rapidly without waiting on a full aim-down-sights animation | 
| Cover Selection | Camera & Movement | Movement Only (if snapping feels off) | Stops camera swings from accidentally sticking your character to the wrong wall | 
| Holster in Vehicle | Automatic | Automatic | Automatically tucks weapons away when entering cars so you stay clean around cops | 
Important Tip:
Switching Targeting to Free Aim does not automatically shut off every assist. Make sure you manually toggle Shooting Assist and Drive-By Assist to Off to, otherwise close-range tracking will still kick-in during combat.
Best GTA 6 Movement and Accessibility Settings on Controller
In GTA 6, thanks to its default control scheme, sprint in movement is now mapped to L3 instead of repeated taps. So, under the Gameplay → Movement setting, certain tweaks completely change how Leonida feels. Also, under the Gameplay → Accessibility settings, Rockstar has hidden some massive quality-of-life upgrades in GTA 6, so it’s worth taking a look too:

Best GTA 6 Camera Settings to Improve Controller Aim
Since GTA 6 targets 30 FPS on consoles, excess screen shake or motion blur can make your aim feel heavier and gameplay a bit choppy. So jump into your Camera and Display tabs to improve controller aim while using GTA 6 weapons:

Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy assured the Public Health Foundation of India (PHFI) of the State government’s full support for establishing its Institute of Public Health Sciences (IPHS) Deemed-to-be University in Hyderabad, setting June 2, 2028, as the deadline for completing the proposed campus and promising assistance with land, funds, permissions and other requirements.
Speaking at the foundation-laying ceremony and unveiling of the campus master plan on Saturday, Mr. Reddy said the government was committed to developing the institution into a world-class university that would contribute to public health education, research and healthcare in India and internationally.
He further added that the proposed university was not merely another educational institution but a project of global significance. Expressing confidence in its potential, he said he hoped that in the coming years, people would discuss the PHFI university alongside established institutions such as Harvard and Oxford.
The Chief Minister recalled how institutions such as the Indian School of Business (ISB) had contributed to Hyderabad’s emergence as an educational and knowledge hub. He said individuals who had established successful institutions had helped create a distinct identity for the city and that the PHFI university would add to this legacy.
PHFI Chairman Rajat Gupta said the university aspired to achieve excellence through world-class faculty, students, international collaborations and infrastructure.
PHFI IPHS Chancellor Dr. K. Srinath Reddy said PHFI aspired to become the world’s leading public health institution with the establishment of the university in Hyderabad. Dr. Reddy said the foundation’s work involved advancing multidisciplinary education and research through multi-sectoral implementation and multi-stakeholder engagement. The objective was to improve life expectancy, strengthen health systems, align policies across sectors with population health goals and encourage active community engagement.
Pro-Chancellor Sanjay Zodpey said the university was being conceived as a long-term institution that would serve generations of students, researchers, public health professionals and communities. He said the public health challenges of the 21st century required professionals with interdisciplinary perspectives, evidence-based knowledge and a commitment to equity and social impact.
Vice-Chancellor M. Vishnu Vardhana Rao outlined the university’s academic journey and expansion plans. The Indian Institute of Public Health Hyderabad was established in 2008 under the aegis of PHFI, with the objective of advancing public health through education, research and community engagement. The institution received recognition as a deemed-to-be university from the University Grants Commission in 2025, with Hyderabad as its main campus and Bengaluru as another campus, he said.
With the proposed campus and modern infrastructure, the institution plans to expand its academic offerings to at least six postgraduate programmes, two undergraduate programmes, PhD programmes and institute-level Master of Public Health programmes. It aims to build an academic community of approximately 2,500 students and research scholars over the next five years.
Dr. Rao said the university’s research priorities would include infectious diseases and pandemic preparedness, non-communicable diseases, maternal and child health, One Health, mental health and disability. Digital health, artificial intelligence and data science would serve as cross-cutting areas across its research activities, he added.

Humyn Labs’s $47 Mn Physical AI Play Humyn Labs is capitalising on the physical AI gold rush. The startup has raised $47 Mn, via debt and equity, to scale its business of recording humans for training robots. As questions over privacy and consent linger, how is Humyn Labs building its warchest to dominate physical AI? Funding Global Ambition: The round comprised $26 Mn in equity investment, which was led by Accel. The remaining $21 Mn was raised via debt from Lighthouse Canton and Trifecta Capital. The infusion will go towards expanding robot deployment operations to Brazil, South Korea and India, while strengthening its data collection hardware and processing capabilities. The corpus will also help scale the startup’s presence in San Francisco, London and Seoul. A Rapid Rise: Founded earlier this year, the startup claims to have already $50 Mn in ARR within six months of operation. This pace of growth, coupled with the burgeoning physical AI data collection market, appears to have caught the attention of global investors. But the bigger ace up the startup’s sleeve is its tech stack and the scale of its operations. A Sprawling Empire: Humyn Labs has developed its own two-camera hardware to record people performing everyday tasks. It then uses its software to process and label the footage, which is then used by robots for training. Overall, its data collection operations span more than 20 countries across Latin America and Asia. The Contradictory Core: Beyond the headlines, the startup’s business model has raised serious questions around privacy, consent and data ownership. Recordings inside homes and factories could capture personal information, which has made consent and storage safeguards critical. Even deeper lies a stark labour paradox: workers are recording the very movements that will be used to train machines designed to automate their jobs. Amid this backdrop, it will be interesting to see how Humyn Labs balances privacy safeguards, data usage and fair compensation. You can now purchase the 512GB Steam Machine like a normal console
Valve has worked through the waitlist for the smaller version of its gaming PC.
Valve has announced that it's completed all of the waitlist orders for the smaller 512GB model of the Steam Machine and is now letting anyone buy it while supplies last. The change should make the experience of buying the Linux gaming PC a bit closer to the consoles it competes with, though Valve's announcement doesn't suggest dealing with RAMaggedon has gotten any easier.
It's not clear how many 512GB Steam Machines are available, but rather than set up another waitlist, the company says it will mark the model as "out of stock" once it sells through its current supply. Things are a bit more complicated for the 2TB model. Valve has "finished getting purchase invites out to all reservation holders" and anyone who joined the waitlist later will be able to keep their place in line. Because there are more people on the waitlist than units available to buy, though, Valve is closing the list to new sign-ups and marking the 2TB model as out of stock on Steam.
The company says Steam Machines will still be made, but it sounds like availability will fluctuate and the price could change. "We don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we'll be able to offer them," Valve says in its announcement. "The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained."
The company originally instituted a waitlist as a way to manage interest in the Steam Machine after the Steam Controller became difficult to buy due to high demand. Valve has also been constrained by the current price of memory and storage, which has been driven up by the data center buildout powering the AI industry. Launching the Steam Machine for $1,049 was never Valve's plan, but a high price and limited supply appear to have tied the company's hands. Valve says it expects to have more to share about Steam Machine availability in January.

The Delhi High Court on Thursday (November 19, 2026) stayed proceedings before the Lokpal against Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh in connection with a corruption complaint concerning promotions at the National Productivity Council (NPC).
A Bench of Justice Subramonium Prasad and Justice Renu Bhatnagar sought responses from the Lokpal and the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) on a petition by Mr. Singh challenging the Lokpal’s March 4, 2025, and October 26, 2026, orders and the October 28 notice directing him to appear for proceedings under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act.
The court listed the matter for further hearing on January 20 next year.
The complaint alleges irregularities and corruption in recruitment and promotions at the NPC. The allegations against Mr. Singh relate to his decision to forward an advisory committee report concerning the promotions to the NPC’s Governing Body for appropriate action, instead of directing the organisation to act on the report.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, representing the CBI, submitted that the issue may require deeper examination by the court.
Senior advocate Vikas Singh, appearing for the Defence Secretary, said that the Lokpal’s October 26, 2026 order and October 28, 2026 notice are founded on the January 6, 2025 order and January 7, 2025 notice, both of which have already been quashed by the High Court.
He said the Lokpal directed a hearing against the petitioner for the second time “without crossing the threshold” laid down by the High Court in its November 28, 2025, judgment in the same case.
Mr. Singh contends that he had no role in the formation of the Departmental Promotion Committees (DPCs) or in the promotions in question, as he assumed charge as Secretary, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), only on April 21, 2023. The promotions were made on March 28, 2023.
The High Court, in its judgment dated November 28, 2025, in Mr. Singh’s earlier petition, held that the Lokpal had failed to record the statutorily mandated prima facie satisfaction before directing a hearing.

Singapore-based robotics startup Botsync has raised $11 Mn (about ₹103 Cr) in a funding round led by IvyCap Ventures to upgrade its factory automation software and mobile robots. It also plans to expand its engineering and project delivery teams in India to support deployments globally. Capital 2B, AppWorks, Iterative, AngelCentral, Genesis Alternate Investments, and angel investor Nalin Advani also participated in the funding round, which followed the startup’s Series A extension led by SGInnovate in January. With the latest round, Botsync’s total funding has moved past the $20 Mn mark, it said. Most of the fresh capital will go towards upgrading Botsync’s MAG mobile robots and adding AI features to SyncOS, its software for coordinating robots and other factory equipment. The new features will help manufacturers increase throughput, predict maintenance needs, and analyse operational data. How Botsync Makes Money Founded in 2017 by Nanyang Technological University graduates Rahul Nambiar, Nikhil Venkatesh, and Prashant Trivedi, Botsync primarily serves automotive and FMCG manufacturers that regularly move goods between production lines, storage areas, and dispatch bays. Its MAG range includes lifters, conveyors, tuggers, and forklifts and can handle loads of up to 1.5 tonnes. Botsync sells MAG robots and SyncOS together or separately. SyncOS assigns tasks and manages traffic across Botsync’s own robots and third-party equipment, and connects them with systems such as enterprise resource planning software. Botsync's business model combines hardware sales and software-led automation, with customers historically having the option to purchase robots through upfront capex arrangements or adopt opex-based models to spread the cost over time. The startup has also offered subscription-based software services and explored a Robotics-as-a-Service (RaaS) model in the past. At a global automaker’s body shop, Botsync supplied both products. SyncOS coordinated the robots delivering parts to the assembly line. Botsync said the deployment allowed the automaker to take one forklift out of service, reassign two workers, and improve productivity by 12.5%. Where Botsync Is Expanding Botsync says it has completed more than 70 projects and executed over 2 Mn production tasks at 99% uptime. Its customers include Caterpillar, Ford, Nestle, Honda, Coca-Cola, and Kimberly-Clark. To support more deployments, Botsync plans to deepen partnerships with local systems integrators and automation providers in India, where it runs a Bengaluru office and experience centre. Overseas, it plans to expand its presence in Australia and build its US business. This comes as the broader Indian industrial control and factory automation market, which was valued at $16.7 Bn in 2025, is projected to grow at a CAGR of 11.4% and reach $23.4 Bn by 2030, according to MarketsandMarkets. India’s robotics and automation market includes Addverb, GreyOrange, Anscer Robotics, and Ati Motors, alongside global automation providers. The Inc42 Take: Can Botsync Scale Beyond Custom Deployments? Botsync's proposition addresses a practical manufacturing problem – automating material movement without requiring factories to overhaul their entire infrastructure. Its combination of hardware and software, enterprise customer base and reported deployments across multiple countries provide an early indication of commercial traction. At the same time, physical AI is emerging as a promising frontier for India's deeptech ecosystem, as advances in AI, sensors and robotics allow machines to perceive, learn and respond to real-world environments. However, these startups face high hardware development and manufacturing costs, while factory deployments often require customisation to fit existing infrastructure. This can make standardisation, margin expansion and faster customer acquisition difficult. Long enterprise sales cycles, maintenance requirements, and the need for specialised engineering talent add to the operational burden. While Botsync has demonstrated deployment traction, scaling SyncOS across diverse factory environments without extensive customisation will be critical for its success.
